Report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  McCauley ,  If.  S.  Navy,  commanding 
TJ.  8.  B.  Fort  Henry ,  regarding  the  capture  of  schooner  Anna. 

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

Cedar  Keys,  Fla. ,  February  27,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  evening  of  the  26th  instant  the  schooner  Anna,  Captain 
H.  Hanson,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  was  captured  whilst  endeav¬ 
oring  to  evade  the  blockade  by  armed  boats  of  this  vessel  inside  the 
bar  off  the  mouth  of  the  Suwanee  River. 

She  is  loaded  with  75  bags  of  salt,  3  bags  coffee,  9  boxes  soap,  12 
kegs  nails,  4  kegs  powder,  7  barrels  and  21  cases  merchandise  (con¬ 
tents  unknown). 

Captain  Hanson  acknowledges  the  fact  of  endeavoring  to  run  the 
blockade. 

The  prize  has  been  sent  to  Key  West. 

Very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley, 

Acting  Lieutenant,  Commanding  U.  S.  B.  Fort  Henry.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy,  of  the  arrival  of 
Colonel  Good,  TJ.  S.  Army ,  and  the  rescinding  of  order  for  removal 
of  inhabitants  of  Key  West. 

No.  75.]  U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West ,  February  28,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  pleasure  to  inform  you  that  the  country  is  saved  the 
dishonor  which  would  have  resulted  from  the  carrying  out  of  Colonel 
Morgan’s  General  Order  No.  10,  enclosed  in  my  communication  of  the 
26th  instant. 

At  the  moment  that  the  proscribed  families  had  assembled  to  embark 
for  the  rebel  lines  under  that  order  the  steamer  Cosmopolitan  arrived, 
having  on  board  Colonel  Good  and  the  Forty -seventh  Pennsylvania 
Regiment.  Colonel  Good,  being  the  senior  of  Morgan,  rescinded  the 
absurd  order,  to  the  great  joy  of  the  inhabitants  of  this  key. 

1  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Nickerson ,  JI.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  II  S. 
schooner  James  S.  Chambers ,  regarding  capture  of  the  Spanish  sloop 
Relampago  and  schooner  Ida. 

U.  S.  Schooner  James  S.  Chambers, 

Charlotte  Harbor ,  Florida ,  March  7,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report,  viz:  I  dispatch 
for  Key  W  est  this  day  the  Spanish  sloop  Relampago ,  together  with 
cargo  taken  from  schooner  Ida ,  a  list  of  which  is  enclosed,  in  charge 
of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  William  A.  Smith,  with  a  prize  crew  of  6  men. 

The  circumstances  of  the  capture  are  as  follows:  On  the  evening  of 
the  3d  instant  a  sail  was  reported  from  the  masthead,  apparently  enter¬ 
ing  the  passage  between  Pine  and  Captiva  islands,  about  6  miles  to  the 
south  of  our  anchorage.  I  dispatched  two  armed  boats  in  charge  of 
Acting  Master  William  H.  McLean  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Wil¬ 
liam  A.  Smith.  About  11  a.  m.  the  following  day  a  sail  was  reported 
to  the  south  of  us,  seaward;  I  got  underway  and  ran  out  to  her.  She 
proved  to  be  the  sloop  above  named  in  charge  of  my  officers.  Mr. 
McLean  reports  that  after  proceeding  to  a  point  where  he  could  com¬ 
mand  the  inlet  between  Pine  and  Captiva  islands  he  landed  and  waited 
for  daylight,  when  he  discovered  a  sloop  standing  in  for  the  entrance. 
The  wind,  at  the  time  was  blowing  strong  from  the  north,  and  a  rough 
sea,  the  tide  setting  out.  She  not  being  able  to  enter,  bore  away  a  few 
miles  down  the. coast,  and  came  to  anchor  1£  miles  from  the  beach.  He 
then  put  out  with  the  boats  and  pulled  to  her,  and  boarded  her.  The}7 
were  not  aware  of  the  approach  of  our  boats  until  they  were  boarded. 
They  then  threw  their  flag  overboard,  which  was  recovered  by  our 
boats. 

It  was  an  old  Spanish  flag,  made  to  resemble  a  rebel  flag  by  attach¬ 
ing  a  piece  of  blue  cloth  and  seven  stars.  Her  cargo,  as  far  as  known, 


380 


BAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


consists  of  coffee,  liquors,  soldiers’  shoes,  etc.  There  were  six  persons 
on  board;  four  of  them  I  send  in  the  sloop,  the  other  two  remain  on 
board  this  vessel,  and  I  shall  take  the  first  opportunity  of  sending  them 
to  Key  West.  I  also  send  all  the  papers  found  on  board,  together  with 
the  flag. 

The  following  are  the  circumstances  connected  with  the  schooner  Ida: 

About  4  p.  m.  on  the  4th  instant,  while  lying  by  the  sloop  taking 
off  some  of  the  men,  a  sail  was  reported  to  the  south  of  us,  standing 
in  for  the  land;  I  left  the  sloop  in  charge  of  Mr.  Smith  and  went  in 
chase  of  the  sail,  which  proved  to  be  a  schooner.  When  within  a  mile 
and  a  half  I  threw  a  shot  across  her  bow,  which  she  did  not  regard, 
but  continued  her  course  for  the  beach  (distant  about  2  miles)  with¬ 
out  showing  any  colors.  I  continued  the  chase,  firing  at  her,  until  she 
was  beached.  A  few  moments  after  she  struck,  men  were  seen  run¬ 
ning  for  the  woods,  leaving  her  with  her  sails  set.  She  was  beached 
about  midway  of  Sanibel  Island,  15  miles  to  the  south  of  this  place. 
I  came  to  anchor  about  li  miles  from  her,  and  waited  for  the  sea  to 
become  smooth  enough  to  land  in  order  to  save  or  destroy  her  cargo. 
The  following  morning  I  sent  boats  on  shore  and  found  her  bilged. 
She  was  a  small  schooner  of  pilot-boat  build;  had  hailed  from  Key 
West;  she  had  the  name  of  Ida  on  her  stern,  but  her  place  of  hailing 
painted  out.  We  took  several  boat  loads  of  her  cargo,  which  con¬ 
sisted  principally  of  liquors;  we  set  fire  to  her  and  left  her.  There 
were  no  papers  found  on  board;  a  small  rebel  flag  was  found  on  board, 
which  I  send.  After  we  had  got  underway  a  man  was  seen  coming- 
down  to  the  wreck,  and  waived  his  blanket  to  us.  I  sent  a  boat  and 
took  him  on  board.  He  represents  himself  as  a  passenger  on  board 
the  schooner,  named  James  S.  Bishop,  of  Florida;  that  he  left  Havana 
the  27th  of  February  in  the  schooner,  bound  for  the  Suwanee  Fiver; 
that  she  was  formerly  named  Esecon ,  of  Key  W est,  commanded  at  this 
time  by  a  man  named  De  Coste,  formerly  of  Key  West.  I  sent  the 
said  James  S.  Bishop  in  the  sloop  to  Key  West;  I  also  sent  a  correct 
list  of  the  cargo  taken  from  the  schooner. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Luther  Nickerson, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  JD.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Nickerson ,  II.  S.  Ntwy,  requesting  the  services 

oj  a  tight-draft  vessel  to  prevent  trading  in  vicinity  of  Charlotte 

Harbor ,  Florida. 

U.  8.  Schooner  James  S.  Chambers, 

Charlotte  Harbor ,  March  7, 1863. 

Sir:  Information  has  reached  me  from  sources  that  I  deem  reliable 
that  there  are  numerous  small  craft  trading  along  this  coast  in  this 
immediate  vicinity,  especially  about  Punta  Rasa  and  up  the  Sanibel 
fju'er-  There  are  many  islands  between  this  place  and  Punta  Rasa 
that  afford  the  facilities  of  landing  cargoes  unobserved. 

If  not  presuming  too  much,  I  would  take  the  liberty  of  requesting 
ot  you  a  small  craft  of  light  draft,  of  sufficient  size  to  carry  a  howit¬ 
zer,  to  cruise  among  the  islands.  M}7-  boats  are  too  small  "for  such  a 
purpose. 

I  send  on  the  sloop  Daniel  Kane,  ordinary  seaman,  who  has  been 
attached  to  this,  vessel  since  she  left  Philadelphia,  and  has  not  been 
able  to  do  duty  in  that  time.  I  would  respectfully  request  a  man  in 
his  place.  Among  the  prize  crew  of  the  sloop  is  William  H.  Frost, 
rated  as  chief  boatswain’s  mate  on  board  this  vessel,  whom  I  wish  to 
bring  to  your  notice.  He  is  a  very  deserving  man,  that  can  always  be 
relied  upon,  strictly  moral  and  temperate,  and  I  think  fully  deserving 
of  promotion. 

By  the  paymaster’s  report,  we  have  on  hand  this  day  provisions  for 
three  weeks. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  Nickerson, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Squadron ,  Key  West. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  con¬ 
ditions  in  Apalachicola  Rimer ,  with  a  view  to  destruction  of  Confed¬ 
erate  gunboats. 

No.  91.]  U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  March  7,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  communi¬ 
cation  of  the  10th  of  February,  instructing  me  to  examine  into  the 
subject  of  the  reports  which  I  forwarded  from  Lieutenant-Commander 
Grosman,  and  the  practicability  of  an  expedition  for  capturing  or 
destroying  the  rebel  gunboats  on  the  Apalachicola,  etc. 

I  have  made  the  enquiries  and  find  that  the  river  has  a  bar  at  the 
mouth,  where  it  empties  into  St.  George’s  Sound,  with  only  6  feet  water 
on  it  at  the  highest  spring  tides;  therefore  the  gunboats  building  on 
that  river  can  not  be  formidable  as  ocean  steamers.  1  think  they  are 
intended  for  river  defense  only,  for  the  reason  that  the  legislature  of  the 
State  of  Georgia,  at  its  last  session,  passed  a  large  appropriation  of 
money  to  place  obstructions  in  the  rivers  of  that  State,  and  from  refu¬ 
gees  and  contrabands  I  learn  that  the  rebels  have  fortified  a  bluff  80 
miles  from  the  mouth  of  the  river  and  there  obstructed  the  navigation 
by  driving  piles,  etc.  Above  these  obstructions  the  rebel  gunboats 
are  preparing  and  building. 


382 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  Port  Royal,  which  is  the  lightest  draft  effective  steamer  in  my 
squadron,  tried  to  get  over  the  bar  into  the  river  at  high  spring  tide, 
and  after  being  aground  one  week  in  the  effort,  failed  to  get  over. 
Nothing,  therefore,  can  be  effected  by  a  steam  force  until  the  light- 
draft  Mississippi  gunboats  are  released  from  that  river  and  are  put 
under  my  orders.  To  attempt  it  with  small  boats  would  be  quixotic, 
as  the  river  is  sinuous,  with  frequent  abrupt  bends,  and  the  current 
rapid,  insomuch  that  the  enemy  would  get  information  of  our  attempted 
ascent  long  before  we  could  reach  them. 

To  meet  a  raid  on  our  blockading  vessels  by  their  gunboats,  I  have 
stationed,  with  necessary  orders,  the  following  vessels  to  guard  the 
passes  of  St.  George’s  Sound,  viz:  The  Penguin ,  steamer;  Port  Royal , 
steamer;  Somerset ,  steamer;  Hendrick  Hudson ,  steamer,  and  the  bark 
Amanda.  1  think  that  those  vessels  will  be  able  to  successfully  repel 
and  capture  any  force  they  may  send  out  to  attack. 

In  necessarily  putting  so  many  steamers  before  one  port,  my  force 
for  cruising  and  blockading  other  points  is  so  far  diminished  that  I 
request  several  more  to  be  sent  me. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

At  Anchor  off  Indian  River  Inlet, 

East  Florida,  March  11,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  on  the  10th  instant  we 
captured  the  sloop  Petee,  6  tons  burden,  of  Savannah,  from  Nassau,

New  Providence,  while  attempting  to  run  the  blockade  at  this  inlet 
with  a  cargo  of  50  sacks  salt,  and  manned  with  the  following  persons,

Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Railey,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  to  the  United 
States  district  attorney  at  Key  West,  regarding  proceedings  against 
the  sloop  Petee ,  destroyed  March  10 , 1863. 

U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  March  27,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  request  that  the  proper  proceedings  be  taken  (to  pre¬ 
vent  any  future  claim  by  the  English  Government)  against  the  sloop 
Petee,  6  tons,  captured  while  on  a  voyage  from  Nassau  to  Indian  River 
Inlet,  while  attempting  to  run  the  blockade  at  said  inlet. 

She  was  captured  by  the  U.  S.  bark  Gem  of  the  Sea,  with  a  cargo 
of  50  sacks  of  salt,  and  both  vessel  and  cargo  being  almost  worthless 
and  not  of  sufficient  value  to  justify  the  sending  of  her  into  port, 
Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  I.  B.  Baxter,  commanding  the  Gem  of 
the  Sea,  destroyed  the  vessel  and  her  cargo.  The  only  papers  found 
on  board  were  the  shipping  articles.  The  Huntsville  brought  down 
the  three  prisoners  found  on  board,  viz:  Charles  Brown,  captain; 
Daniel  Petersen,  mate;  John  Morgan,  seaman. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

[Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

To  the  U.  S.  District  Attorney,

His  cargo  consists  of  207  bales  of  cotton  (mostly  sea  island).  I  send

Boat  expedition  from  U.  S.  hark  Roebuck  in  St.  Andrew's  Bay , 

March  20,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  reports  and  correspondence. 

No.  136.]  U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  April  21,  1863. 

Sir:  I  enclose  herewith  the  report  of  Acting  Master  John  Sherrill, 
commanding  the  bark  Roebuck,  of  an  unfortunate  affair  in  which  Acting 
Master  James  Folger  and  the  launch’s  crew  of  11  men  were  engaged, 
and  which  resulted  in  the  death  of  2  of  the  men  and  the  wounding  of  6. 

It  seems  that  Captain  Sherrill,  having  heard  that  a  vessel  was  loading 
with  cotton  up  St.  Andrew’s  Bay,  sent  up  his  launch  and  crew  to 
reconnoiter.  For  some  reason,  of  which  I  am  not  advised,  Mr.  Folger, 
in  charge  of  the  party,  made  a  landing.  The  boat’s  crew  were  fired 
upon  by  a  large  guerrilla  force,  with  fatal  effect,  and  barely  escaped 
with  their  lives,  Mr.  Folger  himself  paying  dearly  for  his  incautious¬ 
ness,  as  the  report  shows.  I  think  the  landing  was  ill-advised. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Gomdg.  Eastern  Gidf  Blockdg.  Sguadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

[Endorsement.] 

Enquiries  should  be  made  as  to  the  orders  given  to  this  officer. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Sherrill,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  bark  Roebuck. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay ,  March  20,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  inform  the  Department  that  this  morning  I  sent  the 
launch  of  this  ship  with  an  armed  crew  of  11  men,  in  charge  of  Acting 
Master  James  Folger,  up  the  bay  on  a  reconnoissance.  The  boat 
returned  at  2  o’clock  p.  m. ,  the  crew  having  been  attacked  by  a  guer¬ 
rilla  party  of  over  50  men,  and  met  with  the  following  severe  loss: 

Killed— Thomas  King,  seaman;  Ralph  B.  Snow,  ordinary  seaman. 

Wounded— Acting  Master  James  Folger,  severely;  Robert  Wilkes, 
captain  forecastle,  mortally;  Andrew  K.  Snyder,  landsman,  mortally; 
Neil  O’Donnell,  landsman,  mortally;  Charles  Sweet,  seaman,  slightly; 
George  H.  French,  ordinary  seaman,  slightly. 

The  body  of  Ralph  B.  Snow  was  not  brought  off.  Thomas  Wylie 
(ordinary  seaman)  and  James  Kitchen  (landsman)  deserve  much  credit 
for  bringing  the  boat  off  safely,  when  nearly  all  the  rest  of  the  crew 
were  killed  or  wounded. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J ohn  Sherrill, 

Acting  Master,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  Comag.  TJ.  S.  Bark  Roebuck. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

Sir:  1  have  to  report  the  following  casualties  of  the  attack  by  guer¬ 
rillas  upon  our  boat’s  crew  at  St.  Andrew’s  town,  Fla. : 

Killed. — Thomas  King,  seaman,  shot  through  the  heart;  Ralph  B. 
Snow,  ordinary  seaman,  reported  shot  through  the  head;  his  body  was 
not  recovered — 2. 

.  Wounded  mortally.—  Robert  Wilkes,  captain  of  forecastle,  wounded 
in  seven  places  with  three  balls  and  four  buckshots;  one  of  the  balls 
entered  fhe  umbilical  region;  another  ball  entered  the  rig'ht  forearm, 
and  grazing  the  elbow  joint,  broke  the  humerus  in  its  lower  third;  the 
other  wounds  are  flesh  wounds.  Neil  O’Donnell,  landsman,  received 
two  balls  in  the  upper  half  of  his  right  humerus,  fracturing  it  badly; 
a  buckshot  in  right  shoulder;  another  buckshot  through  the  auricle  of 
the  right  ear,  lodging  in  the  cheek,  and  still  another  in  the  right  thigh. 
Andrew  K.  Snyder,  landsman,  wounded  in  the  head  with  buckslTot, 
penetrating  the  skull,  and  a  ball  in  right  forearm,  shattering  the  ulna — 3.’ 

founded  severely.  James  holger,  acting  master  and  executive 
officer,  struck  on  the  right  knee,  apparently  by  a  rifle  ball,  which,  after 
grazing  the  upper  extremity  of  the  fibula,  was  lost  in  the  soft  parts; 
George  French,  ordinary  seaman,  received  a  flesh  wound  in  his  right 
forearm  by  a  ball,  and  another,  slight,  on  the  left  hand — 2.

right  foot — 2.

[Enclosures.] 

May  10,  1863. 

Sir:  The  following  is  substantially  the  particulars  as  reported  by 
me  to  headquarters  of  the  attack  made  by  me  on  a  boat  and  crew  at 
St.  Andrew’s  on  the  20th  of  March  last: 


388 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Being  at  the  bay  on  the  morning  of  the  20th  of  March,  with  a  lieu¬ 
tenant,  sergeant,  and  20  men,  a  boat  belonging  to  the  enemy,  carrying 
a  small  howitzer  on  the  bows,  landed  an  armed  party,  consisting  of  an 
officer  and  9  men,  leaving  2  in  the  boat.  They  formed  on  the  beach 
and  proceeded  in  an  easterly  direction  along  the  same. 

Taking  advantage  of  a  bluff  which  concealed  us  from  their  sight,  I 
charged  within  60  or  70  yards  of  them  before  we  were  discovered, 
when  being  the  stronger  party,  I  summoned  them  to  surrender,  which 
they  refused  to  do  by  attempting  to  escape  to  their  boat,  and  knowing 
that  their  cannon  would  give  them  a  great  advantage,  I  ordered  my 
men  to  fire,  which  was  kept  up  with  such  effect  that  but  few  could 
board  the  boat.  After  firing  some  time  the  flag  was  lowered  and  one 
of  the  men  called  out,  “Do  not  fire  on  us  any  more;  we  surrender,” 
whereupon  I  immediately  gave  the  order  to  cease  firing,  and  ordered 
my  men  out  of  the  water.  There  being  some  apparent  hesitation  in 
their  coming  ashore,  they  were  asked  why  they  did  not  come  ashore, 
and  the  answer  as  understood  was,  “We  will  as  soon  as  we  pick  up  a 
drowning  man,”  which  privilege  was  granted  them.  They  pulled  out 
to  the  man,  and  immediately  made  sail  on  the  boat  and  escaped. 

W.  J.  Robinson, 

Cajptain ,  Commanding  Company ,  C.  S.  Army. 

Commander  of  the  U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

Blockading  Port  of  St.  Andrew’s  Bay.

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay ,  May  10,  1863. 

Sir:  Your  communications  of  the  10th  instant,  sent  by  flag  of  truce, 
have  been  received. 

Your  statement  of  the  affair  is  replete  with  falsehood,  as  no  demand 
was  made  to  surrender  before  being  fired  upon. 

With  one  so  devoid  of  all  honorable  rules  of  warfare  I  decline  hold¬ 
ing  further  communication.  As  to  hereafter  “  quarter  being  denied,” 
none  has  been  shown  by  or  expected  from  one  who  stoops  to  guerrilla 
warfare. 

I  am,  sir,  yours,  etc., 

John  Sherrill, 

Acting  Master ,  U.  S.  Navy,  Comdg.  U.  S.  Bark  Boebuck.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  announcing  the  death  of  Acting  Master 

Folger,  IT.  S.  Navy. 

No.  189.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West,  June  1,  1863. 

_  Sir:  Your  letter  of  May  4,  relative  to  the  unfortunate  boat  expedi¬ 
tion  sent  from  the  Roebuck  on  March  20,  and  directing  that  “enquiries 
should  be  made  with  regard  to  the  orders  given  Mr.  Folger,  as  he 
appears  to  have  exposed  his  boat’s  crew  by  making  a  landing  when  on 
a  reconnoissance,”  has  been  received. 

Acting  Master  Sherrill,  commanding  the  Roebuck,  reported  to  me 
in  person  that  Mr.  Folger  had  acted  solely  on  his  own  responsibility  in 
landing,  and  contrary  to  his  orders,  and  that  no  blame  attached  to  any 
other  officer.  As  Mr.  Folger  has  since  died  of  the  wounds  received  on 
that  occasion,  any  further  enquiry  seems  unnecessary. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Gomdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Expedition  to  the  Ocklockonee  River  for  the  purpose  of  cutting  out  the 
schooner  Onward,  March  20-33,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  IT.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  reports. 

No.  128.]  U.  S.  Frigate  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West ,  April  21,  1863. 

Sir:  I  enclose  herewith  (marked  129)  the  report  of  an  expedition 
from  the  U.  S.  bark  Amanda,  for  the  purpose  of  cutting  out  the 
schooner  Onward,  about  to  load  in  the  Ocklockonee  River  with  a  cargo 
of  cotton.  The  expedition  resulted  in  the  destruction  of  the  vessel, 
and  this  result  was  accomplished,  as  the  report  shows,  in  the  face  of 
obstacles,  and  was  characterized  from  first  to  last  by  the  exhibition  of 
much  coolness  and  bravery.  I  regret  to  report  the  death  of  James 
Mooney,  seaman,  shot  through  the  heart,  and  the  wounding  of  five  men 
and  of  Acting  Master  R.  J.  Hoffner,  commanding  the  expedition.  The 
latter  has  a  musket  ball  lodged  in  his  neck  and  not  yet  extracted. 
Under  advice  of  the  board  of  medical  survey,  I  have  granted  him  per¬ 
mission  to  proceed  North,  as  stated  in  my  communication  No.  124. 

1  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

.  Theodores  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear- Admiral,  Oomdg .  East .  Gulf  Rlockdg .  Sguadrou% 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secu'etary  of  the  Navy.

First  Report  of  Acting  Master  Hoffner,  II.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson, 

St.  Marks  Blockading  Station,  Thursday,  Alarch  86,  1863. 

Sir:  I  send  you  the  earliest  information  of  our  whereabouts,  and 
the  success  of  our  expedition,  although  attended  with  very  many  diffi¬ 
culties  and  more  fatality  than  I  anticipated.  My  report,  as  well  as 
this  note,  is  written  while  lying  on  my  back  and  in  some  pain;  still  I 
am  in  hopes  that  you  will  be  able  to  make  out  enough  to  feel  satisfied 
that  1  have  done  all  in  my  power  to  finish  the  work  to  your  satisfac¬

state  full  accounts  verbally.  I  am  in  hopes  to  be  on  board  to-morrow, 
when  I  will  give  you  the  full  particulars.  Myself  and  wounded  men

Detailed  report  of  Acting'  Master  Hoffner,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

Friday,  March  20,  1863,  left  the  ship,  in  charge  of  two  boats  manned 
by  27  men.  2  officers,  and  a  pilot,  to  proceed  to  the  Ocklockonee 
River,  for  the  purpose  of  cutting  out  and  capturing  a  schooner  sup¬ 
posed  to  be  loaded  with  cotton.  At  10  a.  m.,  fairly  underway;  at  12, 
thick  fog,  lost  sight  of  launch;  at  2  p.  m.,  clearing  off,  made  the 
launch  to  windward  and  found  ourselves  about  halfway  along  Dog 
Island,  wind  east;  beat  up  to  east  end  of  the  island  and  found  the 
wind  and  tide  ahead  and  too  strong  to  make  way  against.  At  8  p.  m. 
made  a  harbor  for  the  nig'ht;  at  daylight,  March  21,  underway,  strong 
breeze  eastward,  working  to  windward;  sea  heavy  for  boats,  causing 
me  to  work  up  inside  shoal.  At  Turkey  Point, ‘when  close  inshore, 
had  three  shots  fired  at  us  from  salt  works,  said  to  be  worked  by  a 
man  named  Jackson;  after  clearing  shoals  worked  up  to  South  Point 
[S.  W.  Cape];  wind  still  ahead  and  too  much  distance  to  finish  my 
work;  anchored  for  the  night.  March  22,  at  daylight,  worked  up 
to  Baldliead  [Bald]  Point,  and  waited  for  night  tide;  started  again 
at  8  and  got  foul  of  a  quantity  of  oyster  banks;  at  11  worked  clear, 
took  launch  in  tow,  and  with  a  fair  wind  sailed  for  the  mouth  of  the 
Ocklockonee  River.  About  2  a.  m.,  March  23,  arrived  at  the  head  of 
the  bay  and  could  not  find  the  entrance,  beating  about  till  daylight; 
boat,  grounded  some  dozen  of  times.  I  became  fearful  of  discovery’ 
and  instructed  the  pilot  to  find  his  way  out  of  a  complete  trap,  and,  if 
possible,  get  deep  water  and  run  back.  Just  then  the  mouth  of  the 
livei  appealed  open,  and  all  hands,  wishing  and  agreeing,  concluded 
to  steer  for  and  proceed,  in  search  of  the  schooner;  wind  fair.  About 
8  a.  m.  came  in  . sight  of  a  dismasted  vessel  lying  close  to  starboard 
bank;  at  same  time  found  we  were  discovered  by  the  people  on  board 
who  manned  their  boats  and  made  for  the  shore.  I  dispatched  the 
launch  to  cut  the  boat  off,  but  found  her  a  little  too  late.  The  launch 
with  Mr.  Shaffer,  boarded  the  schooner  a  few  minutes  after  8  a.  m.  and 
I,  with  the  sloop. m  about  two  minutes  after,  and  took  charge  under 
the  flag  of  the  United  States  of  America;  captured  at  same  time  an  old 
man  and  bov,  but  could  gather  little  information  from  them;  hove  up 
anchor  and  put  launch  ahead;  having  about  two  hours  tide,  towed  down 
tfie river.  About  11a.  m.  tide  done;  anchored  about  2  miles  belowthe 
terry;  at  5  underway,  launch  ahead,  relieving  the  oarsmen  every  two 
hours;  about  8  got  clear  of  the  entrance  in  safety,  steering  for  the  bav 
channel;  about  9  unfortunately  grounded  (having  run  one-half  the 
distance  to  sea);  made  every  effort  to  get  off,  and  after  losing  an  anchor 
had  to  let  the  vessel  lay  until  return  of  tide;  set  the  watches  and 
allowed  the  men  to  take  the. first  good  sleep  since  leaving  the  ship;  at 
daylight,  March  24,  tide  suiting  early,  vessel  all  afloat;  started  again 
with  about  two  hours’  work  to  clear  all  danger,  when,  after  moving 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


393 


about  a  half  mile  and  sounding  in  the  boat,  found  we  had  taken  the 
wrong  channel,  and  grounded  again;  got  out  the  anchor  and  lines  to 
the  shore  and  worked  hard  to  get  her  off,  but  of  no  avail;  made  ready 
to  fire  the  vessel,  and  cleaned  up,  recapped,  and  primed  afresh  all  small 
arms,  howitzer  loaded  with  canister,  and  all  fully  prepared  for  defense; 
the  ground  before  us  being  a  pine  forest,  and  with  some  knowledge 
(from  the  old  man  taken)  of  the  troops  being  some  distance,  concluded 
to  wait  the  next  tide.  About  11 : 30  a.  m.  discovered  horsemen  approach¬ 
es'  at  some  distance;  they  wheeled  off  and  appeared  to  be  going  away; 
all  hands  to  quarters,  the  tide  going  down  so  low  as  to  ground  the 
boats;  about  12  found  the  horsemen  about  40,  and  various  squads  of 
foot,  (in  all  about  200)  coming  quite  near,  running  from  tree  to  tree  and 
taking  position  to  attack.  At  this  time  one  gun  tired  from  the  shore 
was  answered  with  10  muskets  from  the  vessel,  at  the  nearest  persons; 
the  battle  had  begun;  sharp  tire  from  the  shore  with  Minie  rifles,  every 
shot  striking  on. board  the  vessel.  The  howitzer,  with  canister,  was 
then  tired,  but  with  what  effect  was  not  known,  the  shore  party  being 
concealed  behind  trees.  Our  firing  was  kept  up  brisk  when  anything 
appeared  to  be  shot  at.  One  man  was  shot  by  our  musketry,  when  a 
squad  appeared  of  some  20;  we  dropped  a  shrapnel  among  them;  the 
effect  must  have  been  severe,  as  all  that  could  get  away  left;  some  of 
them  remained,  and  I  have  every  reason  to  believe  a  number  were 
wounded.  The  howitzer  not  having  a  good  chance  to  work,  I  fired  but 
few  shots  with  it,  but  depended  more  on  musketry,  the  little  breastwork 
that  we  were  enabled  to  get  up  keeping  our  men  safe  up  to  this  time. 

1  he  tide  flowing  fast  and  boats  floating,  I  concluded  to  fire  the  vessel, 
embark  howitzer,  and  retreat  in  boats;  having  the  anchor  out  astern 
and  the  vessel  drawing  but  3£  feet  of  water,  was  fearful  of  her  swing¬ 
ing  close  inshore,  as  we  were  not  more  than  250  yards  from  the  shore 
then.  After  holding’  on  about  one  and  one-half  hours,  unlimbered 
and  embarked  howitzer  under  cover  of  musketry,  embarked  launch’s 
crew,  applied  the  match  at  four  different  fires,  jumped  into  the  sloop 
and  attempted  to  leave.  On  swinging  from  the  vessel  found  that  the 
boats  touched;  all  hands  jumped  out  and  dragged  them  about  half  a 
mile  over  mud  flats;  during  this  time  the  whole  force  of  the  enemy 
playing  upon  us  in  good  style.  James  Mooney  at  this  time  was  killed 
instantly;  shot  through  the  heart,  the  ball  passing  through  his  body. 
At  the  same  time  I  received  a  rifle  ball  in  the  right  side  of  the  neck, 
passing  around  the  back,  and  lodging  in  the  left  side,  deeply  imbedded 
in  the  muscles.  Other  men  were  struck  about  the  same  time,  but  no 
man  except  one  failed,  every  one  doing  his  best  under  all  circum¬ 
stances,  working  or  fighting,  and  being  ably  assisted  by  Mr.  Shaffer. 
After  hard  dragging  and  perfectly  exhausted,  we  succeeded  in  getting 
in  deep  water  and  out  of  danger.  I  would  call  your  attention  to  Henry 
Leavey,  who,  after  a  severe  wound  in  the  chest,  and  losing  his  own 
boat,  caught  mine  and  remained  on  board  some  five  minutes  before 
giving  up.  After  getting  in  the  channel  1  concluded  to  make  for  the 
St.  Marks  blockade  for  assistance,  and  arrived  on  board  the  U.  S.  S. 
Hendrick  Hudson ,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  David  Cate,  about 
3  p.  m.,  where  every  comfort  and  attention  that  lay  in  the  power  of 
commander,  officers,  and  men  were  given  us,  particularly  the  wounded. 
Myself,  with  Mr.  Shaffer  and  crew,  do  offer  our  thanks  for  the  kind¬ 
ness  received  on  board  the  Hendrick  Hudson. 

Richard  J.  Hoffner, 

Acting  Master  and  Executive  Officer.

East  Pass,  St.  George's  Sound ,  March  27,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  the  following  casualties,  the  result  of  an  attack 
on  the  expedition  sent  by  you  to  cut  out  the  schooner  Onward,  at  the 
Ocklockonee  River,  on  Tuesday  morning,  March  24,  1863:  James 
Mooney,  captain  forecastle,”  New  York,  killed;  Owen  McManus,  cox¬ 
swain,  England,  slight  wound  in  the  arm;  Samuel  Reynolds,  landsman, 
New  York,  wound  in  the  leg;  William  Wallace,  landsman,  England, 
slight  wound  in  head,  ball  passing  through  the  ear;  James  Halsen, 
coxswain,  Norway,  slight  scalp  wound;  Benjamin  Davis,  quartermas¬ 
ter,  Virginia,  wound  in  the  hand;  Matthew  Evans,  very  slight  wound 
in  back  of  the  hand;  Richard  J.  Hoffner,  acting  master,  severe  wound 
in  the  neck. 

Of  the  eight  wounded  James  Halsen,  Benjamin  Davis,  and  Matthew 
Evans  are  able  to  return  to  duty.

Peport  of  Acting  Master  Pennell,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  bark 
Ethan  Allen ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Gypsy,  formerly 
the  Grace  E.  Baker. 

U.  S.  Bark  Ethan  Allen, 

St.  Joseph's  Bay,  Fla.,  March  21h  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  1,0  report  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
Gypsy,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  formerly  the  Grace  E.  Baker ,  of 
Key  West,  by  this  vessel,  under  my  command,  on  the  20th  instant,  35 
miles  west  of  this  bay.  The  following  are  the  particulars :  On  the  19th 
instant,  at  3: 30  p.  m.,  the  lookout  at  the  masthead  reported  a  sail  stand¬ 
ing  in  for  the  bay.  At  4  p.  m.  she  opened  out  past  the  woodland  on  the 
point,  bringing  her  in  full  view  of  this  vessel  from  on  deck,  and  about 
3  miles  distant.  She  immediately  altered  her  course  to  the  westward. 
I  got  underway  and  gave  chase.  The  wind  being  light  and  the  ship’s 
bottom  very  foul,  1  did  not  come  up  with  her  until  next  morning,  when 
I  made  her  out  close  inshore.  I  stood  in  as  near  as  was  prudent  and 
sent  boats  to  board  her.  Soon  after  our  boats  left  the  ship  I  saw  a 
boat  plying  between  the  schooner  and  the  shore,  and  a  man  on  the 
beach;  shortly  after  our  boats  boarded  her,  her  boat  returned  on  board. 
The  officer  in  charge  of  our  boats  took  charge  of  the  schooner,  ran  her 
down  to  the  ship,  and  sent  the  captain  on  board  with  his  papers.  On 
looking  at  the  papers  I  saw  that  the  manifest  did  not  agree  with  the 
captain’s  statement  of  cargo  on  board.  I  placed  Acting  Master’s  Mate 
John  E.  Stickney,  with  a  crew  from  this  vessel,  in  charge,  and  ordered 
him  to  proceed  to  this  bay.  The  wind  being  light  from  the  eastward, 
I  did  not  get  back  until  yesterday.  The  schooner  came  in  this  after¬ 
noon.  I  have  been  on  board  and  examined  the  cargo  as  far  as  possi¬ 
ble  without  breaking  bulk.  The  manifest  calls  for  300  sacks  salt,  12 
reams  paper,  2  boxes  containing  plated  forks  and  spoons,  and  3  of  knives

and  fcn-ks..  I  lincl  but  3  boxes  and  2  bales  of  paper  on  board;  one  of 
the  boxes  is  partly  burst  open  and  contains  files  and  wrenches  and  other 
implements  for  mechanics’  use.  One  of  the  boxes  is  12  feet  lone-  and 
1  *°ot square,  and  by  the  appearance  does  not  contain  knives  and  forks.

U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  March  26,  1863. 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  is  ready  for  sea, 
you  will  proceed  in  the  direction  of  Havana  until  within  about  10  miles 
of  the  land;  thence  to  the  westward  as  far  as  Port  Cabanas,  and  from 
thence  in  a  slightly  zigzag  course  toward  the  Quicksand  Passage.  On 
nearing  the  edge  of  the  reef,  you  will  pass  around  to  the  southward 
and  westward  of  the  Tortugas,  to  the  northward  of  which  you  will 
cruise  until  by  the  tenth  da}"  from  this  date  you  will  be  at  Tampa  Bay, 
and  there  deliver  to  the  gunboat  Tahoma  all  the  provisions  and  coal 
you  can  spare,  reserving  but  one  week’s  provisions  for  yourself  and 
enough  coal  to  bring  you  to  this  place.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Willcomb ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  capture 
of  the  British  schooner  Pacifique. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

Off  St.  Marhs ,  March  £7,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  arrived  here  from  Apalachi¬ 
cola  Ba}r  this  morning  and  resumed  the  blockade  of  this  port,  relieving 
the  U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson. 

On  my  arrival  I  found  anchored  here  the  schooner  Pacifique ,  of 
Quebec,  under  English  colors,  and  purporting  to  be  from  Cienfuegos, 
Cuba,  bound  to  St.  John’s,  Newfoundland,  which  had  been  seized  by 
the  U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson .  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Commanding 
David  Cate. 

He  informed  me  that  her  papers  were  all  correct,  and  requested  me 
to  endorse  them  with  him,  which  I  declined  on  the  grounds  that  I  con¬ 
sidered  her  position  as  extremely  suspicious.  He  endorsed  them. 

After  the  departure  of  the  Hendrick  Hudson ,  I  made  a  careful  exam¬ 
ination  of  the  schooner’s  papers,  including  log  book  and  charts.  They 
were  apparently  correct,  with  the  exception  of  the  log  book,  which 
contained  several  discrepancies  such  as  follows:  March  19,  Sandy 
Cay  in  sight,  latitude  obs.  24°  19';  21st,  Salt  Cay  light  SW.  by  S.,  14 
miles  distant;  23d,  latitude  obs.  27°  58',  which  would  put  her  at  least 
30  miles  clear  of  and  to  the  northward  of  Little  Bahamas.  After 
careful  investigation,  I  have  concluded  to  take  possession  of  her  as  a 
prize  to  this  steamer,  and  send  her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

I  herewith  enclose  a  complete  list  of  the  officers  and  crew  of  this 
vessel. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  ve^  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  L.  W illcomb, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Engagement  with  Confederates  on  Gadsden's  Point ,  Tampa  Bay ,  by 
boat's  crew  f  rom  the  U.  8.  bark  Pursuit ,  March  27,  1863. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy. 


No.  134.]  U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West ,  April  21,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  the  following: 

On  the  27th  ultimo,  as  the  bark  Pursuit  was  lying  off  Gadsden’s 
Point  in  Tampa  Bay,  on  blockade,  a  smoke  was  discovered  on  the 
beach,  and  shortly  afterwards  three  persons  made  their  appearance, 
wavinga  white  flag.  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Randall,  in  command 
of  the  Pursuit,  supposing  them  to  be  escaped  contrabands  or  others, 
wishing  to  communicate  with  the  vessel,  sent  a  boat  in,  in  charge  of 
Acting  Master  H.  K.  Lapham,  with  a  flag  of  truce  flying.  On  the 
boat  nearing  the  beach,  two  of  the  parties  were  seen  to  be  clothed  in 
female  apparel,  with  their  hands  and  faces  blackened,  and  one  of  them 
appeared  to  be  overcome  with  joy,  exclaiming,  “Thank  God!  Thank 
God!  I  am  free.”  On  the  boat  touching  the  beach,  the  female  dresses 
were  thrown  off,  and  it  then  became  evident  that  they  were  white 
men,  disguised  for  the  purpose  of  decoying  the  boat  on  shore.  Imme¬ 
diately  afterwards  about  100  armed  men  arose  from  the  bushes  around 
about  and  demanded  the  surrender  of  the  boat,  which  being  refused, 
they  fired  a  volley  of  musketry  into  her,  wounding  the  officer  in  charge 
and  three  of  the  crew.  The  fire  was  returned  by  the  boat’s  crew, 
some  firing  and  the  rest  hauling  the- boat  off  until  they  were  out  of 
range.  As  soon  as  the  firing  commenced,  the  Pursuit  was  sprung 
and  her  battery  brought  to  bear,  and  four  shells  fired  amongst  the 
rebels,  but  probably  without  effect. 

The  gunboat  Talioma,  arriving  at  Tampa  Bay  the  next  day,  her 
commander  having  been  informed  of  the  treacherous  conduct  of  the 
rebels,  ordered  the  Pursuit  down  the  bay,  and  proceeded  with  the 
U.  S.  schooner  Beauregard  up  to  bombard  the  town.  It  blowing  a 
norther  at  the  time,  it  was  impossible  to  do  anything  more  than  to  try 
the  range  of  the  Beauregard's  rifle,  which  was  done  with  satisfactory 
results.  On  the  2d  instant,  the  commander  of  the  Talioma,  while 
returning  to  his  vessel  from  a  closer  inspection  of  the  battery,  had 


398

three  shots  fired  at  him.  The  Beauregard  was  then  sent  as  near  the 
battery  as  was  possible,  and  both  vessels  commenced  firing-  on  the 
town,  hitting  some  of  the  houses,  but  what  other  damage  was  done 
could  not  be  ascertained.  I  herewith  enclose  the  acting  assistant 
surgeon’s  report  of  the  wounded  on  board  the  bark  Pursuit. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Pursuit. 

U.  S.  Bark  Pursuit, 

Off  Gadsden? s  Point ,  Tampa  Bay ,  March ,  ,f7,  1863. 

Sir:  I  am  obliged  to  report  an  act  of  shameful  treachery  committed 
by  the  rebels  under  a  flag  of  truce.  The  circumstances  are  as  follows: 
Last  night,  at  about  10  p.  m.,  a  small  fire  was  discovered  on  the  beach 
at  Gadsden’s  Point,  which  bears  N.  h  W.,  2  miles  distant.  Supposing 
it  to  have  been  made  by  escaped  contrabands  who  were  desirous  of 
coming  to  the  ship,  1  was  about  to  send  a  boat;  but  on  further  consid¬ 
eration  1  deemed  it  more  prudent  to  wait  until  daylight.  In  the 
morning  no  signs  of  anyone  could  be  seen  on  shore.  About  noon, 
however,  a  small  smoke  was  discovered  on  the  beach,  and  three  per¬ 
sons  were  seen  waving  a  flag  of  truce.  It  being  evident  that  they 
wished  to  communicate  with  the  ship,  I  sent  the  first  cutter  with  an 
armed  crew,  under  charge  of  Acting  Master  Henry  K.  Lapham,  who 
pulled  toward  them  with  a  white  handkerchief  flying  as  a  flag  of  truce. 
On  nearing  the  beach  two  of  the  persons  were  found  to  be  clothed  in 
female  apparel;  their  faces  and  hands  were  blackened,  and  one  of  them 
appeared  to  be  overcome  with  joy,  wringing  her  hands  and  repeatedly 
exclaiming,  “Thank God!  Thank  God!  1  am  free!”  As  soon,  how-

At  this  signal  about  100  men  arose  from  ambush  and  demanded  the

most  miraculous  that  any  of  the  boat’s  crew  should  have  escaped,  as 
the  rebels  were  no  less  than  100  in  number,  and  not  over  30  yards 
distant  from  the  boat.  She  could  easily  have  been  captured  were  it 
not  for  the  cool  and  determined  manner  in  which  she  was  defended. 
The  only  comment  that  I  can  make  on  the  conduct  of  Mr.  Lapham  and 
the  boat’s  crew  is  that  they  have  proved  themselves  to  be  truly  brave 
men. 

Regretting  my  inability  to  communicate  more  briefly  a  faithful 
detail  of  the  events,  1  have  the  honor  to  remain, 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  P.  Randall,

Admiral:  Your  letter  of  the  24th  instant  enclosed  me  a  communica¬ 
tion  from  R.  W.  Shufeldt,  U.  S.  consul-general,  Havana. 

I  do  not  agree  with  the  consul  that  the  information  afforded  him  by 
one  of  the  crew  of  the  Confederate  steamer  Cuba  was  correct,  or  even 
given  with  the  intention  of  telling  the  truth. 

I  have  had  a  lookout,  furnished  with  signals,  kept  at  Sea  Horse  Key 
light-house,  from  whence  the  mouth  of  the  Suwanee  River  is  distinct. 
I  have  had  boats  out,  spending  forty-eight  hours  at  a  time,  laying  in 
wait  behind  North  Key.  My  boats  have  several  times  been  in  the 
Suwanee  River  and  have  cut  down  all  the  beacons  and  stakes  there¬ 
about.  I  should  have  thought  it  rather  late  in  the  war  for  that  stale 
expedient  that  has  been  employed  by  the  rebels  of  endeavoring  to 
harass  officers  bv  bringing  them  under  the  unfavorable  notice  of  their 
commanders  by  such  reports.

99*]  U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  March  13,  1863. 

Sir:  I  would  call  the  attention  of  the  Government  to  some  peculiar 
facts  connected  with  the  region  of  the  Rio  Grande,  suggested  by  the 
recent  release  of  the  British  brig  Magicienne  by  the  officers  of  the 
district  court  at  this  place. 

This  vessel  has  been  mentioned  as  suspicious  in  the  extracts  from 
consular  and  other  dispatches  furnished  to  me  by  the  Department, 
and  also  as  having  sailed  from  England  for  Matamoras  on  the  6th  of 
January.  She  was  captured  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Onward  and  sent  in  here 
for  adjudication;  but,  on  February  28,  the  district  attorney  addressed 
the  following  official  communication  to  the  prize  commissioners,  and 
she  was  accordingly  released: 

Sir:  At  the  request  of  the  British  vice-consul  I  examined  to-day,  in  your  presence, 
the  depositions  taken,  and  the  invoices,  bills  lading,  and  other  papers  relating  to  the 
British  brig  Magicienne,  lately  sent  into  this  port  as  prize,  and  to  the  cargo  of  that 
vessel.  I  can  not  consistently  commence  proceedings  against  the  Magicienne.  I  can 
see  nothing  on  which  to  base  a  demand  for  condemnation,  nor  even  for  a  certificate 
for  probable  cause  of  seizure.  I  advise  that  the  Magicienne  and  cargo  be  restored 
by  the  prize  commissioner  to  the  master  and  claimant. 

I  do  not  know  what  evidence  was  submitted  in  the  case;  but  assum¬ 
ing  that  her  cargo  may  have  consisted  wholly  or  partially  of  contra¬ 
band  of  war,  it  might  be  urged,  in  view  of  the  existing  hostilities 
between  Mexico  and  France,  that  it  doe's  not,  therefore,  follow  that 
such  articles  were  intended  to  be  smuggled  into  Texas  for  the  use  of 
the  rebels,  but  that  it  is  fair  to  suppose  they  were  destined  for  the 
Mexicans,  and,  in  support  of  such  a  supposition,  it  has  been  noticed 
that  vessels  are  constantly  being  cleared  from  our  Northern  ports  for 
Matamoras,  laden  with  all*  sorts  of  articles,  even  including  such  as  are 
clearly  contraband.  It  is  somewhat  remarkable,  however,  that  the 
requirements  of  a  legitimate  trade  with  this  port  should  have  increased 
to  such  an  enormous  extent  in  so  short  a  time  as  is  represented;  and  it 
will  readily  occur  to  the  Government  that,  unless  this  trade  can  be 
restricted  in  some  way,  the  object  of  blockading  our  Southern  coast 
must  necessarily,  in  a  great  measure,  be  frustrated.  Whether  such

EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


restrictions  can  be  effected  by  our  cruisers — especially  in  view  of  this 
case  of  the  A fagidenne — or  whether  the  occupation  of  Brownsville  by 
a  sufficient  military  force  is  possible  and  calculated  to  secure  the  object 
desired,  is  now  suggested  for  the  consideration  of  the  Government. 

It  is  proper  to  state  that  (I  understand)  the  cargo  of  the  Magicienne 
was  not  broken  out  and  examined  in  this  port;  and  although  the  fact 
of  her  having  contained  contraband  of  war  may  have  been  fully  shown, 
and  may  have  been  considered  insufficient  for  her  detention,  yet  an 
examination  might  have  revealed  (for  example)  clothing  or  accouter¬ 
ments  marked  “C.  S.  A.,”  which  could  hardly  have  been  intended  for 
the  Mexicans.  And  in  this  connection  I  would  remind  the  Department 
that  the  mere  fact  of  contraband  would  be  sufficient  to  warrant  her 
being  seized  by  our  cruisers  and  sent  in  for  adjudication,  and  that  a 
search  for  such  further  proof  of  complicity  with  the  rebels,  as  is  sug¬ 
gested  above,  would  be  impossible  at  sea,  as  all  such  proof  would  nat¬ 
urally  be  stowed  well  out  of  reach. 

The  steamer  Peterhoff,  captured  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Vanderbilt  while 
bound  (apparently)  to  Matamoras,  is  now  in  this  port,  and  although  I 
fancy  there  can  be  no  doubt  about  her,  yet  similar  considerations  to 
those  suggested  above  would  release  her  also. 

Respectfully,  /

No.  106.J  U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  Afarch  19, 1863. 

Sir:  Referring  to  the  subject  of  my  letter  of  March  13, 1  would  sug¬ 
gest,  in  case  the  military  occupation  of  the  Rio  Grande  can  not  be  under¬ 
taken  at  present,  that  an  arrangement  with  the  French  for  a  joint 
blockade  of  that  river  would,  if  practicable,  produce  the  desired  result 
perhaps  even  more  effectually  than  could  be  done  in  any  other  way. 
A  representation  to  the  French  authorities  that  English  capitalists  are 
openly  pouring  into  Matamoras  munitions  of  war  of  every  description, 
avowedly  for  the  supply  of  the  Mexicans,  ought  certainly  to  induce 
them  to  blockade  that  port,  and  then  a  similar  force  on  our  part  would 
seal  up  the  place  entirely,  as  against  any  set  of  papers  that  a  vessel 
could  carry. 

Whether  such  an  arrangement  can  be  made  without  any  “  entangling 
alliances,”  whether  it  can  not  be  informally  agreed  upon  betAveen 
Admiral  Farragut  and  the  French  admiral,  or  whether  the  entire  ques¬ 
tion  can  not  be  turned  to  some  further  advantage  in  our  relations  with 
France,  is  for  the  Government  to  consider  and  determine. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

No.  120.]  IT.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  April  1863. 

Sir:  Referring  once  more  to  the  subject  of  my  dispatches,  Nos.  99 
and  106,  dated  March  13  and  19,  relative  to  the  condition  of  affairs  in 
the  \  lcmity  of  Matamoras,  I  have  to  inform  the  Department  that  the 
British  schooner  Agnes ,  with  a  cargo  of  cotton  and  with  papers  show¬ 
ing  a  regular  clearance  from  Matamoras,  was  captured  near  the  Tortu¬ 
ga  by  the  schooner  Two  Sisters  (a  tender  to  this  vessel)  and  brought 
into  this  port  yesterday  for  adjudication. 

1  his  vessel  was  built  in  Louisiana  and  was  formerly  owned  there, 
but  now  shows  a  provisional  register  signed  by  the  British  consul- 
general  at  Havana.  On  a  first  examination  of  her  papers  the  district 
attorney  was  of  opinion  that  no  cause  of  action  could  lie  against  her, 
but  on  further  consultation  with  him  I  have  directed  the  vessel  to  be 
libeled  as  a  prize  in  order  to  make  it  a  test  case  for  the  future  guidance 
of  our  cruisers  in  making  captures.  The  reasons  that  impelled  me  to 
this  course  are  that  from  intercepted  correspondence  lately  found  on 
board  a  prize  I  learn  that  the  rebel  Government  are  seizing  all  the  cot¬ 
ton  they  can  lay  hands  on  in  Florida  and  paying  the  planters  for  it  at 
an  arbitrary  rate  fixed  by  themselves,  and  that  they  are  exporting  it 
at  their  own  risk  in  order  to  meet  the  demands  for  foreign  loans. 
Officers  are  appointed  for  this  purpose,  and  great  discontent  is  mani¬ 
fested  by  the  professed  speculators  in  this  line  at  the  interference  with 
their  business.  It  is,  therefore,  fair  to  suppose  that  these  provisions 
are  coextensive  with  the  authority  of  the  rebel  Government,  and  that 
in  this  case,  as  in  the  other,  the  real  ownership  is  covered  up  from 
observation  by  false  papers. 

I  learn  also,  from  passengers  taken  in  the  Agnes,  that  there  are  at 
present  from  180  to  200  vessels,  of  all  nations  (many  of  them  Ameri¬ 
can,  and  having  regular  clearances  from  the  Northern  ports  of  the 
United  States),  off  the  mouth  of  the  Rio  Grande,  waiting  to  discharge 
their  cargoes  and  receive  cotton  instead,  and  that  previous  to  this 
rebellion  there  were,  at  most,  but  half  a  dozen  vessels  trading  with 
that  port  during  the  whole  year.  In  view  of  all  these  facts,  I  would 
reiterate  my  opinion  as  to  the  necessity  of  some  immediate  action  to 
close  this  port  for  all  purposes  of  general  trade,  either  by  military 
occupation  of  our  own  interior  frontier,  or  by  instituting  a  joint 
blockade  with  the  French. 

1  shall  send  copies  of  my  three  letters  to  the  Department  on  this 
subject,  by  the  first  opportunity,  to  Rear-Admiral  Farragut,  for  his 
information. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdy.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Lientenant-Commander  English, 

IT.  S.  Navy,  regarding  cooperation. 

U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  March  1863. 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  is  ready  for  sea, 
you  will  receive  from  this  vessel  two  launches  (with  howitzers  and  the 
crews  otherwise  armed),  and  you  will  proceed  with  all  dispatch  to 
Cedar  Kevs,  avoiding  all  communication  by  which  the  object  of  your 
expedition  can  be  known,  or  even  surmised,  without,  however,  suffer¬ 
ing  any  attempt  to  evade  the  blockade  that  may  fall  under  your 
immediate  notice  to  pass  unheeded. 

On  arriving  at  Cedar  Keys,  you  will  communicate  with  Acting 
Lieutenant  Edward  Y.  McCauley,  commanding  the.  U.  S.  S.  Fort 
Henry ,  and  arrange  with  him  the  details  of  the  following  plan: 

The  two  launches  of  this  ship,  together  with  your  own  and  such 
other  boats  of  the  Sagamore  and  Fort  Henry  as  can  be  spared  (having 
due  regard  to  the  safety  and  efficiency  of  the  latter  vessel  during  the 
absence  of  the  expedition)  will  constitute  a  force  under  the  immediate 
command  of  Acting  Lieutenant  McCauley,  for  the  purpose  of  scouring 
the  entire  coast  between  the  Suwanee  River  and  the  Anclote  Keys. 
You  will  take  the  expedition  in  your  vessel  first  to  the  mouth  of  the 
Suwanee  River,  and  dispatch  them  inside,  and  thence  along  the  coast 
to  the  southward,  with  orders  to  capture  all  vessels  they  may  find  on 
the  way,  or  failing'  that  to  destroy  them.  In  the  meantime  you  will 
manage  your  own  vessel  so  as  to  render  the  most  efficient  support 
possible  to  the  expedition.  Passing  to  the  southward  of  Cedar  Keys, 
you  will  continue  the  process  above  indicated,  paying  especial  attention 
to  Crystal  River,  Chassahowitzka  River  and  Bayport.  After  the  boats 
shall  have  passed  inside  of  St.  Martin’s  Reef,  it  would  seem  the  best  plan 
for  you  to  go,  in  the  Sagamore ,  to  cruise  between  the  southern  point 
of  that  reef  and  North  Anclote  Key,  until  rejoined  by  the  expedition. 

Should  information  reach  you  inducing  a  belief  that  greater  damage 
could  be  done  to  the  rebels  by  first  scouring  the  coast  inside  of  St. 
Martin’s  Reef  before  visiting  the  Suwanee  River,  you  are  at  liberty 
to  do  so,  and  you  can  not  too  highly  appreciate  the  importance  of  tak¬ 
ing  the  enemy  by  surprise,  whereby  a  greater  blow  can  be  inflicted  on 
them  and  with  less  probability  of  loss  on  our  side. 

Much  must  necessarily  be  left  to  your  discretion  in  the  matter,  and 
I  confidently  expect  no  insignificant  results  from  the  expedition  if 
arranged  with  judgment  and  executed  with  the  celerity  and  dash  which 
I  look  for  in  yourself  and  Lieutenant  McCauley,  for  there  is  reason  to 
believe  that  all  this  portion  of  the  coast  is  thickly  lined  with  vessels 
whose  only  object  is  to  run  the  blockade  with  valuable  cargoes. 

On  the  accomplishment  of  this  duty,  and  having  left  Lieutenant 
McCauley  and  his  portion  of  the  expedition  on  board  their  own  vessels, 
you  will  return  to  this  port  with  the  launches  of  the  St.  Lawrence 
and  report  to  me. 

Respectfully,  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Earl  English,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Gunboat  Sagamore.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  English,  II.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Sagamore. 

U.  S.  Boat  Sagamore, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  April  9 ,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  jTour  letter  of  instruction  dated  March  24,  I 
received  from  the  frigate  St.  Lavrrence  her  first  and  second  launches, 
accompanied  with  a  party  of  46  men  and  marines,  under  charge  of 
Acting  Master’s  Mate  Boyle  and  Gunner  Ferguson,  and  proceeded  to 
Cedar  Keys;  arriving  here  on  the  28th  ultimo,  communicated  with 
Lieutenant-Commander  E.  Y.  McCauley,  and  made  all  preparations 
for  starting  the  expedition.  It  was  not,  however,  until  the  2d  instant 
that  the  weather  would  admit  of  boats  leaving  the  vessel,  upon  which 
day  I  took  them  in  tow  and  proceeded  down  the  coast  and  dispatched 
them  inshore.  Enclosed  I  send  Lieutenant-Commander  McCauley’s 
report. 

I  am  satisfied  had  it  not  blown  a  gale  of  wind  at  the  time  the  party 
arrived  off  Bayport,  every  vessel  in  there  would  have  been  captured 
or  destroyed,  notwithstanding  the  battery  and  rifle  pits. 

It  is  not  often  we  hear  of  open  boats  attacking  a  battery  on  shore, 
protected  as  this  was,  and  succeed  in  silencing  and  driving  them  from 
their  guns. 

The  contrabands  that  made  their  escape  from  Crystal  River  report 
the  courier  brought  news  of  the  attack  the  same  afternoon,  and  that 
the  rebels  had  four  killed  and  many  wounded,  and  that  he  had  been 
dispatched  along  the  coast  collecting  troops  at  contemplated  points  of 
attack. 

During  the  time  the  expedition  was  inside  of  St.  Martin’s  Reef,  and 
so  on  up  to  the  mouth  of  the  Suwanee  River,  this  vessel,  accompanied

Detailed  report  of  Acting  Lieutenant  McCauley,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Fort 

Henry. 

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla.,  April  9 ,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  and  directions,  I  took  charge  of 
the  armed  boat  expedition,  consisting  of  the  St.  Lawrencd  s  two  first 
launches,  the  Sagamore1  s  launch  and  cutter,  the  Fort  Henry’s  launch 
and  cutter,  and  a  cutter  ambulance  in  charge  of  Assistant  Surgeon  J. 
Stevens. 

On  the  evening  of  the  2d  instant,  at  7  o’clock,  we  left  the  Sagamore 
and  stood  in  for  Bayport  and  anchored  in  4  feet  water  at  1  o’clock 
a.  m.  At  daylight  we  found  ourselves  2  miles  to  leeward  of  Bayport, 
with  a  strong  westerly  breeze  and  ebb  tide  against  us.  The  first 
launch  proved  so  sluggish  and  heavy  that  we  spent  two  hours  in  reach¬ 
ing  the  entrance  of  the  harbor  through  a  most  intricate  and  shallow 
channel.  This  waste  of  time  gave  the  rebels  leisure  to  make  all  prepa¬ 
rations  for  our  reception.  The  outer  anchorage,  where  vessels 
usually  take  in  their  cargoes,  was  clear  of  sail.  Two  small  schooners 
and  two  sloops  were  run  into  a  bayou  and  grounded  on  the  banks, 
which  were  thickly  covered  with  trees,  but  a  large  schooner,  laden 
with  cotton  and  ready  for  sea,  was  at  anchor  in  the  bay,  evidently  of 
too  great  draft  to  be  moved.  I  dispatched  the  Sagamore’s  second 
cutter,  in  charge  of  Master’s  Mate  Fleming,  to  capture  a  sloop  lying 
inshore  to  the  southward  of  the  harbor.  They  dashed  after  her,  car¬ 
rying  their  boats  over  the  flats,  and  took  possession  of  her.  She 
proved  to  be  the  Helen ,  of  Crystal  River,  loaded  with  corn.  She  was 
destroyed  by  fire.  Her  crew  was  brought  on  board  the  first  launch. 
They  informed  me  that  Bayport  was  defended  by  a  battery  of  two 
guns  and  a  company  of  rebel  soldiers,  besides  other  auxiliaries,  and 
gave  the  above-mentioned  information  of  the  cotton  schooner.  Hav¬ 
ing  cleared  boats  for  action,  I  led  the  launches  on  to  capture  or  destroy 
the  schooner.  On  reaching  within  900  yards  the  battery  opened  on 
us  with  round  shot,  and  the  woods  around  the  harbor  concealed  a  good 
number  of  riflemen,  who  kept  up  a  brisk  fire  upon  us,  all  equally  badly 
aimed,  for  although  we  were  from  twenty-five  to  thirty-five  minutes 
under  fire,  but  one  man  was  wounded  on  our  side. 

On  getting  within  4C0  yards  the  launches  opened  fire  with  their 
howitzers.  A  man  was  then  seen  to  leave  the  schooner  and  in  a  few 
seconds  after  the  flames  spread  over  her.  For  about  fifteen  minutes 
the  battery  answered  our  fire  with  grape,  but  the  fire  from  the  Saga- 
mords  launch  was  so  rapid  and  well  directed,  and  finally  a  shrapnel 
from  her  gun  falling  in  the  midst  of  the  enemy  there,  their  guns  were 
deserted  and  our  attention  was  turned  to  shelling  the  riflemen  in  the 
woods.

Tlie,  Fort  Henry  s  launch’s  howitzer  broke  its  clamp  plate  after  the 
second  discharge  and  was  disabled.  After  the  thirteenth  round  the 
second  launch  s  gun  was  disabled  by  the  same  kind  of  accident.  She 
did  not  withdraw  from  under  tire,  but  held  her  position  and  kept  up  a 
warm  rifle  discharge.  The  first  launch  was  so  unwieldy,  the  tide 
wind,  and  sea  so  strong,  that  we  could  not  keep  bows  on  to  the  bat¬ 
tery;  constantly  grounding.  She  seemed  hardly  to  be  affected  by  the 
oais.  i  got  her  anchor  out  astern,  but  she  dragged  it,  and  brouo-ht 
up  about  350  yards  from  the  battery,  where  she  was  bravely  followed 
by  the  Sagamore  s  launch,  to  whose  effective  fire  she  is  indebted  for 
getting  off  unscathed. 

i  ^oac^eir  °f  °Yr  howitzer,  J.  Baptiste,  of  the  Sagamore ,  had  been 
shot  through  the  shoulder;  his  place  was  promptly  supplied  by  Louis 
Vascom,  whose  conduct  under  fire  and  afterwards  was  [a]  subject  of 
praise  from  all  who  witnessed  it. 

By  this  time  the  schooner  was  ignited  to  such  an  extent  that  ren¬ 
dered  extinguishing  impossible.  Having  gained  my  object  in  her 
destruction  and  the  clearing  of  the  battery,  the  disabling  of  two  of  my 
guns,  the  unwieldiness  of  the  first  launch,  which  made  it  difficult  to 
bring  her  gun  to  bear;  the  uncertainty  of  aim  in  the  sea  that  was  run¬ 
ning,  and  consequent  waste  of  ammunition,  and  the  warnings  of  Mr. 
Ashley,  the  pilot,  that  if  the  ebb  tide  found  us  there  we  should  be 
left  aground,  made  me  give  up  my  design  of  trying  to  set  the  vessels 
in  the  bayou  on  fire  by  shelling.  We  then  began  a  heavy  pull  out  of 
range,  a  feat  which  we  accomplished  in  the  first  launch  in  half  an  hour, 
daring’  which  time  the  rebels  returned  to  their  guns  and  saluted  us 
with  a  steady  fire  from  a  rifled  fieldpiece  they  brought  up. 

We  anchored  outside  the  range  of  their  guns  for  rest  and  food.  I 
found  the  first  launch’s  bow  had  suffered  from  the  strain  of  the 
24-pounder  to  such  an  extent  that  two  rounds  more  would  have  disa¬ 
bled  her  entirely.  The  Sagamores  gun,  having  stranded  its  breeching, 
was  the  only  gun  I  could  depend  upon  for  future  service.  Jury  fittings 
were  skillfully  made,  but  were,  of  course,  unreliable. 

My  course  was  then  for  the  mouth  of  the  Chassahowitzka,  which 
we  barely  reached  that  night  in  time  to  find  a  slight  shelter  against  the 
N.  W.  gale,  which  blew  with  violence,  filling  the  light  boats  and 
launches  with  water,  and  reducing  our  howitzer  ammunition  by 
drowning. 

The  men  and  officers  who  spent  that  cold  night  baling  and  pulling 
about,  with  the  usual  accompaniment  of  loss  of  kedges,  etc.,  without 
a  murmur,  deserve  to  be  remembered  by  the  rear-admiral  when  he 
requires  the  services  of  hardy,  resolute  seamen. 

Without  delay,  at  daylight  we  got  underway,  and  by  taking  the  first 
launch  in  tow,  forty-eight  hours  after  leaving  Bayport  we  reached 
Crystal  River,  a  rebel  express  having  preceded  us  there  by  forty-one 
hours.  The  first  launch  having  been  rendered  still  more  unwieldy  by 
the  alteration  of  her  trim,  consequent  to  consumption  of  ammunition, 

I  did  not  think  it  proper  to  proceed  up  the  Crystal  River  to  any  dis¬ 
tance.  1  sent  Mr.  Babson  in  with  the  Sagamore's  launch  and  second 
cutter  to  reconnoiter.  He  reported  the  river  clear  of  sail  and  the 
channel  so  shallow  that  even  his  light  launch  had  difficult}'  in  getting 
by  the  channel  stakes. 

W e  left  Crystal  River  that  afternoon  and  passed  the  Homosassa,  a 
small  creek  with  a  boat  channel  of  about  4  feet  water. 


408  EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

Next  night  we  entered  the  Withlacoochee,  where  I  took  possession 
of  a  deserted  house,  and  sent  half  the  crews  of  the  boats  ashore  at  a 
time  to  obtain  rest  and  dry  their  clothing  and  arms. 

Next  day  we  visited  the  mouth  of  the  Waccasassa  and  returned  to 
the  Fort  Henry  at  8  p.  m.,  havingtugged  that  first  launch  against  head 
winds,  and  for  the  most  part  of  the  time  adverse  tides,  a  distance  of  at 
least  75  miles  in  five  days. 

On  the  8th  we  started  for  the  Suwanee  and  entered  the  river;  night 
coming  on,  owing  to  delays  occasioned  by  the  first  launch,  we  did  not 
have  time  to  proceed  up,  but  found  here  as  elsewhere  that  the  news  of 
our  approach  had  preceded  us,  and  not  a  sail  was  visible.  We 
attempted  to  return,  but  the  first  launch  made  us  pass  another  night 
in  the  boats. 

In  your  report,  pray  mention  to  the  rear-admiral  that  if  the  expedi¬ 
tion  has  been  poor  in  its  results,  he  will  please  take  into  consideration 
the  fact  that  the  weather  has  been  most  adverse  for  a  boat  expedition. 
I  was  amply  supplied  with  force  and  material,  and  the  men  and  officers 
seconded  me  in  a  manner  to  have  insured  success  in  any  undertaking. 
My  orders  were  obeyed  with  the  greatest  precision  and  alacritj^,  and 
not  a  single  disagreeable  incident  occurred  during  the  five  days  we  were 
toiling  along  under  the  hot  sun  against  head  winds,  tides,  and  bitter 
cold  nights. 

Will  you  please  mention  to  Captain  Schenck,  commanding  U.  S. 
flagship  /St.  Lawrence ,  the  notice  of  Louis  Vasconi’s  conduct,  also  the 
coxswain*  of  the  first  launch  for  perfect  attention  to  his  duty. 

I  recommend  to  you  the  captain  of  the  Sagamore,  s  launch’s  howit¬ 
zer.  Where  all  behaved  well,  these  men  were  remarkable. 

This  is  the  second  time  that  I  have  to  report  to  the  commander  of 
the  Sagamore  the  notice  I  have  taken  of  Mr.  Babson’s  conduct  under 
fire. 

I  find  I  have  a  valuable  officer  in  Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineer 
Charles  Minnerly. 

I  enclose  you  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  J.  Stevens’s  report  of  the 
wounded  man.  A  man  on  the  Fort  Henry’s  launch  was  also  struck  by 
a  spent  ball;  the  injury  was  very  slight. 

Mr.  Ashley,  the  pilot,  was  infallible  in  his  knowledge  of  the  shoals 
and  bars.  Out  of  sight  of  all  landmarks,  he  found  his  wav  through 
shoals  where  the  best  water  was  but  4  feet  with  a  confidence  and  skill 
which  enabled  him  to  perform  every  promise  he  made  me. 

When  the  news  of  our  attack  reached  Crystal  River,  7  contrabands 
took  advantage  of  the  excitement  to  escape  and  arrived  safely  on  board 
the  Fort  Henry.  Will  you  please  take  them  to  Key  West,  as  also  two 
prisoners  captured  in  the  prize  Annie ,  and  two  others  captured  in  the 
prize  Ranger. 

You  have  furnished  this  vessel  with  provisions  for  twenty -five  days. 

Allow  me  also  to  thank  you  for  the  valuable  advice  you  gave  me  on 
starting. 

Very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley, 

Acting  Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  U.  S.  S.  Fort  LLenry.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  East  Gulf  Squadron. 

U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West ,  April  21,  1863. 

Sir:  Under  date  of  March  24,  I  directed  Lieutenant-Commander 
English  to  proceed  in  the  gunboat  Sagamore ,  accompanied  by  the  two 
armed  launches  of  this  vessel,  to  Cedar  Keys,  there  to  arrange  the 
details  of  a  boat  expedition,  under  the  immediate  command  of  Lieu¬ 
tenant-Commander  McCauley,  for  the  purpose  of  scouring  the  coast 
between  the  Suwanee  River  and  the  Anclote  Keys,  where  it  was 
believed  many  small  craft  were  engaged  in  evading  and  violating  the 
blockade. 

A  launch  and  cutter  from  the  Sagamore  and  others  from  the  Fort 
Henry ,  together  with  an  ambulance  boat,  were  added  to  the  force,  and 
the  whole  proceeded  direct  to  Bayport,  while  the  Sagamore  remained 
in  the  offing,  to  prevent  the  escape  of  the  rebel  vessels.  The  weather 
throughout  was  most  unfavorable,  and  many  unforeseen  obstacles 
presented  themselves  at  every  step;  but  yet  the  main  object  of  the 
expedition  was  handsomely  accomplished.  The  sloop  Helen ,  of  Crystal 
River,  loaded  with  corn,  was  burned,  and  then  the  boats  made  a  move¬ 
ment  toward  a  large  schooner  at  anchor  inside,  loaded  with  cotton 
(said  to  contain  300  bales),  but  were  arrested  by  the  tire  of  a  2-gun 
battery  on  shore  and  of  a  goodly  number  of  riflemen  concealed  in  the 
woods.  A  brisk  engagement  of  half  an  hour  ensued,  and  the  rebels 
were  driven  from  their  guns  and  rifle  pits,  wrth  some  loss — certainly 
1  killed  and  3  wounded,  and  probably  more — although  our  launches 
and  their  guns  were  partially  disabled  by  their  own  rapid  firing  and 
consequent  violence  of  the  recoil;  fortunately  the  enemy’s  aim  was  so 
wild  that  their  shot  went  mostly  over  the  heads  of  our  party,  and  but 
one  man  was  hurt  on  our  side,  and  he  not  seriously.  This  little  action 
.  seems  to  have  been  conducted  with  coolness  and  judgment  and  to  have 
been  fought  with  spirit  and  bravery. 

Meantime  the  rebels  had  set  fire  to  the  schooner,  and  the.  engage¬ 
ment  was  continued  on  our  side  by  shelling  the  woods,  until  all  possi¬ 
bility  of  their  extinguishing  the  flames  had  disappeared,  when,  as  our 
object  had  been  accomplished,  as  several  of  our  guns  had  been  dis¬ 
abled,  and  as  the  pilot  gave  warning  that  the  tide  would  soon  leave 
the  boats  high  and  dry,  they  retired  beyond  the  range  of  the  battery 
and  waited  there  until  the  masts  of  the  schooner  fell  and  until  the  ves¬ 
sel  herself  had  entirely  disappeared. 

The  expedition  then  proceeded  to  the  Chassahowitzka  River,  thence 
to  Crystal  River,  the  Homosassa,  the  Withlacoochee,  and  the  Wakassa 
[WaccasassaJ;  but  they  were  so  much  delayed  by  head  winds  and  cur¬ 
rents,  and  by  the  sluggishness  of  one  of  the  launches  that  they  neces¬ 
sarily  made  but  slow  progress,  only  75  miles  in  five  days,  and  conse¬ 
quently  the  news  of  their  coming  preceded  them,  and  of  course  noth¬ 
ing  was  found  within  their  reach  along  the  coast.  The  same  causes 
prevented  their  effecting  a  surprise  on  extending  their  operations  to 
the  Suwanee  River. 

Lieutenant-Commander  McCauley  speaks  in  the  highest  terms  of 
the  conduct  of  his  men,  their  alacrity,  spirit,  and  coolness,  both  while 
under  fire  from  the  enemy  and  while  laboring  along  the  coast,  day 
and  uight,  under  every  disadvantage  of  wind,  tide,  and  weather. 

I  enclose  the  report  of  the  medical  officer  of  the  expedition,  and 
also  a  sketch  of  the  affair  at  Bayport.  It  should  have  been  mentioned 


410 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


that,  on  the  appearance  of  our  force  at  Bayport,  several  launches 
were  moved  inside  the  bayou,  where  they  could  not  be  reached  with¬ 
out  undue  exposure  of  the  men,  and  where  no. adequate  results  could 
be  obtained. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Hear- Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  BZkdg.  Squadron.

Reports  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Baxter,  JJ.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  JJ.  S.  hark  Gem  of  the  Sea,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British 
schooner  Maggie  Fulton. 

U.  S.  Bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 

At  Anchor  off  Indian  River  Inlet,  Fla.,  April  8,  1863. 
Sir:  Agreeable  to  your  order,  1  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the 
capture  made  this  day  by  the  U.  S.  bark  Gem  of  the  Sea  of  the  English 
schooner  Maggie  Fulton,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  from  Green 
Turtle  Cay,  Abaco,  while  attempting  to  run  the  blockade  at  Indian  Fiver 
Inlet,  East  Fla.,  loaded  with  a  general  cargo  and  manned  with  the  fol¬ 
lowing  named  persons:  John  T.  Foberts,  captain;  John  F.  Prinder, 
mate;  William  Harvey,  seaman;  and  Christopher  Fisher,  cook.  I  have 


412 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


sent  the  above  schooner  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  Henry  B.  Carter, 
and  a  prize  crew  to  Key  West  for  adjudication,  with  the  whole  of  her 
former  crew  as  witnesses. 

The  following  is  a  detailed  account  of  her  capture: 

This  morning  we  were  lying  at  anchor  2  miles  off  from  Indian  River 
Inlet,  with  the  wind  light  from  S.  E.  and  weather  foggy.  At  9  a.  m. 
the  fog  lifted  and  we  discovered  a  schooner  about  4  miles  to  the  N.  E. 
from  us  standing  to  the  southward;  we  fired  a  gun  to  bring  her  to,  to 
which  she  paid  no  attention,  but  kept  on  her  course.  I  immediately 
got  underway  and  went  in  chase  of  her,  but  shortly  after  we  lost  sight 
of  her,  as  the  fog  thickened  and  did  not  see  her  again  until  3  p.  m., 
when  we  made  her  close  inshore  about  3  miles  distant  from  us,  stand¬ 
ing  to  the  northward  for  the  inlet.  The  water  being  too  shoal  for 
us  to  approach  much  nearer  with  the  vessel,  we  lowered  our  boats 
and  captured  her.  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  herewith  a  copy  of  the 
invoice  of  cargo  on  board  the  above  schooner,  and  also  a  list  of  officers 
and  men  who  are  entitled  to  share  in  the  prize  money. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Baxter, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


U.  S.  Bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 

At  Anchor  off  Indian  Liver  Inlet ,  East  Fla.,  April  9,  1863. 

Sir:  I  last  had  the  honor  to  report  to  you  under  date  of  March  25, 
per  U.  S.  gunboat  Huntsville ,  giving  you  a  detail  of  my  proceedings 
up  to  that  date,  ivhich  were  of  little  interest. 

I  now  have  the  gratification  to  report  the  capture  made  by  this  vessel 
on  the  8th  instant  of  the  English  schooner  Maggie  Fulton,  26  tons,  of 
Nassau,  New  Providence,  from  Green  Turtle  Cay,  Abaco,  loaded  with 
salt  and  a  general  assortment  of  merchandise,  while  attempting  to  run 
the  blockade  at  this  inlet.  I  have  placed  Acting-  Volunteer  Master 
Henry  B.  Carter  on  board  of  her  as  prize  master,  with  a  prize  crew, 
and  sent  her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication  with  all  of  her  former  crew 
as  witnesses. 

I  am  confident  that  no  vessels  have  run  in  or  out  of  either  Jupiter 
or  Indian  River  inlets  since  the  6th  of  March,  1863,  as  our  boats  are 
in  the  river  whenever  the  bar  will  permit  them  to  cross.  They  were 
up  the  river  a  few  days  past  as  far  as  St.  Sebastian  River  and  down  to 
Jupiter  Inlet.  The.  bar  at  Jupiter  Inlet  is  nearly  dry  at  low  water. 

I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  herewith  a  report  of  the  capture  of 
schooner  Maggie  Fulton  for  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  and  also  a  dupli¬ 
cate;  also  receipt  of  small  arms. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Baxter, 

Acting  Volunteer'  Lieutenant,  U.  S.  Navy,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.
