Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Grosman ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding 
V.  S.  8.  Somerset ,  suggesting  the  feasibility  of  an  expedition  in  St. 
Marks  River. 


Sir: 


U.  S.  S.  Somerset, 

St.  George’s  Sound ,  April  If  1863. 


I  have  just  learned  by  the  testimony  of  an  intelligent  refugee  on 
board  the  Hudson  that  the  fort  at  St.  Marks  mounts  but  8  guns,  the 
largest  caliber  being  a  12-pounder. 

He  also  tells  me  that  a  cotton  schooner  is  loading  at  that  place  with 
a  crew  composed  of  those  who  left  the  prize  captured  by  the  boats  of 
the  bark  Amanda ,  and  not  burned,  through  bad  management. 

As  I  can  light  3  guns,  one  IX-inch  and  two  32-pounders,  right 
ahead,  and  can  protect  my  steam  drum  and  boiler  with  barrels  of  sand 
or  bags  of  coal,  as  the  reach  during  my  position  in  which  I  shall  be 
exposed  to  the  enemy’s  lire  will  be  only  2£  miles  (the  extreme  range 
of  their  guns),  and  consequently  with  the  flood  tide  I  will  be  under 
such  a  fire  but  twenty  minutes  at  the  utmost,  I  think  there  is  no  ques¬ 
tion  as  to  my  ability  to  ascend  the  river,  capture  the  Spray  and  cotton 
schooner,  besides  any  other  small  vessels  lying  there,  driving  the 
enemy  out  of  a  fort  only  fortified  with  dismounted  guns  (after  I  leave 
them),  and  treating  with  the  people  of  Newport,  but  a  short  distance 
above.  There  may  be  a  bank  in  this  place  with  gold  or  silver  stored 
in  its  vaults,  and  that  will- add  to  the  success  of  an  expedition  promis¬ 
ing  in  every  way  to  be  glorious. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  F.  Crosman, 

Lieutenant- Commander,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailet, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gidf  Squadron.

U.  S.  Schooner  Wanderer, 

At  Sea ,  off  Egmont  Key ,  Fla.,  Lat.  37°  15' ,  Long.  83°  15' , 

April  17,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  this  day  made  a  seizure  of  the  schooner  Annie  B  at  the 
above-mentioned  latitude  and  longitude,  the  nearest  land  being  Egmont 
Key,  bearing  N.  E.,  distant  35  miles.  Her  cargo  consists  of  17  bales 
of  cotton,  is  from  Anclote  River,  bound  to  Havana.  Having  no  papers 
nor  flags  on  board,  I  consider  her  a  lawful  prize. 

There  were  no  public  ships  nor  vessels  in  sight  at  the  time  of  cap¬ 
ture. 

'  Most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Baxter ,  B.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  TJ.  S.  baric  Gem  of  the  Sea,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British

U.  S.  Bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 

At  Anchor,  off  Lndian  River  Lnlet ,  F.  Fla.,  April  19,  1863. 
Sir:  I  last  had  the  honor  of  addressing  you  under  date  of  April  8, 
per  prize  schooner  Maggie  Fulton,  giving  you  a  detail  of  her  capture. 
I  now  have  the  honor  ito  report  to  you  that  on  the  18th  day  of  April, 
1863,  we  captured  the  British  schooner  Lnez,  4  tons,  of  and  from 
Nassau,  New  Providence,  while  attempting  to  run  the  blockade  at 
Indian  River  Inlet.  She  was  manned  with  the  following-named  per¬ 
sons:  George  R.  Edgett,  captain;  George  Holdham,  mate;  and  William 
Jones,  cook.  Her  cargo  consisted  of  15  sacks  salt  and  14  pounds 
shoe  thread,  and  the  only  paper  found  on  board  of  her  is  her  register, 
which  1  will  forward  with  her  crew  to  the  senior  officer  commanding 
Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron,  the  first  opportunity,  for  his 
disposal. 

The  schooner  being  old  and  leaky,  I  do  not  deem  her  and  her  cargo 
of  sufficient  value  to  justify- me  in  sending  her  into  port  for  adjudica¬ 
tion.  I  therefore  will  destroy  her  and  her  cargo,  with  the  exception 
of  the  shoe  thread,  which  I  will  save  for  the  bark’s  use. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  417 

The  following  is  a  detailed  account  of  the  capture  of  the  above- 
mentioned  schooner: 

On  the  18th  day  of  April,  1863,  at  5:20  p.  m.,  while  we  were  lying 
at  anchor  1^  miles  off  from  Indian  River  Inlet,  with  the  wind  light 
from  the  east,  we  discovered  her  10  miles  south  from  us,  close  in  to  the 
land,  steering  to  the  northward,  but  shortly  after  discovering  her  she 
tacked  to  the  south.  Judging  it  was  her  intention  to  run  the  blockade 
at  Indian  River  Inlet,  and  was  trying  to  dodge  us  until  dark,  when 
she  would  attempt  to  run  in,  I  therefore  lowered  two  boats  and  sent 
them  in  chase  of  her.  At  9:30  p.  m.  the  boats  returned  to  the  bark 
with  the  schooner,  having  captured  her  6  miles  south  of  the  inlet. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Baxter, 

Acting  Volunteer  lieutenant,  U.  iS.  Navy ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Treasury 

regarding  measures  for  trie  restriction  of  trade  in  the  Rio  Grande. 

Navy  Department,  April  1863. 

Sir:  Circumstances  indicate  that  there  is  an  active  trade  carried  on 
with  the  rebels  by  way  of  Matamoras,  on  the  Rio  Grande.  Since  the 
opening  of  the  rebellion  the  trade  with  that  port  has  increased  to  such 
an  extent  as  to  leave  no  room  to  doubt  that  a  constant  commercial 
intercourse  is  carried  on  between  it  and  our  frontier. 

In  a  recent  dispatch  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodoras  Bailey, 
he  states  that  he  learns  from  passengers  in  the  prize  schooner  Agnes , 
from  Matamoras,  that  there  are  at  present  from  180  to  200  vessels  of 
all  nations,  many  of  them  Americans,  and  having  regular  clearances 
from  the  Northern  ports,  off  the  mouth  of  the  Rio  Grande,  waiting  to 
discharge  and  receive  their  cargoes  and  receive  cotton  instead,  and 
that,  previous  to  this  rebellion,  there  were  at  most  but  half  a  dozen 
vessels  trading  with  that  port  during  the  whole  year. 

There  appears  to  be  no  means  at  present  of  checking  the  abuse  in 
question,  except  by  occupying  and  holding  the  frontier;  but  our  own 
vessels  and  our  own  citizens  should  not  take  advantage  of  this  condi¬ 
tion  of  affairs,  and  indirectly  aid  the  insurgents,  by  shipping  merchan¬ 
dise  to  Matamoras  peculiarly  adapted  to  the  Southern  market,  and 
which  is  transshipped  or  resold  to  the  insurgents,  and  receive  in  return 
the  products  of  the  South. 

I  have  made  this  communication  to  you  so  that  any  measure  which 
may  suggest  itself  to  you  to  restrict  the  trade  between  Northern  ports 
and  Matamoras,  and  check  the  growing  and  injurious  illicit  intercourse 
with  the  insurgents,  may  be  adopted,  if  you  think  proper. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Hon.  S.  P.  Chase, 

Secretary  of  the  Treasury.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S .  Navy ,  transmitting 
reports  regarding  an  attempt  to  determine  the  character  of  a  foreign 
vessel  of  war  on  the  high  seas. 


No.  130.1  U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West ,  April  1863. 

Sir:  I  transmit  herewith  copies  of  reports  from  Captain  William  M. 
Walker,  commanding1  steamer  De  Soto ,  and  from  two  of  his  officers, 
relative  to  a  very  remarkable  occurrence  between  that  vessel  and  some 
other  one,  calling  herself  the  French  corvette  Suffren ,  and  I  would 
urge  the  speedy  attention  of  the  Government  to  the  circumstances  of 
the  case,  lest  serious  results  should  grow  out  of  its  repetition. 

In  view  of  the  incidents  attending  the  destruction  of  the  steamer 
Hatteras — if  not  upon  general  principles  alone — it  can  not  be  expected 
that  the  commanding  officer  of  a  United  States  cruiser  will  be  content 
with  a  mere  assurance  (in  answer  to  a  hah)  of  the  friendly  or  neutral 
character  of  an  armed  vessel,  particularly  in  the  dark;  and  if,  in  addi¬ 
tion,  the  strange  vessel  should  permit  himself  to  indulge  in  an  arrogant 
or  insolent  tone,  approaching  in  appearance  to  the  audacity  often  dis¬ 
played  by  the  rebels,  it  can  not  be  wondered  at  if  mistakes  should  arise, 
and  if  a  damaging  broadside  should  be  the  next  feature  of  the  case.  I 
imagine  there  are  many  impulsive  officers  who  would  fail  to  show  the 
forbearance  exercised  by  Captain  Walker  in  this  instance,  and  who 
would  have  resorted  to  more  emphatic  means  of  enforcing  his  rights 
than  by  the  discharge  of  a  musket  across  the  stranger’s  bow. 

If  the  rule  of  action  in  similar  cases  is  to  conform  to  this,  the  object 
for  which  our  cruisers  are  sent  out  will  scarcely  be  accomplished;  but  I 
trust  the  French  admiral,  when  the  matter  shall  be  brought  to  his 
notice,  will  be  as  mindful  of  our  belligerent  rights  as  was  Vice-Admiral 
Sir  Alexander  Milne  in  his  circular  of  February  16,  and  also  that  our 
own  officers  may  exercise  due  firmness  in  ascertaining  the  character  of 
all  vessels  found  near  our  coast. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdcj.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


[Enclosures.] 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Key  West,  April  f  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  night  of  the  2d  instant,  between  11  and  12  p.  m.,  when 
in  latitude  23°  56'  N.,  and  longitude  83°  55'  W.,  and  steering  to  the 
northward  and  eastward,  a  steamer  was  reported  crossing  our  wake; 
we  immediately  stood  to  the  southward  to  intercept  her. 

As  we  ran  toward  her  it  was  discovered  that  she  was  burning  bitu¬ 
minous  coal,  and  soon  she  seemed  to  be  increasing  her  speed.  Our 
intention  of  communicating  with  her  must  have  been  apparent,  but  as 
she . did  not  regard  it,  we  fired  a  musket  to  indicate  our  purpose  more 
decidedly;  to  this  she  paid  no  attention  whatever,  neither  stopping  nor 
slowing  her  engine.  We  then  hailed  her  and  directed  her  to  heave  to, 
but  no  intelligible  reply  reached  us,  nor  was  there  any  indication  on 
her  part  of  an  intention  to  stop;  we  then  fired  another  musket,  hailed 
her  repeatedly,  directing  her  to  stop,  and  declared  our  desire  to  com- 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  419 

municate  by  boat,  which  the  stranger  in  reply  said  he  would  not 
receive. 

We  continued  to  maintain  our  position  on  the  port  beam  of  the 
stranger,  and  again  informed  him  that  we  wished  to  send  a  boat 
aboard  of  him.  Finally  he  replied  in  French,  “Very  well,  bear  a 
hand,”  and  stopped.  We  then  lowered  a  boat,  and  I  directed  Acting 
Master  Martine  to  go  and  ascertain  what  vessel  it  was.  It  proved  to 
be  a  French  corvette,  the  Suffren ,  we  believe. 

It  is  to  be  observed  that  I  could  form  no  judgment  respecting  the 
true  character  of  this  vessel  without  nearing  her;  that  she  did  not 
choose  at  first  to  stop,  nor  could  I  for  a  long  time  comprehend  any 
reply  she  made  to  our  hail.  I  am  well  aware  that  we  can  exercise  no 
authority  over  a  ship  of  war  on  the  high  seas,  but  it  seems  to  me  that 
it  was  due  to  the  relations  subsisting  between  France  and  the  United 
States  that  the  commander  of  the  corvette  should  have  immediately 
stopped  and  satisfied  me  of  the  character  of  his  ship,  knowing  well  that 
it  was  my  duty  to  enquire  into  it.  I  regret  to  believe  that  the  spirit 
displayed  by  him  on  this  occasion,  if  not  disapproved  by  the  French 
admiral  commanding  in  these  seas,  may  lead  to  painful  collisions. 

The  case  here  recited  belongs  to  a  class  of  extreme  delicacy,  calling 
for  the  exercise  of  much  forbearance,  and  with  which  we  are  liable  to 
have  to  deal  at  any  moment,  with  nothing  better  than  our  fallible 
judgment  to  guide  us;  for  notwithstanding  that  during  two  }mars  past 
we  have  been  in  the  exercise  of  belligerent  rights,  it  is  yet  not  sur¬ 
prising  that  with  respect  to  the  forms  and  ceremonies  to  be  observed 
in  arresting  and  boarding  vessels  on  the  high  seas  such  various  and 
imperfect  notions  should  prevail  and  that  the  rights  we  may  or  may  not 
exercise  in  regard  to  them  should  still  be  so  vague  and  undetermined, 
for  we  have  no  convention  with  maritime  powers  on  the  subject  to 
which  we  might  refer,  nor  do  I  know  of  any  general  order  or  regulation 
of  the  Navy  Department  to  direct -us.  Although  your  own  order  No. 
2  is  more  explicit  on  the  subject  than  any  other  of  which  I  am  cogni¬ 
zant,  it  does  not  contemplate  in  its  provisions  such  a  case  as  1  now 
present  you.  All  that  I  know  bearing  on  such  a  case  is  that  writers 
have  defined  to  some  extent  the  ceremony  with  which  national  ships 
are  to  enquire  of  and  declare  to  each  other  their  character,  and  that 
all  publicists  concede  that  the  right  of  visit  does  not  apply  to  national 
ships,  which  are  clothed  with  immunity  from  the  exercise  of  any 
jurisdiction  other  than  that  of  the  sovereign  power  to  which  they  owe 
allegiance. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  M.  Walker, 

Captain ,  II.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

Herewith  I  enclose  the  statements  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Brad¬ 
ford  and  Acting  Master  Martine.

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

A  t  Sea ,  Apr  il  3,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  following  conversation  which 
occurred  alongside  of  the  French  corvette  Suffren.  In  obedience 
to  your  orders,  I  took  charge  of  the  first  cutter  to  board  the  strange 
steamer  off  our  beam  and  ascertain  her  character  and  flag,  and,  if  a 
friend,  to  say  that  we  regrettedmuch  to  detain  him,  but  the  exigencies  of 
war  made  it  unavoidable.  Arrived  alongside,  asked  for  a  line,  which  was 
given  us.  Her  commander  then  asked,  ‘ 11  What  ship  is  that?”  1  replied, 
“  The  De  SotoJ  He  asked,  “  What  is  the  De  Soto?  ”  I  said,  “The 
U.  S.  S.  De  SotoJ  He  then  said,  “Have  you  any  dispatches  for 
me?”  I  answered,  “No.”  He  then  said,  “I  understood  you  to  say 
that  you  had  dispatches  for  me.”  I  next  asked  what  steamer  it  was. 
He  answered,  “The  French  corvette  Suffren .”  I  then  said  that  I 
wished  to  come  aboard.  He  said,  ‘  ‘  I  told  you  I  did  not  wish  to  com¬ 
municate  with  you,  but  if  you  wish  any  assistance  I  would  give  it. 
You  came  too  near;  what  did  you  want?”  “We  wished  to  ascertain 
the  character  of  your  ship;  the  circumstances  of  war  make  it  neces¬ 
sary  to  know  what  she  is.”  “This  is  a  friend;  we  are  not  at  war,  and 
this  is  the  high  sea;  I  shall  report  your  captain  to  our  admiral,”  was 
his  reply.  I  told  him  that  we  could  not  understand  a  word  he  had  said. 
He  replied,  “I  did  not  wish  you  to  understand.”  I  asked  where  he 
was  from.  He  answered,  “1  have  no  questions  to  answer;  we  are 
friends;  I  think  that  is  enough,”  and  turned  and  left  the  side  and  gave 
orders  to  go  ahead.  This  communication  was  in  English. 

Y ery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  L.  Martine, 

Acting  Master,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Captain  W.  M.  Walker, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  De  Soto.

Speed  on  recent  trial  trip,  12  knots;  draft  aft,  8  feet;  forward,  5  feet. 
Rig,  three-masted  schooner.  The  river  is  at  present  obstructed  with 
three  heavy  chains  across  the  narrow  part  of  the  channel;  two  shore 
batteries  of  six  guns  each,  commanding  obstructions.  Reports  an 
ironclad  steamer  being  built  at  Columbus,  diamond  shaped,  her  draft 
to  be  from  4  to  5  feet;  intended  only  for  use  in  the  bay.  The  captain 
of  the  Essex  carries  the  cotton  at  his  own  request  for  ballast,  without

Also  brought  off  a  fine  canal  boat  90  feet  long,  which  I  understood  was 
employed  to  carry  contraband  articles.  It  will  be  useful  to  me  for

Report  of  Captain  Walker,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 
regarding  convoy  duty  performed  for  Brigadier-  General  Ullman , 
TJ.  S.  Army,  in  the  steamer  Matanzas. 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico,  April  26,  1863. 

Sir:  In  my  communication  to  you  of  the  16th  instant  I  informed  you 
of  my  having  acceded  to  the  request  of  Brigadier-General  Ullman  to 
convoy  him,  with  270  officers,  in  the  steamer  Matanzas  to  the  Missis¬ 
sippi. 

We  had  to  work  hard  all  night  to  be  ready,  having  been  compelled 
to  blow  out  our  boilers  and  patch  them  before  we  could  be  ready  to 
start. 

Having  convoyed  the  Matanzas  to  the  South  W est  Pass — a  service 
which  was  acknowledged  in  a  very  flattering  letter  from  the  general— 
and  finding  the  water  at  the  time  too  salt  to  permit  us  to  fill  our  tanks, 
which  were  nearly  empty,  we  ran  over  to  the  Bajmu  La  Fourche,  in 
the  expectation  of  perhaps  performing  some  good  service,  and  at  the 
same  time  have  the  advantage  of  smooth  water  to  make  some  further 
necessary  repairs.  These  completed,  we  returned  to  the  Mississippi, 
where  we  remained  for  a  few  hours  filling  water,  and  thence  we 
steered  out  to  intercept  the  cotton  which  I  had  reason  to  believe  was 
afloat.  W e  were  not  lucky  enough  to  pick  up  a  steamer  which  had 
run  out  with  800  bales,  but  we  made  prizes  of  the  schooner  General 
Prim,  schooner  Rapid,  sloop  Jane  Adelie,  and  sloop  Bright,  with  full 
cargoes;  all  of  which  I  have  ordered  to  Key  West  for  adjudication, 
and  shall  now,  in  pursuance  of  your  instructions,  proceed  toward  Cape 
Catoche. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


423 


After  giving-  time  enough  for  the  dispatch  of  business  by  the  court 
at  Ke}^  West,  I  will  return  to  that  port  for  the  officers  and  crew  sent 
in  the  prizes,  whose  loss  I  shall  feel  very  much  in  consequence  of  my 
having  but  a  very  short  complement,  and  I  trust  you  will  see  the 
importance  of  increasing  it  by  at  least  ten  prime  men  to  meet  the 
extraordinary  demands  which  may  at  any  moment  be  made  for  prize 
crews,  etc. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  M.  Walker, 
Captain ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico,  Lcit.  26°  21'  N.,  Lon.  83°  1+9'  W.,  April  26, 1863. 

Sir:  I  have  this  day,  in  the  latitude  and  longitude  above  specified, 
taken  possession  of  the  schooner  Clarita,  G.  It.  Gammon,  master, 
sailing  under  a  provisional  certificate  of  registry  dated  at  Havana  on 
the  30th  December,  1862,  and  signed  John  V.  Crawford,  acting  consul- 
general  in  Cuba,  represented  to  be  bound  from  Havana  to  Matamoras, 
and  for  the  following  reasons  I  have  ordered  her  to  Key  West  for 
adjudication: 

1st.  She  was  far  out  of  the  track  which  she  should  have  followed 
from  Havana  to  Matamoras;  that  being  in  the  vicinity  of  blockaded 
ports  gives  the  strong  presumption  de  jure  that  she  had  been  so  placed 
with  the  intention  to  violate  the  blockade;  that  the  real  but  concealed 
destination  of  the  Clarita  was  a  blockaded  port  of  the  United  States. 

2d.  Her  papers  are  very  incomplete.  On  demanding  of  her  master 
his  log  book,  the  mutilated  log  book  sealed  up  herewith  is  the  only  log 
book  that  was  produced.  This  mutilation  of  the  log  book  is  to  be 
considered  an  act  of  the  most  aggravated  nature  and  sufficient  of  itself 
to  establish  guilt. 

On  examination  of  the  chart  of  the  Clarita ,  which  appears  to  be  a 
new  one,  and  is  sent  herewith  under  seal,  the  position  of  the  vessel 
from  day  to  day  is  not  marked  upon  it  in  the  usual  manner;  but  it  will 
be  seen  that  her  position  on  the  24th  of  April  is  pricked  through  the 
chart  and  corresponds  with  the  reckoning  found  upon  the  slate  on 
board  of  the  Clarita ,  used  in  working  up,  and  which  her  master 
admitted  to  be  the  reckoning  of  the  vessel  for  the  24th  and  25th  of 
April. 

It  will  next  be  seen  that  tracing  backward  (in  point  of  time)  from  these 
admitted  positions,  there  is  pricked  on  the  chart  the  track  of  the  vessel 
around  the  Tortugas,  and  considering  the  well-established  direction  of 
the  currents  in  that  vicinity,  the  Clarita  could  not  have  been  carried 
to  the  northward  unless  intentionally.  At  the  time  that  we  descried 
her  she  was  on  the  starboard  tack,  apparently  standing  N.  N.  W.  The 
wind  was  light  and  from  N.  E.  The  slate  above  referred  to,  as  also  a 
certified  copy  of  it,  is  herewith  sealed  up. 

I  am,  sir,  with  great  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  M.  Walker, 

Captain,  U  S.  Navy. 

The  Judge  of  the  United  States  District  Court, 

At  Key  West ,  Fla.

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Wavy,  to  Captain  Walker , 
U.  S.  JVavy ,  commanding  E.  S.  S.  De  Soto ,  defining  the  cruising 

ground  of  that  vessel ,  and  urging  vigilance  against  the  C.  S.  steamers 

Florida  and  Alabama. 

U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  April  38,  1863. 

Sir:  Your  several  letters  have  been  received,  and  I  have  to  con¬ 
gratulate  you  upon  your  success  in  intercepting  the  enemy’s  vessels. 

Since  writing  your  previous  orders  (of  April  3)  I  have  received 
information  which  is  corroborated  by  your  experience  and  which  had 
caused  me  to  regret  that  you  were  not  within  my  reach,  that  I  might 
give  you  different  instructions. 

You  will  therefore  consider  your  previous  orders  revoked,  and  will 
take  as  the  general  limits  of  your  cruising  ground  the  space  included 
between  the  parallels  of  25°  and  29°  north  latitude  and  the  meridians 
of  83°  and  87°  west  longitude,  within  which  it  is  believed  you  will  be 
most  likely  to  intercept  many  vessels  bound  to  and  from  the  various 
rebel  ports. 

It  is  also  my  present  intention  to  send  the  steamer  Huntsville  to  the 
same  cruising  ground  so  soon  as  she  is  ready,  and  the  gunboat  Sagamore 
is  now  on  the  same  line  of  travel  to  the  southward. 

It  seems  probable  from  your  letters  that  the  Clarita  will  prove  a 
good  prize,  but  at  the  same  time  it  is  necessary  to  inform  you  that  the 
court  at  this  place  have  very  materially  modified  their  views  upon 
the  general  subject  of  vessels  bound  to  and  from  Matamoras,  since  my 
conversation  with  you. 

Of  course  the  limits  of  your  cruising  ground,  as  above  indicated, 
are  not  rigid,  in  case  of  chasing  anything,  for  example,  or  for  other 
good  cause. 

There  are  rumors  in  Havana,  communicated  to  me  by  the  acting 
consul-general,  that  the  rebel  cruiser  Florida,  or  Oreto,  is  hovering 
about  the  Bahama  Banks;  other  reports  represent  the  rebel  cruiser 
Alabama  as  being  somewhere  in  this  vicinity.  Although  there  seems 
but  little  to  confirm  these  rumors,  yet  I  would  caution  you  to  increased 
vigilance  and  circumspection  in  approaching  strange  vessels,  lest  the 
reports  should  prove  more  correct  than  seems  probable. 

I  enclose  a  memorandum  of  information  gleaned  from  the  corre¬ 
spondence  of  the  acting  consul-general  at  Havana  relative  to  vessels 
engaged  in  running  the  blockade. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Captain  Wm.  M.  Walker,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Steamer  JDe  Soto .

Correspondence  regarding  the  firing  upon  British  schooner  Dream ,  off 
the  coast  of  Cuba,  April  °38,  1863. 

Letter  of  enquiry  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  II.  S. 

Navy. 

Navy  Department,  May  1%,  1863. 

Sir:  Lord  Lyons  lias  invited  the  attention  of  the  Department  of 
State  to  the  representations  of  the  master  of  the  British  schooner 
Dr  ’■ earn  that  his  vessel  was  repeatedly  fired  into  by  a  gunboat  supposed 
to  belong  to  the  United  States.  The  circumstances  are  narrated  as 
follows: 

To-day  (April  28,  Caracoa,  Cuba),  we  were  fired  at  five  times  by  a  Northern  gun¬ 
boat,  in  addition  to  two  shots  across  our  bow;  one  of  the  shots  was  of  grape  and 
canister  and  penetrated  our  rigging.  It  occurred  about  1  to  1:30  o’clock  and  we 
were  compelled  to  put  in  here  for  safety.  The  gunboat  is  now  about  1  mile  off  and 
watching  our  movements.  The  firing  at  us  was  done  within  2  miles  from  the  shore. 
*  *  *  The  gunboat  is  a  small  sailing  pilot  boat  with  one  gun  amidships,  apparently 
an  18  or  24  pounder — more  probably  the  latter.  She  is  now  lying  off  and  on,  within 
about  a  mile  of  this  port. 

Please  enquire  if  the  act  complained  of  was  committed  by  one  of 
the  vessels  of  your  squadron,  and  if  so,  furnish  the  Department  with 
a  report  of  the  circumstances.  The  Dream  had  left  Havana  that 
morning. 

You  will  be  careful  to  enjoin  upon  those  to  whom  you  entrust  com¬ 
missions,  and  especially  to  those  in  charge  of  tenders,  a  strict  observ¬ 
ance  of  the  rights  of  neutrals.  Inexperienced  and  often  uninformed 
as  these  officers  are  of  the  important  trusts  committed  to  them,  they 
must  carefully  abstain  from  trespassing  upon  the  jurisdiction  of  other 
powers  or  infringing  on  those  principles  which  the  laws  of  nations  have 
well  established  and  defined.  No  one  should  be  permitted  to  have  a 
distinct  command  without  a  copy  of  the  instructions  of  the  18th  of 
August,  1862,  and  he  must  also  understand  that  it  is  not  allowable  to 
blockade  a  neutral  port. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theod.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  report  of  Acting  Ensign 
Williams,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  schooner  Annie. 

Nos.  178.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West ,  May  36,  1863. 

Sir:  Your  letter  of  the  12th  instant,  relative  to  a  complaint  made 
by  the  master  of  the  British  schooner  Dream ,  has  been  received. 

I  enclose  herewith  copies  of  all  the  papers  in  my  possession  relat¬ 
ing  to  the  transaction.  The  accounts  in  the  Diario  de  la  Marina  are 
characterized  by  the  exaggeration  natural  to  those  who  sympathize 
with  our  enemies;  and  that  of  Captain  Simpkins  is  probably  still 
further  colored  by  the  consciousness  of  an  intention  (temporarily  frus¬ 
trated  by  the  Annie)  of  materially  assisting  those  enemies.  The  report 
of  Acting  Ensign  Williams  is  clear  and  conclusive,  and  seems  to  have 
been  satisfactory  to  the  Spanish  officers. 

Mr.  Williams  is  a  zealous  and  capable  officer,  but  seems,  in  the 
ardor  of  the  chase,  to  have  pushed  his  belligerent  rights  to  the  extreme 
limit;  and  to  avoid  the  possibility  of  any  future  complications  I  have 
directed  him  not  to  extend  his  cruising  beyond  the  southern  edge  of 
the  Florida  Reefs. 

The  Annie  is  armed  with  a  light  12-pounder  howitzer,  which  has 
been  magnified  by  the  emotions  of  Captain  Simpkins  in  the  exact  pro¬ 
portion  that  he  has  diminished  the  distance  from  land  at  the  time. 

I  enclose  a  pamphlet  of  squadron  instructions  (as  furnished  to  every 
vessel  under  my  command),  with  two  of  the  articles  marked. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg .  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Williams,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  schooner  Annie. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Annie, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  May  10,  1863. 

Sir:  I  herewith  respectfully  submit  the  following  statement  in 
regard  to  firing  on  an  English  schooner  while  cruising  on  the  coast  of 
Cuba: 

On  the  28th  April,  at  11:30  a.  m.,  made  a  schooner  standing  to  the 
W.  N.  W.;  stood  for  her  to  the  westward  until  1  p.  m.,  when  she 
showed  British  colors,  upon  which  we  set  our  ensign  and  fired  a  shot 
across  her  bow.  The  schooner  simply  dipped  her  colors  and  kept  on, 
when  I  fired  another  shot,  upon  which  she  kept  off  dead  before  the 


428 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


wind  and  took  no  notice  of  us,  after  which  fired  five  shot  at  her,  all 
striking  close  by;  and  one,  exploding-  close  to  her,  parted  his  main  sheet. 
When  judging  him  to  be  about  miles  from  the  land  and  being  very 
cautious  not  to  exceed  my  limit,  I  hauled  off  and  the  schooner  con¬ 
tinued  in  and  anchored. 

At  the  time  of  hauling  off,  the  Morro  Castle  bore  E.  i  N.  true  and 
table-land  of  Mariel  S.  by  W.  J  W.,  making  my  position,  at  the  least, 
distant  3^  miles  from  land.  On  the  29th  April  at  2  p.  m.,  having  had 
light  winds  all  day,  I  was  boarded  by  an  officer  from  the  Spanish  gun¬ 
boat  General  Lejo ,  he  wishing  to  know  what  the  firing  was  yesterday, 
the  name  of  the  vessel,  and  also  my  name. 

I  showed  the  officer  my  position  on  the  chart  and  explained  the 
cause  of  the  firing.  He  left  apparently  satisfied,  and  requested  I  would 
not  fire  within  6  miles  of  his  coast.  Through  the  night  calm,  and  at 
10  p.  m.  was  boarded  by  a  boat  from  the  Spanish  gunboat  Neptuna , 
he  wishing  to  know  whether  this  vessel  was  Federal  or  a  Confederate 
man-of-war,,  and  upon  my  handing  him  my  papers  to  look  at  he 
refused,  saying  he  only  wished  to  know  whether  Federal  or  a  Confed¬ 
erate  man-of-war,  and  then  left  me,  also  requesting  me  not  fire  within 
6  miles  of  the  coast,  and  the  steamer  then  stood  away  to  the  south¬ 
eastward. 

On  the  forenoon  of  the  1st  May  I  was  hailed  by  a  Spanish  gunboat 
(supposed  to  be  the  General  Lejo).  He  hailing,  wished  to  know  if 
that  was  the  Annie,  Captain  Williams,  and  on  being  answered  in  the 
affirmative,  he  replied  “Good  morning,  captain,”  and  stood  on  to  the 
southward.  The  above  is  a  correct  statement  of  the  chase  of  the 
schooner  and  my  communications  with  the  Spanish  gunboats. 

1  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  S.  Williams, 

Acting  Ensign ,  Commanding. 

Commander  Robert  Handy, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Ship  Dale.

facts,  relative  to  the  condition  of  vessels  under  my  command  and  the

The  great  number  of  prizes  brought  in,  although  gratifying  as  an 
e\  idence  of  vigilance  and  activity  on  the  part  of  the  cruising  vessels, 
ought  rather  to  be  considered  as  indicative  of  the  brisk  trade  carried 
on  along  this  coast  and  of  the  importance  of  enabling  me  to  break  it 
up  entirely. 

As  matters  now  stand.  I  am  unable  to  guard  the  coast  as  I  deem 
necessary,  and  1  would  therefore  most  urgently  request  the  Depart¬ 
ment  to  send  me  at  once  three  steamers  and  two  barks,  all  of  light 
draft,  great  speed,  and  heavy  armament,  besides  a  flagship. 

The  Magnolia  and  Ethan  Allen  can  always  be  employed  to  advan¬ 
tage  on  this  station,  provided  they  are  ini  good  condition,  but  the 
delay  in  recovering  their  services  will  be  injurious,  and  in  the  mean¬ 
time  I  would  desire  others  in  their  places. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey,

U.  S.  Flagship  St.  Lawrence, 

Key  West,  April  29,  1863. 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  is  ready  for  sea 
you  will  proceed  first  to  within  sight  of  the  entrance  to  Havana, 
thence  along  the  coast  of  Cuba  to  the  westward,  keeping  outside  of 
Spanish  jurisdiction,  as  far  as  Bahia  Honda;  from  there  you  will  stand 
to  the  northward  and  westward,  giving  the  Tortugas  a  berth  of  some 
50  or  60  miles,  and  continue  on  in  the  direction  of  Mobile.  Your 
ultimate  cruising  ground  will  be  from  40  to  100  miles  to  the  southward 
and  eastward  of  Mobile  Bar,  where  it  is  believed  you  will  be  most 
likely  to  pick  up  vessels  that  may  have  succeeded  in  evading  the 
blockade  at  that  place,  or  that  may  be  waiting  for  a  favorable  oppor¬ 
tunity  to  get  in.  I  would  suggest  that  you  endeavor  each  morning  to

find  yourself  about  100  miles  from  the  bar,  and  that  you  work  in  to 
within  about  40;  but  on  no  account  will  you  show  your  vessel  within 
sight  of  the  blockading  fleet  or  of  the  land,  unless  it  be  in  chase. 

The  De  Soto  is  cruising  between  latitude  25°  and  29°  N.,  and  lon¬

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Rogers ,  U.  S.  Wavy ,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  S.  Huntsville ,  regarding  the  capture  by  that  vessel  of  the 

Confederate  sloop  Minnie. 

U.  S.  S.  Huntsville, 

Key  West ,  April  30,  1863. 

Sir:  In  compliance  with  your  order,  I  Avould  respectfully  state  that 
while  lying  at  anchor  off  Charlotte  Harbor  on  the  6th  instant  a  sail 
was  reported  to  me  before  daylight.  I  immediately  got  underway, 
went  in  chase,  and  in  about  thirty  minutes  captured  the  Confederate 
sloop  Minnie ,  it  being  not  quite  daylight  at  the  time. 

I  put  an  officer  and  crew  on  board,  and  as  day  broke  discovered  two 
schooners  inshore  of  us,  6  to  8  miles  distant,  and  standing  not  toward 
us,  but  toward  the  land. 

Supposing  them  to  be  blockade  runners,  I  immediate^  gave  chase 
and  in  the  course  of  an  hour  came  up  with  the  U.  S.  schooners  Beau¬ 
regard  and  Stonewall ,  neither  of  which  were  in  sight  at  the  time  of 
the  capture  of  the  Minnie. 

The  truth  of  this  statement,  I  believe,  you  are  aware  of,  being  on 
board  at  the  time.  It  can  also  be  substantiated  by  the  affidavits  of  one 
or  two  of  the  officers  of  the  ship. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  C.  Rogers, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Huntsville. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron,  Key  West ,  Fla.

Information  received  from  William  M.  Martin ,  mechanic ,  belonging  to 
the  Confederate  ironworks ,  Columbus ,  6ra. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Port  Royal, 

Apalachicola  Bay ,  J/ay  -A  1863. 

Sir:  William  M.  Martin  reports  that  he  came  from  Columbus,  Ga., 
which  place  he  left  April  22.  There  are  not  any  troops  at  Columbus. 
An  ironclad  vessel  is  being  built  there;  her  length  is  120  feet,  depth 
from  10  to  12  feet;  her  frame  is  all  up,  and  were  at  work  plank¬ 
ing  her  outside  and  ceiling  her;  boilers  are  in.  She  is  to  be  a  pro¬ 
peller;  her  engines  are  from  the  old  river  steamer  Times.  The  mill 
for  rolling  out  the  iron  is  in  progress  of  construction;  they  have  but 
little  iron  on  hand  to  use.  She  can  not  be  ready  before  November 
next.  She  is  built  of  green  pine  timber;  frame  timber  1  foot  square. 
From  Columbus  he  went  overland  to  Chattahoochee;  while  there  he 
visited  the  rebel  gunboat  Chattahoochee  on  or  about  the  24th  ultimo. 
She  has  six  guns  mounted,  broadside  guns  6-inch  bore.  Saw  only 
three  or  four  officers,  and  about  forty-five  men.  Ship  about  100  feet 
long,  two  engines,  cylinders  36-inch  bore  and  24-inch  stroke;  two 
propellers  7  feet  diameter;  three-masted,  two  square  sail  yards,  one 
on  foremast  and  one  on  mainmast.  Hull  painted  black  and  has  a 
bowsprit.  The  general  belief  of  the  people  in  that  vicinty  is  that  the 
Chattahoochee  will  never  come  down  the  river;  one  of  her  own  crew 
made  the  same  assertion.  There  is  a  regiment  of  troops  at  Chatta¬ 
hoochee.  The  river  is  not  very  well  fortified,  as  far  as  he  could  learn, 
but  is  obstructed  with  two  hulls  of  old  river  steamers,  and  rocks, 
spiles,  and  two  chains  stretched  across  the  river.  One  hundred  con¬ 
scripts  are  guarding  the  obstructions.  There  is  quite  a  strong  Union 
sentiment  among  the  workmen  and  farmers  in  and  about  Columbus, 
which  place  is  the  great  depot  for  the  manufacturing  of  arms  and 
clothing.  He  has  been,  a  resident  of  that  city  (Columbus)  about  four 
years,  and  he  well  knows  that  there  is  a  strong  Union  feeling  with 
the  people  there  and  in  the  surrounding  country.  He  saw  no  troops 
on  his  way  down  to  Apalachicola  after  leaving  Chattahoochee,  as  he 
avoided  them.  On  or  about  the  10th  of  April  the  women  turned  out 
en  masse  and  broke  open  the  stores  for  food  and  clothing.  Provisions 
were  very  scarce  and  at  very  high  prices.  The  troops  wrote  to  their 
wives  and  families  that  they  will  soon  lay  down  their  arms  and  give 
up  fighting  if  the  rebel  Government  does  not  provide  for  their  fam¬ 
ilies,  and  the  general  belief  of  the  troops  is  that  the  South  will  be 
whipped  eventually.  He  visited  Fosterville,  Tenn.,  on  or  about  the 
10th  of  last  March,  at  which  place  were  the  pickets  of  the  rebel  Gen¬ 
eral  Joe  J ohnston’s  army,  at  which  place  he  made  an  effort  to  pass  to  the 
Union  lines,  but  was  checked  by  the  rebel  pickets.  The  general  feel¬ 
ing  in  Tennessee  was,  the  hopes  that  the  Union  Army  would  again 
advance  and  hold  Shelbyville  and  the  adjacent  country.  Even  at 
Atlanta,  Ga.,  many  were  praying  that  the  Union  Army  would  come 
there.  There  was  a  bread  riot  at  Atlanta  on  the  day  of  his  arrival 
there,  the  women  turning  out  and  sacking  the  stores  for  food  and 
clothing;  this  was  in  March.  After  leaving  Chattahoochee  he  traveled 
about  35  miles  by  land  to  a  place  called  Canida  Creek;  passing-  through 
the  country,  very  few  men  were  to  be  seen,  but  plenty  of  females, 
who  seemed  to  be  suffering  for  clothing  and  food.  At  Canida  Creek 
he  made  a  bargain  with  two  fishermen,  who  had  come  up  with  fish,  to 
carry  him  to  Apalachicola,  as  he  represented  to  them  that  he  was

438 


desirous  to  go  there  to  purchase  steel.  He  left  Cam  da  Creek  this 
morning  at  5:30  a.  m.  and  arrived  here  this  afternoon. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  U.  Morris, 

.  ,  .  .  Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Admiral  Iheodorus  Bailey,

Report  of  Feting  Master  Sherrill ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 
bark  Roebuck ,  regarding  the  capture  by  that  vessel  of  the  British 
schooner  Emm, a  Amelia. 

U.  S.  Bark  Koebuck, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay ,  May  2,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  of  the  seizure  this 
day  of  the  British  schooner  Emma  Amelia,  85|f  tons,  Thomas  Best, 
master,  while  attempting  to  run  the  blockade  at  this  place.  At  day¬ 
light  a  sail  was  discovered  in  the  offing  steering  E.  N.  E.  for  the  bar 
at  the  entrance  of  this  bay,  and  distant  from  it  about  3  miles,  the 
wind  at  the  time  being  light,  from  the  northwest.  1  immediately  dis¬ 
patched  two  armed  boats,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  K.  F.  Cook  and 
Acting  Ensign  G.  M.  Pulsipher,  in  pursuit,  and  as  soon  as  they  were 
discovered  by  the  schooner  she  changed  her  course  to  the  southward 
and  set  square  sail.  At  8  a.  m.  the  boats  boarded  her,  the  bar  bearing 
E.  N.  E.,  distant  about  7  miles.  She  had  no  colors  set,  though  English 
and  American  were  found  on  board.  The  master  said  he  was  bound  to 
New  Orleans,  and  had  been  standing  in  to  make  the  land  to  correct  his 
reckoning.  The  course  he  was  steering  and  position  were  deemed  by 
me  sufficient  reasons  for  seizing  her  as  a  prize,  her  papers  being 
apparently  correct,  and  I  shall  send  her  under  charge  of  Acting  Ensign 
G.  M.  Pulsipher  and  a  prize  crew  of  four  men,  with  her  former  mas¬ 
ter  and  two  men,  to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

I  enclose  herewith  a  complete  list  or  muster  roll  of  officers  and  crew 
of  this  vessel  at  time  of  capture.  No  other  vessels  in  sight.  Cargo 
consists  of  wines,  flour,  etc. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Sherrill, 

Acting  .Master,  JJ.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  U.  S.  bark  Roebuck. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 

transfer  of  fag. 


No.  158.] 


U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West ,  May  5 ,  1863. 


Sik:  I  have  to  report  that  the  frigate  St.  Lawrence  being  now  ready 
to  return  north,  agreeably  to  the  orders  of  the  Department,  I  have 
directed  Commander  Colhoun  to  proceed  with  her  to  Boston,  Mass. 

In  consequence  of  this  I  have  this  day  transferred  my  flag  to  the 
steamer  ALagnolia ,  inasmuch  as  the  condition  of  her  boiler  renders  her 
incapable  of  cruising,  and  I  am  advised  that  her  new  boiler  will 
“probably  be  ready”  about  the  middle  of  June.  As,  however  the 
internal  arrangements  of  this  vessel  will  not  admit  of  my  living  on 
board  of  her '  without  extensive  alterations  (involving  an  expense 
which  would  not  be  justified  by  the  temporary  nature  of  the  service), 
I  have  established  an  office  in  the  storehouse  on  shore  for  the  trans¬ 
action  of  business  until  the  arrival  of  another  flagship. 

I  have  also  ordered  the  bark  Ethan  Allen  to  Boston,  Mass.,  for 
repairs,  the  necessity  for  which  was  shown  by  the  reports  enclosed  in 
my  letter  of  April  28. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Rogers ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  S.  Huntsville ,  regarding  the  chase  of  a  steamer  supposed 

to  be  the  Cuba ,  from  LLavana. 

U.  S.  S.  Huntsville, 

Off  Lake  Ocala ,  May  5,  1863. 

Sir:  By  the  Hendrick  Hudson  I  have  the  honor  to  send  a  report  of 
my  cruise  to  this  date. 

In  accordance  with  your  orders  I  touched  at  Havana,  and  from  the 
consul  learned  that  one  or  two  steamers  were  nearly  ready  for  sea,  and 
that  one  of  them,  the  Cuba,  would  sail  that  same  night. 

This  decided  me,  after  obeying  your  orders  as  to  running  down  the 
coast  of  Cuba,  to  steer  directly  for  this  place. 

On  leaving  Havana  a  lead-colored  blockade-running  steamer  followed 
me  out,  but  as  we  watched  her  closely  she  finally  returned  to  the  harbor. 

On  the  second  morning  out,  and  when  about  halfway  between  Tor- 
tugas  and  St.  Andrew’s,  at  daybreak  we  discovered  a  white  steamer, 
without  masts,  and  answering  in  every  respect  to  the  Cuba,  steering 
the  same  course  as  ourselves. 

We  immediately  gave  chase,  and  for  two  or  three  hours  had  every 
prospect  of  capturing  her,  as  we  steadily  overhauled  her,  having  a 
strong  breeze  in  our  favor;  but  toward  noon  it  became  calm  and  she 
gradually  outsteamed  us,  and  after  an  exciting  chase  of  140  miles  we 
lost  sight  of  her  at  dark. 

I  then  made  all  dispatch  for  this  place,  hoping  that  I  might  again 
have  the  good  luck  to  intercept  her. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  435 

I  shall  remain  here  long  enough  to  ascertain  whether  this  is  her  des¬ 
tination,  when  I  shall  proceed  to  my  station  oil'  Mobile. 

Hoping  that  my  next  effort  may  be  more  successful, 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  C.  Rogers, 

Acting  I  olunteer  Lieutenant ,  Comdg.  U.  S.  S.  Huntsville. 
Acting  Bear- Admiral  Tiieodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron ,  Key  1 Vest,  Fla.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey , 
TJ.  S.  Navy ,  forwarding  information  regarding  the  channel  for  mails 
from  Europe  to  the  Southern  States. 

Navy  Department,  May  7,  1863 

Sir:  The  following  is  an  extract  from  a  dispatch,  dated  the  18th 
ultimo,  received  by  the  Secretary  of  State  from  the  U.  S.  consul  at 
Liverpool: 

A  man  who  professes  to  know,  and  who  has  given  me  information  which  I  have 
found  correct,  tells  me  a  very  valuable  rebel  mail  was  sent  from  here  on  the  14th  of 
March,  via  New  York  and  Nassau.  He  says  from  Nassau  it  is  to  be  taken  in  Adderly 
&  Co.’s  boat  to  Bumany  [Bernini],  on  the  northwest  part  of  Abaco,  and  from  there 
over  to  Mosquito  Inlet,  on  the  coast  of  Florida,  thence  up  the  Indian  River  to 
[New]  Smyrna,  etc.  Now,  I  do  not  know  enough  about  these  localities  to  decide 
upon  this  plan,  but  feel  it  to  be  my  duty  to  report  it  for  what  it  is  worth,  the  more 
so  from  the  fact  that  I  learn  this  is  to  be  one  of  the  regular  mail  channels  between  this 
country  and  the  South.  There  can  be  no  doubt  but  what  mails  are  constantly  being 
carried  by  way  of  New  York. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  Theo.  Batley,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Willcomb ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U  S.  S. 

Stars  and  Stripes ,  regarding  the  escape  of  a  schooner  off  St.  Marks , 
Fla. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

Off  St.  Marks,  May  7 ,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  morning  of  the  5th  instant,  at  8:30  a  m. ,  the  fog  light¬ 
ened  up,  and  we  discovered  a  side-wheeled,  schooner-rigged  steamer 
in  the  S.  S.  W.,  about  9  miles  off.  I  immediately  got  underway  and 
gave  chase,  but  soon  perceived  that  she  was  leaving  this  vessel  very 
fast.  1  chased  her  until  11:30  a.  m.,  when  I  lost  sight  of  her  about 
30  miles  S.  S.  W.  from  St.  Marks  light-house.  We  carried  34  pounds 
of  steam  and  were  making  70  revolutions.  The  chase  must  have  been 
going  at  the  rate  of  14  miles  per  hour.  We  were  doing  all  we  could 
to  get  up  near  enough  to  give  her  a  shot,  but  could  not,  and  I  had  the 
mortification  to  see  her  disappear. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  L.  Willcomb, 

Acting  Afaster ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron , 

Flagship  St.  Lawrence ,  Key  West,  Fla. 


Correspondence  regarding  the  license  of  the  schooner  Sea  Lion ,  captured 

at  Mobile ,  May  9 ,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  copy  of  license. 

No.  253.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  July  1863. 

Sir:  The  schooner  Sea  Lion  was  lately  captured  coming  out  of  the 
port  of  Mobile  loaded  with  cotton  and  sent  to  this  port  for  adjudica¬ 
tion.  She  exhibited  at  the  time  of  her  capture  a  license  to  bring 
cotton  to  New  Orleans  from  a  Mr.  Dennison,  who  appeared  to  be  a 
special  agent  of  the  Treasury  Department.  1  send  herewith  enclosed, 
marked  254,  a  copy  of  this  paper.  I  am  credibly  informed  that  Mr. 
Denison  has  answered,  in  reply  to  the  question  whether  this  license 
was  intended  to  apply  to  blockade  ports  as  well  as  to  bring  the  cotton 
through  the  military  lines  by  land,  that  the  license  was  granted  in 
pursuance  of  an  order  of  General  Banks,  and  that  he  did  not  think  it 
necessary  to  enquire  how  the  property  should  come  to  New  Orleans. 
Under  this  license,  it  seems,  the  favored  parties  at  New  Orleans  sent 
their  agent  to  Mobile,  bought  the  cotton,  had  it  shipped  in  the  name 
of  a  Mobile  firm,  and  consigned  by  the  papers  to  aMobilian  at  Havana. 
When  captured,  it  was  claimed  that  the  vessel  was  really  going  to  the 
mouth  of  the  Mississippi  River  or  to  New  Orleans  for  the  orders  of 
Brott,  Davis,  and  Shons,  the  parties  named  in  the  license. 

This  is  not  only  trading  with  the  enemy,  pure  and  simple,  but  it  is 
trading  with  the  enemy  through  a  closely  blockaded  port.  It  seems 
to  me  that  if  this  action  is  sustained,  it  amounts  to  a  virtual  abandon¬ 
ment  of  the  blockade  of  all  the  ports  to  which  these  or  other  favored 
parties  may  choose  to  trade,  and  that  it  possibly  has  some  importance 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


437 


in  connection  with  our  foreign  relations.  I  have  thought  it  a  matter 
proper  to  be  represented  to  you. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

[Enclosure.] 

Custom-House,  New  Orleans, 

Collector’’  s  Office ,  Februiry  16,  1863. 

The  U.  S.  military  and  other  authorities  at  New  Orleans  permit 
cotton  to  be  received  here  from  beyond  the  U.  S.  military  lines,  and 
such  cotton  is  exempt  from  seizure  or  confiscation.  An  order  is  in 
my  hands  from  Major-General  Banks  approving  and  directing  this 
policy.  The  only  condition  imposed  is  that  cotton  or  other  produce 
must  not  be  bought  with  specie. 

All  cotton  or  other  produce  brought  hither  from  the  Confederate 
lines  by  Brott,  Davis  and  Shons  will  not  be  interfered  with  in  any 
manner,  and  they  can  ship  it  direct  to  any  foreign  or  domestic  port. 

[k-  s.]  _  George  S.  Dennison, 

Special  Agent  of  the  Treasury  Department  and 

Acting  Collector  of  Customs.

D.  G.  Farragut,

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico,  May  If  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  inform  you  that  last  evening,  being  in  20  fathoms  of 
water  and  in  latitude  29°  40',  longitude  87°  37',  I  seized,  for  attempted 
violation  of  the  blockade,  the  schooner  Sea  Bird,  of  Havana,  D.  M. 
Allen,  master.  She  is  American  built,  was  sailing  under  a  provisional 
certificate  of  registry,  dated  April  28, 1863,  signed  John  V.  Crawford, 
acting  consul-general  in  Cuba,  and  sealed  with  the  seal  of  her  Brit- 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  439 


tannic  Majesty’s  consulate  in  Cuba  and  was  cleared  from  Havana  for 
Matamoras. 

From  the  moment  we  could  discern  her  she  was  standing  N.  by 
W.,  with  the  wind  from  W.  S.  W. 

In  reply  to  my  hail  her  master  stated  that  he  was  “bound  to 
Mobile.” 


Her  papers  are  incomplete;  she  has  no  log  book;  was  far  out  of  her 
track,  and  accordingly  I  have  ordered  her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

It  is  proper  I  should  add  that  for  the  better  security  of  the  Sea  Bird 
and  the  preservation  of  her  cargo  I  took  out  of  her  6  demijohns  of 
spirits,  said  to  belong  to  her  crew,  which  I  shall  deliver  to  the  prize 
commissioners  on  my  arrival  at  Key  West.

Oliver  S.  Breese  on  the  J  6th  of  May  in  the  latitude  of  28°  N. ,  longitude

At  4  p.  m.  a  sail  was  reported  from  the  masthead  standing  to  the 
eastward,  the  wind  being  W.  S.  W.  at  that  time.  We  being  to  the 
leewaid  other,  distant  12  miles,  I  immediately  stood  in  for  the  shore

shore,  and  lowered  our  sails,  sent  topmasts  down,  and  let  go  anchor. 
Consequently  the  sail  did  not  see  us  until  she  was  within  3  miles  of  us'. 
At  6:30  she  saw  us  and  closehauled  to  the  wind,  making  all  sail,  i

Report  of  Acting  T  olunteer  Lieutenant  Couthouy ,  TJ  S.  Navy,  regard¬ 
ing  trade  with  Matamoras ,  Mexico. 

13  West  Cedar  Street, 

Boston ,  May  16,  1863. 

Sir:  In  compliance  with  your  verbal  instructions  of  12th  instant,  I 
have  the  honor  to  transmit  herewith  a  copy  of  a  communication 
addressed  by  me  on  19th  March,  1862,  to  Flag-Officer  W.  W. 
McKean,  at  that  time  commanding  the  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading 
Squadron,  in  relation  to  the  systematic  abuse  of  the  privileges  of  a 
neutral  port  by  vessels  clearing  at  Northern  ports  for  Matamoras  with 
cargoes  whose  true  and  ultimate  destination  was  Brownsville,  in 

rn  / 

lexas. 

There  can,  I  tnink,  be  no  moral  and  scarcely  a  legal  doubt  that 
nine-tenths  of  the  cargoes  which  within  the  past  twelve  months  have 
gone  up  the  Rio  Grande,  nominally  consigned  to  merchants  in  Mata¬ 
moras,  were,  in  fact,  destined  to  supply  the  rebels  in  Texas,  and  were 
securely  stored  in  the  warehouses  of  Brownsville  within  twenty-four 
hours  after  their  simulated  sale  on  the  Mexican  side  of  the  river. 

A  residence  of  four  years  in  Brownsville,  from  October,  1849,  to 
November,  1853,  and  my  position  as  presiding  officer  of  the  branch  of 
the  Commercial  and  Agricultural  Bank  of  Texas  there  established, 
enabled  me  to  become  well  acquainted  not  only  with  all  the  leading 
merchants  and  traders  on  both  sides  of  the  Rio  Grande  as  high  up  as 
Monterey,  but  with  the  whole  commerce  with  Mexico,  whether  of 
exports  or  imports,  and  I  can  not  recall  a  single  instance  in  all  that 
time  of  a  vessel  arriving  at  Matamoras  with  a  cargo  of  provisions, 
groceries,  and  other  supplies  of  such  magnitude  and  value  as  within 
the  last  few  months  has  found  its  way  thither  almost  weekly,  osten¬ 
sibly  for  Mexican  consumption. 

Nor  can  I  remember  the  importation  during  the  whole  of  those  four 
years  of  so  much  as  a  solitary  cargo  of  provisions  or  other  supplies  in 
an  English  bottom.  The  whole  of  the  pseudo  Mexican  trade  by  the 
channel  of  the  Rio  Grande,  carried  on  so  extensively  by  English  ves 
sels  at  the  present'time,  has  its  explanation  and  origin  in  the  market 
opened  up  in  Texas  by  the  necessities  of  that  and  adjacent  States  in 
arms  against  the  Federal  Government,  consequent  upon  the  blockade 
of  their  maritime  ports.  Matamoras  is  but  the  Mexican  synonym  of 
Brownsville  so  far  as  this  trade  is  concerned.  The  merchants  and  the 
warehouses  of  the  one  city  are  those  of  the  other  also. 

From  the  garita  on  the  Matamoras  bank  of  the  river,  alongside 
which  a  vessel  may  lie  and  go  through  the  forms  of  a  sale  of  her  cargo 


442 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQtTADKOiSf. 


in  Mexico,  it  is  but  a  stone’s  cast  to  Stillman’s  levee  in  Brownsville, 
on  which  it  may  with  impunity  be  landed  immediately  after  by  the 
Texan  purchaser.  I  have  been  tauntingly  informed  by  persons 
engaged  in  the  traffic  that  this  was  the  course  of  procedure,  and  have 
no  doubt  they  spoke  the  truth,  although  owing  to  the  subtlety  of  the 
precautions  taken  to  avoid  violating  the  letter  of  international  law,  it 
may  be  very  difficult  to  establish  the  fact  in  a  majority  of  the  cases  of 
vessels  captured  and  sent  in  for  adjudication  by  our  cruisers,  under 
suspicion  of  using  the  trade  with  Matamoras  as  a  cloak  to  cover  the 
real  object  of  furnishing  supplies  to  Texas.  I  can  not  flatter  myself 
that  either  the  facts  or  suggestions  herewith  submitted  to  the  Depart¬ 
ment  have  the  merit  of  novelty,  yet  as  they  are  the  result  of  personal 
observation,  and  in  the  opinion  of  Francis  H.  Upton,  esq.,  counsel  for 
the  captors  in  the  case  of  the  Peterhoff ,  not  without  importance  in 
their  bearings  on  the  question  of  the  true  character  and  destination  of 
her  cargo,  I  trust  to  be  excused  for  occupying  so  much  of  its  valuable 
time  with  them,  and  remain, 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jos.  P.  Couthouy, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington  City ,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Captain  Walker ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 
regarding  tl\e  "burning  of  the  Confederate  steamer  Cuba. 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico,  May  18,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  yesterday  at  noon  discov¬ 
ered  the  smoke  of  a  steamer  and  stood  for  it.  Soon  after  we  made 
the  steamer  and  pressed  after  her  to  the  very  extent  of  our  power.  At 
6  p.  m.  she  stopped  and  two  boats  pushed  off  from  her,  carrying  her 
officers  and  crew.  I  immediately  lowered  and  took  out  of  the  steam¬ 
er’s  boats  her  principal  officers,  as  a  security  for  the  lives  of  my  own 
men,  and  then  boarded  the  steamer. 

As  soon  as  the  boats  had  got  alongside  of  her  the  flames  burst  out, 
as  I  had  anticipated,  when  I  hoisted  the  recall.  Afterwards,  having 
had  the  assurance  Jhat  there  was  no  danger  of  her  blowing  up,  1  went 
near  enough  to  the  burning  ship  to  lead  our  hose  on  board,  but  all 
efforts  to  suppress  the  flames  were  unavailing,  and  by  sunset  the 
famous  Confederate  ship  Cuba  sank  beneath  the  waters  of  the  Gulf,  in 
latitude  28°  47',  longitude  87°  58'. 

It  is  estimated  upon  reliable  authority  that  the  cargo  of  the  Cuba 
was  worth  in  Havana  nearly  $400,000,  and  if  landed  in  Alabama  would 
have  been  worth  from  a  million  to  a  million  and  a  quarter.  I  have  her 
officers  and  crew  on  board,  and  shall  deliver  them  to  the  custody  of  the 
authorities  at  Key  West. 

1  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  M.  Walker, 
Captain ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Secretary  of  the  Navy, 

Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Rogers ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  com¬ 
manding  IT.  S.  S.  Huntsville ,  regarding  the  capture  ly  that  vessel  of 
the  Spanish  steamer  Union. 

.  U.  S.  S.  Huntsville, 

Lat.  27°  55'  N,  Long.  85°  13'  W.,  May  If  1863. 
Sir:  Under  the  above  date  and  position  I  have  the  honor  to  report 
to  you  the  capture  of  the  Spanish  steamer  Union ,  of  and  from  Havana, 
with  a  clearance  for  Matamoras,  but  from  his  position,  which  is  some 
260  miles  to  northeastward  of  its  proper  course  (also  steering  north- 
erly  when  discovered),  as  well  as  from  information  gained  and  packages 
found  on  board,  directed  to  parties  in  Mobile,  undoubtedly  bound  to 
the  latter  port. 

This  opinion  is  confirmed  by  the  statements  of  prisoners  on  board 
the  Huntsville ,  recently  taken  from  the  Confederate  steamer  Cuba, 
which  vessel  I  chased  100  miles  to  southward  of  Mobile,  she  escaping 
under  cover  of  the  night;  but  on  the  following  morning,  being  hard 
pressed  by  the  U.  S.  S.  De  Soto,  her  captain  and  owner  set  fire  to  her 
and  took  to  their  boats. 

With  the  above  facts,  taken  in  connection  with  the  absence  of  some 
and  irregularity  of  other  documents  essential  to  proving  the  honesty 
of  her  voyage,  I  deemed  it  my  duty  to  make  a  prize  of  her  and  send 
her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

She  is  a  small  tugboat  of  115  tons,  built  in  Philadelphia  two  years 
since,  and  recently  used  in  Havana  for  towing  purposes,  Her  crew 
consists  of  11  persons,  chiefly  Spanish,  and  3  passengers,  probably 
Americans.  Her  cargo  an  assorted  one  and  of  considerable  value. 

Please  find  enclosed  muster  roll  of  officers  and  crew  on  board  at 
date  of  capture. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  C.  Rogers, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

company.

mails.  From  another  prisoner  I  learned  A.  W.  Babcock  was  seen  by

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Rogers ,  U.  8.  JYavy,  command¬ 
ing  JJ.  8.  8.  Huntsville ,  regarding  the  cruise  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Huntsville, 

Key  West ,  May  88,  1863. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  my  cruise: 

Leaving  Key  West,  I  touched  at  Havana  and  there  learned  that  one 
or  two  steamers  were  ready  for  sea  with  contraband  cargoes,  one  of 
which  was  the  Cuba. 

I  therefore  proceeded  to  my  station  with  all  dispatch,  after  obeying 
your  orders  as  to  running  down  the  coast  of  Cuba. 

On  the  second  day  discovered  a  suspicious  steamer  standing  north¬ 
erly,  to  which  we  gave  chase,  but  after  following  her  140  miles  she 
escaped  by  superior  speed. 

I  have  since  learned  she  was  the  General  Buckner ,  from  Havana  for 
Mobile. 

Off  Lake  Ocala  found  the  Hendrick  Hudson ,  with  whom  I  com¬ 
municated. 

This  place  can  hardly  be  one  of  much  use  as  a  port  of  entryq  being 
a  mere  inlet  on  the  beach  much  exposed  to  the  sea,  with  the  surf  con¬ 
stantly  breaking,  and  apparently  no  depth  of  water. 

Leaving  here,  I  steered  to  southeastward  of  Mobile  and  there  cruised 
until  want  of  coal  obliged  me  to  leave. 

On  May  13,  about  100  miles  to  southeast  of  Mobile,  fell  in  with  the 
Confederate  schooner  A.  J.  Hodge ,  of  Mobile,  from  Nassau,  for  the 
former  port  with  an  assorted  cargo.  Made  prize  of  him  and  sent  him 
to  Key  West  for  adjudication  in  charge  of  a  prize  officer  and  crew. 

On  May  16  again  made  a  suspicious  steamer  and  gave  chase,  over¬ 
hauling  her  rapidly,  when  she  threw  overboard  cargo,  and  night  com¬ 
ing  on  she  escaped  after  a  chase  of  90  miles. 

But  1  had  driven  her  into  the  track  of  the  Be  Soto ,  with  whom  I 
had  communicated  the  early  part  of  the  day,  and  the  following  morn¬ 
ing  she  fell  in  with  and  overhauled  her  so  "fast  that  they  took  to  their 
boats,  having  previously  set  fire  to  the  steamer,  which  burned  to  the 
water’s  edge.  She  was  the  notorious  Cuba. 

At  the. request  of  Captain  Walker,  I  have  brought  16  of  her  crew 
to  Key  West,  now  subject  to  your  orders.

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

Ceder  Keys ,  Fla. ,  May  22,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  morning  of  the  14th  instant  the  boats  of  the  Fort  Henry 
captured  a  flat  in  Waccasassa  Bay  loaded  with  corn.  The  flat  not  being 
seaworthy  has  been  sent  ashore. 

This  morning  our  boats  captured  the  sloop  Isabella  in  Waccasassa 
Bay,  from  Tampa,  bound  to  No.  4  Key.  No  cargo.  The  crews  of 
the  flat  and  sloop  escaped  to  the  shore,  with  the  exception  of  one  old 
man  belonging  to  the  sloop,  whose  infirmity  prevented  his  running. 

I  forwarded  to  Key  West  in  the  sloop  2,900  pounds  of  corn,  part  of 
the  cargo  of  the  flat;  also  25  pounds  cotton. 

Very  respectfullv,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

Ed.  Y.  McCauley,

letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  State  regard¬ 
ing  vessels  cleared  for  Matamoras. 


Nayy  Department,  May  2%,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  note  of 
the  19th  instant  enclosing  a  copy  of  a  dispatch  from  Mr.  Adams  of 
the  1st  instant. 

There  is  no  doubt  that  an  organized  plan  has  been  formed  in  Great 
Britain  to  furnish  the  rebels  with  supplies  by  vessels  cleared  nomi¬ 
nally  for  Matamoras,  but  with  contingent  destination  for  Brownsville, 
as  indicated  in  the  circular  of  Bennett  and  W ake,  agents  for  the  Mata¬ 
moras  line  of  steamers.  Admiral  Bailey,  in  one  of  his  late  dispatches, 
says  there  were  over  200  vessels  olf  the  Bio  Grande  when  in  ordinary 
times  there  are  but  6  or  8.  Of  course  the  traffic  in  which  they  are 
engaged  is  principally  for  the  rebels  through  Texas. 

Whether  anything  can  be  done  “to  defeat  these  machinations,” and 
prevent  this  illicit  trade,  except  as  indicated  in  the  closing  paragraph 
of  Mr.  Adams’s  letter,  “the  possession  of  the  eastern  bank  of  the 
river,”  is  doubtful.  An  effective  naval  blockade  of  the  Bio  Grande, 
which  is  a  neutral  highway  for  Mexico  and  ourselves,  is  impracticable. 
It  appears  to  me  desirable  on  many  accounts  that  there  should  be  a 
military  force  in  western  Texas,  and  that  we  should  have  possession 
of  Brownsville  at  as  early  a  day  as  possible.  The  possession  of  the 
Mississippi  Biver  will  be  some  check  on  smuggling  operations,  but 
until  the  blockade  runners  are  stopped  entirely  on  the  Bio  Grande, 
we  shall  experience  difficulty  in  Texas  and  Arkansas. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 


Hon.  Vm.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State. 


Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Captain  Walker ,  II.  S.  Navy,  commanding  II.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 
regarding  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Mississippian,  of  Biloxi. 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico,  May  21,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  on  the  19th  instant  I  seized, 
for  violation  of  the  blockade,  proclaimed  and  instituted  by  the  Presi¬ 
dent  of  the  United  States,  the  schooner  Mississippian  of  Biloxi,  laden 
with  187  bales  of  cotton  and  4  barrels  of  turpentine,  from  Mobile, 
bound  to  Havana. 

On  boarding  her,  I  found  in  all,  six  persons,  not  one  of  whom  would 
acknowledge  himself  to  be  her  master  or  supercargo,  nor  one  among 
them  who  at  first  would  admit  that  he  spoke  or  comprehended  English. 

Her  colors  and  papers  had  no  doubt  been  thrown  overboard.  The 
only  paper  of  importance  that  I  found  was  a  permit  to  sail,  signed  by 
F.  Buchanan,  admiral.  I  supplied  her  with  provisions,  gave  her  a 
boat,  placed  a  prize  master  and  crew  on  board  of  her,  and  ordered  her 
to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

On  the  20th,  at  5:45  p.  m.,  being  about  61  miles  southeast  of  Pensa¬ 
cola  light,  we  descried  the  smoke  of  a  steamer,  gave  chase,  and  soon 
got  sight  of  the  vessel  and  gained  on  her  so  rapidly  that  she  throw

Capture  of  the  sloop  Fashion ,  May  21+,  1863. 

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Morris,  IT.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  report  of  officer  in 

command  of  expedition. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Port  Royal, 

Off  Apalachicola ,  Fla. ,  May  25,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  transmit  herewith  the  report  of  Acting 
Master  Edgar  Van  Slyck,  who  commanded  a  boat  expedition  from  this 
vessel,  Avhich  resulted  in  the  capture  of  the  sloop  Fashion ,  having  on 
board  50  bales  of  sea-island  cotton. 

Learning  that  a  vessel  laden  with  cotton  was  45  miles  above  the 
town  of  Apalachicola,  waiting  for  an  opportunity  to  run  the  blockade, 
and  fearing  she  might  escape  through  Indian  Pass,  I,  on  the  23d  instant, 
dispatched  the  launch,  first  cutter,  and  a  captured  boat  under  charge 
of  Mr.  Van  Slyck,  with  orders  to  capture  her  if  possible. 

The  able  manner  in  which  the  expedition  was  conducted,  the  river 
being  very  narrow,  current  strong,  and  the  sloop  in  the  vicinity  of  an 
encampment,  reflects  great  credit  upon  Mr.  Van  Slyck. 

The  sloop  tender  Brockenborough  was  within  signal  distance  of  this 
vessel  when  the  capture  was  made  by  the  boats. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  U.  Morris, 

Lieutenant- Commander,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington  City,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Van  Slyck,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Port  Royal, 

Apalachicola  Bay ,  May  26,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  the  23d  of  May,  I  took  the 
launch,  Assistant  Paymaster  George  A.  Sawyer  with  the  first  cutter, 
Acting  Master’s  Mate  William  F.  Raynolds  with  a  captured  boat, 
carrying  [in]  all  41  men,  and  proceeded  up  Apalachicola  River,  intend¬ 
ing  to  capture  the  sloop  Fashion,  loaded  with  50  bales  of  sea-island 
cotton. 

As  I  learned  Fort  Gadsden  contained  a  number  of  troops,  I  deemed 
it  necessary  to  pass  under  cover  of  the  night.  The  current  being  very 
strong  against  us,  compelled  a  prolonged  pull  of  eight  hours.  We  suc¬ 
ceeded  in  passing  at  2  o’clock  after  midnight  of  the  24th  without  being 
discovered.  At  10  a.  m.  we  reached  Canida  Creek,  45  miles  up  the 


448 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


river,  at  which  place,  after  proceeding  2  miles  up  and  satisfying  our¬ 
selves  that  it  was  impossible  for  a  sloop  to  go  farther,  we  commenced 
our  return.  At  Devil’s  Elbow  we  saw  where  the  vessel  had  been 
repaired,  and  burned  everything  there.  Farther  down  the  river  we 
saw  a  barge,  which  indicated  the  near  whereabouts  of  the  sloop. 
After  sending  William  E.  Raynolds  in  the  captured  boat  to  the  mouth 
and  up  Owl  Creek,  I,  with  the  launch,  and  Assistant  Paymaster 
George  A.  Sawyer  with  the  first  cutter,  proceeded  2  miles  up  the  first 
creek  above  Owl  Creek,  where  we  discovered  and  captured  her  with¬ 
out  any  resistance.  We  learned  a  rebel  camp  was  within  6  miles  and 
of  easy  access  to  her  defense.  Owing  to  the  heavy  rain  at  that  time 
our  surprise  was  complete.  After  one  discharge  of  the  12-pounder 
howitzer,  we  immediately  cut  her  lines  and  vigorously  towed  her  from 
the  creek  to  the  river,  where  we  burned  the  barge,  and  proceeded  on 
our  return.  In  passing  Fort  Gadsden  we  fired  one  discharge  of  can- 
nister  but  elicited  no  reply. 

I  have  the  honor  to  state  officers  George  A.  Sawyer  and  William  F. 
Raynolds  rendered  me  all  the  assistance  possible,  both  with  advice  and 
energy;  also  I  beg  leave  to  mention  the  patient  endurance  and  meri¬ 
torious  zeal  of  all  the  men  under  my  charge,  having  during  the  week 
pulled  200  miles  against  and  with  a  current  of  3  miles  per  hour.  At  7 
o’clock  a.  m.  of  the  25th  arrived  alongside  of  the  vessel  with  no 
casualties. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

[Edgar  Van  Slyck,] 

Acting  Master. 

Lieutenant-Commander  George  U.  Morris, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Gunboat  Port  Royal.

Off  Apalachicola ,  Fla. ,  June  1,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  communi¬ 
cation  of  May  11.  I  send  by  the  Hendrick  Hudson  “Master’s  Mate 
William  F.  Raynolds,  attached  to  this  vessel,  in  charge  of  49  bales  of 
sea-island  cotton,  recently  captured  in  the  sloop  Fashion.  I  have 
detained  the  sloop  here,  as  I  do  not  consider  her  seaworthy.  I  also 
send  under  his  charge  five  prisoners,  viz:  A.  W.  Babcock,  Confeder¬ 
ate  mail  agent;  William  Austin,  Confederate  soldier;  George  Ashey, 
Confederate  soldier;  A.  W.  Wing,  who,  I  understand,  has  been 
engaged  superintending  the  obstructions  on  the  river  and  working  on 
the  batteries;  James  Silva,  captain  of  the  captured  sloop  Fashion.  I 
read  the  contents  of  the  captured  mail  bag  and  only  found  three  letters 
which  contained  news  of  importance.  Those,  with  the  rebel  news¬ 
papers,  I  enclose  to  you.  The  remainder,  being  simply  private  letters, 
I  sent  on  shore.  I  also  sent  down  the  refugees. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  U.  Morris,

U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West,  Alay  37,  1863. 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  is  ready  for  sea, 
you  will  proceed  with  her  to  cruise  to  the  northward  and  westward  of 
the  Tortugas.  The  general  limits  of  your  cruising  ground  will  be 
between  25°  and  26°  30,  north  latitude  and  between  83  and  84°  30'  west 
longitude,  although  in  chase  of  anything  there  are  no  limits  other  than 
the  jurisdiction  of  foreign  governments.  You  will  be  vigilant  to  over¬ 
haul  and  examine  all  vessels  you  may  fall  in  with,  and  to  seize  and 
send  in  for  adjudication  all  such  as  may  have  violated  the  blockade  or 
as  may  afford  a  reasonable  ground  of  presumption  that  they  intend 
doing  so.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  JR  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
successful  cruises  of  the  U.  S.  steamers  De  Soto  and  Huntsville. 

No.  186.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West,  May  28,  1863. 

Sir:  It  has  been  the  good  fortune  of  one  of  my  squadron,  the 
De  Soto ,  to  fall  in  with  the  notorious  blockade-running  steamer  Cuba. 
While  cruising  in  the  Gulf  on  the  17th  instant,  Captain  Walker,  of  the 
De  Soto,  discovering  the  smoke  of  a  steamer,  stood  for  it,  and  bv  his 
superior  speed  succeeded,  after  a  chase  of  six  hours,  in  overhauling 
her.  Finding  that  a  capture  was  inevitable,  the  men  and  officers  of 
the  Cuba  set  fire  to  that  vessel  before  she  could  be  boarded  from  the 
De  Soto  and  abandoned  her.  Efforts  were  made  to  put  out  the  tire, 
but  without  success,  and  after  burning  half  an  hour  the  Cuba  went 
down.  Her  cargo  cost  $400, 000  in  specie  at  Havana,  and  was  wTorth 
at  Mobile  a  million  and  a  quarter.  This  cruise  of  the  De  Soto  resulted 
also  in  the  capture  [of]  seven  vessels.  Four  of  these  were  captured 
on  the  same  day,  the  25th  ultimo,  sailing  together  from  Mobile  to 
Havana.  They  had  but  one  navigator.  Their  names  were  the  Rapid 
and  General  Prim,  schooners,  and  the  Bright  and  Jane  Adelie , 
sloops,  and  all  were  loaded  with  cotton.  On  the  26th  (the  succeeding 
day)  the  De  Soto  captured  the  schooner  Clarita,  and  on  the  13th 
instant  the.  schooner  Sea  Bird.  A  few  days  since  she  made  her 
seventh  prize,  the  Mississippian ,  loaded  with  187  bales  of  cotton. 
She  has  just  returned  to  this  port  for  coal. 

The  Huntsville  returned  to  this  port  a  few  days  since  after  a  cruise 
of  much  interest.  On  the  4th  instant  she  gave  chase  to  the  steamer 
Eugenia  (since  captured  by  the  blockading  fleet  off  Mobile),  but  after 
a  chase  of  142  miles  lost  sight  of  her  in  the  darkness.  On  the  13th 
instant  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  W.  C.  Rogers,  commanding  the 
Huntsville,  captured  the  schooner  A.  J.  Hodge,  bound  into  Mobile 
from  Nassau.  On  the  16th  he  gave  chase  to  the  Cuba ,  which  escaped 
him  by  superior  speed,  but  ran  into  the  track  of  the  De  Soto,  by  which 
she  was  destroyed,  as  above  stated.  On  the  19th  of  May,  Captain 
Rogers  overhauled  and  captured  the  steamer  Union,  bound  to  Mobile. 
Ihe  capture  of  these  vessels  and  others  has  throwui  a  great  number  of 
prisoners  upon  our  hands.  Wre  have  no  fit  place  to  confine  them,  nor 
could  they  accommodate  them  at  the  fort.  The  supply  steamers  com¬ 
municate  at  long  intervals,  and  it  therefore  became  necessary  to 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.

release  them,  and  they  are  now  at  large  on  the  island.  Many  of  the 
captains  and  supercargoes  of  the  blockade-running  vessels  have  been 
cap tuied  for  the  second  or  third  time,  and  for  the  lack  of  proper 
piison  accommodations  have  been  released.  I  commend  this  subject 
to  the  consideration  of  the  Department.  Since  I  took  command  43 
vessels  have  been  captured  by  the  vessels  of  this  squadron  and  declared 
good  prizes;  others  have  been  released  by  the  court,  and  others  still 
destroyed  at  Indian  River  and  other  places  along  the  coast. 

Many  prizes  have  been  sent  in  by  the  West  India  and  West  Gulf 
squadrons,  making  the  number  that  have  come  in  for  adjudication 
since  January  1,  1863,  to  be  70.
