Report  of  Captain  Walker ,  U.  S.  No  a  n/,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  De 
Soto ,  regarding  prisoners  captured  in  prizes  to  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Key  West ,  May  3 9 ,  1863. 

Sir:  There  are  now  remaining  on  board  this  ship  22  prisoners,  who, 
in  addition  to  those  heretofore  sent  in,  make  in  all  66  men  captured  by 
me  in  this  ship  since  her  departure  from  this  port  on  the  17th  ultimo. 

Among  these  are  experienced  navigators,  men  familiar  with  all  the 
coasts  of  the  Gulf,  daring  seamen,  capable  engineers,  skillful  artisans, 
etc.;  in  fine,  aftercareful  reflection,  I  am  satisfied  that,  considering  the 
present  state  of  the  country,  it  would  be  difficult  to  select  an  equal 
number  of  men  whose  services  might  be  more  important  to  the  public 
enemy,  whose  appreciation  of  their  value  is.  attested  by  the  high  rates 
of  compensation  at  which  many  of  them  have  been  employed,  of  which 
I  have  presented  the  most  conclusive  testimony. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  M.  Walker, 

Captain ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla. 


Reqoort  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  IT.  S.  Navy ,  transmitting 
opinion  of  court  of  enquiry  regarding  the  wreck  of  the  U.  S.  bark 
Amanda .,  in  St.  George’s  Sound ,  May  39,  1863. 

Nos.  207.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West ,  June  18,  1863. 

Sir:  I  enclose  herewith  the  proceedings  of  a  court  of  enquiry  into 
the  loss  of  the  U.  S.  bark  Amanda. 

I  have  not  ordered  a  general  court-martial  in  the  case,  partly  because 
great  injury  would  result  to  the  public  service  and  partly  because  it 
would  seem  unnecessary  in  view  of  the  act  of  Congress  (No.  165) 
approved  July  17,  1862,  section  17. 


452 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


I  have  ordered  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  George  E.  Welch,  late 
commanding  officer  of  the  Amanda ,  to  return  north  by  the  first  public 
conveyance  and  report  to  the  Department  by  letter  on  his  arrival,  and 
I  was  hesitating  whether  to  do  the  same  with  Acting  Volunteer  Lieu¬ 
tenant  David  Cate,  commanding  the  steamer  Hendrick  Hudson ,  not 
only  on  account  of  his  inefficiency  on  the  occasion  of  the  AmandcCs 
disaster  (as  set  forth  in  the  record  of  the  court  of  enquiry),  but  also 
on  account  of  the  general  disorganization  of  his  own  vessel,  when  he 
relieved  me  from  my  embarrassment  by  applying  for  leave  of  absence 
on  the  ground  of  a  probable  loss  otherwise  of  from  $6,000  to  $10,000. 
I  have  accordingly  ordered  Lieutenant-Commander  C.  J.  McDougal  to 
the  command  of  the  Hudson ,  and  would  request  that  Acting  Volunteer 
Lieutenant  Cate  be  not  returned  to  this  squadron. 

I  have  also  ordered  Acting  Assistant  Paymaster  E.  B.  Southworth, 
late  of  the  Amanda ,  to  go  north  for  the  settlement  of  his  accounts; 
and  at  his  request  have  allowed  his  steward,  although  an  enlisted  man, 
to  accompany  him. 

Two  other  officers  of  the  Amanda ,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant 
Samuel  Howard  and  Acting  Master  Joseph  E.  Jones,  1  have  ordered,  at 
the  request  of  the'U.  S.  deputy  marshal  at  this  place,  to  take  charge  of 
the  condemned  prize  schooner  John  Williams ,  loaded  with  prize  goods, 
and  take  her  to  New  York.  The  first  of  these  officers,  Acting  Volun¬ 
teer  Lieutenant  Howard,  has  voluntarily  allowed  two  officers  of 
inferior  grade  to  be  put  over  his  head  as  executive  officer  of  the 
Amanda ,  while  he  has  done  duty  as  a  watch  officer.  I  can  not  therefore 
place  him  in  a  position  due  to  his  rank,  and  would  request  that  he  be 
ordered  elsewhere.  The  other,  Acting  Master  Jones,  represented  to 
me  that  his  wife  is  about  to  suffer  amputation  of  the  leg,  and  I  have 
given  him  three  weeks  leave  of  absence  after  his  arrival  at  New  York, 
with  orders  to  return  to  this  squadron,  which  order  I  hope  he  will  be 
allowed  to  obey. 

Acting  Master’s  Mate  Nathaniel  L.  Ledyard,  also  of  the  Amanda , 
has  been  condemned  b}^  medical  survey,  and  I  have  ordered  him  home 
with  a  recommendation  that  he  be  dropped  from  the  Navy  as  worthless. 

The  rest  of  the  Amanda? s  officers  and  men  have  been  distributed 
among  the  different  vessels  of  the  squadron,  partly  to  fill  vacancies 
occasioned  by  the  outfit  of  tenders,  and  partly  in  exchange  for  some 
whose  terms  of  service  will  shortly  expire,  and  who  will  return 
north  in  the  Magnolia.  A  few  also  have  been  transferred  to  vessels 
belonging  to  the  West  India  Squadron. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Hast  Gulf  JBlockdg .  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

U.  S.  S.  Magnolia,  Key  West,  June  <9,  [1863]. 

By  virtue  of  authority  contained  in  act  *  *  *  July  17,  1862,  a 

naval  court  of  enquiry  is  hereby  ordered  to  convene  at  Key  West,  on 
board  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Magnolia ,  at  10  o’clock  a.  m.  on  the  10th  day 
of  J une,  or  as  soon  thereafter  as  practicable,  for  the  investigation  of 
the  circumstances  attending  the  loss  of  the  U.  S.  bark  Amanda. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


453 


The  court  will  be  composed  of  the  following'  officers,  any  two  of 
whom  are  empowered  to  act,  viz: 

Captain  George  F.  Emmons,  U.  S.  Navy;  Commander  H.  S.  New¬ 
comb,  U.  S.  Navy;  Lieutenant-Commander  R.  F.  Bradford,  U.  S. 
Navy;  and  Lieutenant-Commander  C.  J.  McDougal,  U.  S.  Navy,  is 
hereby  appointed  the  judge-advocate. 

The  basis  of  the  enquiry  is  contained  in  the  accompanying  papers,  viz: 

1.  Extract  (copy)  of  a  report  from  Lieutenant-Commander  A.  F. 
Grosman. 

2.  Report  from  Lieutenant-Commander  George  U.  Morris. 

3.  Report  from  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  George  E.  Welch. 

4.  Report  from  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  David  Cate. 

But  the  court  will  examine  into  every  circumstance  relating  to  the 
loss  of  the  Amanda ,  and  to  the  subsequent  operations,  with  a  view  of 
showing  from  the  evidence  whether  any  blame  attaches  to  her  com¬ 
manding  officer,  to  anyone  else  on  board  of  her,  or  to  any  other  per¬ 
son  belonging  to  the  Navy  of  the  United  States. 

And  the  court  will  report  the  facts  of  the  case  as  they  believe  them 
to  be  correct  from  the  hearing  of  the  evidence;  and  also  an  opinion 
as  to  the  propriety  and  expediency,  or  otherwise,  of  further  proceed¬ 
ings  in  the  case. 

T.  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 


Opinion  of  the  court. 

Key  W  est,  June  17,  1863.  - 

Finished  with  evidence  (some  20  witnesses)  in  the  case  of  the  loss 
of  the  U.  S.  bark  Amanda,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  G.  E.  Welch, 
near  East  Pass,  in  St.  George’s  Sound,  Florida,  May  29  last. 

Found  the  evidence  very  conflicting,  the  record  containing'  some 
104  pages. 

Recapitulated  and  commented  upon  the  same,  and  presented  a  report 
same  day  of  8  pages,  which  expressed  the  “expediency  and  propriety 
of  further  proceedings.” 

It  appears  that  this  cj'clone  was  severe  also  at  the  West  Pass,  pro¬ 
ducing  a  current  of  some  8  knots  per  hour,  which  wrecked  the  coal 
bark  Andrew  Manderson  on  Sand  Island,  and  washed  away  a  large 
pile  of  coal  here  as  at  East  Pass,  and  the  U.  S.  sloop  Brockenborougli 
was  obliged  to  run  on  shore  to  prevent  being  driven  across  the  sound 
onto  the  enemy’s  shore.  The  U.  S.  schooner  Wanderer  rode  out  the 
blow  at  sea,  but  sprung  her  foremast.  Some  200  tons  of  coal  was  lost 
and  the  guns  of  the  Amanda,  besides  some  ammunition  and  stores,  all 
of  which  ought  to  have  been  saved. 

Examined  the  following  witnesses: 

1.  Captain  Welch,  who  was  allowed  to  be  present.  [Testimony  of 
18  witnesses  omitted.] 

Result  and  opinion: 

The  court  respectfully  submit  the  accompanying  record  as  the  result 
of  their  examination  into  the  loss  of  the  IJ.  S.  bark  Amanda,  Acting 
Volunteer  Lieutenant  George  E.  Welch,  near  East  Pass,  in  St.  George’s 
Sound,  Florida,  May  29, 1863,  having  appended  thereto  extracts  from 
the  log  books  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson  and  bark  Amanda ,  with 
certain  notes  that  passed  between  their  commanders  upon  the  occasion. 


454  EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 

From  this  evidence  it  will  be  seen  that  the  weather  and  falling  barom¬ 
eter  indicated  a  blow  for  several  days  before  it  finally  culminated  in  a 
hurricane  or  cyclone,  which  was  the  primary  cause  of  the  final  loss  of 
the  Amanda. 

It  is  also  in  evidence  that,  notwithstanding  these  unfavorable  indica¬ 
tions  and  the  severity  of  the  gale  on  the  27th  and  28th  of  May,  many 
of  the  usual  precautions  were  neglected  for  the  safety  of  the  vessel. 

For  instance,  after  the  Amanda  had  struck  on  Dog  Island  her  exec¬ 
utive  officer,  Acting  Master  J ones,  testifies  that  she  had  30  fathoms 
of  chain  in  either  chain  locker,  and  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant 
[Samuel]  Howard  testifies  that  40  fathoms  were  left  in  the  port  and 
75  fathoms  of  chain  in  the  starboard  locker. 

And,  although  the  court  are  in  some  doubt  (owing  principally  to  the 
violence  of  the  gale)  whether  the  Amanda  could  have  ridden  out  the 
blow,  even  with  the  additional  precaution  of  veering  more  cable,  back¬ 
ing  anchors,  sending  down  yards,  masts,  etc.,  yet,  from  the  partially 
sheltered  cove  in  which  she  lay,  the  good  holding  ground,  and  the 
length  of  time  one  of  her  anchors  had  been  embedded  in  the  mud,  she 
may  possibly  have  held  on,  and  the  court  think  it  not  only  unfortunate, 
but  highly  culpable,  that  these  precautions  were  not  taken. 

While  on  shore  on  Dog  Island,  and  after  being  driven  off  by  a 
sudden  change  of  wind  and  driving  across  the  sound  toward  the  main¬ 
land,  the  evidence  is  conflicting  in  regard  to  her  condition,  her  manner 
of  driving,  as  well  as  whether  she  was  dragging  one  or  more  anchors. 

The  court  are  therefore  still  in  doubt  whether  during  this  time  (a 
period  of  from  one  to  one  and  one-half  hours,  according  to  the  testi¬ 
mony)  any  additional  precautions  would  have  brought  her  up. 

It  appears  that  the  stream  anchor  was  let  go  during  this  time  and 
the  hawsers  attached  to  it  immediately  parted,  and  she  finally  struck 
a  second  time  on  the  shoal  flats  of  the  mainland,  where,  from  the  com¬ 
bined  effects  of  the  hurricane  and  high  water,  she  was  finally  left 
standing  in  an  upright  position  some  200  to  300  yards  from  the  beach, 
with  her  head  to  the  eastward  and  her  port  batter}^  commanding  the 
shore,  having  the  Hendrick  Hudson  in  company  to  afford  protection 
in  case  of  necessity. 

The  court  are  unable  from  these  facts,  or  anything  adduced  in  the 
testimony,  to  see  any  justifiable  reason  for  abandoning  and  destroying 
the  Amanda ,  and  much  less  for  doing  this  until  her  battery  and  every¬ 
thing  of  value  had  been  removed  from  her. 

From  anything  that  appears  to  the  contrary  in  the  evidence,  or 
within  the  knowledge  of  the  court,  she  might  have  maintained  her 
position  without  the  assistance  of  the  Hendrick  Hudson,  and  with  her 
battery  of  six  32s  of  42  hundredweight,  one  20-pound  Parrott  rifle,  and 
a  12-pounder  howitzer  defied  all  the  guns  the  rebels  could  have  prob¬ 
ably  brought  against  her  for  a  week,  if  not  for  a  month. 

There  is  no  evidence  other  than  of  Captain  Welch  that  any  consid¬ 
erable  number  of  rebels  were  seen  from  the  Amanda ,  and  from  the 
weight  of  testimony  it  is  doubtful  if  they  were  armed.  No  artillery 
was  seen,  and  from  the  testimony  of  the  executive  officer  of  the 
Amanda  there  was  no  military  force  known  to  be  stationed  nearer  than 
Shell  Point,  some  40  miles  distant,  and  these  had  nothing  larger  than 
6-pounder  fieldpieces.  It  is  well  known  that  the  country  adjacent  is 
low  and  marshy,  intersected  by  crooked  rivers  and  bayous,  making  it 
difficult  to  transport  men  and  supplies,  much  less  heavy  guns,  and  if 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


455 


it  had  been  possible  for  the  cavalry  force,  before  alluded  to,  with  their 
small  guns  to  have  occupied  the  most  advantageous  point  on  the  main¬ 
land  near  the  wreck  (known  as  Topsail  Bluff  and  distant  about  1  mile) 
two  days  after  the  wreck,  the  court  do  not  believe  that  they  could  have 
done  any  harm,  or  for  any  time  withstood  the  replies  of  the  Amanda's 
guns. 

How  far  this  catastrophe  may  have  finally  been  brought  about  or 
influenced  by  the  apparent  indecision  of  Captain  Cate,  who  was  the 
senior  officer  present  in  command  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Hendrick,  Hudson , 
may  better  appear  by  reference  to  the  record  and  the  notes  appended 
thereto. 

Although  Captain  Welch  appears  finally  to  have  assumed  the  respon¬ 
sibility  of  not  only  destroying  his  guns,  but  of  firing  and  abandoning 
his  vessel,  it  does  not  satisfactorily  appear  to  the  court  that  Captain 
Cate  sufficiently  interested  himself  in  preventing  this,  either  by  taking 
and  preserving  a  nearer  position  to  the  wreck,  or  by  giving  some  defi¬ 
nite  and  decided  orders  after  or  while  on  board  of  the  Amanda ,  thereby 
tacitly  consenting  to  his  junior  assuming  responsibility  that  more 
properly  belonged  to  him,  Captain  Cate. 

What  took  place  subsequently  on  board  of  the  Hendrick  Hudson ,  on 
her  spar  deck  and  in  the  presence  of  all  hands — see  the  record — (and 
which,  under  the  precept,  became  a  proper  subject  of  enquiry)  will  go 
far  to  show  the  revising  power  the  weight  that  was  attached  to  rank 
and  seniority  in  this  instance,  and  it  does  not  satisfactorily  account 
for  the  reticence  of  Captain  Cate  of  assuming  all  his  prerogatives,  but 
will,  to  a  certain  extent,  account  for  and  palliate  the  only  instance  of 
insubordination  reported  on  the  part  of  a  portion  of  the  Amanda's  crew. 

►Such  a  public  and  disgraceful  exhibition  is  destructive  to  all  order 
and  discipline  on  shipboard,  and  the  court  hope  and  believe  of  very 
rare  occurrence  in  our  Navy.  So  far  as  the  language  of  Captain  Cate 
applied  to  his  senior  officer,  Lieutenant-Commander  Crosman  (who  was 
not  present  at  the  time),  he  is  exonerated  by  a  note  from  the  latter, 
who  is  not  willing  to  believe  he  applied  such  language  to  him,  and  no 
other  witness  but  Captain  Welch  appears  to  have  heard  it. 

Having  thus  fully  examined  into  and  presented  the  main  points  in 
this  case,  the  court  will  not  perhaps  be  expected  to  indicate  more 
decidedly  than  they  have  al ready  done  an  opinion  of  its  merits. 

They  certainly  think  it  both  “expedient  and  proper”  that  further 
proceedings  should  follow,  therefore  venture  to  submit  it  with  the 
remark  that  both  Captain  Cate  and  Captain  Welch  have  testified  to  the 
faithful  performance  of  duty  on  the  part  of  their  respective  officers  and 
crew  throughout  this  gale. 

Geo.  F.  Emmons, 

Captain ,,  U.  S.  Navy ,  and  President  of  the  Court.

Past  Pass,  St.  George's  Sound ,  June  3,  1863. 
Sir:  Upon  the  29th  ultimo  I  was  ordered  by  Lieutenant-Commander 
Morris  to  proceed  to  this  place,  relieve  the  Hudson,  send  that  steamer

to  report  to  him,  and  also  furnish  all  possible  information  relating  to 
the  loss  of  the  U.  S.  bark  Amanda. 

I  enclose  a  copy  of  the  orders. 

I  arrived  upon  the  31st  ultimo  and  the  U.  S.  S.  Hudson  was  sent  by 
me  to  West  Pass  upon  the  1st  of  June.  Up  to  that  date  I  had  not 
succeeded  in  forming  an  opinion  in  regard  to  the  action  taken  by  Act¬

from  Lieutenant-Commander  Morris,  send  a  boat  to  him  with  the  sub¬ 
stance  of  the  report  1  make  to  you. 

Yesterday  I  took  my  steamer  up  to  within  half  a  mile  of  Topsail 
Bluff.  I  lowered  two  boats  and  visited  the  wreck.  She  was  in  18 
inches  of  water,  lay  within  150  yards  of  the  shore,  broadside  to,  and 
could  not  have  brought  her  guns  to  bear  upon  Topsail  Bluff,  which 
was  upon  her  port  quarter,  where  Lieutenant  Welch  informs  me  he 
saw  apparent  preparations  to  erect  a  battery,  which,  from  the  situation 
of  his  ship,  would  have  raked  a  defenseless  vessel. 

The  tide  ebbed  and  flowed  in  the  ship,  her  chains  were  parted,  and 
the  Hudson  lay  so  far  off  that  her  Parrott  rifle  could  not  reach  the 
shore.  There  was  no  chance  of  saving  the  ship  herself. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Commanding  Welch  will  make  his 
report  to  you  in  person,  and  I  presume  it  is  supererogatory  in  me  to 
dwell  upon  this  circumstance. 

The  six  32s.,  a  quantity  of  shot  and  shell,  the  water  tanks,  some 
casks  and  spars  which  remain  lashed  together  as  a  raft  since  the  blow¬ 
ing  up  of  the  bark,  I  am  going  to  try  to  save.  The  copper  and  part  of 
the  chains  I  think  may  also  be  secured.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Crosman ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 
U.  S.  S.  Somerset ,  regarding  the  conduct  of  that  vessel  in  a  violent 
gale. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset, 

West  Pass,  St.  Georgds  Sound ,  May  30,  1863. 
Sir:  *  *  *  On  the  night  of  the  25th  it  commenced  to  blow 
freshly  from  the  eastward  and  northeast.  On  the  26th  the  wind  steadily 
increased  in  force.  In  the  afternoon  I  let  go  my  second  anchor.  The 
wind  still  increased  in  violence,  but  yet  remained  at  the  same  point  of  the 
compass.  On  the  27th  it  was  blowing  a  violent  gale.  The  bark  Man- 
derson  was  on  shore.  Boats  could  not  live  and  no  opportunity  of  aid¬ 
ing  her  existed.  All  the  lighters  and  small  craft  were  driven  on  shore 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


457 


or  went  down  at  their  anchors.  A  splendid  lifeboat  given  me  by  the 
Circassian ,  securely  moored  to  a  pile  driven  into  the  mud  by  a  pile 
driver,  which  pile  was  9  inches  in  diameter,  broke  the  stake  off  and 
was  driven  on  shore  and  ruined.  The  Brockenborough  had  to  be 
beached  to  save  her  crew. 

The  wind  increased  to  almost  a  hurricane.  The  Port  Royal  com¬ 
menced  to  drag  and  went  astern  some  300  yards.  I  let  go  my  last 
spare  anchor,  and  veered  to  the  bitter  end 'of  my  starboard  bower, 
bringing  an  equal  strain  upon  all  chains.  I  was  now  convinced  this 
was  a  cyclone,  and  from  the  wind’s  holding  the  same  direction  and 
increasing  in  force,  that  we  were  right  in  the  path  of  the  storm,  which 
must  have  been  approaching  us  in  a  N.  W.  direction. 

(My  supposition  became  conviction  when,  after  the  gale  subsided  a 
little,  the  wind  came  out  from  W.  It  was  then  daylight;  I  got  all  my 
anchors  as  quickly  as  possible  and  during  the  light  wind  shifted  my 
berth  to  the  E.  N.  E.  of  Sand  Island.  Here  I  let  go  all  three  anchors, 
veered  my  whole  scope,  and  rode  out  comfortably  the  other  half  of  the 
gale  from  S.  W.) 

At  S  on  the  night  of  the  27th  I  started  my  engine  and  kept  it  work¬ 
ing  at  its  full  stroke,  yet  the  chains  were  like  harp  strings.  Fearful 
tlie  bitts  would  give  wajq  I  took  the  end  of  my  best  bower  chain  down 
the  fire-room  hatch  through  a  hole  cut  in  the  bulkhead  separating  the 
fire  room  from  the  fore  peak,  up  around  two  beams  and  a  carline 
through  the  fore  timbers  and  clinched  the  end  to  its  own  part.  The 
floor  timbers  are  too  slight  to  be  relied  upon  as  a  fastening-  for  the 
chains. 

From  10  until  2:30  it  blew  a  hurricane.  Whole  seas  came  over  the 
bows.  Everything  was  battened  down  forward,  and  the  deck  was 
flooded  constantly.  The  gangway  doors  were  nailed  with  bucklers,  yet 
the  sea  stove  them  from  their  hinges,  and  I  was  obliged  to  place  shores 
against  them,  the  ends  being-  cleated.to  the  deck.  The  squalls  were 
terrific  and  it  seemed  impossible  for  anything  to  stand  their  violence. 

There  was  hardly  any  lull  between  them  and  this  was  merely  a  very 
slight  slacking  down.  The  tide  or  current  caused  by  the  water  being 
all  blown  toward  this  pass,  rushed  past  at  the  rate  of  8  knots. 

It  was  impossible  to  touch  bottom  with  the  heaviest  boat  grapnel 
lashed  to  a  32-pounder  shot. 

By  good  luck  a  fire  was  burning  on  shore,  and  compass  bearings  told 
me  through  the  night,  as  the  faint  glimmer  shone  through  the  spray, 
that  we  had  not  moved. 

At  daylight  I  found  the  Somerset  had  not  dragged  a  particle,  and 
after  the  other  half  of  the  gale  had  subsided,  I  found  the  only  injury 
she  had  sustained  was  some  two  or  three  of  the  five  sponsons  under  the 
bow  slightly  splintered.  These  I  have  since  removed  and  replaced  with 
good  and  stouter  ones. 

I  have  been  thus  verbose,  inasmuch  as  it  may  be  gi-atifying  to  you 
to  learn  that  the  Somerset  proves  to  be  so  staunch.  At  sea  it  is  a  dif¬ 
ferent  matter. 

*  *  *  *  *  *  .* 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  F.  Crosman, 

Lieutenant-  Commander,  U.  S.  Navy.

Rejyort  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
urgent  need  of  reinforcements  for  his  command. 


No.  188.] 


U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West,  May  30,  1863. 


Sir:  Referring  to  my  letter  of  April  28, 1  would  ask  to  be  informed 
if  it  is  the  policy  and  intention  of  the  Department  to  grant  my  request 
for  the  reinforcement  of  this  squadron,  as  otherwise  1  wish  to  avail 
myself  of  additional  tenders,  although  less  efficient  for  my  purposes. 

The  steam  tug  Sunflower  has  arrived  out  on  the  station,  and  although 
of  12-feet  draft  and  carrying  but  live  days’  fuel  and  ten  days’  water,  1 
have  sent  her  to  cruise  within  a  hundred  miles  to  the  northwest  of  the 
Tortugas,  at  which  place  she  can  get  supplies  of  coal  and  water,  until 
obliged  to  return  here  for  provisions.  But,  although  I  hope  she  may 
do  good  service  there,  it  would  embarrass  me  to  employ  profitably 
another  similar  vessel  with  the  same  defects.  It  is  essential  that  the 
offshore  cruisers  between  the  Tortugas  and  Mobile,  and  within  that 
line  (by  whom  nearly  all  the  captures  are  made),  should  be  able  to  keep 
at  sea  the  greater  part  of  the  time;  and  the  inshore  cruisers  on  this  coast 
must  combine  with  this  quality  a  light  draft  of  water. 

Of  course  I  would  prefer  the  reinforcements  to  be  sent  out  from  the 
North,  where  their  armament  and  outfit  can  be  more  efficiently  sup¬ 
plied  and  arranged;  but  should  I  be  compelled  to  resort  to  the  more 
imperfect  expedient  of  purchasing  additional  tenders,  I  shall  require 
at  least  20  seamen,  25  ordinary  seamen,  and  55  landsmen  to  be  sent 
out  to  me.  Indeed,  several  of  the  vessels  are  already  short  of  their 
complement  of  men,  partly  from  furnishing  crews  for  their  tenders 
and  partly  from  sending  home  their  sick;  and  I  would  request  that 
one-fourth  of  these  numbers  be  sent  out  as  soon  as  possible. 

If,  in  addition  to  this,  the  Department  would  order  a  band  to  be 
brought  out  in  the  flagship,  I  should  not  only  be  gratified,  but,  judg¬ 
ing  from  the  statistics  of  the  British  army  and  navy,  1  am  of  opinion 
that  important  hygienic  results  would  be  secured  for  her  ship’s  com¬ 
pany,  which,  in  this  climate,  is  well  worthy  of  serious  consideration; 
but  I  would  not  desire  a  band  to  the  exclusion  of  other  recruits. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Oomdg.  Bast  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Van  Sice,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  JJ.  S.  S. 
Sunflower ,  regarding  the  capture  by  that  vessel  of  the  schooner  Echo ,

U.  S.  S.  Sunflower, 

Lat.  85°  39'  N,  Long.  83°  £ 7 '  IF,  May  31,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  4:45  this  morning  made  a 
sail  bearing  N.  W.  by  N.,  standing  to  the  southward  and  eastward; 
immediately  gave  chase,  and  at  5:30  came  up  to  him  and  fired  a  blank 
cartridge,  when  he  hove  to,  but  did  not  set  any  colors  until  after  being 
boarded,  when  he  set  the  English  flag.  Sent  an  officer  with  boat’s  crew 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


459 


on  board.  The  captain  of  her  then  came  on  board  with  his  papers. 
She  proved  to  be  the  schooner  Echo ,  of  Halifax,  from  Matamoras, 
cleared  for  New  York,  with  185  bales  of  cotton  on  board,  60  bales  of 
which  purporting  to  belong-  to  the  captain  were  certified  on  the  invoice 
by  the  American  consul.  The  other  125  bales  there  is  no  invoice  for 
and  no  American  consul’s  certificate.  This,  together  with  his  having- 
seven  passengers  on  board,  while  his  clearance  only  calls  for  five  (the 
excess  of  two  being-  a  Dr.  Farmer  and  wife  from  Texas),  also  from 
other  conflicting  stories,  induced  me  to  take  him  in.  When  the  cap¬ 
tain  first  came  on  board  he  was  very  much  agitated  when  I  asked 
him  for  the  certificate  for  the  125  bales.  He  then  said  that  it  belonged 
to  the  British  consul,  afterwards  that  it  belonged  to  a  party  in  New 
York,  and  still  later  that  he  did  not  know  to  whom  it  belonged.  He 
also  complained  very  much  at  my  towing  him  in  to  Key  West  (it  being- 
calm),  although  some  time  afterwards  he  said  he  intended  to  go  into 
Key  West  for  supplies.  Dr.  Farmer  pretends  to  be  a  refugee  South¬ 
ern  Union  man,  and  says  that  the  captains  of  the  vessel,  she  having- 
two  pretending  to  be  brothers,  are  very  strong  secessionists,  especially 
the  younger  one.  At  the  time  of  the  capture  there  were  no  other 
vessels  in  sight. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edw.  Van  Sice, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  I).  C.

Report  of  Lieutenant-  Commander  Me  Cauley ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  command¬ 
ing  if.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry ,  regarding  the  capture  in  Wacccisassa  Ray 

of  the  sloop  Isabella  and  two  other  vessels. 

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  June  2,  1863. 

Admiral:  On  the  22d  May  we  captured  the  sloop  Isabella  in  Wac- 
casassa  Bay.  I  loaded  her  with  2,900  pounds  of  shelled  corn  and  a 
hag  of  cotton,  and  sent  her  on  the  23d  ultimo  to  Key  West  in  charge 
of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  David  Axe,  with  two  seamen  and  an  infirm 
old  prisoner. 

On  the  30th  ultimo  one  of  our  boats  captured  in  Waccasassa  Bay  a 
copper-fastened  sloop  boat;  she  was  manned  by  two  soldiers,  who 
escaped,  and  a  refugee,  who  assisted  in  the  boat’s  capture. 

On  the  30th  ultimo  I  again  sent  1113^  launch  to  cruise  in  Waccasassa 
Bay.  She  returned  this  morning  with  a  scow  loaded  with  56  bales  fair 
cotton,  averaging  over  500  pounds  each.  She  was  manned  by  four 
Confederate  soldiers,  bound  to  Bayport.  The  cotton  I  will  send  to 
Key  West  by  the  schooner  David  Faust ,  the  prisoners  by  the  U.  S. 
schooner  Beauregard. 

Having  obtained  some  information  about  the  schooner  Frolic ,  now 
lying  at  Bayport,  loaded  with  cotton,  ready  to  run  the  blockade,  I 
have  sent  my  launch  with  the  Beauregard  to  that  point,  having  made 
arrangements  with  Acting  Ensign  Hamlin  which  I  think  will  probably 
insure  her  capture. 

Very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley, 

Lieut.  Comdr. ,  XT.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry. 

Bear- Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Squadron.

Circular. 

I  he  following  .order,  having  been  issued  by  the  U.  S.  district  judge 
at  this  place,  is  hereby  promulgated  for  the  information  and  guidance 
of  officers  placed  in  charge  of  prizes  and  ordered  to  this  port: 

District  Court  of  the  United  States 

for  the  Southern  District  of  Florida, 

June  4,  1863. 

Ordered,  That  whenever  a  capture  is  reported  to  one  of  the  prize  commissioners, 
he  shall  go  on  board  the  vessel,  seal  up  the  hatches,  and  see  that  the  vessel  is  prop¬ 
erly  anchored.  The  personal  baggage  of  the  master,  crew,  and  passengers,  consist¬ 
ing  of  their  wearing  apparel  and  pocket  money  for  immediate  expenses  (not  exceeding 
for  the  master  or  any  passenger  $25,  and  for  any  of  the  crew  $15  each),  shall  be 
restored  to  them  at  the  time  they  leave  the  vessel.  No  whole  pieces  of  goods,  nor 
whole  packages  of  merchandise,  nor  anything  else  that  is  not  properly  denominated 
personal  baggage  for  the  use  of  the  party,  shall  be  restored  by  the  commissioner. 
He  shall  take  charge  of  the  chronometer  and  other  instruments  of  navigation,  and 
gather  together  the  loose  effects  and  put  them  in  store  under  his  own  charge.  No 
application  for  the  restoration  of  any  other  articles  than  those  herein  permitted  to  be 
restored  by  the  prize  commissioner  will  be  heard  by  the  judge  except  in  open  court, 
on  a  claim  filed. 

William  Marvin,  Judge. 

All  officers  of  the  Navy  bringing  prizes  to  this  port  will  yield  every 
assistance  in  their  power  to  the  prize  commissioner  for  the  due  per¬ 
formance  of  this  order,  and  will  not,  of  their  own  authority,  permit 
anything  to  be  taken  out  of  the  vessel.  When  practicable,  a  list  will 
be  prepared  by  the  captors,  before  reaching  port,  of  the  “loose  effects” 
claimed  as  private  property,  and  the  articles  will  be  marked  with  the 
claimant’s  name. 

T.  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear- Admired,  Comdg.  East  Gidf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Hill ,  TT.  S.  Navy,  executive  officer  of  the 
TJ.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  sloop  Florida. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

St.  Marks  Bay ,  Fla.,  June  J±.  1863. 

Sir:  I  beg  leave  to  submit  the  following  report  of  the  capture  of  the 
sloop  Florida ,  of  St.  Marks,  Fla. : 

According  to  your  order  of  June  3,  1863,  I,  accompanied  by  Acting 
Assistant  Surgeon  Benjamin  Marshall,  Acting  Master  George  Ashbury, 
and  Master’s  Mate  Henry  B.  Conklin,  proceeded  with  the  first  and  sec¬ 
ond  cutters  to  the  mouth  of  St.  Marks  Kiver,  where  we  discovered  the 
Florida  at  anchor  about  2  miles  above.  Immediately  upon  perceiving 
us  she  got  underway,  endeavoring  to  escape  up  the  river.  We  fol¬ 
lowed  in  pursuit,  and  after  a  two  hours’  chase  succeeded  in  capturing 
her,  the  crew  escaping  by  running  the  vessel  ashore.  She  proved  to 
be  a  small  sloop  loaded  with  6  bales  of  cotton  and  a  half  barrel  of 
tar,  and  bound  to  Havana.  On  our  way  back  we  discovered  about  50 
mounted  rebels  stationed  upon  Light-House  Point,  near  which  we 
must  pass,  evidently  with  the  intention  of  intercepting  us,  but  owing 
to  two  well-directed  shots  from  the  steamer  they  fled  in  all  directions, 
enabling  us  to  reach  the  ship  in  safety. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  W.  Hill, 

Acting  Master  and  Executive  Officer. 

C.  L.  Willcomb, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes.

U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

Off  Crystal  River ,  Fla. ,  June  5 ,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  39  bales  of  cotton 
under  the  following  circumstances: 

From  information  received  from  Lieutenant-Commander  McCauley 
I  left  Cedar  Keys  June  2  with  a  detachment  of  1  officer  and  12  men 
from  the  U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry ,  and  anchored  same  night  12  miles  off 
the  mouth  of  Crystal  River  and  sent  in  2  armed  boats.  On  the  night 
of  the  3d  instant  succeeded  in  capturing  a  lighter  loaded  with  30 
bales  of  upland  cotton  and  9  bales  of  sea-island  cotton.  Finding  the 
lighter  unfit  to  bring  outside,  I  ran  close  in  with  this  vessel  and  took 
the  cotton  on  deck,  then  scuttled  the  lighter.  Will  leave  immediately 
for  Key  West  with  the  cotton  and  the  crew,  consisting  of  3  men.  No 
papers  of  any  kind  found  on  board.  I  forward  the  list  of  crew  entitled 
to  share  in  the  prize. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  C.  Hamlin, 

Acting  Ensign ,  Commanding .

Report  of  Acting  Rear- Adnniral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
distribution  of  the  crew  of  the  U.  S.  bark  Amanda  among  the  vessels 
of  his  command. 


No.  195.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West,  June  6,  1863. 

Sir:  The  steamer  Hendrick  Hudson  arrived  from  St.  George’s 
Sound  yesterday,  having  on  board  a  portion  of  the  officers  and  crew 
of  the  bark  Amanda,  which  vessel  is  reported  to  have  been  driven 
upon  the  mainland  in  a  hurricane  beyond  the  possibility  of  getting 
her  off.  After  getting  nearly  everything  out  of  her  it  was  deemed 
expedient  to  burn  her,  to  prevent  the  enemy  from  deriving  any  benefit 
from  her  disaster.  I  have  received  no  detailed  report  yet  of  the  cir¬ 
cumstances,  and  can  therefore  only  state  the  bare  fact;  but  of  course 
I  shall  institute  a  court  of  enquiry  into  the  circumstances  of  the  case 
so  soon  as  the  commanding  officer  of  the  vessel  shall  arrive. 

Meantime,  since  this  loss  leaves  the  crew  of  the  Amanda  free  to  be 
distributed  among  the  other  vessels  of  the  squadron,  I  would  withdraw 
the  request  for  25  additional  men  contained  in  my  letter  of  May  30. 
If  any  remain  after  filling  all  vacancies  in  this  squadron,  I  will  furnish 
such  as  are  required  to  the  vessels  of  the  W est  India  Squadron  resort¬ 
ing  to  this  port  for  supplies. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gidf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

the  schooner  a  rifled  gun  from  the  enemy’s  battery  at  Tampa  opened  on  the  boats, 
rowing  its  projectiles  over  and  near  them,  and  kept  up  firing  until  the  schooner 
was  boarded  and  taken  possession  of  without  injuring  anybody,  though  several  shot 
struck  within  a  few  feet  of  the  boats.  Got  the  schooner  off  by  means  of  hedging 
towing,  and  using  the  sails  under  a  sharp  fire  of  a  fieldpiece  of  the  enemy  planted 
on  the  beach  near  the  schooner,  which  was  soon  silenced  by  a  few  shell  from  the 
Parrott  gun. 

She  had  no  flag  or  papers.  Her  name  on  the  stern  was  partially  covered  with 
paint. 


I  enclose  a  list  of  the  officers  and  crew  of  this  vessel  at  the  time  of 
capture.  I  will  send  the  prize  to  Key  West. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  A.  Semmes, 

Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Sir:  Agreeable  to  your  order  of  May  23,  1863,  received  on  the  27th 
ultimo  per  U.  S.  bark  Pursuit ,  1  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that 
on  the  31st  ultimo,  after  giving  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  William 
P.  Randall,  commanding  U.  S.  bark  Pursuit ,  all  the  information  1 
possessed  about  Jupiter  and  Indian  River  inlets  and  the  tributary 
waters,  I  got  the  Gem  of  the  Sea  underway  and  proceeded  for  Key 
W  est. 

I  have  experienced  nothing  but  light  southeast  winds  and  calms  since 
leaving  my  station  off  Indian  River  Inlet,  and  unless  there  is  a  change 
in  the  wind  it  will  be  some  days  before  I  reach  Key  West,  as  the  cur¬ 
rent  is  running  close  in  to  the  shore  at  the  rate  of  2^  knots  per  hour, 
and  I  find  it  impossible  to  work  to  the  southward  with  any  other  wind 
but  a  leading  wind.  I  would  cross  the  Gulf  and  work  up  under  the 
Bahama  Banks  if  I  could  get  sufficient  wind  to  cross  with  without 
drifting  too  far  to  the  northward  to  strike  the  bank. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Baxter,

U.  S.  Steamer  Fort  Henry,

Admiral:  On  the  9th  instant,  off  the  Withlacoochee  River,  our  boats 
captured  a  sloop  boat,  manned  by  Henry  Kelly,  who  acknowledges 
having  several  times  successfully  run  the  blockade. 

On  the  10th  instant,  near  the  same  place,  the  boats  captured  a  skiff 
and  a  large  flat  loaded  with  250  bushels  of  corn  consigned  to  D.  Yulee 
on  the  Homosassa.  She  was  manned  by  two  men,  B.  F.  Maguire  and 
William  Hollins. 

As  directed,  I  send  the  Ezilda  for  repairs  and  forward  by  her  the 
corn  and  two  prisoners,  also  the  three  engineers,  refugees. 

I  would  most  respectfully  suggest  to  the  Rear-Admiral  that  he  would 
send  me  for  a  tender  in  lieu  of  the  Ezilda  a  vessel  of  lighter  draft; 
when  ready  for  sea  she  draws  8  feet  water,  and  in  every  instance  where 
the  Ezilda  has  been  in  chase  of  blockade  runners,  the  chase  has  escaped 
her  by  running  into  shoal  water. 

Henry  Sellwood,  ordinary  seaman,  of  this  vessel,  deserted  from  his 
boat  at  Withlacoochee;  he  was  tracked  some  distance  from  the  boats. 

Very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley,

Destruction  of  salt  works  on  Alligator  Bay,  June  If  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  II.  S.  Navy. 

No.  231.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  July  6,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  received  an  interesting  report  from  Lieutenant- 
Commander  A.  F.  Grosman,  of  the  steamer  Somerset,  from  which  it 
appears  that,  after  having  devoted  about  a  week  to  saving  from  the 
wreck  of  the  Amanda  all  that  could  have  been  turned  to  account  by 


468 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


the  enemy,  as  well  as  what  was  of  service  to  himself  (including  six  32- 
pounders,  a  quantity  of  kentledges,  253  solid  shot,  30  shells,  some 
spars  and  ironwork,  over  100  fathoms  of  chain  cable,  one  hedge,  about 
a  barrel  full  of  loose  grape  and  canister,  and  some  water  casks), 
during  which  operation  his  crew  labored  cheerfully  in  the  sun  and 
water  under  cover  of  the  Somerset's  guns,  he  next  turned  his  attention 
to  sounding  out  the  various  channels  about  the  East  Pass  of  St. 
George’s  Sound,  ascertaining  the  changes  wrought  by  the  recent  hur¬ 
ricane  and  replacing  the  buoys  that  had  been  swept  away.  Having 
satisfactorily  completed  this  work,  he  sent  the  boats  of  the  Somerset 
to  reconnoiter  the  sound  to  the  eastward,  sound  out  some  channels, 
and  specially  to  determine  the  precise  locality  of  some  extensive  salt 
works,  which  had  been  in  operation  since  the  commencement  of  the 
rebellion  near  Alligator  Bay  [Harbor].  This  duty  was  well  performed 
by  Acting  Master  Thomas  Chatfield,  and  on  the  information  gained 
Lieutenant-Commander  Crosman  determined  to  attempt  the  destruc¬ 
tion  of  these  salt  works.  For  this  purpose  the  Somerset  was  brought 
within  1,100  yards  of  the  shore  and  within  range  of  the  works,  the 
woods  were  shelled,  and  the  boats,  with  65  seamen  and  marines,  were 
sent  on  shore,  together  with  a  party  from  the  engineer’s  division,  armed 
with  sledge  hammers  to  break  the  salt  boilers,  all  under  the  immedi¬ 
ate  command  of  Acting  Master  Chatfield.  Those  armed  with  muskets 
were  deployed  as  skirmishers  in  the  rear  of  the  settlements  to  protect 
the  worldng  party,  who  in  their  turn  performed  the  duty  entrusted  to 
them  in  a  thorough  manner.  Four  distinct  stations  were  demolished, 
65  salt  kettles  destroyed,  more  than  200  bushels  of  salt  scattered  over 
the  sand,  and  about  30  huts  and  houses,  wdth  all  their  appurtenances 
for  constructing  and  repairing  the  works,  burned  to  the  ground. 
Lieutenant-Commander  Crosman  compliments  Acting  Master  Chat¬ 
field  upon  the  officerlike  ability^  displayed  in  the  management  of  his 
small-arms  men,  owing  to  which  and  to  the  previous  and  effective  shell¬ 
ing  of  the  woods  no  resistance  was  attempted  by  the  enemy.  Infor¬ 
mation,  however,  was  brought  that  some  cavalry  were  en  route  for  the 
place,  but  the  work  was  handsomely  accomplished  before  their  arrival, 
and  our  force  was  withdrawn  without  the  loss  of  a  single  man. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Crosman  also  confirms  the  report  received 
directly  from  Lieutenant-Commander  George  U.  Morris,  of  the 
steamer  Port  Royal ,  and  indirectly  from  several  other  sources,  of  the 
disaster  of  the  rebel  gunboat  Chattahoochee .  Her  boiler  exploded, 
killing  and  disabling  all  on  board  but  18.  Among  the  killed  were  4 
officers.  The  vessel  is  sunk  and  shattered  past  the  possibility  of 
recovering  and  making  future  use  of  her. 

The  vigilance  and  activity  of  this  squadron  are  attested  by  the  fact, 
mentioned  in  some  intercepted  rebel  correspondence,  that  out  of  52 
vessels  which  have  left  Havana  since  the  1st  of  April  for  the  purpose 
of  running  the  blockade,  but  7  have  succeeded,  and  the  rest  have  been 
brought  into  this  port.  This  statement  speaks  well  for  the  officers 
and  men  under  my  command. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Rlockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Crosman,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Somerset, 

transmitting  reports  of  Acting  Master  Chatfield,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset, 

East  Pass,  St.  Georges  Sound,  June  11^,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  4th  instant  I  steamed  up  toward  the  wreck'  of  the 
Amanda ,  sounding-  carefully  till  within  1,000  yards  of  the  bark, 
when  I  came  to  at  low  water  in  11  feet.  The  shore,  in  a  prolongation 
of  that  line,  was  1,200  yards  distant,  as  I  found  by  two  shots  with 
which  I  searched  the  woods. 

The  morning  of  the  5th  my  boats  got  to  work. 

I  have  landed  upon  Dog  Island,  opposite  the  steepest  part  of  the 
bank,  where  a  vessel  can  haul  in  most  easily  all  six  of  the  wrecked 
barks,  32-pounders  of  42  hundredweight,  a  quantity  of  kentledge,  253 
solid  shot,  some  spars  and  ironwork.  The  guns  have  their  cascabels 
broken  off  and  are  spiked;  30  shell,  whose  fuzes  only  are  damaged,  I 
have  re-fuzed  and  retained  for  the  use  of  this  vessel;  also,  two  chains, 
one  of  45,  the  other  of  60  fathoms,  and  a  very  small  kedge.  About  a 
barrelful  of  loose  grape  and  canister  were  also  found  among  the 
debris,  which  1  am  fitting  for  my  guns. 

Six  water  casks,  some  small  chain  belonging  to  topsail  and  topgallant 
sheets,  spars,  ironwork,  and  a  few  sheets  of  yellow  metal  were  also 
removed;  but  owing  to  the  fact  that  nothing  of  value  to  the  rebels 
now  remained  upon  the  wreck  and  that  many  of  my  men  had  received 
ugly  cuts  and  bruises  from  the  sheets  of  yellow  metal  and  composition 
spikes,  besides  having  to  work  at  times  up  to  their  waists  in  water,  I 
did  not  wreck  the  vessel  quite  so  completely  as  I  should  have  done 
otherwise. 

Nothing  remains  but  the  yellow  metal  and  the  composition  spikes, 
except  some  burned  spars  and  a  little  bent  and  twisted  ironwork. 

Such  is  the  condition  of  my  men’s  health,  in  consequence  of  having 
been  one  year  and  a  month  away  from  a  port  where  they  could  have  a 
run  on  shore,  that  the  slightest  cuts  or  bruises  turn  to  most  malignant 
sores,  and  I  have  a  number  upon  the  list  at  present,  as  well  as  several 
who  are  treated  by  the  doctor  without  being  excused  from  ordinary 
duty,  for  nothing  but  these  causes. 

I  enclose  a  letter  from  the  assistant  surgeon  of  the  vessel,  written 
bjr  my  order,  relating  to  the  health  of  the  crew,  and  I  myself  request 
the  Somerset  be  allowed  a  short  respite  at  Key  West. 

Upon  my  arrival  at  this  pass,  in  attempting  to  run  in  by  the  bar 
buoy,  I  got  ashore.  No  harm  was  done  and  i  backed  off  easily  with 
the  engine  and  waited  till  the  Hudson  came  out,  when  1  followed  that 
steamer  in.  The  buoy  had  drifted  in  the  gale  more  than  a  mile  to  the 
westward. 

I  have  replaced  the  bar  buoy  in  its  original  and  proper  position  and 
have  put  down  also  the  casks  of  the  Amanda,  slung  with  stout  chain 
and  anchored  with  from  500  to  600  pounds  of  kentledge,  in  the  posi¬ 
tions  of  those  buoys  placed  here  by  the  Coast  Survey  and  still  marked 
upon  the  chart. 

I  enclose  a  tracing  of  the  pass,  the  position  of  the  wreck,  with  a  buoy 
marking  the  spot  where  the  Somerset  lay,  which  was  placed  there  by 
me  for  future  guidance. 

The  morning  of  the  12tli  I  sent  my  executive  officer,  Mr.  Chatfield, 
in  the  launch  upon  a  reconnoitering  trip  to  the  eastward,  with  instruc- 


470 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


tions  to  sound  along  the  channel,  and  upon  the  reefs  and  shoals,  ascer¬ 
tain  the  precise  locality  of  the  salt  works,  which  have  been  in  operation 
since  the  commencement  of  this  rebellion,  and  were  said  to  be  situ¬ 
ated  in  the  vicinity  of  Alligator  Bay  [Harbor],  and  note  upon  the 
sketch  I  gave  him,  the  soundings  and  positions  of  the  various  estab¬ 
lishments. 

On  the  morning  of  the  13th,  got  underway,  picked  my  boat  off  the 
east  end  of  Dog  Island,  stood  to  the  eastward,  felt  my  way  with  the 
lead  carefully,  and  came  to  anchor  opposite  the  mouth  of  Alligator  Bay 
[Harbor]  within  1,100  yards  of  the  shore,  and  having  within  easy  range 
of  my  guns  the  most  extensive  set  of  salt  works  I  have  yet  seen  upon 
the  coast. 

I  shelled  the  woods  and  sent  Mr.  Chatfield,  the  executive  officer  in 
command  of  all  the  boats  and  small-arms  men,  ashore  to  destroy  the 
works. 

My  boats  were  protected  with  iron  plating. 

Two  contrabands  came  down,  were  picked  up  by  a  boat  I  sent  on 
shore  after  them,  and  gave  me  some  information  relative  to  other 
works.  These  were  also  destroyed,  I  going  to  one  in  the  launch  and 
Mr.  Chatfield  finishing  the  others. 

I  enclose  his  reports. 

The  expedition  was  entirely  successful.  The  largest  range  of  works 
upon  the  coast  I  think,  which  have  been  so  long  spoken  of  as  in  the 
vicinity  of  East  Pass,  is  at  last  thoroughly  broken  up. 

Sixty-five  salt  kettles  were  destroyed,  more  than  200  bushels  of  salt 
scattered  over  the  sand,  four  distinct  stations  demolished,  and  about 
30  huts  and  houses  with  all  their  apparatus  for  constructing  and  repair¬ 
ing  the  works,  burned  to  the  ground.  We  were  not  opposed  by  any¬ 
one,  all  the  whites  having  fled.  The  horse  company,  however,  was 
expected  there  by  the  contrabands. 

Acting  Master  Chatfield  displayed  much  officer-like  ability  in  his 
management  of  the  small-arms  men  on  shore,  where  more  tact  and 
prudence  are  necessary  than  is  generally  conceded. 

One  of  the  contrabands  above  mentioned,  who  sought  protection  at 
Alligator  Bay  [Harbor],  informs  me  that  at  the  time  he  was  at  work 
near  the  obstructions  of  the  Apalachicola  River,  the  gunboat  Chatta¬ 
hoochee  came  down  to  them  with  the  intention  of  forcing  her  way 
through  and  capturing  the  Port  PoyaVs  boats,  then  upon  an  expedition 
up  that  river;  that  finding  her  means  insufficient,  that  vessel  steamed 
back  toward  the  town  of  Chattahoochee  to  get  more  boats  with  which 
to  achieve  that  object,  and,  owing  to  some  fault  of  the  engineer,  blew 
up,  killing  and  disabling  all  but  18  souls  on  board. 

His  story  is  consistent,  and  he  states  having  himself  seen  the  guns 
at  the  town  and  the  graves  of  the  men.  Four  officers  were  killed. 
One  of  the  guns  is  at  Tallahassee. 

He  also  states  that  the  officials  abandoned  for  the  present  all  attempts 
to  recover  the  spars  and  rigging,  but  devote  all  their  means  toward 
the  completion  of  the  ironclad  building  at  Columbus,  which,  according 
to  my  notion,  will  be  of  about  as  much  service  in  getting  down  the 
river  as  the  famed  Chattahoochee  itself. 

Various  reports  are  current  about  this  ironclad,  and  the  prevalent 
idea  now  is  that  she  draws  7  or  8  feet  water.  If  so,  she  can  not  cross 
the  bar  off  the  town.

I  he  state  of  their  blood  is  so  vitiated  that  I  think  such  a  respite  is 
requisite.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Chatfield,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  preparatory  reconnoissance. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

East  Pass,  St.  George’s  Sound ,  Fla.,  June  If  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  of  reporting  that  in  obedience  to  your  order 
of  the  11th  instant  I  fitted  out  the  ship’s  launch,  taking  with  me  10 
men,  with  provisions  for  three  days,  and  left  the  ship  at  6  o’clock  a.  m. 
on  the  morning  of  the  12th. 

Following  your  instructions,  I  proceeded  to  the  eastward,  in  the 
direction  of  Alligator  Bay  [Harbor].  At  7  a.  m.,  a  heavy  squall  com¬ 
ing  up,  I  was  obliged  to  run  into  a  small  cove  at  the  east  end  of  Dog 
Island,  where  I  anchored  and  awaited  the  passage  of  the  storm. 

At  11  a.  m. ,  the  weather  clearing  up,  I  continued  my  course  to  the 
eastward,  observing  the  locality  of  the  shoals,  taking  soundings  in 
from  fathoms  to  8  feet  water,  noting  them  upon  the  accompanying 
chart. 

At  the  distance  of  about  2  miles  from  the  mouth  of  Alligator  Bay 
[Harbor]  discovered  a  range  of  salt  works,  but  was  unable  to  find  more 
than  10  feet  of  water  at  the  distance  of  1^  miles  from  the  shore. 

Reconnoitering  the  shore  at  the  distance  of  from  one-half  to  three- 
quarters  of  a  mile,  I  discovered  several  other  ranges  of  salt  works,  the 
most  extensive  of  which  are  situated  at  the  mouth  of  Alligator  Bay 
[Harbor],  at  which  place  there  is  good  anchorage  in  12  feet  water  at 
the  distance  of  about  a  mile  from  the  beach. 

Continuing  my  course  some  distance  farther  toward  South  W7est 
Cape,  and  finding  no  more  works  of  any  kind,  I  finished  my  observa¬ 
tions  at  7  p.  m.  and  worked  off  to  Dog  Island  Reef,  where,  the  wind 
being  ahead  and  the  night  coming  in  dark,  I  anchored  and  lay  until 
daylight. 

Getting  underway  at  daylight  next  morning,  I  was  on  my  passage 
returning  to  the  ship  when  I  discovered  her  underway  standing 
toward  us.  I  reported  on  board  at  8:30  o’clock  a.  m. 

I  am  of  the  opinion  that  an  expedition  to  break  up  the  salt  works 
would  be  attended  with  but  little  danger,  as  the  ground  is  too  open 
for  an  ambush  to  be  successful  and  the  operations  of  the  men  can  be 
conducted  under  cover  of  the  guns  of  the  vessel. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Chatfield, 

Acting  Master ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Lieutenant-Commander  A.  F.  Crosman,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Comdg.  U.  S.  S.  Somerset ,  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron , 

East  Pass ,  St.  George's  Sound ,  Fla.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Chatfield,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset,  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

East  Pass,  St.  Georg  eh  Sound,  Fla.,  June  If  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  instructions  directing  me  to  organize  a 
landing  party  for  the  purpose  of  destroying  the  salt  works  at  Alli¬ 
gator  Bay  [Harbor],  I  have  the  honor  to  report  as  follows: 

At  12  o’clock  m.,  assisted  by  Acting  Master  Alexander  Waugh  and 
Master’s  Mate  Thomas  M.  Toombs,  1  landed  in  the  launch,  two  cutters 
and  a  spare  boat,  with  53  seamen  and  the  marine  guard,  in  all  65 
muskets,  together  with  a  party  from  the  engineer’s  division,  armed 
with  sledges  to  break  the  salt  “boilers.  Immediately  upon  landing  I 
detailed  a  working  party,  sent  out  the  marines  as  pickets,  and  deployed 
the  remainder  of  my  force  as  skirmishers  in  the  rear  of  the  huts  to 
protect  the  working  party  in  case  of  attack. 

There  were  destroyed  at  this  place  three  separate  ranges  of  works, 
in  all  45  salt  boilers,  about  200  bushels  of  salt,  and  8  buildings,  large 
and  small,  thus  thoroughly  breaking  up  the  establishments.  We  met 
with  no  opposition,  and  returned  to  the  vessel  at  3  p.  m. 

At  5  o’clock  p.  m. ,  by  your  order,  I  took  the  two  cutters  and  spare 
boat,  carrying  40  men  and  a  contraband  as  guide,  and  proceeded  about 
5  miles  up  Alligator  Bay  [Harbor],  where  I  landed  and  destroyed 
another  range  of  5  boilers  and  burned  1  building. 

Returning,  I  arrived  on  board  at  8:30  p.  m. ,  the  party  under  my 
command  having  destrojmd  9  buildings  and  50  salt  boilers  during  the 
day. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Chatfield, 

Acting  Master,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Lieutenant-Commander  A.  F.  Crosman,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Comdg.  TJ.  S.  S.  Somerset ,  Eastern  Gulf  Bloekdg.  Squadron,

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U  S.  Navy ,  giving  list  of 
prizes  captured  by  the  vessels  of  his  command. 

No.  204.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West ,  June  16,  1863. 

Sir:  Since  my  communication  dated  May  28  and  numbered  186  the 
following  prizes  have  been  made  by  vessels  of  this  squadron: 

May  If — A  flatboat,  with  225  bushels  corn,  by  the  Fort  Henry. 
May  <22. — Sloop  Isabella ,  no  carg-o,  by  the  Fort  Henry. 

May  62f. — Sloop  Fashion ,  49  bales  cotton,  by  the  Port  Royal. 

May  31. — Schooner  Echo ,  125  bales  cotton,  by  the  Sunflower. 

June  1. — A  scow,  56  bales  cotton,  by  the  Fort  Henry. 

June  3. — A  lig-hter,  39  bales  cotton,  by  Fort  Henry  and  Beauregard. 
June  6. — Schooner  Statesman ,  50  to  75  bales  cotton,  by  the  Tahoma. 
June  13. — Pushmataha ,  some  loose  cotton,  by  the  Sunflower. 

You  will  perceive  by  the  above  list  that  the  Fort  Henry  has  dis¬ 
played  much  activity.  The  prizes  made  by  her  have  been  the  result 
of  boat  expeditions  which  have  been  out  constantly  and  which  have 
been  attended  with  enterprise  and  incident. 

The  circumstances  attending-  the  capture  of  the  Fashion  by  the  Port 
Royal  were  detailed  in  the  reports  that  I  forwarded  some  time  since. 


474 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  Sunflower  made  both  of  her  prizes  off  Tortugas.  The  last  prize, 
the  Pushmataha ,  had  thrown  over  her  cargo  before  capture. 

The  Statesman  was  cut  out  from  under  the  guns  of  a  battery  at 
Tampa  by  the  boats  of  the  Tahoma.  The  rebels  had  evidently  regarded 
this  battery,  which  mounted  among  other  pieces  a  rifled  gun,  as  afford¬ 
ing  a  complete  protection  to  the  schooner.  On  the  approach  of  the 
boats,  however,  a  fieldpiece  was  brought  to  bear  upon  them  from  the 
beach,  in  addition  to  the  battery,  and  though  many  of  the  shot  fell 
within  a  few  feet  of  the  boats,  no  person  was  struck,  and  the  schooner 
being  all  ready  for  getting  underway,  her  cable  was  slipped,  and  by 
aid  of  the  boats  and  of  her  sails  she  was  soon  out  of  range. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  July  6,  1863. 

Sir:  The  supply  steamer  Circassian  captured,  on  the  16th  of  June, 
the  sloop  John  Wesley ,  near  St.  Marks,  with  12  bales  of  cotton.  The 
sloop  proved  unseaworthy.  The  cotton  has  been  adjudicated  by  this 
prize  court  and  condemned  as  prize  of  war.  Judge  Marvin,  of  this 
district  court,  has  made  an  order  to  have  this  cotton  shipped  to  New 
York  for  sale  by  Mr.  J.  C.  Clapp,  the  marshal  of  this  district  of 
Florida,  113  Wall  street,  New  York,  who  is  now  in  New  York  to 
attend  to  the  sale  of  prize  propert}^  condemned  here. 

T  on  will  therefore  be  pleased  to  take  this  cotton  (12  bales)  on  board 
and  deliver  the  same  to  the  marshal  aforesaid  on  your  arrival  in  New 
York. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral.

Report,  of  Lieutenant- Commander  ALorris ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  giving  infor¬ 
mation  obtained  from  a  deserter'  regarding  the  destruction  of  the 
C.  S.  S.  Chattahoochee. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Port  Royal, 

Off  Apalachicola,  Fla.,  June  18,  1863. 

1  have  the  honor  to  inform  3Tou  that  a  deserter,  calling  himself 
J.  C.  Cook,  lately  ship’s  cook  of  the  rebel  gunboat  Chattahoochee 
came  on  board  this  vessel  on  the  morning  of  the  8th  instant.  He 
voluntarily  took  the  oath  of  allegiance.  I  will  send  him  to  you  by 
the  first  conveyance.  I  gain  the  following  information  from  him: 

He  says  that  he  was  conscripted  into  the  Confederate  service  on  or 
about  beptember  2,  1862;  was  taken  to  Tallahassee,  at  which  place  he 
shipped  for  the  rebel  gunboat  Chattahoochee  (being  a  seaman)  in 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


475 


preference  to  joining  an  infantry  company.  He  remained  on  board 
said  gunboat  until  the  27th  day  of  May,  on  which  day  she  was 
destroyed  by  the  explosion  of  her  boiler.  At  12  m.  on  said  day  she 
was  lying  at  anchor  at  Blountstown  Bar  with  steam  up,  ready  to  run 
hack  to  the  town  of  Chattahoochee,  from  which  place  she  had  come  the 
day  previous.  Lhe  men  were  at  dinner,  when  suddenly  she  exploded, 
killing  18  men  and  wounding  badly  some  10  or  12  others,  also  some 
slightly,  hhe  sank  that  afternoon.  Among  the  killed  were  three 
engineers,  viz,  Messrs.  Fagan,  Hodges,  and  Arents;  one  midshipman, 
Mr.  Mallory;  the  purser’s  clerk,  and  pilot.  The  exact  cause  of  the 
explosion  he  does  not  know,  but  says  that  the  chief  engineer,  who  was 
carried  on  shore  b}r  him  and  some  others  of  the  crew,  and  who  survived 
some  three  or  four  hours,  said  that  the  cause  was  by  there  being  no 
water  in  the  boilers,  and  that  the  donkey  engine  was  just  then  started 
to  fill_  them  when  the  accident  occurred.  The  river  steamer  William 
JL  1  oung  came  down  from  Chattahoochee  at  midnight  of  same  day  and 
took  the  captain  and  six  men  up  as  far  as  Ochesee,  at  which  place  she 
remained  until  8  a.  m.  of  the  28th,  when  she  ran  down  to  Blountstown 
Bar  and  took  on  board  the  dead  and  wounded,  which  she  conveyed  to 
Chattahoochee,  where  the  dead  were  interred  and  the  wounded  sent  to 
Columbus  on  the  following  day.  After  the  dead  were  buried  the 
4  oung  again  went  down  to  the  wreck  and  got  the  big  guns,  which 
were  carried  to  Columbus.  He  remained  in  Chattahoochee  until  the 
evening  of  June  5,  when  he  took  to  the  woods  with  the  determination 
and  express  purpose  of  reaching  the  blockade  if  possible.  At  1  p.  m. 
last  Saturday  he  arrived  at  Rickoe’s  Bluff,  from  whence  by  land  he 
proceeded  to  Canida  Creek,  at  which  place  he  reached  on  the  6th 
instant,  when  he  got  a  canoe  and  came  to  Apalachicola  at  11  p.  m. 
Here  he  visited  a  friend  and  got  some  clothing.  At  midnight  he  left 
Apalachicola  and  came  direct  to  this  vessel.  He  corroborates  the 
statements  concerning  the  Chattahoochee  which  I  have  previously  sent 
y°u- 

Since  his  arrival  I  have  learned  from  several  other  sources — Dr. 
Chapman  and  others — that  his  statement  is  perfectly  correct.  Four 
of  the  wounded  have  since  died.  Several  belonged  to  Apalachicola. 
There  can  be  no  doubt  but  that  she  is  destroyed. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

[Geo.  U.  Morris], 
Lieutenant- Commander,  U.  iS.  Wavy. 

Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

P.  S. — Since  writing  the  above,  Elias  Lee,  quartermaster  of  and 
deserter  from  the  late  rebel  gunboat  Chattahoochee ,  came  on  board  on 
the  morning  of  the  20th  instant  and  voluntarily  took  the  oath  of  alle¬ 
giance.  He  corroborates  the  statements  of  others  relative  to  the  rebel 
gunboat. 

Owing  to  incompetency  I  have  discharged  my  pilot,  and  said  Lee  is 
so  highly  recommended  by  Union  people  as  being  one  of  the  best 
pilots  not  only  in  the  sound  but  also  on  the  coast,  and  as  the  bad  steer¬ 
ing  of  this  vessel  necessitates  mj^  having  a  pilot,  I  will  retain  him,  with 
your  permission. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  U.  Morris, 

Lieutenant- Commander,  U.  S.  Wavy.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Nickerson ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S. 
schooner  James  S.  Chambers ,  regarding  the  capture  by  that  vessel  of 
the  schooner  Rebekah. 

U.  S.  Schooner  James  S.  Chambers, 

At  Sea^  Lat.  37°  15 ',  Long.  83°  20',  June  18,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report,  viz: 

On  the  morning  of  the  18th  instant,  when  about  30  miles  to  the  west 
of  Charlotte  Harbor,  Fla.,  a  sail  was  discovered  to  the  west  of  us, 
about  9  miles  distant,  steering  north.  I  directed  my  course  for  her, 
seeing  which  she  changed  her  course  directly  from  us.  After  a  seven 
hours’  chase  we  came  up  with  her  and  sent  an  officer  on  board.  She 
proved  to  be  the  schooner  Rebekah ,  and,  as  appears  by  her  papers, 
owned  by  a  British  merchant  in  Havana.  The  captain  reports  that 
he  was  bound  for  Matamoras.  She  has  but  a  small  amount  of  cargo 
on  board,  consisting  of  liquors,  etc.  When  we  boarded  her  Tampa 
Bay  bore  N.  E.  by  E.,  distant  30  miles.  My  reasons  for  making  the 
capture  are,  first,  she  being  found  so  far  from  the  route  to  Mata¬ 
moras,  and  also  the  course  she  was  steering  when  first  discovered,  and 
afterwards  evidently  trying  to  escape  from  us.  I  dispatch  her  for  Key 
West,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  William *J.  Eldredge,  with 
a  prize  crew  of  6  men.  1  retain  one  of  the  crew  of  the  schooner  on 
board  this  vessel,  and  I  shall  improve  the  first  opportunity  of  sending 
him  to  Key  West. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Luther  Nickerson, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

Harriet. 


U.  S.  Gunboat  Tahoma, 

Tampa  Bay ,  Flor  ida ,  June  22,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  of  the  capture  of  the  English 
schooner  Harriet  by  this  vessel  about  10  a.  m.  the  18th  instant  in 
latitude  28°  04'  N.,  longitude  82°  57'  W.,  in  3*  fathoms  of  water, 
Anclote  Keys  bearing  N.  by  E.,  distant  about  7  miles. 

The  Harriet  was  discovered  shortly  after  daylight,  the  18th  instant, 
and  chased  to  where  she  was  captured,  all  possible  measures,  except 
running  ashore,  being  resorted  to  to  avoid  capture. 

The  captain  acknowledged  to  me  that  he  was  trying  to  run  the 
blockade. 

I  enclose  herewith  a  list  of  the  officers  and  crew  of  this  vessel. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  A.  Semmes, 

Lieutenant-  Commander.

U.  S.  Bark  Pursuit, 

Off  Indian  River  Inlet ,  East  Coast  Florida ,  June  23,  1863. 
Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  this  morning,  the  23d 
instant,  at  6  a.  m.,  a  sail  was  discovered  in  Indian  River,  12  miles 
north  of  the  inlet.  Two  boats  were  immediately  dispatched,  Acting 
Ensign  Peter  Heede  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  James  H.  Barry  in 
charge.  They  succeeded  in  capturing  her  and  arrived  at  this  vessel  at 
4  p.  m.  She  proved  to  he  the  sloop  Kate  from  Nassau,  New  Provi¬ 
dence,  with  an  assorted  cargo.  She  had  no  colors  or  papers  of  any 
description  on  hand.  The  captain  acknowledged  that  he  left  Nassau 
on  the  20th  instant  for  the  express  purpose  of  running  the  blockade. 
The  vessel  leaves  for  Key  West  to-morrow  for  adjudication.  I  have 
the  honor  to  enclose  a  full  list  of  the  officers  and  crew  entitled  to  share 
in  the  prize.  No  other  vessels  were  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 
I  have  the  honor  to  remain,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  P.  Randall, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

i  11^  desirable  that  the  fraudulent  practices  mentioned  by  Mr  Liais

It  seems  to  me  that  some  measures  should  be  taken  in  concert  with

ade  in  the  insurgent  States  was  instituted.  Admiral  Bailey  informs  the 
Department  that  over  200  vessels  are  off  the  mouth  of  the  Rio  Grande 
when  ordinarily  there  are  but  6  or  8.  Our  rights  as  a  nation  ought  not 
to  be  sacrificed  because  a  new  question  has  arisen  that  has  not  heretofore 
been  ad]udicated  or  settled  by  diplomatic  arrangement.  Because  the 
Rio  Grande  is  a  neutral  highway,  it  is  not  to  be  used  to  our  injury 
yet  we  know  such  to  be  the  fact,  and  it  seems  to  me  some  effectual 
steps  should  be  taken  to  correct  the  evil.  It  can  be  done,  I  apprehend 
in  a  manner  satisfactory  to  both  countries,  and  a  principle  be  estab¬ 
lished  that  will  be  conformable  to  international  law.  I  must  ask  you  to 
excuse  me  for  earnestly  pressing  this  subject  upon  your  consideration. 

I  would  also  invite  your  special  attention  to  that  portion  of  the  dis¬

of  the  schooner  Robert  Anderson ,  with  British  papers,  was  to  run  a 
regular  mail  from  Belize  to  Matamoras  for  the  Confederate  Govern¬ 
ment.  TV  ould  it  not  be  well  to  inform  the  Secretary  of  War  of  the 
facts  in  relation  to  Vallez,  at  New  Orleans,  that  General  Banks  maybe

Report  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Boyle ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S. 

schooner  Two  Sisters ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  schooner.  Frolic. 

U.  S.  Tender  Two  Sisters, 

Off  Crystal  River ,  June  26,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  on  the  25th  instantoff 
Cedar  Kej^s  two  schooners  hove  in  sight  close  hauled  and  presenting 
a  suspicious  appearance.  Being  at  a  loss  to  decide  which  one  to  chase, 
I  concluded  to  send  the  boat  in  charge  of  Master’s  Mate  Chester  to 
board  the  smaller  vessel  while  I  chased  the  larger  one,  which  I  gained 
on  gradually,  and  soon  made  her  out  to  be  a  large  schooner  loaded 
with  cotton.  The  chase  kept  off  gradually  until  she  steered  S.  E. 
The  wind  freshening,  I  continued  to  gain  on  her  rapidly.  At  11  a.  m. 
made  out  the  U.  S.  S.  Sagamore  standing  toward  us.  At  12:30 
we  were  in  7  feet  water  and  about  2  miles  from  the  chase,  when  I 
opened  fire  on  her  with  the  howitzer.  She  then  commenced  to  heave 
cargo  overboard.  Our  shot  falling  short,  I  ceased  tiring  until  I  got 
close  to,  when  I  fired  a  5-second  shell  which  exploded  close  alongside  of 
her.  She  then  hauled  down  her  flying  jib  and  hove  to,  hoisting  English 
colors.  I  was  then  in  6  feet  of  water.  Having  no  boat  (my  boat 
being  in  chase  of  the  other  vessel),  I  kept  her  hove  to  at  short  range 
until  the  boats  of  the  Sagamore  came  up  and  took  possession  of  her. 
She  proved  to  be  the  English  schooner  Frolic ,  from  Crystal  River 
bound  to  Havana,  with  a  cargo  of  160  bales  of  cotton  and  40  barrels 
turpentine.  Captain  English  took  charge  of  her,  directing  me  to  fol¬ 
low  to  Cedar  Keys.  At  6  p.  m.  our  boat  returned,  having  boarded  the 
other  vessel,  which  proved  to  be  the  tender  Stonewall. 

On  26tli  instant,  at  1  p.  m.,  got  underway  in  company  with  the 
prize  for  Key  West,  and  when  off  Crystal  River  I  concluded  to  stand 
to  the  eastward  in  hopes  of  finding  the  cotton  the  prize  had  thrown 
overboard  during  the  chase,  and  I  succeeded  in  finding  all  of  it,  which 
consisted  of  7  bales. 

Yer}^  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Boyle, 

Acting  Master’s  Mate ,  Commanding. 

Commander  H.  S.  Newcomb, 

U  S.  Flagship  Magnolia.

Report  of  Lieutenant-  Commander  Me  Cauley ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 

77.  S.  S.  Fort  Ilenry ,  commending  the  conduct  of  Acting  Master 

Smith ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  in  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Anna  Maria  and 

other  vessels. 

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  June  30,  1863. 

Admiral:  On  the  27th  instant  I  visited  Deadman’s  Bay  with  the 
Fort  LLenry,  leaving  the  tender  S.  Jackson  to  watch  Cedar  Keys.  An 
expedition  of  5  of  the  boats  of  this  vessel  brought  out  of  the  Stein- 
hatchee  River  the  schooner  Anna  Maria ,  loaded  with  cotton.  A  con¬ 
traband  who  demanded  the  protection  of  the  flag  informs  me  that  her 
captain,  a  man  by  the  name  of  Shaw,  pretty  well  known  at  Key  West, 
had  gone  the  previous  day  to  Tallahassee. 

In  obedience  to  your  direction,  in  General  Order  No.  1,  I  report 
Acting  Master  R.  B.  Smith  for  his  enterprise  in  making'  captures. 
He  is  the  officer  who,  with  the  boats  of  this  vessel  and  Sagamore,  cut 
the  G.  Z.  Rrockenborough  out  of  Apalach[icola]  River,  under  guerrilla 
fire;  he  captured  the  Annie  in  this  vessel’s  launch;  commanded  the 
boats  of  this  vessel  that  captured  the  Ranger;  also  the  scow  load  of 
corn  lately  forwarded,  and  has  now  captured  the  Anna  Maria  7  miles 
up  the  Steinhatchee  River. 

Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  Stevens  was  transferred  to  the  J.  S. 
Chambers  on  her  arrival,  in  accordance  with  Dr.  Tourtellotte’s  orders. 
Not  having  received  at  that  time  Dr.  Stevens’s  orders,  I  transferred 
him  and  his  steward,  but  did  not  permit  the  nurse  to  go. 

Ihe  officers  and  crew  of  the  Fort  Henry  are  gratified  with  the  rear- 
admiral’s  appreciation  of  their  exertions,  in '  their  small  sphere  of 
action,  contracted  as  it  is  by  the  unseaworthiness  of  the  Fort  Henry 
herself,  which  precludes  visiting  other  points  of  the  coast  under  their 
surveillance,  which  if  attended  to  might  offer  more  opportunities  for 
harassing  the  enemy. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley, 

1  nontenant-  Commander,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  Comdg  TJ.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Rlockdg.  Squadron.

Letter  from  Acting  Fear- Admiral  Bailey ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  to  Rear-Admiral 
Farragut ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  forwarding  papers  relating  to  the  case  of  the 
British  schooner  Comet. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Magnolia, 

Key  West ,  July  3,  1863 . 

.  Sir:  I  enclose  herewith  copies  of  a  letter  from  her  Britannic  Majesty’s 
vice-consul  at  this  place,  a  list  of  articles  allege^  to  have  been  missing 
from  the  British  schooner  Comet  when  in  charge  of  the  prize  crew 
from  the  U.  S.  gunboat  JCancvwha,  a  letter  from  myself  to  Captain 
Goldsborough,  a  letter  from  Lieutenant-Commander  W.  K.  Mayo  to 
Captain  Goldsborough,  and  a  report  from  Acting  Master  Thomas  C. 
Dunn  to  Lieutenant-Commander  Mayo. 

When  this  matter  was  reported  to  me  the  Kanawha! s  people,  having 
been  discharged  by  the  district  court,  were  on  board  the  steamer  Eugenie, 
to  return  to  this  vessel.  I  had  issued  the  order  to  detain  them  that  the 
proper  investigation  should  be  had,  when  the  prize  master  came  to  me 
with  the  former  captain  of  the  prize  and  represented  that  the  alleged 
depredations  had  been  committed  by  others  than  this  prize  crew,  also 
belonging  to  the  Kanawha ,  who  had  been  in  charge  of  the  Comet  dur¬ 
ing  the  night  previous  to  her  leaving  for  this  place.  Of  course,  there¬ 
fore,  no  investigation  could  be  had  here,  and  I  referred  the  question 
to  the  commanding  officer  off  Mobile,  not  only  as  being  an  alleo-ed 
breach  of  naval  discipline,  but  as  a  matter  which  would  be  referred  to 
ie  British  Government. 

The  statement  of  Acting  Master  Dunn  appears  perfectly  satisfactory 
to  me,  although  the  whole  affair  has  passed  out  of  my  hands;  but  the 
peculiar  tone  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Mayo’s  letter  (together  with 
his  injudicious  use  of  adjectives,  his  incorrect  statement  of  points,  his 
wild  reasoning,  and  his  arbitrary  conclusions)  has  induced  the  belief 
that  he  is  intellectually  incapable  of  grasping  the  fact  that  the  accusa¬ 
tion  comes  from  others  than  myself,  and  that  he  requires  some  judi¬ 
cious  advice  as  to  the  proper  temper  to  be  preserved  in  his  official 
correspondence.  I  would  therefore  leave  the  matter  in  your  bands 
as  his  immediate  superior  and  commanding  officer,  for  such  action  as 
will  correct  these  little  defects  and  enhance  the  value  of  Lieutenant- 
Gommander  Mayo’s  talents  in  the  services  of  the  Government. 

Respectfully, 

.  7  _  .  7  .  Tiieodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Sguadron. 

Rear-Admiral  D.  G.  Farragut,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Western  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  you  herewith  a  copy  of  a  communi¬ 
cation  received  by  me  from  Lieutenant-Commander  E.  Y.  McCauley 
in  relation  to  the  brave  assault  made  by  Oi’derly  Sergeant  Nugent  and 
4  men  upon  a  rebel  breastwork  fortification.  In  this  assault  the 
orderly  sergeant  and  his  comrades  drove  a  guard  of  11  rebels  into 
the  swamp,  capturing  their  arms  and  destroying  their  camp  equipage, 
withholding  his  fire  with  manly  and  commendable  discretion  lest  he 
should  wound  or  kill  a  woman  who  was  among  the  fugitives.  I  would 
respectfully  suggest  whether  the  conduct  of  Orderly  Sergeant  Nugent 
does  not  bring  him  within  that  class  of  men  who  should  receive  the 
medal  of  honor  authorized  by  Congress  to  be  given  to  “such  petty 
officers,  seamen,  and  marines  as  shall  most  distinguish  themselves  by 
gallantry  in  action,”  etc. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

T.  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  /Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,
