U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  June  17 ,  1863. 

Admiral:  Having  had  need  of  an  extra  boat  to  relieve  those  of  this 
vessel  watching  along  the  coast  between  this  and  the  Crystal  River,  I 
had  the  sloop  boat,  captured  on  the  9th  instant,  fitted  up.  Orderly 
Sergeant  C.  Nugent  superintended  the  work  with  skill  and  zeal.  On 
the  11th  instant  she  was  manned  by  6  of  the  guard  of  this  vessel  and 
sent  in  charge  of  Sergeant  Nugent  to  the  Withlacoochee  with  orders 
to  watch  for  the  appearance  of  the  Frolic. 

On  the  15th  instant  he  reconnoitered  6  miles  up  the  Crystal  River; 
a  log  breastwork  attracting  his  attention,  he  landed  with  4  men  and 
drove  a  guard  of  11  rebel  soldiers  into  the  swamp.  One  shot  was 
fired  by  the  officer  in  command,  which  took  effect  in  the  sergeant’s 
waist  pouch.  The  fire  was  not  returned  by  the  guard,  the  sergeant’s 
gallantry  not  permitting  it,  as  there  was  a  woman  among  the  fugitives. 

A  number  of  papers  were  found,  which  I  forward.  The  deserter 
mentioned  in  one  is  the  Hy.  Sellwood,  ordinary  seaman,  deserter 
from  one  of  my  boats.  Apparently  the  squad  numbered  13  men  on 
the  rolls. 

The  order  given  by  Captain  Chambers  in  another  paper  about  call¬ 
ing  on  the  crew  of  the  Frolic  to  defend  the  place  in  case  of  our 
attack,  [is]  interesting,  if  it  be  true  that  she  sails  under  British  colors. 

Enclosed  please  find  list  of  the  marines  who  manned  the  guard  boat 
and  of  the  arms,  etc. ,  brought  off.  They  had  no  means  for  bringing

off  the  tents  and  camp  equipage.  I  will  forward  the  arms,  etc.,  to 
Key  West  by  the  U.  S.  schooner  Two  Sisters. 

Very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley,

Report  off  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  requesting  a 
commanding  officer  for  the  flagship. 

No.  228.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  July  6‘,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  pleasure  to  report  the  arrival  of  this  vessel  on  the 
evening  of  the  1st  instant,  and  that  my  flag  was  transferred  to  her  on 
the  morning  of  the  4th. 

From  the  fact  that  Lieutenant-Commander  Chandler  has  been  sent 
out  in  charge  of  the  vessel  and  that  he  is  at  the  same  time  detached 
from  this  squadron,  I  fear  it  was  the  intention  of  the  Department  that 
I  should  command  my  own  flagship;  but  with  the  amount  of  attention 
demanded  of  me  by  my  more  important  duties  as  commander  in  chief  of 
the  squadron,  it  is  impossible  for  me  to  do  this  properly,  and  I  am  not 
satisfied  to  leave  it  to  her  executive  officer.  The  San  Jacinto ,  being’ a 
vessel  of  the  second  class,  would,  I  suppose,  as  flagship,  be  assigned  to 
a  commander;  I  would  therefore  request  that  one  of  the  following 
officers,  viz,  Commander  James  H.  Strong,  Commander  Reed  Werdeif 
Commander  Edward  Donaldson,  Commander  John  C.  Howell  Com¬ 
mander  George  H.  Cooper,  Commander  John  C.  Febiger,  Commander 
Somerville  Nicholson,  be  ordered  to  command  her,  if  consistent  with 
the  views  of  the  Department  and  not  distasteful  to  the  officer  himself. 
Among  these  I  would  prefer  to  have  Commander  Howell. 

Should  such  an  arrangement  be  impossible  or  inexpedient,  I  propose 
to  transfer  Lieutenant-Commander  F.  \ .  McCauley  to  the  command 
of  this  vessel  and  to  relieve  him  with  Lieutenant-Commander  Quacken- 
bush  in  the  command  of  the  Fort  Henry.  In  that  event  I  would  desire 
to  have  a  lieutenant  sent  out  as  executive  officer  of  this  vessel  and  if 
possible,  a  graduate  of  the  Academy  as  a  drill  officer. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Van  Sice ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U  S.  S. 

Sunflower,  regarding  the  chase  by  the  U  S.  S.  Sunflower  of  the 

U  S.  S.  Union  for  a  supposed  blockade  runner. 

U.  S.  S.  Sunflower, 
Tortugas,  July  6,  1863. 

Sir:  I  beg  to  report  that  yesterday  morning  at  2  o’clock,  while 
cruising  to  the  northward  of  the  Quicksand  Passage,  made  a  steamer 
heading  for  the  passage.  Immediately  went  to  quarters  and  gave 
chase.  After  coming  up  some  on  him,  commenced  firing  to  bring  him 
to.  After  firing  several  shell,  he  stopped,  when  I  ceased  firing.  A  few 
minutes  afterwards  lie  started  off  at  full  speed,  when  I  again  shelled 
him  and  continued  chasing  and  shelling  him,  until  I  finally  succeeded 
in  bringing  him  to  after  a  three-hours’  chase.  She  proved  to  be  the 
U.  S.  S.  Union.  Without  being  presumptuous,  allow  me  to  suggest 
it  would  be  better  for  our  armed  steamers  to  ascertain  a  vessel’s  char¬ 
acter  before  endeavoring  to  run  away  from  her. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edw,  Van  Sice, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Expedition  in  Peace  Greek ,  Charlotte  Harbor ,  Florida ,  for  the  capture 
of  schooner  Ann  and  a  small  sloop ,  July  6-9 ,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Master  Browne,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  bark  Restless. 

U.  S.  Bark,  Restless, 
Charlotte  Harbor,  Fla. ,  July  10,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  1: 30  p.  m.  of  the  6th  instant, 
having  learned  from  two  refugees,  named  James  Henry  Thompson 
and  Milledge  Brannen,  that  two  vessels  were  seen  at  daylight  that 
morning  off  Cape  Haze  attempting  to  run  out,  loaded  with  cot¬ 
ton,  1  dispatched  Acting  Ensigns  Eason  and  Russell  and  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter’s  Mate  Browne,  with  the  first  and  second  cutters  of  this  ship  with 
33  of  our  crew,  and  the  refugees  as  pilots,  all  armed  and  equipped,  to 
the  tender  sloop  Rosalie ,  which  was  at  that  time  stationed  behind  Pine 
Island,  with  written  instructions  to  Acting  Ensign  Charles  P.  Clark, 
commanding  th z  Rosalie.  The  surgeon  of  this  ship,  Doctor  Page,  accom¬ 
panied  the  expedition.  Our  boats,  not  finding  the  Rosalie  at  Pine 
Island,  proceeded  up  Peace  Creek  to  Punta  Gorda  and  anchored  until 
the  next  morning  (the  7th),  when  they  discovered  the  Rosalie  about 
5  miles  above  them.  It  appears  that  the  Rosalie  had  changed  her 
position  to  the  mouth  of  Peace  Creek,  when,  discovering  the  two  ves¬ 
sels  some  miles  above  at  anchor,  she  attempted  to  go  to  them  and  had 
gone  thus  far  when  she  grounded,  the  vessels  meanwhile  getting 
underway  and  sailing  up  the  creek  out  of  sight.  The  boats,  together 
with  the  sloop,  now  slowly  proceeded  up  the  creek,  the  sloop  frequently 
grounding.  About  sunset  it  being  impossible  to  get  farther  with  the 
sloop,  the  boats  anchored  for  the  night. 

At  6  o’clock  the  following  morning,  the  8th  instant,  the  first  and 
second  cutters,  in  command  of  Acting  Ensigns  Eason  and  Russell,  pro¬ 
ceeded  5  miles  farther  up  to  Horse  Creek,  where  they  found  the  two 


488 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


vessels,  the  schooner  Ann,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  and  a  small 
sloop,  both  apparently  loaded  with  cotton.  No  one  was  on  board  of 
them.  Mr.  Eason  with  5  men  took  possession  of  the  schooner,  and 
Mr.  Russell  with  2  men  of  the  sloop,  and  towed  them  with  the  boats 
to  the  Rosalie.  By  means  of  poling,  towing,  and  sailing,  the  Rosalie 
the  boats  and  the  two  prizes  arrived  at  Punta  Gorda  at  dark,  where 
they  anchored  for  the  night.  At  daylight  on  the  moring  of  the  9th, 
the  prize  schooner,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Eason,  and  the  prize 
sloop,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Russell,  got  underway  and,  with  the 
RosaUe  and  the  boats,  arrived  at  this  vessel  about  2  o’clock  p.  m. ;  the 
Rosalie,  on  account  of  the  rough  weather,  taking  the  prize  sloop  in  tow 
oft  Cape  Haze. 

I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  a  copy  of  my  instructions  to  Acting 
Ensign  Charles  P.  Clark,  commanding  the  Rosalie. 

The  commanding  officer  of.  the  Gem  of  the  Sea,  which  has  relieved 
this  vessel  at  this  station,  having  occasion  to  send  the  Rosalie  to  Key 
West,  I  embrace  the  opportunity  of  sending  the  prizes  in  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  Clark  commanding  her. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding .

Letter  of  commendation  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Acting  Master 
Browne,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U,  S.  bark  Restless. 


U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  July  18,  1863. 

Sir:  It  is  gratifying  to  me,  so  soon  after  your  arrival  on  the  sta¬ 
tion,  to  have  occasion  to  commend  you  for  planning,  and  the  officers 
and  men  of  the  Restless  and  Rosalie  for  executing,  the  expedition  up 
Peace  Creek,  which  resulted  in  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Ann  and 
a  small  sloop.  Enterprises  of  this  sort,  when  successfully  accom¬ 
plished,  are  of  far  greater  value  than  the  mere  amount  of  the  capture, 
by  disheartening  the  enemy  and  encouraging  our  own  men. 

You  will  read  this  letter  to  the  officers  and  crew  of  the  Restless  at 
general  muster. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailet,

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  requesting  the  approval  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment  of  a  promotion  for  Acting  Ensign  Clark,  U.  S.  Navy. 

No.  249.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  July  18,  1863. 

Sir:  As  I  have  already  informed  the  Department,  the  prize  sloop 
Rosalie  was  taken  into  the  service  on  the  appraisement  of  the  court,

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Acting  Master 
Zerega ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Antona,  to  cruise  in  search 
of  the  U  S.  Army  schooners  Tortugas  and  Matchless. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  July  7,  1863. 

Sir:  You  will  please  prepare  your  vessel  for  sea  with  all  possible 
dispatch,  and  as  soon  as  she  is  ready  proceed  with  her  to  the  Tortugas 
and  enquire  into  the  following  matter:  It  has  been  reported  to  me 
that  the  army  schooner  Toidugas  left  that  place  on  the  1st  instant  for 
this  port,  and  although  the  wind  and  weather  have  been  favorable  since 
then,  she  has  not  yet  arrived.  The  army  schooner  Matchless  was  also 
to  have  started  from  there  on  the  5th,  and  she,  too,  has  failed  to  arrive. 
It  is  possible  that  the  Tortugas  may  have  got  aground  on  the  quick¬ 
sands  on  the  reef,  and  the  Matchless  may  either  have  gone  to  her  assist¬ 
ance  or  not  have  sailed  at  the  appointed  time.  It  is  also  possible  that 
the  Tortugas  may  have  been  dismasted  in  a  squall,  and  be  drifting  with 
the  Gulf  Stream.  But  as  a  vague  rumor  has  arrived  at  the  same  time 
with  this  news  that  a  privateer  bark  was  supposed  to  be  prowling  in 
that  vicinity,  it  is  not  impossible  that  one  or  both  of  these  schooners 
may  have  been  surprised  and  captured  by  her.  You  will  therefore  be 
careful  to  have  your  vessel  thoroughly  prepared  for  action  in  approach¬ 
ing  any  strange  vessel.  Should  you  find  either  of  the  two  schooners  in 
distress,  you  will  render  her  every  assistance  in  your  power;  otherwise 
you  will  continue  on  to  the  Tortugas,  gather  all  the  information  possi¬ 
ble  relating  to  this  matter,  return  with  all  possible  dispatch  to  this 
place,  and  report  to  me.  Enquire  particularly  into  the  rumor  of  a 
privateer,  and  whether  anything  like  burning  vessels  have  been  seen 
from  the  Tortugas  or  elsewhere. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  requesting  the 
prompt  return  to  his  command  of  the  U  S.  S.  Magnolia. 

No.  238.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  July  11,  1863. 

Sir:  In  sending  the  Magnolia  north  for  new  boilers,  agreeably  to 
the  orders  of  the  Department,  I  would  most  urgently  request  that  she 
may  be  returned  to  this  squadron,  as  from  her  great  speed  and  capacity, 
together  with  her  light  draft,  she  is  eminently  adapted  to  the  duty  of 
carrying  supplies  to  the  vessels  on  permanent  blockade  along  the  coast, 
and,  incidentally,  also  of  capturing  blockade  runners  while  passino- 
back  and  forth.  I  know  of  no  vessel  that  could  perform  this  service 
with  equal  advantage  to  the  public  interests,  and  her  temporary 
incapacity  has  been  of  serious  detriment  by  obliging  me  to  charter 
merchant  vessels  or  to  withdraw  the  fast  cruisers  from  the  important 
duty  of  the  offshore  blockade  in  order  to  keep  the  others  supplied. 
I  therefore  hope  that  the  necessary  work  to  render  her  efficient  may 
be  hurried  as  much  as  possible. 

I  would  also  request  that  two  additional  24-pounder  howitzers  be 
added  to  her  armament. 

1  would  further  remind  the  Department  that  the  Magnolia  is  a  fourth- 
rate,  and  would  state  that  in  consequence  of  this  a  commander  is  natu- 
rally  averse  to  be  assigned  to  her;  at  the  same  time,  I  consider  it 
important  tor  many  reasons  that  she  should  be  in  charge  of  a  regular 
officer.  °  " 

Respectfully, 

.  ±.  „  ,  ,  .  ,  Theodorus  Bailey,

Boat  expeditions  from  U.  S.  steamers  Somerset  and  Stars  and  Stripes 
to  St.  Marks  River  and  Marsh's  Island ,  Apalachee  Bay ,  July  12 
and  15,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  July  30,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  an  expedition,  consisting  of  5  armed 
boats  from  the  steamer  Somerset  and  3  from  the  steamer  Stars  and 
Stripes,  together  with  an  ambulance  boat,  the  whole  under  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Crosman,  and  numbering  130  persons,  started  up  the  St. 
Marks  River  on  the  night  of  the  12th  instant,  mainly  with  a  view  to 
making  a  thorough  reconnoissance,  and,  incidentally,  also  to  inflicting 
such  damage  upon  the  enemy  as  the  circumstances  might  render  feas¬ 
ible.  Every  precaution  was  taken  to  avoid  observation  until  such  time 
as  an  opportunity  should  present  itself  for  striking  an  unexpected 
blow;  but  the  promise  of  rain  was  not  kept,  and  this,  together  with  the 
unfortunate  vigilance  and  promptness  of  a  picket  stationed  at  Port 
Leon,  rendered  further  secrecy  impossible.  A  few  shots  were  ex¬ 
changed,  and  one  of  our  men  was  slightly  wounded,  and  as  their  signal 
fires  and  alarm  guns  showed  an  instant  state  of  readiness,  as  also  it 
was  known  that  600  rebel  troops  could  be  concentrated  at  an  hour’s 
notice,  the  boats  were  withdrawn,  having  first  ascertained  that  the 
channel  was  obstructed  about  1,000  yards  below  Port  Leon,  so  that  the 
vessels  could  not  pass  up.  Under  the  circumstances  any  further  opera¬ 
tions  in  that  direction  were  wisely  abandoned,  beyond  throwing  a  few 
shell  at  the  trains,  which  were  bringing  in  troops  from  Tallahassee,  and 
burning  the  stairway  of  the  light-house,  where  a  lookout  is  kept. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Crosman  then  turned  his  attention  to  some 
salt  works  on  Marsh’s  Island,  near  the  Ocklockonee  River,  from  which 
it  was  supposed  the  men  had  probably  been  called  in  for  the  defense 
of  St.  Marks,  and  where  consequently  our  men  destroyed  50  salt 
boilers,  together  with  the  buildings  attached  and  some  60  bushels  of 
salt,  without  opposition  or  loss,  beside  capturing  3  prisoners  and  res¬ 
cuing  6  contrabands. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Crosman  is  warm  in  his  commendation  of 
the  officers  and  men  of  both  vessels  acting  under  his  orders,  both  as  to 


494 


BAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


their  spirit  and  efficiency,  and  I  am  constrained  to  express  the  same 
opinion  of  him. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Detailed  report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Crosman,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  D.  S.  S. 

Somerset. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset, 

East  Pass ,  St.  George! s  Sound ,  July  16,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  5th  I  requested  Lieutenant-Commander  Morris  to  send 
me  the  Chambers  at  this  place,  that  I  might  leave  that  vessel  to  main¬ 
tainable  blockade  while  I  went  to  St.  Marks  to  relieve  the  Stars  and 
Stripes  in  case  she  needed  coal,  as  I  expected,  and  to  destroy  all  the 
salt  works  in  that  vicinity. 

On  the  8th  the  Chambers  anchored  in  East  Pass. 

The  morning  of  the  12th  got  underway  for  St.  Marks,  anchored  off 
Ocklockonee  Shoal  at  about  3  p.  m.,  13  miles  from  the  light-house,  and 
fired  a  gun  upon  my  arrival.  The  Stars  and  Stripes  was  soon  along¬ 
side.  Captain  Willcomb  told  me  he  had  plenty  of  coal,  and  I  would 
have  returned,  but  it  occurred  to  me  that  no  moon  would  be  up  that 
night;  that  it  was  nearly  change;  that  there  was  generally  a  smart 
breeze  during  the  night;  that  the  tides  were  spring  and  neap,  or  nearly 
so,  and  I  ordered  him  to  prepare  all  his  men  and  boats  for  a  night 
expedition. 

After  the  shades  of  evening  had  shut  in  the  vessels  from  the  vigilant 
gaze  of  the  rebel  pickets  in  the  light-house  both  ships  got  underway, 
steamed  up  to  the  bar,  and  anchored. 

At  9  p.  m.  five  boats  from  the  Somerset  and  three  from  the  Stars 
and  Stripes  shoved  off,  formed  line  ahead,  and  pulled  for  the  mouth  of 
the  river.  The  oars  were  all  muffled  and  a  spare  set  of  mufflers  was 
in  each  boat.  Each  man  had  his  metal  bayonet  scabbard  covered  with 
blue  flannel  and  a  white  cap  to  be  put  on  at  the  order.  Handcuffs  and 
spare  trailing  lines  were  also  provided  to  secure  the  prisoners. 

Before  starting  the  officers  were  told  the  object  of  the  expedition, 
which  was  the  first  intimation  they  received.  This  was  to  pass  up  the 
St.  Marks  to  the  Wakulla  River  above  the  hospital,  land,  storm  the 
battery  and  spike  the  guns,  then  embark,  make  a  dash  at  Newport, 
capture  the  Spray ,  make  prize  of  all  the  cotton  in  that  neighborhood’ 
burn  the  Government  buildings,  which  are  extensive  and  valuable,  and 
come  down  the  river  in  the  Spray ,  whose  two  guns  beside  our  own 
rifles  would  effectually  scour  the  banks. 

No  precaution  was  neglected,  and  all  were  enthusiastic  and  sanguine 
of  success. 

.  With  the  young  flood  tide,  at  9  p.  m.,  we  pulled  for  the  mouth  of  the 
river.  On  entering  it  the  pilot  came  into  my  boat  and  the  line  pro¬ 
ceeded  slowly  and  silently,  threading  its  way  among  the  oyster  bars 
and  numerous  shoals  of  the  channel.  I  led  the  boats,  and  the  Somerset1  s 
boats  preceded  those  of  the  Stars  and  Stripes ,  the  ambulance  boat 
bringing  up  the  rear.  We  numbered  130,  all  told. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


495 


The  picket  fires  could  be  seen  dimly  burning  near  the  light-house 
and  about  the  solid  ground  to  the  east  of  the  river,  and  one  faint  light 
showed  itself  at.  Port  Leon  about  1^  miles  from  the  battery  at  St. 
Marks,  near  which  light  we  must  pass  within  less  than  10(4  yards. 
The  clouds  which  in  starting  had  obscured  the  stars  were  fast  fading 
away,  and  the  fresh  breeze  too  had  died  entirely  out.  Yet  there  was 
no  moon,  and  I  hoped  we  might  pass  unobserved  by  keeping-  close 
against  the  west  bank,  where  the  boats  would  be  projected  against  the 
high  swamp  grass  of  the  shore.  I  had  given  orders  that  if  we  should 
be  fired  upon  by  a  picket,  no  one  was  to  return  it  without  an  order. 

Pulling  silently  and  slowly  close  in  to  the  grass,  no  noise  could  be 
heard,  save  the  plash  of  the  water  as  it  struck  the  bows  of  the  boats 
and  rippled  past,  and  we  reached  Port  Leon,  when  the  picket  hailed 
us.  All  the  boats  laid  on  their  oars.  I  replied  to  his  hail,  that  I  had 
been  fishing  down  the  river  and  was  going  up  to  St.  Marks  to  sell  the 
fish. 

He  hailed  again  and  told  me  to  come  on  shore.  I  replied  that  I  was 
coming,  and  whispering  to  my  executive  officer  to  keep  the  boats  in 
their  present  position,  went  toward  the  fire  with  the  intention  of  cap¬ 
turing  the  guard  before  they  could  give  the  alarm.  Presently  a  brand 
was  thrown  in  the  air,  the  fire  commenced  to  burn  brightly,  two  or 
three. caps  snapped,  then  apparently  having  found  one  that  would  go, 
the  picket  sent  a  bullet  through  the  biceps  muscle  of  one  of  my  men 
in  the  launch.  Four  or  five  shots  were  given  us,  and  seeing  the  signal 
fires  blazing  up  brightly  all  about  the  east  part  of  the  river,  knowing 
the  surprise  was  now  over  and  no  chance  of  effecting  our  purpose 
remained,  I  gave  orders  to  return  the  fire. 

Two  signal  guns  were  fired  from  the  battery,  and  everything 
denoted  consternation  and  alarm  upon  the  part  of  the  enemy.  Had 
I  kept  on  I  should  have  pulled  through  a  narrow  river  exposed  for  1 
mile  to  the  raking  fire  of  the  battery,  to  the  fire  of  skirmishers  upon 
the  east  bank,  and  probably  by  the  time  I  arrived  my  force  would 
have  been  so  reduced  as  to  make  an  assault  the  result  of  mere  folly. 
I  therefore  with  much  regret  gave  the  order  to  retreat,  formed  the 
line  in  reverse  order,  bringing  up  the  rear  myself,  and  pulled  quietly 
back;  the  Stars  and  Stripes’  launch  which  I  had  ordered  to  lead  the 
retreat,  on  account  of  her  great  draft  of  water,  capturing  a  sailboat 
with  compass,  provisions,  cigars,  charts,  etc.,  on  the  way.  Two  men 
who  were  in  the  boat  jumped  out  and  had  to  wade  some  2  miles 
through  swamps  to  reach  solid  ground. 

We  reached  the  ships  at  5  a.  m.  on  the  13th. 

Meade,  the  man  wounded,  will  soon  be  well  again,  as  his  wound  is 
quite  slight. 

The  afternoon  of  the  13th  two  cars  were  seen  to  come  into  St. 
Marks  and  shortly  after  another  train,  no  doubt  bringing  troops  from 
Tallahassee. 

I  steamed  in  toward  Spanish  Hole,  shelling  the  troops  about  the 
light-house,  the  Stars  and  Stripes  doing  the  same.  The  morning  of 
the  14th  I  anchored  in  Spanish  Hole,  sent  a  boat  on  shore  to  pull  to 
pieces  a  shed  at  the  light-house  that  I  might  have  material  to  build  a 
coal  bin  around  my  steam  drum,  and  also  stakes  to  put  down  upon  the 
bars  of  the  river. 

I  went  myself  then  to  the  last  stake,  which  marks  the  point  of  an 
oyster  bar  about  1,000  yards  to  the  southward  of  Port  Leon,  and  found 
a  scow  sunk  with  about  100  tons  of  stone,  right  in  the  channel.  My 


496 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADKON. 


vessel  was  all  ready  to  go  up,  and  had  it  not  been  for  this  obstruction, 
insurmountable  as  it  is,  I  am  quite  sure  I  could  have  whipped  the 
rebels  from  their  battery,  spiked  the  guns,  captured  the  Spray,  and 
destroyed  Newport. 

I  neglected  to  state  that  the  Spray  came  down  on  the  13th  within 
about  4  miles  of  my  vessel  and  hoisted  a  flag  of  truce.  I  responded 
with  one  at  the  fore,  and  when  a  boat  came  from  her,  sent  Mr.  Chat- 
field,  the  executive  officer,  in  the  launch  with  a  flag  of  truce  to  com¬ 
municate  with  her.  The  object,  1  think,  was  to  reconnoiter,  but  the 
only  question  they  desired  to  propound  was  in  relation  to  the  white  and 
yellow  flag  at  the  main,  which  they  had  supposed  to  be  a  flag  of  truce. 

The  Spray’s  boat  met  mine  equally  distant  from  the  vessels.  No 
information  whatever  was  elicited. 

On  the  15th  1  landed  and  burned  out  the  stairway  of  the  light-house, 
besides  a  quantity  of  corn  stored  there.  I  think  it  will  be  some  time 
before  the  rebel  pickets  can  use  the  light-house  as  a  lookout. 

.  Giving  up  all  idea  of  taking  the  battery  on  account  of  the  obstruc¬ 
tions,  I  got  underway  at  9  a.  m.  of  the  15th,  and  in  company  with  the 
Stars  and  Stripes  steamed  down  to  the  northward  of  Ocklockonee 
Bay.  Here  we  arrived  at  12:30,  and  all  the  boats  were  sent  on  shore 
to  destroy  the  salt  works.  My  executive  officer,  Mr.  Chatfield,  had 
command  of  the  expedition,  and  performed  his  duty  in  a  highly  credita¬ 
ble  and  officer-like  manner.  1  enclose  his  report: 

Some  60  bushels  of  salt,  a  number  of  shanties,  and  50  salt  boilers 
were  destroyed. 

Three  white  men  and  six  negroes  were- also  captured,  the  latter 
coming  off  voluntarily. 

I  will  send  them  to  you  by  the  first  opportunity. 

Oil  the  16th  I  got  underway,  parted  company  with  the  Stars  and 
Stripes ,  and  arrived  here  in  the  evening. 

During  the  night  expedition  up  the  river,  ashore  at  the  salt  works, 
and  during  the  time  Captain  Willcomb  was  cooperating  with  me,  I  was 
much  pleased  with  the  activity  and  ardor  with  which  he  obeyed  my 
instructions.  His  officers  and  men  also  did  their  duty,  and  the  execu¬ 
tive  officer  of  the  Stars  and  Stripes  was  always  careful,  energetic,  and 
attentive.  As  regards  my  own  officers,  I  have  frequently  written  of 
Mr.  Chatfield,  who  merits  the  favorable  consideration  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment,  and  all  did  their  whole  duty. 

1  regret  the  failure  of  a  long-cherished  scheme,  but  would  not  have 
regretted  it,  I  am  confident,  had  the  weather  proved  propitious.  Had 
that  rascally  picket  not  proved  so  vigilant  and  wakeful,  the  attempt 
would  have  been  a  complete  success,  and  1  should  have  had  the  pleasure 
of  sending  you  perhaps  600  or  700  bales  of  cotton.  Or  had  the  night 
proved  what  the  clouds  seemed  to  presage,  a  dark  and  rainy  one,  the 
tale  would  have  been  different. 

I  enclose*  a  sketch  of  the  battery,  a  tracing  of  the  river,  and  have 
drawn  a  diagram  illustrating  the  position  of  the  scow,  or  obstruction 
in  the  channel. 

I  am  still  convinced,  sir,  that  with  my  men  drilled  as  they  are  so  as 
to  be  obedient  to  the  bugle  call  when  acting  as  skirmishers,  I  can  whip 
the  lebels  off  of  the  point  at  8t.  Marks.  But  to  achieve  any  great 
lesult  I  would  like  200  or  300  soldiers;  with  them  and  my  own  men 
1  could  march  up  to  Newport,  capture  any  quantity  of  cotton,  perhaps 


*  See  page  500.

1,000  bales,  then  come  down  the  river  to  St.  Marks,  storm  the  fort, 
cut  the  wires,  tear  up  the  railroad  track,  and  throw  the  guns  into  the 
river,  returning  to  the  ships  in  the  Spray. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Chatfield,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  expedition  to  Marsh’s  Island 

for  the  destruction  of  salt  works. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset,  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Off  Ocklockonee  Bay ,  Fla. ,  July  16,  1863. 

'  Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  your  order 
directing  me  to  organize  an  expedition  for  the  purpose  of  destroying 
the  salt  works  on  Marsh’s  Island,  Apalachee  Bay,  I  left  the  ship  at 
1  o’clock jp.  m.  J uly  15,  with  the  two  cutters  and  launches,  carrying  a 
force  of  TO  officers  and  men.  The  gig  accompanied  the  expedition  as 
an  ambulance  boat,  in  charge  of  Assistant  Surgeon  Cooke. 

Having  ascertained  that  there  were  two  different  sets  of  works  upon 
the  island,  1  landed  my  whole  force,  threw  out  pickets  and  deployed  a 
line  of  skirmishers  to  protect  the  working  parties. 

I  found  at  this  place  some  contrabands,  who  informed  me  that  there 
were  no  troops  upon  the  island,  all  having  left  one  week  before. 

W e  here  destroyed  27  salt  boilers,  about  60  bushels  of  salt,  and  burned 
all  the  buildings,  etc.,  thus  thoroughly  breaking  up  the  establishments. 

Six  of  the  10  or  12  contrabands  found  at  this  place  claiming  my 
protection,  I  brought  them  off  with  me,  and  they  are  now  on  board. 

The  boats  from  the  U.  S.  S._  Stars  and  Stripes  landed  about  one-half 
mile  to  the  right  of  us,  destroyed  23  boilers,  etc.,  and  captured  3 
prisoners. 

Uniting  our  forces,  we  reconnoitered  the  whole  island,  and  ascer¬ 
taining  that  there  were  no  more  works  of  any  kind,  we  returned  to  the 
ship,  arriving  on  board  at  7  o’clock  p.  m. 

The  combined  result  of  the  expedition  was  the  destruction  of  50  salt 
boilers,  together  with  their  buildings,  etc. ,  and  60  bushels  of  salt,  the 
capture  of  3  prisoners,  and  bringing  off  of  6  contrabands. 

We  met  with  no  opposition  and  returned  without  any  accident. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Chatfield, 

Acting  Master,  TJ.  S.  Nawy. 

Lieutenant-Commander  A.  F.  Crosman,  U.  S.  Navjr, 

Comdg.  TJ.  S.  S.  Somerset,  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Willcomb,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 
regarding  expedition  in  St.  Marks  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

St.  Marks  Bay ,  Fla. ,  July  19,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  12th  instant  U.  S.  S.  Somerset ,  Lieutenant-Commander 
A.  F.  Crosman,  arrived  here.  I  immediately  went  on  board,  when 
Captain  Crosman  informed  me  that  he  intended  to  proceed  up  to  St. 
Marks  with  all  the  available  force  at  his  and  my  command.  I  told 
him  I  was  ready.  At  8:45  p.  m.  my  first,  second,  and  third  cutters, 
under  command  of  Acting  Master  L.  W.  Hill,  accompanied  by  Acting 
Master  George  Ashbury,  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  Benjamin  Marshall, 
Acting  Assistant  Paymaster  John  J.  Pratt,  Acting  Master’s  Mate 
Henry  B.  Conklin,  and  42  armed  men,  left  this  vessel  and  went  along¬ 
side  the  Somerset.  About  9  p.  m.  they  left  the  Somerset  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  up  the  St.  Marks  River.  Unfortunately  they  were  discovered 
by  the  enemy’s  picket,  about  2£  miles  below  the  fort,  and  were  tired 
at  by  the  picket  as  well  as  the  fort,  and  were  obliged  to  abandon  the 
expedition  and  return  to  the  ship. 

The  object  of  the  expedition  was  to  surprise  the  fort,  spike  the 
guns,  and  make  prisoners  of  the  garrison  and  proceed  up  to  St.  Marks, 
capture  the  rebel  steamer  Spray  and  such  other  vessels  as  they  might 
find,  then  proceed  up  to  Newport  and  destroy  the  foundry  and  machine 
shop  at  that  place. 

Captain  Crosman  and  myself  the  following  day  took  my  first  cutter 
and  an  armed  crew  and  proceeded  up  the  river  to  sound  and  stake  out 
the  channel  and  to  try  and  get  our  ships  up,  but  we  found  a  large 
barge  full  of  stone  sunk  across  the  channel  about  1^  miles  below  Port 
Leon,  so  that  it  is  impossible  for  an}^  vessel  drawing  over  4  feet  of 
water  to  pass  by  it,  even  at  high  tide. 

On  the  morning  of  the  15th,  at  6  a.  m.,  Captain  Crosman  and  myself 
went  on  shore  in  my  gig  at  the  light-house  and  set  fire  to  the  wooden 
steps  and  burned  all  the  woodwork  inside,  so  as  to  prevent  them  from 
using  it  as  a  lookout  station.  At  9  a.  m.  I  got  underway  from  Spanish 
Hole,  the  Somerset  following,  and  proceeded  close  up  to  the  mouth  of  the 
Ocklockonee  River,  and  came  to  about  3  miles  from  Pawtuxett  Point, 
armed  all  our  boats,  and  landed  in  two  divisions;  Somerset’s  boats 
landed  about  1  mile  outside  of  mine.  For  the  success  of  this  expedi¬ 
tion  I  respectfully  refer  you  to  the  enclosed  report  of  Acting  Master 
L.  W.  Hill.  They  destroyed  about  $30,000  worth  of  property  and 
captured  three  white  prisoners,  which  I  turned  over  to  Captain 
Crosman. 

At  2  p.  m.  Captain  Crosman  and  myself  went  on  shore  in  my  gig 
and  landed  at  another  point  and  set  fire  to  and  destroyed  several 
buildings. 

I  have  no  casualties  to  report.  I  should  have  landed  and  destroyed 
these  salt  works  before,  but  did  not  think  it  prudent  with  so  small  a 
force  as  I  had  at  my  command,  as  they  have  always  kept  one  or  two 
companies  at  that  place;  but  they  were  recalled  to  St.  Marks  the  day 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.

bef°re,  as  they  were  anticipating  an  attack  up  there.  The  Somerset 
left  heie  on  the  lbth  for  her  station. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  L.  Willcomb, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 
Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailet,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Hill,  U.  S.  Navy,  executive  officer  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and 

Stripes. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

St.  Marks,  Fla. ,  July  16,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order,  I  beg  leave  to  submit  the  following- 
report :  & 

On  the  12th  of  July,  according  to  instructions,  I,  accompanied  by 
Acting  Master  George  Ashbury,  Acting  Assistant  Paymaster  John  J. 
Pratt,  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  Benjamin  Marshall,  and  Master’s 
Mate  Henry  B.  Conklin,  proceeded  with  42  armed  men  in  the  first, 
second,  and  third  cutters,  and  reported  to  Captain  Grosman  on  board 
U.  S.  S.  Somerset  for  duty. 

We  immediately  proceeded  in  company  with  his  boats  up  St.  Marks 
River,  with  the  object  of  taking  the  fort  near  St.  Marks,  of  capturing 
the  rebel  steamer  Spray,  and  any  other  vessel  in  that  locality,  but 
upon  arriving  at  Port  Leon,  1^  miles  from  the  fort,  we  were  discov¬ 
ered  and  fired  upon  by  the  enemy’s  pickets,  and  immediately  after¬ 
wards  from  the  fort  itself,  when  we  returned  to  our  respective  vessels. 

In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  July  15,  I  also  have  to  report  that 
we  proceeded  to  Ocklockonee  Bay,  where  the  force  was  divided  into 
parties.  One,  consisting  of  all  our  own  boats  under  my  command, 
landed  on  Pawtuxett  Point,  where  we  discovered  two  extensive  salt 
works,  consisting  of  23  salt  boilers,  several  houses,  a  large  number  of 
wagons  and  other  implements,  besides  a  large  quantity  of  salt,  all  of 
which  property,  valued  at  $30,000,  was  destroyed  or  rendered  useless 
to  the  enemy.  After  which  we  returned  to  our  vessels,  bringing  three 
white  prisoners. 

I  have  no  casualties  to  report. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  W.  Hill, 

Acting  Master,  Executive  Officer. 

Chas.  L.  Willcomb, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Stars  and,  Stripes.

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Williams ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  JJ.  S. 
schooner  Annie ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  whaleboat  Alice ,  from 
Havana ,  (Juba. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Annie, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  July  13,  1863. 

Sir:  I  herewith  respectfully  submit  the  report  of  the  capture  of  the 
whaleboat  Alice,  from  Havana,  the  11th  instant,  bound  to  Tampa. 
Upon  my  reaching1  the  Northwest  Channel  light-house,  I  was  boarded 
by  the  keeper,  who  reported  a  suspicious  boat,  with  6  men  in  her,  hav¬ 
ing  been  seen  in  behind  Cotteral’s  Key,  and  he  feared  an  attack  on  the 
light-house  after  dark.  I  anchored  and  sent  my  boat,  and  also  the 
keeper’s,  fully  manned  and  armed,  and  found  the  above-mentioned 
boat. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  S.  Williams, 

Acting  Ensign,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Zerega ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Jasmine,  regarding  the  capjture  of  the  sloop  Relampago. 

U.  S.  S.  Jasmine, 

Lat.  36°  Iff  N,  Long.  82°  If  W.,  July  If  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  I  have  this  day  captured 
the  sloop  Relampago ,  loaded  with  an  assorted  cargo  (among  which  are 
JO  copper  tubes  for  a  boiler),  cleared  from  Havana  July  10,  1863,  and 
bound  to  Matamoras. 

W e  saw  her  at  daylight  about  7  miles  to  the  eastward  of  us,  stand¬ 
ing  to  the  northward  and  eastward  with  the  wind  from  the  southward 
and  eastward. 

When  we  came  within  range  of  our  guns  we  hoisted  our  colors  and 
fired  a  blank  charge,  upon  which  she  hove  to,  but  did  not  show  any 
colors. 

Her  answer  to  the  hail  of  “Where  are  you  bound?”  was  “Key 
West.”  ...  ' 

Her  captain,  William  Hudson,  came  on  board  with  his  papers, 
among  which  1  could  not  find  any  register.  While  I  was  examining 
his  papers  a  steamer  burning  black  smoke  was  reported  in  sight,  and 
we  went  in  chase  of  her.  After  chasing  her  six  hours  I  gave  up  the 
attempt  and  returned  to  the  sloop,  which  I  took  in  tow  for  Key  West. 

Enclosed  please  find  a  list  of  all  the  officers  and  crew  on  board  this 
steamer  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 

No  other  vessel  in  sight. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Alfred  L.  B.  Zerega, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Jasmine. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  to  Lieutenant- 
Cornrnander  McDougal ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Hen¬ 
drick  Hudson,  to  proceed  off  Cape  San  Bias  in  search  of  cotton 
thrown  overboard  by  blockade  runner. 


U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  July  16,  1863. 

Sir:  You  will  prepare  your  vessel  for  sea  with  all  possible  dispatch 
for  an  absence  of  fifteen  days,  postponing  all  repairs  that  are  not  abso¬ 
lutely  necessary  until  your  return. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Jouett  reports  that  while  chasing  a  vessel 
to  the  westward  of  Cape  San  Bias,  [Fla.],  a  day  or  two  ago,  she  threw 
overboard  upward  of  300  bales  of  cotton,  in  order  to  escape  from  him. 
It  is  probable  that  a  large  portion  of  this  cotton  may  be  recovered  by 
an  early  effort  to  do  so.  You  will  therefore  see  Lieutenant-Com¬ 
mander  Jouett  and  obtain  from  him  all  the  information  possible  rela¬ 
tive  to  the  precise  locality  where  it  was  thrown  overboard,  and  then 
proceed  to  the  spot  (without,  however,  neglecting  the  ordinary  duties 
of  a  cruiser  in  case  of  falling  in  with  any  vessel)  and  pick  up  as  much 
of  it  as  possible. 

Having  performed  this  duty,  you  will  return  to  this  port. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Lieutenant-Commander  C.  J.  McDougal,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson.

Report  of  Captain  Gillis,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Ossipee,  West  Gulf  Squadron. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Ossipee, 

Off  Mobile,  July  17,  1863. 

Admiral:  *  *  * 

18th  July. — About  1  o’clock  a.  m.,  while  at  anchor  off  the  Swash 
Channel,  the  Aroostook  and  Kennebec  at  their  positions  to  the  east¬ 
ward,  they  made  signal  “A  steamer  running  out  this  pass,  standing 
S.  E.”  We  got  underway  and  stood  in  chase;  overhauled  and  passed 
the  gunboats,  smoke  of  chase  in  sight;  at  daylight  discovered  her  to 
be  a  side-wheel  steamer,  and  also  another  steamer  on  our  port  beam 
making  black  smoke;  signalized  the  Kennebec  to  run  for  her;  discov¬ 
ered  a  third  steamer  about  standing  for  us;  soon  after  she  stood  for 
the  steamer  we  were  in  pursuit  of  and  fired  several  guns;  the  chased 
vessel  hove  to  and  we  saw  her  boarded  and  seized  as  a  prize  by  the 
U.  S.  S.  De  Soto,  she  showing  her  number  in  answer  to  ours;  we 
closed  in  and  found,  about  70  miles  southeast  of  our  anchorage  off 
Mobile,  the  prize  to  be  the  James  Battle,  from  Mobile  for  Havana, 
cargo  600  or  more  bales  of  cotton,  rosin,  crew,  and  passengers.  I 
told  Captain  Walker,  of  the  De  Soto,  we  had  chased  her  from  off 
Mobile  and  that  I  would  send  to  the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy 
our  list  of  crew  and  officers,  and  directed  him  to  send  the  prize  to  New

the  blockade  proclaimed  and  instituted  by  the  President  of  the  United 
States. 

The  steamer  William  Bagley  is  said  to  be  laden  with  700  bales 
cotton. 

I  send  on  board  by  the  same  conveyance  and  by  your  order  Charles 
Frisk,  master  of  the  William  Bagley. 

At  the  time  of  taking  possession  of  the  William  Bagley  the  U.  S. 
steamers  Ossipee  and  Kennebec  were  in  sight.

U.  S.  S.  Ossipee, 

July  18,  1863. 

I  do  hereby  certify  that  I  was  chased  from  morning  by  a  U.  S.  gun¬ 
boat  and  from  noon  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Ossipee.  At  11:02  p.  m.  the 
Ossipee  being  within  short  range,  a  gun  was  fired  at  me,  upon  which 
I  hove  to. 

No  other  gun  was  fired. 

The  U.  S.  S.  De  Soto,  coming  up  soon  after,  passed  between  us,  and, 
lowering  a  boat,  boarded  me  and  sent  me,  with  my  papers,  on  board 
the  De  Soto,  from  whence  1  was  removed  to  the  vessel  capturing  me. 

I  hove  to  for  or  surrendered  to  the  U.  S.  S.  Ossipee. 

Chas.  Frisk, 

Commanding  Prize  Steamer  Wm.  Bagley. 


Report  of  Captain  Walker,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  De  Soto,  disputing  the  claims 
of  Captain  Gillis,  TJ.  S,  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Ossipee,  regarding  the  captures. 

U.  S.  Ship  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico,  JulyW,  1863. 

Sir:  The  morning  of  Saturday  the  18th  found  us  lying  to  in  lati¬ 
tude  29°  21',  longitude  87°  08',  the  position  1  had  selected  at  night. 

At  5:15  discovered  a  smoke  bearing  nearly  west;  stood  for  it.  At 
6:15  made  another  smoke  on  the  beam,  bearing  N.  by  E.,  and  at  6:30 
a  sail  abaft  the  beam.  Pressed  on  our  course,  when  at  length  it  was 
believed  that  the  steamer  ahead  was  an  armed  vessel  mounting  heavy 
guns  cleared  for  action.  We  now  gained  very  slowly  upon  her.  At 
7:15  showed  our  colors,  to  which  she  did  not  reply;  after  which  threw 
a  shot  in  her  direction,  to  which  she  paid  no  attention,  but  changed  her 
course,  increased  her  speed,  and  commenced  throwing  cotton  over¬ 
board.

and  sent  an  officer  on  board  the  Bagley  to  take  possession,  who  was

[crew]  was  going  on,  the  executive  officer,  engineer,  and  other  officers,

ford  to  give  the  William  Bagley  in  charge  of  the  officer  from  the 
Ossipee ,  and  so  soon  as  I  could  give  the  matter  attention  I  sealed  up

whom  they  had  been  received,  and  sent  them,  accompanied  by  her  mas¬ 
ter,  on  board  to  Captain  Gillis,  to  whom,  at  the  same  time,  I  addressed 
at  midnight,  the  hastily  written  letter,*  whereof  I  enclose  a  copy. 

I  can  not  conclude  this  paper  without  expressing  my  surprise  at  the 
act  of  Captain  Gillis,  which  dispossessed  me  of  a  prize  within  the  limits 
of  your  command.  I  would  be  glad  to  learn  that  his  course,  which 
appears  so  high  handed,  may  be  justified  by  considerations  of  public 
safety  or  necessity  which  were  not  revealed  to  me. 

No  officer  has  a  higher  respect  than  I  have  for  the  prerogative  of 
rank,  nor  would  I  have  its  functions  abridged,  but  it  should  be  exer¬ 
cised  with  consideration  and  discretion  under  heavy  responsibility.  In 
the  instance  to  which  I  now  call  attention  Captain  Gillis  appears  to 
have  exercised  it  without  due  consideration  for  myself,  his  equal  in 
rank,  and  with  an  utter  disregard  of  that  comity  which  should  have 
led  him  to  refrain  from  all  unnecessary  interference  with  the  ships 
under  the  special  orders  of  the  admiral  commanding  the  Eastern  Gulf 
Blockading  Squadron. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  M.  Walker, 

Captain ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron . 


Report  of  Captain  Walker,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  De  Soto,  regarding  the  cap¬ 
ture  of  the  steamer  William  Bagley. 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico,  July  W,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  on  the  night  of  the  18th 
instant  in  latitude  27°  31',  longitude  86°  10',  1  seized  and  took  posses¬ 
sion  of,  for  violation  of  the  blockade  proclaimed  and  instituted  by 
the  President  of  the  United  States,  the  steamer  William  Bagley , 
Charles  Frisk,  master,  of  and  from  Mobile,  laden  with  750  bales  of 
cotton  and  bound  to  Havana. 

After  I  was  in  possession  and  her  master  and  her  papers  had  been 
brought  on  board  this  ship,  the  U.  S.  S.  Ossipee  came  up  followed  by 
the  Kennebec,  whereupon  Captain  Gillis,  of  the  Ossipee ,  sent  a  boat  on 
board  the  prize  to  take  possession,  when  the  officer  sent  by  Captain 
Gillis  reported  to  him  that  she  was  in  possession  of  the  De  Soto.

The  necessary  organization  of  the  prize  was  being  carried  on  on 
board  of  her  by  my  orders,  when  Captain  Grillis  sent  an  officer  direct¬ 
ing  me  to  send  the  master  of  the  William  Bagley  with  his  papers  on 
board  to  him,  claiming,  without  right,  I  think,  the  William  Bagley  as 
a  prize  to  the  Ossipee. 

With  this  order,  as  in  duty  bound,  I  complied,  and  at  the  same  time

What  disposition  was  made  of  the  prize  I  know  not,  as  I  immedi¬ 
ately  resumed  my  cruise. 

At  the  time  of  the  capture  of  the  William  Bagley  by  this  ship  the 
U.  S.  steamers  Ossipee  and  Kennebec  were  within  signal  distance.

Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Rear-Admiral  Farragut,  IT.  S. 

Navy,  regarding  the  disagreement  between  the  commanding  officers  of  the  TL  S. 

steamers  De  Soto  and  Ossipee. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  July  88,  1863. 

Sir:  I  gather  from  what  Captain  Walker,  commanding  the  De  Soto, 
tells  me,  that  there  existed  some  misunderstanding  at  the  time  of  the 
taking  of  the  prize  steamer  William  Bagley  between  himself  and 
Captain  Gillis  as  to  which  was  the  real  captor,  and  accordingly  I 
enclose  a  copy  of  his  report  of  the  affair  as  best  expressing  the  view 
that  he  takes  of  the  matter,  though  the  question  as  to  which  is  the 
actual  captor  is  perhaps  of  more  theoretical  than  practical  importance; 
at  least,  it  does  not  affect  the  distribution  of  the  prize  money. 

It  seems  that  both  the  De  Soto  and  the  Ossipee  were  in  chase  of  the 
Bagley;  that  about  midnight  the  De  Soto,  by  reason  of  her  superior 
speed,  overhauled  her,  the  Ossipee  then  being  astern  of  the  De  Soto; 
that  in  that  position  she  fired  a  gun,  though  for  this  act  there  existed 
no  real  necessity,  the  De  Soto  being  close  aboard  the  prize;  that  on 
approaching  sufficiently  near  the  chase  the  De  Soto  sent  a  boat  on 
board,  and  put  an  officer  and  prize  crew  in  possession,  and  sent  the 
master  of  the  prize  with  his  papers  on  board  the  De  Soto,  all  of  which 
was  accomplished  before  the  Ossipee  had  so  much  as  lowered  a  boat. 
Matters  standing  in  this  position  Captain  Gillis  thereupon,  by  virtue 
of  his  superior  rank,  dispossessed  Captain  Walker  of  his  prize,  and 
put  his  own  officer  and  prize  crew  on  board.  I  think  the  proceeding 
was  not  in  accordance  with  either  the  custom  of  the  service  or  with 
legal  precedent.  I  hope  this  action  of  Captain  Gillis  will  not  raise 
questions  that  will  delay  and  embarrass  the  court  in  determining  the 
case. 

Upon  this  state  of  the  case  I  trust  I  shall  not  be  found  to  be  in  con¬ 
flict  with  any  views  you  may  have  of  the  case,  when  I  add  that  it 
seems  clear  to  me  that  this  is  a  capture  in  which  the  De  Soto ,  Ossipee 
and  Keymebec  are  equally  entitled  to  share,  and  that  while’  you  are 
entitled  to  one-twentieth  part  of  such  sum  as  may  be  awarded  to  the 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  511 

Kennebec  and  Ossipee,  I  am  entitled  to  one-twentieth  part  of  such  sum 
as  may  be  awarded  to  the  De  Soto.  I  send  a  statement  to  that  effect. 

Ir  you  coincide  with  me  in  this  view  of  our  relative  rights  in  the 
case  and  the  rights  of  our  respective  vessels,  will  you  be  kind  enough 
to  sign  and  forward  the  .statement  to  whatever  prize  court  you  may 
hav  e.  selected  for  the  adjudication  of  the  case.  I  refer  you  to  the 
opinion  of  Judge  Marvin,  which  I  sent  you  a  few  days  since,  as  to  the 
necessity  for  a  statement  of  this  character,  assented  to  by  the  respec¬ 
tive  parties  entitled  to  share,  being  submitted  to  the  prize  court  in 
cases  of  conflicting  claims  before  any  decree  for  distribution  can  be 
made. 

Please  advise  me  as  to  the  disposition  you  make  of  the  prize,  and 
whether  you  agree  with  me  in  the  views  I  have  expressed  above. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Statement  of  facts  regarding  the  capture  of  the  prize  steamer  William  Bagley,  agreed  to 
between  Rear-Admiral  D.  G.  Farragut,  commanding  the  Western  Gulf  Blockading 
Squadron,  and  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey,  commandiug  the  Eastern  Gulf 
Blockading  Squadron. 

That  the  William  Bagley  was  captured  on  the  night  of  the  18th  of 
July,  1863,  in  latitude  27°  31',  longitude  86°  10'.  That  she  was  taken 
possession  of  in  the  first  instance  by  Captain  William  M.  Walker, 
commanding  the  U.  S.  S.  De  Soto ,  a  vessel  of  the  Eastern  Gulf  Block¬ 
ading  Squadron,  and  subsequently  was  placed  in  charge  of  an  officer 
and  prize  crew  from  the  U.  S.  S.  Ossipee,  a  vessel  of  the  Western 
Gulf  Blockading  Squadron,  by  order  of  Captain  Gillis,  commanding 
the  Ossipee,  and  the  senior  officer  present.  That  the  De  Soto ,  Ossipee , 
and  Kennebec  are  entitled  to  share  in  the  prize,  all  being  present  at  the 
capture. 

That  Rear-Admiral  Farragut  is  entitled  to  one-twentieth  of  such 
shares  as  may  be  awarded  to  the  Ossipee  and  Kennebec,  and  Acting 
Rear-Admirai  T.  Bailey  is  entitled  to  one-twentieth  of  such  share  as 
may  be  awarded  to  the  De  Soto. 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  disposition  of  the 

steamer  James  Battle  and  cargo. 


No.  252.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  July  23,  1863. 

Sir:  The  James  Battle  arrived  here  on  the  21st  instant  with  600 
bales  of  cotton,  a  prize  to  the  De  Soto.  She  is  one  of  a  large  fleet  of 
blockade  runners  carrying  on  a  steady  and  successful  trade  between 
Mobile  and  Havana. 

The  Battle  was  the  finest  packet  on  the  Alabama  River  and  was 
altered  to  suit  her  for  a  blockade  runner,  at  a  large  expense.  The 


512 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Warren,  Fannie,  William  Bctgley,  W.  II.  Smith,  Alabama,  Alice 
Vivian,  and  St.  Mary's  are  other  vessels  of  the  same  class.  The  De  Soto 
is  the  only  vessel  I  have  with  sufficient  speed  to  overtake  any  of  these 
traders.  I  have  stationed  her  to  the  northwest  of  Tortugas  in  their 
track,  and  a  week  never  passes  that  she  does  not  sight  some  one  of 
them.  At  the  time  of  the  capture  of  the  Battle  another  was  in  sight, 
to  which  the  De  Soto  gave  chase.  The  Sunflower  is  also  off  Tortugas 
and  has  chased  several,  but  in  most  cases  they  escape  both  these 
cruisers  by  superior  speed.  I  feel  confident  that  if  the  Department 
will  send  me  two  swift  steamers  like  the  De  Soto,  I  can  effectually  put 
a  stop  to  this  lucrative  traffic.  1  have  directed  that  the  cotton  on  the 
Battle  be  sent  north  in  the  ship  General  Cobb,  if  the  marshal  can  make 
his  arrangements  with  the  captain,  and  that  the  Battle  herself  be  sent 
to  New  Orleans  for  sale  at  the  marshal’s  convenience,  she  being  par¬ 
ticularly  adapted  to  the  carrying  of  plantation  produce. 

I  should  have  stated  above  that  the  Hendrick  Hudson  and  Huntsville 
have  both  at  various  times  given  chase  to  one  or  other  of  the  above- 
named  steamers,  but  failed  to  make  capture  by  reason  of  their  inferior 
speed. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Bear- Admiral. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Beport  of  Lieutenant- Commander  McCauley,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding 
cm  engagement  in  Waccasassa  Biver,  July  W,  1863. 

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  August  5,  1863. 

Admiral:  In  obedience  to  the  order  contained  in  your  dispatch  of 
the  29th  ultimo,  I  communicate  the  following  as  the  details  of  the 
reconnoissance,  in  which  P.  Doran  (seaman)  and  J.  Bishop  (seaman) 
lost  their  lives : 

On  the  20th  ultimo,  at  early  daylight,  the  launch  was  fitted  out  with 
ten  days’  rations  and  ordered  “to  proceed  off  Bayport,  to  keep  out  of 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


513 


sight  during  daytime  behind  an  island  there,  and  at  nighttime  to 
endeavor  to  intercept  the  blockade  runners.”  Two  of  my  officers 
being  sick,  another  away  in  charge  of  a  prize,  and  needing  the  services 
or  a  tomth  for  other  duty,  I  was  obliged  to  put  the  launch  in  charge  of 
the  chief  boatswain’s  mate.  I  forbade  the  ascent  of  Crystal  River, 
little  imagining  a  necessity  of  the  kind  in  respect  to  the  Waccasassa.’ 

In  passing  the  latter  a  large  amount  of  loose  cotton  floating  down- 
stream  attracted  attention,  and  the  probability  of  making  a  good  cotton 
capture  induced  Boatswain’s  Mate  Gillespie  to  pull  up  the  river. 
Coming  to  a  narrow  part,  they  were  fired  into  from  both  banks  by 
about  50  or  60  rifles.  Doran  and  Bishop  sprang  to  their  gun.  The 
former  received  a  rifle  ball  through  the  neck,  severing  the  carotid 
artery,  and  expired  instantly;  Bishop  was  shot  through  the  body,  and 
lived  about  half  an  hour.  The  launch  being  protected  by  her  spars 
in  cranes,  none  of^  the  rest  of  the  crew  was  materially  hurt.  On 
receiving  a  return  fire,  the  rebels  decamped,  and  in  a  few  minutes  the 
launch  pulled  out  of  range  and  returned  alongside  at  midnight. 

On  the  afternoon  of  the  21st  the  deceased  were  buried  in  the  ceme¬ 
tery  on  Sea  Horse  Key  with  the  customary  ceremonies. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley, 

Lieut.  Commander ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  TJ.  S.  8.  Fort  Henry. 

Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

astern.  At  about  5: 30  he  again  altered  to  the  southward,  when  I  came

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
'injury  to  the  public  service  caused  by  the  vacancy  in  the  judgeship) 
of  the  U.  S.  district  court  at  Key  West,  Fla. 

No.  251.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  July  23,  1863. 

Sir:  I  feel  it  incumbent  upon  me  to  call  your  attention  to  the  very 
grave  detriment  that  is  resulting  to  the  public  service  by  reason  of  the 
vacancy  that  now  exists  in  the  judgeship  of  the  U.  S.  district  court  for 
this  district. 

The  fact  that  the  bench  of  this  court  is  unfilled  embarrasses  every 
proceeding  of  a  judicial  character,  for  the  remaining  U.  S.  officials,  the 
district  attorney,  the  marshal,  the  clerk  of  the  court,  the  prize  com¬ 
missioners,  are  unable  to  take  anj^  important  step  without  the  sanction 
of  a  judge  unless  they  choose  to  assume  a  considerable  degree  of  judi¬ 
cial  responsibility  and  to  exercise  doubtful  powers. 

Meantime  prizes  are  arriving  every  few  clays  which  should  be  adju¬ 
dicated  upon  here — high-pressure  Mississippi  steamers,  for  instance, 
such  as  the  James  Battle,  sent  in  yesterday  by  the  De  Soto ,  with  600 
bales  of  cotton.  These  steamers,  though  admirably  adapted  to  the 
Southern  waters,  are  useless  at  the  North  and  ill  fitted  to  make  the 
voyage.  They  must,  however,  be  sent  on  or  else  the  responsibility  of 
transferring  the  cargo  and  making  proper  disposition  of  the  vessel 
must  be  taken  by  those  not  properly  chargeable  with  such  duties. 

In  view  of  these  facts  and  also  of  the  greatly  increased  expenditure 
in  prize  cases  resulting  from  the  absence  of  the  prize  judge,  I  would 
respectfully  suggest  that  an  appointment  be  made  of  some  person 
competent  to  fill  the  office  and  who  will  at  once  assume  its  duties.  As 
Key  West  was  never  healthier  than  now,  I  do  not  think  that  any  con¬ 
sideration  as  to  the  season  should  deter  a  judge  from  coming  down 
forthwith.  If  none  other  can  be  found,  I  am  of  opinion  that,  should 
the  President  request  it,  Judge  Marvin,  who  is  now  in  New  York  and 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


515 


who  has  tilled  the  position  of  admiralty  judge  for  twenty  years  with 
such  unfaltering  rectitude  and  rare  ability,  would  resume  the  office 
until  a  lit  successor  could  be  obtained. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

.  .  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Hear- Admiral  Comdg .  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Sguadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Namy. 


Letter  f  rom  Rear-Admiral  Farragut  to  Acting  Rear- Admired  Bailey 

U.  S.  Navy. 


U.  S.  Flag  Steamer  Tennessee,  July  £6,  1863. 

Dear  Admiral:  Your  dispatch  in  relation  to  the  stealing  of  certain 
articles  from  the  passenger  Don  Higena,  of  the  Comet ,  captured  by  the 
Kanawha  and  S6nt  to  Ivuy  W  est?  lias  boon  received.  I  regret  that 
Lieutenant-Commander  Mayo  should  have  allowed  his  judgment  to 
give  way  in  the  manner  he  did  in  his  letter.  Although  I  agree  with 
you  that  the  officer’s  statement  is  perfectly  satisfactory,  still  it  was  an 
official  representation  of  a  foreign  consul  and  called  for  circumspec¬ 
tion  on  your  part;  but  I  have  no  doubt  that  these  men  would  say  any¬ 
thing  to  give  trouble,  as  they  almost  invariably  do  when  you  meet 
with  a  perverse  disposition,  and  I  believe  the  whole  representation  a 
fabrication,  and  that  all  these  articles  were  for  commercial  purposes, 
and  not  entitled  to  respect  as  private  property. 

Our  war  has  been  conducted  with  the  greatest  liberality  on  our 
part,  while,  so  far  as  I  know,  we  have  been  taken  advantage  of  when¬ 
ever  it  was  possible  for  them  to  do  it. 

The  part  that  the  English  people,  if  not  the  Government,  is  playing- 
in  this  struggle  with  us  is  as  great  a  disadvantage  to  us  as  the  rebels, 
and  we  are  unable  to  help  ourselves;  but  I  trust  it  will  not  be  so  long. 
I  regret  that  I  am  not  twenty  years  younger  and  could  live  to  see  it 
all  fairly  settled.  But  God  will  settle  it  all  right  in  His  good  time. 
1  will  say  this  for  the  British  officers  whom  I  have  met,  that  they  do 
not  approve  the  conduct  of  their  countrymen  and  regret  that  there 
should  be  such  just  cause  for  complaint  against  them.  I  suppose  they 
are  much  as  the  good  and  honest  people  of  our  country  were  on  the 
subject  of  filibustering. 

I  shall  attend  to  your  letter  and  admonish  Lieutenant-Commander 
Mayo  of  his  impropriety  in  addressing  such  a  letter  to  his  command¬ 
ing  officer  when  a  superior  officer  is  a  party  in  the  complaint. 

Very  respectfully, 


D.  G.  Farragut, 

Rear-Admiral. 


Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Order  of  Acting  Bear- Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Crosman,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Somerset , 
regarding  expedition  up  St.  Marks  Biver ,  Florida. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  July  27,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  directed  the  schooner  Chambers  and  the  steam  tug 
Marigold  to  report  to  you  with  a  view  of  granting  you  the  permis¬ 
sion,  so  often  asked,  to  organize  an  expedition  up '  the  St.  Marks 
River.  In  yielding  to  your  request,  I  am  conscious  that  in  the  event 
of  failure  I  might  be  thought  to  have  acted  injudiciously  in  entrusting 
the  execution  of  the  project  to  a  comparatively  inexperienced  officer; 
but  from  the  fact  that  the  plan  originated  with  yourself,  from  the  long 
consideration  that  you  have  given  the  subject,  and  from  the  zeal^ 
energy,  and  ability  that  you  have  already  displayed,  not  only  in  the 
performance  of  whatever  duty  has  presented  itself  to  you,  but  also  in 
the  efficiency  and  discipline  of  your  vessel,  I  have  been  induced  to 
believe  that  this  expedition  could~  not  be  entrusted  to  better  hands.  I 
trust,  therefore,  that  you  will  display  a  degree  of  discretion  in  making 
your  preparation  for  this  little  affair  equal  to  the  other  qualities  for 
which  I  have  given  you  credit.  The  force  placed  at  your  disposal  is 
deemed  more  than  adequate  for  the  accomplishment  of  the  object  pro¬ 
posed,  as  you  will  leave  the  Chambers  to  maintain  the  blockade  at  the 
Last  I  ass  during  your  absence,  and  will  take  the  Marigold  and  the 
Stars  and  Stripes  with  the  Somerset.  If,  however,  you  should  have 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


517 


leceivecl  information  since  communicating'  with  me  which  would 
render  the  result  of  the  expedition  at  all  doubtful,  or  if  the  aspect  of 
affairs  on  the  river  should  lead  you  to  question  the  correctness  of  your 
previous  information,  or  to  feel  the  smallest  want  of  confidence  in  your 
ability  to  succeed,  you  will  then  consider  the  present  expedition  as  a 
mere  reeonnoissance  en  force,  and  will  postpone  the  attack  until  you 
can  be  reinforced  to  such  a  degree  as  to  insure  success. 

On  returning  from  this  expedition,  the  Stars  and  Stripes,  the  Som¬ 
erset,  and  the  Chambers  will  resume  their  previous  stations  on  the 
blockade,  and  the  Marigold  will  be  sent  to  this  place  with  the  reports 
and  results  of  the  affair. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  McDougal ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding 
cotton  discovered  in  the  vicinity  of  Cape  San  Bias ,  Florida. 

U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson, 

Key  West ,  July  2 9 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  while  on  a 
cruise  1  found  on  the  beach,  on  and  in  the  vicinity  of  Cape  San  Bias, 
138^  bales  of  cotton,  all  of  which  I  succeeded  in  getting,  and  have 
brought  them  to  this  place  and  entered  them  in  the  U.  S.  district 
court  for  adjudication,  as  a  part  of  the  cargo  of  a  rebel  steamer,  name 
unknown. 

The  cotton  was  strewn  all  up  and  down  the  beach,  and  had  evidently 
been  washed  on  shore  but  a  short  time  previously. 

On  or  about  the  15th  instant,  the  U.  S.  S.  R.  R.  Cuyler  chased  a 
rebel  steamer  some  distance  to  the  westward  of  Cape  San  Bias,  and 
made  her,  in  her  efforts  to  escape,  throw  overboard  a  part  of  her  cargo, 
which,  I  think,  is  the  same  that  1  have  recovered. 

The  seizure  was  made  on  the  19th,  20th,  21st,  22d,  and  26th  instants, 
a  part  on  each  day. 

1  herewith  enclose  a  list  of  those  entitled  to  share  in  the  capture. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  J.  McDougal, 

Lieutenant-  Commander ,  Comdg.  TJ.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  McDougal ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  command¬ 
ing  TJ.  S.  S.  LLendrick  Hudson ,  regarding  expedition  for  the  recovery 
of  cotton  thrown  overboard  from  a  blockade  runner. 

U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson, 

Key  West,  July  30,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  the  16th  instant,  I  left  this  port 
on  the  17th  and  proceeded  to  sea.  I  shaped  a  course  for  Cape  San 
Bias,  making  the  light-house  on  that  point  shortly  after  daylight  on 
the  19th.  About  9  a.  m.  of  that  date  a  solitary  bale  of  cotton  was 
discovered  and  secured.  I  then  cruised  about  in  the  neighborhood  of 
the  place  the  cotton  had  been  thrown  overboard,  but  without  finding 
any  more.  The  day  was  one  well  adapted  for  seeing  distant  objects^ 
and  the  lookouts  were  vigilant,  an  officer  with  the  glass  being  at  the 
masthead  nearly  the  entire  time. 

I  then  became  convinced  that  most,  if  not  all,  of  it  had  been  carried 
to  the  eastward,  and,  being  near  St.  Andrew’s  and  St.  Joseph’s,  and 
having  stores  for  the  vessels  at  those  places,  I  concluded  to  proceed 
and  deliver  them  and  at  the  same  time  find  how  the  wind  had  been  for 
the  past  week. 

The  Roebuck  I  communicated  with  early  on  the  20th,  and  about  noon 
of  the  same  day  I  also  supplied  the  J.  L.  Davis,  at  St.  Joseph’s,  with 
what  I  had  on  board  for  her.  From  these  vessels  I  ascertained  that 
the  wind  had  been  from  the  southward  and  westward  for  the  week 
previous,  which  convinced  me  that  a  part,  if  not  all,  the  cotton  was  in 
the  neighborhood  of  Cape  San  Bias.  As  soon  as  I  finished  with  the 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


519 


J.  L.  Davis  I  got  underway  and  proceeded  down  the  land  and  close 
to  the  shore  in  3  fathoms  water.  About  6  miles  to  the  northward 
of  Cape  San  Bias  the  first  bale  was  discovered  on  the  beach  just  at  the 
water’s  edge,  and  from  that  point  cotton  could  be  seen  all  along  the 
shore.  The  men  and  boats  were  at  once  set  to  work  and  by  night  we 
had  on  board  33  bales.  The  next  morning,  the  21st,  we  commenced 
again  at  daylight,  and,  working  down  the  beach  with  the  steamer, 
succeeded  in  getting  off  72|-  bales. 

The  next  day,  the  22d,  we  recovered  28  bales,  the  last  20  of  which 
we  got  on  St.  \  incent's  Island.  Just  as  we  secured  the  last  bale  the 
Port  Royal  made  her  appearance  from  the  West  Pass,  supposing  us  to 
be  an  English  steamer  discharging  cargo.  Having  scoured  the  beach 
around  and  being  satisfied  no  more  cotton  remained,  I  followed  the 
Port  Royal  into  West  Pass,  delivered  mails  and  stores  both  to  her  and 
the  schooner  Chambers ,  and  early  next  morning  (the  23d)  proceeded  to 
East  Pass,  communicating  and  delivering  stores  to  the  Somerset ,  and 
then  kept  on  to  St.  Marks,  where  I  anchored  all  night,  communicating 
with  the  Stars  and  Stripes. 

Early  next  morning  I  got  underway  and  returned  to  the  West  Pass, 
stopping  a  short  time  at  East  Pass  and  overhauling  the  American 
schooner  Anna  Maria ,  on  a  cruise  from  Pensacola  in  search  of  cotton. 
The  next  day  (the  25th),  it  being  very  bad  weather,  I  remained  at  West 
Pass,  and  on  the  morning  of  the  26th  got  underway  and  again  pro¬ 
ceeded  off  Cape  San  Bias  to  see  if  any  more  cotton  had  come  on  shore. 
I  succeeded  in  getting  4  more  bales,  and  am  satisfied  that  no  more 
remains  in  that  neighborhood.  Possibly  some  might  have  gone  as  far 
to  the  eastward  as  Cedar  Keys,  but  my  coal  getting  short,  and  the 
engineer  complaining  so  much  of  the  engine,  I  decided  on  returning 
to  this  place,  which  I  did,  after  stopping  at  West  Pass  for  the  mails, 
and  arriving  here  yesterday,  the  29th  instant. 

From  the  Port  Royal  I  received  for  passage  to  this  place  the  follow¬ 
ing  men: 

John  Conley,  Edward  Smith,  and  John  Calahan,  deserters  from  the 
First  Regiment  of  Georgia  Regulars,  and  Joseph  Delano,  a  refugee, 
all  of  whom  have  taken  the  oath  of  allegiance. 

I  also  brought  from  the  Port  Royal  one  sick  man  for  the  hospital, 
who  was  transferred  there  yesterday. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  J.  McDougal, 

Lt.  Comdr .,  U.  S.  Navy ,  Comdy.  U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

in  lallahassee,  and  that  50  miles  from  St.  Marks,  at  Bainbridge,  were 
a  company,  or  part  of  a  company,  while  at  Quincy,  some  30  miles,  I 
think,  were  stationed  the  remainder,  making  in  all  700  men  as  the 
entire  available  force  to  be  got  into  St.  Marks  within  a  day.  Two 
hours  would  be  perhaps  sufficient  for  the  400  men  to  arrive  from  Tal¬ 
lahassee,  but  I  did  not  expect  to  have  been  exposed  to  their  fire  until 
I  should  have  disabled  the  guns  of  the  battery  and  captured  the  Spray. 
After  that,  which  certainly  would  not  have  occupied  more  than  half  an 
hour,  I  would  have  sent  my  boats  down  to  Tort  Leon,  g-one  up  with 
the  main  body  to  Newport,  which  I  could  have  reached  before  infantry 
could  march  the  distance  on  a  corduroy  road,  as  I  should  go  in  the 
steamer  Spray,  and  by  at  once  burning  the  bridge  and  destroying  the 
boats,  prevent  any  reinforcements  getting  to  the  point  or  peninsular 
upon  which  stood  Port  Leon  and  the  light-house.  The  work  of  cap¬ 
turing  cotton,  burning  all  public  workshops,  putting  cotton  bales  upon 
the  Spray  to  protect  my  men,  and  making  all  other  necessarv  arrange¬ 
ments  would  be  done  probably  before  the  troops  could  arrive  at  New¬ 
port.  Then  using  the  guns  of  the  Spray  to  scour  the  one  bank  of  the 
river  upon  which  I  could  be  attacked,  together  with  my  own  rifles,  all 
the  time,  if  disabled  by  artillery,  having  the  option  of  running  the 
vessel  into  the  grass,  setting  fire  to  her,  and  marching  safely  down  to 
Port  Leon  without  any  hindrance,  having  a  battery  to  pass  whose  guns 
were  harmless,  I  think  the  plan  does  not  seem  rash  or  foolhardy. 

But  I  expected  to  get  quite  close  to  the  battery  that  night  before  I 
was  discovered  and  then  carry  it  by  a  coup  de  main,  a  work  sailors  are 
specially  fit  for,  as  you  know,  sir,  and  that  done,  all  else  was  easy. 

As  I  am  the  only  officer  who  has  had  the  opportunity  of  attempting 
this  project,  and  as  I  have  failed,  I  shall  deem  it  an  especial  favor  if 
you  will  let  me  try  again,  sure  of  doing  all  that  any  equal  number  of 
men  on  the  station  can  do. 

The  pickets  are  doubtless  more  upon  the  alert  now  than  before,  and 
they  may  have  been  alarmed  into  making  arrangements  for  a  more 


522 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


rapid  means  of  getting  reinforcements.  I  would  like,  therefore,  the 
cooperation  of  two  or  three  hundred  troops,  who  might  load  at  the 
light-house,  push  up  to  Newport,  hold  the  bridge,  destroy  the  cotton, 
and  either  wait  for  me  or  push  on  to  St.  Marks,  where  I  would  be 
with  the  Spray  and  the  battery. 

This  would  create  a  diversion  and  would  allow  of  our  more  thor¬ 
oughly  finishing  the  work. 

It  is  a  scheme  I  have  cherished  most  fondly,  and  had  the  elements 
proved  propitious,  am  confident  that  night  would  have  witnessed  a 
success.  _  As  it  is,  I  ardently  hope  you  will  permit  me  to  lead  another, 
since  it  is  impossible  to  get  up  the  river  in  ships  now,  and  until  the 
stones  have  been  removed  by  divers,  which  will  read  better  than  the 
account  of  a  retreat. 

If  it  is  determined  on  to  attack  by  vessels,  the  Somerset  is  the  only 
vessel  upon  the  station  fit  to  go  up,  for  the  river  is  too  narrow  to  turn 
m  above  Fort  Leon  except  at  the  Forks,  and  my  vessel  steers  equallv 
well  at  either  end.  Excuse  me,  sir,  if  I  have  been  guilty  of  bad  taste 
in  suggesting  what  you  already  know. 

Should  x  ou  permit  this  expedition,  and  kindly  allow  me  to  retrieve 
rf C  C  °*i  su^cf^s’  1  would  be  much  gratified  if  Lieutenant-Commander 
McDougal,  of  the  Hudson,  could  act  in  the  place  of  the  Stars  and 
/Stripes,  if  it  meets  with  your  approval. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  F.  Grosman,

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

St.  Marks  Bay,  Fla.,  July  31,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  29th  instant,  being  informed  that  there  was  a  sloop 
loading  up  the  Chopchoppa  [Sockockhoppee?]  River,  I  sent  two  armed 
boats  20  miles  up  that  river  with  the  object  of  capturing  her  or  any 
other  vessel  which  they  might  find,  but  they  returned  on  the  following 
morning  and  reported  that  there  was  no  vessel  of  any  kind  up  there. 

On  the  30th  Jacob  Parker  (contraband)  came  off  to  this  ship  and  I 
have  shipped  him. 

Provisions  on  board  for  seventy-five  days. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  L.  Willcomb,

capturing  the  above-mentioned  schooner,  which  they  found  secreted  in 
a  small  creek  near  Fort  Myers.

old,  and  with  your  permission  I  shall  be  pleased  to  retain  her  as  a 
tender  to  this,  vessel,  as  she  will  be  of  g-reat  service  in  making  the 
blockade  at  this  point  effective.

Navy  Department,  August  5 ,  1863. 

Sir:  The  Secretary  of  State,  under  date  of  30th  ultimo,  informs  this 
Department  that  the  charge  d’affaires  of  the  United  States  at  Madrid 
announces  the  revocation  of  the  order  issued  by  the  captain-general  of 
Cuba,  to  the  effect  that  vessels  of  war  under  our  flag  should  not  be 
permitted  to  communicate  with  the  shore  without  formally  entering 
the  port  of  Havana.
