Report  of.  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
crippled  condition  of  the  squadron  under  his  command. 

No.  265.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Tahoma, 

Key  West,  August  6,  1863. 

Sir:  1  have  again  to  represent  to  the  Department  the  sorely  crip¬ 
pled  condition  of  the  squadron  under  my  command.  The  steamers 
1  enguin  and  Magnolia  having  gone  North  for  new  boilers  I  have 
received  in  their  stead  the  Sunflower  and  the  Marigold;  but  their  verv 
limited  capacity  compels  me  to  restrict  their  sphere  of  action  within 
exceedingly  narrow  limits,  namely,  to  cruising  in  the  vicinity  of  the 
lortugas,  where  they  can  obtain  coal  every  few  days.  In  the  mean¬ 
time,  the  De  Sotos  boilers  have  so  far  given  out  that  on  the  recom¬ 
mendation  of  the  fleet  engineer  I  have  requested  the  Bureau  to  order 
new  ones  tor  that  vessel;  and  now  the  Hendrick  Hudson's  propeller 
has  become  loose  on  the  shaft,  and  it  will  be  necessary  for  her  to  go 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


527 


Noith  and  be  docked.  Lhe  Tahoma  is  here,  undergoing'  repairs,  and 
several  weeks  are  yet  needed  to  render  her  efficient;  thus  confining 
6  JJun ,  which  is  next  to  the  De  Soto  in  speed,  to  the  blockade 
at  iampa  Bay.  I  he  _  Port  Royal ,  Somerset ,  and  Fort  Ilenry  also 
require  extensive  repairs,  but  I  am  wholly  unable  to  relieve  them  for 
that  purpose,  and  I  fear  by  the  time  I  can  do  so  that  the  bad  weather 
^wll  render  it  hazardous  to  bring  them  down  here.  In  order  to  do 
anything  toward  keeping  up  the  offshore  blockade  between  the  Tor- 
tugas  and  Mobile,  where,  doubtless,  a  large  number  of  vessels  will  now 
be  thrown,  in  consequence  of  the  operations  at  Charleston,  I  have 
been  obliged  to  send  the  San  Jacinto  out  to  cruise  and  to  hoist  my 
flag  on  board  the  Tahoma. 

Respectfully,  T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg .  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Albury;  after  which  you  will  proceed  with  the  Sea  Bird  to  cruise 
within  the  following  limits,  viz:  Between  the  parallels  of  26°  and  28° 
north  latitude,  and  between  the  meridians  of  83°  ancl  85°  west  longi¬ 
tude,  keeping  generally  near  a  line  drawn  diagonally  from  N.  W.  to 
S.  E.  of  that  square.  In  chasing,  of  course,  there  are  no  limits  besides 
those  imposed  by  the  jurisdiction  of  neutral  powers,  but  otherwise  it 
is  important  that  you  remain  within  the  space  designated. 

The  bark  Restless  is  cruising  within  the  same  limits  as  assigned  to 
the  Sea  Bird. 

The  object  of  your  cruising  is  to  intercept  and  capture  all  enemy’s 
vessels  or  others  engaged  in  violating  the  blockade;  in  the  perform¬ 
ance  of  which  duty  you  will  be  guided  by  the  orders  and  circulars 
already  furnished  you. 

You  will  return  to  this  port  for  provisions  when  necessary;  mean¬ 
time  you  can  obtain  wood  and  water  either  at  Tampa  Bay  or  at  Char¬ 
lotte  Harbor,  as  may  be  most  convenient. 

Respectfully, 


T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Acting  Master  Chas.  P.  Clark,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Schooner  (i tender )  Sea  Bird.

Report  of  Acting.  Master  Willcomb ,  U  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

stars  and  Stripes,  stationed  off  St.  Marks ,  Fla. ,  regarding  the  chase 
and  escape  of  a  steamer. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

St.  Marks  Bay,  Fla.,  August  11,  1863. 

SlK;  (1)!'  ^'e  1' 'tli  instant,  at  3:30  p.  m.,  the  smoke  of  a  steamer  was 
T\F°F om  m  ,  ^  ^  immediately  got  underway  and  gave  chase. 

At  4:3 0  a  schooner  hove  in  sight  in  the  S.  W.  At  5  p.  m.  I  had 
gained  so  much  on  the  chase  that  I  could  see  her  hull.  She  was  a 
large  side-wheel  boat  with  walking  beam,  white  smokestack,  and  one 
mast. 

I  then  fired  a  gun  as  signal  for  the  schooner  to  know  that  I  was 
chasing  the  steamer,  so  that  she  might  endeavor  to  cut  her  off;  but 
theie  was  i  ery  little  wind  and  she  could  do  nothing,  but  answered  my 

II  ^  ^’mg  several  times  at  the  chase.  I  took  the  schooner  to  be 
the  Fox.  At  6  p.  m.  I  got  within  7  miles  of  the  chase,  and  at  sun¬ 
down  I  was  not  more  than  6  miles  from  her,  and  at  7:30  p.  m.  I  was 
about  5  miles  astern  of  her,  when  it  set  in  very  dark,  and  at  7:45  p.  m. 
we  lost  sight  of  her,  and  at  8:30  I  was  obliged  to  give  up  the  chase 
and  return  to  my  anchorage. 

T"o  hours  more  of  daylight  and  she  would  have  been  mine. 

I  have  onty  10  tons  of  coal  on  board  this  morning. 

On  the  13th  the  Fox  arrived  here,  and  I  took  the  liberty  of  sending 
a  letter  to  Lieutenant-Commander  G.  U.  Morris,  at  West  Pass,  by  her, 
to  let  him  know  that  1  am  nearly  out  of  coal. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  L.  Willcomb, 
Acting  Master,  Commanding.

Report  of  Lieutenant-  Commander  English,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding 
U.  S.  S.  Sagamore,  regarding  an  attack  upon  New  Smyrna,  ana l 
reporting  the  capture  of  sloop  Clara  Louisa  and  schooners  Southern 
Rights,  Shot,  and  Ann. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Sagamore, 

Key  West,  August  12,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  afternoon  of  the  28th  I  attacked  New  Smyrna  with  the 
U.  S.  dispatch  steamer  Oleander  and  schooner  Beauregard  and  boats 
belonging  to  this  vessel  and  the  schooner  Para,  which  vessel  was  sta¬ 
tioned  off  blockading  that  place.  The  Oleander  took  the  Beauregard 
in  tow,  crossed  the  bar  and  anchored  abreast  the  place,  giving  it  a 
good  shelling,  the  boats  going  up  past  the  town.  We  captured  one 
sloop  loaded  with  cotton,  one  schooner  not  laden;  caused  them  to 
destroy  several  vessels,  some  of  which  were  loaded  with  cotton  and 
about  ready  to  sail.  They  burned  large  quantities  of  it  on  shore, 
which  we  could  not  prevent.  Landed  a  strong  force,  destroyed  all  the 
buildings  that  had  been  occupied  by  troops.  In  landing  the  party  was 
fired  upon  by  a  number  of  stragglers  concealed  in  the  bushes.  The 
conduct  of  all  connected  with  the  expedition  was  most  praiseworthy. 
From  the  handsome  dash  in  which  it  was  made  I  attribute  our  success, 

n  w  r — vol  17 - 34 


530 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


particularly  in  coming  off  without  haying  anyone  injured.  The  sloop  I 
sent  to  Port  Royal  with  the  Oleander ,  the  schooner  I  have  brought  to  this 
place  for  adjudication.  Having  operated  with  Rear-Admiral  Dahl- 
gren’s  vessels,  I  made  a  report  to  him  of  the  affair,  as  well  as  to  the 
Secretary  of  the  Navy,  which  letters  I  have  sent  north  by  the  Oleander. 

On  the  morning  of  the  8th  I  captured  the  English  sloop  boat  Clara 
Louisa  10  miles  north  of  Indian  River.  On  the  afternoon  of  the  same 
day  off  Gilbert’s  Bar,  I  captured  the  English  schooners  Southern 
Rights  and  Shot /  at  the  same  time  and  place  I  captured  the  American 
schooner  Ann,  of  Key  West,  Fla.  1  am  satisfied  his  intentions  were 
to  ha\e  run  in  at  Jupiter  Inlet  or  Indian  River,  according  to  circum¬ 
stances,.  with  those  vessels.  She  sailed  from  Abaco  on  Monday,  the 
3d,  arrived  at  Sand  Cay  Thursday  night,  sailed  from  Sand  Cay  on 
L  riday  night  in  company  with  the  two  schooners  above  mentioned, 
and  remained  with  them  until  the  time  of  capture. 

I  have  stationed  the  Beauregard  at  the  Haul  Over,  13  miles  above 
Cape  Canaveral,  where  cargoes  have  been  landed  and  others  taken  in, 
with  orders  for  him  to  proceed  to  Jupiter  Inlet  when  it  is  necessary 
to  communicate  with  the  bark  Pursuit  for  stores. 

I  found  it  impossible  to  close  Jupiter  Inlet;  therefore  consider  it 
important  to  have  a  vessel  of  some  kind  stationed  at  that  place  con¬ 
stantly. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Earl  English, 
Lieutenant-  Commanded'. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Pensacola  Bay ,  August  16 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  between  the  hours  of  7 
and  8  this  morning-  several  of  the  officers  and  men  of  this  vessel

Report  of  Captain  Walker,  B.  S.  Navy,  proposing  a  search  of  the  baggage  found  on  board 

the  prize. 

U.  S.  Ship  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico ,  August  32,  1863.. 

Sir:  On  the  day  of  the  capture  of  the  Confederate  steamer  Alice 
Vivian ,  a  falling  barometer  and  the  threatening  aspect  of  the  weather, 
together  with  a  consideration  of  the  season  of  the  year,  all  admonished 
rue  to  send  the  prize  into  port  with  the  least  delajr;  therefore  at  the 
time  of  separation  from  her  I  had  not  had  time  to  ascertain  the  char¬ 
acter  of  the  passengers  transferred  from  her  to  this  ship. 

Upon  examination  I  find  that  among  these  men  are  several  of  the 
staff  of  General  Slaughter,  C.  S.  A. 

I  am  informed  that  General  Slaughter  had  embarked  on  board  the 
steamer  with  all  his  staff,  but  that  a  few  hours  previous  to  her  leaving 
Mobile  Bay  he  returned  to  the  city,  accompanied  by  Captain  Aldrich, 
of  his  staff,  and  perhaps  others;  whether  with  the  intention  of  rejoin¬ 
ing  the  steamer  I  can  not  learn,  but  from  the  fact  that  the  baggage  of 
Captain  Aldrich  and  others  had  been  on  board  it  is  probable  that  such 
had  been  his  intention. 

The  destination  of  General  Slaughter  is  Texas,  whither  he  was  going 
to  raise  a  brigade. 


534 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADKON. 


On  my  arrival  at  Key  West,  to-morrow  probably,  I  shall  suggest 
that  the  baggage  and  papers  belonging  to  these  officers  be  submitted 
to  the  scrutiny  of  General  Woodbury. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  M.  Walker, 

Captain ,  TJ.  S  Navy.

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Lieutenant- 
Commander^  Me  Doug  at,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  Assistant  Surgeon 
Pratt ,  C.  S.  Army ,  a  prisoner  from  the  prize  steamer  Alice  Vivian. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  August  21,  1863. 

Sir:  You  will  please  receive  on  board,  from  the  prize  steamer  Alice 
Vivian  as  a  prisoner  of  war,  Dr.  T.  T.  Pratt,  an  assistant  surgeon  in 
the  Confederate  Army,  who  was  captured  en  route  from  Mobile  to 
Havana. 

Dr.  Pratt  represents  himself  as  being  under  military  orders  for 
Texas,  and  says  that  the  difficulties  of  getting  there  by  land  had 
induced  the  rebel  authorities  to  allow  him  to  attempt  this  mode  of 
reaching  his  destination;  but  he  urges  the  existence  of  a  cartel  or 
agreement  of  some  kind,  by  which  medical  officers  are  exempted  from 
the  ordinary  results  of  capture,  as  applied  to  others.  I  have  received 
no  notice  of  such  arrangement,  and  if  it  exists,  I  conceive  it  to  apply 
only  to  such  medical  officers  as  may  be  taken  on  the  field  of  battle 
and  in  the  exercise  of  their  professional  duties.  In  addition  to  this 
the  U.  S.  consul-general  at  Havana  writes  me  under  date  of  July  28 
as  follows: 

I  have  information  from  a  very  reliable  source  that  the  British  house  of  Brooks, 
Douglass  &  Co.,  of  Havana  (whose  Mr.  Douglass  has  a  brother  residing  in  Mobile)! 
received,  per  steamer  Alice,  an  order  from  the  Confederate  Commissary" Department,’ 
through  the  Douglass,  of  Mobile,  for  a  very  large  quantity  of  medicines,  etc.  One 
item  is  300  ounces  of  quinine.  I  understand  the  army  in  Mobile  are  in  great  need 
of  these  supplies;  and  if  they  do  not  reach  them,  the  Confederate  forces  will  be  in  a 
very  bad  way. 

It  is  not  a  violent  supposition,  therefore,  that  Dr.  Pratt  may  have 
been  ordered  to  Havana  to  expedite  the  purchase  and  shipment  of

board  the  prize  steamer  Nit  a,  brought  in  here  yesterday),  and  in  that 
case,  as  I)r.  Pratt  would  have  been  employed  in  a  commercial  capacity 
by  the  lebel  Government,  of  course  his  commission  would  not  carry

Report  of  Rating  Rear- R dmira l  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
operations  of  the  prize  steamer  James  Battle ,  Rugust  23  to  September*' 
18,  1863 ,  under  command  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Semmes,  U  S. 
Navy. 

No.  299.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  September  22,  1863. 

Sir:  Having  received  information  from  the  acting  U.  S.  consul- 
general  at  Havana  that  one  or  more  steamers  were  about  to  attempt  a 
violation  of  the  blockade  at  some  point  between  Tampa  Bay  and  St. 
Marks,  I  dispatched  notice  to  that  effect  to  the  commanding  officers 
of  the  blockading  vessels,  and  at  the  same  time  obtained  from  the  U.  S. 
deputy  marshal  at  this  place  the  temporary  use  of  the  prize  steamer 
James  Battle  to  scour  the  coast.  She  was  hurriedly  fitted  out  with  two 
rifled  and  two  smoothbore  12-pounders,  manned  from  the  crew  of  the 
Tahoma ,  placed  under  charge  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Semmes, 
and  dispatched  up  the  coast  on  the  23d  of  August.  Information  sub¬ 
sequently  reached  me  that  one  of  the  reported  steamers  had  been 
repeatedly  chased  off  the  coast  by  our  blockading  vessels,  and  had 
returned  to  Havana;  and  it  appears  that  another  attempted  to  get  into 
the  Suwanee  River,  but  was  prevented  by  the  presence  of  the  Battle. 
Owing  to  the  Battle  having  got  aground,  and  remained  so  for  twelve 
days,  she  was  unable  to  continue  the  expedition  up  the  Suwanee, 
where  a  small  steamer  was  supposed  to  be;  but  by  a  sudden  descent 
upon  Bayport  she  performed  a  more  important  service,  by  frighten¬ 
ing  the  rebels  into  destroying  (by  fire)  a  still  larger  steamer  and  a 
large  warehouse  filled  with  cotton.  There  was  no  loss  of  any  sort  on 
our  part,  and  I  consider  the  expedition  as  sufficiently  successful.  I 
enclose  Lieutenant-Commander  Semmes’s  report. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Rcting  Rear- Rdmiral,  Comdg.  Blast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

and  sea,  Loth  ahead,  increasing,  and  the  weather  looking  bad,  I  returned 
to  an  anchorage  inside  of  the  light.  At  8  p.  m.,  the  weather  being 
more  promising,  I  started  again,  and  on  the  following  day  sighted 
Sanibel  Island  and  Charlotte  Harbor.  The  25th,  at  daylight,  then  off 
Tampa  Bay,  called  out  the  Huntsville  by  using  bituminous  coal,  with 
the  view  of  delivering  provisions  and  getting  some  firemen  from  her, 
but  it  being  too  rough  for  boat  work  we  were  obliged  to  go  inside. 
The  same  night,  at  midnight,  left  for  Cedar  Keys,  near  the  bar  of 
which  anchorage  we  were  obliged  to  run  for  shelter  the  following  day 
in  a  gale  of  wind.  On  the  27th,  having  received  reinforcements  from 
the,  Tort  Henry ,  we  left,  intending  to  go  up  the  Suw7anee  River  after 
an  English-built  steamer  seen  on  that  stream.  Here  our  difficulties 
commenced.  The  pilot  upon  whom  I  relied  to  carry  the  vessel  into 
the  mouth  of  the  river  did  not  (experience  subsequently  proved  it) 
know  where  to  look  for  it.  The  result  was  the  vessel  was  run  ashore 
twice,  and  gotten  off  at  next  high  water  following,  but  on  running' 
ashore  a  third  time  she  lay  twelve  days. 

Whilst  ashore,  feeling  doubtful  of  the  pilot’s  competency,  I  sent  a 
boat  to  the  northwest  to  sound,  and  to  look  for  the  mouth  of  the 
ii\ei.  YV  hen  the  boat  was  about  5  or  6  miles  distant  a  steamer  was 
discerned  standing  in  toward  the  land.  Bituminous  coal  was  burned 
by  us  to  decoy  her,  but  the  stranger,  discovering  our  boat,  turned 
seaward  ana  r._ .  -  out.  That  night,  as  the  steamer  appeared  to  stop 
a.  long  distance  offshore,  sent  two  armed  boats  to  the  mouth  of  the

sounded  the  pass  through  the  reef  and  one  of  them  went  up  to  the 
forks  of  the  river.  I  afterwards  sounded  it;  scant  6  feet  can  be  car¬ 
ried  through  a  passage  (which  must  be  passed  at  high  slack  water) 
varying  from  70  to  100  feet  in  width,  until  the  river  is  entered,  when 

thei  e  appears  to  be  plenty  of  room.  No  other  passage  into  the  river 
was  found.

U.  b.  Tender  Fox, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  August  25,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  left  Key  West  July  27  in 
obedience  to  your  instructions,  and  proceeded  to  my  cruising  ground 
between  the  Aucilla  and  Suwanee  rivers,  stopping  to  deliver  mails  and 
dispatches  to  the  Huntsville  at  Tampa  Bay,  the  Fort  Henry  at  Cedar 
Keys,  and  the  Stars  and  Stripes  at  St.  Marks. 

On  the  10th  instant  at  7  a.  m.  the  lookout  raised  black  smoke  and  I 
made  all  sail  in  chase.  At  10  I  made  him  out  to  be  a  lead-colored  river 
steamer  with  a  white  smokestack  and  one  mast.  The  wind  dying  away 
however,  he  gained  on  me  rapidly,  so  that  at  noon  he  was  hull  down5 
and  at  2  p.  m.  his  smoke  had  disappeared  entirely. 

His  course  was  about  N.  N.  E.  My  position  at  meridian  was,  bv 

observation,  latitude  29°  06' N.,  longitude  84°  25' W.  J 

Standing  to  the  northward  through  the  afternoon,  the  lookout  raised 
black  smoke  to  the  northward  and  eastward  at  5  o’clock  and  I  made  all 
sail  in  chase.  At  5:  30  raised  another  smoke,  and  this  appearing  the 
nearer  of  the  two,  I  kept  off  for  it.  At  0  made  out  two  steamers  stand¬ 
ing  in  the  same  direction,  the  second  one  resembling  the  one  we  had 
chased  in  the  morning.  At  6:30  opened  on  him  with  the  rifle  at 
extreme  elevation,  using  Hotchkiss  shell  with  20-second  fuzes,  but  the 
shells  m  every  instance  burst  high  in  the  air  and  not,  I  should  iudsre 
at  more  than  two-thirds  range.  J  s

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Baxter,  U.  S.  Navy,  command- 
ing  L  .  fe.  bark  Gem  of  the  Sea,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  sloop 
Richard,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence. 


U.  S.  Bark  Gem  oe  the  Sea, 

Charlotte  Harbor,  September  3,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  on  the  night  of  the  31st 
ultimo  1  captured  the  sloop  Richard,  of  5  tons,  hailing  from  Nassau 
New  Proi  idence,  laden  with  8^  bales  of  cotton.  Her  crew  made  their 
escape  on  shore,  except  Henry  Brown  (colored),  who  belongs  to  Nas¬ 
sau,  New  Providence. 

.  I  have  sent  the  above-named  sloop  to  Key  West,  in  charge  of  Act¬ 
ing  Ensign  W.  H.  Winslow  and  a  prize  crew,  for  adjudication,  with 
Henry  Brown  as  a  witness. 

.  The  following  is  a  detailed  account  of  her  capture:  Having  received 
information  from  refugees  that  the  above-named  sloop  was  lying 
about  15  miles  up  Peace  Creek  and  40  miles  from  this  ship,  laden  with 
cotton,  intending  to  run  the  blockade,  on  the  31st  ultimo,  at  noon,  I 
sent  an  expedition,  consisting  of  the  launch  and  first  cutter,  armed 
and  manned  with  20  men,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  W.  H.  Winslow 
and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Charles  A.  Edgcomb,  accompanied  by  Henry 
W  est,  a  refugee,  acting  as  their  pilot,  with  orders  to  Mr.  Winslow  to 
proceed  up  Peace  Creek  and  bring  the  sloop  out  if  possible. 

Mr.  Winslow  returned  on  board  the  following  morning  at  6  a.  m., 
1st  instant,  from  the  expedition,  having  found  the  sloop  lying  at 
anchor  27  miles  up  Charlotte  Harbor,  near  the  entrance  to  Peace 
Creek,  and  captured  her,  finding  no  one  on  board  but  the  above- 
named  negro. 

The  above-named  sloop  has  an  English  register,  but  is  owned  by 
John  Mooney  and  James  Fuell,  both  living  in  West  Florida. 

I  am  sorry  to  have  to  state  that  John  A.  Smith,  seaman  on  board 
this  vessel,  was  severely  wounded  in  the  right  hand  while  on  the  expe¬ 
dition  to  capture  the  within-named  sloop,  by  the  accidental  discharge 
of  a  rifle  in  the  hands  of  William  Smart,  seaman,  also  belonging  to  this 

n  w  r — vol  17 - 35 


546 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


vessel.  The  hand  was  so  badly  shattered  that  the  surgeon  was  obliged 
to  amputate  it,  and  he  is  now  doing  well. 

It  gives  me  pleasure  to  call  your  attention  to  the  zeal  which  Acting 
Ensign  William  H.  Winslow  exhibited  throughout  the  expedition  and 
the  admirable  behavior  of  the  men  under  him,  and  also  of  Henry  West, 
a  refugee,  who  volunteered  his  services  as  their  pilot. 

Enclosed  herewith  is  a  list  of  officers  and  men  who  are  entitled  to 
share  in  the  prize  money. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Order  of  Acting  Rear- Admired  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Captain  Walker, 
U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  De  Soto ,  regarding  the  cruising 
ground  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  September  3, 1863. 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  is  ready  for  sea  you 
will  proceed  to  execute  the  verbal  instructions  I  have  given  you,  after 
which  you  will  be  pleased  to  cruise  on  the  parallel  of  29°  30'  north  lati¬ 
tude,  between  the  meridians  of  86°  and  88°  west  longitude.  These 
limits  are  not  to  be  considered  as  altogether  rigid,  and  you  can,  at  your 
discretion,  extend  them  to  the  northward,  eastward,  or  westward;  but 
as  the  San  Jacinto  will  be  ordered  to  cruise  on  the  parallel  of  29° 
between  the  meridians  of  85°  30'  and  87°  30'  and  the  Huntsville  on  the 
parallel  of  28°  30'  between  the  meridians  of  85°  and  87°  you  will  see 
that  any  great  departure  to  the  southward  of  the  line  indicated  will 
defeat  the  general  plan  for  intercepting  any  vessels  bound  in  or  out  of 
Mobile,  besides  causing  an  unnecessary  expenditure  of  coal  by  mutual 
chasing. 

You  will  return  to  this  port  when  in  want  either  of  coal  or  provisions. 
Respectfully,

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  sani¬ 
tary  conditions  at  Key  West. 

No.  286.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  September  6 ,  1863. 

Sir:  Understanding  from  the  public  prints  and  from  private  corre¬ 
spondence  that  a  general  impression  prevails  at  the  North,  probably 
based  upon  the  sad  condition  of  the  steamer  Alabama ,  to  the  effect  that 
the  yellow  fever  has  been  epidemic  at  this  place,  I  deem  it  a  duty,  as 
well  as  a  pleasure,  to  state  to  the  Department  that,  so  far  from'  this 
being  the  case,  not  a  single  instance  of  yellow  fever,  or  of  anything 
approaching  to  it,  has  made  its  appearance,  either  in  the  town  or  har- 
bor,  during  the  entire  season,  and  the  health  of  the  place  is,  in  every 
respect,  remarkably  good. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blkdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Capture  of  the  Confederate  steamer  Alabama ,  September  12,  1863. 

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Mayo,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TT.  S.  S.  Kanawha. 

U.  S.  S.  Kanawha, 

Ship  Island ,  September  13 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  yesterday  from  early  daylight 
a  strange  nondescript  steamer  was  seen  at  anchor  off  the  Chandeleur 
[Islands].  There  was  not  a  thing  under  my  command  here  to  pursue 
it.  At  4  p.  m.,  12th,  a  United  states  steam  bark  was  seen  chasing 
another  fine  steamer  toward  the  same  light-house.  Now,  the  first 
(nondescript)  steamer  got  underway  and  stood  for  Horn  Island  Pass, 
and,  though  somewhat  pressed  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Tennessee ,  was  able  to 
enter  this  sound.  She  met  the  Jackson  and  Calhoun  near  Round 
Island,  and  I  learned  from  a  refugee  from  Biloxi  was  burned  up.  This 
was  the  Confederate  blockade  violator  Fox. 

The  Tennessee ,  after  the  Fox  entered  the  sound,  headed  off  the  other 
steamer,  which  took  refuge  and  escaped  from  both  her  and  the  San 
Jacinto  by  running  into  the  shoal  water  behind  the  Chandeleurs. 
From  my  lookout  at  the  masthead  of  this  ship  1  was  witness  to  this 
chase  and  the  escape.  I  immediately  dispatched  the  Eugenie ,  armed 
steamer,  under  Acting  Ensign  N.  M.  Dyer,  having  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Charles  H.  Greene  on  board  as  probable  prize  master. 
The  Eugenie  came  up  on  west  side  of  the  Chandeleurs,  in  less  than  7 
feet  water,  and  possessed  as  prize  the  Confederate  steamer  Alabama , 
from  Havana  for  Mobile,  cargo  assorted.  The  Tennessee ,  Acting 
Volunteer  Lieutenant  George  Wiggin,  sent  boats  also  to  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Greene.  This  vessel  was  now  in  possession  of  the  Eugenie 
and  Tennessee,  having  escaped  from  the  San  Jacinto ,  then  at  anchor  near 
to  the  Chandeleur  light-house.  The  route  of  the  Eugenie  and  prize  to 
this  place  lay  near  to  the  San  Jacinto .  Lieutenant-Commander  Ralph 
Chandler  ordered  Lieutenant-Commander  Greene  to  yield  the  prize 
to  him,  and  he,  without  communicating  with  this  established  naval 
station,  although  only  11  miles  off,  stood  away  for  Key  West. 

As  the  Alabama  had  escaped  the  San  Jacinto,  and  her  deditio  beino- 
to  two  vessels  of  this  squadron,  I  sent  the  Tennessee ,  and  recalled  the 
ban  Jacinto  and  Alabama  to  this  port.  I  have  taken  charge  of  the 
Alabama ,  sent  her,  with  proper  crew,  to  the  nearest  prize  court  to 
wit,  New  Orleans,  and  this  paper  will  be  mailed  by  Prize  Master  N  ?M 
Dyer  in  New  Orleans. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  K.  Mayo, 

TT  „  Lieutenant- Commanded'. 

Hon.  Gideon  W7elles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Chandler,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto, 

regarding  the  capture. 

U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto, 

At  Sea,  Lat.  29°  1,5'  N,  Lang.  88°  15'  W,  September  If  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  concerning 
the  capture  of  the  rebel  steamer  Alabama: 

On  the  11th  instant,  at  2  o’clock  p.  m.,  latitude  29°  02'  N.,  longi¬ 
tude  87°  32'  W.,  the  masthead  lookout  reported  black  smoke,  bearing 
about  south.  I  steered  for  it  under  full  steam,  and  soon  discovered 
that  the  smoke  originated  from  a  steamer,  and  that  the  steamer  was 
steering  to  the  northward.  As  soon  as  she  discovered  the  San  Jacinto 
she  kept  away  to  the  westward,  and  the  chase  was  continued  until  7 
p.  m.,  when  it  became  too  dark  to  see  her.  1  felt  confident  that  the 
steamer  was  a  blockade  runner  and  that  she  was  bound  to  Mobile,  and 
accordingly  shaped  such  courses  during  the  night  as,  in  my  opinion, 
would  intercept  her.  On  the  morning  of  the  12th  instant  she  was  dis¬ 
covered  from  aloft,  bearing  N.  N.  W.,  and  I  immediately  steered  for 
her,  going  at  full  speed.  The  San  Jacinto  gained  on  the  chase  fast 
during  the  day,  until  we  were  up  with  the  light  on  the  north  point  of 
the  Chandeleur  Islands,  when  I  deemed  it  unsafe  to  chase  farther  with 
the  ship,  but  came  to  anchor  with  the  light-house  bearing  east,  about 
2  miles  distant,  and  dispatched  the  first  cutter  under  command  of 
Lieutenant-Commander  J.  N.  Quackenbush  to  continue  the  chase.  In 
the  meantime  the  Tennessee ,  which  was  in  sight,  kept  away  and  stood 
to  the  southward,  close  inshore  on  the  east  side  of  the  Chandeleur 
Islands,  and  the  Eugenie ,  which  came  from  Ship  Island,  passed  bjq 
heading  for  the  strange  steamer.  At  6  p.  m.  the  strange  sail,  that 
afterwards  proved  to  be  the  unarmed  rebel  steamer  Alabama,  ran  on 
shore  in  plain  sight  of  this  ship,  in  about  latitude  29°  56'  N.,  longi¬ 
tude  88°  52'  W.,  on  one  of  the  shoals  on  the  inside  of  the  Chandeleur 
Islands,  and  was  taken  possession  of  b}r  the  steamer  Eugenie  before 
the  first  cutter  of  this  ship  reached  her.  The  vessels  in  sight,  and,  in 
my  opinion,  entitled  to  share  in  the  prize,  were  the  San  Jacinto ,  the 
Tennessee,  and  the  Eugenie. 

I  took  possession  of  her  as  soon  as  she  was  brought  to  where  this 
ship  was  at  anchor,  and  subsequently  delivered  her  to  Lieutenant- 
Commander  W.  K.  Mayo,  of  the  gunboat  Kanawha,  who  claimed  a 
prior  right.  All  the  papers  are  in  his  possession,  and  it  is  therefore 
impossible  for  me  to  state  the  size,  cargo,  etc.,  of  the  Alabama.  I 
have  the  honor  to  transmit  a  list  of  the  officers  and  men  of  this  ship. 


552 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


On  the  afternoon  of  the  13th,  while  in  chase  of  the  Alabama ,  passed 
another  steamer  burning  black,  smoke,  which  I  was  afterwards 
informed  was  the  Fox ,  another  blockade  runner,  and  as  soon  as  it  was 
dark  saw  a  bright  light  bearing  about  N.  N.  E.,  and  believe  it  to  have 
been  the  Fox  on  fire. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  Chandler, 

Lieut.  Commander ,  U.  S.  Nary ,  Comdg.  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Captain  Walker ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  if.  S.  S.  L)e  Soto , 
regarding  the  capture  of  the  steamer  Montgomery. 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Gulf  of  Mexico,  September!'  13 ,  1863. 

Sir:  1  have  to  inform  you  that  this  day,  in  latitude  28°  32'  longi¬ 
tude  87°  12',  I  seized  for  attempted  violation  of  the  blockade  procla¬ 
mation,  and  instituted  by  the  President  of  the  United  States,  the 
steamer  Montgomery ,  Richard  Roach,  master,  who  represents  that  the 
steamer  sailed  under  British  colors,  is  from  Havana  with  an  assorted 
cargo,  and  was  bound  to  Mobile. 

On  demanding  the  papers  of  the  Montgomery ,  her  master  declared 
that  he  had  no  papers.  I  have  accordingly  ordered  her  to  New  Orleans 
for  adjudication. 

The  chase  to-day  was  continued  nine  hours  under  both  steam  and 
sail.  Three  months  ago  we  should  have  concluded  it  in  one-fourth  of 
the  time,  but  now  the  crippled  condition  of  the  ship  soon  becomes 
apparent  to  the  enemy,  and  thus  hope  sustains  to  the  last  the  effort  to 
escape  us.  The  whole  tribe  of  blockade  runners  has  been  watching 
this  ship — they  tell  me  so — and  are  as  well  informed  as  I  am  in  regard 
to  the  tinkering  upon  her  at  Key  West  and  the  general  inefficiency  of 
her  boilers. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  M.  Walker, 

.  .  .  Captain ,  if.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla.

an<  ^om  the  direction  it  trailed  I  was  under  the  impression 
that  the  vessel  was  steering  about  S.  E.  As  soon  as  the  chase  after 
the  Alabama  was  discontinued  for  the  night  I  determined  to  steer  such 
a  course  as  in  my  judgment  would  during  the  first  part  of  the  night 
intercept  the  steamer  bearing  N.  W.,  and  if  unsuccessful  in  that 
to  endeavor  to  have  the  Alabama  in  sight  in  the  morning.  The  shin  was 
accordingly  steered  E.  N.  E.  £  E.,  and  not  meeting  with  anything,  at 
midnight  the  course  was  changed  to  N.  W.  £  W.  I  had  no  apprehen¬ 
sions  of  the  Alabama’s  trying  to  get  into  Mobile  that  night,  as  she  was 
too  tar  oft,  and  my  idea  was  that  she  would  steam  slow  up  to  within 
easy  distance  and  remain  until  the  next  night  to  run  the  blockade. 
Un  the  morning  of  the  12th  the  Alabama  was  in  sight,  and  during  the 
chase,  winch  I  reported  in  my  communication  to  vou,  at  2  p.  m.  on 
the  12th,  the  same  steamer  that  I  had  endeavored  to  cut  off  the  nio-ht 
before  hove  in  sight,  steering  toward  Horn  Island. 

The  San  Jacinto’s  course  was  so  directed  that  neither  steamer  could 
escape  to  the  eastward  of  the  Chandeleur  Islands,  and  at  2  jj.  m.  the 
Tennessee  hove  in  sight  to  the  nothwarcl  of  us,  thus  rendering  it  impos¬ 
sible  for  the  smaller  steamer,  which  I  was  afterwards  informed  was  the 
Tox,  to  escape.  I  therefore  directed  all  my  energies  to  the  capture  of 
the  Alabama .  The  commanding*  officer  of  the  Tennessee  informed  me 
Oil  the  evening  of  the  12th  instant  that  the  steamer  running  for  Horn 
Island  was  the  Fox y  and  that  he  knew  her  well;  that  he  ran  as  near  the 
reef  as  he  dared  to  go  in  chase  of  her,  and  that  she  had  got  through 
the  passage  to  the  eastward  of  Horn  Island,  where  the  gunboat 
Calhoun  and  another  one  had  pressed  her  so  hard  that  she  was  run  on 
shore  by  her  own  people  and  fired.  I  am  confident  that  the  steamer  seen 
by  rue  on  the  11th  at  6:30  p.  m.  was  the  same  one  that  ran  into  Mis¬ 
sissippi  Sound  on  the  evening  of  the  12th,  and  as  soon  as  it  was  dark 
a  bright  light  as  of  a  vessel  burning  was  distinctly  in  sight  from  the 
deck  of  this  ship,  bearing  from  our  anchorage  about  N.  N.  E.  I  also 
feel  confident  that  the  San  Jacinto  was  the  cause  of  the  steamer’s  run¬ 
ning  into  Mississippi  Sound,  and  consequently  of  her  being  chased  by 
our  gunboats  and  subsequently  burned. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  Chandler, 

Lieutenant-  Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy,  Comdg.  San  Jacinto.

Reports  of  Captain  Walker,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  capture  hy  that 
vessel  of  the  steamer  Leviathan. 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

South  West  Pass,  September  22,  1863. 

Sir:  We  ran  into  the  South  West  Pass  this  morning  for  the  purpose 
of  receiving  officers  and  men  who  had  been  placed  in  charge  of  prizes 
ordered  to  New  Orleans. 

Before  crossing  the  bar  we  received  information  that  a  few  hours 
previously  a  steamer  had  been  boarded  by  a  band  of  rebels  and  carried 
out  of  the  river. 

We  immediately  stood  to  sea,  and  as  we  had  just  run  in  from  the 
eastward  without  seeing  her,  it  was  fair  to  presume  that  she  had  run 
off  to  the  southward,  and  we  shaped  our  course  accordingly. 

It  was  not  long  before  we  made  a  sail  from  the  masthead,  and  after 
a  run  of  about  35  miles  we  captured  the  Leviathan. 

The  Leviathan  is  a  new  and  very  fast  screw  steamer,  amply  supplied 
with  coal  and  provisions  for  a  cruise,  and  has  a  picked  crew. 

I  feel  great  satisfaction  in  announcing  this  success,  for  when  the 
Boston,  a  very  much  inferior  vessel,  was  carried  off  some  months  ago  by 
a  similar  enterprise  we  soon  fell  upon  her  track,  and  thus  had  the  oppor¬ 
tunity  of  witnessing  the  desolation  she  had  spread  in  her  path,  black¬ 
ening  the  seas  in  her  wake  with  the  charred  memorials  of  many  fine 
ships. 

I  shall  send,  the  Leviathan  with  her  desperate  band  to  New  Orleans. 

I  am,  sir,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  M.  Walker, 

Captain ,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Secretary  of  the  Navy, 

Washington,  D.  C.

We,  the  subscribers,  seamen  and  others,  do,  and  each  of  us  does, 
hereby  agree  to  and  with  Franklin  Buchanan,  of  the  Confederate 
States  Navy,  in  manner  and  form  following,  that  is  to  say: 

In  the  first  place  we  do  hereby  agree,  for  the  considerations  herein¬ 
after  mentioned,  to  enter  the  service  of  the  Navy  of  the  Confederate 
States,  and  in  due  and  seasonable  time  repair  on  board  such  vessel  of 
the  Navy  as  we  may  be  ordered  to  join,  and  during  the  term  of  the 
existing  war  with  the  United  States,  and  until  the  return  to  the  Con¬ 
federate  States  of  the  vessel  in  which  we  may  be  serving  on  a  foreign 
station  at  the  expiration  of  said  war,  provided  by  and  upon  the 
conditions  of  the.  act  of  Congress,  approved  March  2,  1837,  entitled 

An  act  to  provide  for  the  enlistment  of  boys  for  naval  service  and 
to  extend,  the  term  of  the  enlistment  of  seamen,”  and  February  20, 
1845,  entitled  “An  act  to  amend  an  act  entitled  ‘An  act  to  provide  for 
the  enlistment  of  boys  for  the  naval  service  and  to  extend  the  term  of 
the  enlistment  of  seamen,’”  and  adopted  by  an  act  entitled  “An  act 
to  provide  for  the  organization  of  the  Navy  of  the  Confederate  States,” 
approved  March  16,  1861,  unless  sooner  discharged  by  proper  author¬ 
ity,  to  the  utmost  of  our  power  and  ability,  respectively,  to  discharge 
our  several  duties,  and  in  everything  to  be  conformable  and  obedient 
to  the  several  requirings  and  lawful  commands  of  the  officers  who  may 
fiom  time  to  time  be  placed  near  us. 

Secondly.— We  do  also  oblige  and  subject  ourselves  to  serve  during 
the  term  aforesaid,  and  we  do  severally  oblige  ourselves  during  such 
service  to  comply  with  and  be  subject  to  such  laws,  regulations,  and 
discipline  of  the  Navy  as  are  or  that  may  be  established  by  the  Con¬ 
gress  of  the  Confederate  States  or  other  competent  authority. 

^  Thirdly.—  The  said  Franklin  Buchanan,  for  and  in  behalf  of  the 
Confederate  States,  does  hereby  covenant  and  agree  to  and  with  the

Report  of  Acting  Marten'  Owens ,  U  S.  Navy,  commanding  U  S.  S. 

Clyde ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Amaranth ,  of  Boston. 

U.  S.  S.  Clyde, 

Tortug as  Harbor,  September  %7,  1863. 

Sin.  W  hile  cruising  off  to  the  W.  S.  W.  of  Log'gerhead  light- 
f ie  masthead  lookout  reported  at  1  p.  m.  a  strange  sail  bearing 
b.  by  b.  and  steering  N.  W.  At  1:30  made  her  out  to  be  a 
schoonei  under  mainsail,  foresail,  and  jib.  At  1:45  she  set  the  flying 
pC  Vv  e  called  ail  hands  to  quarters  and  fired  a  shot  astern  of  'her 
winch  she  took  no  notice  of;  we  fired  another,  which  struck  one-fourth 
ot  a  mile  ahead  of  her;  as  soon  as  the  shot  struck  they  set  their  main¬ 
top  staysail  and  kept  on  their  course.  When  I  saw  this  1  immediately 
niccl  the  thud  at  her,  which  fell  10  yards  short,  when  thej^  immedi- 
ately  hove  to.  I  came  up  with  her  at  3  p.  m.  She  was  in  latitude,  at 
that  time,  24°  25'  N.,  longitude  83°  30' W.,  and  no  other  vessel  in 
sight,  Loggerhead  light-house  bearing  E.  N.  E.,  distant  30  miles. 
Sent  a  boat  alongside.  Upon  examination  of  the  papers  she  proved 
to  be  the  schooner  Amaranth,  of  Boston,  with  a  cargo  of  200  boxes  of 
sugar,  11,000  cigars,  and  4  cases  of  merchandise.  I  opened  her  hatches 
and  examined  the  character  of  the  cargo,  which  I  found  all  the  articles 
the  bills  of  lading  called  for.  The  only  thing  that  I  condemn  her  on 
is  her  cargo  and  not  heaving  to  when  fired  at.  I  took  her  in  tow  and 
brought  her  into  this  place,  and  I  think  it  my  duty  to  send  her  to  Key 
West  for  adjudication.  In  looking  over  her  papers  I  found  some  of 
them  signed  by  two  captains,  which  looks  very  suspicious.  Not  hav¬ 
ing  anyone  acquainted  with  the  reef,  I  therefore  sent  my  pilot  on  board 
to  take  her  to  Key  West. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  humble  and  obedient  servant, 

A.  A.  Owens, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  Steamer  Clyde. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Bast  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron,  Key  West.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Rockwell ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 
tender  Two  Sisters ,  regarding  expeditions  to  Bay  port,  Fla.,  in  search 
of  a  steamer. 

U.  S.  Tender  Two  Sisters, 

Key  West,  September  — ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  of  making  the  following  report.  Having 
received  information  on  the  5th  instant,  while  lying  in  Cedar  Keys,  of 
the  presence  of  a  steamer  in  Bayport,  I  immediately  proceeded  to 
cruise  olf  that  place,  arriving  there  on  the  morning  of  the  6th.  On 
the  7th  saw  two  sails  inshore,  and  on  standing  for  them,  found  them 
to  be  two  boats  from  the  Fort  Henry  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


561 


Mate  Hancock,  who  had  been  sent  down  the  coast  to  watch  the  move¬ 
ments  of  the  steamer  inshore.  I  took  the  boats  in  tow,  and  the  next 
morning',  taking'  advantage  of  a  flood  tide,  stood  inshore  to  endeavor 
to  discover  the  main  channel  through  St.  Martin’s  Reef.  Having 
arrived  within  about  4  miles  of  Bayport,  I  anchored,  having  barely 
sufficient  water  to  float  the  vessel.  \\  ith  the  aid  of  a  glass,  I  soon  dis¬ 
covered  the  steamer  lying  near  the  shore,  partly  covered  with  bushes. 
She  was  painted  lead  color,  had  side-wheels,  one  pipe  painted  white, 
one  mast  with  a  standing  gaff  upon  it,  and  her  after  end  was  covered 
with  a  rounding  top,  apparently  painted  yellow.  Being  unable  to  do 
anything  more  that  tide,  stood  offshore  to  a  sufficient  depth,  and 
feeling  assured  that  she  could  never  leave  the  harbor  in  the  night,  as 
soon  as  it  was  dark,  stood  for  Cedar  Keys  to  give  information  of  her 
whereabouts  to  Captain  McCauley  of  the  Fort  Henry.  I  weighed 
again  the  same  evening  to  return,  taking  the  Fort  Henry’s  armed 
launch  with  me.  At  daylight  saw  a  sail  offshore,  which  proved  to  be 
the  tender  Annie ,  Acting  Ensign  Williams  in  command,  and  Avhom  I 
detained  to  carry  any  information  that  I  could  procure  to  Cedar  Keys. 
Stood  inshore  with  both  vessels  until  within  10  miles  of  Bayport, 
when  the  wind  failing  I  took  the  Fort  Henry’s  launch  and  the  Two 
/Sisters’  boats,  and  went  inshore  to  within  4  miles  of  Bayport,  discov¬ 
ering  the  steamer  to  be  still  there,  but  the  weather  being  very  squally 
and  rainy  was  unable  to  accomplish  my  purpose  of  finding  the  channel, 
everything  being  obscured.  On  returning  on  board,  dispatched  the 
Annie  to  Cedar  Keys  with  the  information  that  the  steamer  was  still 
there.  On  the  12th,  the  weather  being  again  clear,  stood  in  toward 
Bayport,  taking  advantage  of  a  flood  tide,  and  when  within  3i  miles  of 
Bayport,  saw  the  reef  and  the  channel  stakes.  Anchored  near  the 
reef,  and  sent  an  armed  boat  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Mon¬ 
tague  to  sound  out  the  channel,  which  dut}^  he  performed  in  a  satis¬ 
factory  manner,  going  within  1  mile  of  the  battery.  As  the  boat  was 
returning,  the  rebel  flag  was  hoisted  on  the  battery,  when  I  threw  a 
shell  in  toward  it,  but  found  we  were  out  of  range.  The  tide  failing 
I  stood  out  again.  The  steamer  had  been  hauled  in  behind  the  island 
on  which  the  town  of  Bayport  stands  since  my  last  reconnoissance, 
and  was  still  further  disguised  with  bushes. 

On  returning  on  board  Mr.  Montague  reported  having  found  no 
less  than  6  feet  of  water  at  any  place,  and  the  channel  through  the 
reef  not  less  than  100  yards  wide.  I  blockaded  the  place  during  the 
next  day,  and  in  the  evening  stood  for  Cedar  Keys,  arriving  the  14th, 
and  finding  an  expedition  just  starting  for  Bayport,  consisting  of  the 
steamer  James  Battle ,  schooner  Annie ,  with  boats,  etc.  The  steamer 
immediately  took  the  Two  Sisters  in  tow,  and  1  went  on  board  the 
steamer  to  render  what  assistance  I  could.  We  arrived  off  Bayport 
the  next  day,  and  had  the  pleasure  of  witnessing  the  destruction  of 
the  steamer,  and  a  large  warehouse  apparently  containing  cotton,  and 
of  participating  in  a  bloodless  victoxy,  won  from  the  fears  of  the 
enemy. 

Respectfully, 

C.  H.  Rockwell, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Tpieodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Morris ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 
TJ.  S.  S.  Port  Royal ,  regarding  the  destruction  of  salt  works  near 
St.  George's  Sound,  Florida. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Port  Royal, 

St.  George's  Sound,  Fla. ,  October  3,  1863. 
Sir:  Having  received  information  that  there  were  some  salt  works 
2£  miles  hack  on  the  mainland  and  16  miles  by  water,  I  yesterday  dis¬ 
patched  Acting  Master  E.  Van  Slyck  in  the  launch  to  destroy  them. 
He  returned  to-day  without  casualties,  having  destroyed  6  boilers  and 
kettles,  2  large  vats,  and  all  the  utensils  for  making  salt. 

Ve^  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  U.  Morris, 

Lieutenant-  Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Baxter ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  TJ.  S.  bark  Gem  of  the  Sea,  regarding  the  caqoture  of  the  British 
schooner  Director. 

U.  S.  Bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 
Charlotte  Llarbor,  October  3,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  on  the  evening  of  the 
30th  ultimo  I  captured  the  British  schooner  Director,  2xVo,  of  and  from 
Nassau,  New  Providence,  laden  with  20  small  bags  of  Bahama  salt  and 
1  barrel  rum,  manned  with  two  men,  viz,  Robert  Johnson  (captain) 
and  Thomas  Valentine  (colored  seaman),  while  attempting  to  run  the 
blockade  at  Punta  Rasa,  bound  for  Peace  Creek,  but  cleared  from 
Nassau  for  Key  West.  The  schooner  being  old  and  unseaworthy,  1  do 
not  deem  her  and  her  cargo  of  sufficient  value  to  authorize  me  to  send 
her  in  for  adjudication;  1  therefore  shall  destroy  her. 

The  following  is  a  detailed  account  of  her  capture:  September  the 
30th,  while  the  U.  S.  sloop  Rosalie  (tender  to  this  vessel),  under  the  com¬ 
mand  of  Acting  Master  Peter  F.  Coffin,  blockading  the  passage  which 
runs  into  this  harbor,  and  also  to  the  entrance  of  Sanibel  River,  they 
discovered  a  small  schooner  coming  out  of  Terraceia  Creek  and  making 
for  the  entrance  to  Sanibel  [Caloosa]  River.  Mr.  Coffin  immediately 
sent  his  boat  in  chase  and  captured  her.  She  proved  to  be  the  above- 
named  schooner,  and  brought  her  to  this  vessel,  agreeable  to  my  order. 
Her  crew,  Robert  Johnson  and  Thomas  Valentine,  I  will  send  to  Key 
W est  by  the  Union  for  your  disposal. 

^  This  Robert  Johnson  is  the  man  whose  buildings  I  burned  on  Peace 
Creek  the  2d  of  September  last,  they  being  a  rendezvous  for  guerillas. 

I  have  good  authority  in  saying  that  this  Johnson  is  an  old  blockade 
runner  and  a  notorious  villain.  He  has  been  captured  and  paroled 
twice,  once  at  Philadelphia  and  once  at  Key  West,  and  am  informed 
that  he  broke  his  parole  both  times.  I  am  also  informed  by  Captain 
Wade  S.  Rigby  and  Enoch  Daniels  (refugees  living  on  the  islands  in 
the  vicinity  of  this  harboi’)  that  this  Robert  Johnson  is  the  man  who 
captured  the  schooner  Laura  at  the  entrance  to  Sanibel  River  in  Decem¬ 
ber,  1862.  The  Laura  was  from  Key  West,  with  the  mail  for  this 
squadron  and  stores  for  the  U,  S.  S.  Penguin 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


568 


I  have  deemed  it  advisable  to  send  Captain  Rigby  to  Ke3^  West  by 
the  Union  as  a  witness,  he  wishing  to  go  to  Key  West  to  purchase  a 
tew  articles  for  his  family.  With  your  permission  Captain  Rigby 
would  wish  to  return  to  this  harbor  by  the  first  opportunity  to  his 
family. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Baxter, 

Acting  Volunteer  lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla. 


Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Commander 
Newcomb ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Tioga ,  regarding  the 
cruising  ground  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  October  5,  1863. 

Sir:_  So  soon  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  is  ready  for  sea 
you  will  proceed  in  her  to  cruise  on  the  parallel  of  28°  30'  north  lati¬ 
tude,  between  the  meridians  of  85°  and  87°  west  longitude.  These 
limits  are  not  to  be  considered  as  altogether  rigid,  and  you  can  at 
your  discretion  extend  them  to  the  eastward  or  westward;  but,  as  the 
De  Soto  is  cruising  on  the  parallel  of  29°  30',  between  the  meridians  of 
86°  and  88°,  and  as  the  San  Jacinto  will  be  asssigned  to  the  parallel  of 
29°,  between  the  meridian  of  85°  30'  and  87°  30',  you  will  see  that 
any  great  departure  to  the  northward  of  the  line  indicated  would 
defeat  the  general  plan  for  intercepting  vessels  bound  in  and  out  of 
Mobile,  besides  causing  an  unnecessary  expenditure  of  coal  by  mutual 
chasing.  You  will  return  to  this  port  when  in  want  of  coal/  Should 
you  take  any  prizes,  you  will  send  them  to  New  Orleans  for  adjudica¬ 
tion,  and  if  possible  take  means  to  recover  the  prize  master  and  crew 
before  returning  here. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Commander  Id.  S.  Newcomb,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  G  unboat  Tioga.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Burgess ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S. 

schooner  Beauregard ,  regarding  the  seizure  in  Key  West  Harbor  of 

the  sloop  Last  Trial. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  October  6 ,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  an  order  received  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral 
Theodoras  Bailey  I  have  visited  and  searched  the  sloop  Last  Trial , 
lying  in  this  harbor,  and  find  her  loaded  with  26  sacks  of  salt  and 
without  papers  or  colors.  The  only  man  on  board  (Thomas  Merlin) 
represents  that  she  is  five  da}7s  out  from  Havana,  and  cleared  for 
Nassau,  New  Providence;  that  she  met  with  heavy  weather  to  the 
westward  of  this,  and  had  to  throw  overboard  a  portion  of  the  cargo, 
and  that  she  put  in  here  in  distress  and  that  she  intended  to  run  the 
blockade.  Her  captain  (George  Elliot)  had  already  left  the  vessel, 
but  was  arrested  by  the  provost- marshal,  by  order  from  Admiral 
Bailey.  Before  his  arrest  he  admitted  to  Mr.  Edward  Howe,  prize 
commissioner  of  this  place,  that  he  intended  to  run  the  blockade,  and 
it  was  on  this  information  that  she  was  visited  and  searched.  I  have 
seized  her  as  a  prize  of  war. 

The  following  United  States  vessels  were  within  signal  distance  and 
entitled  to  share  in  the  capture:  San  Jacinto ,  Dale ,  Huntsville, 
Tahoma ,  Tioga ,  Wanderer,  Eugenie,  Marigold,  and  Sunflower,  and 
tender  schooners  Sea  Bird  and  Fox. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Francis  Burgess, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding . 

i  Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C. 

[Endorsement.] 

This  capture  will  scarcely  pay  the  costs. 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Fades,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  baric

vessel. 

U.  S.  Bark  J.  L.  Davis, 

St.  Joseph's  Bay,  Fla.,  October'  7,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  of  the  circum¬ 
stances  of  picking  up  a  lot  of  cotton  by  this  vessel  and  forwarded  to 
Key  West  by  the  U.  S.  bark  Roebuck. ' 

duly  23,  1863,  discovered  a  number  of  bales  of  cotton  drifting  about 
outside  of  this  harbor;  sent  boats  and  picked  it  up  and  landed  it  on 
St.  Joseph’s  Point;  saw  also  a  number  of  bales  that  had  drifted  on 
shore  along  the  coast,  both  north  and  south  of  this  place;  sent  a  party 
of  men  and  had  it  rolled  up  out  of  the  water,  and  as  soon  as  possible 
thereafter  sent  boats  and  had  it  brought  down  to  and  landed  on  St. 
J oseph  s  Point.  In  this  way  collected  64  bales,  which  I  forward  by  the 
Roebuck  to  Key  West;  also  two  packages  of  loose  cotton. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  Fales, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  W7elles,

Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Acting  Master 
Fates ,  TJ.  S.'  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  bark  J.  L.  Davis ,  regarding 
the  disposition  of  cotton  captured  by  the  latter. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West ,  October  If  1863. 

Sir:  Your  letter  of  October  7,  relative  to  captured  cotton,  has  been 
received.  After  a  careful  consideration  of  the  circumstances  (in  con¬ 
nection  with  my  General  Order  No.  2,  dated  January  1,  and  my  two 
special  orders  to  yourself,  dated  August  28  and  September  21)  it  has 
been  found  impossible  at  this  office  to  seize  upon  and  duly  appreciate 
the  precise  difficulty  that  has  presented  itself  to  your  mind,  unless  it 
be  a  doubt  whether  by  proceeding  as  in  a  case  of  salvage  you  might 
not  receive  a  larger  amount  of  money  than  if  treated  as  prize  of  war. 
If  this  is  the  cause  of  your  embarrassment,  I  would  refer  you  to  sec¬ 
tion  9  of  the  act  for  the  better  government  of  the  Navy,  approved 
July  17,  1862,  and.  lest  that  should  not  be  sufficiently  explicit,  I  would 
state  further  that  in  case  of  salvage  there  is  either  an  additional  delay 
(over  prize  cases)  of  a  year  and  a  day,  or  else  the  amount  divided  is 
only  one-eioffith  instead  of  one-half. 

Should  this  explanation  fail  to  cover  the  ground  of  your  doubts, 
perhaps  a  recapitulation  of  the  facts  and  regulations  may  reach  the 
desired  point. 

On  August  21  you  first  reported  the  circumstance  of  the  capture, 
and  on  the  28th  you  were  directed  to  send  the  cotton  here  for  adjudi¬ 
cation  as  prize,  with  the  usual  reports  and  crew  lists,  and  with  an 
officer  who  was  cognizant  of  the  facts.  This  required,  among  other 
things,  a  letter  to  the  judge  of  the  United  States  district  court,  con¬ 
taining  the  full  particulars  of  the  seizure,  a  letter  to  the  Secretary  of 
the  Navy  containing  the  like  information,  and  a  letter  to  the  admiral 
commanding  the  squadron,  detailing  the  circumstances  of  the  capture; 
also  General  Order  No.  12,  of  the  Navy  Department,  dated  April  6, 
1863,  requires  that  the  prize  list  required  by  law  to  be  transmitted  to 
the  Navy  Department  (viz,  one  to  the  Secretary  and  one  to  the  Fourth 
Auditor,  which  last  you  have  not  sent)  will  exhibit  not  only  the  name 
and  rank,  or  rating,  but  also  the  rate  of  annual  or  monthly  pay  of 
each  person  borne  on  the  list  at  the  time  of  the  capture  to  which  the 
list  refers.

At  that  time  information  had  been  received  at  this  office  which  ren¬ 
dered  it  certain  that  this  cotton  was  a  portion  of  that  thrown  over¬ 
board  from  the  rebel  steamer  Alabama  when  chased  by  the  U.  S.  S. 
Cuyler ,  and  a  large  quantity  of  the  same  lot  had  already  been  con¬ 
demned  as  prize  in  this  court,  of  which  you  were  informed. 

On  September  21  you  were  directed  to  send  the  cotton  in  the 
Roebuck  to  this  place  and  to  comply  with  all  the  regulations,  laws, 
and  circulars  relating  to  prize  matters,  copies  of  which  have  been  duly 
furnished  to  you,  and  you  were  recommended  to  study  such  matters 
diligently  in  order  to  avoid  mistakes  and  consequent  delay. 

It  was  supposed  that  these  instructions  were  adapted  to  the  meanest 
capacity  and  that  no  misunderstanding  of  them  was  possible,  but  if 
the  matter  is  not  sufficiently  clear  to  you  now  the  case  would  appear 
hopeless.  As  this  is  not  the  first  instance  where  it  has  been  necessary 
to  call  your  attention  to  orders  and  circulars  duly  furnished  you,  and 
as  the  time  of  this  office  can  not  be  occupied  in  the  constant  reitera¬ 
tion  of  such  matters,  as  also  several  minor  omissions  or  inaccuracies 
on  your  part  have  been  permitted  to  pass  unnoticed,  you  are  hereby 
admonished  that  any  similar  case  hereafter  will  cause  your  being- 
deprived  of  your  command  and  returned  to  your  previous  subordinate 
position. 

Respectfully. 


Theodorus  Bailey,

Capture  of  the  steamer  Mail ,  October  15 ,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Master  Gould,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TL  S.  S.  Honduras. 

U.  S.  S.  Honduras, 

At  Sea,  October  16,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  to  the  Department  that  on  the  15th  instant,  at 
about  6:30  p.  m.,  in  latitude  27°  57'  N.,  longitude  83°  09'  W.,  1  cap¬ 
tured  the  steamer  Mail,  Captain  Gilpin,  under  British  colors,  from 
Bayport,  Fla.,  and  bound  to  Havana,  Cuba,  with  176  bales  of  cotton 
and  6  barrels  of  turpentine,  100  bales  being  long  staple,  the  remain¬ 
der  short.  Her  crew  consists  of  captain,  mate,  and  12  men.  Upon 
their  persons  and  baggage  were  found  about  $2,500,  about  $1,200 
in  specie,  the  remainder  in  Confederate  and  Southern  bank  notes. 
According  to  her  British  register  she  was  built  in  Glasgow,  Scotland, 
in  1860;  she  is  179  feet  in  length,  breadth  of  beam  18  feet,  depth 
of  hold  7  feet;  she  is  198  tons  (English  measure),  her  engine  is  85 
horse  power. 

The  chase  lasted  six  hours  and  was  very  exciting.  I  shall  send  her 
to  Key  West  for  adjudication.  At  the  time  of  the  capture  the  U.  S. 
schooner  Fox  was  within  signal  distance  and  is  entitled  to  share  in  the 
prize. 

Enclosed  is  a  list  of  officers  and  men  attached  to  this  ship  at  the 
time  of  the  capture. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  N.  Gould, 

TT  _.  .  Acting  Master,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Rockwell,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  schooner  Two  Sisters. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Two  Sisters, 

Key  West ,  November - ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report:  At  3:20 
p.  m.  on  the  15th  of  October,  while  lying  at  anchor  under  Anclote 
Keys,  in  compan}T  with  the  U.  S.  schooner  Sea  Bird ,  a  steamer  was 
reported  bearing  about  N.  N.  W.,  and  steering  apparently  S.  S.  W. 
At  3:35  I  weighed  and  stood  to  the  northward,  the  Sea  Bird  weighing 
at  the  same  time  and  standing  offshore.  Soon  after  the  U.  S.  S.  Hon¬ 
duras  appeared  in  sight,  chasing  the  steamer.  At  3:50  I  tacked  and 
stood  offshore,  the  steamer  gradually  nearing  me  and  apparently  try¬ 
ing  to  weather  the  Sea  Bird  and  this  vessel,  out  of  range.  At  4:20  I 
set  my  ensign  and  pennant  and  tired  a  percussion  shell  at  her,  but 
found  she  was  still  out  of  range.  The  firing,  however,  caused  him  to 
alter  his  course  more  to  windward.  At  5  p.  m.  the  tender  Fox 
appeared  in  sight  offshore,  and  perceiving  the  steamer,  tacked  to  cut 
her  off.  At  5:55  the  steamer  rounded  to  and  steered  for  the  Hon¬ 
duras.  At  6:15  the  Honduras  closed  with  the  steamer  and  took  pos¬ 
session  of  her,  she  proving  to  be  the  British  steamer  Mail ,  from  Bay- 
port,  bound  to  Havana.  At  the  time  of  the  capture,  within  no  more 
than  4  miles  distance  from  the  prize,  were  the  tenders  Fox ,  Two 
Sisters ,  and  Sea  Bird ,  all  entitled  to  share. 

Respectfully, 

Chas.  H.  Rockwell, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Ashbury,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  schooner  Fox. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Fox, 

Off  Bayport,  Fla.,  October  15,  1863. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  5  p.  m.  this  day  the  lookout 
raised  black  smoke  to  the  northward.  I  immediately  made  all  sail  in 
chase,  and  at  5:20  made  the  chase  to  be  a  steamer  standing  about 
W.  S.  W.  and  pursued  by  one  steamer  and  two  schooners.

Gaining  rapidly  on  him,  he  hauled  down  his  jibs  and  stood  to  north¬ 
ward  and  westward,  directly  in  the  wind’s  eye.  At  6:15,  the  distance 
still  lessening,  the  chase  hove  to  and  was  shortly  after  boarded  by  a 
boat  from  the  pursuing  steamer.  At  6:40 1  ran  alongside.  The  vessel 
proved  to  be  the  British  steamer  Mail,  from  Bayport,  Fla. ,  for  Havana 
with  a  cargo  of  cotton,  then  in  charge  of  a  prize  master  from  U .  S.  S. 
Honduras.  In  accordance  with  orders  from  Acting  Master  Gould, 
commanding  Honduras ,  I  sent  an  officer  and  five  men  on  board  to  assist 
in  taking  the  prize  into  Tampa.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Clark,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  schooner  Sea  Bird. 


U.  S.  Schooner  Sea  Bird, 

Of  Key  Anclote ,  West  Coast  of  Florida ,  October'  15 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  while  at  anchor  under  Key 
Anclote,  in  company  with  U.  S.  (tender)  schooner  Too  Sisters ,  we 
made  out  black  smoke  by  N.  W.  at  about  3  o’clock  this  afternoon. 

Getting  underway  with  a  westerly  wind,  I  stood  off  to  the  S.  W., 
while  the  Two  Sisters  went  to  the  northward.  W e  soon  made  out  a 
steamer  running  about  south,  with  another  steamer  in  chase  of  her. 
As  we  worked  out,  the  chase  hauled  to  the  westward  until  she  made  a 
schooner,  which  proved  to  be  the  U.  S.  schooner  Fox.  (The  Two 
Sisters  had  by  this  tacked  ship  and  followed  us  on  to  the  S.  W.)  The 
chase  then  hauled  to  the  northward,  and  at  6:15  was  brought  to  by  a 
gun  from  the  U.  S.  S.  Honduras ,  to  whom  she  became  a  prize.  The 
tender  schooners  Fox ,  Two  Sisters ,  and  Sea  Bird  were  in  sight  at  the 
time  of  capture.  The  prize  proved  to  be  the  steamer  Mail ,  from  Bay- 
port,  with  160  bales  of  cotton  and  some  spirits  turpentine. 

I  enclose  a  list  of  officers  and  men  attached  to  this  vessel. 

Respectfully, 


Charles  P.  Clark, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  Tender. 


Lieutenant-Commander  R.  Chandler, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto. 


Destruction  of  the  steamer  Scottish  Chief  and  sloop  Kate  Dale ,  in 
Hillsboro  Hirer ,  October  16-17 ,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  October  62Jh  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  the  destruction  of  the  blockade-running 
steamer  Scottish  Chief  and  of  the  sloop  Kate  Dale,  in  Hillsboro  River, 
by  an  armed  expedition  from  the  U.  S.  gunboats  Tahoma  and  Adela. 


East  gulp  blockading  squadkon.  571 

Having  learned  that  these  vessels  were  loading  with  cotton  and 
about  to  sail,  and  being  apprehensive  that  by  reason  of  their  light 
draft  they  would  escape  the  blockading  vessel,  I  sent  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Semmes  to  Tampa  Bay  to  destroy  them.  It  was  planned 
between  myself  and  Captain  Semmes  that  he  should,  with  the  Tahoma , 
assisted  by  the  Adela ,  divert  attention  from  the  real  object  of  the 
expedition  by  shelling  the  fort  and  town,  and  that  under  cover  of 
the  night  men  should  be  landed  at  a  point  on  old  Tampa  Bay,  distant 
from  the  fort,  to  proceed  overland  to  the  point  on  the  Hillsboro  River 
where  the  blockade  runners  lay,  there  to  destroy  them.  This  plan 
was  successfully  carried  out,  but  not  without  a  considerable  loss. 

On  the  16th  instant  the  Tahoma  and  Adela  ran  in  abreast  of  the 
batteries  and  shelled  them  slowly  during  the  day;  the  firing  was  in 
an  unusual  degree  accurate  and  precise.  At  dark,  as  soon  as  the 
moon  went  down,  a  force  consisting  of  Acting  Ensigns  J.  P.  Randall 
and  J.  G.  Koehler,  with  60  men  from  the  Tahoma ,  and  of  Acting  Ensigns 
Strandberg  and  Balcli  and  Acting  First  Assistant  Engineer  [George  M.] 
Bennet,  with  40  men  from  the  Adela ,  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate 
Crane  and  Mr.  J.  A.  Thompson,  guides,  was  landed  at  Ballast  Point. 
The  expedition  was  under  the  immediate  command  of  Acting  Master 
T.  R.  Harris,  executive  officer  of  the  Tahoma.  The  line  of  march 
was  quietly  taken  up  for  the  river,  under  the  guidance  of  Mr.  J.  A. 
Thompson,  who,  being  too  ill  to  walk,  was  borne  in  a  litter.  A  march 
of  14  miles  (rendered  circuitous  by  the  necessity  of  avoiding  houses, 
creeks,  etc.)  brought  the  party  before  daylight  to  the  river  bank.  As 
soon  as  it  was  light  the  vessels  were  discovered  on  the  opposite  bank;  the 
force  was  thereupon  moved  to  a  point  opposite  where  they  lay,  and 
those  on  board  brought  under  aim  of  the  rifles  and  ordered  to  send  a 
boat,  which  they  did.  A  detachment  thereupon  was  sent  to  bring  over 
the  vessels  and  to  make  prisoners  of  those  on  board.  At  this  time  two 
men  succeeded  in  escaping  from  the  vessels,  who  carried  the  alarm  to 
the  garrison.  The  vessels  meantime  were  fired  effectually  and  the 
force  thereupon  set  out  upon  its  return.  Encountering  an  armed 
party  near  the  beach,  a  charge  was  made,  and  two  rebels  made  pris¬ 
oners.  The  beach  finally  was  safely  reached  without  loss,  and  pickets 
were  stationed  and  the  party  rested,  waiting  the  arrival  of  the  boats, 
then  being  dispatched  from  the  Tahoma  and  Adela.  While  so  resting, 
word  was  brought  that  a  detachment  of  cavalry  and  one  of  infantry 
was  advancing;  the  party  was  formed  to  resist  an  attack,  and  the 
boats  having  arrived  the  embarkation  commenced.  W  hile  this  was 
proceeding  the  rebels  opened  fire.  The  first  and  second  divisions, 
with  7  prisoners,  proceeded  in  an  orderly  manner  to  the  boats; 
the  third  division  (spread  out,  that  the  rebels  might  not  fire  into  a 
mass)  returned  the  fire  energetically  and  with  great  coolness  and 
bravery.  The  Adela  meantime  shelled  the  woods  (in  which  the  rebels 
were  concealed  and  from  which  they  fired)  with  shrapnel.  The  first 
and  second  divisions  having  embarked,  the  rear  guard,  on  receiving 
the  order  so  to  do,  followed.  This  rear  guard  stood  nobly  to  their 
post,  protecting  the  retreat  under  an  extremely  severe  fire  from  a  con¬ 
cealed  enemy — loading  and  firing  with  the  coolness  of  target  practice, 
and  finally  leaving  quietly  at  the  word  of  command,  bearing  with 
them  their  wounded.  The  rebels  were  under  the  command  of  Captain 
(late  U.  S.  Senator)  Westcott,  and  were  so-called  regulars. 


572 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  retreat  to  the  boats  was  admirably  conducted  by  Acting  Master 
Harris,  and  the  expedition  throughout  was  characterized  by  a  dis¬ 
ciplined  courage  on  the  part  of  both  officers  and  men.  The  force 
suffered  severely  at  the  beach,  and  both  courage  and  discipline  were 
called  for.  Our  loss  was  as  follows: 

Killed. — James  Worrall,  seaman,  Tahoma;  John  Roddy,  seaman, 
Adela ;  Joseph  O’Donnell,  seaman,  Adda. 

Ten  were  wounded  (including  Acting  Ensigns  Randall  and  Koehler), 
two  seriously.  Five  were  made  prisoners. 

In  reporting  these  losses  Lieutenant-Commander  Semmes  observes: 

I  regret  sincerely  our  loss,  yet  I  feel  a  great  degree  of  satisfaction  in  having 
impressed  the  rebels  with  the  idea  that  blockade-running  vessels  are  not  safe,  even 
up  the  Hillsboro  River. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Baieet, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Oomdg.  East  Gulf  RlJcdg.  Squadron.

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Semmes,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IJ.  S.  S.  Tahoma. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Tahoma, 

Tampa  Bay ,  Fla. ,  October  20,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  for  your 
information: 

Upon  our  arrival  here,  on  the  13th  instant,  finding  that  the  steamer 
Scottish  Chief  and  the  sloop  Kate  Dale  were  loaded  with  cotton  and 
ready  to  run  the  blockade,  1  had  to  change  the  place  of  landing  a  force 
from  Old  Tampa  Bay  to  Ballast  Point,  about  5  miles  below  the  town 
of  Tampa. 

On  the  16th,  the  Adela  in  company,  we  Avent  abreast  of  the  batteries 
and  shelled  them  at  our  leisure.  The  practice  with  the  200-pounder 
Parrott  was  beautiful,  but  the  fuzes  acted  badly.  While  in  this 
position,  with  a  view  of  deceiving  the  rebels,  I  placed  some  stakes  to 
the  northward  and  eastward,  as  if  intending  to  land  there.  This  had 
the  desired  effect,  for  that  night  quite  a  force  was  sent  there  to  oppose 
a  landing.  Toward  4  o’clock  in  the  afternoon  I  backed  off  into  deeper 
water  and  at  dark  received  on  board  officers,  men,  and  boats  from  the 
Adela.  As  soon  as  the  moon  ivent  down  this  vessel  was  moved  abreast 
of  Ballast  Point,  and  a  force  of  100,  exclusive  of  officers  and  guides, 
was  landed. 

When  the  boats  returned  I  moved  about  midnight  abreast  of  the 
batteries  again.  The  following  morning,  at  daylight,  we  fired  the 
heavy  rifle  gun,  simply  to  keep  the  rebels  busy. 

For  the  details  of  the  expedition  on  shore  I  respectfully  refer  you 
to  the  report,  herewith  enclosed,  of  Acting  Master  [T.  R.]  Harris,  the 
executive  officer  of  this  vessel,  who  was  in  command. 

I  am  satisfied  from  the  way  in  which  the  vessels  were  scattered  about 
the  river  that  more  could  not  haATc  been  accomplished. 

The  Adela  having  signalized  me  about  noon,  the  17th,  that  our  force 
was  on  the  beach,  I  sent  boats  to  take  them  off  as  soon  as  possible. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


573 


From  the  testimony  of  witnesses  I  feel  assured  that  the  most  effectual 
means  were  adopted  by  Acting  Master  Harris  for  the  protection  of  his 
command. 

The  officers  and  men  mentioned  in  the  enclosed  report  of  Acting 
Master  Harris  constituted  a  rear  guard,  and  according  to  verbal  reports 
behaved  nobly. 

Those  not  particularly  mentioned  remained  in  line  of  battle  until 
ordered  to  their  boats. 

Acting  Master’s  Mate  [H.  A.]  Crane  and  Mr.  J.  A.  Thompson, 
guides,  did  their  duty  well,  though  the  latter  had  to  be  carried  in  a 
litter  a  long  time. 

The  march  to  the  river  and  back,  I  am  informed,  was  made  in  good 
time  and  very  quietly.  The  escape  of  two  prisoners  from  one  of  the 
vessels  burned  was  the  only  thing  that  showed  the  presence  of  our 
force. 

The  morning  of  the  18th  I  communicated  by  flag  of  truce,  meeting 
Captain  [John]  Westcott,  the  commander  at  Tampa,  from  whom  I 
learned  the  condition  of  the  men  left  on  shore. 

We  have  in  our  possession  2  prisoners  of  war  and  5  blockade 
runners  (one  of  them  severely  wounded),  all  of  whom,  except  the 
wounded  man,  I  send  by  the  Honduras. 

The  vessels  destroyed  were  of  light  draft,  not  over  1  feet,  and  would 
have  probably  eluded  me. 

Our  total  loss  is  as  follows: 

Killed. — James  Worrall,  seaman,  Tahoma;  John  Roddy,  seaman, 
Adela;  Joseph  O’Donnell,  seaman,  Adela. 

Wounded. — J.  P.  Randall,  acting  ensign,  Tahoma;  J.  G.  Koehler, 
acting  ensign,  Tahoma;  Jonathan  Murray,  boatswain’s  mate,  Tahoma; 
Henry  Palmer,  coxswain,  Tahoma;  William  Curtin,  ordinary  seaman, 
Tahoma;  George  [H.]  Fitzgerald,  ordinary  seaman,  Tahoma ;  Nicholas 
Lund,  ordinary  seaman,  Adela;  John  Hannibal,  quarter  gunner, 
Adela;  Charles  H.  Dodge,  steerage  boy,  Adela;  Frederick  Klasson, 
carpenter’s  mate,  Adela. 

Prisoners. — John  Collins,  master  at  arms,  Tahoma:  John  McDonald, 
seaman,  Tahoma;  John  Hilton,  ordinary  seaman,  Tahoma ,  wounded; 
Thomas  Donnelly,  fireman,  Adela. 

But  five  of  the  wounded,  including  the  one  taken  prisoner,  need 
medical  treatment,  and  only  two  of  them  have  serious  wounds. 

I  regret  sincerely  our  loss,  yet  I  feel  a  great  degree  of  satisfaction 
in  having  impressed  the  rebels  with  the  idea  that  blockade-running 
vessels  are  not  safe  even  up  the  Hillsboro  River. 

October  22. —I  communicated  by  flag  of  truce  again  this  morning 
with  the  view  of  getting  Mr.  Crane’s  family,  whom  Captain  Westcott 
intended  to  send  to  me,  but  for  some  reasons  the}7  didn  t  come.  I  send 
by  the  Honduras  three  refugees  received  by  flag  of  truce.  Boys, 
McKnight  and  Spencer,  sent  some  time  since  to  the  Huntsville ,  were 
landed.'"’  The  enclosed  private  letters  (except  the  one  to  Judge  Whit¬ 
worth,  which  was  captured  on  board  one  of  the  vessels  destroyed)  were 
received  by  flag  of  truce. 

I  enclose  a  list  of  prisoners.  The  man  Mobley  is  a  druggist  and 
consumptive.  They  are  very  anxious  to  get  him  back,  and  the  surgeon 
who  met  me  on  Sunday  intimated  that  probably  General  Finegan 
might  propose  an  exchange.  Nothing  heard  from  General  Finegan

Report  of  casualties  on  the  U.  S.  S.  Tahoma. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Tahoma, 

Tampa  Bap,  October  W,  1863. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  the  following  casualties,  which 
occurred  to  the  officers  and  men  under  your  command  during  the 
engagement  of  the  17th  instant: 

Killed. — James  Worrall,  seaman;  body  not  recovered. 

Severely  wounded. — J.  F.  Randall,  acting  ensign.  Wounded  in  two 
places — one,  a  rifle  ball,  having  passed  completely  through  the  neck 
immediately  below  the  lower  jaw,  wounding  several  small  arteries  and 
the  external  jugular  vein  of  the  right  side.  The  other,  evidently  a 
buckshot,  entering  the  right  arm  and  lodging  in  the  biceps  muscle. 
Doing  well. 

Jonathan  Murray,  seaman.  A  rifle  ball,  entering  the  posterior  por¬ 
tion  of  the  right  buttock  and  passing  obliquely  upward  through  the 
glutteus  muscles  and  making  its  exit  near  the  anterior  superior  spinous 
process  of  the  ilium. 

John  Hilton,  ordinary  seaman.  A  rifle  ball,  entering  the  upper  por¬ 
tion  of  the  side  of  head  and  passing  out  near  the  place  of  entry. 

William  Curtin,  ordinary  seaman.  Rifle  ball,  striking  him  on  the 
right  shin  just  above  the  ankle  joint  and  splintering  the  bone  slightly. 

Slightly  wounded. — John  G.  Koehler,  acting  ensign.  Spent,  ball, 
striking  him  on  the  left  leg  near  the  knee,  bruising  but  not  breaking 
the  skin. 

George  H.  Fitzgerald,  landsman.  Flesh  wound  of  the  index  finger 
of  the  right  hand. 

Henry  Palmer,  coxswain.  Spent  ball,  striking  him  on  the  side  near 
the  spine. 

All  of  the  above  wounded,  I  am  happy  to  say,  are  doing  well. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  H.  Gunning, 
Assistant  Surgeon,  JJ.  S.  Navy.
