Report  of  Acting  Master  Harris,  U.  S.  Navy,  executive  officer  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Tahoma. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Tahoma, 

Off  Tampa,  October  18,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  of  an  expedition, 
under  my  command,  made  a  few  miles  into  the  interior  of  Florida,  which 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


575 


resulted  in  the  capture  and  burning  of  the  steamer  Scottish  Chief  and 
sloop  Kate  Dale ,  both  loaded  with  cotton  and  ready  to  run  the  blockade. 

The  force  landed  consisted  of  Acting  Ensigns  J.  P.  Randall  and  J.  G. 
Koehler  with  60  men  from  this  vessel,  and  Acting  Ensigns  Strandberg 
and  Balch  and  Acting  First  Assistant  Engineer  Bennet,  with  40  men 
from  the  U.  S.  S.  Adda ,  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Crane  and  Mr.  J. 
A.  Thompson,  guides,  all  well  armed  and  supplied  with  three  days’ 
rations. 

At  11  p.  m.,  October  16,  having  quietly  landed  on  the  western  shore 
of  the  bay  in  six  boats,  I  took  up  the  line  of  march  for  the  Hillsboro 
River,  carrying  along  a  small  boat  to  be  used  in  crossing  the  river  or 
any  creek  should  it  be  necessary  to  do  so.  I  avoided  the  roads  and 
houses  as  much  as  possible  so  as  to  prevent  discovery.  After  march¬ 
ing  4  or  5  miles  we  were  obliged  to  abandon  the  boat,  she  delaying  us 
too  much,  and  I  had  her  concealed  about  a  quarter  of  a  mile  from  our 
trail.  After  this  wre  moved  along  very  rapidly  under  the  direction  of 
our  excellent  guides,  and  reached  the  banks  of  the  Hillsboro  River 
about  4  a.  m.  October  17,  having  marched  about  14  miles.  Having 
stationed  lookouts,  the  party  lay  down  till  daylight.  Shortly  after 
daylight  we  discovered  the  steamer  and  sloop  on  the  opposite  side  of 
the  river  about  2  miles  above  us.  The  force  was  immediately  moved 
to  a  point  opposite  where  they  lay  and  those  on  board  ordered  to  send 
a  boat  to  us.  When  the  boat  reached  [us]  I  sent  Acting  Ensigns  Ran¬ 
dall  and  Balch,  with  a  suitable  number  of  men,  on  board  of  the  ves¬ 
sels,  where  they  made  prisoners  of  all  except  two,  who  escaped  on  the 
Tampa  side.  Hauling  the  vessels  over,  I  fired  both  effectually. 

The  other  steamer  having  been  represented  to  me  as  being  5  miles 
farther  up  the  river,  and  too  far  gone  to  be  repaired,  and  the  schooner 
Neptune  being  sunk  in  the  river  near  Tampa,  I  determined  not  to 
attempt  any  more,  and  immediately  took  up  the  line  of  march  for  the 
beach,  hoping  to  get  there  before  the  garrison  in  the  town  of  Tampa 
could  be  alarmed.  No  one  was  encountered  until  near  the  beach,  when 
a  scouting  party  was  discovered  in  citizens’  dress,  on  foot  and  armed, 
and  upon  whom  we  immediately  charged,  capturing  two.  Having 
reached  the  beach  and  placed  out  a  picket  guard,  we  halted  and  rested. 
Very  soon  the  picket  guard  informed  me  of  the  presence  of  a  party  of 
cavalry  lurking  about  the  woods,  upon  which  information  I  ordered 
the  party  to  be  prepared  for  a  fight  should  the  rebels  attack  us  before 
our  boats,  then  approaching,  could  arrive.  When  the  boats  had  neared 
the  beach,  and  I  had  ordered  all  but  about  twenty,  including  officers,  to 
embark,  the  rebels  opened  a  sharp  fire  with  their  rifles  on  the  boats 
and  those  left  with  me  on  the  beach,  which  was  returned  for  fifteen  or 
twenty  minutes. 

Finding  that  the  enemy,  concealed  by  the  brush,  had  the  advantage' 
of  position,  that  nearly  ail  of  those  ordered  to  the  boats  had  embarked, 
and  that  those  with  me  were  suffering  severely,  I  retreated  to  the 
boats,  bringing  off  all  but  6,  1  of  whom  was  killed  in  the  water  and 
5  who  fell  into  the  hands  of  the  rebels,  2  of  them  being  severely 
wounded.  (One  of  these  wounded  died  the  following  morning  in  the 
hospital  at  Tampa.) 

I  would  respectfully  call  to  your  notice  the  gallant  conduct  of  Acting 
Ensigns  Randall  and  Koehler,  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Crane,  Boat¬ 
swain’s  Mate  Jonathan  Murray,  Captains  of  forecastle  John  Black 


576 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


and  William  Larkin,  Master  at  arms  John  Collins,  Quarter  Gunner 
Thomas  Brooks,  Captain  top  Douglas  Thompson,  Seaman  Arthur 
Ulmer,  Ordinary  seamen  William  Curtin,  John.  Hilton,  and  John 
Roddy,  of  the  Adela ,  mortally  wounded,  and  Landsman  James  Heenan. 
There  were  also  a  few  men  of  the  Adela  whose  names  I  do  not  know 
who  were  all  that  I  recollect  being  on  the  beach. 

The  total  loss  amounts  to  3  killed,  6  wounded,  4  prisoners.  One  of 
the  latter  was  severely  wounded.  A  prisoner  captured  by  us  is  also 
wounded. 

It  being  necessary  for  the  boats,  crowded  as  they  were,  to  move  off 
a  short  distance  to  avoid  the  lire  of  the  enemy,  some  of  the  arms  were 
lost. 

I  am  pleased  to  state  that  all  concerned  remained  in  position  until 
they  were  ordered  to  embark. 

The  force  of  the  enemy  was  between  70  and  80  men,  40  of  whom 
were  cavalry,  all  under  the  command  of  Captain  Westcott,  as  we 
afterwards  learned  by  a  flag  of  truce  from  the  commanding  officer  at 
Tampa. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  R.  Harris, 

Acting  Master  and  Executive  Officer. 

Lieutenant-Commander  A.  A.  Semmes, 

Ccvmmanding  U.  S.  Gunboat  Tahoma. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Stodder,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Adela. 

U.  S.  S.  Adela, 

Tampa  Bay ,  Fla. ,  October  19,  1863. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the  16th 
instant,  at  9  a.  m.,  moved  up  with  the  vessel  under  my  command  (in  obe¬ 
dience  to  instructions)  to  within  2,000  yards  of  the'  battery  at  Tampa. 
At  9:15  a.  m.  opened  fire  on  the  battery  and  town  with  my  20-pounder 
rifle  and  rifled  howitzer.  Eliciting  no' reply  from  the  battery,  fired  at 
intervals  until  4  p.  m.,  when,  in  obedience  to  signal  made,  dropped 
alongside  the  Talioma  and  sent  three  boats  in  charge  of  First  Assist¬ 
ant  Engineer  George  M.  Bennet,  Acting  Ensigns  F.  A.  Strandberg 
and  Edward  Balch,  with  40  men,  armed  and  equipped.  Having 
obtained  permission  from  yourself,  on  the  morning  of  the  17th  at 
8  a.  m.  proceeded  toward  the  western  shore  of  the  bay  in  order  to  get 
my  vessel  nearer  the  battery,  but  unfortunately  run  aground  and  was 
unable  to  get  ofl.  At  10  a.  m.  espied  our  forces  returning  to  the 
beach,  and  immediately  made  signals  to  that  effect.  In  a  few  moments 
descried  rebels  in  the  woods  opposite  this  vessel.  Commenced  shelling 
the  woods  with  shrapnel,  the  rebels  still  moving  toward  our  party  oil 
the  beach.  Continued  covering  our  party  as  well  as  possible  until  all 
gained  the  boats  but  few,  on  whom  the  rebels  made  an  attack.  At  2 
p.  m.  the  boats  from  the  vessel  returned,  bringing  the  partjr  belong¬ 
ing  to  this  vessel,  together  with  the  wounded.  ' 

I  regret  to  report  that  two  men,  Thomas  Donnelly,  fireman,  and 
John  Roddy,  seaman,  are  missing.  Joseph  O’Donnell,  ordinary  sea¬ 
man,  mortally  vrounded  (since  died);  Nicholas  Lund,  ordinary  seaman,

dangerously  wounded;  John  Hannibal  and  Frederick  Klasson,  slightly 
wounded.  Three  prisoners  taken  sent  on  board  your  vessel.

Letter  of  congratulation  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Semmes,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West ,  October  °28,  1863. 

Sir:  Your  report  of  the  expedition  sent  by  you  beyond  Tampa,  for 
the  purpose  of  destroying  the  vessels  in  Hillsboro  River,  has  lieen 
received  and  the  affair  duly  represented  to  the  Navy  Department. 

The  plan  of  operations  seems  to  have  been  arranged  with  skill  and 
judgment,  and  to  have  been  executed  with  coolness  and  bravery;  and 
I  have  to  congratulate  you  and  the  officers  and  men  under  your  com¬ 
mand,  more  especially  Acting  Master  Thomas  R.  Harris  and  the  land¬ 
ing  party  under  his  charge,  upon  the  handsome  manner  in  which  this 
brilliant  little  affair  was  executed.  The  lesson  taught  to  the  rebels  by 
this  expedition,  that  their  movements  can  be  watched  and  thwarted  by 


n  w  r— -vol  17 - 37 


578 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


the  daring  of  our  seamen,  even  when  carried  on  at  a- distance  of  sev¬ 
eral  miles  up  a  river  whose  mouth  is  protected  by  a  fortified  town,  is 
of  no  small  importance,  and  is  calculated  to  depress  them  in  propor¬ 
tion  to  the  audacity  and  discipline  displayed  by  our  men. 

I  regret  exceedingly  that  your  success  should  have  been  attended  by 
the  loss  of  even  a  few  of  the  brave  men  composing  the  expedition,  and 
that  others  are  yet  suffering  from  wounds  received  in  conflict  with  the 
enemy;  but  it  does  not  appear  that  a  different  result  could  have  been 
expected,  and  I  am  too  confident  of  the  temper  of  the  men  in  this 
squadron  to  suppose  that  they  would  hesitate  at  any  exposure  which 
may  be  required  of  them.  1  am  highly  gratified  at  the  reports  of  the 
steadiness  and  discipline  under  fire  exhibited  on  this  occasion. 

You  will  be  pleased  to  read  this  communication  to  the  officers  and 
men  of  your  vessel  at  general  muster.  A  similar  letter  will  be  sent 
to  the  Adela. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Lieutenant-Commander  A.  A.  Semmes,  U.  S.  Navy,

seem  to  have  been  executed  with  coolness  and  bravery;  and  I  have  to 
congratulate  you  and  the  officers  and  men  under  your  command  upon 
the  handsome  manner  in  which  they  behaved. 

The  lesson  taught  to  the  rebels  by  this  expedition,  that  their  move¬

though  carried  on  at  a  distance  of  several  miles  up  a  river,  whose 
mouth  is  protected  by  a  fortified  town,  is  of  no  small  importance,  and 
is  calculated  to  depress  them  in  proportion  to  the  audacity  and  disci¬ 
pline  displayed  by  our  men. 

I  regret  that  their  success  should  have  been  attended  by  the  loss  of 
even  a  few  of  the  brave  men  composing  the  expedition,  ancl  that  others 
are  yet  suffering  from  wounds  received  in  conflict  with  the  enemy,  but 
it  does  not  appear  that  a  different  result  could  have  been  expected,  and 
I  am  too  confident  of  the  temper  of  the  men  in  this  squadron  to  sup¬ 
pose  they  would  hesitate  at  any  exposure  which  may  be  required  of 
them.  The  reports  of  their  steadiness  and  discipline  under  fire  are 
highly  gratifying. 

You  will  be  pleased  to  read  this  communication  to  the  officers  and 
men  of  your  vessel  at  general  muster. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Harris,  U.  S.  Navy,  commending  the  gallant 
conduct  of  Acting  Ensign  Randall,  U.  S.  Navy. 

U.  S.  S.  Honduras, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  December  6,  1863. 

Sir:  I  would  respectfully  call  to  the  notice  of  the  Department  the 
gallant  conduct  of  Acting  Ensign  J.  P.  Randall  in  the  late  expedition 
to  Hillsboro  River,  Florida,  sent  out  from  U.  S.  gunboat  Tahoma ,  and 
placed  under  my  command  by  Lieutenant-Commander  Semmes,  the 
result  of  which  you  are  already  aware.  Mr.  Randall’s  energy  and 
daring  and  his  coolness  under  tire  rendered  his  services  of  the  utmost 
importance  to  me,  and  not  until  shot  down  did  he  cease  to  exhibit  the 
most  noble  bearing. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  R.  Harris, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  October  31,  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  afternoon  of  the 
20th  instant  the  Fort  ILenrfs  tender,  the  Annie ,  commanded  by  Act¬ 
ing  Ensign  J.  S.  Williams,  captured  off  Bayport  the  British  schooner 
Martha  Jane ,  from  Bayport  bound  to  Havana,  loaded  with  26,609 
pounds  (as  per  manifest)  sea-island  cotton.  There  was  also  found  on 
the  persons  of  the  captain  and  crew  $1,206.88  in  gold,  silver,  and 
United  States  Treasury  notes,  and  $127.70  in  Confederate  States 
money.  The  money  I  "have  forwarded  to  the  prize  commissioners  at 
Key  West. 

I  send  to  Key  West,  in  the  prize,  her  captain  and  supercargo.  The 
balance  of  her  crew,  3  men,  I  will  bring  to  Key  West  in  the  Fort 
LLenry. 

Enclosed  I  forward  Ensign  Williams’  report  of  the  capture. 

Very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Baxter ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  lark  Gem  of  the  Sea,  regarding  capture  of  a  loat  containing 
four  men. 

U.  S.  Bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 

Charlotte  Harbor ,  October  33,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  on  the  morning  of  the 
21st  instant  I  captured,  with  my  boat,  off  the  entrance  to  this  harbor,  a 
small,  open,  fiat-bottomed,  sloop-rigged  boat,  with  1  barrel  turpen¬ 
tine  and  4  men,  named  as  follows:  George  Anderson,  James  Grunsell, 
Benjamin  Kemp,  and  Richard  Maires  (a  former  marshal  of  Key  West). 
They  reported  that  they  sailed  from  Clearwater  Harbor,  40  miles  to 
the  northward  of  Tampa,  on  the  17th  instant,  bound  for  Nassau,  New 
Providence,  without  any  papers  whatever. 

The  barrel  of  turpentine  and  4  prisoners  I  will  send  to  Key  West 
the  first  opportunity,  for  your  disposal. 

The  boat  is  of  no  value. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Baxter, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  U.  S.  N.,  Commanding . 
Senior  Officer, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron ,  Key  West,  Fla.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Fleming,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Sagamore. 

U.  S.  S.  Sagamore, 

Cedar  Keys,  Fla. ,  November  3,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  28th  of  October  I  sent 
the  schooner  Annie  (tender),  Acting  Ensign  James  S.  Williams  com¬ 
manding,  and  the  launch  from  this  vessel.  Acting  Ensign  Louis  R. 
Chester  in  charge,  to  cruise  off  Bayport  and  Crystal  River  to  intercept 
any  vessels  attempting  to  enter  or  come  out  from  those  places.  I  am 
happy  to  inform  you  that  they  met  with  success  by  capturing,  about 
30  miles  from  Bayport,  the  British  schooner  Meteor,  of  29  tons,  with 
an  assorted  cargo,  from  Havana,  cleared  for  Matamoras,  but  the  mas¬ 
ter  says  bound  to  St.  Marks,  Fla. 

I  herewith  enclose  copies  of  reports  from  the  officers  mentioned 
above  relative  to  the  capture.  I  send  the  schooner  to  Key  West  to-day 
in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Charles  R.  Fleming,  accompanied  by 
Acting  Master’s  Mate  George  W.  Wilson  and  three  men,  having  taken 
two  men  out  of  her,  whom  1  have  on  board  this  vessel  and  will  send  to 
Key  West  by  the  first  opportunity  unless  otherwise  directed. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  E.  Fleming, 

Lieutenant-  Commander,  Commanding .

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Williams,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  schooner  Annie. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Annie, 

At  Sea ,  30  Miles  S.  W.  from  Bayport ,  October  30 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  herewith  respectfully  submit  the  following’  reports  of  the 
cruise  of  this  vessel,  together  with  your  armed  launch,  and  also  the 
capture  of  the  British  schooner  Meteor. 

At  3  p.  m.  of  the  28th  I  made  a  sail  to  the  northward  which  proved 
to  be  a  sloop  standing  about  S.  E.  I  immediately  sent  the  launch  to 
the  N.  E.  so  as  to  intercept  her,  should  she  get  inside  the  reef,  while 
I  followed  her  up  outside  in  7  feet  of  water.  At  dark  I  lost  sight  of 
the  sloop  and  came  to  anchor  to  await  the  return  of  the  boats,  wrhen  I 
saw  the  launch  tire  three  shots  at  her.  At  9  a.  m.  of  the  29th  the  launch 
returned,  having  got  near  enough  to  fire  at  her,  but  she  lost  sight  of 
the  chase  shortly  after  dark.  After  resting  the  crew  we  set  sail  for 
Bayport  and  made  a  reconnoissance  of  the  harbor  in  the  launch,  and 
returned  to  the  schooner  at  dark.  The  men  being  very  much  fatigued, 
I  allowed  the  boat  to  lay  alongside  through  the  night.  At  7  a.  m.  of 
this  date  made  schooner  to  the  southward  standing  northward  and  gave 
chase,  together  with  the  launch,  the  schooner  gaining  fast  on  the  chase 
until  10  a.  m.,  when  I  fired  several  shots  at  her.  At  1  p.  m.  it  fell  calm, 
when  I  sent  my  boat  with  four  men  in  charge  of  Quartermaster  James 
Peterson  to  board  her  (the  launch  just  in  sight  astern).  At  2  p.  m.  mj^ 
boat  boarded  her  and  found  her  to  be  the  British  schooner  Meteor ,  from 
Havana  on  the  19th  instant,  bound  to  St.  Marks  with  a  general  assorted 
cargo,  in  charge  of  and  owned  by  Captain  Anthony  Bado.  At  3:30 
p.  m.  the  launch  came  up  and  I  gave  the  schooner  in  charge  of  Acting 
Ensign  Chester  and  made  sail  in  company  for  Cedar  Keys. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  S.  Williams, 

Acting  Ensign ,  Commanding , 

Lieutenant-Commander  C.  E.  Fleming, 

Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Sagamore. 


Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Chester,  B.  S.  Navy,  commanding  the  launch  of  the  U.  S.  S. 

Sagamore. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Sagamore, 

Cedar  Keys ,  November  1,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report,  viz: 

In  obedience  to  your  orders  I  left  this  ship  on  the  28th  ultimo  with 
the  launch  and  light  howitzer  and  was  taken  in  tow  of  the  schooner 
Annie ,  tender  to  this  vessel.  We  arrived  off  Bayport  at  3  p.  m.  the 
same  dav,  and  came  to  off  the  harbor,  intending  to  reconnoiter  the  bay 
and  harbor  at  nights;  shortly  after  we  made  a  sail  standing  to  the  south¬ 
ward  and  eastward.  I  immediately  took  the  launch  and  stood  inshoie, 
in  order  to  intercept  her  entrance  into  Bayport  and  the  schooner  stood 
to  the  northward  to  prevent  her  running  out  to  sea.  I  shortly  made 
her  out  to  be  a  sloop  standing  toward  me.  I  was  within  3  miles  ot  the 
land  when  she  discovered  me,  and  she  immediately  went  about  and 
stood  to  the  northward.  I  gained  on  her  constantly,  and  when  within 


582 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


three-quarters  of  a  mile  I  fired  three  shell,  two  of  them  exploding 
close  on  board  of  her.  She  paid  no  attention,  but  kept  on  her  course, 
and  darkness  coming  on,  amidst  a  heavy  squall,  we  lost  sight  of  her. 
I  then  stood  in  for  Homosassa  River  and  anchored.  At  daylight  on 
the  29th  stood  in  along  the  land  with  the  hope  of  discovering  the  sloop, 
but  not  seeing  her  I  stood  out  S.  W.  and  arrived  alongside  the  Annie 
at  8  a.  m.  At  4  p.  m.  I  took  the  launch  and  stood  in  for  Bayport.  1 
proceeded  close  enough  to  see  plainly  that  there  were  no  vessels  in 
that  port.  The  rebels  hoisted  their  flag  on  their  battery  on  discover¬ 
ing  my  approach.  At  7:30  p.  m.  returned  to  the  Annie.  At  7:30 
a.  m.  on  the  30th  instant  [ultimo]  discovered  a  sail  to  the  southward 
and  westward.  1  immediately  stood  in  for  the  land  to  intercept  her 
entrance  into  Bayport.  The  Annie  got  underway  and  stood  for  her. 
At  11  a.  m.  the  wind  died  away  to  a  calm  and  I  hauled  up  and  stood 
for  the  chase.  At  3  p.  m.  I  came  within  range  and  fired  a  shell  and 
she  lowered  her  jib,  and  I  boarded  her.  She  proved  to  be  the  schooner 
Meteor ,  from  Havana,  bound  to  St.  Marco  [St.  Marks,  Fla.].  Finding 
she  was  a  prize  I  took  her  in  charge  and  proceeded  with  her  to  this 
place. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Louis  R.  Chester, 

Acting  Ensign ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Chas.  E.  Fleming, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Gunboat  Sagamore. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Rudd,  U.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  S.  Somerset,  regarding  cotton  captured  at  Apalachicola, 
Fla.,  October  30,  1863. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset, 

West  Pass ,  St.  George' ‘s  Sound ,  Fla.,  December  15,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  30th  of  October,  while 
on  a  scouting  expedition  at  the  town  of  Apalachicola,  I  found  10  bales 
of  cotton  secreted  in  a  warehouse,  which  I  captured  and  brought  off. 
A  negro  named  Frank  Cook  claimed  to  be  the  owner  and  stated  that 
he  had  kept  them  hid  there  for  some  months  to  prevent  them  from 
falling  into  rebel  hands.  Some  of  the  rebels  in  town,  however,  knew 
that  the  cotton  was  there,  and  we  did  not.  In  my  opinion  the  real 
owner  did  not  make  his  appearance.  I  have  sent  'the  cotton  to  Key 
W est  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Honduras,  and  respectfully  forward  the  prize 
list  of  this  vessel  at  the  time  of  the  capture.  The  U.  S.  S.  J.  S.  Cham¬ 
bers  was  at  anchor  at  West  Pass,  but  not  within  signal  distance  when 
the  cotton  was  captured. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  Budd, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Commanding  So?nerset. 
Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  November  3,  1863. 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  is  ready  for  sea 
you  will  proceed  in  her  to  cruise  on  the  parallel  of  28°  30'  north  lati¬ 
tude,  between  the  meridian  of  85°  and  87°  west  longitude.  These 
limits  are  not  to  be  considered  as  altogether  rigid,  and  you  may,  at 
your  discretion,  extend  them  to  the  eastward  or  westward;  but  as 
the  De  Soto  will  be  directed  to  cruise  on  the  parallel  of  29°  30', 
between  the  meridians  of  86°  and  88°,  and  as  the  San  Jacinto  will 
also  be  sent  to  the  parallel  of  29°,  between  the  meridians  of  85°  30' 
and  87°  30',  you  will  see  that  any  great  departure  to  the  northward  of 
the  line  indicated  would  defeat  the  general  plan  for  intercepting  ves¬ 
sels  bound  in  and  out  of  Mobile,  besides  causing-  an  unnecessary 
expenditure  of  coal  by  mutual  chasing  among  our  own  cruisers.  You 
will  return  to  this  port  by  the  22d  instant.  Should  you  take  any 
prizes  you  will  send  them  to  this  place  for  adjudication.  *” 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blkdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Rockwell ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 

schooner'  Two  Sisters ,  regarding  the  cruise  of  that  vessel  on  the  west 

coast  of  Florida. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Two  Sisters, 

Key  West,  November  f  1863. 

Sir:  In  accordance  with  orders  received  from  Captain  Temple, 
desiring  a  report  of  every  cruise,  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the 
following  report: 

1  left  Key  West  September  28  and  proceeded  up  the  coast.  On 
the  30th  anchored  in  Tampa  Bay  and  communicated  with  the  steamer 
Adela.  October  1  proceeded  to  sea  cruising;  on  the  4th  spoke  the 
tender  Annie  on  a  cruise,  and  proceeded  to  the  northward  in  company. 
At  4:30  p.  m.,  Bayport,  bearing  S.  S.  E.,  20  miles  distant,  saw  a 
sloop  standing  along  to  the  southward  in  shoal  water,  on  St.  Martin’s 
Reef.  Made  all  sail  in  chase,  the  sloop  hauling  his  wind  as  soon  as  he 
saw  us,  running  inshore;  chased  her  until  we  were  in  7  feet  of  water, 
gaining  on  her  rapidly.  Finding  the  water  too  shoal,  I  immediately 
armed  the  boat  and  sent  her  in  chase,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s 
Mate  J.  A.  Montague.  Night  setting  in,  however,  he  lost  sight  of 
her  in  the  darkness  and  she  escaped,  although  he  continued  the  chase 
in  every  available  direction  until  midnight. 

On  the  6th  anchored  at  Cedar  Keys  to  make  necessary  repairs  on 
sails;  lay  .there  until  the  9th,  when,  taking  the  Fort  Henry's  second 
cutter,  with  an  officer  and  crew,  proceeded  on  a  cruise  down  the  coast. 

On  the  10th,  having  anchored  off  Bayport,  just  in  sight  of  the  land, 
1  took  the  Fort  Henry's  boat  and  proceeded  in  to  reconnoiter  the  coast 
in  the  vicinity  of  the  town.  When  within  3  miles  of  the  town  saw  a 
boat  coming  out  containing  2  men,  who  evidently  mistook  us  for  a 
small  blockade  runner.  I  ran  for  them,  intending  to  capture  them  if 
possible,  but  they  ran  for  the  battery,  not  letting  us  get_  within  musket 
range  of  them.“  Having  accomplished  my  object  of  coming  in,  I 
returned  to  the  vessel. 

On  the  11th,  sent  a  boat  ashore  on  Anclote  Keys  to  reconnoiter  the 
coast  in  the  vicinity  of  Anclote  River.  Discovering  nothing,  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  down  the  coast,  and  on  the  13th  dispatched  both  boats,  in  charge 
of  Acting  Master’s  Mates  Hancock  and  Montague  into  Clearwater 
Harbor  to  reconnoiter  the  mainland  inside  the  keys  bordering  that 
portion  of  the  coast.  They  proceeded  along  a  range  of  10  miles  of 
coast  discovering  no  vessels  or  evidences  of  breach  of  the  blockade 
at  that  place.  A  party  of  about  30  men,  armed,  were  observed  in  the 
bushes  watching  their  movements,  but  as  1  had  ordered  them  not  to 
land  unless  for  some  necessary  purpose,  no  attack  was  made.  _  The 
next  day  I  beat  down  the  coast  until  Tampa  light-house  was  in  sight, 
at  which  point  I  communicated  with  the  U.  S.  schooner  Sea  Bird ,  and 
returned  with  her  to  an  anchorage  off  Anclote  Keys.  On  the  15th 
assisted  in  the  capture  of  the  steamer  Mail ,  the  particulars  of  which 
1  have  given  in  a  former  report.  On  the  morning  of  the  16th  anchored 
in  Cedar  Keys.  On  the  morning  of  the  18th  received  the  mails  and 
stores  for  the  fleet  from  the  U.  S.  S.  Honduras ,  having  received  orders 
from  Lieutenant-Commander  McCauley,  commanding  the  Fort  Henry, 
to  deliver  them  at  their  several  destinations.  Proceeded  on  this  duty, 
communicating  with  the  Stars  and  Stripes  off  St.  Marks  the  20th;  the 
Sagamore  at  East  Pass  on  the  21st;  the  Somerset  and  J.  S.  Chambers 


586 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


at  the  West  Pass  on  the  22d;  the  J.  L.  Davis  at  St.  Joseph’s  on  the 
23d,  and  the  Restless  at  St.  Andrew’s  on  the  same  day. 

On  the  24th  started  on  my  return  to  Cedar  Keys,  and  having 
received  the  mails  from  the  J.  L.  Davis  in  passing,  arrived  at  Cedar 
Keys  on  the  26th,  sending  the  mails  by  the  Sea  Bird.  On  the  30th 
sailed  for  Key  West  to  accompany  the  Fort  Henry ,  and  render  assist¬ 
ance  if  necessary,  but  as  she  started  ahead  of  us,  on  account  of  calms, 
we  saw  no  more  of  her. 

On  the  1st  November  communicated  with  the  Tahoma  at  Tampa 
Bay,  and  the  Sea  Bird  off  Sarasota.  On  the  3d  arrived  in  Key  West, 
having  experienced  much  bad  weather  during  the  cruise,  and  having 
received  some  injuries,  rendering  a  few  repairs  necessary. 

Respectfully, 

Chas.  H.  Rockwell, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comuianding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Burgess ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 

schooner  Beauregard ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
Volante. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

Off  Indian  River ,  Fla. ,  November  6 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  On  the  5th  instant, 
at  9: 30  a.  m.,  while  lying  at  anchor  at  Cape  Canaveral,  the  man  at  the 
masthead  lookout  reported  a  sail  bearing  S.  E.  by  E.,  distant  about  10 
miles,  and  as  the  weather  was  calm  at  the  time  I  sent  an  armed  boat  in 
chase,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  H.  B.  Colby,  who  succeeded 
in  overtaking  her  about  noon.  She  proved  to  be  the'British  schooner 
Volante ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  with  a  cargo  consisting  of  salt, 
dry  goods,  etc.,  from  Nassau,  bound  to  Matamoras,  but  as  she  was  so 
far  out  of  the  regular  track  for  Matamoras  and  as  things  looked  very 
suspicious,  I  seized  her  and  sent  her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Francis  Burgess, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.

U.  S.  Schooner  Annie, 

At  Sea ,  20  miles  West  of  Bay  port,  November  7,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
Paid,  from  Havana,  under  the  following  circumstances: 

While  standing  to  the  northward  this  morning,  at  8:30  a.  m.  a  sail 
was  reported  from  aloft  to  the  N.  W.  I  immediately  made  all  sail  in 
chase.  At  9,  the  wind  being  light,  your  second  cutter,  in  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  Chester,  started  for  the  chase  and  boarded  her  at  about 
11  a.  m.  It  being  calm  all  day  I  did  not  get  up  to  the  schooner  until 
1  p.  m.  Everything  appertaining  to  the  vessel  is  in  charge  of  Ensign 
Chester. 

1  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  S.  Williams,

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Chester,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  a  launch  from  the  U.  S.  S. 

Sagamore. 

U.  S.  S.  Sagamore, 

Off  Cedar  Keys,  Fla. ,  November  8,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report: 

In  accordance  with  your  instructions  I  started  with  an  armed  boat 
for  the  purpose  of  guarding  the  different  rivers  between  here  and  Bay- 
port,  in  company  with  the  schooner  Annie.  Nothing  of  any  importance 
transpired  until  the  morning  of  the  7th,  when  we  discovered  a  sail  to 
the  northward  and  westward,  apparently  standing  in  for  the  land.  The 
wind  being  light,  we  immediately  gave  chase  with  our  boat  and  suc¬ 
ceeded  in  boarding  her  at  11  a.  m.,  in  about  latitude  28°  36',  longitude 
82°  55',  depth  of  water  4  fathoms.  Upon  examination  she  proved  to 
be  the  schooner  Paul,  from  Havana,  with  an  assorted  cargo.  Consid¬ 
ering  her  a  prize,  I  brought  her  here  for  your  further  orders. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Louis  R.  Chester, 
Acting  Ensign ,  U.  S.  S.  Sagamore. 

Lieut.  Commander  Chas.  E.  Fleming, 

Commanding  Cunboat  Sagamore.

Cruising  instructions  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy 
to  Captain  Scott ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Be  Soto. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  November  £0,  1863. 

Sir:  You  will  proceed  with  the  vessel  under  your  command  to  cruise 
in  and  about  the  North  East  Providence  Channel,  for  the  purpose  of 
intercepting  and  capturing  any  vessels  that  you  may  encounter  on  the 
high  seas  which  may  have  violated  the  blockade  instituted  by  the 
U.  S.  Government,  or  which  may  afford  a  reasonable  ground  for  sus¬ 
picion  that  they  intend  doing  so.  You  will  make  yourself  familiar 
with  my  General  Order  No.  2,  dated  January  1, 1863  (it  is  presumed 
that  you  are  already  familiar  with  the  circular  instructions  issued  by 
the  Department  under  date  May  14,  1862,  and  August  18,  1863),  and 
be  governed  thereby  in  making  captures.  Should  a  chase  carry  you 
within  sight  of  any  neutral  foreign  country,  too  much  care  can  not  be 
exercised  to  determine  with  accuracy  your  own  position  and  the  posi¬ 
tion  of  the  chase  at  different  stages  of  the  operation,  with  a  view  to 
refuting  any  false  allegations  that  may  be  subsequently  made  by  our 
enemies  or  their  sympathizers  of  any  violation  of  neutral  territory. 

The  general  limits  of  your  cruising  ground  may  be  stated  as  between 
the  parallels  of  25°  and  27°  north  latitude,  and  between  the  meridians 
of  75°  and  77°  west  longitude;  but  the  entire  waters  and  islands  to  the 
northward  and  westward  of  Crooked  Island  Passage  have  just  been 
placed  within  the  limits  of  my  command,  and  until  other  vessels  can 
be  assigned  to  particular  portions  of  this  ground  much  will  necessa¬ 
rily  be  left  to  your  discretion.  The  Tioga  will  follow  you  with  similar 
orders  to  these  in  a  few  days,  and  efforts  will  be  made  to  increase  this 
force  on  and  about  the  Bahama  Banks. 

In  the  event  of  taking  prizes  you  will  send  them  to  some  Northern 
port  for  adjudication,  if,  in  your  opinion,  their  importance  and  their 
ability  to  go  upon  our  coast  in  the  winter  time  should  render  it  advis¬ 
able.  Otherwise  you  will  send  them  to  this  place. 

You  will  return  here  when  necessary  for  further  supplies  of  coal  or 

P'lt  isTot  improbable  that  by  extending  your  observations  on  the 
parallel  of  28°  as  far  as  longitude  79°  west,  and  on  the  meridian  of  75° 
as  far  as  latitude  24°  north,  the  chances  of  successful  cruising  may  be

Report  of  Acting  Master  Rockwell ,  IT.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 

schooner  Two  Sisters ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 

Maria  Alberta  November  27,  1863. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Two  Sisters, 

Off  Anclote  Keys ,  West  Coast  of  Florida ,  November  28,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  of  the  capture 
of  the  English  schooner  ATaria  Alberta  on  the  27th  instant  by  this 
vessel. 

During  the  night  of  the  26th  instant  I  anchored  on  St.  Martin’s 
Reef,  in  the  latitude  28°  45'  N.,  longitude  82°  50'  W.  At  daylight 
on  the  27th  discovered  a  sail  bearing  S.  E.,  distant  about  9  miles; 
weighed  anchor  and  made  all  sail  in  chase.  The  chase  was  soon 
made  out  to  be  a  schooner  under  the  English  flag,  evidently  endeav¬ 
oring  to  work  over  the  reef  to  Bayport.  Continued  chasing,  finding 
very  shoal  water,  and  dragging  over  the  bottom  continually.  At 
8:30  commenced  firing  shell  at  her,  but  at  the  second  fire  tore  up 
the  chock  from  the  deck,  and  was  consequently  obliged  to  fire  with 
the  gun  secured  with  ropes,  which  process,  lacking  steadiness,  mate¬ 
rially  interfered  with  the  accuracy  of  the  firing.  She  paid  no  atten¬ 
tion  to  the  explosion  of  projectiles  near  her,  but  continued  endeavoring 
to  enter  the  harbor.  At  this  time  a  pilot  boat  came  out  of  the  harbor 
and  passed  near  her,  but  immediately  went  back  into  the  harbor.  At 
the  time  of  commencing  to  fire  at  her  I  launched  my  boat  with  an 
armed  crew  and  sent  her  in  [charge]  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Mon¬ 
tague.  The  chase,  finding  that  the  boat  would  intercept  her,  soon 
kept  off  to  the  S.  S.  W.  and  made  all  sail  to  run  offshore.  In  keep¬ 
ing  off  in  the  chase  this  vessel  ran  onto  a  bed  of  rocks  and  lay  three- 
quarters  of  an  hour,  but  floating  at  10:45  a.  m.  we  followed  in  chase, 
the  boat  having  continued  in  pursuit  while  we  were  ashore.  We  con¬ 
tinued  to  gain  rapidly  on  her  until  12:20,  when,  on  firing  a  shell  over 
her,  she  rounded  to  and  was  boarded  by  the  boat  at  the  same  time 
that  this  vessel  came  up  with  her.  She  proved  to  be  the  schooner 
ATaria  Alberta,  cleared  from  Havana  for  Matamoras,  but  endeavoring 
to  run  the  blockade  into  Bayport.  She  had  English  papers  and  flag, 
and  was  loaded  with  an  assorted  cargo. 

Respectfully, 

C.  H.  Rockwell, 

Acting  Afaster,  Commanding . 

Lieutenant-Commander  R.  Chandler, 

Commanding  Flagship  San  Jacinto.

Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Brigadier- 
General  Woodbury,  U.  S.  Army,  regarding  proqoosed  organization  of 
a  volunteer  force  for  operations  between  Charlotte  Harbor  and  Tampa 
Bay. 

December  2,  1863. 

My  Dear  General:  Mr.  Enoch  Daniels,  a  refugee  from  the  main¬ 
land  near  Charlotte  Harbor,  arrived  here  to-day  for  the  purpose  of 
consulting  you  with  reference  to  raising  a  volunteer  force  to  occupy 
and  conquer  the  country  between  Charlotte  Harbor  and  Tampa  Bay, 
from  which  section  of  the  rebel  State  about  1,500  head  of  cattle  are 
furnished  weekly  for  the  supply  of  the  rebel  army  in  the  field. 

Mr.  Daniel  hopes,  if  you  think  well  of  his  adventure,  to  organize 
recruits  among  the  refugees  at  present  in  Key  West,  who  will  be 
required  to  be  mustered  into  the  service,  armed,  equipped,  and 
rationed,  and  a  small  body  of  regular  volunteers,  say  100,  well  com¬ 
manded  as  a  nucleus.  If  you  think  well  of  his  proposition,  1  will 
endeavor  to  furnish  the  required  transportation  to  Peace  Creek  or 
Charlotte  Harbor,  and  the  protection  which  can  be  afforded  by  the 
neighboring  blockading  vessels. 

Begging  you  to  hear  his  story  and  judge  of  its  feasibility, 

I  remain,  general,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Sguad/rori. 

Brigadier-General  [D.  P.  Woodbury]. 


Destruction  of  extensive  salt  works  in  Lake  Ocala  and  St.  Andrew'1 s 
Bay,  Florida,  December  2,  10,  and  18,  1863,  under  the  direction  of 
Acting  Master  Browne,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U  S.  bark  Restless. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  IT.  S.  Navy. 

No.  391.1  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  December  28,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  gratification  of  reporting  a  very  important  service 
performed  by  the  blockading  force  at  St.  Andrew’s  Sound,  under  the 
command  of  Acting  Master  William  R.  Browne,  in  destroying  a  very 
extensive  and  valuable  quantity  of  salt  works,  both  at  Lake  Ocala  and 
in  St.  Andrew’s  Bay.  The  circumstances  are  as  follows: 

On  December  2  a  boat  was  dispatched  from  the  bark  Restless,  then 


n  w  r — vol  17 - 38 


594 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


lying  at  St.  Andrew’s  Sound,  to  Lake  Ocala  (some  20  miles  to  the 
westward),  where  Acting  Ensign  James  J.  Russell  landed  with  his 
men  and  marched  some  5  miles  inland  to  Kent’s  salt  works — con¬ 
sisting  of  three  different  establishments — and  utterly  destroyed  them. 
There  were  6  steamboat  boilers  at  this  place,  cut  in  half  lengthwise, 
and  7  kettles  made  expressly  for  the  purpose,  each  holding  300  gal¬ 
lons.  They  were  in  the  practice  of  turning  out  130  bushels  of  salt 
daily.  Beside  destroying  these  boilers,  a  large  quantity  of  salt  was 
thrown  into  the  lake,  2  large  flatboats,  and  6  ox  carts  were  demolished, 
and  17  prisoners  were  taken,  who  were  paroled  and  released,  as  the 
boat  was  too  small  to  bring  them  away. 

On  the  10th  of  December  Acting  Ensign  Edwin  Crissey  arrived  at 
St.  Andrew’s  Sound  from  the  East  Pass  of  Santa  Rosa  Sound,  with  the 
stern-wheel  steamer  Bloomer  and  her  tender,  the  sloop  Caroline.,  hav¬ 
ing  heard  of  the  expedition  to  Lake  Ocala,  and  placed  his  command  at 
the  disposal  of  Acting  Master  Browne  for  more  extensive  operations 
near  St.  Andrew’s.  Accordingly,  3  officers  and  48  men  were  sent  from 
the  Restless  to  the  Bloomer ,  and  she  proceeded  to  West  Bay,  where  the 
rebel  Government’s  salt  works  were  first  destroyed,  which  produced  400 
bushels  daily.  At  this  place  there  were  27  buildings,  22  large  boilers, 
and  some  200  kettles,  averaging  200  gallons  each;  all  of  which  were 
destroyed,  together  with  2,000  bushels  of  salt  and  some  storehouses  con¬ 
taining  three  months’  provisions,  the  whole  estimated  at  half  a  million 
of  dollars.  From  this  point  the  expedition  proceeded  down  the  bay, 
destroying  private  salt  works,  which  lined  each- side  for  a  distance  of 
7  miles,  to  the  number  of  198  different  establishments,  averaging  2 
boilers  and  2  kettles  each,  together  with  large  quantities  of  salt;  507 
kettles  were  dug  up  and  rendered  useless,  and  over  300  buildings  were 
destroyed,  together  with  27  wagons  and  5  large  flatboats.  The  entire 
damage  to  the  enemy  is  estimated  by  Acting  Master  Browne  at  three 
millions  of  dollars.  Thirty -one  contrabands  employed  at  these  works 
gladly  availed  themselves  of  this  opportunity  to  escape,  and  were  of 
great  service  in  pointing  out  the  places  where  the  kettles  were  buried 
for  concealment. 


In  the  meantime,  while  these  operations  were  going  on.  Acting 
Master  Browne  got  underway  in  the  bark  Restless  and  ran  up  to  within 
800  yards  of  the  town  of  St.  Andrew’s,  which  had  been  reported  to 
him  by  deserters  as  being  occupied  only  by  a  military  force  for  the 
last  ten  months,  and  commenced  shelling  the  place  and  some  soldiery, 
who  made  a  speedy  retreat  to  the  woods.  Selecting  the  weathermost 
houses  for  a  target,  the  town  was  fired  by  the  third  shell  and  32  houses 
were  soon  reduced  to  ashes.  No  resistance  was  offered  to  our  people 
throughout  the  affair. 

Acting  Master  Browne  reports  that  his  work  is  not  yet  half  done, 
as  there  are  over  100  salt  works  in  East  and  West  bays,  which  he  con¬ 
templates  destroying.  He  also  speaks  in  high  terms  of  Acting  Ensigns 
James  J.  Russell  and  Charles  N.  Hicks  and  the  48  men  from  the  Rest- 
less,  as  also  of  Acting  Ensign  Edwin  Crissey  and  the  6  men  belonging 
to  the  Bloomer ,  for  the  prompt  manner  in  which  they  carried  out  his 
orders. 

Respectfully, 


Theodokus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Bastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 
Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Browne,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  bark  Restless,  regarding 

expedition  to  Lake  Ocala  under  the  direction  of  Acting  Ensign  Russell,  IT.  S.  Navy,  of 

that  vessel. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay,  Fla .,  December  7,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  communicate  to  you  that  just  about  dusk 
on  the  evening  of  December  2  we  descried  from  our  masthead  a  black 
smoke,  a  long  distance  seaward,  moving  westward.  I  supposed  it  to  be 
a  steam  blockade  runner,  bound  in  somewhere  on  the  coast,  and,  being 
credibly  informed  that  Lake  Ocala  has  been  resorted  to  as  a  place 
for  running  and  receiving  cargoes,  I  fitted  out  the  first  cutter  and  9 
men  under  the  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  J.  J.  Russell  with  orders  to 
proceed  up  the  coast  as  far  as  Lake  Ocala,  in  hopes  of  cutting  her  out 
if  that  was  her  destination. 

I  also  ordered  him  (in  case  he  found  no  vessel  there)  to  land  his 
party,  with  the  exception  of  enough  to  take  charge  of  the  boat,  and 
proceed  up  the  cart  road  which  leads  from  the  sea  to  Kent’s  salt  works, 
5  miles  inland,  and  destroy  the  whole  affair,  and  well  did  he  accom¬ 
plish  his  mission. 

After  reaching  the  lake,  no  vessel  being  in  sight,  he  landed  his  party 
and  marched  to  the  works,  and  effectually  destroyed  them,  consisting 
of  three  different  establishments,  having  6  steamboat  boilers  cut  in 
half  lengthways,  and  7  iron  kettles  made  expressly  for  the  purpose, 
each  holding  300  gallons,  and  turning  out  130  bushels  of  salt  per  day. 
He  also  hove  a  large  quantity  of  salt  into  the  lake,  and  on  his  return  to 
the  boat  he  demolished  2  large  flatboats  and  6  ox  carts,  used  for 
hauling  salt  or  cargo. 

Seventeen  prisoners  were  taken,  but,  the  boat  being  too  small  to 
convey  them  to  the  ship,  it  was  thought  advisable  to  release  them, 
after  administering  an  oath  never  to  take  up  arms  against  the  United 
States  Government.  You  will  please  find  enclosed  a  chart  of  the  lake; 
also  2  Confederate  newspapers  found  upon  the  person  of  one  Jordon, 
overseer  of  the  works. 

I  would  respectfully  call  your  attention  to  Acting  Ensign  J.  J. 
Russell  and  the  men  under  his  command  who  composed  this  expedi¬ 
tion  as  deserving  great  praise  in  destroying  so  effectually  one  of  the 
most  extensive  salt  works  upon  this  coast,  to  accomplish  which  took 
ten  hours  of  hard  labor. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Browne,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  bark  Restless,  regarding 
expedition  to  St.  Andrew's  Sound  under  the  direction  of  Acting  Ensign  Crissey,  TJ.  S. 
Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Bloomer. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew’s  Bay ,  Florida,  December  15,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  on  the  morning  of  December  10  the 
U.  S.  S.  Bloomer,.  Captain  Edwin  Crissey,  and  sloop  Caroline ,  her 
tender,  came  to  this  place  from  East  Pass,  Santa  Rosa  Island,  to  render 
us  assistance  in  the  destruction  of  the  numerous  salt  works  on  this 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  597 

bay,  having  heard  of  our  dash  a  few  days  before  on  the  Government 
salt  works  at  Lake  Ocala,  7  miles  from  Santa  Rosa  Bay. 

Captain  Crissey  tendered  me  the  Bloom, er  and  Caroline  for  the  accom¬ 
plishment  of  that  object,  informing  me  if  I  would  place  men  and  arms 
on  board  of  his  vessel  he  would  stay  and  render  me  all  the  assistance 
he  possibly  could.  I  gladly  availed  myself  of  the  opportunity,  and 
placed  48  men  and  3  officers,  armed  and  provisioned  for  4  days,  on 
board,  and  ordered  him  to  proceed  to  Bear  Creek  (at  the  head  of  North 
Bay)  and  if  possible  cut  out  a  schooner  loaded  with  100  bales  of  cotton, 
which  lay  4^  miles  up  the  creek.  This  accomplished,  to  proceed  to  W est 
Bay  and  destroy  the  extensive  Government  salt  works,  which  yielded 
daily  400  bushels  of  salt,  while  I  would  destroy  the  headquarters  of 
the  rebel  companies  stationed  at  St.  Andrew’s  (to  protect  the  numerous 
salt  works  on  East  and  West  Bay),  numbering  277  men,  who  held  it 
with  one  fieldpiece  to  keep  the  hands  employed  at  the  Government 
salt  works  supplied  with  tish,  oysters,  etc.,  and  to  prevent  contra¬ 
bands  and  refugees  from  coming  off  to  the  blockade.  These  men 
were  always  upon  the  alert  for  an  opportunity  to  shoot  our  men  who 
land  for  wood  on  the  main,  there  being  none  on  the  island.  At  8  p.  m. , 
the  wind  freshening  ahead,  I  came  to  and  ordered  the  steamer  to  pro¬ 
ceed  on  her  misson.  At  daylight  next  morning  I  got  underway  with 
the  bark  and  ran  up  to  within  800  yards  of  the  town.  Before  opening 
upon  it  we  saw  2  cavalry  officers  and  numerous  infantry,  who  quickly 
fled  after  our  second  shot  to  the  woods  where  their  companions  lay 
concealed. 

Selecting  the  largest  group  of  houses  we  succeeded  in  firing  it,  our 
third  shell  bursting  in  one  of  the  houses  at  the  southeast  end.  The 
wind  being  E.  S.  E.  communicated  the  flames  quickly  to  the  others, 
consisting  of  32  houses  and  shanties,  which  were  speedily  reduced  to 
ashes,  and  will  no  more  afford  shelter,  as  heretofore,  to  the  enemy, 
from  which  the}7  watched  the  proceedings  of  all  which  took  place  in 
or  about  this  harbor. 

I  would  now  most  respectfully  call  your  particular  attention  to  the 
expedition  on  board  the  Bloomer  and  the  almost  incalculable  destruc¬ 
tion  of  salt  works,  salt,  provisions,  materials,  etc,.,  pertaining  to  the 
manufacture  of  this  essential  article,  which  they  accomplished. 

The  Government  works  [were]  under  the  command  of  a  Mr.  Clen- 
denin,  which  turned  out  daily  400  bushels  of  salt.  This  was  one  of 
the  best  located  in  West  Bay,  being  situated  in  a  marsh,  the  water  of 
which  yielded  75  gallons  of  salt  to  100  gallons  of  water.  It  was  in  fact 
a  complete  village,  covering  a  space  of  three-fourths  of  a  square  mile, 
employing  many  hands  and  16  ox  and  mule  teams  constantly  to  haul 
salt  to  Eufaula  Sound,  and  from  thence  conveyed  to  Montgomery,  at 
which  place  it  is  selling  at  fabulous  prices — $40  and  $45  per  bushel. 

At  this  place  were  27  buildings,  and  22  large  steam  boilers,  and  300 
kettles  averaging  200  gallons  each,  which  cost  the  Government  $5  per 
gallon,  all  of  which  were  totally  destroyed,  besides  2,000  bushels  of 
salt,  and  storehouses  filled  with  corn  meal,  bacon,  sirup,  and  other 
provisions,  enough  to  supply  those  employed  three  months,  the  whole 
of  which  was  so  effectually  destroyed  that  every  vestige  of  this  salt 
village  has  entirely  disappeared,  the  whole  of  which  can  not  be  esti¬ 
mated  of  a  less  value  than  $500,000. 

After  which  they  proceeded  down  the  bay  and  destroyed  the  salt 
works  which  lined  each  side  for  7  miles  (belonging  to  private  indi¬ 
viduals),  numbering  at  least  198  different  works,  averaging  2  boilers 


598 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


and  10  kettles  each;  also  destroying  a  large  quantity  of  salt.  Five 
hundred  and  seven  kettles  were  dug  up  and  rendered  useless;  over  300 
buildings  of  various  sizes,  used  as  storehouses,  etc.,  were  destroyed, 
together  with  27  wagons  and  carts  and  5  large  flatboats. 

These  works,  with  the  Government  works,  could  not  have  cost  less 
than  $3,000,000. 

Thirty-one  contrabands  (two  of  whom  were  females)  belonging  to 
these  works  gladly  gave  themselves  up  to  us  and  assisted  materially 
in  destroying  the  works  and  digging  up  kettles,  which  were  buried  in 
the  swamp  and  would  never  have  come  to  light  had  they  not  pointed 
them  out  to  us. 

This  bay  was  considered  a  safe  place  to  pursue  the  making  of  salt,  and 
on  either  side  for  7  miles  there  could  be  seen  one  continued  string  of 
salt  works.  A  Mr.  Blunt,  an  intelligent  man,  who  had  been  engaged 
in  this  business,  said  the  swamps  in  this  bay  were  the  best  adapted  in 
the  whole  Confederacy  for  the  location  of  salt  works,  as  the  continued 
drought  in  this  region  for  the  past  three  years  had  caused  the  evapo¬ 
ration  of  nearly  all  the  fresh  water,  leaving  at  least  75  per  cent  of  salt 
in  the  water  remaining.  Besides  this,  the  salt  made  here  was  of  better 
quality  than  that  procured  at  any  other  place,  not  excepting  the  cele¬ 
brated  salt  works  in  Virginia,  and  the  destruction  we  had  made  would 
be  “a  greater  blow,  and  more  severely  felt,  than  the  falling  of 
Charleston.” 

But  our  work  is  not  yet  half  done.  There  are  over  100  salt  works 
in  East  and  West  bays,  which  I  contemplate  destroying.  I  send  for 
your  disposal  21  contrabands,  reserving  the  remainder  for  boat’s  crew 
and  to  assist  in  finding  buried  kettles,  etc.,  of  the  other  works. 
Enclosed  please  find  various  letters  collected  at  the  destroyed  works. 
I  would  most  respectfully  call  your  attention  to  Acting  Ensigns  James 
J.  Russell  and  Charles  N.  Hicks,  of  this  vessel,  and  the  men  under 
their  command,  for  the  prompt  manner  in  which  they  carried  out  my 
orders  and  cooperated  with  Captain  Crissev,  of  the  Bloomer ,  whose 
force  of  6  men  made  the  total  of  51  men  and  1  officers  engaged  in 
this  expedition. 

Very  respectfulty,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Corndg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  T Vest,  Fla.

Additional  report  of  Acting  Master  Browne,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  operations  in  St. 

Andrew’s  Bay. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew’s  Bay,  Fla. ,  December  20 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report: 

On  the  evening  of  the  18th  instant,  having  finished  repairing  the 
boilers  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Bloomer ,  which  were  so  much  out  of  repair  that 
we  could  not  proceed  to  the  final  destruction  of  the  remaining  salt  works 
in  this  bay  until  the}'  had  undergone  a  hasty  and  partial  repairing  and 
supplied  with  four  extra  days’  fuel  (pine  wood),  I  repaired  on  board 
with  Acting  Ensigns  James  J.  Russell  and  Henry  Eason  and  47  men. 
As  the  moon  was  quite  large,  I  concluded  not  to  make  a  start  until 
after  she  had  set,  but  the  wind,  which  had  been  light  from  the  N.  IV., 
suddenly  freshened  to  a  double  reef  topsail  breeze.  At  10:30  it  blew 
still  harder,  so  much  so  that  it  was  thought  by  Captain  Crissey  and 
the  pilot  that  the  steamer  would  not  be  able  to _ stem  the  strong  ebb 
tide  at  that  time  running,  especially  as  the  boilers  leaked  so  badly 
on  the  expedition.  The  fires  were  nearly  extinguished,  besides,  we 
had  her  tender,  a  sloop  of  some  60  tons,  alongside  to  tow,  the  wind 
being  dead  ahead.  But  as  my  men  were  all  on  board  and  provisioned 
only  for  four  days  and  Captain  Crissey  anxious  to  return  to  his 
station,  his  time  of  absence  having  already  expired,  1  determined  to 
make  the  attempt.  At  11:30,  steam  being  up,  we  weighed  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  on,  and  so  strong  was  the  wind  and  the  tide  against  us  that  we 
gained  onl}"  1  mile  in  three  hours,  the  captain  and  pilot  saying  we 
must  give  it  up.  I  urged  them  to  keep  on,  as  after  midnight  1  was 
confident  the  wind  would  moderate,  and  at  3  a.  m.  the  tide  would  turn 
in  our  favor.  At  1:30  a.  m.  the  wind  began  to  abate,  and  at  3  a.  m. 
the  tide  turned. 

We  had  now  only  got  as  far  as  Red  Fish  Point,  a  distance  of  4  miles 
from  our  starting  point,  at  11:  30  p.  m.  By  daylight  we  were  through 
the  narrowest  part  of  the  bay,  and  at  the  commencement  of  the  salt 
works,  10  miles  above  St.  Andrew’s. 

The  officers  and  men  were  landed  under  the  cover  of  our  guns  and 
occupied  the  rest  of  the  day  in  destroying  the  remaining  salt  works, 
90  in  number,  with  a  large  number  of  kettles  and  boilers  and  30  build¬ 
ings  or  salt  sheds. 

The  pickets  stationed  at  Parker’s  house  seeing  us  gave  the  alarm, 
and  the  rebels  destroyed  the  remaining  works  by  setting  them  on  fire 
to  keep  them  from  being  destroyed  by  us. 

We  skirted  this  bay  for  a  distance  of  15  miles,  10  of  which  were 
covered  near  the  beach  with  some  300  salt  works,  all  of  which  the 
enemy  destroyed  with  the  exception  of  the  90  we  demolished. 

Having  cleared  the  three  arms  of  this  extensive  bay  of  salt  works 
we  returned  to  this  ship.  On  our  way  back  we  saw  large  fires  in  West 


600 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Bay  in  the  direction  of  some  salt  works  we  had  not  destroyed  and 
supposed  the  rebel,  Captain  Robinson,  had  ordered  them  to  be  destroyed 
to  prevent  us  from  doing  it,  which  proved  to  be  the  case.  Upon  my 
arrival  at  the  ship  I  found  three  deserters  from  Anderson’s  company 
had  come  off  and  delivered  up  their  arms  and  said  they  were  ready  to 
take  the  oath  of  allegiance  to  the  United  States  Government  and  that 
all  the  privates  in  the  companies  of  Anderson  and  Robinson  were 
heartily  tired  of  the  war;  even  Captain  Anderson  had  resigned  and 
gone  home,  and  33  men,  and  now,  all  the  salt  works  in  this  vicinity  were 
destroyed,  many  would  starve  to  death. 

The  oath  of  allegiance  was  administered  to  three  of  these  men,  and 
who  joined  this  ship,  having  entered  the  service  for  one  year.  Within 
the  past  ten  days  290  salt  works,  33  covered  wagons,  12  flatboats,  2 
sloops  (5  tons  each),  6  ox  carts,  4,000  bushels  of  salt,  268  buildings  at 
the  different  salt  works,  529  iron  kettles  averaging  150  gallons  each, 
105  iron  boilers  for  boiling  brine  [were  destroyed],  and  it  is  believed 
from  what  we  saw  that  the  enemy  destroyed  as  many  more  to  prevent 
us  from  doing  so.  Forty-eight  contrabands  and  prisoners  have  been 
taken  and  five  deserters  from  the  army  have  come  and  delivered  them¬ 
selves  up  and  entered  our  service.  Seventeen  persons  have  been 
paroled  after  taking  the  oath  of  allegiance  not  to  take  up  arms 
against  us. 

In  conclusion  permit  me  to  add  that  52  men  and  4  officers  were 
employed  in  the  destruction  of  these  works — 47  men,  3  officers,  and 
myself  from  the  Restless ,  5  men  and  1  officer  from  the  Bloomer — all  of 
which  deserve  great  praise  for  the  prompt  manner  in  which  they  car¬ 
ried  out  my  every  order. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne. 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  /Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla. 


Commendatory  letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Acting  Master 
Browne,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  bark  Restless. 


U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  December  28,  1863. 

Sir:  You  will  be  pleased  to  accept  for  yourself,  and  to  convey  to 
the  officers  and  men  under  your  command,*  my  commendation  for  the 
very  important  service  performed  in  the  destruction  of  the  extensive 
and  valuable  salt  works,  both  at  Bake  Ocala  and  in  St.  Andrew’s  Bay. 
I  have  taken  great  pleasure  in  reporting  the  details  of  these  operations 
to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  as  another  instance  of  the  zeal  and  energy 
which  animate  this  squadron  and  as  another  severe  blow  to  the  enemy. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  later  operations  in 

St.  Andrew's  Bay. 


U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  T Vest,  January  % 7 ,  186 f 

Sir:  It  affords  me  pleasure  to  report  to  the  Department  that  the 
promise  made  by  Acting'  Master  W illiam  R.  Browne,  commanding  bark 
Restless ,  at  the  conclusion  of  his  last  report  concerning  the  destruction 
of  extensive  salt  works  in  the  vicinity  of  St.  Andrew’s  Bay,  namely, 
that  he  would  complete  the  work  so  handsomely  begun,  appears  to 
have  been  kept.  He  reports  that  he  went  on  board  the  stern-wheel 
steamer  Bloom, er,  with  2  officers  and  47  men  belonging  to  the  Restless , 
and  proceeded  up  the  bay,  against  very  unfavorable  circumstances  of 
darkness,  wind,  and  tide,  some  10  miles  above  St.  Andrew’s,  where  his 
force  was  landed,  and  destroyed  some  90  additional  salt  works,  together 
with  all  the  boilers,  kettles,  and  buildings  attached  to  them;  where¬ 
upon  the  enemy  commenced  the  destruction  of  some  200  more,  which 
were  in  advance  of  our  party,  and  thus  saved  us  from  all  further  trouble, 
except  skirting  along  the  bay  for  the  distance  of  15  miles,  to  make 
sure  that  the  work  of  destruction  had  been  well  performed  by  them. 
Deserters  from  Captain  Anderson’s  and  Robinson’s  companies  reported 
subsequently  that  both  officers  and  men  had  broken  up  and  gone  home, 
as  the  destruction  of  the  salt  works,  which  they  were  ordered  to  guard, 
had  been  so  complete,  and  6  of  them  have  enlisted  in  the  Navy,  after 
taking  the  oath  of  allegiance. 

Acting  Master  Browne  again  speaks  in  terms  of  commendation  of 
the  officers  and  men  engaged  in  this  service,  including  Acting  Ensign 
Crissey  and  the  five  men  composing  the  crew  of  the  steamer  Bloomer. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Bast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Fleming ,  £7.  /S'.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Sagamore , 
regarding  vessels  reported  as  trading  between  Suwanee  River  and 
Harcana. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  December  7,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  information  from  a  reliable  source  that  the  following- 
vessels  are  trading  between  Suwanee  River  and  Havana,  viz  :  Steamer 
Little  Lilly ,  steamer  Union ,  steamer  Lsabel ,  steamer  (not  known). 

And  that  the  Little  Lilly  makes  two  trips  to  the  Suwanee  per  month 
with  the  regularity  of  a  mail  packet,  two  pilots  being  stationed  at  the 
mouth  of  the  river  to  pilot  them  in.  If  it  be  possible  I  would  like  to 
have  those  pilots  captured  and  the  stakes  marking  the  entrance 
removed  to  a  locality  that  would  insure  those  steamers  being  plumped 
on  shore. 

I  hope  to  be  able  to  send  the  steamer  Nita  to  Cedar  Keys  in  about 
a  fortnight,  when,  through  your  vigilance  and  disposition  of  vessels 
and  boats,  I  shall  hope  to  hear  of  your  success  in  capturing  the  four 
steamers.  The  stakes  should  be  moved  in  the  night. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

T.  Bailey, 

Acting  LI  ear- Admiral. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Charles  E.  Fleming, 

Commanding  Steamer  Sagamore. 


Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Semmes ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  blockade  at  Tampa, 
Fla. ,  regarding  measures  for  trapping  blockade  runners. 


[U.  S.  Flagship]  Dale, 

December'  8,  1863. 

Sir:  I  understand  that  the  channels  in  and  out  of  Bayport  and  the 
rivers  on  your  station,  where  the  rebels  are  in  the  habit  of  running 
the  blockade,  are  buoyed,  or  staked  out.  I  wish,  where  you  find  that 
to  be  the  case,  that  you  will  send  boats  and  pilots  in  the  night  and 
change  the  position  of  those  stakes,  buoys,  or  marks  in  such  new  loca¬ 
tion  as  will  infallibly  plump  their  vessel's  on  shore.  The  pilots  should 
at  the  same  time  be  ordered  to  observe  carefully  the  situation  of  the 
channel  from  which  they  remove  the  marks,  so  that  our  own  vessels 
may  not  get  into  the  trap  set  for  our  enemies. 

After  carrying  out  this  order,  watch  carefully  the  nets  thus  set  and 
pounce  upon  your  prey  when  aground. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc. , 


Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral. 


Lieutenant-Commander  A.  A.  Semmes, 

Commanding 'Blockade  at  Tampa ,  etc.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
fitting  of  the  steamer  Nitafor  service. 


U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West ,  December  13,  1863. 

Sir:  Referring  to  letters,  No.  290,  of  September  10,  and  No.  308, 
of  October  3, 1  would  state  that  I  hope  to  have  the  steamer  Nita  ready 
for  service  within  the  present  month,  when  she  will  be  sent  to  cruise 
between  the  Suwanee  River  and  Bayport.  Her  armament  will  consist 
of  one  rilled  12-pounder  howitzer,  in  pivot,  forward;  two  heavy  12- 
pounder  howitzers,  in  broadside,  forward;  one  smooth  24-pounder 
howitzer,  in  pivot,  aft,  and  I  have  fixed  her  complement  of  officers 
and  men  together  at  46. 

I  would  therefore  request  an  early  decision  as  to  whether  she  can  be 
considered  a  regular  cruiser  or  whether  she  can  act  only  as  a  tender. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey,

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Adm  iral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  Acting  Volun¬ 
teer  Lieutenant  Baxter,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  to  render  assistance  to  company 
of  refugee  rangers  to  be  landed  on  an  island  in  Charlotte  Harbor. 

Confidential.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  December  16,  1863. 

Sir:  Brigadier -General  Woodbury  has  commanded  the  organization 
of  a  company  of  refugee  rangers,  intended  to  operate  on  the  main¬ 
land  in  the  vicinity  of  Charlotte  Harbor  and  Tampa  Bay,  in  conjunc¬ 
tion  with  some  regular  troops  and  under  his  own  immediate  orders. 
Some  25  or  30  men  are  already  enlisted  and  placed  in  charge  of  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Meyers,  of  the  Forty-seventh  Regiment  Pennsylvania  Volun¬ 
teers.  This  detachment  is  sent  up  in  the  Sunflower  to  be  landed  on 
one  of  the  islands  in  Charlotte  Harbor  (Useppa  Island  is  considered 
the  best  for  their  present  purposes),  under  your  directions,  with  a  view 
to  obtaining  further  recruits  from  the  refugees  and  other  inhabitants 
of  that  vicinity,  and  to  await  there  the  arrival  of  the  general,  or  orders 
from  him. 

You  will  therefore  render  them  every  assistance  in  your  power  and 
protect  them  with  your  guns  and  all  the  force  under  your  command, 
if  necessary. 

Respectfully,  [T.  Bailey,] 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Sherrill ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  bark. 

Roebuck ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner  Ringdove. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

Off  Indian  River ,  December  19 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
Ringdove ,  23  tons,  of  and  from  Nassau,  with  a  crew  of  five  men,  on 
the  17th  instant. 

Soon  after  daylight  a  sail  was  discovered  to  southward  standing 
apparently  for  this  ship,  the  wind  being  fresh  from  S.  E.,  rugged  sea, 
and  passing  squalls.  At  8:15  he  changed  his  course  as  if  to  run  past, 
when  I  fired  three  shell  from  the  rifled  gun  and  made  ready  to  follow 
him,  upon  which  he  hauled  in  for  the  beach  and  ran  aground  near  the 
bar  off  Indian  River  Inlet.  I  dispatched  two  armed  boats  in  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  Pulsipher  and  a  master’s  mate  [William  H.]  Bradford, 
who  succeeded  in  boarding  the  schooner  and  after  a  while  in  getting 
her  afloat  and  inside  the  bar  in  smooth  water.  Her  cargo  [consisted 
of  ]  190  bags  salt,  3  bags  coffee,  2  half  chests  tea,  and  3  barrels  whisky. 

The  only  papers  found  on  board  were  register,  crew  list,  and  clear¬ 
ance.  No  log  book  or  colors.  Got  the  schooner  out  safely  this  a.  tn. 
and  will  dispatch  her  to  Key  West  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Pulsi¬ 
pher  and  a  prize  crew  for  adjudication.  I  enclose  a  list  of  the  officers 
and  crew  attached  to  this  vessel  at  time  of  above  capture. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Sherrill, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C.

Destruction  of  the  steamer  Powerful ,  by  the  U.  S.  tender  Fox ,  at  the

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy. 

No.  392.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  December  28,  1863. 

Sir:  It  gives  me  great  pleasure  to  call  the  attention  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment  to  a  very  important  service  performed  by  the  schooner  Fox ,  a 
tender  to  the  San  Jacinto ,  under  the  command  of  Acting  Master 
George  Ashbury.  The  circumstances  are  as  follows: 

On  the  20th  of  December  a  steamer  was  discovered  in  the  mouth  of 
the  Suwanee  River,  apparently  at  anchor  or  aground.  The  Fox  imme¬ 
diately  beat  up  toward  her  until,  when  within  about  three-quarters  of 
a  mile  of  the  steamer,  she  grounded  in  8£  feet  water,  and  opened  upon 
her  with  the  howitzers,  at  the  same  time  sending  an  armed  boat  in  to 
capture  the  steamer.  An  attempt  was  made  to  intimidate  our  people 
by  mounting  a  piece  of  stovepipe  on  a  chair  to  represent  a  forecastle 
gun,  and  a  log  of  wood  on  a  camp  stool  for  a  stern  gun,  but  this  device 
of  the  enemy  failed  in  its  object,  and  Acting  Ensign  Marcellus  Jack- 
son  boarded  the  steamer,  from  which  everybody  had  made  their  escape 
to  the  shore.  She  proved  to  be  a  side-wheel  vessel,  painted  lead  color, 
with  black  smokestack,  two  masts,  and  a  walking- beam  engine.  Neither 
cargo,  personal  effects,  papers,  nor  anything  to  indicate  her  name 
were  found  on  board,  but  from  the  description  she  is  supposed  to  have 
been  the  Little  Lily ,  formerly  the  Nan-Nan ,  and  before  that  the 
Flushing.  The  water  was  found  running  rapidly  into  the  engine 
room;  none  of  our  people  were  competent  to  stop  the  leak  or  work 
the  engine;  the  channel  was  exceedingly  intricate  and  narrow,  and 
night  was  rapidly  coming  on.  Under  these  circumstances,  Acting 
Ensign  Jackson  set  fire  to  the  vessel,  agreeably  to  orders  from  Acting 
Master  Ashbury;  and  in  returning  to  the  Fox,  pulled  up  all  the  stakes 
by  which  the  channel  was  marked  out  for  about  a  mile  and  a  half. 
The  destruction  of  this  steamer  is  reported  as  having  been  complete, 
and  if  it  prove  to  have  been  the  Little  Lily,  it  is  a  most  fortunate  cir¬ 
cumstance,  as  her  speed  was  supposed  to  be  greater  than  that  of  any 
vessel  in  this  squadron. 

Again,  on  December  24,  a  vessel  was  discovered  by  the  Fox,  stand¬ 
ing  in  for  the  Suwanee  River,  and  after  a  chase  of  two  hours,  and  the 
firing  of  several  shells,  she  was  hove  to.  Being  ordered  by  Mr.  Ash¬ 
bury  to  send  a  boat  on  board,  the  stranger  put  his  helm  up,  with  the 
evident  intention  of  running  the  Fox  down,  and  came  down  upon  the 
starboard  quarter,  carrying  away  the  boat  davits,  but  doing  little 
other  damage,  as  the  Fox  was  immediately  kept  away.  While  his  ves¬ 
sel  was  paying  off  Mr.  Ashbury  directed  a  rifie  shot  to  be  fired  for  the 
purpose  of  intimidation,  but  a  heavy  sea  was  running  at  the  time  and 
the  bullet  took  effect  on  the  captain  of  the  strange  vessel,  who  was  at 
the  wheel,  passing  through  his  leg,  but  without  touching  an  artery. 
The  vessel  was  then  boarded  and  proved  to  be  the  British  schooner 
Edward ,  from  Havana,  bound  to  the  Suwanee  River,  with  a  cargo  of 
lead  and  salt,  and  was  accordingly  seized  as  a  prize. 

In  addition  to  these  achievements,  I  would  remind  the  Department 


608 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


that  the  Fox  was  one  of  the  three  tenders  that  assisted  the  Honduras 
in  capturing  the  British  steamer  Mail. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral  Gomdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Ashbury,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  schooner  Fox,  tender  to 

the  U.  S.  S,  San  Jacinto. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Fox, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  Deceniber  28,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  left  this  port  in  obedience,  to 
your  instructions  on  the  9th  instant,  the  repairs  to  the  vessel  having 
been  completed,  and  proceeded  to  my  cruising  ground.  On  the  10th, 
in  a  gale,  I  had  the  misfortune  to  lose  the  starboard  quarter  boat,  a 
heavy  sea  striking  it.  On  the  19th,  having  a  favorable  opportunity,  I 
stood  in  to  3  fathoms  oil'  the  Suwanee  and  anchored.  On  the  20th  at 
11  a.  m.  the  lookout  aloft  descried  a  steamer  some  miles  up  the  coast. 
1  got  underway  at  once  and  beat  up  toward  her.  At  12,  being  in  2 
fathoms,  I  anchored  at  3  miles  distance,  the  steamer  having  apparently 
anchored  or  got  ashore.  Sending  a  boat  ahead  to  sound,  and  finding 
enough  water  for  some  distance,  I  stood  in,  but  at  12:30  struck  in  82 
feet,  but  succeeded  in  getting  off  without  much  difficulty  or  any 
injury.  At  this  time  boats  could  be  plainly  seen  passing  and  repass¬ 
ing  from  the  steamer  to  the  shore.  1  opened  tire  on  her  and  at  2:30 
sent  Acting  Ensign  [Marcellus]  Jackson  with  an  armed  boat’s  crew 
with  instructions  to  destroy  her  if  possible,  her  situation,  being  almost 
surrounded  with  oyster  beds,  rendering  any  attempt  to  get  her  out 
with  my  imperfect  facilities  nearly  hopeless.  The  boat  returned  at 
sunset,  having  accomplished  the  object.  Mr.  Jackson  reports  her  as 
being  a  side-wheel  vessel,  painted  a  light  lead  color,  with  black  smoke¬ 
stack,  two  masts,  and  a  walking  beam.  Neither  cargo,  personal 
effects,  papers,  nor  anything  to  indicate  her  name  were  found  on  board. 
She  was  apparently  of  English  build.  She  was  entirely  deserted, 
although  her  machinery  was  still  warm;  a  couple  of  “quakers”  were 
bearing  on  the  schooner,  water  was  running  into  her  engine  room,  and 
she  was  anchored  in  the  channel  leading  to  the  mouth  of  the  Suwanee. 
Mr.  Jackson  reports  this  channel  as  being  very  narrow  in  places  and 
extremely  intricate  although  well  staked  out. 

In  returning  to  the  schooner  he  followed  this  channel  and  pulled  up 
nearly  all  the  stakes  from  a  short  distance  above  the  steamer  to  its 
mouth,  a  distance  of  a  mile  and  a  half  or  more.  I  have  no  doubt  that 
the  steamer  is  rendered  perfectly  useless,  the  flames  having  enveloped 
the  hull  in  a  short  time  after  the  fire  was  ignited.  After  dark  I  put 
to  sea  and  the  next  day  stood  up  the  coast  sighting  the  land,  but  saw 
nothing. 

On  the.  22d,  off  St.  Marks,  I  spoke  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes  and 
received  from  her  a  supply  of  water. 

On  the  24th,  at  4  p.  m.,  the  lookout  aloft  raised  a  sail  to  the  S.  E. 
Made  all  sail  in  chase,  and  after  a  chase  of  two  hours,  firing  several 
shells  at  her,  the  chase  hove  to,  by  hauling  down  his  jib.  Running 
near  him  I  ordered  him  to  lower  his  foresail  and  send  his  boat  on  board,

oiir  boat  being  unsafe  in  so  heavy  a  sea  as  was  then  running.  Instead

My  provisions  running  low  I  started  at  the  same  time  for  this  port 
and  arrived  at  my  anchorage  this  day  at  10  o’clock.

Powerful. 

No.  51.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Dale,

Sir:  Referring  to  my  communication  dated  December  28,  1863 
(numbered  392),  I  have  to  inform  the  Department  that  the  steamer,  the 
destruction  of  which  by  the  U.  S.  schooner  Fox  is  therein  detailed, 
was  the  Powerful ,  and  not  the  Nan-Nan  (or  Little  Lily )  as  I  had 
surmised. 

Lieutenant-Commander  McDougal  has  since  visited  the  wreck  and 
destroyed  the  machinery,  which  the  rebels  were  preparing  to  take 
away. 

I  trust  that  the  Department  will  see  fit  to  notice  by  promotion  the 
service  performed  by  Acting  Master  Ashbury  in  destroying  the  steamer. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Bailey,
