Expedition  to  Myacca  River ,  for  transportation  of  refugee  rangers 
from  Useppa  Island  to  the  mainland ,  December  %lf-30,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Baxter,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  bark  Gem 

of  the  Sea,  transmitting  reports. 

U.  S.  Bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 

Charlotte  Harbor ,  January  3,  1864- 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  that  agreeable  to  the  request  of 
Lieutenant  Meyers,  of  the  Forty-seventh  Regiment  Pennsylvania  V ol- 
nnteers,  now  in  command  of  the  refugee  rangers  on  Useppa  Island, 
I  sent  on  the  21th  ultimo  the  launch  and  second  cutter,  armed  and 
manned  with  14  men  and  provisions  for  eight  days,  in  charge  of  Act¬ 
ing  Ensign  J.  H.  Jenks,  with  orders  to  proceed  to  Useppa  Island,  [Flor¬ 
ida],  there  take  on  board  Captain  Daniels  and  15  refugee  rangers,  under 
his  command,  and  also  to  take  two  small  boats  for  the  use  of  the 
refugee  rangers,  and  proceed  with  them  to  the  mainland  at  a  point 
designated  by  Captain  Daniels  in  the  mouth  of  the  Myacca  River, 
[Florida],  and  land  them  for  the  purpose  of  scouting  through  the  coun¬ 
try  for  recruiting,  and  then  to  remain  there  or  in  the  vicinity  with 
his  men  and  boats  until  Captain  Daniels  and  his  men  returned,  or  his 
provisions  were  exhausted,  for  the  purpose  of  covering  their  retreat 
and  taking  them  away. 

On  the  26th  ultimo  the  sloop  Rosalie  arrived  from  Key  West,  and  on 
the  morning  of  the  28th  ultimo  I  sent  her  up  to  the  mouth  of  the 
Myacca  to  Took  after  our  boats  and  assist  them  in  case  they  were 
attacked  by  the  rebels. 

On  the  30th  ultimo  at  8  o’clock  p.  m.  Acting  Ensign  J.  H.  Jenks 
returned  on  board  with  the  launch  from  the  expedition,  reporting  the 
other  boats  and  Rosalie  on  their  way  to  this  vessel,  and  bringing  with 
him  John  Brown  (seaman),  who  was  severely  wounded  in  the  groin  by 
a  rifleball  that  morning  while  in  a  skirmish  with  the  rebels. 

On  Mr.  Jenks’s  arrival  at  the  point  designated  by  Captain  Daniels, 
he  landed  the  refugee  rangers,  who  left  for  the  interior,  having  an 
understanding  with  them  that  they  were  to  return  to  that  point  within 
seven  days.  He  then  landed  with  his  men  and  encamped  within  50 
yards  of  his  boats  for  their  comfort  and  convenience  and  making 
every  preparation  to  avoid  a  surprise  by  the  rebels. 

On  the  30th  ultimo  at  about  4:30  a.  m.  the  camp  was  alarmed  by 
hearing  noises  in  the  bushes  in  different  directions,  as  though  men 
were  crawling  toward  them.  At  first  Mr.  Jenks  thought  they  were 
Captain  Daniels’  men  coming  in,  and  on  being  hailed  by  our  pickets, 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


611 


u  Who  comes  there?’'  they  answered  “Captain  Daniels  and  his  men.” 
Mr.  Jenks  then  ordered  them  to  halt  and  advance  one  at  a  time  and 
give  the  countersign.  On  giving  this  order  he  was  answered  by  the 
discharge  of .  about  40  muskets  and  rifles  into  his  camp.  He  then 
returned  their  fire  with  spirit  and  fell  back  to  the  boats,  when  the 
.  Rosalie  opened  fire  and  routed  the  rebels.  Mr.  Jenks  then  manned 
his  boats  and  went  alongside  the  Rosalie.  At  10  o’clock  a.  m. ,  Captain 
Daniels  and  his  men  not  having  made  their  appearance,  and  being 
short. of  provisions  and  having  one  man  wounded,  Mr.  Jenks  returned 
to  this  ship  with  his  boats,  accompanied  by  the  Rosalie ,  where  they 
all  arrived  the  following  morning,  31st  ultimo. 

I  immediately  provisioned  the  two  boats  and  Rosalie  and  sent  them 
back  to  the  mouth  of  the  Myacca  River,  with  orders  to  remain  there 
six  days,  unless  Captain  Daniels  and  his  men  made  their  appearance 
sooner. 

The  Rosalie  and  boats  returned  to  the  ship  the  following  morning, 
1st  instant,  with  Captain  Daniels  and  five  of  his  men,  six  having 
deserted  him  the  third  night  after  landing,  and  the  remaining  four  he 
had  left  up  the  country,  not  knowing  where  they  were. 

I  can  not  close  this  report  without  calling  your  attention  to  the  admi¬ 
rable  behavior  and  bravery  of  Acting  Ensign  J.  H.  Jenks  and  the  men 
under  him  on  this  occasion.  The  coolness  and  bravery  of  Mr.  Jenks 
and  the  gallant  men  under  him  have  elicited  my  warmest  encomiums, 
and  as  an  evidence  of  their  efficiency  1  beg  leave  to  state  that  they 
saved  their  four  boats  and  camp  equipage  and  brought  them  off  safe, 
losing  but  one  rifle. 

1  enclose  herewith  Acting  Ensign  J.  H.  Jenks’  and  Acting  Master 
Peter  F.  Coffin’s  detailed  reports  of  the  above  affair. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Baxter,

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Jenks,  U  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

U.  S.  Bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 

Charlotte  Harbor ,  December  31 , 1863. 

Sir:  Agreeable  to  your  orders,  I  left  this  ship  on  the  24th  instant  at 
1  o’clock  p.  m.  with  launch  and  second  cutter,  armed  and  manned  with 
14  men  and  provisioned  for  eight  days,  and  proceeded  to  Useppa 
Island,  where  I  took  on  board  Captain  E.  Daniels  and  15  of  the  refugee 
rangers,  and  proceeded  for  a  point  designated  by  Captain  Daniels  on  the 
mainland,  6  miles  from  the  mouth,  on  the  Myacca  River,  where  we 
arrived  on  the  25th  instant,  5:30  p.  m.  Landed  with  Captain  Daniels 
and  5  of  his  men,  under  cover  of  the  boats,  and  reconnoitered  the  ground 
for  half  a  mile  around  there.  Disembarked  the  men,  stationed  pickets, 
formed  camp,  and  threw  up  breastwork  to  cover  my  boats  in  case  of 
an  attack.  Having  made  arrangements  with  Captain  Daniels  how  he 
should  approach  us  on  his  return,  he  left  with  his  men  for  up  the  coun¬ 
try.  6  p.  m.,  saw  a  large  fire,  apparently  on  Peace  Creek,  east  side. 
6:15  p.  m.,  another  fire  on  west  side,  apparently  in  answer.  26th 


612 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADKON. 


instant,  reconnoitered  the  ground  for  several  miles  and  planted  stakes 
along  the  shore  in  3  feet  of  water.  27th  instant,  7:30  p.  m. ,  the  enemy’s 
scouts  reconnoitered  our  position  and  fired  a  shot.  Doubled  pickets 
and  kept  the  men  under  arms  till  daylight.  28th  instant,  4  o’clock 
p.  m. ,  sloop  Rosalie  arrived  and  took  up  a  covering  position  about  80 
yards  distant.  About  6  p.  m.  saw  two  fires  3  or  4  miles  distant.  8  o’clock 
p.  m.,  enemy’s  scouts  attempted  to  surprise  our  pickets;  fired  on  them, 
but  they  escaped;  men  remained  under  arms  the  remainder  of  the  night. 
About  midnight  discovered  a  person  with  a  torch  in  his  hand,  about 
three-fourths  of  a  mile  distant;  he  waved  it  over  his  head  some  time, 
then  extinguished  it.  29th  instant,  first  part  of  the  day  discharged  all 
small  arms,  cleaned  and  reloaded  them,  went  out  and  examined  the  ground 
for  some  distance  and  found  the  trail  of  men  and  horses  in  different 
directions.  About  noon  took  the  launch  and,  with  the  pilot  of  the 
Rosalie ,  started  up  the  river  on  a  reconnoissance;  found  a  good  posi¬ 
tion  for  a  camp  about  l£  miles  above,  where  the  Rosalie  could  cover 
our  boats  without  danger  to  them;  moved  camp  to  it,  as  the  Rosalie 
could  not  assist  me  where  I  then  was.  The  Rosalie  took  a  shelling 
position  about  200  yards  distant  from  the  shore.  About  8  o’clock  p.  m. 
heard  noise  about  old  camp  ground.  Short  time  after  saw  a  large  fire 
there;  thinking  it  might  be  Captain  Daniels  and  his  men  returned, 
started  a  fire  in  answer  and  sent  a  boat  with  2  men  to  ascertain,  and  if  so, 
to  tell  them  how  to  approach  us;  but  being  unable  to  ascertain,  they 
returned.  Every  precaution  was  taken  to  avoid  a  surprise ;  then  endeav¬ 
ored  to  ascertain  who  they  were,  their  number  and  object.  Heard 
distant  voices  and  the  sound  of  dogs,  apparently  on  the  trail  for  some 
time.  30th  instant,  about  4  o’clock  a.  m. ,  discovered  persons  advancing 
through  the  tall  grass  a  short  distance  from  my  pickets.  Challenged 
them  twice,  but  received  no  answer;  challenged  again,  and  received 
answer  that  it  was  Captain  Daniels  with  his  men;  ordered  them  to  halt, 
then  to  advance  one  at  a  time  and  give  the  countersign,  intending  to 
disarm  them  as  they  came  in  so  as  to  avoid  treachery.  This  order 
being  given,  they  arose  and  opened  fire  within  15  yards  of  the  picket 
line,  in  a  half  circle,  the  heaviest  firing  on  the  right,  where  they  tried 
to  cut  us  off  from  our  boats.  Pickets  returned  the  fire,  fell  back,  and 
kept  up  a  brisk  fire  for  about  five  minutes.  Being  heavily  pressed 
by  superior  numbers,  fell  back  to  the  beach.  Gave  the  signal  for  the 
Rosalie  to  open  fire.  Kept  up  the  fire  for  about  five  minutes,  and  find¬ 
ing  it  impossible  to  resist  their  superior  numbers,  ordered  the  boats 
to  be  manned,  which  was  done  in  good  order,  still  keeping  up  a  fire  on 
them.  In  the  act  of  shoving  off,  John  Brown  (seaman)  was  wounded  in 
the  leg.  The  enemy  was  within  15  yards  of  the  boats  at  the  time. 
Went  alongside  of  the  Rosalie  with  my  boats,  and  had  it  not  been  for 
her  our  loss  would  have  been  very  heavy;  her  shells  burst  over  and 
among  them,  driving  them  back  from  the  beach.  Kept  up  a  brisk  fire 
on  them  until  they  were  out  of  range.  At  daylight  went  on  shore 
with  boats  and  took  off  all  camp  equipage  left  there.  Captain  Daniels 
not  having  arrived  according  to  agreement,  and  believing  that  he  had 
been  captured,  I  started  for  the  ship  with  the  boats,  in  company  with 
the  j Rosalie,  but  the  wind  dying  away  I  left  the  Rosalie ,  and  with  the 
launch  and  wounded  arrived  on  board  the  ship  at  8  o’clock  p.  m.  Saw 
several  rebels  on  different  points  of  the  mainland  on  our  way  down, 
who  saluted  us  with  yells.  I  should  judge  by  the  line  of  fire  that  the 
enemy  numbered  30  or  40  men,  armed  with  Colt’s  revolving  rifles,  shot¬ 
guns,  etc.  1  should  judge  their  loss  in  killed  and  wounded  at  least  6 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


613 


or  8;  a  number  were  seen  to  fall  by  my  men  on  shore;  I  saw  2  fall 
myself;  several  of  the  men  were  struck  in  different  parts  of  their  cloth¬ 
ing  and  received  slight  scratches  from  shot.  My  boats  and  equipments 
were  struck  in  many  places.  The  men  behaved  with  the  utmost  cool¬ 
ness  and  precision  during  the  entire  affair,  courting  the  enemy’s  fire,

holland  (boatswain’s  mate)  were  conspicuous  for  daring,  rendering  great 
assistance  in  scouting,  even  inside  the  enemy’s  lines.

J.  H.  Jenks,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Coffin,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  tender  Rosalie,  sent  to  the  relief 

of  Acting  Ensign  Jenks. 

U.  S.  Sloop  Rosalie, 
Charlotte  Harbor ,  Dece'mber  31 ,  1863. 

Sir:  Agreeable  to  your  orders  I  left  the  bark  at  Charlotte  Harbor, 
on  the  28th  instant,  to  go  up  the  Myacca  River  in  search  of  your  boats, 
and  upon  finding  them  to  operate  with  them. 

At  4  o’clock  p.  m.  I  arrived  in  the  Myacca  River  and  found  the  launch 
and  second  cutter,  Acting  Ensign  J.  H.  Jenks  in  command,  and  refu¬ 
gees’  boats  at  an  encampment  about  one-fourth  of  a  mile  from  the 
mouth.  I  anchored  about  80  yards  off  the  breastwork,  which  had 
been  thrown  up.  At  8  o’clock  p.  m.  the  camp  was  alarmed  by  rebel 
scouts,  but  as  nothing  could  be  seen  of  them  all  quieted  away  again. 
At  9:30  p.  m.  we  were  aroused  again  by  the  camp  being  alarmed,  but 
nothing  was  seen  of  those  prowling  about  in  the  vicinity  of  the  camp. 
About  the  same  time  a  light  was  seen  about  3  miles  off,  which  appeared 
like  a  torch.  During  the  remainder  of  the  night  all  remained  quiet. 
On  the  29th  instant  Mr.  Jenks  and  my  pilot  went  up  the  river  to 
reconnoiter  and  returned  at  2:30  p.  m.,  and  having  found  a  more 
skeltered  position  for  a  camp  we  agreed  to  move  up  to  it.  It  was 
about  li  miles  from  the  first  camp  ground,  on  a  point  of  land  about 
50  yards  wide,  and  extended  so  far  out  in  the  river  that  it  afforded  me 
a  chance  to  put  the  sloop  in  a  position  to  rake  across  in  front  of  the 
camp  and  cover  them,  should  they  be  attacked  and  have  to  fall  back 
to  the  boats.  At  4  o’clock  all  things  had  been  removed  to  the  new 
camp,  and  the  sloop  was  anchored  about  200  yards  off  the  shore  in 
position  for  shelling.  During  the  early  part  of  the  evening  noises 
were  heard  in  the  neighboring  palmettoes,  as  if  some  one  stealing 
through  toward  the  camp.  The  pickets  were  doubled  and  the  greatest 
vigilance  was  kept,  the  men  under  arms  all  the  time.  At  8:15  a.  m.  a 
large  fire  was  seen  at  the  deserted  camp  ground,  and,  supposing  it  to 
be  friends  returning  from  the  scouting  expedition, _  a  fire  was  imme¬ 
diately  kindled  in  our  new  camp  to  acquaint  them  of  our  position,  but 
instantly  the  fire  was  extinguished  and_  suspecting  something  wrong 
our  camp  fire  was  put  out  and  all  stood  in  readiness  for  action.  Dur¬ 
ing  the  afternoon  the  sloop  Matilda ,  with  refugees  Brannen,  Thomp¬ 
son,  and  Arnold,  came  alongside  and  supplied  us  with  beef  and  venison, 
and  stating  that  they  had  permission  to  hunt  in  the  vicinity  I  allowed 


614 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  • 


them  to  cross  the  river  and  land  on  the  opposite  side.  Through  the 
night  we  repeatedly  heard  the  noise  of  persons  crawling  through  the 
bushes,  but  could  not  find  their  exact  position.  At  4:45  a.  m.  the 
pickets  heard  noises  near  them  and,  though  they  could  see  nothing, 
they  challenged  them  twice,  but  received  no  answer.  I  then  heard 
Mr.  Jenks  challenge  them,  and  he  received  an  answer  that  it  was 
Captain  Daniels  and  his  men.  Mr.  Jenks  then  said,  UA11  right,’1  and 
ordered  them  to  halt  and  one  at  a  time  to  advance  and  give  the  coun¬ 
tersign.  He  had  hardly  spoken  when  he  was  saluted  with  a  volley 
from  an  extended  line  of  rebels  across  our  whole  front  line  of  pickets. 
The  fire  was  returned  briskly,  and  then  they  were  ordered  to  fall  back 
on  the  camp.  On  reaching  the  camp  a  smart  fire  was  kept  up  for  a 
minute  and  a  half,  and  then  our  men  closed  up  and  I  opened  fire  from 
the  howitzer  with  shrapnel  and  canister.  The  rebels  fell  back  and 
the  boats’  crews  embarked  and  came  alongside,  having  one  man  (John 
Brown,  seaman)  wounded  in  the  leg.  I  continued  shelling  the  bushes 
and  using  small  arms  for  about  twenty  minutes,  and  then,  until  day¬ 
light,  I  occasionally  sent  a  shell  in.  At  dajdight  the  boats  went 
ashore,  collected  all  the  camp  equipments  and  returned  to  the  sloop, 
and  then  I  weighed  anchor  and  stood  down  the  river  to  the  mouth, 
where  1  anchored  and  got  breakfast.  It  was  then  10  o’clock  in  the 
forenoon,  and  at  11  o’clock  I  weighed  anchor  and  started  for  the  bark, 
to  have  the  wounded  attended  to.  At  3  o’clock  it  died  away  calm  and 
I  was  obliged  to  anchor,  and  Mr.  Jenks  took  the  launch  and,  with  the 
wounded,  started  for  the  bark.  About  4  o'clock  p.  m.,  light  breeze 
springing  up,  weighed  anchor  and  stood  on,  and  9:30  p.  m.  anchored 
near  Pine  Key  [Island]  for  the  night.  December  31  at  daylight 
weighed  anchor  and  stood  for  the  bark,  and  came  to  at  7:30  a.  m.  near 
by.  Please  allow  me  the  pleasure  of  bringing  to  your  notice  the  con¬ 
duct  of  Mr.  Jenks,  who,  though  deprived  of  sleep  for  two  days,  ever 
kept  the  strictest  vigilance  about  the  camp,  and  in  the  engagement 
with  the  rebels  was  foremost  in  the  ranks,  encouraging  his  men  to 
action,  and,  when  compelled  to  leave  the  camp,  was  the  last  man  to 
leave  the  shore.  Also,  the  men  under  his  command  can  not  be  sur¬ 
passed  in  bravery,  for,  though  heavily  pressed  by  superior  numbers, 
they  stood  their  ground  and  fought  desperately  until  ordered  to  fall 
back. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peter  F.  Coffin, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  Tender  Rosalie. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  I.  B.  Baxter,  U.  S.  Navy,

U.  S.  S.  Sunflower, 

Tampa  Bay,  December  26,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture,  by  the  above  steamer 
under  my  command,  of  the  Confederate  sloop  Hancock,  from  Havana, 
bound  into  Crystal  River  with  salt,  borax,  etc. 

I  took  her  on  the  24th  instant,  just  out  of  sight  of  Egmont  (Tampa 
Bay)  light-house.  Previous  to  boarding  him  he  had  thrown  his  chart 
and  rebel  flag  overboard,  but  [I]  found  in  the  captain’s  valise  his  con¬ 
tract  with  the  owner  for  the  performance  of  the  voyage  from  Crystal 
River  to  Havana  and  back  to  a  Confederate  port. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edw.  Van  Sice, 

'  Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


U.  S.  S.  Sunflower, 

Tantpa  Bay,  December  26,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  24th  instant,  while  lying  at  anchor  under  Egmont  [Key] 
in  company  with  the  Tahoma,  made  a  sail  in  the  offing;  got  underway, 
in  obedience  to  signal,  and  ran  out.  She  proved  to  be  the  schooner  Sea 
Bird,  coming  in.  Made  another  sail  off  to  the  westward,  gave  chase,  and 
snortly  overhauled  her,  just  out  of  sight  of  the  light-house.  She 
proved  to  be  the  sloop  Hancock,  from  Havana,  bound  into  Crystal 
River  or  any  Confederate  port.  Her  cargo  consists  of  some  20  sacks 
salt  and  3  barrels  of  borax,  some  little  rum,  etc.  Previous  to  my  board¬ 
ing  him  he  had  thrown  his  chart  and  rebel  flag  overboard,  as  he  after¬ 
wards  acknowledged.  On  searching’  the  captain’s  valise  I  found  his 
contract  with  the  owner  to  perform  the  voyage  from  Crystal  River  to 
Havana  and  back  to  a  Confederate  port.  She  carried  to  Havana  3,100 
pounds  sea-island  cotton.  There  are  three  persons  on  board,  namely, 
Fredk.  White,  captain;  Bartholomew  Blanco,  seaman,  and  Edward 
Walker,  passenger.  You  wished  me  to  capture  one  of  the  pilots  in 
this  neighborhood.  I  think  you  will  find  a  pretty  good  one  in  the 
person  of  this  Fredk.  White,  the  captain  of  the  sloop. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  Van  Sice, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla.

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  December  28,  1863. 

Sir:  It  is  believed  that  the  steamers  Mary  Ann,  Powerful,  Laura, 
and  Little  Lily  are  engaged  in  running  the  blockade  between  Havana 
and  the  Suwanee  River.  Others  may  also  be  similarly  emplo}^ed. 

So  soon,  therefore,  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  is  ready  for 
sea  you  will  proceed  to  cruise  in  her,  with  a  view  to  breaking-  up  this 
traffic. 

The  general  limits  of  your  cruising  ground  may  be  stated  as  between 
the  meridians  of  83°  and  85°  west  longitude,  on  the  parallel  of  28° 
north  latitude;  but  these  limits  are  not  to  be  considered  as  altogther 
ngid,  and  you  will  exercise  a  sound  discretion  in  either  increasing 
or  decreasing  your  distance  from  the  mouth  of  the  Suwanee  River  as 
circumstances  may  render  advisable. 

The  tenders  Fox  and  Annie  are  specially  charged  with  watching  the 
mouth  of  the  river,  well  inshore. 

Respectfully, 

.  ,  n  .  7  .  ,  ^  Theodorus  Bailey,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Willcomh ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 

Stars  and  Stripes ,  regarding  the  destruction  of  the  Confederate 

schoone)'  Caroline  Gertrude ,  with  cargo  of  cotton ,  off  Ocklockonee 

River. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

St.  Marks  [ Apalachee\  Bay ,  December  30 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  night  of  the  28th  instant, 
at5p.  m.,  we  discovered  a  vessel  inside  of  the  bar  at  the  mouth  of 
the  Ocklockonee  River.  I  immediately  got  underway  and  steamed 
for  her. 

At  6 : 30  p.  m.  came  to  and  dispatched  the  first  and  second  cutter 
(one  up  the  north  and  other  the  south  channel),  under  command  of 
Acting  Master  Thomas  Smith,  accompanied  by  Acting  Ensign  C. 
Carven,  Acting  Master’s  Mates  Henry  B.  Conklin  and  ChaiTes  P. 
Turner,  the  pilot,  and  Acting  Assistant  Paymaster  J.  J.  Pratt  and 
Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineer  William  Hopkins  as  volunteers, 
with  20  armed  men,  with  orders  to  capture  and  bring  the  vessel  out. 

At  2 : 30  a.  m. ,  the  29th  instant,  Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineer 
William  Hopkins  came  alongside  with  13  prisoners  from  the  prize, 
which  he  reported  to  be  the  Confederate  schooner  Caroline  Gertmide , 
with  a  cargo  of  69  bales  of  cotton,  bound  to  Havana,  Cuba,  and  that 
she  was  aground  about  100  yards  from  the  beach  on  an  oyster  bank, 
and  also  stated  that  Mr.  Smith  thought  that  she  would  float  off  at 
high  water. 

At  8  a.  m.,  finding  that  the  vessel  was  not  afloat,  I  dispatched 
orders  and  lines  to  Mr.  Smith  to  raft  the  deck  load  of  cotton  and 
prepare  a  breastwork  of  the  same  material  for  shelter  to  his  men  in 
case  of  an  attack  by  the  enemy  and  to  send  all  papers  and  colors  found 
on  board  this  vessel.  ■ 

At  1  p.  m.  Mr.  Smith  sent  me  word  that  he  had  rafted  45  bales  of 


618 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


cotton  to  the  mouth  of  the  river  and  prepared  a  breastwork  of  cot¬ 
ton.  About  this  time  the  enemy’s  cavalry  made  their  appearance  in 
large  numbers  and  began  a  brisk  fire,  which  was  returned  by  our  men 
from  behind  the  cotton,  the  enemy  being  behind  trees  and  stumps, 
etc.  The  fire  was  kept  up  so  lively  that  our  men  could  not  show  their 
heads  without  being  a  target  for  at  least  50  rifles.  After  a  sharp 
engagement  of  two  hours  with  them,  and  finding  we  could  not  save 
the  vessel  (an  old  affair)  or  any  more  of  the  cotton,  at  3:30  set  fire  to 
her  and  she  was  totally  destroyed,  with  balance  of  her  cargo. 

At  8  p.  m.  the  boats  returned  to  this  vessel  with  43  bales  of  cotton 
(2  being  lost),  which  I  now  have  on  board  and  shall  send  to  Key  West 
by  first  opportunity,  with  all  the  papers  found  on  board  and  the  pris¬ 
oners,  14  in  all.  No  colors  were  found  on  board  and  no  other  vessel 
was  in  sight  at  the  time  of  capture. 

In  conclusion,  I  would  add  that  the  officers  and  men  on  the  expedi¬ 
tion  acted  with  gallantry  and  coolness  and  my  orders  were  promptly 
obeyed  and  executed  by  the  officers  in  command  of  the  boats. 

1  have  no  casualties  to  report. 

The  officer  in  command  of  the  rebels  was  killed  in  the  engagement, 
and  one  of  the  passengers  was  slightly  wounded  while  attempting  to 
escape. 

Had  I  waited  to  save  the  schooner,  even  if  it  could  have  been  done, 
I  should  have  lost  all  the  cotton  outside,  as  the  weather  began  to  be 
very  bad  by  the  time  the  boat  reached  the  ship,  and  it  blew  a  gale  all 
night. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  L.  Willcomb, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Randall ,  U.  S.  Wavy ,  trans¬ 
mitting  report  regarding  the  destruction  of  the  Austin  salt  works , 
St.  Joseph's  Bay. 

U .  S.  Bark  Pursuit, 

St.  Joseph's  Bay ,  December  31 ,  1863. 
Sir:  Soon  after  my  arrival  at  this  place  I  became  convinced  that 
there  were  two  salt  works  in  active  operation  at  the  head  of  the  bay, 
about  14  miles  distant  from  our  anchorage.  1  availed  myself  of  the 
first  opportunity  to  reconnoiter  them  and  visited  one  of  them  in  person. 
It  was  the  smaller  one  of  the  two,  and  of  minor  importance,  as  the  imple¬ 
ments  employed  were  six  kettles  of  about  150  gallons  each.  They  were 
broken  and  can  never  be  made  of  much  use.  Not  having  time  to  visit 
the  Austin  works,  the  more  important  of  the  two,  I  returned  on  board 
and  subsequently  sent  an  expedition  under  command  of  Acting  Ensign 
Norman  McLeod,  who  entirely  destroyed  them.  1  have  the  honor  to 
forward  to  you  his  report  of  the  expedition. 

With  much  respect,  sir,  1  have  the  honor  to  remain, 

Your  obedient  servant, 


Wm.  P.  Randall, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 


Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey,  . 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla.

U.  S.  Bark  Pursuit, 

St.  Joseph's  Bay ,  Fla.,  December  31,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders,  I  left  this  vessel  on  the  30th  in¬ 
stant  for  the  purpose  of  destroying  the  Austin  salt  works,  situated  at 
the  head  of  St.  Joseph’s  Bay.  The  expedition  consisted  of  2  armed 
boats  and  22  men,  one  of  the  boats  being  under  the  charge  of  Acting 
Master’s  Mate  Henry  W.  Richdale.  We  left  the  ship  at  9:30  a.  m. 
and  arrived  opposite  the  salt  works  at  1  p.  m.,  but  owing  to  the 
extensive  flats  that  make  out  in  that  vicinity  it  was  impossible  to  get 
the  boats  within  three-fourths  of  a  mile  of  the  shore.  Leaving  a  suf¬ 
ficient  guard  with  the  boats,  we  proceeded  to  the  works,  which  we 
found  to  consist  of  three  boilers  from  10  to  15  feet  in  length,  set  in 
brick.  At  about  20  yards  from  the  boilers  was  an  artificial  pond  or 
vat  about  40  feet  in  diameter  from  which  water  was  forced  to  the 
boilers  through  5  couplings  of  2-inch  pipe.  Owing  to  the  weight  of 
the  boilers,  it  was  impossible  to  remove  them,  but  they  were  rendered 
entirely  useless  by  having  holes  broken  in  them  by  the  sledges  which 
we  took  for  that  purpose.  The  masonry  work  was  also  demolished 
and  the  pipes  rendered  useless  by  twisting  them  around  trees.  Con¬ 
nected  with  the  establishment  was  a  small  house  and  several  cords  of 
wood,  which  we  destroyed  by  fire.  We  met  with  no  opposition,  and 
it  is  evident  that  the  place  was  evacuated  on  our  approach.  We 
arrived  at  the  ship  at  8  p.  m. 

I  have  the  honor  to  remain,  sir,  very  respectfully, 

Your  obedient  servant, 


N.  McLeod, 
Acting  Ensign. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  William  P.  Randall, 

TJ.  S.  Bark  Pursuit.

Order  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  V.  S.  Navy,  to  Acting  Volun¬ 
teer  Lieutenant  Harris ,  U.  S.  Nary,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Hon¬ 
duras ,  for  the  transportation  of  troops  to  Caloosahatchee  River. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Hey  West,  January  J,  186 f 

Sir:  The  vessel  under  your  command  is  hereby  detailed  to  assist  in 
conveying  a  detachment  of  the  Forty-seventh  Regiment  Pennsylvania 
Volunteers  to  the  Caloosahatchee  River,  under  the  orders  of  Briga¬ 
dier-General  D.  P.  Woodbury,  U.  S.  Army,  commanding  district  of 
Key  West  and  Tortugas. 

You  will  therefore  receive  on  board  such  persons,  stores,  etc.,  as  he 
may  direct  and  accompany  the  army  schooner  Hatchless  (or  tow  her 
if  necessary)  to  her  destination. 

General  Woodbury  will  himself  take  passage  in  your  vessel,  and  you 
will  obey  such  directions  as  he  may  give  in  carrying  out  the  objects  of 
this  expedition,  returning*  to  this  place  when  he  shall  have  discharged 
your  vessel  from  further  attendance. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 
Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Thos.  R.  Harris,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Steamer  Honduras. 


Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  McCauley,  U.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  TJ.  S.  S.  Tioga ,  regarding  the  capture  of  a  schooner  off  Great 
Bahama  Lsland. 

U.  S.  S.  Tioga, 

Off  Great  Bahama  Lsland ,  January  J,  186 f 
Admiral:  This  morning  at  10  o’clock,  whilst  laying  off  S.  W.  point 
of  Great.  Bahama  Island,  a  schooner  was  reported  in  sight  and  shortly 
afterwards  was  distinctly  seen  coming  down  before  the  wind,  heading 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


621 


about  N.  W.  As  soon  as  we  started  in  chase  she  hauled  by  the  wind, 
heading  toward  S.  E.  point.  On  coming  within  range  a  blank  car¬ 
tridge  was  fired  to  bring  her  to.  Mr.  Brisco  boarded  and  reported  her 
as  having  on  board  a  cargo  of  salt,  liquors,  coffee,  arms,  shoes,  and 
cigars,  bound  from  Nassau  to  Havana.  I  have  seized  her  on  the 
grounds  that  she  was  out  of  the  route  for  vessels  bound  to  the  south¬ 
ward  from  New  Providence,  that  her  cargo  is  manifestly  contraband 
of  war  and  of  export  in  Havana,  not  import,  that  she  hauled  her 
wind  when  chased,  evidently  with  the  intention  of  getting  within  the 
limits  of  foreign  jurisdiction  to  evade  capture,  and  also  that  informa¬ 
tion  received  by  me  points  to  her  as  one  of  five  schooners  which  have 
been  preparing  to  run  the  blockade  from  Nassau.  The  master’s  asser¬ 
tions  about  having  been  obliged  to  stand  off  to  northward  in  conse¬ 
quence  of  calms,  etc. ,  which  he  made  to  me,  are  untrue,  as  during  the 
past  night  the  Tioga  was  hove  to  off  the  Isaacs,  when  it  blew  a  mod¬ 
erate  breeze.  The  Tioga  and  her  prize  were  over  5  miles  from  the 
nearest  land  at  the  time  of  the  capture  by  bearings  and  estimated  gun 
range,  and  was  about  85  miles  to  the  northward  of  the  port  of  clear¬ 
ance,  standing  directly  for  the  blockaded  coast  about  Indian  River. 

The  captain  when  first  boarded  pretended  that  he  could  not  speak 
English,  but  he  has  since  been  able  to  express  his  views  fluently. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley, 

Lieutenant- Commander,  JJ.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  U.  S.  S.  Tioga. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West,  Fla. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding 
cooperation  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Honduras  with  army  expedition  to 
Caloosahatchee  River. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  January  6,  1861+. 

Sir:  Referring  to  my  letter,  No.  385,  of  December  IT,  1  have  to 
report  that  (Brigadier- General  Woodbury  having  completed  his 
arrangements  for  going  up  the  coast,  with  a  view  to  preventing  any 
further  supply  of  cattle  to  the  rebel  army  from  southern  Florida)  the 
steamer  Honduras  was,  at  his  request,  placed  at  his  disposal  to  convoy 
and  assist  the  expedition.  General  Woodbury  went  in  the  Honduras 
to  direct  the  operations  in  person.  One  company  of  the  Forty -seventh 
Regiment  Pennsylvania  Volunteers  accompanied  him  in  the  quarter¬ 
master’s  schooner  Matchless ,  and  more  than  30  of  the  refugee  rangers  had 
already  preceded  him  to  Charlotte  Harbor,  where  large  numbers  of 
recruits  were  confidently  expected  to  join  them  from  the  mainland. 

The  general  left  yesterday  and  will  establish  his  force  at  Fort  Myers, 
about  12  miles  from  the  mouth  of  the  Chattahoochee  [Caloosahatchee] 
River,  for  the  present.  Should  his  expectations  of  the  reinforcements 
likely  to  join  him  from  the  surrounding  country  prove  correct,  he 
will  be  able  to  push  his  operations  on  to  Tampa  and  to  occupy  that 
place. 

In  the  meantime  the  Honduras  and  other  vessels. on  the  blockade 
have  orders  to  assist  and  cooperate  with  this  expedition  to  the  extent 


622 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


of  their  ability,  and  I  am  prepared  to  render  such  further  assistance 
as  may  be  needed. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Chandler,  JJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 

JJ.  S.  S.  San  Jacinta ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Roebuck. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

At  Sea ,  January  7,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Roebuck , 
taken  by  this  vessel  at  8: 15  a.  m.  this  day,  after  a  chase  of  two  hours. 
She  cleared  from  Havana  on  Monday,  the  4th  instant,  and  was  bound 
to  Mobile.  I  have  taken  the  captain  and  two  men  on  board  this  ship, 
as  the  accommodations  are  so  small  on  board  the  schooner,  leaving  two 
of  her  crew  to  testify  before  the  courts  She  is  a  new  vessel  and  a  fast 
sailer  and  would  make  a  good  tender.  Her  captain  tells  me  that  he 
paid  $8,000  in  gold  for  her  cargo  in  Havana,  and  the  vessel  he  was 
offered  $5,000  for.  Her  cargo  is  assorted,  and  among  other  things 
she  has  clothing  and  lead.  I  send  Acting  Ensign  Charles  Cunningham, 
with  two  petty  officers  and  four  men  in  charge  of  the  prize.  Her 
nautical  instruments  are  the  best  I  have  seen  in  some  time,  and  the 
chronometer  and  sextant  would  be  useful  to  the  Government. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  Chandler, 

Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Letter  from  Acting  Ensign  Russell ,  JJ.  S.  Navy ,  of  the  JJ.  S.  lark 

Restless ,  to  Acting  Ensign  Crissey,  JJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  JJ.  S.  S. 

Bloomer ,  requesting  his  assistance. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew’s  Bay ,  Fla. ,  January  9 ,  186 J. 

Sir:  Captain  Browne  has  requested  me  to  communicate  to  you  and 
give  you  a  brief  epitome  of  what  has  transpired  here  since  you  left, 
and  also  to  request  your  services  once  more  in  this  quarter. 

Nineteen  refugees  and  a  large  number  of  contrabands  have  come  off 
to  us  lately.  They  are  mostly  all  from  Georgia  and  Alabama.  From 
them  we  learn  that  Robinson’s  company  remain  at  their  same  station, 
and  that  there  is  a  strong  Union  sentiment  manifested  by  a  large 
majority  of  them,  also  by  numbers  of  inhabitants  of  this  section,  and 
that  it  only  required  a  demonstration  from  our  side  to  make  them  all 
enroll  themselves  under  the  standard  of  the  Union. 

The  schooner  also  remains  in  Bear  Creek — loaded  or  not,  we  do  not 
know. 

Some  of  the  salt  works  in  both  bays  have  resumed  operations  and 
need  a  visit  from  us. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


623 


There  is  also  a  small  steamer  in  the  Chipola  River,  which  we  might 
possibly  capture.  She  is  used  to  convey  salt  from  a  large  salt  ware¬ 
house  at  the  head  of  East  Bay,  through  a  cut-off  into  the  Chattahoochee 
River,  and  thence  to  the  interior.  Everything  will  be  in  operation  by 
the  time  you  come  here. 

*  *  *  *  *  *  * 

In  conclusion,  Captain  Browne  would  like  to  know  by  the  earliest 
opportunity  if,  and  when,  you  will  come.  He  also  transmits  his  best 
wishes  to  yourself  and  Captain  Dustin  and  wishes  to  see  you  here  soon. 
*****  *  * 

Truly,  yours, 

.  James  J.  Russell. 

Acting  Ensign  Crissey, 

TJ.  S.  A.  Bloomer ,  East  Pass,  Fla. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Sherrill,  U  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  bark 

Roebuck ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner  Susan,  off 

Jupiter  Inlet,  January  11,  186 J. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

Off  Indian  River  Inlet,  January  12,  1861 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  of  the  capture,  on 
the  11th  instant,  of  the  English  schooner  Susan,  about  6  tons,  J.  F. 
Pinder,  master,  and  crew  of  3  men,  laden  with  43  bags  salt  and  sundry 
boxes  dry  goods,  by  the  boats  of  this  vessel,  within  500  yards  of 
Jupiter  Inlet,  in  the  attempt  to  run  in  there. 

A  clearance  from  Abaco,  $265  in  Confederate  notes,  and  English 
colors  were  found  on  board;  had  no  colors  set  at  time  of  capture. 

The  captain  says  he  was  bound  to  Sand  Point. 

At  the  time  this  vessel  was  captured  an  army  tug  was  near  and 
stood  offshore  3  miles,  capturing  another  schooner,  also  bound  in. 

The  cargo  I  shall  send  to  Key  West  for  adjudication,  retaining  the 
vessel  to  be  used  as  a  guard  boat  in  the  sound. 

I  enclose  herewith  a  list  of  the  officers  and  crew  of  this  vessel  entitled 
to  share  in  the  above  capture. 

I  remain,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Sherrill, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Sears ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 
Honeysuckle,  claiming  a  share  in  the  prize  schooner  Susan,  captured 
by  TJ.  S.  bark  Roebuck  January  11,  186 J. 

II.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  January  23,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  beg  to  state  that  this  vessel  was  in  pursuit  and  within  hailing 
distance  of  the  English  schooner  Susan,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence, 
when  she  was  captured  by  a  boat  from  the  U.  S.  bark  Roebuck,  on 
the  11th  day  of  January,  1864,  Jupiter  Inlet  light-house  bearing  west, 


624 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


1  mile  distant.  Since  arriving  here  I  have  learned  that  the  com¬ 
mander  of  the  Roebuck  reported  this  vessel  as  an  army  steam  tug 
passing  at  the  time;  but  this  is  a  mistake.  I  discovered  the  Susan 
at  or  about  11  a.  m.  of  the  said  morning,  and  immediately  changed 
our  course  to  cut  her  off  from  the  land.  About  ten  minutes  before  we 
reached  the  Susan  I  saw  the  Roebuck?  s  boat  coming  out  from  Jupiter 
Inlet.  The  boat  reached  the  Susan  before  it  could  be  done  by  us. 
Therefore  I  do,  in  behalf  of  the  officers  and  crew  of  this  vessel,  claim 
a  share  in  the  said  schooner  Susan. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Cyrus  Sears, 

Acting  Ensign ,  Commanding.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Sherrill ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  an  expedi¬ 
tion  to  Jupiter  Inlet  and  the  capture  of  the  Confederate  sloop  Maria 
Louise  and  British  schooner  Susan. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

Off  Indian  River  Inlet ,  January  12 ,  1861. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  learning  from  refugees  small 
vessels  frequently  ran  into  Jupiter  Inlet  from  the  Bahamas  I  deemed 
it  my  duty  to  attempt  the  capture  of  them,  and  accordingly,  on  the 
8th  instant,  fitted  out  two  armed  boats,  under  the  command  of  Acting 
Ensign  G.  M.  Pulsipher  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  W.  H.  Bradford, 
and  sent  them  into  the  sound  with  orders  to  proceed  to  Jupiter  Inlet 
and  capture  all  vessels  attempting  to  run  in  or  out. 

The  boats  returned  last  evening,  bringing  with  them  the  Confeder¬ 
ate  sloop  Maria  Louise  (8  tons  register  and  owned  at  Savannah),  John 
Makin,  master,  a  crew  of  2  men,  and  3  passengers,  laden  with  about 
3,000  pounds  sea-island  cotton,  captured  on  the  10th  instant  2  miles 
from  Jupiter  Inlet  while  trying  to  run  out.  She  had  a  Confederate 
register,  but  no  colors.  On  the  persons  of  the  captain  and  passengers 
were  found  $725.95  in  gold  and  silver,  3  gold  watches,  and  $240  in 
Confederate  notes,  which  were  taken  possession  of.  This  man  Makin 
ran  out  of  Savannah  in  October  last.  The  passenger  Shackleford, 
on  whom  $480  in  gold  was  found,  appears  from  papers  taken  to  have 
acted  as  agent  for  the  shippers. 

,  The  boats  also  brought  the  English  schooner  Susan ,  of  Nassau  (about 
6  tons),  J.  H.  Binder,  master,  and  crew  of  3  men,  laden  with  43  bags 
salt  and  sundry  boxes,  as  dry  goods,  etc. ,  eight  days  from  Green  Tur¬ 
tle  Cay,  captured  within  500  yards  of  the  bar  at  Jupiter  Inlet  in  the 
attempt  to  run  in. 

The  captain  says  he  was  bound  to  Sand  Point,  [Fla.].  A  clearance 
from  Abaco  and  English  colors  were  found  on  board;  had  no  colors  set 
at  time  of  capture. 

At  the  time  of  capture  an  army  tug  was  near,  and  stood  offshore 
about  3  miles  and  captured  another  schooner,  which  Pinder  says  was 
bound  in.  I  have  taken  the  cargoes  of  both  vessels  on  board  this  ship, 
as  I  did  not  deem  it  prudent  to  send  a  crew  to  Key  West  in  such  frail 
crafts,  and  the  sloop  leaked  quite  badly.  The  schooner  was  exactly  the 
boat  I  required  for  inside  work.  I  have  fitted  my  howitzer  on'  her, 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  625 

and  shall  dispatch  her  this  evening  under  charge  of  Acting  Ensign 
(x.  M.  Pulsipher  and  a  crew  to  Jupiter  Inlet,  hoping  thereby  to  cap- 
ture  more  of  these  vessels  before  news  reaches  Nassau  that  the  place 
is  well  guarded. 

I  trust  you  may  approve  of  my  action  in  retaining  the  schooner. 

The  cargoes  and  sloop  will  be  sent  to  Key  West  for  adjudication  by 
earliest  available  opportunity. 

I  he  refugees  now  on  shore  here  are  encroaching  quite  severely  on 
our  stock  of  ship’s  stores,  and  wish  a  vessel  might  be  sent  to  convov 
them  to  Key  West. 

I  remain,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Sherrill, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Mast.  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla. 


Report  of  Acting  Blaster  Chatfield ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S. 
schooner  Two  Sisters,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  schooner  William , 
off  the  Suwanee  River. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Two  Sisters, 

Off  Suwanee  River,  January  13,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  while  passing  down  the  coast, 
off  the  mouth  of  Suwanee  River,  at  4:45  p.  m.  saw  a  sail  bearing  W. 
S.  W.  Immediately  gave  chase  and  soon  discovered  that  she  was  a 
schooner  and  that  she  was  steering  in  a  northerly  direction,  trying  to 
pass  to  windward  of  us  and  get  nearer  the  land,  and  using  every  means 
to  avoid  communicating  with  us.  The  wind  dying  out,  I  dispatched 
an  armed  boat  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Montague,  who  succeeded 
in  boarding  her  at  about  7  p.  m.,  after  first  hailing  and  then  firing  in 
order  to  bring  her  to.  In  answer  to  Acting  Ensign  Montague’s  ques¬ 
tions,  the  captain  informed  him  that  he  was  in  ballast,  bound  to  New 
Orleans,  and  that  he  was  upon  the  coast  in  consequence  of  his  vessel 
being  in  a  leaky  condition.  Upon  examining  his  papers,  she  proved  to 
be  the  schooner  William,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  with  salt,  bag- 
ging,  and  rope,  instead  of  ballast.  Mr.  Montague  informs  me  that  the 
captain  hesitated  to  exhibit  his  manifest,  and  it  was  only  when  he 
demanded  it  that  he  gave  it  up.  The  papers  appear  to  be  correct, 
except  that  the  shipping  articles  are  not  certified  and  he  has  no 
crew  list. 

As  the  capture  was  made  in  6  fathoms  water,  upon  a  part  of  the 
coast  entirely  out  of  the  track  of  vessels  bound  to  New  Orleans,  and 
trying  to  get  still  nearer  the  land,  I  have  deemed  it  my  duty  to  send 
her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication.  I  also  send  what  papers  were  found 
on  board,  together  with  the  vessel’s  log  book. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Chatfield, 

Actg.  Master,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  Comdg.  TJ.  S.  Schooner  Two  Sisters. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Sears ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  IT.  S.  S. 
Honeysuckle ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner  Fly ,  off 
Jupiter  Inlet. 

U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  January  If  186 f 
Sir:  1  beg  to  report  to  you  the  capture  of  the  English  schooner 
Fly ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  under  the  following  circumstances: 

Noon,  January  11,  1864,  Jupiter  Inlet  light-house  bearing  west,  1 
mile  distant,  while  communicating  with  a  boat  from  the  U.  S.  bark 
Roebuck ,  which  had  just  taken  a  small  schooner  within  hailing  dis¬ 
tance,  a  sail  was  sighted  bearing  E.  S.  E.,  6  miles  distant,  standing- 
in  for  the  land  before  the  wind.  Went  in  pursuit,  and  when  within  2 
miles  of  her  she  was  hauled  by  the  wind  on  the  starboard  tack,  head¬ 
ing  N.  N.  E.,  at  the  same  time  showing  the  English  flag. 

At  1  p.  m.  fired  a  shot  across  her  bow,  when  she  was  hove  to.  Sent 
a  boat  on  board  with  an  officer,  to  examine  her  papers  and  cargo.  Not 
finding  the  cargo  to  agree  with  the  manifest,  and  that  the  vessel  was 
greatly  out  of  the  course  of  her  voyage,  as  the  clearance  showed  that 
'she  was  bound  from  Green  Turtle  Cay  to  Key  West,  I  took  the  vessel 
in  tow  as  a  prize,  bringing  her  to  this  port.  At  the  time  of  capture 
the  boats  of  the  U.  S.  bark  Roebuck  were  about  4  miles  distant. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Cyrus  Sears, 

Acting  Ensign ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Burgess ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,'  commanding  TJ.  S. 
schooner  Beauregard ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
Minnie ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

Off  Cape  Canaveral ,  Fla. ,  January  16,  186 J. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  On  the  15th 
instant,-  at  7 :  30  a.  m. ,  while  on  a  cruise,  1  discovered  a  sail  close  inshore, 
about  20  miles  to  the  southward  of  Mosquito  Inlet.  I  immediately 
gave  chase,  the  vessel  making  all  sail  and  steaming  about  N.  E. 
During  the  chase,  which  lasted  six  hours,  I  fired  14  shot  and  shell,  but 


628 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


she  showed  no  colors  and  made  every  effort  to  escape.  I  boarded  her 
about  noon;  she  proved  to  be  the  British  schooner  Minnie ,  of  Nassau, 
New  Providence,  from  Nassau,  bound  to  Halifax,  Nova  Scotia,  with  a 
cargo  consisting  of  salt,  liquors,  and  earthenware,  and  as  she  had  a 
suspicious  appearance,  I  seized  her  as  a  prize  of  war  and  send  her  to 
Key  West  for  adjudication.  There  were  no  other  vessels  in  sight  at 
the  time. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Francis  Burgess,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Willcomb?  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 
Stars  and,  Stripes ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  steamer  Laura,  off 
the  OcklocTconee  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

St.  Maries  [ Apalachee\  Bay,  January  19,  186 J. 
Sir:  The  prize  steamer  Laura ,  hailing  from  St.  John,  New  Bruns¬ 
wick,  was  captured  by  this  vessel  near  the  mouth  of  the  Ocklockonee 
River  under  the  following  circumstances: 

At  4:35  p.  m.  of  the  18th  instant  a  sail  was  reported  in  a  S.  W.  direc¬ 
tion,  and  1  immediately  got  underway  and  gave  chase. 

At  4:50  p.  m.  another  vessel  was  reported,  apparently  in  pursuit  of 
the  first-mentioned  sail,  which  convinced  me  that  the  pursued  vessel 
was  a  blockade  runner.  I  stood  to  the  W.  by  S.  with  a  view  to  cut 
her  off,  and  fired  several  shots  at  her,  which  fell  short;  she  then  hauled 
in  for  the  South  West  Cape  and  both  vessels  were  soon  lost  sight  of  in 
the  darkness  of  night;  but  I  continued  standing  in  toward  the  river, 
and  at  6:50  p.  m.  again  discovered  her  about  1  mile  distant,  when  1 
anchored  my  vessel  in  10  feet  of  water  and  dispatched  two  armed  boats 
to  capture  her,  which  they  succeeded  in  doing.  At  8:10  p.  m.  she  was 
aground,  but  soon  and  easily  got  off  and  brought  alongside  this  ves¬ 
sel,  where  she  arrived  at  11  p.  m.  She  proved  to  be  a  blockade 
runner,  the  steamer  Laura,  hailing  from  St,  John,  New  Brunswick, 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


629 


and  purporting  to  be  from  Havana,  loaded  with  merchandise  and 
cigars.  Five  prisoners  were  found  on  hoax’d.  She  was  bound  in  [to] 
a  Confederate  port  in  this  vicinity.  The  captain,  with  15  others, 
escaped  in  a  boat.  At  daylight  on  the  19th  instant  the  other  vessel, 
which  I  took  to  be  one  of  our  gunboats,  proved  to  be  U.  S.  S.  Hen¬ 
drick  Hudson,  and  was  discovered  in  a  S.  E.  direction  and  within  sig¬ 
nal  distance.  I  have  concluded  to  send  the  cotton  captured  on  the, 
schooner  Caroline  Gertrude  by  the  steamer  Laura  to  Key  West,  sub¬ 
ject  to  adjudication;  also  all  papers  found  on  board  the  latter  vessel 
and  her  colors  (English). 

There  being  a  quantity  of  spirits  and  wines  on  board,  and  for  the 
better  preservation  and  for  fear  of  its  causing  any  ti’ouble,  have  put 
it  on  board  the  U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson ,  to  be  delivered  to  the  order 
of  the  judge  of  United  States  district  court  at  Key  West. 

I  herewith  enclose  a  full  list  of  officei's  and  crew  attached  to  this 
vessel  at  the  time  of  capture  of  the  blockade-runner  steamer  Laura. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  L.  Willcomb,

Report  of  Lieutenant-  Commander  McDougal ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  command- 
ing  TJ  S.  S.  Hendrick  LLudson ,  regarding  capture  of  the  steamer 
Laura ,  off  the  Ocklockonee  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson, 

Off  St.  Marks ,  Lila. ,  January  19,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  to  report  the  capture  of  the  blockade-running  steamer 
Laura  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes  under  the  following  cir¬ 
cumstances: 

Yesterday  morning,  at  about  8:30  a.  m.,  when  about  3  miles  off  the 
mouth  of  the  Suwanee  Kiver,  a  steamer  was  discovered  about  6  miles 
distant  from  us,  bearing  about  N.  W.  by  W.  \  W.,  apparently  at  a 
stand  and  evidently  waiting  for  the  weather  to  clear  up  before  running 
into  the  river.  Conceiving  at  once  her  true  character  I  immediately 
gave  chase,  which  she  shortly  perceiving,  kept  to  the  W.  N.  W.  and 
steamed  at  her  best  rate,  I  following.  At  this  time  it  was  calm  and  we 
did  not  seem  to  gain  any  on  the  stranger,  though  steaming  as  hard  as 
was  prudent.  About  10  a.  m.  a  fresh  breeze  sprung  up  right  ahead, 
which  gradually  increased  in  strength  until  it  was  blowing  a  half  a  gale 
of  wind,  accompanied  by  a  heavy  head  sea.  I  then  perceived  that  we 
were  gaining  on  her.  In  this  manner  I  chased  her  70  miles,  drawing 
gradually  nearer,  and  was  getting  anxious,  lest  in  the  dark  and  among 
the  shoals  off  South  West  Cape  he  might  escape,  when  to  my  great 
delight  the  Stars  and  Stripes  was  discovered  on  the  starboard  bow  in 
full  chase  and  steering  so  as  to  cut  him  off  to  the  eastward.  Just  at 
dark  I  was  near  enough  to  bring  him  in  range,  and  fired  7  shots  at 
him  with  the  20-pounder  Parrott  rifle,  all  of  which  could  be  seen  to 
strike  in  his  immediate  vicinity. 

Shortly  after  this  the  water  shoaled  so,  and  I  was  so  near  South 
West  Cape  (in  2  fathoms  water),  that  I  deemed  it  imprudent  to  run 


630 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


any  farther,  and  anchored.  At  this  time  the  Stars  and  Stripes  was 
nearer  him  than  1  was,  and  I  felt  convinced  that  he  could  not  escape. 
Immediately  on  anchoring-  I  discovered  that  the  chase  did  not  move, 
and  at  once  correctly  divined  that  she  was  ashore;  which  proved  to  be 
the  case.  I  was  then  on  the  point  of  sending  my  boats  in  to  her,  but 
reflecting  that  long  before  they  could  reach  her  she  would  be  in  the 
possession  of  the  Stars  and  Stripes ,  I  refrained  from  so  doing.  At 
this  time  and  during  the  entire  night,  I  had  both  vessels  in  plain  sight 
from  the  deck  of  this  vessel.  At  about  9  o’clock  p.  m.  I  saw  a  Coston 
light  burned  on  board  the  prize  which  was  answered  from  the  Stars 
and  Stripes ,  which  convinced  me  that  the  capture  had  been  made.  A 
dangerous  shoal  extended  between  my  vessel  and  the  Stars  and  Stripes , 
and  I  therefore  concluded  to  wait  until  morning  before  moving.  In 
the  morning  the  Stars  and  Stripes  came  around  to  where  I  was  lying 
and  piloted  me  to  where  the  prize  was,  the  prize  crew  having  in  the 
meantime  gotten  her  afloat.  She  proved  to  be  the  Laura ,  with  an 
assorted  cargo  and  evidently  from  Havana,  bound  to  some  Confederate 
port.  Undoubtedly  her  original  destination  was  the  Suwanee  River, 
but  being  chased  from  thence  by  this  vessel,  her  next  effort  was  to  get 
into  the  Ocklockonee  River  or  the  nearest  available  place.  Acting 
Master  Charles  L.  Willcomb,  who  made  the  capture,  will  send  her  to 
Key  West  and  prepare  the  necessary  reports,  etc.  I  herewith  enclose 
a  list  of  officers  and  crew  of  this  vessel  entitled  to  share  as  joint  cap- 
tors  with  the  Stars  and  Stripes  in  any  prize  money  accruing  from  her. 

In  justice  to  Acting  Master  Willcomb,  I  have  to  say  that  he  mani¬ 
fested  great  skill,  energy,  and  judgment  in  the  part  he  took,  and  it  is 
due  mainly  to  him  and  the  discretion  he  displayed  that  the  steamer 
was  captured.  In  the  night,  and  with  her  light  draft  of  water,  she 
might  easily  have  eluded  me,  among  the  shoals  that  exist  hereabouts, 
and  I  desire  that  his  services  may  be  fully  appreciated  and  trust  they 
may  be  rewarded  accordingly. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  J.  McDougal, 

Lieut.  Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  U  S.  S.  LLendrick Hudson. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

U.  S.  Navy.] 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
return  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Honduras  from  expedition  in  cooperation  with 
Brigadier-  General  Woodbury ,  IT  S.  Army. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Ney  West,  January  19 ,  186 J 

Sir:  Referring  to  my  letter  (No.  9)  of  the  6th  instant,  relative  to 
the  expedition  to  the  vicinity  of  Charlotte  Harbor  under  the  personal 
direction  of  Brigadier-General  Woodbury,  I  have  to  report  the  return 
of  the  Honduras  with  the  general  on  board,  after  having  established 
a  military  post  at  Fort  Myers,  on  the  Chattahoochee  [Caloosahatchee] 
River.  As  yet,  however,  the  expectation  of  receiving  recruits  for  the 
refugee  rangers  from  the  surrounding  country  has  not  been  justified 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


631 


by  the  event,  for  not  only  had  a  month  passed  at  our  latest  advices 
without  any  accession  to  their  force,  but  six  of  those  already  enlisted 
had  deserted  to  the  enemy  and  had  combined  with  them  to  attack  our 
men.  In  spite  of  these  circumstances,  which  occurred  before  the  gen¬ 
eral’s  arrival  there  with  a  company  of  the  Forty-seventh  Regiment 
Pennsylvania  Volunteers,  and  in  view  of  the  fact  that  this  defection 
appears  to  have  been  arranged  among  the  deserters  before  leaving  this 
place,  I  am  not  prepared  to  say  that  our  hopes  of  rousing  the  country 
to  violent  opposition  against  the  burden  and  oppression  of  rebel  rule 
are  wholly  unreasonable;  but  I  am  inclined  to  the  opinion  that  the  dis¬ 
affected  population  of  that  region  will  require  the  support  of  a  much 
larger  force  than  can  possibly  be  spared  from  here  in  order  to  induce 
them  to  incur  the  risk  of  joining  us  in  sufficient  numbers  to  produce 
any  impoi'tant  results.  From  3,000  to  5,000  men  embarked  in  steam¬ 
ers  of  light  draft  would  undoubtedly  insure  to  us  the  possession  of  the 
whole  peninsula;  but  in  the  meantime  the  project  will  be  thoroughly 
tested  with  the  means  at  our  disposal. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blkdg.  /Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Browne ,  U  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  bark 

Restless ,  regarding  proposition  made  by  Union  men  of  Marianna , 

Fla. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew’s  Bay ,  Fla.,  January  19,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report: 

On  the  afternoon  of  the  16th  instant  a  person  appeared  on  the  main¬ 
land  at  this  place  with  a  flag  of  truce.  He  was  a  mile  or  more  distant, 
and  was  supposed  to  be  a  refugee  or  contraband,  many  of  whom  have 
lately  come  off  to  this  ship.  I  dispatched  Acting  Ensign  Hicks  in 
a  boat  to  him,  and  he  was  allowed  to  come  on  board  without  my 
knowledge. 

He  represented  himself  a  good  Union  man  having  business  with  me 
on  behalf  of  good  Union  men  of  Marianna.  I  took  him  into  my  cabin, 
where  he  remained  during  his  stay  on  board.  He  made  substantially 
the  following  statement:  That  there  was  a  schooner  of  60  tons  burden, 
named  the  Fain,  lying  at  Bear  Creek,  North  Bay,  about  20  miles  from 
here  and  partly  loaded  with  cotton  (of  this  fact  I  was  already  aware); 
that  she  would  carry  about  120  bales;  that  he,  George  W.  Maslin,  was 
the  agent  in  this  mission  for  four  Union  men  of  Marianna,  named  John 
T.  My  rick,  Alderman,  Moore,  and  Burnett,  one  or  two  of  whom  owned 
part  of  the  cotton  on  board  the  vessel.  All  had  determined  to  get 
away  from  the  Southern  Government,  if  possible,  except  Burnett, 
whom  domestic  affairs  compelled  to  remain. 

My  rick  also  wished  to  pay  for  some  goods  purchased  in  New  York 
just  before  the  war.  As  the  only  way  to  accomplish  these  objects 
they  proposed  to  buy  with  Confederate  money  the  vessel  and  some 
cotton  they  could  procure  to  complete  the  cargo,  together  with  the 


632 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


remaining  interest  in  that  already  on  board,  and  bring  the  vessel  and 
cargo  to  this  place,  Maslin,  who  desired  to  leave,  acting  as  captain, 
and,  if  possible,  obtain  my  permission  to  proceed  to  Pensacola  or  Kej- 
West,  where,  on  proof  of  their  loyalty,  they  hoped  to  be  allowed  to 
sell  their  vessel  and  cargo,  or,  if  I  should  refuse  such  permission,  to 
land  their  cargo  upon  the  island  here  and  await  your  action. 

The  four  men  are  known  by  refugees  here  to  be  true  and  loyal  men. 
Captain  Maslin  says  he  is  an  Englishman  who  has  been  in  this  country 
about  twelve  years,  residing  most  of  that  time  at  Key  West,  and  has 
taken  out  his  first  papers  of  naturalization.  While  on  board  he  took 
the  oath  of  allegiance. 

I  told  Captain  Maslin  I  could  make  no  promise  whatever,  or  in  any 
way  compromise  myself  or  Government;  that  if  the  vessel  came  down 
to  me  I  should  take  possession  of  her,  in  the  same  way  as  if  she  were 
lawful  prize,  and  refer  the  whole  matter  to  you.  Captain  Maslin  said 
he  would  report  my  answer  to  his  principals  and  thought  they  would 
be  willing  to  bring  the  cargo  and  schooner  down  and  deliver  them  into 
my  possession,  to  await  the  action  of  the  proper  authorities  in  the 
matter. 

I  warned  him  against  attempting  to  run  out,  and  in  order  to  guard 
against  surprise,  I  told  him  where  to  anchor.  He  brought  two  letters 
with  him,  which  I  enclose. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  B.  Browne,

Capture  of  schooner  William  A.  Kciin  and  seven  prisoners ,  in  Bear 
Creek ,  by  boat  expedition  from  U.  S.  bark  Restless ,  January  22, 186 J. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  II.  S.  Navy,  commending  the  conduct  of  Acting 
Ensign  Russell,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

No.  48. J  U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West ,  February  3 , 186 A 

Sir:  In  forwarding  the  enclosed  report  of  Acting  Master  Browne, 
commanding  the  U.  S.  bark  Restless,  of  this  squadron,  I  feel  it  a  pleasure 
to  add  my  commendation  of  the  spirited  conduct  of  Acting  Ensign 
James  J.  Russell,  the  officer  to  whose  tact  and  courage  the  capture 
therein  detailed  is  justly  due.  It  is  not  often  that  a  success  occurs 
more  signal  and  complete,  or  that  an  officer,  almost  single-handed,  cap¬ 
tures  and  brings  away  in  custody  7  prisoners  and  a  valuable  prize  out 
of  the  very  hands  of  the  enemy. 

Mr.  Russell  had  been  sent  on  shore  with  instructions  to  cross  a  neck 
of  land  a  mile  or  so  in  width,  to  East  Bay,  to  reconnoiter  the  position 
of  a  large  schooner,  loaded  with  cotton  and  tobacco,  supposed  to  be 
concealed  in  a  bayou  on  the  other  side  of  the  bay.  This  reconnois- 
sance  was  preliminary  to  an  attack  in  force  with  armed  boats.  One 
seaman  and  a  man  who  had  deserted  to  us  only  the  day  previous,  and 
was  still  in  his  rebel  uniform,  were  detailed  to  accompany  him. 

While  proceeding  across  the  neck  of  land,  through  the  woods,  Mr. 
Russell  came  suddenly  upon  the  owner  and  one  of  the  crew  of  the 
schooner  crossing  for  the  purpose  of  watching  the  movements  of  the 
Restless.  W  ith  a  promptness  and  presence  of  mind  that  characterized 
all  his  conduct  on  this  occasion  Mr.  Russell  at  once  made  these  men 
his  prisoners.  _  He  learned  from  them  that  they  had  come  over  from 
the  mainland  in  a  boat,  which  they  had  left  waiting  for  them  in  charge 
of  three  men.  Mr.  Russell  at  once  marched  his  prisoners  with  his  own 
paity  to  the  boat  and  took  prisoners  the  three  men.  He  determined 
to  push  on  the  enterprise  and  ascertaining  that  the  schooner  lay 
moored  in  a  remote  bayou  on  the  other  side  of  the  bay  in  charge  of  two 
men,  he  ordered  his  five  prisoners  into  the  boat,  first  disarming  them, 
ana  compelled  them  to  row  him  across  the  bay  and  up  a  creek 
approachable  only  by  a  difficult  channel,  to  the  place  where  the 
schooner  lay  concealed.  Boarding  her  he  found  himself  with  his  two 
men  in  the  enemy’s  country  in  possession  of  a  valuable  prize  and  seven 
prisoners.  Not  venturing  to  trust  to  the  pilotage  of  any  of  the  cap- 
tu red  party,  Mr.  Russell  sent  two  negro  boys,  who  were  oystering  near 
\  their  father,  who,  it  appeared,  knew  the  channel  well,  and 
assisted  by  him  and  the  prisoners,  got  the  schooner  underway  and  out 
into  the  bay,  wheie,  it  falling  calm,  he  was  compelled  to  anchor  over 
night,  during  which  he  kept  constant  guard  over  his  seven  prisoners 
lest  a  i  ecapture  should  be  attempted.  The  next  morning  he  again  got 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


635 


the  schooner  underway  and  brought  his  bold  exploit  to  a  successful 
conclusion  by  anchoring  her  under  the  guns  of  the  Restless. 

The  Department  will  remember  that  Mr.  Russell  is  the  officer  under 
whose  charge  the  expedition  was  placed  that  destroyed  the  salt  works 
at  Lake  Ocala  on  the  2d  of  December,  and  who  was  so  warmly  com¬ 
mended  by  his  commanding  officer  for  the  skill  and  judgment  he  dis- 
p layed  on  that  occasion. 

Again,  on  the  10th  of  December  Mr.  Russell  bore  a  conspicuous 
part  in  the  expedition  that  destroyed,  on  that  day,  the  extensive  and 
valuable  salt  works  at  St.  Andrew’s,  owned  in  great  part  by  the  rebel 
Government,  and,  finally,  on  the  18th  of  December,  he  again  won  the 
favorable  report  of  his  commanding  officer  by  the  energy  that  he  then 
displayed  in  completing  the  work  of  breaking  up  the  immense  salt 
factories  that  extended  for  miles  along  the  coasts  and  in  the  interior. 
In  consideration  of  these  services  I  would  recommend  that  for  the 
ability  shown  in  the  destruction  of  the  salt  works  of  such  great  value 
to  the  rebels  Mr.  Russell  be  promoted  to  the  grade  of  acting  master, 
the  appointment  to  bear  date  December  2,  1863,  and  that  for  his  serv¬ 
ices  in  taking  a  prize  from  an  enemy  more  than  double  his  superior  in 
numbers  he  be  promoted  to  the  grade  of  acting  volunteer  lieutenant, 
the  appointment  to  bear  date  January  22,  1861. 

The  prompt  recognitions  of  zeal  and  ability  heretofore  given  have 
greatly  stimulated  and  encouraged  the  officers  and  men  of  this  squad¬ 
ron  in  all  matters  of  enterprise,  and  I  have  every  reason  to  be  satisfied 
with  their  general  conduct  and  their  interest  and  pride  in  the  discharge 
of  their  duties. 

Very  respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Browne,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  Bark  Restless. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew’s  Bay ,  Fla. ,  January  !S3,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  schooner  William 
A.  Kain  and  cargo  by  this  vessel  under  the  following  circumstances: 
I  had  for  several  weeks  been  aware  that  a  schooner  loaded  with  cotton 
was  lying  in  Bear  Creek,  several  miles  up  the  bay.  I  had  several 
times  attempted  to  capture  her,  but  the  creek  was  long,  narrow,  and 
crooked,  and  the  channels  intricate,  and  I  had  been  unable  to  accom¬ 
plish  her  capture.  Within  the  past  week  the  schooner  had  come  out 
of  the  creek  and  down  into  Watson’s  Bayou,  there  to  watch  for  an 
opportunity  to  run  the  blockade.  Being  informed  of  this  fact  I  deter¬ 
mined  to  send  Acting  Ensign  James  J.  Russell  and  Acting  Ensign 
Henry  Eason  in  command  of  the  first  and  second  cutters,  armed  and 
manned,  on  the  night  of  the  22d  instant  to  effect  her  capture.  I  thought 
best  to  first  send  Mr.  Russell  in  the  daytime  with  two  men  to  the  main¬ 
land,  to  ascertain  if  possible  the  exact  position  of  the  vessel,  fearing 
that  unless  this  precaution  were  taken,  the  moon  being  quite  bright, 
the  cutters  in  their  search  might  be  discovered  and  the  schooner  fired. 
I  instructed  Mr.  Russell  that  after  ascertaining  her  position  he  should 
return  if  possible  before  dark  to  take  command  of  the  first  cutter,  and 


636 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


in  conjunction  with  Mr.  Eason,  in  command  of  the  second  cutter,  to 
capture  her.  Mr.  Russell  was  to  make  a  signal  from  the  beach,  from 
which  the  first  cutter  was  to  take  him.  In  accordance  with  my  orders 
Mr.  Eason  and  the  two  boats  left  the  ship  at  dark  and  proceeded  to 
stations  agreed  upon,  where  they  waited  all  night  for  Mr.  Russell  and 
returned  to  the  ship  this  morning.  I  then  began  to  entertain  strong 
fears  that  Mr.  Russell  had  been  taken  prisoner.  About  10  o’clock 
a.  m.  the  schooner  appeared  in  sight,  coming  down  the  bay.  Mr. 
Russell  with  the  two  men  had  effected  her  capture.  He  reports  that 
while  reconnoitering  he  found  two  men  in  a  yawl  on  the  shore,  whom 
he  captured,  and  who  proved  to  be,  one  the  supercargo  of  the  schooner 
and  part  owner  of  her  cargo,  the  other,  one  of  her  crew.  From  these 
he  learned  that  the  captain,  mate,  and  another  of  the  crew  were  on 
shoie  spying  out  the  position  of  the  bark  preparatory  to  running-  out. 
Keeping  the  two  already  captured  with  him  he  found  and  captured 
the  other  three.  From  them  he  learned  the  position  of  the  schooner 
and  determined  to  take  her.  He  compelled  his  prisoners  to  row  him¬ 
self  and  men  to  the  schooner,  of  which  he  took  possession.  On  board 
he  found  two  more  of  her  crew.  Seeing  two  young  negroes  in  a  boat 
who  were  the  sons  of  an  old  negro  pilot  near'  by  named  Mazalina,  he 
sent  them  for  their  father,  who  soon  came  off.  Mr.  Russell  then  got 
underway  and,  with  the  assistance  of  the  negro  pilot,  brought  the 
schooner  out  of  the  bayou  into  East  Bay,  where,  for  want  of  wind,  he 
was  compelled  to  anchor  until  this  morning,  when  he  ag-ain  got  under¬ 
way  and  came  to  the  ship. 

By  papers  found  on  board,  it  appears  that  the  William  A.  Rain  is 
loaded  with  57  bales  of  cotton  and  2,626  pounds  of  tobacco,  bound  to 
Havana.  I  he  name  of  the  captain  is  George  K.  Saylor,  and  that  of 
the  supercargo  Henry  McCauley.  Upon  the  person  of  the  super¬ 
cargo  was  found  Confederate  bonds  for  $10,000,  with  8-per-cent  cou¬ 
pons  attached. 


I  shall  forthwith  forward  the  vessel  and  cargo,  together  with  all  her 
papers,  to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

I  beg  leave  to  present  to  your  favorable  consideration  Acting  Ensiun

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Russell,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  Expedition. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay ,  Fla .,  January  2 3 ,  186//. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  obedience  to  your  orders,  I 
landed,  accompanied  by  two  men,  and  proceeded  across  the  mainland  to 
Ferry  Point  for  the  purpose  of  ascertaining  the  position  of  the  schooner 
reported  to  be  in  Watson’s  Bayou.  On  my  arrival  there  I  found  a 
yawl  boat,  with  two  men  in  her,  on  the  lookout  down  East  Bay.  I  took 
them  prisoners,  and  found  one  of  them  to  be  the  owner  of  the  cargo  on 
board  the  schooner  and  the  other  one  of  the  crew.  From  them  I 
learned  that  the  captain,  mate,  and  another  of  the  crew  were  spying 
the  position  of  the  bark,  preparatory  to  running  the  blockade.  Keep¬ 
ing  the  two  in  custody,  I  proceeded  to  capture  the  other  three,  in  which 
attempt  I  was  successful.  From  them  1  learned  the  exact  position  of 
the  schooner,  and  determined  to  capture  her.  Compelling  the  pris¬ 
oners  to  pull  me,  I  went  on  board,  where  1  found  two  more  men,  and 
getting  underway,  proceeded  from  Watson’s  Bayou  (where  she  was 
then  lying)  into  East  Ba}u  There  being  no  wind,  I  was  obliged  to 
anchor  until  morning.  At  sunrise  I  again  got  underway  and  returned 
to  the  bark,  where  I  arrived  at  10:30  a.  m. 

The  cargo  of  the  schooner  consisted  of  57  large  bales  of  cotton  and 
30  boxes  of  tobacco.  1  obtained  the  vessel’s  register,  manifest,  clear¬ 
ance,  and  other  papers,  and  $10,000  in  Confederate  bonds.  1  learned 
from  the  captain  and  owner  soon  after  their  capture  that  it  was  their 
intention  to  run  the  blockade  the  first  opportunity.  I  will  here  men¬ 
tion  that  Mr.  George  K.  Saylor,  the  captain,  and  Mr.  Henry  McCauley, 
the  owner  of  the  schooner,  as  well  as  her  entire  crew,  rendered  me 
material  assistance  in  bringing  the  schooner  to  this  vessel.  I  can  not 
close  without  recommending  to  your  favorable  notice  John  Oxford, 
seaman,  and  Andrew  C.  Jordan,  landsman,  who  accompanied  me  on 
the  expedition,  and  who,  after  a  toilsome  march  through  the  woods 
during  the  day,  were  vigilant  and  active  all  night,  thus  materially  aid¬ 
ing  the  successful  accomplishment  of  my  plans. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  J.  Russell, 

Acting  Ensign. 

Acting  Master  W.  R.  Browne, 

Commanding  U.  S.  Bark  Restless. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Sherrill ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S. 
bark  Roebuck,  regarding  the  loss  of  the  prize  sloop  Mary,  en  route 
to  Key  West. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

Off  Indian  River  Inlet,  January  27,  1861/.. 
Sir:  I  have  to  report  the  loss  of  the  prize  sloop  Mary  on  the  night 
of  22d  instant  under  the  following  circumstances: 

She  sailed  about  dark  under  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Pulsipher 
and  prize  crew  for  Key  West.  Mr.  Pulsipher  reports  that  about  half 
an  hour  after  sailing  fie  discovered  she  was  making  water  very  fast, 
and  immediately  turned  back,  but  soon  filled,  becoming  unmanage¬ 
able.  Seeing  the  impossibility  of  fetching  this  ship,  he  let  go  both 


638 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


anchors,  but  the  cable  of  one  parting,  drifted  rapidly  toward  the  beach, 
wind  blowing  on  a  strong  breeze.  When  the  launch  reached  the  sloop 
she  was  near  the  breakers.  The  people  were  all  taken  off  and  brought 
on  board  this  ship. 

The  sloop  went  well  up  on  the  beach,  bursting  out  her  sides  and 
raising  the  deck.  The  cotton  was  nearly  all  saved  and  is  now  on 
board  this  vessel,  though  somewhat  damaged. 

Mr.  Pulsipher  has  been  very  active  and  energetic,  always  willing 
and  prompt  in  the  performance  of  his  duties,  and  I  think  well  deserv¬ 
ing  of  promotion. 

No  blame  can  attach  to  him  for  the  loss  of  the  Alary ,  as  the  leak 
was  very  sudden  and  beyond  his  control. 

Eighty-six  refugees  are  now  on  shore  at  Hutchinson’s  Island. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Sherrill, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla. 

P.  S.  30th. — I  shall  send  all  the  cargoes  and  prisoners  by  the 
Hendrick  Hudson  if  possible. 


Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  TJ.  S.  Wavy,  to  Acting

ing  his  inability  to  suspend  the  blockade. 


U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  January  2 8 ,  186 f 

Sir:  In  reply  to  your  communication  of  January  19,  enclosing  a 
letter  to  yourself  from  John  T.  Myrick  (relative  to  a  proposed  plan 
for  running  a  cargo  of  cotton  out  of  St.  Andrew’s  Bay,  with  a  view  to 
delivering  it  over  to  the  blockading  squadron  there  and  afterwards, 
on  proof  of  the  owner’s  loyalty,  applying  to  obtain  it  for  their  own 
benefit),  I  have  to  state  that  by  a  decision  of  the  United  States  dis¬ 
trict  judge  at  this  place,  “only  the  President,  acting  under  authority 
of  laws  of  Congress,  could  license  such”  an  arrangement.  The 
admiral  of  the  fleet  can  not  suspend  the  laws  of  Congress  nor  the 
blockade. 

You  can  communicate  this  to  the  persons  mentioned  in  your  letter 
at  }rour  discretion. 

Respectfully, 


T.  Bailey,
