Report  of  Acting  Master  Murphy,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  capture 
of  British  steamer  Rosita  by  army  transport  steamer  Western  Metrop¬ 
olis,  January  28,  186 J 

Chelsea,  Mass.,  February  J,  186 f 
Sir:  I  submit  to  you  a  report  of  the  capture  of  steamer  Rosita  with 
British  colors  flying,  on  the  28th  day  of  January,  1864,  by  steamer 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


639 


Western  Metropolis ,  bound  from  New  Orleans  to  New  York.  The 
Western  Metropolis  not  being  an  armed  vessel,  the  captain  requested 
the  passengers  to  arm  themselves  to  capture  a  blockade  runner,  or 
supposed  to  be,  that  she  was  in  chase  of  right  ahead,  about  80  miles 
from  Key  West.  After  two  or  three  hours’  chase  the  prize  ran  down 
to  us.  Captain  Hilton  requested  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Lewis 
W.  Pennington  to  go  on  board  of  her  and  capture  her.  I  offered  my 
services,  which  Avere  accepted,  to  assist  in  her  capture.  In  company 
with  Lieutenant  L.  W.  Pennington,  First  Lieutenant  G.  C.  Steward, 
U.  S.  Army,  second  mate,  and  a  boat’s  crew  of  4  men,  went  on  board 
and  found  that  she  Avas  from  Havana,  bound  to  Nassau.  By  her  papers 
she  had  liquors,  cigars,  and  an  assorted  cargo.  W  e  convinced  ourselves 
that  she  was  a  prize  and  took  charge  of  her  by  sending  the  captain, 
officers,  and  crew  on  board  the  Western  Metropolis  and  sending  a  haAvser 
to  her  and  taking  her  in  tow  into  Key  W est.  Captain  Hilton  requested 
us,  after  she  was  fast,  to  leave  the  steamer  Rosita  in  charge  of  Mr. 
Cowan,  second  mate  of  Western  Metropolis ,  and  then  come  on  board, 
which  we  did.  The  prize  was  left  at  Key  West  with  a  prize  crew  on 
board  from  the  flagship. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  S.  Murphy, 
Acting  Master ,  U.  S.  Wavy. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  U.  S.  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
capture  of  British  steamer  Rosita  hy  army  transport  steamer  West¬ 
ern  Metropolis ,  January  88,  186 lh 


U.  S.  Flagship  San  .Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  January  89,  186J 

Sir:  I  have  to  report  that  the  steamer  Western  Metropolis  (in  the  serv¬ 
ice  of  the  Quartermaster’s  Department  of  the  Army)  arrived  here  this 
morning  with  the  steamer  Rosita,  which  vessel  she  had  captured  as 
a  prize  while  running  from  Havana  to  Mobile  with  an  assorted  cargo. 
The  prize  was  turned  over  to  me  by  the  captors,  and  I  have  caused  the 
steps  necessary  for  her  adjudication  to  be  taken  in  the  district  court  at 
this  place.  The  Western  Metropolis  had  only  three  muskets  on  board, 
but  no  ammunition  for  them,  and  the  capture  was  mainly  due  to  the 
address  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Pennington,  U.  S.  Navy,  a 
passenger. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of 'Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
destruction  of  salt  works  in  the  vicinity  of  St.  Joseph's  Bay. 


U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  January  30 ,  186 If. 

Sir:  It  gives  me  pleasure  to  report,  more,  however,  as  an  evidence 
of  the  zeal  and  efficiency  manifested  by  this  squadron  than  on  account 
of  the  importance  of  the  achievement,*  that  some  salt  works  in  the 
vicinity  of  St.  Joseph’s  Bay  have  been  destroyed  by  the  bark  Pursuit , 
under  the  command  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Randall.  One 
establishment  consisting  of  6  kettles  of  150  gallons  each  and  another 
consisting  of  3  boilers  set  in  masonry,  together  with  all  the  buildings 
and  apparatus  attached,  are  reported  as  having  been  entirely  demol¬ 
ished  and  rendered  useless  to  the  enemy. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Burgess ,  U.  iS.  Navy ,  commanding  II.  S. 

schooner  Beauregard ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  sloop 

Racer ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

Off  Cape  Canaveral ,  Fla. ,  February  1 ,  1861/.. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  On  the  31st 
day  of  January,  1864,  while  on  a  cruise,  Cape  Canaveral  bearing  S.  W. 
by  W.,  distant  15  miles,  at  4  p.  m.  discovered  a  sail  bearing  W.  N.  W. 
and  steaming  S.  E.,  and  as  the  wind  was  light  at  the  time,  I  furled  my 
sails  and  sent  an  armed  boat  in  pursuit,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s 
Mate  H.  B.  Colby,  who,  after  an  exciting  chase  of  four  hours,  over¬ 
took  her  close  in  to  the  breakers  about  10  miles  to  the  northward  of 
Cape  Canaveral.  She  proved  to  be  the  British  sloop  Racer ,  of  Nassau, 
from  New  Smyrna,  Fla.,  bound  to  Nassau  with  a  cargo  of  cotton  (20 
bales).  I  therefore  seized  her  as  a  prize  of  war  and  send  her  to  Key 
West  for  adjudication. 

1  beg  leave  to  mention  Acting  Master’s  Mate  H.  B.  Colby,  who  has 
used  unusual  energy  in  assisting  in  the  capture  of  this  sloop,  as  also 
on  former  occasions.  There  were  no  other  vessels  in  sight  at  the  time 
of  the  capture. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Francis  Burgess, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy, ' Washington ,  D.  C.

It  is  not  unlikely  that  the  enemy  may  attempt  to  build  flatboats  at

Capture  uf  the  steamer  Cumberland ,  February  5 ,  1861+. 

Report  of  Captain  Scott,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  De  Soto. 

U.  S.  S.  De  Soto, 

Off  Mobile ,  February  5 ,  186 1+. 

Sir:  I  have  the  pleasure  to  inform  you  that  I  have  been  successful 
in  capturing  the  steamer  Cumberland  on  the  morning  of  the  5th  of 
February,  in  latitude  29°  40'  N.,  longitude  87°  30'  W.,  in  attempting 
to  run  the  blockade. 

I  can  not  give  you  any  information  regarding  her  cargo,  as  the 
weather  will  not  permit.  I  believe  her  cargo  consists  chiefly  of  arms 
and  ammunition.  I  have  sent  her  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  L.  H. 
Partridge,  with  orders  to  Key  West,  who  will  give  you  all  the  infor¬ 
mation  regarding  her.  She  has  for  one  article  100  barrels  of  gun¬ 
powder. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  H.  Scott, 

Captain. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  copy  of  circular. 

U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  February  11,  1861+. 

Sir:  It  gives  me  unusual  gratification  to  report  the  capture  of  the 
Anglo-rebel  steamer  Cumberland  on  the  5th  instant  by  the  U.  S.  S. 
De  Soto ,  not  only  because  she  is  so  valuable  a  prize  as  to  constitute  a 
serious  loss  to  those  engaged  in  violating  the  blockade,  but  also  because 
her  cargo  consisted  largely  of  arms  and  munitions  of  war,  and  still 
more  because  it  is  confidently  reported  that  she  was  intended  to  become 
a  rebel  privateer. 

She  arrived  in  Havana  late  in  September  last  and  commenced  mak¬ 
ing  extensive  repairs,  which  did  not  appear  to  be  at  all  necessary. 
Since  that  time  I  have  received  nine  different  dispatches  from  the 
U.  S.  vice-consul-general  at  Havana  (Mr.  Savage,  whose  untiring  zeal 
in  communicating  valuable  information  has  been  of  infinite  service  to 
me  throughout  the  period  of  my  command  here),  giving  me  the  details 
of  her  movements  and  preparations.  Early  in  December  the  reports 
of  her  intended  operations  assumed  such  tangible  form  that  I  issued 
the  circular,  of  which  the  enclosed  is  a  copy,  for  the  information  of 
this  squadron  and  to  insure  extraordinary  vigilance  with  a  view  to  her 
capture.  On  the  31st  of  January  she  at  last  left  Havana,  but  was 
driven  into  Marie!  by  one  of  our  vessels,  probably  by  the  San  Jacinto, 
which,  together  with  the  De  Soto,  had  been  hurried  off  from  here  on 
that  day  specially  to  intercept  her.  Again,  on  the  3d  instant,  she  left 
Mariel  for  Mobile,  and  although  she  reports  having  passed  within 
sight  of  the  San  Jacinto  on  the  night  of  the  4th  without  being  herself 
discovered,  vet  the  distribution  of  our  cruisers,  which  is  made  with  a 
view  to  such  a  contingency,  caused  her  to  come  within  sight  of  the 
De  Soto  at  daylight,  and  after  a  chase  of  less  than  two  hours  she  was 
captured  by  that  vessel. 


644 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  Cumberland  is  a  vessel  of  about  700  tons  and  is  reported  to  be 
fast,  although  quite  an  old  steamer.  So  soon  as  an  order  from  the 
court  can  be  obtained  she  will  be  sent  north  for  sale,  with  a  crew 
composed  of  men  from  this  squadron  whose  terms  of  service  have 
expired  and  who  are  here  awaiting  an  opportunity  to  return  home  for 
their  discharge. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East.  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

CIRCULAR. 

No.  60.]  Key  West,  December  10 ,  1863. 

Information  has  been  received  that  the  steamer  Cumberland ,  now 
lying  at  Havana  and  intended  as  a  rebel  privateer,  is  ready  for  sea. 
A  certain  person  is  daily  expected  there  from  Nassau,  on  whose  arrival 
she  will  sail.  It  is  believed  she  will  be  under  the  command  of  Daniel 
Graham,  formerly  of  New  Orleans,  who  has  a  commission  as  a  navy 
officer  from  the  rebel  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  and  who  has  authority 
from  the  same  source  to  appoint  his  subordinates  for  the  present  voy¬ 
age.  Her  chief  engineer  will  be  a  man  named  Armstrong.  Daniel 
Golding,  Luke  Shaw,  David  Pennel,  and  one  or  two  others  are  men¬ 
tioned  as  officers  and  engineers. 

Several  men  are  engaged  and  their  board  is  being  paid  for,  but  they 
think  they  are  merely  going  on  a  blockade  running  trip.  The  object, 
however,  is  to  go  into  Pensacola  Bay  and  if  possible  to  cut  out  a  fine 
steamer  or  to  destroy  as  many  vessels  as  possible,  and  in  case  of  their 
capture  to  produce  their  commissions  and  claim  to  be  considered  as 
prisoners  of  war.  As,  however,  some  other  point  of  attack  may  be 
selected,  exceeding  vigilance  is  enjoined  upon  everyone  connected 
with  this  squadron,  not  only  to  guard  against  surprise,  but  also  to 
avoid  an_\r  deception  that  may  be  attempted  upon  them.  This  circular 
will  be  read  on  the  quarter-deck  of  every  vessel  in  this  squadron  at 
general  muster  immediately  on  its  receipt. 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  On  the  4th 
instant  at  10:30  a.  m.  I  sent  a  boat  inside  of  Jupiter  Inlet  in  charge 
of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  H.  B.  Colby,  to  examine  Jupiter  Narrows 
and  vicinity  for  blockade  runners,  and  at  9  p.  m.  same  day,  at  Jupiter 
Narrows,  discovered  boat  Lydia ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  on  her 
way  down  to  the  inlet  from  Sand  Point,  Florida,  bound  to  Nassau  with 
a  cargo  consisting  of  2  bales  cotton  and  5  barrels  turpentine;  therefore 
she  was  seized  as  a  prize  of  war  by  my  officer,  and  brought  to  me  at 
Jupiter  Inlet,  where  she  arrived  this  day  (February  6).  I  shall  send 
her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication.  There  was  no  other  United  States 
vessel  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Francis  Burgess, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Browne,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  bark  Restless. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew’s  Bay ,  Fla.,  February  17,  186f 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report: 

Learning  that  the  rebels  had  erected  new  Government  salt  works 
on  West  Bay,  on  the  site  of  the  old  salt  works  destroyed  by  us  in 
December,  and  that  they  had  a  force  of  50  men  armed  and  stationed 
there  for  protection,  I  fitted  out  the  first  cutter,  manned  with  13  men, 
under  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  James  J.  Russell,  with  orders  to  pro¬ 
ceed  up  the  Gulf  coast  20  miles,  and  march  inland  7  miles  to  the  salt 
works  and  attack  them  in  the  rear,  while  Acting  Ensign  Hemw  Eason 
with  10  men,  in  command  of  the  second  cutter,  would  proceed  by  the 
inside  passage  and  attack  them  in  the  front  at  the  same  time. 

The  expedition  was  entirely  successful,  the  works  being  abandoned 
upon  the  appearance  of  our  men,  Messrs.  Russell’s  and  Eason’s  party 
joining  at  the  appointed  time,  and  immediately  proceeded  in  the 
destruction  of  everything  connected  with  the  manufactories,  consisting 
of  26  sheet-iron  boilers,  averaging  881  gallons,  and  19  kettles,  averaging 
200  gallons,  making  an  aggregate  of  26,706  gallons,  which  cost  in 
Montgomery  $5.50  per  gallon.  These  boilers  and  kettles  were  cut  up 
or  broken  to  pieces,  some  600  bushels  of  salt  wrere  thrown  into  the 
bay,  all  the  chimneys  and  furnaces  hauled  down,  and  everything  ren¬ 
dered  completely  useless  for  any  further  operations.  Seven  slaves 
fled  to  us  for  protection,  and  assisted  in  the  destruction  of  this  estab¬ 
lishment,  which  had  only  been  in  operation  ten  days. 

This  work  covered  a  space  of  half  a  square  mile,  the  boilers  and 
kettles  alone  costing  $146,883. 

Our  party  returned  to  the  ship  next  day,  bringing  7  contrabands 
and  6  shotguns.  You  will  please  find  enclosed  a  drawing  of  the  boilers 
and  kettles. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Tiieodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Second  report  of  Acting  Master  Browne,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  bark  Restless. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew ’s  Bay,  Fla.,  February  19,  186 A 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  of  making  the  following  report: 

Having  gained  information  that  a  large  barge  would  leave  the 
Wetappo  River  on  or  about  the  18th  instant  for  East  Bay,  with  all  the 
material  on  board  necessary  for  erecting  a  large  salt  work,  and  on  her 
return  intending  to  bring  back  a  cargo  of  salt  (her  capacity  1,500 
bushels),  I  fitted  out  the  second  cutter  with  11  men,  under  charge 
of  Acting  Ensign  Henry  Eason,  and  gig  with  7  men,  under  charge  of 
Master’s  Mate  F.  Grant,  to  effect  her  capture  on  her  passage  down, 
and  with  orders  if  after  waiting  five  days  and  not  seeing  the  barge,  to 
land  and  destroy  all  the  salt  works  in  the  vicinity. 

According  to  my  instructions  the  boats  left  the  ship  at  8  p.  m.  the 
17th  instant,  and  proceeded  to  a  bayou  on  the  S.  W.  side  of  East  Bay 
selected  as  a  place  of  ambush  and  which  the  barge  must  necessarily 
pass.  After  lying  in  wait  the  appointed  time  and  seeing  no  appear¬ 
ance  of  the  barge,  the  men  were  landed  and  destroyed  all  the  works  at 
hand,  15  in  number,  among  which  were  some  of  the  largest  Govern¬ 
ment  salt  works  ever  erected  in  Florida,  the  whole  of  which  were 
successfully  destroyed,  consisting  of  5  large  steamboat  boilers  and  23 
kettles,  together  with  16  log  houses,  1  flatboat,  a  large  quantity  of  salt, 
vats,  tanks,  and  other  materials  connected  with  the  manufacture  of  this 
article.  After  destroying  the  above  they  returned  to  the  ship,  bringing 
with  them  6  contrabands  found  at  this  place. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Master,  Comma/nding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Tiieodorus  Bailey, 

Oomdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla.

Boat  expeditions  from  the  TJ.  S.  /S.  Tahoma  for  the  destruction  of  salt 
works  near  St.  Marks ,  Fla .,  February  17-19  and  £6-87,  186 f 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

IT.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  March  6 ,  186 4-. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  two  expeditions  have  recently 
been  fitted  out  from  the  U.  S.  S.  Tahoma  for  the  destruction  of  exten¬ 
sive  salt  works,  the  property  of  the  rebel  Government,  in  the  neigh¬ 
borhood  of  St.  Marks,  Fla. 

The  first  expedition  left  the  ship  on  the  morning  of  the  17th  of 
February  in  two  detachments.  One  under  command  of  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter  E.  C.  Weeks  and  the  other  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  J.  G. 
Koehler.  The  salt  works  being  some  7  miles  in  extent,  the  first 
detachment  commenced  at  one  end  of  the  line,  the  other  at  the  other. 
A  day  and  a  night  of  unremitting  labor  was  spent  in  the  work  of 
destruction,  when  the  expedition  returned  safely  to  the  vessel,  having- 
marched  through  swamps  and  dense  woods  a  distance  of  45  miles  and 
successfully  accomplished  the  object  of  the  undertaking. 

On  the  27th,  a  week  later,  a  second  expedition  was  planned  and  car¬ 
ried  through  with  equal  success,  the  object  being  to  destroy  some 
Government  works  at  Goose  Creek,  some  10  miles  distant.  The 
party  was,  in  this  case  also,  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  Weeks,  and 
the  works  to  be  destroyed  were  under  the  protection  of  a  rebel  cavalry 
company,  whose  pickets  the  expedition  succeeded  in  eluding.  Twelve 
prisoners  were  brought  off,  one  the  captain  of  an  infantry  company 
raised  for  coast  service. 

^  The  works  destroyed  by  these  two  expeditions  produced  for  the 
Confederates  2,500  bushels  of  salt  per  diem.  1  enclose  herewith 
Lieutenant-Commander  Harmony’s  list  forwarded  tome  of  the  articles 
captured  and  destroyed. 

V ery  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Harmony,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Tahoma, 
regarding  first  expedition  under  command  of  Acting  Master  Weeks,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Tahoma, 

St.  Marks  [ Apalachee ]  Bay,  February  21,  1861/.. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  result  of  an  expedition,  sent  by 
me  on  the  17th  instant  to  destroy  some  salt  works,  about  40  miles  to  the 
eastward.  On  the  morning  of  the  16th  1  sent  Mr.  Weeks,  the  execu¬ 
tive  officer,  on  shore  to  confer  with  the  leading  men  among  the  refu¬ 
gees,  and  find  out  whether  they  would  assist  me  if  I  wished  them  to 
do  so.  The  same  evening  the  boat  returned  with  a  note  from  him  say¬ 
ing  that  the  refugees  to  the  number  of  96  had  expressed  a  desire  to  go 
with  him,  requesting  me  to  send  rations  for  two  days  for  100  men,  and, 
if  possible,  some  fine  powder  for  shotguns  (the  only  arms  those  men 
on  shore  have).  The  next  morning  (17th)  I  sent  two  boats  in  charge 
of  Acting  Ensign  J.  Green  Koehler,  with  20  armed  men,  and  all  the 


650 


EAST'  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


tools  I  had  on  board  to  destroy  the  kettles,  boilers,  etc.,  used  in  mak¬ 
ing  salt;  also  sent  the  rations  and  5  pounds  of  priming  powder.  Act¬ 
ing  Master  Weeks  was  to  have  met  the  boats  at  the  mouth  of  the 
Warrior  River.  It  had  been  blowing  a  stiff  gale  from  the  north 
during  the  night,  and  was  still  blowing  very  fresh  when  I  sent  the 
boats  off;  the  wind  had  blown  the  water  from  the  mouth  of  the  river, 
and  they  were  unable  to  get  closer  to  the  beach  than  within  -4  miles 
(the  boats  being  unable  to  get  in).  Mr.  Weeks,  with  8  men  from  this 
ship,  and  the  96  refugees,  then  pushed  on  for  the  works,  reach¬ 
ing  there  Friday  morning  at  early  daylight,  having  marched  fully  45 
miles.  They  all  set  to  work  at  once,  working  all  that  day  and  night 
until  Saturday  morning,  destroying  everything  that  could  in  any  way 
be  used  at  the  salt  works.  Mr.  Koehler,  in  the  meanwhile  (with  com¬ 
mendable  energy),  under  sail,  ran  down  about  35  miles  farther  to  the 
eastward,  determined  to  find  a  landing,  and  then,  with  the  thermome¬ 
ter  down  to  29°  waded  with  his  boat’s  crew  several  hundred  yards  to 
the  shore.  In  his  boat  were  all  the  provisions,  etc.,  I  had  sent  on 
shore.  He  commenced  destro}ring  on  the  eastern  end  of  the  long  line 
of  works,  which  extended  about  7  miles,  working  up  to  where  the 
other  party  were  employed.  After  effectually  destroying  everything 
they  could  lay  hands  upon,  the  party  started  to  return  at  about  10 
a.  m.,  Saturday,  marching  all  night,  arriving  here  this  morning  at 
about  9  o’clock,  having  marched  over  80  miles  by  forced  marches,  and 
rowed  some  30  miles.  This  includes  going  and  returning,  in  a  direct 
road.  I  suppose  the  place  they  went  to  was  not  over  30  miles,  but 
the  swamps  they  were  compelled  to  cross,  and  rivers  to  head,  increased 
the  distance  from  10  to  15  miles  each  way.  Not  an  article  was  lost, 
and  no  one  was  injured  except  a  refugee,  whose  gun  accidentally  going- 
off'  put  a  couple  of  buckshot  in  his  leg.  He  is  not  seriously  hurt,  I 
am  happy  to  sajL  I  append  herewith  a  list  of  articles  destroyed  and 
captured. 

In  conclusion,  I  can  not  speak  in  too  high  terms  of  Acting  Master 
E.  C.  Weeks,  who  commanded  the  expedition.  This  officer  performed 
the  duty  assigned  him  with  alacrity  and  cheerfulness.  I  take  great 
pleasure  in  bringing  him  to  your  notice  as  an  officer  of  courage  and 
skill,  and  most  heartily  recommend  him  for  promotion.  He  has  been 
in  the  Navy  since  the  war  commenced,  and  has  seen  much  hard  service; 
was  honorably  mentioned  in  action  with  Forts  St.  Philip  and  Jackson. 

Acting  Ensign  Koehler  also  deserves  much  credit  for  zeal  and 
energy.  Second  Assistant  Engineer  J.  L.  Yanclain  volunteered  for 
the  affair  and  rendered  good  service.  The  men  all  behaved  admir¬ 
ably,  and  express  the  greatest  anxiety  to  go  again.  All  of  them  have 
sore  feet,  and  I  will  have  to  let  them  lay  by  for  a  few  days,  when  I 
shall  send  them  over  to  some  salt  works  about  10  miles  from  here. 
Those  works  we  destroyed,  and  those  I  intend  destroying,  have  been 
in  full  operation  for  several  months  past,  and  ought  to  have  been 
destroyed  long  ago.  The  commanding  officer  of  the  Stars  and  Stripes 
knew  of  them,  but  made  no  effort  to  do  anything,  although  some  of 
them  were  within  plain  view,  and  he  could  get  liis  ship  within  4  miles 
of  them. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  B.  Harmony, 

Lieutenant-  Commander. 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blkdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Harmony,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Tahoma, 

regarding  expedition  to  Goose  Creek,  under  command  of  Acting  Master  Weeks,  U.  S. 

Navy. 

U.  S.  S.  Taiioma, 

Off  St.  Marks ,  Fla. ,  February  27,  186b- 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  of  the  successful  result  of  an 
expedition  to  Goose  Creek  to  destroy  a  large  number  of  salt  works, 
which  have  been,  as  I  am  informed,  in  active  operation  for  several 
months  past. 

From  a  man  who  came  off  from  St.  Marks  about  a  week  ago  I 
thoroughly  informed  myself  as  to  the  locality  and  also  the  station  of 
pickets,  several  of  whom  1  had  seen  from  the  ship.  I  concluded  from 
the  information  so  obtained  that  I  could  send  a  force  on  a  foggy  night 
between  the  points  without  being  observed,  and  that  they  might  finish 
their  work  before  any  information  could  be  sent  to  the  cavalry  com¬ 
pany  encamped  some  6  miles  back.  This  company  numbered  about 
35  men. 

Last  night  proving  favorable,  I  dispatched  three  boats  with  Acting 
Master  L.  W.  Hill,  Acting  Ensign  Shaw,  and  Pilot  W.  Wells,  all 
under  command  of  Acting  Master  E.  C.  Weeks,  executive  officer,  to 
attempt  their  destruction,  directing  him  not  to  make  the  attempt  if  he 
was  seen  by  the  pickets  on  Shell  Point,  which  he  had  to  pass  within 
1,000  yards.  Fortunately  he  was  not  discovered,  and  pushed  on  to 
the  scene  of  his  work.  Immediately  on  landing  he  took  his  whole 
force  and  surrounded  the  different  houses,  capturing  all  the  people 
who  were  in  them.  He  then  threw  out  a  number  of  pickets  and  com¬ 
menced  the  work  of  destruction.  Having  heard  from  one  of  the 
negroes  that  there  were  5  white  men  in  some  houses  about  2  miles 
back,  he  sent  Mr.  Shaw  with  6  men  to  capture  them,  which  duty  that 
officer  performed. 

After  they  had  entirely  destroyed  everything  that  could  be  of  any 
use,  the  party  disembarked  on  their  passage  out  of  the  creek.  They 
were  observed  by  the  pickets,  but  fortunately  when  too  late  for  them 
to  do  any  injury.  The  boats  arrived  on  board  the  ship  at  1  o’clock, 
having  been  absent  nineteen  hours.  They  brought  off  12  prisoners, 
one  of  whom  is  a  captain  of  an  infantry  company  raised  for  coast 
service,  another  a  man  who  has  been  in  the  Army  as  a  lieutenant,  who 
lost  his  leg  and  was  recently  discharged;  his  wound  has  not  yet  healed. 
The  latter  and  2  other  men,  who  are  over  50  years  of  age  and  sick,  I 
shall  parole  and  send  up  to  St.  Marks  to-morrow.  They  can  be  of  no 
use  to  us,  nor  can  they  do  us  any  injury  in  the  rebel  States.  To  keep 
them  will  be  an  unnecessary  expense  and  trouble.  The  officers  on  the 
expedition  deserve  credit  for  the  effectual  manner  in  which  they  per¬ 
formed  the  work  assigned  them.  I  send  herewith  a  list  of  articles 
destroyed.  The  effect  of  my  work  on  the  salt  works  to  the  eastward 
and  those  on  Goose  Creek  will  induce  these  people  to  believe  that  we 
are  disposed  to  annoy  them  when  we  can  get  at  them,  notwithstanding 
their  cavalry  patrols.  The  prisoners  inform  me  that  the  force  along 
the  coast  has  been  increased  where  there  are  any  works,  and  would 
have  been  in  a  day  or  two  at  the  point  we  landed  last  night.  They, 
however,  had  felt  quite  secure,  as  they  supposed  we  knew  of  the  cav¬ 
alry  company  so  near  them.  I  have  destroyed  works  so  far  at  which 
2,400  bushels  were  made  daily,  1,500  at  the  first  and  900  at  the  latter. 
This,  at  $12.50  a  bushel,  is  quite  an  item.  This  is  the  price  at  which 


652 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


it  is  sold,  for  at  the  works,  which  fact  I  discovered  by  overhauling 
their  account  books. 

Every  man  who  is  engaged  in  making  salt  is  exempt  from  military 
service  if  he  makes  20  bushels  daily,  which  the  Government  takes  at 
the  market  price,  $12.50.  Hence,  all  who  are  captured  are  legitimate 
prisoners  of  war,  as  they  are  aiding  and  abetting  the  enemy.  The 
boats  brought  off  2  contrabands. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

■  D.  B.  Harmony, 

Lieutenant- Commander,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdy.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  requesting  orders 
to  participate  in  the  attack  upon  Mobile. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  February  18, 186 f. 

Sir:  Judging  from  the  many  circumstances  that  have  come  to  my 
knowledge  that  the  time  is  not  far  distant  when  an  attack  will  be  made 
upon  Mobile,  I  would  esteem  it  a  great  favor  if  the  Department  would 
direct  Rear-Admiral  Farragut  to  send  for  me,  with  such  of  my^  squad¬ 
ron  as  may  be  available  and  adapted  to  that  service,  in  time  to  partici¬ 
pate  in  the  affair.  With  the  San  Jacinto ,  Tioga,  Tahoma ,  and  Saga¬ 
more  I  feel  confident  that  good  service  could  be  rendered,  and  I  could 
readily  provide  for  the  duties  of  this  squadron  during  my  absence. 
May  I  request  to  be  informed  of  your  decision  in  this  matter. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron , 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
departure  of  the  TJ.  S.  steamers  Huntsville  and  De  Soto  to  Havana 
for  repairs  in  dry  dock.. 

No.  71.1  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  February  25,  186 f 

Sik:  I  have  to  inform  the  Department  that  I  sent  the  Huntsville  to 
Havana  on  the  12th  for  the  pui-pose  of  going  upon  the  dry  dock  and 
having  such  repairs  put  upon  her  bottom  and  rudder  pintles  as  were 
needed.  As  this  was  accomplished  without  difficulty,  I  have  now 
ordered  the  De  Soto  there  to  get  a  leak  in  her  bottom  stopped.  The 
commanding  officers  of  these  vessels  were  instructed  to  draw  upon  the 
Navy  Department  for  the  amount  of  gold  necessary  to  pay  expenses; 
and  there  is  reason  to  believe  that  it  will  be  more  than  refunded  to 
the  Government  through  their  increased  speed  when  they  again  get 
to  sea. 

Respectfully, 

Theodores  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Smith ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  command¬ 
ing  TJ.  S.  S.  Rita,  regarding  the  capture  of  floating  cotton  from 
Turning  steamer  reported  to  he  the  Nan-Nan. 

U.  S.  S.  Nita, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  February  26,  186 J. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  daylight  on  the  morning  of 
February  24,  while  at  anchor  off  the  West  Pass  of  the  Suwanee  River, 
1  discovered  a  steamer  in  the  East  Pass  bound  out.  I  immediately 
started  in  pursuit,  going  around  the  intervening  shoals  with  the  ship 
and  sending  both  my  boats  across.  In  the  excitement  she  got  ashore 
and  threw  overboard  about  60  bales  of  cotton  to  lighten  her.  The 
tide  was  ebbing,  and  seeing  escape  impossible  the  officers  and  crew 
abandoned  her  at  7:20  a.  m.  At  7:25  I  perceived  that  she  was  on  fire, 
and  in  five  minutes  she  was  one  solid  sheet  of  flame  from  bow  to  stern. 
At  8  a.  m.  the  boats  arrived  alongside  her,  but  could  not  board  on 
account  of  the  intense  heat.  About  the  same  time  I  anchored  in  54 
feet  water  and  recalled  the  boats  and  commenced  collecting  the  float¬ 
ing  cotton. 

At  1  p.  m.  a  boat  from  the  Sagamore  arrived  alongside,  and  the 
officer  in  charge  offered  assistance.  Considering  the  cotton  all  safe, 
being  nearly  all  rafted  together  and  anchored,  and  having  anchored 
the  steamer,  I  did  not  accept  his  offer.  I  waited  only  the  ebb  tide  to 
tow  the  cotton  alongside.  At  5:45  p.  m.  the  boats  arrived  alongside 
with  the  cotton.  At  7:30  p.  m.  it  was  all  on  board  and  stowed.  I  am 
informed  by  a  refugee  that  her  name  was  Nan-Nan ,  and  commanded 
by  William  (alias  Barney)  Pennington. 

She  came  down  to  the  West  Pass  three  times,  but  finding  it  closely 
blockaded  she  returned  and  finally  concluded  to  attempt  the  East  Pass. 
On  the  22d  I  saw  her  come  down  within  about  2  miles  of  the  mouth  of 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


655 


the  river,  and  after  watching  us  for  a  few  hours  she  returned  again. 
She  was  armed  with  a  6-pounder  iieldpiece  and  plenty  of  ammunition. 
A  quantity  of  canister  and  shot  was  visible  in  the  bottom  of  the 
vessel.  1  send  you  one  of  the  canister.  The  barrels  and  rammers  of 
a  quantity  of  muskets  were  also  taken  from  the  wreck.  I  am  informed 
that  she  fired  on  U.  S.  schooner  Sea  Bird  a  short  time  since.  She 
was  a  side-wheel,  walking  beam,  iron  steamer,  with  2  masts,  2  flag- 
staffs,  and  1  smokestack;  and  her  engine  is  marked  “Morgan  Iron 
Works,  New  York,  I860.”  The  Clyde  has  remained  to  blockade  the 
river  during  my  absence.  I  shall  return  to-morrow.  I  have  shipped 
the  cotton  by  the  schooner  Vapor  for  $100,  to  be  discharged  within 
twenty -four  hours  after  his  reporting  to  the  proper  authority,  unless 
he  arrives  on  Sunday  or  a  Sunday  intervenes,  or  very  stormy  weather. 

I  have  also  to  report  that  while  running  for  the  above  steamer  I  got 
ashore  twice,  but  can  not  perceive  that  the  ship  is  injured  at  all, 
except  that  probably  her  copper  paint  is  scraped  off  somewhat. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Smith,

Capture  of  cotton  in  Suwanee  River ,  February  26,  186 f 

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Hooper,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Clyde. 

U.  S.  S.  Clyde, 

Key  West ,  Fla.,  March  2,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  9  o’clock  on  the  morning  of 
the  26th  ultimo  1  sent  two  boats  with  armed  crews  (one  in  charge  of 
W.  B.  Rankin,  acting  ensign,  the  other  in  charge  of  C.  F.  Palmer, 
acting  master’s  mate)  up  the  Suwanee  River  for  the  purpose  of  cap¬ 
turing  a  quantity  of  cotton  which  I  learned  was  secreted  about  10 
miles  up  the  river.  At  10  o’clock  on  the  morning  of  the  27th  one  of 
the  boats  returned  with  intelligence  that  they  had  got  67  bales  of  cot¬ 
ton  on  an  old  scow  and  wanted  more  assistance  to  tow  it  alongside  the 
ship.  I  immediately  sent  all  the  available  force  I  could  and  had  it 
alongside,  and  at  7  p.  m.  had  it  stowed  on  board  and  brought  to  Key 
West  for  adjudication. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Quincy  A.  Hooper, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Comdg.  IJ.  S.  S.  Clyde. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington. 


N.  B.— There  was  no  other  vessel  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture 
or  entitled  to  share  in  prize  money. 

Respectfully, 

Q.  A.  Hooper, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Commanding . 


Detailed  report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Hooper,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Clyde. 

U.  S.  S.  Clyde, 

Key  West,  March  2,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  obedience  to  your  orders  of 
the  22d  ultimo,  I  got  underway  at  4:30  p.  m.  and  proceeded  out  the 
North  West  Passage,  then  stood  W.  N.  W.  till  to  the  northward  of  Tor- 
tuo-as,  then  northerly  till  in  28°  40'  N.  latitude,  then  east  northerly 
tilf  5  o’clock  p.  m. ;  on  the  24th  came  to  anchor  at  Cedar  Keys;  at  5: 30 
got  underway  again  for  Suwanee  River  and  came  to  anchor  at  10  in

658 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


2  fathoms  water  off  the  mouth  of  Suwanee  River;  25th,  at  day¬ 
light,  saw  the  U.  S.  S.  Nita  about  2  miles  inshore;  got  underway  and 
ran  into  7  feet  of  water  and  anchored  alongside  of  her.  Captain  Smith 
of  the  Nita  reported  that  he  had  burned  a  steamer,  Nan-Nan ,  and 
captured  55  bales  of  cotton  the  day  previous,  and  that  there  were  sev¬ 
eral  bales  that  had  gone  adrift  that  he  could  not  get.  At  10  a.  m.  sent 
the  first  cutter  with  an  armed  crew  in  charge  of  Mr.  Jones,  acting 
ensign  and  executive  officer,  inside  to  see  if  he  could  pick  up  any  more 
cotton  or  discover  if  there  were  any  more  vessels  inside  to  run  the 
blockade;  at  2  p.  m.  Mr.  Jones  returned  to  the  ship  with  3  men  he  had 
captured  inside,  after  chasing  them  about  2  miles  and  firing  several 
shot  at  them.  They  reported  that  there  were  about  70  bales  of  cotton 
6  or  7  miles  up  the  river  secreted  in  a  creek.  I  immediately  sent  two 
boats  with  armed  crews,  one  in  charge  of  Mr.  Jones,  the  other  in 
charge  of  Mr.  Dexter,  master’s  mate,  taking  one  of  the  prisoners  as 
guide. 

February  26,  at  7  a.  m. ,  the  boats  returned  and  reported  they  had 
mistaken  the  river  and  could  not  find  the  cotton.  At  9  a.  m.  sent  the 
boats  in  again  with  fresh  crews  (the  others  being  completely  exhausted) 
in  charge  of  Mr.  Rankin,  acting  ensign,  and  Mr.  Palmer,  master’s 
mate  (the  U.  S.  S.  Nita  underway,  bound  to  Cedar  Keys  to  land  her 
cotton  captured  the  day  before).  Boats  gone  all  day. 

February  27,  at  10  a.  m.,  Mr.  Palmer  returned  to  the  ship,  stating 
that  Mr.  Rankin  had  sent  him  back  for  more  assistance;  that  they  had 
found  67  bales  of  cotton  up  a  creek  about  10  miles  from  the  vessel  on 
an  old  scow;  that  they  could  not  get  the  scow  out  on  account  of  trees 
having  been  felled  across  the  creek  to  stop  up  the  passage;  that  they 
had  rafted  the  cotton  and  had  towed  it  down  to  the  East  Pass.  I  sent 
the  boat  right  back  again  with  a  fresh  crew;  also,  my  other  boat  to 
assist  in  towing  the  cotton  alongside,  which  they  succeeded  in  doing 
by  5  o’clock  p.  m.,  and  at  7  had  the  cotton  in  on  deck  and  stowed. 
The  U.  S.  S.  Nita  returned  at  4  this  p.  m. 

Februarjr  28,  at  2  p.  m.,  got  underway;  at  9  came  to  anchor  at 
Cedar  Ke}7s. 

February  29,  took  on  board  30  tons  of  coal. 

March  1,  at  10  o’clock  a.  m.,  got  underway,  proceeded  with  all  pos¬ 
sible  dispatch  for  Key  West,  where  we  came  to  anchor  at  8  o’clock 
this  p.  m. 

1  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Quincy  A.  Hooper, 

Acting  Volunteer/'  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  U.  S.  8.  Clyde.

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Rankin,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  boat  expedition  from  the 

U.  S.  S.  Clyde. 

U.  S.  S.  Clyde, 

Off  Suwanee  River,  Fla. ,  February  27,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  obedience  to  your  orders,  I 
proceeded  jmsterday  with  an  armed  boat’s  crew  of  five  men,  accom¬ 
panied  by  a  refugee  as  guide,  up  the  Suwanee  River  for  the  purpose 
of  discovering  and  capturing,  if  possible,  a  quantity  of  cotton,  which 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


659 


was  reported  to  be  on  board  a  tiat  and  concealed  in  one  of  the  creeks 
communicating  with  the  river,  and  which  was  also  reported  to  belong 
to  the  so-called  Confederate  States  Government. 

At  a  point  which  I  judged  to  be  about  10  miles  from  the  river’s 
mouth  I  entered  a  small  creek,  up  which  1  proceeded  about  half  a 
mile,  where  I  discovered  67  bales  of  cotton. 

It  appearing  to  me  inexpedient  to  remove  the  cotton  in  the  flat,  I 
proceeded  to  unload  and  float  it  down  the  creek  to  the  Suwanee. 
Before  getting  all  the  cotton  out  of  the  creek  I  was  reinforced  by 
Acting  Master’s  Mate  Palmer,  from  this  vessel,  in  charge  of  an  armed 
boat’s  crew. 

After  forming  the  whole  into  a  raft  in  the  Suwanee,  I  proceeded  to 
tow  it  down  the  river.  At  about  2  o’clock  a.  m.  of  this  day  I  got  out 
of  the  river.  At  daylight,  finding  myself  farther  from  the  ship  than 

1  anticipated,  I  dispatched  Mr.  Palmer  in  his  boat  to  report  to  you 
and  request  you,  if  you  thought  proper,  to  send  assistance,  as  my  men 
were  exhausted  with  the  arduous  labors  they  had  performed  during 
the  previous  twenty-four  hours. 

At  about  9  a.  m.  the  raft  grounded  on  an  oyster  bar,  soon  after 
which  the  U.  S.  schooner  Annie  hove  in  sight,  stood  in  as  near  as  pos¬ 
sible,  and  anchored.  Leaving  2  men  in  charge  of  the  cotton,  I  went 
on  board  the  Annie  for  the  purpose  of  getting  assistance  in  case  Mr. 
Palmer  should  fail  to  return  to  the  ship  and  notify  you.  Acting  Mas¬ 
ter  Williams,  commanding  the  Annie,  stated  that  he  was  unable  to  take 
the  cotton  on  board  his  vessel,  but  promised  to  remain  where  he  could 
protect  me  until  assistance  came  from  you.  He  refreshed  both  me  and 
my  men  with  coffee  and  food  and  I  returned  to  the  raft.  At  about  1 
o’clock  p.  m.  the  Clyde  hove  in  sight,  and  soon  after  Acting  Master’s 
Mate  Dexter  arrived  with  a  fresh  crew  and  orders  for  me  and  1113^  crew 
to  return  on  board  the  Clyde.  I  accordingly  reported  on  board  about 

2  o’clock  p.  m. 

It  gives  me  pleasure  to  state  that  Mr.  Palmer  and  all  the  men  placed 
under  my  command  obeyed  my  orders  promptly  and  labored  with 
great  zeal  and  energy  to  accomplish  the  object  of  the  expedition. 

While  among  the  islands  at  the  mouth  of  the  river  1  discovered  a 
boat  with  a  number  of  men  in  it.  Being  unable  to  satisfy  myself  they 
were  not  enemies  endeavoring  to  recapture  the  cotton  I  had  taken,  I 
ordered  some  rifles  to  be  discharged  at  them,  after  which  I  heard  no 
more  from  them. 

Verv  respectfully,  W.  B.  Rankin, 

Acting  Ensign ,  U  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Q.  A.  Hooper, 

Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Clyde.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding 
blockade  running  in  Ocklockonee  River. 

No.  83.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  March  186 f. 

Sir:  Your  letter  of  February  13,  enclosing  the  copy  of  one  from  the 
U.  S.  minister  at  Paris,  relative  to  blockade  running  at  the  Ocklockonee 
River,  has  been  received,  and  1  have  sent  an  additional  tender  (the 
Annie)  to  attend  specially  to  that  portion  of  the  coast.  Blockading  ves¬ 
sels  have  been  constantly  stationed  off  St.  Marks  and  at  the  East  Pass  of 
St.  George’s  Sound,  anj  from  the  time  of  my  having  assumed  com¬ 
mand  of  this  squadron  the  attention  of  both  has  been  directed  to  the 
Ocklockonee  River,  in  consequence  of  which  (as  will  be  seen  by  a  ref¬ 
erence  to  my  reports)  repeated  boat  expeditions  have  been  sent  there, 
resulting  sometimes  in  captures  and  sometimes  in  the  destruction  of 
salt  works,  not  without  frequent  little  skirmishes  with  the  enemy.  By 
my  direction,  also,  boats  have  been  sent  up  this  river,  in  common  with 
most  of  the  other  rivers  on  the  coast  of  Florida,  by  night,  with  a  view 
to  shifting  the  stakes  which  mark  out  the  channels,  in  order  that  block¬ 
ade  runners  might  be  deceived  and  run  ashore,  where  they  would  be 
at  the  mercy  of  our  boats.  1  am,  therefore,  disposed  to  think  that 
the  amount  of  blockade  running  in  this  region  has  been  overestimated; 
but  with  the  schooner  Annie  cruising  permanently  at  the  mouth  of  the 


662 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


river,  there  will  be  very  little  more  of  it  in  future.  It  is  but  a  short 
time  since  the  steamer  Laura  and  a  schooner  loaded  with  cotton  were 
captured  in  this  vicinity. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Browne ,  U  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  bark 
Restless ,  requesting  'instructions  regarding  f  urnishing  supplies  to 
refugees  and  the  enlistment  of  ex- Confederates. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrews  Bay ,  Florida ,  March  1 ,  186  Jh 
Sir:  1  take  the  liberty  to  send  to  Key  West  for  your  disposal  refu¬ 
gees  and  contrabands  as  per  enclosed  list.  *  *  * 

Refugees  and  contrabands,  including  women  and  children,  are  daily 
arriving  at  this  place,  frequently  in  a  destitute  and  suffering  condition. 
A  few  fish  are  caught  here;  but  little  else  can  be  obtained  to  supply 
life.  I  have,  in  a  number  of  instances,  issued  half  rations  to  these  per¬ 
sons  to  keep  them  from  starvation,  and  also  in  some  cases  issued  a  few 
articles  of  clothing  and  small  stores  to  relieve  actual  suffering.  I  have 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


663 


the  honor  to  ask  whether  I  am  justified  in  this  practice  and  authorized 
to  continue  it.  I  have  several  times  enlisted  men  who  have  been  in 
the  rebel  service,  after  taking-  the  oath  promulgated  by  the  President. 
I  have  the  honor  to  ask  whether  I  shall  continue  to  do  so  when  satis¬ 
fied  that  such  persons  are  trustworthy  and  fit  for  the  service. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Browne ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  bark 

Restless ,  requesting  instructions  regarding  the  case  of  two  deserters. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay ,  Florida ,  March  0,  186 S 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  transmit  herewith  a  letter  written  by 
Charles  Parker  and  Augustus  Stevens,  two  deserters  from  the  rebel 
Army,  who  deserted  from  one  of  the  rebel  companies  stationed  at  St. 
Andrew’s  last  year  and  came  off  to  the  Roebuck  and  enlisted  in  that 
vessel  and  deserted  from  her  and  were  conscripted  into  the  rebel  ser¬ 
vice  again  shortly  after  the}T  left  the  Roebuck ,  and  were  serving  in 
Robinson’s  company  when  1  arrived  here.  I  am  well  satisfied  that 
they  have  long  ago'repented  of  having  left  our  service,  and  have  done 
all  they  could  to  induce  Robinson’s  company  to  desert  and  come  to  us. 

The  mothers  of  each  are  good  Union  women  and  solely  dependent 
upon  them  for  support.  I  have  learned  from  refugees  and  deserters 
who  have  since  come  off  that  this  was  their  motive  and  object  in  leav¬ 
ing.  Mrs.  Parker  is  one  of  the  strongest  Union  women  in  Florida, 
and  from  time  to  time  has  given  us  valuable  information.  The  other, 
Stevens’s  mother,  is  too  old  and  feeble  to  take  care  of  herself,  but  a 
good  and  true  Union  woman. 

Parker  and  Stevens  are  now  secreted  in  the  woods  and  have  been 
there  three  weeks  with  42  other  deserters  from  Robinson’s  company, 
and  immediately  sent  their  muskets  and  cartridge  boxes  to  me,  afraid 
to  come  themselves,  fearful  they  would  have  been  treated  as  deserters, 
which  would  most  assuredly  have  been  the  case,  and  they  would  have 
been  sent  to  Key  West  for  your  disposal. 

At  present  it  is  next  to  an  impossibility  to  capture  them,  as  then- 
place  of  concealment  affords  a  surveillance  of  the  ships  and  plenty  of 
time  to  secrete  themselves  in  some  of  the  impenetrable  swamps  or 
morasses  on  the  approach  of  our  boats. 

Mrs.  Parker  handed  me  the  enclosed  letter,  through  Acting  Ensign 
Henry  Eason,  who  saw  her  on  East  Bay  the  27th  instant.  I  therefore 
transmit  Parker’s  and  Stevens’s  muskets  and  await  your  answer  as  to 
what  steps  I  shall  take  in  the  matter. 

Very  respectfully, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Actinp-  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey. 


664 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  'Williams ,  U  8.  Navy ,  commanding  U  8. 
schooner  Annie ,  regarding  the  destruction  of  a  fine  schooner  in  Dead- 
man’s  Bay ,  Florida . 

U.  S.  Schooner  Annie, 
Deadmarf s  Bay ,  Florida ,  March  0,  1861/ . 
Sir:  I  herewith  respectfully  submit  the  following  report  of  the 
destruction  of  a  fine  schooner  at  this  place: 

I  came  to  anchor  at  9  a.  m.,  with  a  strong  norther  blowing,  distant 
about  5  miles  from  land,  and  at  11  a.  m.  made  a  small  boat  standing 
out  for  us.  Set  English  colors  at  masthead.  At  12  the  boat  put  back 
and  1  gave  chase  with  the  schooner,  setting  the  American  ensign.  At 
12:30  p.  m.  made  a  schooner  inside  the  reefs  and  stood  for  her  until 
1:10  p.  m.,  when  we  anchored  in  6  feet  of  water  (having  gained  rapidly 
on  the  small  boat),  manned  our  boat  with  5  men  in  charge  of  Master’s 
Mate  James  T.  Bowling  to  board  the  schooner.  At  1:45  the  chased 
boat  was  seen  to  go  on  board  and  after  stopping  about  ten  minutes 
were  seen  to  tire  the  schooner  and  leave.  At  2  our  boat  boarded  the 
schooner  and  found  her  to  be  a  new  schooner  of  about  80  tons  (lying 
ashore)  and  loaded  with  an  assorted  cargo,  amongst  which  was  a  large 
quantity  of  ammunition.  Our  boat  remained  on  board  but  a  short 
time,  as  the  fire  was  making  great  headway,  and  in  about  three  minutes 
after  their  leaving  a  heavy  explosion  took  place  blowing  out  her  decks. 
At  3:  30  boat  returned  on  board,  and  at  4  a  small  skiff  was  seen  coming 
off  with  a  white  flag  flying.  At  4:15  the  skiff  came  alongside  and 
contained  1  man,  calling  himself  Allen  A.  Stephens,  and  wished  ammu¬ 
nition,  saying  he  belonged  to  a  company  of  20  men  about  to  rise 
against  the  rebel  Government.  I  allowed  the  man  Stephens  to  go  on 
shore  again  and  told  him  I  would  report  the  case  up  the  coast. 
Stephens  says  the  schooner  burned  arrived  here  on  the  29th  ultimo. 

1  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  S.  Williams, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 
Lieutenant-Commander  David  B.  Harmony, 

Commanding  U.  8.  8.  Tahoma.

Besides  these,  the  sloop  boat  Julia ,  of  10  tons,  without  armament 
(other  than  small  arms),  is  used  as  a  guard  vessel  on  the  inside  of  this 
island,  to  overhaul  all  fishing  boats  and  sponging  vessels.  She  has  one

The  Carmita,  of  56  tons,  is  dismasted,  is  without  armament  or  crew 
of  anjr  sort,  and  is  attached  to  the  storehouse  at  this  place  simply  as  a 
lighter. 

Neither  of  these  two  vessels  should  be  entered  on  the  Navy  Register. 

The  schooner  Ezilda ,  formerly  one  of  the  tenders  of  this  squadron, 
was  formally  surveyed,  condemned,  stripped  of  everything  useful  to 
us,  and  finally  sold  at  public  auction.

Report  of  Commander  Armstrong ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 
San  Jacinto ,  regarding  the  capture  of  a  schooner,  formerly  the  Lealtad , 
carrying  cotton. 

U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto, 

At  Sea,  Lat.  2 If  5f,  Long.  83°  20',  March  11,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  by  th  is  ship  of  a  schooner 
loaded  with  cotton.  The  account  of  the  capture  is  as  follows: 

At  noon  this  day  a  sail  was  seen  and  chase  given.  At  2  p.  m.  we 
came  up  with  and  boarded  a  schooner  having  no  papers  and  loaded 
with  132  bales  of  cotton  and  2  barrels  of  turpentine.  Her  master, 
Edward  J.  Norville,  a  citizen  of  Maryland,  acknowledged  having  run 
the  blockade  at  Mobile  on  the  2d  of  March. 


66G 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  schooner  has  no  name  at  present,  but  was  formerly  called  the 
Lealtad.  The  master  admits  having-  thrown  overboard  a  Confederate 
pass  and  papers  after  passing  the  blockade  at  Mobile.  She  is  a  small 
schooner  of  about  40  tons.  Her  crew  consists  of  a  master,  6  men,  and 
a  passenger  who  is  owner  of  the  vessel  and  cargo. 

I  have  taken  out  the  passenger  and  four  o*f  the  crew,  and  send  in  the 
master  and  two  men.  I  send  her  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Charles 
Cunningham,  to  Key  West  for  adjudication.  There  was  no  other  ves¬ 
sel  within  signal  distance  at  the  time  of  capture,  Tortugas  bearing  by 
compass  S.  E.  by  E.,  distant  31  miles. 

I  enclose  prize  list  of  officers  and  men  entitled  to  share  in  the  capture. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jas.  F.  Armstrong,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Burgess ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 
schooner  Beauregard,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
JIannah ,  from  Nassau ,  New  Providence. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

Off  Mosquito  Inlet ,  Fla.,  March  11,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  On  the  lltli 
instant,  while  lying  at  Mosquito  Inlet,  where  I  had  anchored,  having- 
been  carried  to  the  northward  by  the  late  souther^  winds,  at  10  a.  m. 
discovered  a  small  vessel  in  the  offing  bearing  E.  S.  E.  and  steering  bj^ 
the  wind  to  the  southward  and  westw-ard.  I  immediately  got  underway 
and  gave  chase.  At  12:  30  p.  m.  I  boarded  the  stranger,  who  proved 
to  be  the  British  sloop  Hannah ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  from 
Green  Turtle  Cay,  bound  to  Key  West.  The  Hannah  cleared  from 
Nassau  on  the  5th  of  February  (over  live  weeks  ago)  with  1  bale  cotton 
cloth,  which  the  captain  reports  he  hove  overboard,  and  as  she  had  no 
colors,  and  the  captain  could  not  account  for  being  so  far  out  of  the 
regular  course  for  Key  West  to  my  satisfaction,  I  seized  her  as  a  prize 
of  war  and  send  her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication.  There  was  no  other 
vessel  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 

1  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Eras.  Burgess, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Burgess,  L .  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S. 
schooner  Beauregard,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
Linda ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence. 


U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

Off  Mosquito  Inlet ,  Fla. ,  March  11,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  On  the  11th 
instant,  while  lying  at  Mosquito  Inlet,  having  been  carried  to  the  north- 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


667 


ward  by  the  late  southerly  winds,  at  5:  30  a.  m.  discovered  a  schooner 
trying  to  get  in  at  the  inlet.  1  immediately  sent  a  boat  in  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  H.  B.  Colby  to  capture  her.  There  was  also  a  boat 
sent  from  the  U.  S.  schooner  Norfolk  Packet*  for  the  same  purpose  at 
the  same  time,  but  as  they  were  unacquainted  with  the  channel,  Mr. 
Colby  took  the  lead,  but  by  time  the  boats  arrived  at  the  inlet  the 
schooner  had  already  turned  the  point  and  was  sailing  up  the  river 
with  a  fair  wind  and  tide.  Therefore  Mr.  Colby,  being  in  the  head 
boat,  ran  his  boat  on  shore  and,  with  his  men  well  armed,  jumped  on 
shore  and  ran  up  the  bank  of  the  river  and  headed  the  schooner  off, 
and  after  firing  several  musket  shots,  some  of  which  went  through  her 
sails,  she  lowered  her  sails  and  the  boat  from  the  Norfolk  Packet  boarded 
her.  She  proved  to  be  the  British  schooner  Linda ,  of  Nassau,  New 
Providence,  from  Nassau,  bound  to  New  Smyrna,  Fla.,  with  a  cargo 
consisting  of  salt,  liquors,  coffee,  and  dry  goods.  1  therefore  seized 
her  as  a  prize  of  war  and  send  her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Fras.  Burgess, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting-  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Reports  of  Lieutenant-  Commander  McCauley ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding 
U.  S.  8.  Tioga,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  sloop  Sioallow ,  from, 
Comhahee  Rivet',  South  Carolina. 

U.  S.  S.  Tioga, 

Off  Elbow  [  Cay\  Light,  March  20,  186 f 

Admiral:  This  morning  while  lying  off  Elbow  [Cay]  light,  in  lati¬ 
tude  26°  33'  N.,  longitude  76°  25'  W.,  this  vessel  overhauled  and  cap¬ 
tured  the  sloop  Swallow,  from  the  Combahee  River,  S.  C.,  bound  to 
Nassau,  New  Providence.  We  found  on  board  of  her  180  bales  cotton, 
80  barrels  rosin,  and  25  boxes  tobacco.  She  had  also  on  board  an  old 
set  of  Confederate  colors.  No  papers  were  found.  I  have  sent  the 
prize  to  Boston  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Bingham  and  four  men. 
You  will  see  that  of  the  men  sent,  the  time  of  three  will  be  out  within 
thirty  dai^s.  Also  find  enclosed  description  of  prisoners  taken  in  prize. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

E.  Y.  McCauley, 

Lieutenant-  Commander ,  U  S.  Navy,  Comdg.  TJ.  S.  S.  Tioga. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg,  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla. 


U.  S.  S.  Tioga, 

Off  Elbow  Cay,  Bahama  Banks,  March  21,  1861+ . 

Admiral:  Yesterday  afternoon  I  sent  to  market  the  first  invoice  of 
this  year’s  crop  from  your  plantation  in  these  arables,  consisting  of  180 
bales  cotton,  80  barrels  rosin  (Confed.  “rawsom”),  25  boxes  tobacco, 
making  about  the  most  valuable  prize  the  “Tidy”  has  yet  captured.  It 
was  done  up  in  a  sloop  [Swallow\  of  about  100  tons,  from  Combahee 
River,  South  Carolina,  bound  to  Nassau.  A  dozen  Confederacies  were 
on  board,  of  whom  the  captain  and  one  man  were  sent  north  for  the  usual 
general  good.  They  had  been  out  nine  days  and  had  on  board  at  the 
time  of  capture  half  peck  black  beans,  half  peck  moldy  bread,  and  a 
very  little  coffee,  so  that  the  beggars  should  be  grateful  to  us  for  our 
trouble,  as  they  might  have  starved  before  getting  in.  I  sent  her 
north  in  charge  of  Ensign  Bingham  and  four  men  whose  time  will  be  out 
next  month,  taking  care  to  advise  commander  navy  yard  and  Secretary 
of  Navy  as  you  directed,  but  told  Mr.  B.  to  try  and  bring  me  back  four 
men  with  longer  terms  from  receiving  ship  if  he  could  do  it  by  coax¬ 
ing,  etc.  I  think  I  did  right  in  sending  her  to  Boston,  as  there  was 
no  necessity  of  her  paying  a  tax  to  our  loving  friends— lawyers  and 
marshals  and  company— at  Key  West,  and  the  sloop  herself  will  bring 
$2,000  for  the  Quincy  trade  at  Boston. 


670 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  Tioga  is  much  improved  by  your  attentions  to  her  last  time  at 
Key  West.  She  used  to  steam  7  knots  without  the  blower;  she  now 
makes  nearly  9.  I  have  not  had  a  chance  to  try  her  full  speed  save 
that  we  overhauled  the  Oriental  the  other  day,  hand  over  fist. 

The  sloop  had  a  large  set  of  Confederate  colors  on  board,  so  that  she 
won’t  be  “Don  Jose’d”  by  the  land  sharks  of  Yankeeville. 

I  believe  the  young  man  Temple  don’t  share  in  this  prize;  will  }rou 
please  present  him  with  my  regards,  etc. 

It  has  blackened  up  and  barometer  falling  low,  heavy  squalls  of 
wind  and  rain,  and  we  are  using  the  blower  ( Iloni  soil  qui  mal  y  jpense) 
to  get  on  the  Great  Bank  to  receive  hospitably  the  equinox  visit. 
Bless  us,  how  the  little  darling  does  roll!  She’d  make  a  fine  pendulum 
to  time  fuzes  with.  Three  sharp  rolls  to  the  second! 

I  write  this  to  send  by  any  accidental  schooner  we  may  board  en 
route  to  Key  West.  The  official  communication  I  will  hand  you. 

With  kind  greeting  to  all  your  staff  family, 

I  am,  very  respectfullv,  your  obedient  servant, 

Ed.  Y.  McCauley. 


R  eqyort  of  Lieutenant-  Commander  McDougal ,  U.  8.  Navy ,  commanding 
11.  8.  8.  Hendrick  Hudson ,  regarding  the  sinking  of  the  schooner 
Wild  Pigeon,  blockade  runner. 

U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson, 

Key  West,  Ajoril  If  186 f 

Sir:  1  have  to  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the  21st  ultimo,  just 
before  daylight,  a  schooner  was  discovered  about  2  miles  distant  from 
us.  Running  down  for  her  immediately,  and  maneuvering  to  speak 
-  and  ascertain  her  character,  her  captain  suddenly  luffed  across  my 
bows,  and  in  spite  of  all  I  could  do  to  prevent  it,  by  backing  and  using 
the  helm,  I  struck  the  schooner  directly  amidships,  sinking  her  in 
about  three  minutes.  All  the  crew  were  saved  excepting  one  man, 
who,  in  a  fright,  jumped  overboard  and  drowned  before  I  could  lower 
a  b  iat  to  pick  him  up.  In  the  collision  the  stem  of  this  vessel  was 
slightly  damaged.  I  learned  the  following  particulars  concerning  the 
schooner  from  the  captain  and  crew :  Schooner  Wild  Pigeon,  37  tons, 
from  Havana,  bound  to  any  Confederate  port  on  the  Florida  coast. 
Assorted  cargo,  rebel  papers,  and  a  rebel  flag  on  board.  As  all  on 
board  claimed  to  be  foreigners,  I  put  them  ashore  about  10  miles  from 
Tampa,  first  searching  them  and  taking  all  their  money  with  the  excep¬ 
tion  of  the  amount  allowed  by  the  court,  and  recommended  them  to 
seek  the  protection  of  their  respective  consuls.  The  damage  done  my 
stem  made  it  imperative  on  me  to  go  to  the  nearest  place  for  repairs, 
which  was  Tampa  Bay,  and  after  concluding  the  work  I  again  went  to 
sea.  One  of  the  blockade  runners  being  a  carpenter,  I  retained  him 
to  assist  in  the  work,  and  brought  him  to  this  place,  as  a  witness  in 
the  case.  The  money  taken  from  the  prisoners,  which  consisted  of 
$726,  Confederate  money,  4  doubloons,  1  half,  1  quarter,  and  1  eighth 
doubloon,  and  $3.18  in  silver,  I  have  turned  over  to  the  prize  commis¬ 
sioner  and  taken  his  receipt  for  the  same.  I  will  also  add  that  three  of 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


671 


the  men  taken  were  captured  in  endeavoring  to  run  the  blockade  in 
the  Laura ,  and  that  this  was  at  least  their  second  attempt. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  J.  McDougal, 

Lieutenant-  Commander ,  II  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Hear- Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey,

Order  of  Acting  Rear- Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Fleming ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Sagamore , 
in  reference  to  a  suggested  expedition  to  Suwanee  River  for  the 
capture  of  cotton. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  March  186 h- 

Sir:  Alex.  Odum,  a  refugee  sent  down  here  from  the  Nita ,  pro¬ 
fesses  to  be  the  owner  of  Clay  Landing,  together  with  a  large  tract  of 
land  thereabouts;  to  be  a  pilot  for  the  Suwanee  River;  to  know  where 
some  300  bales  of  cotton  are  stowed  in  that  vicinity,  and  to  be  able 
and  anxious  to  conduct  a  force  up  the  river  for  its  capture,  and  at  the 
same  time  to  bring  away  his  family  and  effects. 

He  represents  that  the  place  is  wholly  without  militar}^  guard,  but, 
on  the  other  hand,  it  is  understood  here  from  different  sources  that 
the  rebel  troops  are  returning  to  their  former  stations  as  coast  guard. 

I  send  the  man  back  to  you  by  the  Honduras  that  you  may  judge  of 
the  probable  feasibility  of  such  an  undertaking,  and  if  confident  of 
success  that  }mu  may  attempt  it  with  the  combined  force  of  the  Saga¬ 
more  and  Nita.  Should  you  deem  it  expedient  to  make  the  attempt, 
you  are  hereby  authorized  to  enter  Odum  on  your  books  as  pilot,  at 
$60  a  month,  from  this  date  until  his  return  to  Key  West. 

The  difficulties  that  occur  to  me,  and  against  which  you  will  have  to 
guard,  are  as  follows:  We  have  no  assurance  of  Odum’s  fidelity, 
beyond  his  having  taken  the  oath  of  allegiance.  The  banks  of  the 
Suwanee  may  be  again  well  guarded,  and  an  ambush  attempted  upon 
our  party;  or,  if  not,  the  cotton  might  bo  burned  on  our  approach. 
If  a  boat  expedition  were  sent  up  by  night,  the  distance  and  the  cur¬ 
rent  would  probably  keep  them  en  route  until  daylight,  or  later,  when 
our  men  would  be  too  much  fatigued  either  to  resist  a  considerable 
force  or  to  carry  off  the  cotton  before  such  a  force  could  be  gathered 
in  from  the  neighborhood.  It  might,  perhaps,  be  possible  to  conceal 
our  party  throughout  the  day  in  the  vicinity,  and  to  make  the  descent 
with  the  men  refreshed  at  daylight  the  next  morning. 

You  will  exercise  a  sound  discretion  in  this  matter,  after  getting  all 
the  information  possible.  One  of  the  tenders  can,  if  necessary,  con¬ 
tinue  the  blockade  of  Cedar  Keys  during  your  absence. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Lieutenant-Commander  Charles  E.  Fleming,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Gunhoat  Sagamore.

Letter  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Rear- 
Admiral  Farragut ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  March  2 If.,  186 f 

My  Dear  Admiral:  Your  letter  of  the  14th  instant  and  the  one  by 
the  Bermuda  without  date  are  received.  The  extraordinary  expedi¬ 
tion  of  General  Gillmore  to  East  Florida,  without  intimation  or 
informing  us  or  General  Banks,  has  met  the  fate  of  other  ill-contrived 
enterprises.  The  troops  have  been  whipped.  With  the  1,500  men 
which  you  tell  me  could  have  been  spared  from  Pensacola  with  the 
necessary  transports  under  the  protection  of  our  gunboats,  a  landing 
could  have  been  made  at  St.  Marks,  Tallahassee  captured,  and  such  a 
diversion  contrived  as  to  have  made  success  to  Gillmore’s  column  more 
than  probable. 

A  refugee  from  the  enemy’s  lines  informs  me  that  the  first  intima¬ 
tion  they  had  of  the  expedition  was  through  the  columns  of  the  New 
York  Times,  which  induced  Beauregard  to  dispatch  9,000  men  from 
Savannah  by  the  Florida  Railroad  to  the  assistance  of  General 
Fin[e]gan. 

^  When  I  heard  of  Gillmore’s  landing  at  Jacksonville  I  proposed  to 
General  Woodbury  to  make  a  diversion  in  his  favor,  but  he  had  no 
transport  and  no  troops  to  spare.  My  vessels  were  at  the  time  cruis¬ 
ing,  repairing,  or  so  situated  on  blockade  that  to  withdraw  them  would 
open  the  ports;  anyhow,  the  information  reached  me  so  late  that  it 
would  have  been  of  no  avail. 

1  reciprocate  with  you  in  perfectly  ignoring  personal  interests  or 
private  feeling,  but  going  in  with  heart  and  soul  for  the  good  of  the 
service  and  the  perpetuation  of  the  nation  in  its  entirety. 

Nothing  will  please  me  more  than  to  hoist  once  more  the  square 
red  flag  and  lead  the  van  of  your  squadron  into  Mobile  Bay,  to  the 
capture  of  forts  Morgan  and  Gaines,  as  well  as  the  city.  Put  me  down 
for  two  chances,  as  the  jackass  said  to  the  monkey  at  the  lion’s  ball. 

I  appreciate  your  kind  invitation  to  join  you  when  the  big  fight  is  to 
come  off,  and  will  be  ready  with  the  San  Jacinto  and  what  gunboats 
may  be  in  hand  at  the  time  you  notify  me,  unless  the  Georgia  and 
Florida ,  rebel  privateers  which  have  escaped  from  France,  shall  be  at 
the  time  menacing  commerce  in  my  neighborhood  or  some  unforeseen 
danger  on  my  station  shall  prevent. 

I  enclose  herewith  the  names  and  draft  of  the  suitable  vessels  to 
take  with  me,  if  within  reach  and  available  at  the  time  you  make  the 
call. 

If  they  can  not  be  spared,  I  will  be  obliged  to  you  for  a  gunboat  as 
you  suggest. 

I  can  make  no  suggestions  without  consultation  and  knowing  what 
tools  we  shall  have  to  work  with,  but  when  vou  get  the  necessary 
troops  to  land,  cut  off  and  isolate  Fort  Morgan,  and  afterwards  Fort 
Gaines.  I  am  subject  to  your  call,  or  even  without  the  latter. 

Trusting  that  your  health  and  usefulness  may  be  preserved  to  the 
country  for  many  years, 

I  remain,  your  friend  and  obedient  servant, 

_  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Rear-Admiral  D.  G.  Farragut, 

Commanding  II  est  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

C.  Campbell,  and  the  schooner  outside,  both  to  meet  at  Sarasota,  the 
object  being  to  intercept  and  capture  the  sloop  and  to  make  a  recon- 
noissance  for  salt  works.  She  was  taken  as  above  by  the  armed  boats 
of  the  htonvwall  and  this  vessel,  the  launch  of  the  bark  J.  L.  Davis 
being  in  signal  distance  at  the  time  of  capture.  I  beg  to  enclose  here¬ 
with  the  report  of  Acting  Master  H.  B.  Carter,  and 'at  the  same  time 
wish  to  commend  the  zeal  and  vigilance  displayed  by  Acting  Master 

.  B.  Cartel  and  Acting  Ensign  George  C.  Campbell  in  accomplishing 
the  most  important  object  of  the  expedition. 

Before  the  boats  got  to  her  the  captain  and  pilot  got  ashore  and 
escaped.  The  three  persons  found  on  board  I  send  down.  They  were 
interested  in  the  cotton  and  acted  very  well  at  the  time  of  the  capture 
aving  pi  evented  the  captain  from  setting  fire  to  her,  although  the 
kindling  wood  was  already  laid  and  they  had  plenty  of  time  to  have 
set  her  on  lire  and  made  their  escape  before  the  boats  got  to  her. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  Van  Sioe,

U.  S.  Schooner  Stonewall, 

Tampa  Bay,  March  28,  186 h. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report:  At  10  a.  m., 
23d  instant,  got  underway  and  stood  out  the  S.  W.  Channel.  At  1:15 
p.  m.  passed  Longboat  Inlet.  In  consequence  of  the  heavy  sea  on 
the  bar,  could  not  communicate  with  the  boats,  but  sighted  them. 
Stood  on  down  the  coast,  wind  N.  N.  W.  At  4:30  p.  m.  came  to 
anchor  outside  the  bar  at  Sarasota  Inlet.  At  4  p.  m.  the  launch  and 
cutter  came  out  of  New  Cut  [Bass]  and  stood  for  the  schooner,  wind 
E.  Communicated  with  Acting  Ensign  G.  C.  Campbell;  gave  him 
orders  to  go  inside  and  camp;  through  the  night  fresh  breezes  from 
east. 

Thursday,  March  24,  at  8:30  a.  m.,  boats  stood  out  the  channel  to 
sound;  found  plenty  of  water  for  the  schooner.  Got  underway  and
