xeport  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Fleming ,  U  S.  Navy ,  commanding 
U.  S.  S.  Sagamore,  regarding  boat  expedition  and  chase  a, nd  destruc¬ 
tion  of  schooners. 

U.  S.  S.  Sagamore, 

Of  Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  April  2,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the  28th 
ultimo  a  schooner  was  discovered  by  our  masthead  lookout,  bearing 
to  the  southward  and  eastward,  and  as  she  was  in  shoaler  water  than 
this  vessel  could  run  in  I  sent  three  boats  to  intercept  her,  as  she  was 
evidently  bound  in  to  one  of  the  rivers  that  empty  on  this  part  of  the 
coast.  Toward  night,  two  of  the  boats  returned  after  an  unsuccessful 
chase  of  five  hours  and  a  half,  and  as  the  weather  looked  threatening, 
with  the  barometer  falling,  1  felt  much  concerned  about  the  safety  of 
the  crew  in  the  absent  boat,  and  this  was  considerably  increased  by 
the  state  of  the  weather  during  that  night,  the  next  day,  and  the  suc¬ 
ceeding  one,  for  it  blew  furiously,  with  heavy  rain  squalls  and  an 
ugly  sea  running. 

"On  the  morning  of  the  31st  the  boat  returned  to  the  ship,  the  crew 
having  undergone  severe  suffering  from  hunger  and  exposure,  but 
they  did  their  duty  nobly  under  all  their  trials,  and  moreover  were 
successful  in  destroying  two  schooners  (with  their  cargoes)  attempting 
to  run  the  blockade.  The  officer  in  charge  of  the  boat,  Acting  Master’s 
Mate  Francisco  Silva,  is  entitled  to  great  credit  for  the  skill,  perse¬ 
verance,  and  energy  he  displayed,  and  I  take  pleasure  in  commending 
him  to  your  favorable  notice. '  Please  find  enclosed  herewith  a  copy 
of  his  report.  The  ship’s  papers  of  the  schooner  Etta,  with  some 
other  articles,  together  with  two  men  taken  from  her,  I  send  to  Ivey 
West  by  the  steamer  Honduras.  One  of  the  men  (Thomas  Martin), 
you  will  observe,  has  his  name  entered  on  the  shipping  articles  as  mate, 
but.  he  sa}Ts  he  did  not  serve  in  that  capacity;  the  other  one’s  name 
(William  Kelly)  does  not  appear  there  at  all;  they  both  claim  to  be 
British  subjects. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  E.  Fleming, 

L  ieutena  n  t-  Com  man  der ,  Commanding . 

Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

Note.— There  were  no  means  of  ascertaining  the  name  of  the  first 
schooner  burned. 

C.  E.  F. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  two 
expeditions  in  St.  Andrew’s  Bay  for  the  destruction  of  salt  works, 
April  2  and  12, 1864,. 

No.  131.]  U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  April  21,  1864- 

Sir:  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  William  R.  Browne,  commanding 
the  bark  Restless  at  St.  Andrew’s  Sound,  reports  the  result  of  two 
more  expeditions,  made  under  his  orders,  to  harass  the  enemy  in  that 
vicinity. 

The  first  consisted  of  8  refugees,  in  a  dugout  canoe,  who  ascended 
the  Wetappo  River  some  20  miles  to  White  Bluffs  [White’s  Bluff] 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


677 


and  there  destroyed  about  2,000  bushels  of  salt,  brought  away  the 
sacks,  and  captured  a  barge  36  feet  long,  11  feet  beam,  and  3  feet 
deep,  sloop  rigged  and  decked,  which  he  is  fitting  up  with  a  howitzer 
tor  further  operations.  A  heavy  rain  had  fortunately  driven  the  cav- 
!l!pr  guard  away  from  the  place  for  shelter,  so  that  no  resistance  was 
ottered.  Twenty-three  refugees  were  brought  off. 

The  other  expedition  consisted  of  22  men  in  the  boats  of  the  Restless , 
who  proceeded  up  East  Bay  during  another  heavj7  rain  storm,  which 
had  again  sent  the  guard  to  look  for  shelter.  They  succeeded  in 
destroying  two  Government  salt  works,  with  300  bushels  of  salt  and 
about  the  same  quantity  of  corn  and  meal,  without  opposition  and 
brought  off  one  contraband. 

Acting  A  olunteer  Lieutenant  Browne  reports  that  there  are  five 
companies  of  rebel  troops  in  that  vicinity  to  guard  the  salt  works,  and 
that  these  works  are  rebuilt  as  fast  as  he  destroys  them. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Baieey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blekdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


R&port  of  Acting  T  olunteer  Lieutenant  Browne,  U.  S.  Na/vy,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  bark  Restless,  regarding  the  result  of  two  expeditions  in  St. 
Andrew’s  Bay ,  April  2  and  12, 186 f  for  the  destruction  of  salt  works. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew'’ s  Bay ,  Fla. ,  April  R ,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  Ascertaining 
that  a  salt  barge  wTe  have  attempted  to  capture  several  times  but  failed  — 
from  our  ignorance  of  her  exact  locality — was  moored  up  the  Wetappo 
River,  near  the  Government  salt  house  at  AVhite  Bluffs,  61  miles  from 
this  ship,  I  determined  to  make  another  trial  in  hopes  that  by  the 
assistance  of  some  Union  refugees,  who  knew  the  exact  position  and  who 
volunteered  to  accompany  us,  we  might  accomplish  our  object  this  time. 
Accordingly  I  fitted  out  an  expedition  of  refugees,  8  in  number  (3  of 
which  had  previously  entered  the  service),  deeming  it  more  prudent  to 
intrust  it  to  them  than  to  expose  my  own  officers  and  men  in  an 
enemy’s  country  so  far  from  the  vessel,  where  I  was  satisfied  that  at 
least  one  company  of  cavalry  and  one  of  infantry  were  to  be  either 
attacked  or  shunned,  they  serving  as  a  guard  at  the  salt  house,  in  which 
were  stored  from  1,500  to  2,000  bushels  of  salt.  Having  provided  the 
men  with  shotguns  belonging  to  themselves,  with  the  exception  of  3 
attached  to  this  vessel,  who  were  furnished  with  rifles,  and  taking  the 
precaution  to  supply  them  also  with  3  axes  to  cut  away  trees  which 
were  felled  across  the  river  at  short  distances  for  5  or  6  miles  below 
the  barge,  they  proceeded  on  their  mission  on  the  evening  of  the  31st 
of  March  in  a  canoe  or  dugout  we  had  previously  captured.  They 
did  not  arrive  at  the  head  of  the  Wetappo,  where  the  barge  lay,  until 
the  morning  of  the  2d,  owing  to  the  obstructions  in  the  river,  which 
had  to  be  cleared  in  order  to  bring  her  out.  Fortunately  for  our 
party,  a  heavy  rain  storm  set  in  and  the  cavalry  company  had  just  left 
the  premises  for  a  place  of  more  shelter  from  the  storm  and  were 
absent  the  whole  day,  which  enabled  our  party  to  empty  all  the  salt 
from  the  storehouse  in  the  river  and  bring  off  the  sacks,  which  occu¬ 
pied  nearly  the  whole  day,  not  one  person  appearing  to  molest  them. 


678 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Having  accomplished  their  object,  they  jumped  into  their  bateau 
(which  pulled  4  oars  and  is  fast)  and  the  remaining-  men  in  the  barge, 
and  proceeded  on  their  way  down,  slowly  poling  and  towing  the  barge 
down  a  very  narrow  and  crooked  river  for  more  than  20  miles.  On 
their  way  down  they  were  detained  in  some  places  two  hours  by  new 
obstructions  occasioned  by  the  heavy  storm,  but  having  picked  up 
some  23  persons,  men,  women,  and  children  (Union  refugees)  in  their 
raid,  they  were  enabled  to  surmount  all  difficulties  and  arrived  safely 
in  sight  of  the  ship  at  sundown  of  the  4th.  One  of  the  party  having 
previously  landed  and  walked  to  the  seabeach  in  sight  of  the  ship, 
communicated  the  affair  to  me,  when  I  immediately  sent  off  the 
first  and  second  cutter  to  their  assistance.  The  wind  being  ahead,  she 
was  towed  from  Davis  Point  to  the  island  abreast  of  the  ship  and 
anchored  at  midnight.  The  next  morning  I  examined  her  and  found 
her  to  be  just  such  a  vessel  as  we  are  in  need  of  for  this  place,  being 
obliged  to  go  with  the  ship  up  the  different  arms  of  the  bay  when  we 
want  wood  to  cover  our  wooding  party,  as  it  has  come  to  my  knowl¬ 
edge  that  persons  are  secreted  in  the  woods  watching  an  opportunity  to 
kill  some  of  our  men  in  retaliation  for  the  injuries  we  have  done  them. 
She  is  nearly  a  new  barge,  36  feet  long,  3  feet  deep,  and  11  feet  beam, 
built  of  2-inch  yellow-pine  plank,  and  is  perfectly  tight,  sloop  rigged, 
and  has  an  open  hatch  amidships  12  feet  long,  in  which  I  have  built  a 
platform  and  laid  a  circle  for  our  12-pounder  howitzer,  which  can  be 
tired  from  almost  any  point  of  the  compass.  She  has  new  lug  main¬ 
sail,  which  1  have  altered  to  a  boom  mainsail,  and  have  made  a  new 
mast  and  bowsprit  and  given  her  a  jib.  I  have  also  built  lee  boards  4 
feet  wide  and  5  feet  deep,  and  think  that  she  will  work  admirably. 
She  will  be  ready  by  the  8th,  and  would  be  just  the  sort  of  craft  for 
covering  parties  of  men  landing  to  destroy  the  extensive  salt  works 
which  are  constantly  being  put  up  on  the  numerous  arms  of  this  bay, 
her  draft  being  only  13  inches,  with  30  men  provisioned  for  one  week. 
I  have  further  to  report  that  boats  are  being  built  up  the  bay  for  the 
purpose  of  keeping  deserters  from  coming  to  us.  On  the  evening  of 
the  12th  I  fitted  out  an  expedition  of  22  men  to  go  up  East  Bay  fori the 
purpose  of  destroying  some  boats  and  2  large  Government  salt  works. 
They  saw  no  boats,  but  learned  they  were  in  West  Bay  and  that  there 
were  5  companies  of  rebel  soldiers — 3  of  cavalry,  and  2  of  infantry — 
there  to  protect  them  and  the  salt  works  (which  are  being  put  up  as 
fast  as  we  destroy  them,  the  location  being  so  good).  The  expedition 
proved  a  success  as  far  as  the  salt  works  were  concerned,  and  Acting 
Ensign  Henry  Eason  deserves  great  credit  for  the  manner  in  which  he 
conducted  the  expedition.  They  succeeded  in  destroying  two  large 
Government  works  which  employed  a  large  number  of  hands.  They 
also  destroyed  a  storehouse  containing  200  bushels  corn,  300  bushels 
salt,  and  50  bushels  meal.  One  contraband  joined  the  expedition  and 
claimed  our  protection.  They  did  this  during  a  heavy  rain  storm  with¬ 
out  expending  a  single  cartridge.  I  have  also  pleasure  in  speaking  of 
Rodney  H.  Powers,  surgeon’s  steward,  and  John  Fort,  yeoman,  who 
took  a  very  active  part  in  the  destruction  of  the  salt  works  and  store¬ 
house. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Ilealy ,  l S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  schooner 

Beauregard ,  'regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner  Spunky. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

St.  Augustine ,  April  9,  1867 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report.  On  the  7th, 
while  cruising  off  Cape  Canaveral,  the  cape  then  bearing  south  by  west 
Id  miles  distant,  I  discovered  a  small  schooner  to  the  northward  and 
eastward.  I  immediately  gave  chase  and  at  9  p.  m.  came  up  with  and 
boarded  her.  She  proved  to  be  the  English  schooner  Spunky ,  of  Nassau, 
New  Providence,  from  Mosquito  Inlet,  bound  to  Green  Turtle  Cay, 
Bahamas,  with  a  cargo  consisting  of  12  bales  of  cotton.  I  seized  her 
as  a  prize  and  took  her  to  St.  Augustine  for  adjudication. 

There  were  no  vessels  or  boats  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  C.  Healy, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  G.

Cuba,  with  a  view  to  communicating  with  the  Powhatan  and  getting  later 
news  from  Havana.  Should  you  learn  nothing  more  from  these  sources,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Smithy  (  .  S.  Navy,  commanding 
IT.  S.  S.  Nita,  regarding  the  capture  of  schooner  Three  Brothers. 

U.  S.  S.  Nita, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  April  13,  186k • 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  4:30  p.  m.  of  April  11, 1864, 
while  running  along  St.  Martin’s  Reef,  I  discovered  a  schooner  at 
anchor  near  the  mouth  of  the  Homosassa  River.  At  5:45  p.  m.,  beino- 
unable  to  steer  directly  for  her  on  account  of  the  intervening  reeC 
sent  both  boats,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  J.  Hancock,  to  board  her.’ 
At  6  p.  m.  we  cleared  the  reef  and  steered  directly  for  the  schooner. 
At  6:30  p.  m.  the  schooner  made  all  sail  and  steered  E.  S.  E.  in  toward, 
and  afterward  S.  E.  partly  along,  the  land,  the  wind  at  the  time  being 
W.  N.  W.  At  6:50  p.  m.,  being  in  5^  feet  water,  I  fired  two  shells  at 
the  schooner,  one  of  which  struck  very  near  her.  At  7  p.  m.  we 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


681 


grounded  in  5  feet  water  and  fired  another  shell,  the  schooner  being 
partly  perceptible  in  the  dark.  8:20  p.  m.,  Mr.  Hancock  (in  the 
cutter)  hailed  the  schooner  and  ordered  him  to  heave  to.  They  not 
complying  with  the  order,  Mr.  H.  fired  several  volleys  of  musketry 
at  them,  which  induced  them  to  let  go  the  anchor  and  haul  down  sails 
about  8:40  p.  m.,  when  he  boarded  and  took  possession  of  her  as  a 
prize.  The  gig  reached  her  some  time  afterwards,  having  been  detained 
by  her  leaky  condition,  several  times  having  to  stop  to  bail  her  out. 
At  ten  minutes  past  midnight  the  cutter  returned,  bringing  three  pris¬ 
oners  from  the  schooner  (which  proved  to  be  the  Three  Brothers ,  from 
Ha\  ana,  with  an  assorted  cargo  and  three  passengers).  The  captain 
and  passengers  had  landed  and  taken  with  them  a  package,  said  to  be 
a  6-pounder  gun.  One  of  the  prisoners  called  himself  Charles  Mashon 
and  conducted  hirnself  very  badly,  using  the  most  insulting  language, 
threatening  the  lives  of  officer  and  crew,  cursing  the  Yankees  and  the 
President,  etc.  I  put  him  in  double  irons  and  confined  him  below 
during  the  night,  I  send  him,  with  two  others,  by  the  Honduras. 
He  (Mashon)  came  on  board  the  schooner  from  the  shore  for  the  pur¬ 
pose  of  piloting  her  into  Bayport,  [Fla.].  At  4:30  a.  m.  of  12th  this 
ship  floated,  and  at  daylight  I  ran  out  into  9  feet  of  water.  At  same 
time  discovered  the  prize,  bearing  S.  E.,  about  12 miles  from  us,  under 
all  sail,  standing  toward  us  with  a  moderate  easterly  wind.  At  10:15 
a.  m.  she  passed  within  hail  and  received  orders  to  proceed  to  Cedar 
Keys,  where  we  both  arrived  last  evening. 

No  papers  or  colors  have  been  found  on  board. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Smith, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Browne,  U.  S.  Navy,  command- 
ing  U.  S.  hark  Restless,  regarding  cruise  in  East  Bay  for  the  destruc¬ 
tion  of  salt  works. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay ,  Florida ,  April  22,  186 J. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  fitted  out  the  bark  on  the 
afternoon  of  the  17th  for  a  cruise  up  East  Bay  to  destroy  salt  works, 
which  are  constantly  being  put  up  as  fast  as  opportunities  occur  after 
we  demolish  them.  She  was  absent  four  days,  and  destroyed  very 
large  works,  the  only  establishment  in  operation  there.  There  are  no 
other  works  on  East  Bay  at  present,  and  I  hardly  think  they  will 
attempt  to  make  salt  on  this  bay  again,  as  they  are  aware  of  our  having 
mounted  a,  howitzer  on  the  barge.  There  are  some  few  small  concerns 
in  operation  on  West  Bay,  and  1  am  only  waiting  an  addition  to  those 
now  there  when  I  shall  fit  out  another  expedition,  and  am  in  hopes  of 
making  quite  a  formidable  raid,  one  that  will  make  it  worth  our  while 
to  report. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Commanding  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Chase,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S. 
schooner  Fox,  regarding  the  chase  and  destruction  of  the  schooner 
Good  Llope  near  the  mouth  of  the  Homosassa  River. 


U.  S.  Schooner  Fox, 

Key  West ,  Fla.,  April  23,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  18th  instant,  at  12  m., 
latitude  28°  34'  N.,  longitude  83°  10'  W.,  saw  a  topsail  schooner  stand- 


684 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


ing  to  the  eastward.  Made  sail  in  chase,  and  when  within  about  2% 
miles  set  our  ensign  and  fired  a  gun.  She  set  the  English  ensign,  but 
did  not  come  to. 

I  afterwards  fired  eight  shot  at  her,  but  without  effect.  She  crossed 
St.  Martin’s  Reef  and  stood  to  the  northward.  Having  run  into  as 
shoal  water  as  I  could,  I  sent  the  boat  armed,  Acting  Ensign  Jackson 
in  charge,  on  the  inside  the  reef  while  I  went  up  outside. 

At  5  p.  m.,  finding  she  could  not  escape,  the  schooner  was  run  ashore 
and  abandoned  near  the  mouth  of  the  Homosassa  River.  Ensign  Jack- 
son  boarded  her,  but  as  there  were  two  armed  rebel  boats  coming  out

Report  of  Acting  Master  I  Tan  Boskirk ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  boat 
expedition  from  the  II  S.  bar k  Pursuit,  for  the  destruction  of  salt 
works  in  St.  Josephs  Bay. 

U.  S.  Bark  Pursuit, 

St.  Joseph's  Bay,  Florida. ,  April  18,  186 f 

,  Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  this  date,  I  left  the  bark  at  2 
o  clock  a.  m.  with  the  first  and  second  cutters,  manned  with  22  armed 
men  and  with  Acting  Ensign  S.  G.  Toothaker.  Proceeded  up  St. 
Joseph’s  Bay  and  landed  in  the  vicinity  of  [Cape]  San  Bias,  about  day- 
light.  Left  the  boats  properly  manned,  and  with  18  men  proceeded 
across  the  peninsula  to  the  light-house.  Found  no  traces  of  anythin «• 
except  wild  cattle.  Proceeded  up  the  beach  some  distance  to  avoid  the 
dense  swamps  through  which  we  struggled  on  our  way  over,  and  on 
returning  found  salt  works,  consisting  of  a  boiler  30  feet  long,  about 
3i  feet  in  diameter,  of  heavy  wrought  iron  and  divided  into  three  sec¬ 
tions,  beneath  which  were  three  furnaces  of  brick  and  mortar.  Here 
were  also  two  shanties,  with  a  quantity  of  provisions,  also  carpenter’s 
tools,  spyglass,  wagon,  and  firewood.  I  ordered  the  destruction  of  said 
property  and  saw  it  accomplished,  except  a  few  articles  which  I  thought 
might  be  serviceable  on  board,  and  accordingly  brought  with  me  to  the 
bark. 

As  it  was  now  getting  late  in  the  day,  the  men  were  much  fatigued 
with  the  march,  and  I  was  expected  on  board,  I  thought  it  injudicious 
to  proceed  farther,  therefore  made  my  way  back  to  the  boats  and 
returned  to  the  bark,  arriving  about  2:30  o’clock  p.  m. 

.  I  desire  to  add  that  from  observations  made  on  the  spot,  my  impres¬ 
sions  are  that  other  salt  works  may  be  found  in  that  vicinity  and  easily 
destroyed.  J 

Respectfully  submitted. 


Act. 


James  Van  Boskirk,

schooner  Beauregard ,  regarding  the  capture  of  British  schooner  Ora- 
moneta ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence. 


U.  S.  Schooner  Beauregard, 

St.  Augustine ,  April  19,  186f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  At  11  p.  m.  on 
the  18th  instant  I  received  information  from  some  fishermen  that  there 
was  a  schooner  inside  the  bar  at  Matanzas  Inlet,  some  20  miles  to  the 
southward  of  this  place.  I  immediately  dispatched  the  gig  and  cut¬ 
ter,  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  H.  B.  Colby  and  E.  M.  Clark,  taking 
one  of  the  fishermen  as  pilot.  They  proceeded  to  the  inlet  through 
the  night  and  arrived  there  at  daylight.  Found  the  schooner  attempting 
to  get  out  over  the  bar,  but  a  few  musket  shots  from  the  boats  brought 
her  to.  They  boarded  and  captured  her  and  brought  her  to  St.  Augus¬ 
tine  for  adjudication.  She  proved  to  he  the  English  schooner  Orarno- 
neta ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  from  Green  Turtle  Cay,  Bahamas, 
bound  to  [New]  Smyrna,  Fla.  She  had  no  cargo  of  any  amount,  only 
50,000  percussion  caps,  a  few  sacks  of  salt,  and  one  roll  of  bagging. 
There  were  no  vessels  or  boats  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  C.  Healy, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


Expedition  for  the  capture  of  cotton  in  Suwanee  River,  April  21, 186  f 

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Fleming-,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Sagamore. 

U.  S.  S.  Sagamore, 

Off  Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  May  5,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  an  expedition  sent  by  me  from 
this  vessel  on  the  21st  ultimo  to  Clay  Landing,  on  the  Suwanee  River, 
has  returned  successful,  having  captured  at  that  place  and  brought 
here  11  bales  of  sea-island  cotton  and  68  bales  of  upland*besides  destroy¬ 
ing  upwards  of  300  bales  it  was  impossible  to  remove,  as  so  much  time 
would  have  been  consumed  in  the  attempt.  The  cotton  not  being  im¬ 
mediately  on  the  river  and  the  enemy  looked  for  at  any  moment,  our 
party  prudently  retired,  lest  being  taken  at  disadvantage  in  the  nar¬ 
row  parts  of  the  river  below,  they  would,  to  secure  their  own  safety, 
have  been  compelled  to  abandon  the  cotton  they  had  already  secured. 

Acting  Ensign  C.  Carven,  the  officer  in  charge,  acted,  I  think,  with 
discretion  and  promptitude,  and  the  satisfactory  manner  in  which  the 
duty  was  performed  will,  I  trust,  entitle  him  and  those  who  were  with 
him  to  favorable  notice. 

Herewith  enclosed  please  find  copy  of  his  report  giving  particulars. 

Ver}^  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  E.  Fleming, 

Lieutenant-  Commander,  Commanding .

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Carven,  TT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  expedition. 

IT.  S.  Gunboat  Sagamore, 

Cedar  Keys,  Fla. ,  April  86,  186 1^. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  the  21st  instant,  I  left  this  ves¬ 
sel  on  that  day  at  about  11  a.  m.  in  the  launch  with  the  howitzer  and 
crew  of  15  men,  having  also  in  my  command  Acting  Master’s  Mate 
F.  Silva  and  4  refugees  (the  latter  to  act  as  guides  and  using  their 
own  boat)  on  an  expedition  up  the  Suwanee  River.  I  arrived  at  the 
mouth  of  the  river  about  4  p.  m.,  proceeded  up  the  same  about  8 
miles  and  encamped  for  three  hours.  I  then  continued  6  miles  farther 
and  reached  Fowler’s  .Bluff,  where  I  landed  the  refugees  and  sent 
them  to  Clay  Landing  to  reconnoiter.  I  then  proceeded  up  some  3 
miles,  where,  entering  a  bayou,  I  concealed  the  boats  among  the  trees 
and  remained  during  the  day.  At  dark  I  stood  up  to  Old  Clay  Land¬ 
ing  (some  4  miles),  which  was  formerly  a  rebel  post.  There  were  signs 
of  a  battery  having  been  mounted.  1  landed  in  person  and  examined 
the  place.  Finding  nothing  worth  capturing  I  stood  up  with  boats, 
passing  spiles  across  the  river,  with  passage  in  center  for  vessels. 
1  wo  miles  farther  I  passed  some  10  bales  cotton  which  had  been 
thrown  in  by  the  refugees  of  my  party,  who  had  landed  below.  One- 
half  mile  farther  up  I  met  the  refugees  floating  down  on  bales  [of]  cot¬ 
ton.  They  told  me  the  rebel  agent  at  the  landing  had  gone  for  assist¬ 
ance.  I  took  them  in  the  boats  and  started  for  the  landing,  with  the 
intention  of  burning  the  cotton.  I  arrived  at  that  place  (situated 
some  35  or  40  miles  from  the  mouth  of  the  river)  at  about  1:30  a.  m., 
on  the  23d  instant.  Finding  no  one  there  I  stationed  pickets  and 
rafted  100  bales  of  cotton  belonging  to  the  rebel  Government,  which  I 
found  stored  i y  houses.  The  men  being  very  much  fatigued,  and 
daylight  near  at  hand,  I  set  fire  to  from  300  to  500  bales  cotton, 
winch  were  stored  in  four  houses,  one  of  which  was  a  steam  cotton  gin 
and  press.  I  spared  one  empty  storehouse,  as  I  understood  from  the 
refugees  it  belonged  to  a  sound  Union  man.  I  then  manned  the  boats, 
took  the  raft  in  tow,  and  proceeded  down  the  river.  At  daybreak,  on 
nearing-  Old  Clay  Landing,  I  made  preparations  to  repel  an  attack  in 
case  information  had  been  conveyed  to  the  enemy.  Finding  no  one 
theie,  I  diiected  Mr.  Silva  to  go  on  shore  and  set  fire  to  the  barracks. 
Immediately  on  our  getting  well  clear  of  the  landing  a  magazine  con¬ 
cealed  in  one  of  the  buildings  exploded,  blowing  it  to  atoms. '  I  reached 
1  owlei  s  Bluff  about  9  a.  m.  I  sent  Mr.  Silva  and  4  men  in  the  refu¬ 
gees  boat  down  to  the  mouth  of  the  river  to  prevent  cotton  floating 
out  to  sea.  _  I  then  landed  to  rest  and  refresh  the  men.  I  seized  a  lot 
of  o  d  rigging  stored  here  (belonging  to  the-  blockade  runner  Pow 
erful,  which  had  been  burned  some  time  since  off  the  mouth  of  the 
river)  to  secure  my  raft  of  cotton.  At  10  a.  m.  I  started  down  the 
liver,  picking-  up  9  bales  of  cotton  lodged  along  the  banks.  I  reached

Instructions  for  cruising  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S. 

Navy ,  to  Captain  Greene ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  San 

Jacinto ,  in  view  of  reported  movements  of  blockade  runners  from 

abroad. 

U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West.  April  % 8 ,  186f 

Sir:  Information  (apparently  authentic)  has  been  received  here  that 
the  rebel  Government  had,  in  Bremen,  two  sailing  ships  under  English 
colors,  viz,  the  Ernestine,  Captain  Peter  Williams,  loaded  with  muskets, 
rifles,  sabers,  and  ammunition;  and  the  Edinburg ,  Captain  J.  Baldwin, 
loaded  with  tents  and  medicines.  Also  a  schooner  under  Italian  colors 
(name  not  given)  loaded  with  opium,  quinine,  chloroform,  and  other 
medicines,  together  with  dry  goods  and  surgical  and  mathematical  instru¬ 
ments.  All  these  vessels  were  to  have  sailed  between  the  1st  and  5th 
of  April  for  Sisal,  Yucatan,  and  arrangements  were  commenced  by  the 
rebel  Government  to  obtain  permission  (from  General  Bazaine,  com¬ 
mander  in  chief  of  the  F rench  forces  in  Mexico)  to  land  these  cargoes 
at  Tampico,  and  to  transport  them  thence  by  land  to  Texas.  Such 
permission,  if  obtained,  was  to  meet  the  vessels  at  Sisal,  otherwise 
they  were  to  take  their  cargoes  to  Nassau  for  shipment  to  Wilming¬ 
ton,  N.  C.  The  agents  of  the  rebel  Government  to  attend  to  these 
cargoes  are  Mr.  Lafitte,  at  Sisal,  and  Mr.  Heyliger,  at  Nassau,  and  the 
original  cost  of  the  cargoes  is  estimated  at  between  $300,000  and 
$400,000. 

So  soon,  therefore,  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  can  be  got 
ready  for  sea,  you  will  be  pleased  to  proceed  in  her  to  latitude  21°  35' 
N.  and  longitude  89°  35'  W.,  where  you  will  anchor  (in  about  12 
fathoms  water)  and  lie  with  banked  fires  for  the  purpose  of  intercept¬ 
ing  these  vessels. 

In  making  captures  of  vessels  that  you  may  encounter  on  the  high 
seas,  which  may  have  violated  the  blockade  instituted  by  the  United 
States  Government,  or  which  may  afford  a  reasonable  ground  of  sus¬ 
picion  that  they  intend  doing  so,  you  will  be  governed  by  the  circulars 
of  the  Department,  dated  May  14,  1862,  and  August  18,  1863,  and  by 
my  General  Order  No.  2,  dated  January  1,  1863.  Should  a  chase  at 
any  time  carry  you  within  sight  of  a  neutral  country,  too  much  care 
can  not  be  exercised  to  determine  with  accuracy  not  only  your  own 
position,  but  also  that  of  the  vessel  chased  at  different  stages  of  the

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Sears ,  U.  S.  Nam,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 
Honeysuckle ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner  Miriam 
of  Nassau ,  New  Providence. 

U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle, 

At  Sea ,  Bat.  25°  25',  Long.  8 If  30',  April  <29,  186 J 
Sir:  I  beg  to  report  to  you  the  capture  of  the  English  schooner 
Miriam ,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence,  by  this  vessel,  under  the  follow¬ 
ing  circumstances:  April  27,  1864,  latitude  23°  56',  longitude  83°  09', 
boarded  the  schoooner  Miriam  from  Havana,  bound  to  New  Orleans! 
The  officer  that  boarded  her  reported  the  papers  correct,  but  the  cargo 
looked  suspicious;  allowed  her  to  proceed  on  her  voyage  with  the 
determination  to  watch  her  movements.  Parted  company  and  steered 
to  the  S.  W.  Lost  sight  of  the  schooner.  At  4  p.  m.  steered  N.  W. 
by  N.  and  at  0  p.  m.  sighted  her  again.  At  that  time  she  was  steering 
by  the  wind  N.  N.  W.  During  the  night  we  kept  her  in  sight.  April 
28  watched  her  movements;  found  that  at  night  all  lights  were  con¬ 
cealed  and  a  lookout  was  kept  at  the  masthead  during  the  day.  April 
29,  at  10  a.  m.,  took  bearings  of  the  Miriam  and  went  in  pursuit  of  a 
schooner  bearing  E.  N.  E.  At  11  a.  m.  spoke  the  schooner;  then  went 
in  pursuit  of  the  Miriam ,  but  could  not  find  her  on  the  bearings  left; 
went  in  search,  and  at  1  p.  m.  saw  her  bearing  W.,  which  position  she 
could  not  have  obtained  without  altering  her  course  after  we  lost  sight 
of  her.  At  5  p.  m.  boarded  her  and  examined  the  cargo;  found  that 
a  great  portion  of  the  cargo  was  not  on  the  manifest.  I  took  the  vessel 
in  tow  as  a  prize.

Upon  examining  the  baggage  of  the  officers  and  crew  we  found  a 
mail  for  the  Confederate  States.  One  of  the  men  on  board  was  recog¬ 
nized  by  one  of  the  officers  of  this  vessel  as  a  resident  of  Savannah, 
Ga.  One  of  the  crew  acknowledged  that  he  belonged  to  that  place,  also, 
and  that  he  ran  the  blockade  in  January,  1864.  The  captain  had  been 
captured  by  a  boat’s  crew  from  the  U.  S.  bark  Roebuck  at  Indian 
River,  Fla.,  while  attempting  to  run  the  blockade. 

The  crew  consisted  of  seven  persons.  There  were  no  vessels  in  sight 
at  time  of  capture. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Cyrus  Sears, 

Acting  Ensign ,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle.

Cruising  instructions  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy , 
to  Commander  Shufeldt ,  U  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Proteus. 


U.  S.  Flagship  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West ,  April  30 ,  186 f 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  vessel  under  your  command  can  be  got  ready  for 
sea,  you  will  proceed  to  cruise  at  your  discretion  (to  the  northward  of 
28°  iatitude  and  to  the  eastward  of  79°  longitude)*  for  the  purpose  of 
intercepting  and  capturing  any  vessels  that  you  majT  encounter  on  the 
high  seas  which  may  have  violated  the  blockade  instituted  by  the 
United  States  Government,  or  which  may  afford  a  reasonable  ground 
of  suspicion  that  they  intend  doing  so.  The  Tioga  will  sail  in  a  few 
days  with  similar  orders,  to  cruise  to  the  southward  of  28°  latitude. 

Before  proceeding  to  your  station  you  are  at  liberty  to  touch  in 
either  at  Havana  or  Matanzas  for  information  that  may  be  useful  to 
you  in  the  performance  of  this  duty. 

In  making  captures  you  will  be  governed  by  the  circulars  of  the 
Department,  dated  May  14,  1862,  and  August  18,  1863,  and  by  m}T 
General  Order  No.  2,  dated  January  1, 1863,  and  should  a  chase  at  any 
time  carry  you  within  sight  of  a  neutral  country  too  much  care  can 
not  be  exercised  to  determine  with  accuracy  not  only  your  own  posi¬ 
tion,  but  also  that  of  the  vessel  chased,  at  different  stages  of  the  opera¬ 
tion,  with  a  view  to  refuting  any  false  allegations  that  may  be  subse¬ 
quently  made  by  our  enemies  of  a  violation  of  neutral  territory.  In 
the  event  of  your  capturing  any  prizes,  you  will  send  them  to  Boston 
for  adjudication,  taking  every  precaution  to  insure  the  return  of  your 
officers  and  men  to  this  place,  and  as  early  as  possible. 

You  will  return  here  when  necessary  for  a  further  supply  of  coal. 

You  are  authorized  to  employ  a  pilot  by  the  month,  with  the  usual 
allowances.  The  rates  of  pay  prescribed  by  the  Department  for 
pilots  are  $60,  $80,  or  $100  per  month,  and  should  you  be  obliged  to 
make  the  payments  in  gold  it  should  be  at  an  equivalent  for  one  of 
the  above  rates  of  pay  computed  in  greenbacks. 

Respectfully, 


T.  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 


Commander  R.  AY.  Shufeldt,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Steamer  Proteus.

Reports  of  Acting  Master  Chase,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S. 
schooner  Fox ,  regarding  the  capture  of  sloop  Oscar,  with  cargo  of 
cotton. 

U.  S.  Schooner  (Tender)  Fox, 

At  Sea ,  May  1,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor- to  report  to  the  Department  that  this  day, 
latitude  26c  05',  longitude  83°  20'  W.,  Cape  Romano,  Florida,  bearing 
E.  by  S.,  distant  85  miles,  after  a  short  chase,  I  boarded  and  took  pos¬ 
session,  as  a  prize  to  the  United  States,  of  the  sloop  Oscar,  with  a  cargo 
of  93  bales  cotton. 

She  had  no  papers  or  flag  that  I  could  find.  The  captain,  Samuel 
Waters,  says  they  were  thrown  overboard,  but  informs  me  that  she 
was  from  St.  Marks,  Fla.,  bound  to  Havana,  and  had  a  Confederate 
register  and  clearance. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  T.  Chase, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


U.  S.  Schooner  (Tender)  Fox, 

Key  West,  May  3,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  vessel  left  this  port  on  the 
28t.h  of  April  on  a  cruise. 

Having  light  northerly  winds,  I  determined  to  make  the  longitude 
of  84°  W.,  and  then  stand  to  the  northward,  as  the  best  track  for 
blockade  runners. 

On  May  1,  at  daylight,  latitude  26°  05',  longitude  83°  20',  saw  a 
sail  to  the  westward  and  after  a  short  chase  came  up  with  her.  On 
boarding  her  I  found  her  to  be  the  sloop  Oscar,  with  a  cargo  of  93 
bales  of  cotton.  She  had  neither  papers  nor  flag;  the  captain  said  they 
were  thrown  overboard,  but  by  whom  he  did  not  know.  He  informed 
me  that  the  Oscar  was  from  St.  Marks,  bound  to  Havana,  and  that 
she  had  a  Confederate  license  and  clearance. 

I  took  possession  of  her  as  a  prize  and  sent  her  to  this  port  in 
charge  of  Acting  Ensign  Jackson,  with  6  men,  as  Mr.  Jackson  was

Report  of  Acting  Master  Van  Sice,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S,  S.  Sunflower,  regarding 

cooperation  extended  by  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Sunflower, 

Tampa  Bay ,  May  8 ,  186f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  arrival  of  the  steamer 
Honduras  on  the  4th  instant,  with  General  Woodbury  and  troops  on 
board,  for  the  purpose  of  making  a  raid  on  Tampa,  in  obedience  to 
your  circular,  I  immediately  took  steps  to  cooperate  with  the  naval 
force  here  under  my  command.  On  the  afternoon  of  the  4th  instant 
I  went  up  to  Tampa  with  Captain  Bowers,  U.  S.  Army,  to  communi¬ 
cate,  to  ascertain  the  strength  of  the  place,  returning  the  same  night. 
On  the  5th  instant,  after  transferring  two  companies  of  the  colored 
troops  to  the  bark  J.  L.  Davis ,  I  took  her  in  tow  and  towed  her  up  to 
Gadsden’s  Point,  the  Honduras  with  the  balance  of  the  troops  coming 
up  in  the  afternoon.  I  then  organized  a  naval  party  (consisting  of  54 
men  from  the  three  vessels,  Acting  Ensign  J.  Id.  Cox,  of  the  J.  L.  Dams , 
Acting  Master’s  Mate  W.  J.  Crosby,  of  the  Honduras ,  and  Acting 
Master’s  Mate  S.  E.  Willits,  of  this  vessel,  all  under  command  of 
Acting  Master  William  Eales)  to  land  with  the  troops  and  assist  in  the 
capture  of  the  place.  After  getting  them  all  on  board  the  Honduras 
we  proceeded  up  the  bay  as  far  as  practicable  and  succeeded  in  landing 
all  before  daylight.  A  7  a.  m.  the  place  was  taken  possession  of, 
capturing  some  40  prisoners,  the  naval  force  capturing  about  one-half, 
which  were  turned  over  to  the  army,  and  a  few  minutes  after  7  the 
Stars  and  Stripes  were  hoisted  in  the  town  by  the  navy. 

I  have  also  to  report  the  capture  of  the  sloop  smack  Neptune  and  a 
quantity  of  cotton,  estimated  at  about  55  bales,  by  the  naval  force. 
Before  closing  this  report  I  desire  to  make  mention  of  the  cheerful 
and  assiduous  cooperation  of  Acting  Masters  William  Fales  and  J.  H. 
Platt.  Acting  Master  Fales  led  his  party  into  the  town  on  the  double 
quick,  capturing  several  prisoners,  wounding  2  who  were  trying  to  get 
away. 

Acting  Master  Fales  speaks  in  high  terms  of  praise  of  the  conduct 
of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  S.  E.  Willits,  and  also  says  that  both  officers 
and  men  behaved  very  well. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient,  servant, 

Edwd.  Van  Sice, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West.  Fla.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Browne ,  U.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  bark  Restless,  regarding  expedition  in  search  of  blockade 
runners  in  West  Bay. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew"1  s  Bay,  Florida ,  May  6,  186 !h 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following-  report: 

Having  learned  from  refugees  that  a  sloop-rigged  boat,  with  a  crew 
of  10  men  and  2  officers,  had  run  the  blockade  at  Mobile  and  had  cap¬ 
tured  a  smack  from  our  forces  at  East  Pass,  which  they  destroyed,  the 
crew  of  which  made  their  escape  after  being  captured,  and  were  accom¬ 
panied  by  two  of  the  sloop’s  crew,  the  remainder  of  which  hauled  the 
sloop  across  into  West  Bay  with  the  assistance  of  the  salt  makers  and 
their  ox  teams,  I  fitted  out  my  first  cutter  and  IT  men,  under  charge 
of  Acting  Ensign  Thomas  Tierney,  and  gave  him  orders  to  search  all 
the  bayous  in  West  Bay.  The  cutter  left  the  ship  on  the  4th  instant, 
and  after  searching  all  the  ba}Tous  as  directed  without  seeing  any  signs 
of  the  sloop,  but  ascertained  she  had  been  hauled  to  Marianna  on  ox 
carts,  after  which  they  made  preparations  to  return  to  the  ship. 

It  is  my  melancholy  duty  to  report  an  accident  which  happened  on 
the  cutter  when  about  ready  to  start,  by  which  Edward  Delaman, 
ordinary  seaman,  lost  his  life  by  the  accidental  discharge  of  a  firearm 
he  was  moving  from  one  part  of  the  boat  to  another,  catching  the 
hammer  afoul  of  an  oar,  discharging  the  piece  and  Edging  the  con¬ 
tents  in  his  right  breast,  passing  through  his  lungs  and  out  his  back. 
He  expired  a  moment  or  two  afterwards.  The  cutter  immediately 
returned  to  the  ship,  arriving  about  6  o’clock  on  the  night  of  the  6th 
instant. 

I  enclose  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  L.  F.  Morse’s  report.  He  will 
be  buried  on  Hurricane  Island. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey,  n

Instructions  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Dear- Admiral 

Bailey ,  U  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  disposition  of  'persons  captured  on 

blockade  runners. 

Navy  Department,  May  9,  1864- 

Sir:  The  following  instructions  will  hereafter  be  observed  with 
regard  to  the  disposition  of  persons  found  on  board  vessels  seized  for 
breach  of  blockade. 

1st.  Bona  fide  foreign  subjects  captured  in  neutral  vessels,  whether 
passengers,  officers,  or  crew  can  not  be  treated  as  prisoners  of  war, 
unless  guilty  of  belligerent  acts,  but  are  entitled  to  immediate  release. 
Such  as  are  required  as  witnesses  may  be  detained  for  that  purpose, 
and  when  their  testimony  is  secured  they  must  be  unconditionally 
released. 

2d.  Foreign  subjects  captured  in  vessels  without  papers  or  colors, 
or  those  sailing  under  the  protection  and  flag  of  the  insurgent  Govern¬ 
ment,  or  employed  in  the  service  of  that  Government,  are  subject  to 
treatment  as  prisoners  of  war,  and  if  in  the  capacity  of  officers  or  crew, 
are  to  be  detained.  If  they  were  passengers  only,  and  have  no  interest 
in  the  vessel  or  cargo,  and  are  in  noway  connected  with  the  insurgent 
Government,  they  may  be  released. 

3d.  Citizens  of  the  United  States  captured  either  in  neutral  or  rebel 
vessels  are  always  to  be  detained  with  the  following  exceptions:  If 
they  are  passengers  only,  have  no  interest  in  vessel  or  cargo,  have  not 
been  active,  in  the  rebellion  or  engaged  in  supplying  the  insurgents 
with  munitions  of  war,  etc.,  and  are  loyally  disposed,  they  may  be 
released  on  taking  the  oath  of  allegiance.'  The  same  privilege  may  be 
allowed  to  any  of  the  crew  that  are  not  seafaring  men,  of  like  antece¬ 
dents,  and  who  are  loyally  disposed. 

4th.  Pilots  and  seafaring  men,  excepting  bona  fide  foreign  subjects, 
captured  in  neutral  vessels,  are  always  to  be  detained.  These  are  the 
principal  instruments  in  maintaining  the  system  of  violating  the  block¬ 
ade,  and  it  is  important  to  hold  them.  Persons  habitually  engaged  in 
violating  the  blockade,  although  they  may  not  be  serving  on  board  the 
vessels,  are  of  this  class,  and  are  to  be  likewise  detained. 

5th.  When  there  is  reason  to  doubt  that  those  who  claim  to  be  for¬ 
eign  subjects  are  in  reality  such,  they  will  be  required  to  state  under 
oath  that  they  have  never  been  naturalized  in  this  country,  have  never 
exercised  the  privileges  of  a  citizen  thereof  by  voting  or  otherwise, 
and  have  never  been  in  the  pay  or  employment  of  the  insurgent  or  the 
so-called  “Confederate  Government.’’  On  their  making  such  state¬ 
ment  they  may  be  released,  provided  you  have  not  evidence  of  their 
having  sworn  falsely.  The  examination  in  cases  that  are  doubtful 
should  be  rigid. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


697 

6th.  When  the  neutrality  of  a  vessel  is  doubtful,  or  when  a  vessel 
claiming  to  he  neutral  is  believed  to  be  engaged  in  transporting  sup¬ 
plies  and  munitions  of  war  for  the  insurgent  Government,  foreign 
subjects  captured  in  such  vessel  may  be  detained  until  the  neutral¬ 
ity  of  the  vessel  is  satisfactorily  established.  It  is  not  advisable  to 
detain  such  persons  under  this  instruction  unless  there  is  good  ground 
for  doubting  the  neutrality  of  the  vessel. 

7th.  Parties  who  may  be  detained  under  the  foregoing  instructions, 
are  to  be  sent  to  a  Northern  port  for  safer  custody,  unless  there  is  a 
suitable  place  for  keeping  them  within  the  limits  of  your  command, 
and  the  Department  furnished  with  a  memorandum  in  their  cases 
respectively. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

^  Secretary  of  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Budd.,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Somerset. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset, 

West  Pass ,  St.  Georges  Sound ,  May  16 , 186 lh 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  night  of  the  12th  in¬ 
stant  I  sent  the  light-draft  boats  of  this  vessel  and  of  the  U.  S.  schooner 
Chambers  to  land  a  detachment  of  troops  under  command  of  Lieuten¬ 
ant  [Thomas]  Hunter,  One  hundred  and  tenth  New  York  Volunteers,  a 
few  miles  below  the  town  of  Apalachicola.  After  landing  the  troops, 
the  officer  in  charge  of  the  boats  (Acting  Ensign  E.  H.  Smith)  was 
instructed  to  proceed  slowly  alongshore,  so  as  to  he  in  communication 
with  them  during  their  march  and  approach  to  the  town,  in  the  rear  of 
which  the  whole  force  was  to  arrive  at  daybreak.  Taking  two  launches 
from  this  ship,  I  arrived  in  front  of  the  place  about  the  same  time,  and 
discovered  a  force  of  about  TO  or  80  of  the  enemy  attempting  to  embark 
in  boats  from  the  upper  end  of  the  wharves.  The  rapid  approach  of 
the  first  launch  caused  them  to  abandon  that  project  and  retreat  through 
the  town,  which  movement  was  hastened  by  a  couple  of  shells  from 
our  howitzer.  They  passed  within  a  short  distance  of  a  portion  of  our 
troops  under  Lieutenant  Hunter,  who  unfortunately  thought  that  they 
were  part  of  his  command,  and  permitted  them  to  gain  time  and  escape 
by  the  up-river  road  without  molestation. 

We  followed  them  about  2  miles,  but  the  density  of  the  undergrowth 
and  number  of  paths  leading  through  the  woods  in  all  directions  ren¬ 
dering  any  further  pursuit  unwise  and  futile,  we  returned  to  the  boats. 

Ascertaining  that  the  commanding  officer  of  the  expedition  (GeorgeW. 
Gift,  lieutenant,  C.  S.  Navy)  was  in  the  sound  with  about  30  men, 
I  dispatched  boats  and  troops  after  him,  but  the  swiftness  of  his  boat 
and  the  approach  of  night  enabled  him  to  escape,  having  been  chased 
by  our  first  launch,  under  command  of  Acting  Ensign  C.  H.  Bran  ting- 
ham,  who  captured  one  of  his  small  boats  and  three  of  his  party. 

The  forces  of  the  enemy  consisted  of  about  100  men,  commanded  by 
the  following  officers: 

Lieutenant  Commanding  George  W.  Gift,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Passed  Midshipman  S.  P.  Blanc,  C.  8.  Navy. 

Passed  Midshipman  H.  L.  Vaughan,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Passed  Midshipman  G.  W.  Sparks,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Passed  Midshipman  W.  S.  Hogue,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Passed  Midshipman  J.  T.  Scharf,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Assistant  Paymaster  M.  L.  Sothoron,  C.  8.  Navy. 

Assistant  Surgeon  M.  Ford,  C.  S.  Navy. 

First  Assistant  Engineer  L.  Campbell,  C.  8.  Navy. 

Third  Assistant  Engineer  A.  De  Blanc,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Master’s  Mate  C.  Frazee,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Volunteers  on  the  expedition. 

Colonel  D.  P.  Holland,  aid  to  governor  of  Florida. 

Surgeon  [E.  D.]  Cherry,  First  Georgia  Regulars. 

A.  G.  Sparks,  signal  officer. 

Captain  [James  R.]  Blount,  Bonaud’s  battalion. 

rheir  object  was  the  capture  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Adela ,  intending,  in  the 
event  of  being  successful,  to  carry  her  into  Mobile  or  burn  her. 

Their  boats  were  fitted  completely  with  muffled  oars,  paddles,  grap¬ 
nels,  and  incendiary  materials,  and  they  had  been  lurking  in  the  vicinity 
of  the  U.  S.  S.  Adela  for  a  day  or  two  previous  to  their  dispersion  by 
the  force  under  my  command.

Additional  report  of  Acting  Volunteer  ieutenant  Budd,  U.  S.  Navy  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 

Somerset,  regarding  prisoners. 

U.  S.  S.  Somerset, 

West  Pass ,  St.  Georg  ds  Sound,  May  21,  1864  ■ 

Sir:  I  send  dowTn  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Honduras,  as  prisoners,  Thomas 
McLean,  citizen  of  Apalachicola;  Anthony  Murray,  citizen  of  Apa¬ 
lachicola;  James  Anderson,  citizen  of  Apalachicola. 

These  men  were  engaged  in  active  cooperation  with  the  enemy  when 
captured.  McLean  enacted  the  role  of  a  scout  or  spy.  Mistaking  our 
troops  for  those  of  the  enemy,  he  gave  them  information  respecting 
my  force  and  position  in  front  of  the  town  on  the  morning  of  the  13th 
instant.  Murray  and  Anderson  were  acting  as  scouts  for  Gift,  keep¬ 
ing  open  his  communications,  and  supplying  him  with  provisions  when 
he  was  absent  from  the  main  body  of  his  command.  When  taken 
they  were  carrying  soldiers  from  the  islands  back  to  the  main. 

Heretofore  all  of  them  have  enjoyed  immunity  from  us  as  citizens. 
Their  local  knowledge  makes  them  dangerous  to  us  and  very  useful  to 
the  enemy.  For  the  latter  they  act  as  scouts,  spies,  and  pilots,  and  in 
this  case  they  were  caught  in  the  act.  They  pretend  to  have  been 
forced  into  Gift’s  service,  but  I  know  them  well  and  earnestly  request 
that  they  will  not  be  permitted  to  return  to  Apalachicola. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  Budd, 

Acting  Volunteer)1  Lieutenant,  Commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Somerset. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Letter  of  commendation  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey,  IT.  S.  Navy,  to  Acting  Volun¬ 
teer  Lieutenant  Budd,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  Somerset. 


[U.  S.  S.  Flagship]  Dale, 

May  31 ,  186. If,. 

Sir:  I  am  much  gratified  with  the  zeal  you  have  displayed  and  the 
good  judgment  you  have  shown  in  the  affair  at  Apalachicola,  by  which 
you  so  completely  frustrated  the  plans  of  the  rebels.  It  was  this  zeal 
in  Lieutenant-Commander  McCauley  when  he  commanded  the  Fort 
Ilenry  that  made  that  vessel  the  terror  of  the  coast  for  50  miles,  and 
the  Somerset ,  her  sister  ship,  bids  fair  to  obtain  under  your  command 
a  like  enviable  reputation.  I  forwarded  your  report  to  the  Secretary 
of  the  Navy,  with  commendation. 

We  are  very  much  in  need  of  two  things  that  you  have,  I  believe,  in 
your  power  to  supply — contrabands  and  3mllow-pine  timber.  I  wish 
you  would  forward  to  this  port  as  many  able-bodied  negroes  as  you 
can  obtain,  and  put  upon  the  schooner  that  I  send  up  with  coal  as  much 
yellow  pine  as  you  can  collect.  There  is  the  greatest  scarcity  of  this 
article  both  here  and  at  the  North. 

Very  respectfully, 


T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 
Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  W.  Budd.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  requesting  infor¬ 
mation  regarding  apportionment  of  prizes  captured  by  the  U.  S. 
supply  steamer  Union. 

No.  154.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West ,  May  If  18,6 f 

Sir:  While  engaged  in  the  duty  of  communicating  with  and  supply¬ 
ing  the  vessels  of  this  squadron  under  orders  from  me,  a  copy  of  which 
is  herewith  enclosed,  the  U.  S.  supply  steamer  Union  captured  on  the 
14th  of  January,  near  Tampa  Bay  and  within  the  limits  of  my  squad¬ 
ron,  the  Confederate  steamer  Mayflower ,  with  75  bales  of  cotton. 
Subsequently,  on  the  26th  of  April,  while  engag-ed  on  similar  duty 
and  acting  under  similar  orders,  the  Union  captured  between  Tampa 
Bay  and  Charlotte  Harbor,  within  the  limits  of  this  squadron,  the 
schooner  O.  K.,  engaged  in  an  attempt  to  run  the  blockade.  Both  of 
these  vessels  have  been  condemned. 

I  would  request  that  the  Fourth  Auditor  be  instructed  to  apportion 
to  me  the  amount  allowed  by  law  to  the  commanding  officer  of  a 
squadron  in  such  cases. 

Very  respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Woods ,  U.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  mortar  schooner •  Sea  Foam,  regarding  the  rescue  of  the  crew 
of  the  sloop  Anna  Eliza,  May  Ilf.,  186 f 

U.  S.  Mortar  Brig  Sea  Foam, 
Brooklyn,  Navy  Yard,  May  18,  186 f 
Sir:  I  respectfully  beg  leave  to  submit  to  you  the  following- report: 
On  the  14th  instant,  at  11:  30  a.  m.,  in  latitude  34°  35'  N.,  longitude 
74°  55'  W.,  fell  in  with  a  vessel  water-logged  and  dismasted,  the 
English  flag  flying  on  the  stump  of  her  mast,  union  down.  After 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


705 


some  difficulty  (the  weather  being  very  rough),  the  sea  making  a  clean 
breach  over  her,  I  succeeded  in  rescuing  the  crew,  seven  in  all.  Her 
captain  reports  her  to  be  the  sloop  Anna  Eliza,  of  Nassau,  New  Provi¬ 
dence,  bound  from  Santee  River,  South  Carolina,  to  Nassau,  with  a 
cargo  ot  10,000  gallons  spirits  of  turpentine.  Nothing  saved  from  the 
wreck. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

D.  C.  Woods, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  Navy. 


Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the _  Navy,  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey , 
u.  S'  A  avy,  regarding  the  disposition  of  persons  captured  on  blockade- 
running  vessels. 

Navy  Department,  May  19,  186 f 
_  Sir..  On  the  9th  instant  instructions  were  sent  to  you  relative  to  the 
disposing  of  blockade  runners.  As  the  forts  North  are  sometimes 
very  crowded,  they  can  not  accommodate  conveniently  this  class  of 
persons,  and  they  are  kept  for  sometime  on  board  the  receivings  ships, 
which  is  not  desirable.  A  short  time  since  the  Secretary  of  War 
stated,  in  reply  to  an  enquiry  from  this  Department,  that  he  knew  of 
no  place  except  theTortugas,  where  there  were  ample  accommodations 
for  the  blockade  runners.  Should,  therefore,  a  large  class  of  these 
persons  come  into  your  hands  it  would  be  well  to  send  the  most  noto¬ 
rious  ones,  citizens  of  the  United  States,  to  the  Tortugas. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 
Secretary  of  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West. 


Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey , 
U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  use  of  prize  vessels  as  coal  hulks. 


Navy  Department,  May  21,  186 f 

Sir:  Your  No.  138,  in  reference  to  the  want  of  vessels  for  coal 
hulks,  has  been  received. 

There  are  no  old  vessels  that  can  be  sent  to  you  for  that  purpose. 
You  are  authorized  to  purchase  prize  vessels  that  may  be  suitable  at 
Key  West,  or,  if  you  think  it  more  economical  and  more  to  the  interest 
of  the  Government,  }mu  can  purchase  at  Havana  for  gold,  as  you 
suggest.  If  they  can  be  obtained  at  Key  WTestit  is  perhaps  more 
advisable  to  do  so,  as  the  Department  has  refrained  so  far  from  resort¬ 
ing  to  a  foreign  port  for  the  purchase  of  vessels  of  any  description 
for  the  naval  service. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theo.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West,  Fla.

U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West ,  May  31,  186 f 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  Hendrick  Hudson  is  ready  for  sea,  you  will  pro¬

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey , 
U.  S.  Navy,  for  a  court  of  enquiry  to  investigate  cause  of  complaint 
made  by  the  Spanish  Minister. 

Navy  Department,  May  33,  186 f 
Sir:  A  complaint  has  been  made  to  the  Department  of  State  by  Mr. 
Tassara,  the  minister  of  Spain — 

That  on  the  morning  of  the  9th  or  10th  of  April  last,  the  United  States  Navy  steamer 
Marigold ,  mail  steamer  from  Key  West,  after  annoying  and  menacing  the  English 
merchant  vessel  Belle,  coming  from  Matamoras,  just  as  she  was  entering  the  port  of 
Havana,  fired  a  cannon  shot  at  her  at  500  yards’  distance  from  the  Morro  Castle. 

Be  pleased  to  convene  a  court  of  enquiry  for  the  purpose  of  a  thor¬ 
ough  investigation  of  the  grounds  of  the  complaint  made  by  Mr.  Tas¬ 
sara,  direct  the  court  to  report  the  facts  ascertained,  with  its  opinion, 
and  transmit  the  record  to  the  Department  as  early  as  practicable. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron  ,  Key  West.

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Eason ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  cooperative 
movements  in  St.  Andrew’s  Bay. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless,  May  26,  186 f 
Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  the  23d  instant,  I  proceeded  to 
the  mouth  of  Bayou  George  [Goose  Bayou?]  with  Lieutenant  Mercer 
and  a  detachment  of  31  of  the  Second  Florida  Cavalry,  at  which  place 
I  arrived  in  the  morning  of  the  24th,  landed  the  soldiers,  and  recon- 
noitered  the  barge  [bayou]  with  the  second  cutter,  but  saw  no  boats  of 
any  account,  they  having  been  destroyed  by  the  rebels.  I  destroyed 
Captain  Robinson’s  picket  house,  and  at  the  head  of  North  Bay,  a  new 
log  house.  On  the  afternoon  of  the  24th  we  proceeded  down  the  bay 
and  when  off  Alligator  Bay  [Bayou]  I  heard  a  bugee  [bugle?].  We 
stood  inshore  and  landed  all  the  soldiers  and  10  of  my  men  to  capture 
a  squad  of  cavalry,  as  we  supposed,  but  learned  there  were  none. 
Being  near  the  numerous  salt  works,  I  destroyed  11  works,  containing 
as  near  as  I  can  recollect,  about  60  kettles.  I  should  think  by  the 
hies  that  200  works  still  remain  on  the  bay.  I  also  learned  from  g’ood 
authority  that  the  salt  makers  have  a  large  quantity  of  new  boilers  on 
hand  to  replace,  the  broken  ones  as  soon  as  possible  after  we  left  the 
bay.  I  also  learned  that  all  the  rebel  troops  had  been  ordered  to  the 
Army  of  Tennessee. 

We  left  North  Bay  on  the  morning  of  the  25th  and  arrived  at  the 
Restless  the  same  evening. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  Eason, 

Acting  Ensign ,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  W.  R.  Browne, 

Comdg.  U.  S.  Bark  Restless ,  St.  Andrew’s  Bay ,  I  la.

house  known  as  the  Parker  house,  a  company  of  cavalry  fired  upon 
the  scow  and  cutter.  I  had  my  men  ready  and  returned  their  fire 
instantly.  In  fifteen  minutes  we  drove  them  to  the  woods;  then  one

Johnson  place  they  showed  themselves  again— -also  another  flag — two 
men  in  dark  clothes.  I  threw  another  shell  in  the  center  of  them, 
which  made  them  scatter  in  all  directions.  They  first  fired  upon  me 
when  the  boats  were  within  60  yards  of  the  beach. 

The  crews  of  both  boats  behaved  beautifully.  No  casualties  on  our 
side.  We  fired  50  rounds  from  the  rifles  and  4  from  the  howitzer.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey , 
TJ.  S.  Navy,  for  the  appraisement  of  powder  taken  from,  the  prize 
steamer  Cumberland. 


Navy  Department,  May  27,  186J. 

Sir:  The  Department  is  informed  by  a  letter  received  from  Prize 
Commissioners  Carpenter  and  Welch,  of  Key  West,  that  there  is  a 
quantity  of  powder  in  the  army  magazine  at  Key  West,  which  was 
landed  from  the  prize  steamer  Cumberland ,  which  they  say  is  reported 
to  be  of  the  best  quality,  and  in  their  opinions  is  suitable  for  naval 
purposes. 

You  are  desired  to  have  same  examined,  and  if  found  to  be  as 
represented  cause  it  to  be  taken  for  the  use  of  the  Navy,  upon  the 
report  of  a  board  of  appraisers  appointed  to  appraise  the  same. 

V  ery  respectfully, 


Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Key  West,  Fla. 


Gideon  Welles,

Sir:  As  soon  as  the  Proteus,  under  your  command,  is  ready'  for  sea, 
you  will  proceed  off  Cardenas  and  from  thence  through  Nicholas 
Channels  on  the  north  side  of  Cuba  to  Cape  Haitien,  communicating 
with  some  one  of  Admiral  Lardner’s  squadron,  and  informing  them 
of  the  privateer  Florida’s  having  sailed  from  St.  Pierre,  Martinique, 
on  the  9th  instant.  After  performing  this  service,  you  will  proceed  to 
the  northward  of  Martinello  [Matanilla]  Reef,  or  to  such  other  point  as 
in  your  judgment,  from  the  information  you  may  gather,  will  best 
effect  the  main  object  of  your  cruise,  which  is,  first,  to  capture,  if

Capture  and  destruction  of  sloop  General  Finegan  {Madge),  May  88, 
186 f,  during  expedition  to  Ilomosassa  River. 

Report  of  Acting  Master  Russell,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  II.  S.  schooner  Ariel. 

U.  S.  S.  Ariel, 

Key  West ,  June  13,  186 f. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  orders  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  cruise  between  Tampa  Bay  and  Homosassa  River.  On 
May  25,  in  Clearwater  Harbor,  boarded  an  army  boat  containing  10 
men  belonging  to  the  Second  Florida  Regiment,  under  the  command 
of  Sergeant  M.  M.  Edwards,  who  was  under  orders  to  proceed  to 
various  places  on  the  coast  to  protect  and  bring  off  several  refugee 
families.  Wishing  to  acquaint  myself  with  some  of  the  prominent 
localities  of  my  cruising  ground,  I  embraced  the  opportunity  of  so 
doing  by  accompanying  the  detachment.  We  landed  at  Clearwater 
and  learned  that  the  rebels  were  obstructing  the  Homosassa  River. 
I  determined  to  proceed  there,  and  at  my  request  the  sergeant  accom¬ 
panied  me  (as  it  did  not  conflict  with  his  orders).  On  May  27,  off 
Anclote  Keys,  spoke  the  schooner  Two  Sisters.  Informing  Acting 
Master  Chatfield  where  I  was  going,  *he  kindly  lent  me  the  assistance 
of  Acting  Ensign  Montague,  6  men,  and  his  boat  to  assist  me.  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  across  St.  Martin’s  reef,  on  my  way,  leaving  the  Troo  Sisters 
at  Chassahowitzka  beacon. 

On  May  28,  at  5:20  a.  in.,  made  a  small  sloop  under  sail,  standing 
inside  of  an  island  to  the  northward  of  Chassahowitzka  River.  I  sent 
two  boats  to  intercept  the  sloop,  which  they  succeeded  in  doing,  but 
not  until  the  crew  had  set  fire  to  her  and  escaped;  but  the  fire  was 
promptly  extinguished  by  Acting  Ensign  Montague  before  it  had  done 
any  damage  whatever. 


710 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  sloop  proved  to  be  the  General  Finegan  (Madge),  from  Crystal 
River  to  Havana.  The  cargo  consisted  of  5  bales  (2,028  pounds)  of 
sea- island  cotton  and  2  barrels  of  turpentine.  The  sloop’s  papers,  a 
small  mail  for  Havana,  a  rebel  flag,  and  several  other  articles,  of  which 
I  enclose  a  list,  were  found  on  board.  The  Two  Sisters  being  only  15 
miles  distant,  I  sent  the  sloop  in  charge  of  two  men  to  remain  there 
until  I  returned. 

On  May  28,  at  5  p.  m.,  arrived  at  the  mouth  of  the  Homosassa  River 
and  anchored.  At  8  p.  m.  I  went  up  the  river  with  3  boats  and  25  men 
to  reconnoiter  and  find  the  channel;  succeeding  in  doing  so.  On  the 
29th,  at  daybreak,  I  got  underway  with  the  Ariel  for  Tiger  Tail 
Island,  which  is  situated  about  10  miles  from  the  mouth  of  the  river. 
When  within  about  2  miles  of  that  place,  a  rebel  flag  was  observed  fly¬ 
ing.  1  sent  the  army  boat  ahead  to  reconnoiter,  while  I  followed 
slowly  with  the  schooner.  When  the  boat  was  within  about  600  or  700 
yards  of  where  the  flag  was  flying,  two  boats  containing  about  8  or  10 
men  each,  pulled  off  in  great  haste.  The  army  boats  pursued  them 
and  filed  at  them,  when  they  ran  their  boats  on  the  beach  and  escaped 
to  the  woods;  we  obtained  the  boats. 

Landing  on  the  island  I  took  possession  of  the  rebel  flag,  a  small 
quantity  of  ammunition,  a  small  brass  one-pounder,  and  some  other 
articles,  of  which  I  enclose  a  list.  About  100  yards  from  where  the 
rebels  had  been  was  the  residence  of  Ex-Senator  D.  L.  Yulee,  which 
was  unoccupied  at  the  time. 

I  found  about  150  piles,  intended  for  the  obstruction  of  the  river. 
They  were  about  12  or  15  feet  long,  and  sharp  at  one  end.  There  were 
also  a  quantity  of  them  at  a  point  about  2  miles  from  the  mouth  of  the 
river. 

I  set  fire  to  them  all,  also  to  the  buildings  where  the  rebel  flag  was 
flying.  But,  sir,  I  have  to  add  that  the  flames  spreading  rapidly,  com¬ 
municated  themselves  to  Mr.  Yulee’s  residence,  and  it  was  burned  to 
the  ground. 

I  got  underway  and  proceeded  to  rejoin  the  Two  S'isters ,  meeting  her 
on  May  31,  off  Bayport  beacon. 

Acting  Master  Chatfield  informed  me  that  the  prize  sloop  he  had 
considered  unseaworthy,  and  she  was  leaking  badly,  so  he  took  the 
cargo  out  and  sank  her. 

I  took  the  cargo  from  the  Two  Sisters  and  bring  it  to  this  place  for 
adjudication. 

On  my  way  down  1  stopped  at  several  places  to  gather  up  refugee 
families  and  their  effects,  who  were  on  their  way  to  Fort  Myers.  1 
omitted  to  mention  that  on  my  way  to  Homosassa  River,  several 
refugees  who  intended  going  to  Fort  Myers  willingly  joined  me  in  the 
expedition. 

The  officers  and  men  whom  I  had  the  honor  to  command  deserve 
great  praise  for  their  energy  and  efficiency. 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Rockwell,  sent  on  board  for  passage 
to  Key  West;  Acting  Master’s  Mate  W.  H.  Howard,  and  Acting 
Master’s  Mate  C.  A.  Fdgcomb  (under  arrest).  I  also  bring  the  mails 
from  Tampa  and  Charlotte  Harbor. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  J.  Russell, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  Schooner  Ariel. 

Captain  Theodore  Ik  Greene, 

Commanding  Flagship  San  Jacinto .

Letter  from  the  prize  commissioner  at  Key  West  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  requesting 
insti  notions  regarding  the  disposition  of  contraband  articles. 


Office  of  the  Prize  Commissioner, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  June  15,  186 Jh 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  the  U.  S.  schooner  Ariel, 
Acting  Master  J.  J.  Pussell  commanding,  arrived  at  this  port  on  the 
J  .i(  h  instant,  and  reports  that  on  May  28,  being  near  the  entrance  to 
the  Ilomosassa  River,  a  rebel  sloop  was  discovered  lying  aground  on  a 
shoal,  and  before  the  Ariel  could  get  near  her  the  crew  set  her  on  tire 
and  left  in  three  boats  for  the  shore,  but  the  Ariel  soon  boarded  her 
and  extinguished  the  lire  and  took  out  the  cargo,  consisting  of  5  bales 
of  cotton  and  2  barrels  of  turpentine.  The  vessel  was  found  to  be  verv 
old  and  unseaworthy,  and  it  was  decided  to  destroy  her. 

On  the  29th  day  of  May  the  Ariel  went  on  an  expedition  up  the 
Homosassa  River,  as  far  as  Tiger  Tail  Island,  where  they  surprised  a 
.Party  of  rebels,  who  ran  away  and  left  the  following  articles,  viz:  1 
1-pounder  and  carriage,  280  rifle  musket  cartridges,  700  percussion 
caps,  3  bags  shot,  1  small  bale  army  blankets,  1  bale  wool,  5  kegs  nails, 
one-half  box  tobacco,  one-half  barrel  sirup,  and  1  yawl  boat. 

They  also  took  from  the  house  of  David  L.  T  ulee  a  large  quantity 
of  letters,  and  before  they  left  the  place  the}7  destroyed  the  prepara¬ 
tions  in  course  of  construction  to  obstruct  the  river,  and  they  also  had 
the  pleasure  to  see  the  house  burned  to  the  ground. 

M  ill  you  have  the  goodness  to  give  instructions  as  to  the  disposition 
of  the  articles  which  are  contraband;  they  have  been  put  in  store  and 
will  await  your  order. 

I  have  also  to  report  the  capture  by  the  U.  S.  supply  steamer  Union, 
on  the  10th  day  of  June,  of  the  sloop  Caroline,  of  Nassau,  with  no 
cargo  on  board.  She  was  captured  one-quarter  of  a  mile  from  Jupiter 
Inlet  and  brought  here. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  W.  Welch, 

Prize  Commissioner. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Captain  Greene,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto. 

U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  June  18,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  would  most  respectfully  report  that  on  the  morning  of  the 
28th  May,  1861,  the  schooner  Ariel,  tender  to  this  ship,  when  cruising 
to  the  northward  of  the  Chassahowitzka  River,  Florida,  fell  in  with 
and  captured  the  sloop  General  Finegan  from  Crystal  River,  bound  to 
Havana.  The  crew  abandoned  the  sloop  and  escaped,  setting  her  on 
fire.  The  fire  was  extinguished  before  it  had  damaged  vessel  or  cargo. 

The  cargo  consisted  of  5  bales  of  sea-island  cotton,  2  barrels  turpen¬ 
tine,  and  several  small  articles,  all  of  which  were  taken  on  board  the 
tender,  brought  to  this  place,  and  delivered  to  the  prize  commissioner. 
The  sloop  being  considered  unseaworthy,  was  destroyed. 

There  was  no  vessel  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture.  The  cotton

Report  of  Acting  Master  Chase ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 

schooner  Fox,  regarding  the  destruction  of  salt  works  between  Suivanee 

River  and  St.  Marks ,  Fla. ,  May  28,  186/+. 

U.  S.  Schooner  (Tender)  Fox, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  June  23, 1861+ . 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  cruising  off  the  coast,  between 
the  Suwanee  River  and  St.  Marks,  I  had  observed  numerous  large  fires 
on  the  shore  and  had  no  doubt  but  that  they  were  salt  works. 

On  the  28th  May  I  sent  a  boat  from  this  vessel  with  an  armed  crew, 
Acting  Ensign  Jackson  in  charge,  to  reconnoiter  the  shore,  and  if 
practicable,  to  destroy  the  works.  The  persons  employed  at  the  place 
tied  at  the  sight  of  the  boat.  Mr.  Jackson  landed  with  8  men  and 
destroyed  25  salt  kettles  of  a  capacity  of  150  gallons  each,  with  all  the 
pumps,  tools,  and  100  bushels  of  clean  salt.  On  the  5th  instant  I 
landed  a  party  about  10  miles  above  Dead  man’s  Bay  and  destroyed 
another  of  these  works,  with  27  kettles  of  about  200  gallons  capacity 
each  (these  were  new  kettles,  and  finely  porcelained  or  cemented  inside), 
and  burned  all  the  houses,  five  in  number,  with  a  large  quantity  of 
tools,  carts,  etc. 

On  the  8th  instant  sent  a  boat  (armed),  Acting  Ensign  Jackson  in 
charge,  up  the  Suwanee  River  20  miles  to  Clay  Landing,  and  captured 
10  bales  cotton;  brought  it  down  and  landed  it  on  one  of  the  keys  at 
the  month  of  the  river,  where  1  think  it  will  be  perfectly  safe  until  1 
return. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  T.  Chase, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla.

Sir:  A  medical  survey  having  recommended  that  the  De  Soto  be 
sent  north  for  sanitary  considerations,  you  will,  as  soon  as  she  is 
ready  for  sea,  proceed  to  Portsmouth,  N.  H.,  and  report  on  arrival  to 
the  honorable  Secretary"  of  the  Navy. 

The  track  you  will  pursue  on  your  return  north  will  be  from 
Matanilla  Rocks,  cutting  diagonally  the  cruising  ground  to  the  north¬ 
ward  of  Bahama  Banks,  or  on  a  line  from  said  rocks  to  latitude  27°  30'  N. , 
and  longitude  76°  45'  W.,  intercepting  the  course  of  the  blockade 
runners  between  Nassau  and  Wilmington. 

On  arriving  at  Portsmouth,  you  will  use  your  best  endeavors  to 
have  the  De  Soto  cleaned,  disinfected,  and  repaired,  so  as  to  enable 
her  to  return  to  the  squadron  as  soon  as  possible.
