Report  of  Acting  Master  Cofin ,  U  S.  Wavy,  commanding  U.  S.  tender 
Rosalie ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  steamer  Emma. 

Tender  Rosalie, 

Charlotte  Harbor ,  Fla.,  June  11,  1861/.. 

;  Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  capture  and  detention  of 
the  steamer  Emma,  under  the  following  circumstances: 

On  the  morning  of  the  9th  instant,  while  coming  up  the  coast,  I 
discovered  said  steamer  within  half  a  mile  of  the  beach,  near  the  mouth 
of  Malco  Inlet  [Marco  Pass],  at  anchor. 

I  hauled  on  the  wind  and  commenced  beating  toward  her,  and  in 
about  an  hour  after  I  discovered  her  I  perceived  her  to  commence 
firing  up,  and  she  was  shortly  underway  and  started  up  the  coast  to 
the  northward,  keeping  close  inshore  and  apparently  trying  to  outrun 
and  keep  to  windward  of  me. 

I  soon  worked  near  enough  to  have  her  within  range  of  m}^  gun, 
whereupon  I  fired  a  shell  toward  her,  after  which  she  bore  down  toward 
me  with  the  American  ensign  ffying. 

Upon  boarding  her  I  found  her  to  have  on  board  a  man  whose  name 
was  not  on  the  crew  list,  also  one  man  short. 

The  captain’s  excuse  for  being  with  his  steamer  in  such  a  position 
not  being  satisfactory  to  me,  I  took  charge  of  her  and  carried  her  to 
Charlotte  Harbor,  where  I  delivered  her  over  to  Acting  Volunteer 
Lieutenant  C.  H.  Rockwell,  commanding  U.  S.  bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 
for  his  investigation,  as  the  Rosalie  is  a  tender  to  that  bark. 

I  am,  sir,  most  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Peter  F.  Coffin, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  Tender  Rosalie. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Rockwell,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  com¬ 
manding  TJ.  S.  bark  Gem  of  the  Sea,  regarding  the  result  of  an 
examination  of  the  papers  of  captured  steamer  Emma. 

U.  S.  Bark  Gem  of  the  Sea, 
Charlotte  Harbor,  Fla.,  June  11,  186 f 
Sir:  In  connection  with  the  enclosed  report,  I  have  the  honor  to 
report  to  you  that  on  investigation  of  the  papers  and  search  of  the 
steamer  Emma  I  find: 

1st.  She  was  captured  at  an  entrance  in  the  coast  where  three  ves¬ 
sels  ran  the  blockade  together  less  than  a  month  ago.  These  three 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  7l7 

had  elotTiere  Captured  by  thc  army  forces  at  Fort  Myers,  after  they 

2d.  On  board  the  steamer  is  one  Holmes,  who  is  not  on  any  of  her 
papers,  and  who  was  captain  of  the  largest  of  the  three  vessels  spoken 
ot  above  as  having  run  the  blockade. 

3d.  Her  manifest  says  her  lading  is  ballast,  stores,  and  fuel.  She 
nas  no  ballast  on  board. 

7^!;  Fhere  *s.on  board  several  tons  of  fine  blacksmith’s  coal,  for 
which  the  captain  says  he  paid  $20  a  ton,  the  whole  costing  over  $300, 
and  which  is  not  mentioned  in  her  manifest.  The  captain  says  this  is 
fuel,  and  then  acknowledges  that  the  steamer’s  furnaces  can  burn  noth- 

®!nAbutfWO-  ,  This  c°al  is  conti’aband  of  war,  and,  I  am  told,  is  worth 
$£>00  a  ton  in  the  so-called  Southern  Confederacy. 

5th.  Those  on  board  the  steamer  have  endeavored  to  throw  over- 
boaicl,  surreptitiously,  portions  of  this  coal  since  her  capture  on  two 
occasions,  until  prevented  by  the  prize  crew. 

(3th.  The  real  fuel  on  board  of  her,  i.  e.,  wood,  was  barely  sufficient 
to  reach  Sambel  Harbor  with,  and  it  was  necessary  to  cut  more  in 
order  to  reach  this  harbor. 

7th.  Though  cleared  for  New  Orleans  via  Pensacola,  they  had  barely 
wood  enough  to  enable  them  to  reach  the  point  where  captured  and 
proceed  inside,  where  fuel  could  be  easily  obtained. 

8th.  The  enemy  are  known  to  have  been  in  communication  with  that 
portion  of  the  coast  Avhere  she  was  captured  quite  recently,  and  it  is 
probable  they  are  still. 

9th.  The  statements  and  explanations  of  the  captain  are  very  con¬ 
tradictory  in  their  character. 

10th.  Her  “shipping  articles”  are  not  endorsed  by  the  collector  of 
the  port  cleared  from  (Key  West). 

11th.  Two  men  called  for  by  the  crew  list  are  not  on  board.  The 
man  Holmes  had  just  been  taken  to  Key  West  as  a  prisoner,  and  had 
taken  the  oath  of  allegiance  there. 

12th.  Three  different  times  after  she  was  captured  she  was  discov¬ 
ered  to  be  on  fire,  and  her  crew,  on  being  requested  to  assist  in  extin¬ 
guishing  the  flames,  would  not  do  so  until  obliged  to  do  so  by  the 
officer  in  charge. 

The  above  are  the  principal  facts  in  the  case,  and  I  have  deemed  it 
my  duty  to  detain  and  send  her  in.  Their  actions  have  been  very  sus¬ 
picious,  and  I  think  there  is  no  doubt  of  an  intention  of  running  'in  for 
a  cargo. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  H.  Rockwell, 

Actg.  Vol.  Lieut.,  U.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  U.  S.  bark  Gem  of  the  Sea. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Fleming,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding 
U.  S.'S.  Sagamore,  transmitting  report  regarding  expedition  for 
the  seizure  of  cotton  in  Suwanee  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Sagamore, 

Off  Cedar  Keys,  Fla.,  June  12,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  6th  instant  I  sent  the 
launch  from  this  vessel,  and  two  boats  from  the  steamer  Clyde,  with 


718 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


24  men  and  4  officers,  on  an  expedition  up  the  Suwanee  River  to  seize 
some  cotton  I  had  been  informed  the  rebels  were  making  use  of  for 
the  purpose  of  constructing  breastworks  on  that  river.  On  the  7th 
the  expedition  reached  the  place,  about  38  miles  up,  in  the  vicinity  of 
Clay  Landing,  and  succeeded  in  capturing  100  bales,  mostly  sea-island 
cotton,  which  had  been  brought  to  this  place. 

In  conclusion,  permit  me  to  say  that  Acting  Ensign  L.  It.  Chester, 
the  officer  in  charge  of  the  expedition,  conducted  it  in  a  manner  to  be 
commended,  returning  his  force  with  no  casualties  and  not  an  article 
missing,  and  the  behavior  of  the  officers  and  men  who  accompanied 
him  was  as  usual  everything  that  could  be  desired. 

Enclosed  herewith  please  find  copy  of  Acting  Ensign  Chester’s 
report. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

[Charles  E.  Fleming,]

[Report  of  same  date  and  like  tenor  to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy.] 

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Sagamore, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  June  12,  186 f 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  orders  of  June  6,  I  proceeded  with  Act¬ 
ing  Master’s  Mate  F.  Silva  on  an  expedition  up  the  Suwanee  River  to 
seize  some  cotton  belonging  to  the  rebels,  supposed  to  be  in  that 
vicinity. 

Our  launch,  howitzer,  and  12  men,  two  boats  from  the  U.  S.  S. 
Clyde ,  with  Acting  Ensign  H.  Jones,  Acting  Master’s  Mate  C.  F. 
Palmer,  and  12  men,  formed  the  expedition.  We  were  joined  while 
on  oiu  way  toward  the  river  by  7  refugees  in  their  own  boat. 

At  5  p.  m.  on  the  7 th  instant  we  arrived  in  the  vicinity  of  Clay 
Landing  and  secured  about  100  bales  of  cotton,  principally  sea-island. 
W  e  rafted  it  and  started  that  same  evening  for  Cedar  Keys  with  it 
in  tow. 

During  the  passage  to  this  station  we  experienced  head  winds  and 
currents,  obliging  us  to  reraft  the  cotton  three  times,  and  delaying 
our  arrival  until  to-day. 

I  beg  leave  to  state  that  the  above-mentioned  officers  used  every 
exertion  to  forward  the  object  of  the  expedition.  The  men  were 
prompt  and  obedient,  performing  their  duties  cheerfully. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  R,  Chester, 

Acting  Ensign ,  in  Charge  of  Expedition. 

Lieutenant- Commander  Charles  E.  Fleming, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Sagamore.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Browne,  IT.  S.  JVavy,  command- 
tng  U.  S.  bark  Restless ,  regarding  cooperative  movements  in  St. 
Andrews  Bay. 

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 

St.  Andrew’s  Bay ,  Florida ,  June  1%,  1861,. 
feiE.  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report: 

On  the  22d  April  we  dispatched  the  barge  up  East  Bay  to  destroy 
all  salt  works  in  operation.  Only  one  was  discovered,  and  that  was 
destroyed..  There  were  at  that  time  some  small  concerns  in  West 
Bay  making  salt,  but  hearing  they  intended  to  erect  extensive  ones 
again  for  the  Government  on  the  old  site  destroyed  by  us  in  December 
last,  I  concluded  not  to  molest  them  until  they  were  more  numerous. 
In  the  meantime  Captain  Woods,  commanding  the  Federal  post  here 
desiring  our  cooperation  on  an  expedition  to  destroy  some  rebel  Gov¬ 
ernment  property,  on  the  23d  of  May  I  dispatched  Acting  Ensign 
Eason  in  the  barge  with  a  crew  of  11  men,  with  howitzer  and  rifles, *to 
cover  the  soldiers  landing  and  retreating  if  necessary.  In  the  mean¬ 
time  our  men  landed  and  destroyed  some  10  or  12  salt  works  in  that 
vicinity,  which  see  in  his  report,  enclosed. 

On  the  27th  of  May,  hearing  that  another  extensive  salt  work  had 
been  erected  up  East  Bay  since  April,  I  determined  to  destroy  it,  and 
if  possible  to  do  so  as  fast  as  they  build  new  ones. 

I  therefore  dispatched  Acting  Ensign  Eason  again  in  the  barge  with 
a  howitzer  and  8  men,  accompanied  by  the  second  cutter  with  ll  men 
armed  with  howitzer  and  rifles,  the  result  of  which  is  detailed  in  his 
report,  enclosed. 

Again  on  the  8th  of  June  the  Federal  soldiers  here  under  Captain 
Woods,  being  out  of  provisions  and  no  prospect  of  a  supply  from  Key 
West  for  some  time,  he  consulted  with  me  the  feasibility  of  procuring 
supplies  of  corn  and  bacon  by  making  a  raid  on  the  saltworks  up  West 
Bay.  Feeling  assured  that  this  could  be  accomplished,  I  directed  Act¬ 
ing  Ensign  W.  B.  Rankin  to  proceed  in  the  barge  with  5  men  from 
this  vessel,  carrying  Captain  Woods  and  40  of  his  men,  taking  our 
howitzer.  We  heard  there  was  a  company  of  cavalry  in  that  vicanity. 
The  expedition  was  successful  and  returned  the  next  day,  having  made 
a  very  successful  raid;  97  salt  works  were  totally  destroyed,  with  all 
their  tools  and  equipments,  etc.  The  barge  was  loaded  with  corn  and 
bacon;  of  the  former,  600  rations,  and  of  the  latter,  320.  Enclosed  is 
Acting  Ensign  Rankin’s  report. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Volunteer  lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla.

U.  S.  Schooner  J.  S.  Chambers, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  t. Tidy  12,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report: 

On  the  13th  June  last  an  armed  boat’s  crew  was  dispatched  from 
this  vessel  in  charge  of  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Henry  E.  Hopkinson  for 
the  Waccasassa  River,  Florida,  in  connection  with  an  armed  boat  from 
the  U.  S.  S.  Clyde.  They  returned  on  the  Kith  ultimo,  with  a  quantity 
of  cotton  captured  on  said  river,  some  34  bags,  which  has  been 
delivered  to  the  proper  authorities  at  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  Nickerson, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C. 


Reports  of  Acting  Master ‘  Gray ,  71.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  store- 
ship  Courier,  regarding  the  loss  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  Storeship  Courier, 

Ashore  on  the  Island  of  Abaco ,  June  15 ,  186 f 

Sir:  I  regret  to  announce  to  you  the  loss  of  this  ship,  she  having  run 
ashore  on  this  island  about  10  miles  south  of  Elbow  Cay  light-house, 
at  about  3  o’clock  on  the  morning  of  the  14th  instant.  The  officers  and 
crew  are  all  safe,  and  I  have  written  to  the  U.  S.  consul  at  Nassau 
requesting  him  to  charter  a  vessel  to  convey  them  to  a  port  in  the 
United  States. 

The  ship  will  prove  a  total  wreck.  Wo  are  now  engaged  in  saving 
stores  and  cargo,  the  latter  in  a  damaged  condition.  The  only  way  1 
have  to  account  for  this  unfortunate  occurrence  is,  that  the  reckoning 
of  the  ship  must  have  been  very  much  out,  or  that  we  experienced  a 
very  strong  westerly  current. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

S.  C.  Gray, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Memorandum  of  an  agreement  between  H.  N.  Farr,  master  and  owner  of  the  schooner 
Samuel  T.  Keese,  and  W  C.  Thompson,  acting  U.  S.  consul  at  Nassau. 


It  is  hereby  agreed  b y  and  between  the  above  parties  that  said 
schooner  shall  proceed  hence  to  Lynyard  Cay,  Great  Abaco  Island,  Baaas 
[Bahamas],  and  take  on  board  the  officers  and  crew  of  the  wrecked 
U.  S.  ship  Courier)',  75  men,  more  or  less,  and  transport  them  to  the 
port  of  Port  Royal,  S.  C.  And  that  the  ship  shall  be  well  and  suffi¬ 
ciently  equipped  and  provided  for  that  purpose  with  all  articles  except 
provisions,  and  that  the  master  shall  lend  them  every  necessary  assist¬ 
ance  on  the  voyage,  and  to  land  at  Port  Royal;  also  "that  he  shall  take 
on  board  and  convey  there  all  the  baggage  of  tbe  officers  and  crew 
and  three  brass  guns  now  on  board  the  Courier,  or  landed  from  her, 
together  with  their  carriages  and  appurtenances.  It  is  also  agreed 
that  said  Captain  H.  N.  Farr  shall  receive  therefor  the  sum  of  $1,000, 
payable  in  gold  coin  by  a  draft  on  the  United  States  Treasury  at 
thirty  days’  sight.  That  said  officers  and  crew  shall  furnish  provisions 
for  the  voyage,  and  that  a  pilot  from  this  place  to  said  Lynyard  Cay 
shall  be  provided  the  vessel  at  this  place. 

W.  C.  Thompson, 

Acting  U.  S.  Consul.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
loss  of  mails  en  route  to  the  Department. 

No.  190.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  June  15 ,  186 f 

Sir:  The  report  is  current  that  two  mails  from  this  port  for  the 
North  have  been  lost.  The  one  went  north  by  the  Nightingale ,  and  on 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  723 

the  arrival  of  that  vessel  at  New  York  could  not  be  found.  The  other 
was  lost  at  sea  by  the  sinking  of  the  Pocahontas  off  Hatteras.  I  can  not 
tell  what  letters  may  have  gone  by  these  mails  to  the  Department,  but 
am  inclined  to  believe  that  communications  of  importance  from  myself 
to  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  were  in  both  the  mails.  If  the  Depart¬ 
ment  will  furnish  me  with  the  numbers  of  such  letters  as  have  failed 
to  come  to  hand,  I  will  at  once  forward  duplicate. 

Respectfully, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 

A.ctg.  Rear-  Admiral,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Rlockdg .  Squadron . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Order  of  Acting  Pear- Admiral  Bailey ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  to  Captain  Greene , 
C.  Navy ,  commanding  U .  S.  S.  San  Jacinto ,  to  proceed  in  search 

of  blockade  runners . 


U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West ,  June  16 ,  186 f 

Sir:  In  case  the  vessels  for  which  you  have  been  waiting  have  not 
as  vet  made  their  appearance,  I  am  inclined  to  believe  that  their  desti¬ 
nation  has  been  altered  and  that  it  will  be  useless  to  delay  longer  in 
the  hope  of  making  them  prizes. 

lou  will  therefore,  unless  }tou  have  good  reason  to  suppose  that  a 
further  delay  would  be  productive  of  good  results,  return  upon  the 
receipt  of  this  order  to  this  port.  On  your  way  to  this  port,  in  case 
you  have  on  board  a  sufficient  supply  of  coal,  you  can  cruise  for  a  few 
days  between  longitude  85°  and  87°  W.,  latitude  24°  and  24°  30'  N., 
making  your  course  between  these  parallels  E.  by  N.  1  N.,  and  W. 
by  S.  \  S.,  steering  from  daylight  till  meridian  to  the  eastward  and 
from  meridian  to  sundown  to  the  westward,  lying  to  at  night. 

There  is  reason  to  believe  that  blockade  runners,  both  from  Sabine 
Pass  and  Galveston,  can  be  intercepted  on  that  line. 

Respectfully, 


Theodorus  Bailey, 

Act.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  GulfBlockdg.  Squadron. 


Captain  T.  P.  Greene,  U.  S.  Navy.

result  of  the  appraisement  of  powder  taken  from,  prize  steamer 
Cumberland. 

No.  204.]  U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  June  23,  186 J. 

Sir:  In  the  Department’s  communication  to  me  of  May  27,  1864,  I 
was  directed  to  have  the  powder  landed  from  the  prize  steamer  Cum¬ 
berland  (consisting  of  100  barrels)  examined,  and  if  found  to  be  as 
represented,  to  cause  it  to  be  taken  for  the  use  of  the  Navy  upon  the 
report  of  a  board  of  appraisers  appointed  to  appraise  the  same.  I 
enclose  herewith  the  papers  relating  to  the  matter,  including  the 
report  of  Captain  McFarland,  L.  S.  Engineer  Corps,  in  charge  of  the 
construction  of  the  fortifications  on  this  island  and  at  Tortugas,  and 
the  report  of  the  board  of  appraisers, 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.

I  have  accordingly  taken  the  powder,  100  barrels  of  100  pounds 
each,  for  the  use  of  the  Navy,  at  20  cents  per  pound,  the  appraised 
value.  There  being  no  room  for  it  on  the  ordnance  ship,  I  have  left 
it  at  the  magazine  at  Fort  Taylor. 

Very  respectfully,

Roebuck ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  sloop  Last  Resort  in  Jupiter 
Inlet ,  Florida. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

Off  Indian  River  Inlet ,  June  30,  186 J. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  j’ou  the  capture  of  the  rebel  sloop 
Last  Resort,  John  Dougherty,  master,  and  crew  of  two  men,  claiming 
to  be  passengers,  and  a  cargo  consisting  of  6  bales  cotton. 

The  capture  was  made  on  the  morning  of  June  30,  at  Jupiter  Inlet, 
35  miles  from  the  bark,  by  the  launch  of  this  vessel,  in  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  E.  H.  Wat  keys,  who  reports  that  he  found  no  papers 
or  flag;  also  that  the  master,  John  Dougherty,  had  made  his  escape. 
The  sloop,  in  my  opinion,  being  unfit  to  send  to  Key  West,  1  have 
taken  her  cargo  on  board  the  bark. 

Enclosed  please  find  crew  list  of  the  bark  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 
I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  L.  Martine,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Budd,  U.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  if.  S.  S.  Merrimac ,  regarding  the  capture  of  sloop  Henrietta ,  of 
Havana ,  July  1 ,  TSVJ. 

U.  S.  S.  Merrimac,  ./Vy  3,  186 f 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  that  at  8  a.  m.  July  1,  in  latitude 
28<J  20'  N.,  longitude  84°  W.,  I  captured  the  sloop  Henrietta ,  of  Havana, 
bound  from  Bayport,  Fla.,  to  the  former  place,  cargo  about  16  bales 
of  cotton.  A  schooner,  afterwards  ascertained  to  be  the  J  S.  Cham¬ 
bers ,  was  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture,  but  not  within  signal  dis¬ 
tance.  The  crew  of  the  sloop  consist  of  Joseph  Napoleon  Talbot, 
master;  Daniel  Robinson,  Bryon  Doughtey,  and  Francis  Allen,  hands; 
M.  Cole,  of  Atlanta,  Ga. ,  passenger.  Enclosed  please  find  prize  list 
and  papers  found  in  prize. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  Budd, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  Merrimac. 
Acting  Rear-Admiral  Theodorus  Bailet, 

Commanding  Eastern  Gidf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Nickerson ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  TJ.  S. 
schooner  James  S.  Chambers,  claiming  a  share  in  the  sloop  Henrietta , 
captured  Judy  1 ,  186 f 

U.  S.  Schooner  J.  S.  Chambers, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  July  12,  186 J 

Sir;  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of,  and  submit  a  claim 
of  this  vessel  to  a  prize  sloop,  Henrietta,  captured  by  the  U.  S.  S. 
Merrimac,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  W.  Budd,  commanding.  The 
following  are  the  circumstances  of  the  capture: 

At  about  5:30  a.  m.  on  1st  instant,  in  latitude  28°  24',  longitude  83° 
24',  a  sail  was  reported  bearing  S.  W.  by  W.  We  were  at  the  time 
heading  S.  by  W.  I  immediately  directed  my  course  for  her,  setting 
all  sail.  At  7 : 30  a.  m.  a  steamer  was  discovered  under  our  lee  quarter, 
bearing  about  N.  N.  W.,  apparently  standing  for  the  sail  alluded  to. 
When  abeam  of  us  persons  could  be  distinctly  seen  on  board  of  her. 
Shortly  after,  the  chase  was  brought  to  by  the  steamer,  at  which  time 
the  ensign  of  the  latter  could  be  plainly  made  out  from  this  vessel. 
We  were  gaining  on  the  sloop  fast  and  should  have  soon  secured  her 
without  assistance. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  Nickerson, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Commander  Shufeldt,  TJ.  S.  _  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 
Proteus,  regarding  the  cruise  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Proteus, 

Key  West,  July  3,  186 J 

Admiral:  Since  my  letter  to  you  of  17th  ultimo,  and  after  going  to 
several  points  among  the  Bahamas,  in  pursuit  of  information,  1  have 
cruised  in  this  ship  to  the  northward  of  Matanilla  Reef. 


728 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


On  the  night  of  25th  ultimo  we  chased  and  overhauled  the  U.  S.  S. 
Bermuda.  During  the  afternoon  of  the  26th  we  chased  a  blockade 
runner,  supposed  to  be  the  Lucy,  from  Nassau  for  Wilmington.  On 
the  27th  we  captured  the  steamer  Jupiter ,  after  a  chase  of  four  hours, 
latitude  29°  10'  N.,  longitude  77°  02'  W.  This  prize  showed  British 
colors,  but  previous  to  capture  had  thrown  overboard  her  papers  and 


cargo. 

I  sent  the  prize  to  Boston  in  charge  of  Acting  Gunner  W.  H.  Pearce, 
leaving  on  board  the  supercargo  and  mate,  together  with  6  of  her  sea¬ 
men.  The  master  and  engineers,  with  15  seamen  and  firemen,  I  have 
brought  to  this  port  and  are  now  on  board,  subject  to  your  order. 

I  sent  the  prize  in  charge  of  the  acting  gunner  because,  in  my 
opinion,  of  the  two  acting  ensigns  remaining  on  board  this  ship,  neither 
is  competent  to  take  a  command. 

On  the  1st  instant  we  chased  for  six  hours  a  fine  steamer,  supposed 
to  be  the  Let  Her  Be,  from  Nassau  to  Wilmington;  in  that  time  she 
gained  upon  us  at  the  least  12  miles. 

I  take  this  occasion  to  say,  from  information  I  have  obtained  and 
from  my  knowledge  of  the  ground,  that  if  I  could  have  a  good  sea¬ 
going  steamer,  capable  of  11  to  12  knots  speed,  and  of  remaining  at 
sea  fifteen  days  in  eveiy  month,  I  could  do  much  toward  breaking  up 
the  illegal  traffic  between  Nassau  and  Wilmington.  The  Proteus 
wants  speed.  During  this  cruise  in  search  of  the  Florida,  and  of 
blockade  runners,  we  have  boarded  and  spoken  2d  vessels,  have 
steamed  nearly  4,000  miles,  and  made  1,070,000  revolutions  of  the 
engines. 

I  am,  very  respectfully, 


R.  W.  Shufeldt, 

Commander. 


Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  Fast  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Order  of  Acting  Bear- Admiral  Bailey,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Captain  Greene, 
U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto,  defiling  the  cruis¬ 
ing  ground  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Dale,  July  5,  186J 

Sir:  So  soon  as  the  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto ,  under  your  command, 
can  be  got  ready  for  sea,  you  will  proceed  to  cruise  on  a  parallel  of 
29°  N.,  between  85°  30'  and  87°  30'.  The  Merrimnc  has  orders  to 
cruise  on  a  parallel  of  29°  30',  between  the  meridians  of  86°  and  88°. 
The  Luka  has  orders  to  cruise  to  the  southward  and  eastward  of 
Mobile,  from  50  to  100  miles  offshore.  Should  you  fall  in  with  the 
latter  vessel  you  will  give  her  commanding  officer  orders  to  cruise  on 
a  parallel  of  28°  30'  N.,  between  the  meridians  of  85°  and  87°.  When 
in  want  of  coal  proceed  to  Tampa  therefor,  and  having  coaled,  return 
to  your  present  anchorage  at  Sand  Key  and  report  to  me. 

Respectfully, 

T.  Bailey, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Captain  T.  P.  Greene,  U.  S.  Navy, 

Commanding  ZT.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto ,

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Cheesman ,  U.  S.  Wavy ,  com- 

tnanding  U.  S.  S.  Magnolia ,  regarding  the  capture  of  three  boats 

from  Reace  Creek ,  near  Ray  port ,  AYa. 

U.  S.  S.  Magnolia, 

At  Sea ,  July  7,  186 J 

Sir:  Being-  at  sea  in  north  latitude  27°  41'  and  west  longitude  78° 
a‘  m*  ° the  4th  instant,  three  sails  were  reported  bearing 
IN.  W.  from  us  by  the  masthead  lookout.  Immediately  stood  for 
them,  but  the  sails  had  disappeared  and  standing  on  this  course  for 
awhile,  saw  three  boats  with  neither  masts  nor  sails  up.  At  11:30 
a.  m.  spoke  them;  they  replied,  they  were  from  Dixie  and  bound  to 
Nassau,  New  Providence,  loaded  with  cotton  and  turpentine  (about  9 
bales  and  8  barrels).  They  were  from  Peace  Creek,  near  Bayport, 
Fla.,  had  been  forty-two  da3rs  on  the  passage,  nine  of  which  they  had 
been  in  the  Gulf,  were  almost  destitute  of  provisions  and  water. 
There  were  two  men  in  each  boat,  making  six  in  all;  the  boats  had 
neither  name  nor  papers. 

The  nearest  land  at  the  time  of  capture  was  the  Middle  Shoal, 
Mata n ilia  Reef,  bearing  S.  by  W.,  distance  about  15  miles.  Were 
obliged  to  stave  in  the  decks  of  the  boats  to  discharge  their  cargoes, 
and  the  boats  were  so  shaky  and  worthless  had  them  scuttled  and  cast 
adrift. 

All  the  men  were  foreigners  with  the  exception  of  one,  whose 
family  is  residing  in  Florida.  All  but  this  one  I  have  set  on  shore  at 
Great  Stirrup  Cay,  Bahamas,  and  intend  to  take  this  man  to  Key  West 
in  the  ship. 

Enclosed  please  find  list  of  officers  and  men  attached  to  this  vessel 
on  the  4th  instant,  and  are  entitled  to  share  in  the  capture  made  on 
that  day. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  S.  Cheesman, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Secretary  of  the  Navy, 

Washington ,  D.  C. 

[Report  dated  July  4, 1864,  and  of  like  tenor,  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral 
Bailey.] 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Martine ,  II.  S.  Wavy ,  commanding  U.  S.  bark 
Roebuck ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner  Terrapin. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

Off  Indian  River  Inlet ,  July  11,  1861. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  capture  of  the  English 
schooner  Terrapin ,  of  Nassau,  Peter  Cummings,  master,  and  crew  of 
2  colored  men  and  1  man  claiming  to  be  a  passenger,  with  a  cargo  of  3 
bales  of  cotton  and  3  barrels  turpentine. 

The  capture  was  made  on  the  evening  of  July  10,  at  Jupiter  Inlet, 
35  miles  from  the  bark,  by  the  launch  of  this  vessel,  in  charge  of  Act¬ 
ing  Ensign  E.  H.  Watkeys,  who  reports  that  he  found  no  papers  or 
flag,  but  on  removing  her  after  hatch  to  put  the  cargo  of  the  sloop 
Last  Resort  in,  the  crew  list  and  clearance  from  Nassau  were  found.

As  soon  as  an  opportunity  offers  will  send  her  to  Key  West  with  the 
cargo  of  the  sloop  for  adjudication. 

Enclosed  please  find  crew  list  of  the  bark  at  the  time  of  the  above 
capture. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  L.  Martine, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Martine ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 

bark  Roebuck ,  regarding  the  capture  of  sloop  Last  Resort ,  in  Jupiter 

Inlet. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 

Off  Indian  River  Inlet ,  July  1°2 , 186 J 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  on  the  29th  of  June  I 
dispatched  the  launch  of  this  vessel,  with  an  armed  crew  of  ten  men  and 
a  coxswain,  under  command  of  Acting  Ensign  E.  H.  Watkeys,  to  Jupi¬ 
ter  Inlet  to  blockade.  On  the  30th  of  J une,  at  11 : 30  a.  m. ,  he  captured 
the  sloop  Last  Resort ,  John  Dougherty,  master,  attempting  to  run  out 
of  the  inlet  with  6  bales  of  cotton. 

The  captain  escaped  into  the  bushes.  No  papers  or  flag  have  been 
found.  There  were  two  passengers  on  board,  viz,  Robert  Day-  and 
George  Coulter. 

At  8  o’clock  on  the  evening  of  the  2d  of  July  the  prize  sloop  arrived 
alongside  the  bark  with  one  passenger,  in  charge  of  John  Findlay  (cox¬ 
swain),  and  one  seaman.  The  next  morning  discharged  the  prize.  Mr. 
Watkeys  and  the  balance  of  his  crew  remained  at  the  inlet  to  endeavor 
to  raise  a  sunken  schooner  supposed  to  contain  6  bales  of  cotton  and  1 
barrel  turpentine. 

On  the  evening  of  July  11,  at  8  p.  m.,  Mr.  Watkeys  returned  with 
the  launch  and  a  prize,  the  schooner  Terrapin ,  of  Nassau,  Peter  Cum¬ 
mings,  master,  and  three  men,  one  of  whom  represented  himself  as  a 
passenger  and  owner  of  the  cotton,  Samuel  Kennard.  Her  cargo  con¬ 
sists  of  3  bales  of  cotton  and  3  barrels  turpentine,  captured  July  10, 
at  5  p.  m.,  attempting  to  run  out  at  Jupiter  Inlet. 

Mr.  Watkeys  also  brought  two  men  and  a  small  boat  which  he  had 
taken  on  the  river.  They  claimed  to  be  Union  men,  and  asserted  that 
they  had  never  been  engaged  in  blockade  running;  all  that  they  had 
was  wrecked  stuff.  They  both  took  the  oath  of  allegiance  before  me, 
which  I  enclose  to  you.  One  of  them  had  previously  taken  it  in  Key 
West  (George  C.  Brantley). 

After  a  rigid  examination  I  could  find  nothing  that  would  warrant 
my  detaining  them;  therefore  I  gave  them  their  boat  and  things  and 
let  them  go. 

I  would  also  respectfully  report  to  you  the  arrival  at  Indian  River 
Inlet  of  26  refugees — 7  men,  6  women,  13  children.  They  wish  to  be 
sent  to  St.  Augustine. 

Mr.  Watkeys  reports  that  out  of  the  sunken  schooner  he  could  only 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  731 

get  what  will  amount  to  about  2  bales  of  cotton;  the  balance  is  all 
decayed. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  L.  Martine, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Corndg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West ,  Fla. 

July  14,  1864. 

Sir:  Since  writing  the  above  I  have  to  report  the  arrival  of  five 
more  refugees.

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  in  obedience  to  your  order,  dated 
June  23,  1864,  I  proceeded  with  the  Two  Sisters  to  the  mouth  of  the 
Suwanee  River,  for  the  purpose  of  securing  a  quantity  of  cotton  left 
there  by  the  tender  Fox.  I  found  the  cotton  sunk  in  the  mud  and 
water  and  badly  broken  up,  and  was  employed  two  days  in  getting  it 
above  high  water,  cleaning  off  the  mud,  and  spreading  it  out  to  dry. 

I  then  proceeded  to  Cedar  Kej^s  and  obtained  90  yards  of  bagging 
from  Lieutenant-Commander  Fleming,  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Sagamore,  with 
which  I  returned  to  the  Suwanee,  repacked  the  cotton,  brought  it  to 
Cedar  Keys,  and  delivered  it  to  Lieutenant-Commander  Fleming,  to  be 
forwarded  to  Key  West. 

The  lot  consists  of  15  round  bales  (or  bags)  marked  Fox,  and  is  all  in 
a  wet  and  damaged  condition. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  Chatfield, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  Two  Sisters.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Russell ,  U  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 

schooner  Ariel ,  regarding  cooperative  expedition  to  Bayport ,  Fla. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Ariel, 

Tampa  Bay ,  Fla. ,  July  25,  186  J 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that,  in  obedience  to  your  orders,  1 
proceeded  to  cruise  between  Tampa  Bay  and  Cedar  Keys.  Stopping 
at  Fort  Myers  to  procure  a  pilot,  1  received  a  communication  from 
Captain  J.  W.  Childs,  commanding  officer  at  that  post,  requesting  the 
means  of  transporting  some  250  troops  to  a  point  convenient  to  Bay- 
port.  Meeting  the  schooner  Sea  Bird  off  Anclote  Keys,  I  requested 
Acting  Ensign  Robbins  to  accompany  me  to  Point  Arrassa  [Punta 
Rasa]  to  assist  in  that  service.  Stopping  at  Tampa  Bay,  I  requested 
the  assistance  of  Captain  Chandler,  of  the  Huntsville,  who  immedi¬ 
ately  dispatched  the  schooner  Stonewall  to  Point  Arrassa  [Punta  Rasa] 
for  the  same  purpose.  The  three  schooners  took  on  board  260  troops, 
Captain  J.  W.  Childs  being  in  command  of  them.  We  proceeded  to 
Anclote  Keys,  the  sloop  Rosalie  taking  part  of  the  troops  from  the 
Stonewall.  On  July  7  we  landed  them  on  the  north  side  of  the 
Anclote  River,  the  Stonewall  and  Rosalie  returning  to  Tampa  Bay. 
The  expedition  left  for  the  purpose  of  making  a  raid  on  Brooksville 
and  then  falling  back  on  Bayport.  I  was  to  meet  them  at  .that  place 
on  the  12th  instant.  Captain  Childs  and  8  men  being  unable  to  march, 
remained  on  board  the  Ariel. 

On  July  10,  in  company  with  the  Sea  Bird,  I  proceeded  to  Bayport; 
the  Sea  Bird,  being  unable  to  get  in  that  place,  anchored  about  4  miles 
off.  I  ran  up  within  100  yards  of  where  the  battery  had  been  located 
and  anchored  at  5  p.  m.,  observing  some  few  men  retreating  from  the 
town  by  the  road. 

I  then  dispatched  Acting  Ensign  Bacon  under  a  flag  of  truce  to 
demand  the  surrender  of  the  town,  if  he  found  anyone  there,  or  to  take 
possession  of  it  if  they  had  evacuated  it.  At  6  p.  m.  Acting  Ensign 
Bacon  returned  and  reported  that  the  male  inhabitants  had  all  fled,  and 
that  there  were  live  or  six  families  residing  there,  and  also  that  there 
were  also  a  few  bales  of  cotton  on  the  wharf  ready  for  shipping. 
Acting  Ensigns  Robbins  and  Dunderdale  arrived  at  this  time  with  ten 
men.  I  immediately  dispatched  them  on  shore  and  requested  Captain 
Childs  to  picket  the  road  with  the  six  soldiers  who  were  fit  for  that 
duty. 

I  then  proceeded  on  shore  and  examined  the  town,  visiting  the  fam¬ 
ilies,  whom  I  found  greatly  frightened,  but  having  no  knowledge  of 
the  expedition  that  was  operating  against  Brooksville.  The  two  guns 
which  I  had  expected  to  find  there  had  been  removed  to  Brooksville 
for  some  time.  Eleven  bags  of  cotton  ready  for  shipping  I  took  pos¬ 
session  of  and  commenced  getting  it  off  that  night.  There  was  also 
some  20  or  30  bales  of  cotton  that  were  lying  loose  in  a  building  for¬ 
merly  used  as  a  schoolhouse,  and  32  bales,  ready  packed,  on  the  road 
about  1^  miles  from  the  town.  There  were  also  some  large  scows  and 
a  number  of  small  boats  there,  but  no  blockade  runners.  The  people 
assured  me  that  but  two  vessels  had  run  the  blockade  from  that  place 
for  the  last  five  months.  Four  contrabands  that  were  there  placed 
themselves  under  my  protection.  Stationing  extra  pickets,  with  strict 
orders  not  to  enter  a  house  or  molest  anyone,  I  waited  until  morning. 
On  the  11th  at  7  a.  m.  our  military  forces  entered  Bayport,  when

I  withdrew  my  pickets,  and  they  took  possession  of  the  town.  I 
requested  a  detail  of  soldiers  from  the  commanding1  officer  for  the  pur¬ 
pose  of  bringing-  all  the  cotton  off  with  me,  which  I  could  have  done 
in  the  large  scows  that  were  there.  The  detail  was  furnished  me,  but 
in  the  meanwhile  all  the  cotton  near  the  place  was  fired  by  the  soldiers, 
although  the  commanding  officer  had  assured  me  that  he  would  protect 
it  and  assist  me  to  remove  it  from  the  place. 

On  the  11th  at  5  p.  in.  the  military  wishing  to  evacuate  the  place,  1 
took  00  men  on  the  Ariel,  besides  the  cotton  I  had  on  board,  and  trans¬ 
ferred  them  to  the  Sea  Bird.  On  the  12th  the  sloop  Rosalie  arrived, 
and  not  coming  inside,  1  sent  40  men  to  her  for  transportation  to  Fort 
Myers. 

Before  leaving  the  place  I  destroyed  the  building  used  as  a  custom¬ 
house,  also  all  boats  and  lighters.  On  the  morning  of  the  13th  we 
succeeded  in  removing  the  troops  from  Bayport,  arriving  at  Anclote 
Keys  on  the  same  da}7. 

Leaving  the  cotton  at  Anclote  Keys  we  proceeded  to  Tampa  Bay, 
and  at  that  place  transferred  all  the  troops  and  prisoners  to  steamer 
Ella  Morse. 

I  returned  to  Anclote  Keys  to  bring  the  cotton  and  arrived  at 
Egmont  Key  with  it  this  day. 

Acting  Ensigns  Robbins,  Bacon,  and  Dunderdale,  and  the  crews  of 
the  Sea  Bird  and  Ariel ,  are  entitled  to  much  commendation  for  their 
untiring  energy  throughout  this  affair. 

I  also  bring  two  deserters  from  the  rebel  army,  who  have  taken  the 
oath  of  allegiance  and  wish  to  join  the  Second  Florida  Regiment. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  J.  Russell, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding .

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Robbins ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S. 
schooner  Sea  Bird,  regarding  cooperative  expedition  to  Bayport ,  Fla. 

U.  S.  Schooner  (Tender)  Sea  Bird, 

Tampa  Bay ,  Fla. ,  July  25,  186 J. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  the  orders  of  Captain  T.  F.  Greene,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto,  dated  the  21st  of  June,  I  proceeded  to  sea  on 
the  22d  ultimo.  On  the  26th  I  communicated  with  Acting  Master  J.  J. 
Russell,  commanding  tender  Ariel,  and  received  from  him  orders  to 
accompany  him  to  Punta  Rasa  for  the  purpose  of  conveying  troops 
from  that  place  to  a  point  near  Bayport.  I  immediately  got  under¬ 
way  and  arrived  at  Punta  Rasa  on  the  28th  ultimo,  in  company  with 
the  tenders  Ariel  and  Stonewall,  duly  1  received  on  board  110 
troops,  including  officers.  I  then  got  underway  and  proceeded  to  sea. 
Arrived  at  Anclote  Keys  on  the  morning  of  the  5th  instant.  At  5 
p.  m.  the  same  day  the  schooner  Stonewall  and  the  sloop  Rosalie 
arrived,  the  Rosalie  having  taken  on  board  part  of  the  troops  from  the 
Stonewall.  I  then  got  underway  and  ran  inside  the  key,  and  on  the 
morning  of  the  8th  instant  landed  the  troops  above  Anclote  River. 

The  object  of  the  expedition  was  to  make  a  raid  on  Brooksville  and 


736 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


then  to  fall  back  on  Bayport.  After  landing  the  troops  I  then  stood 
up  the  coast,  and  on  the  10th  instant,  in  company  with  the  Ariel,  stood 
in  toward  Bayport  and  anchored  about  4  miles  from  the  town,  not 
being  able  to  get  nearer  on  account  of  the  shallowness  of  the  water. 
Taking  10  men  (armed)  in  the  boat  and  with  Acting  Ensign  C.  E.  Dun- 
derdale,  pulled  in  toward  the  town.  In  the  meantime  the  Ariel  stood 
in  and  anchored  within  200  yards  of  the  landing.  Pulling  alongside  of 
the  Ariel,  Captain  Russell  informed  me  that  he  had  sent  Acting  Ensign 
Bacon  to  reconnoiter  under  a  flag  of  truce.  He  soon  returned  with 
the  information  that  all  the  male  portion  of  the  inhabitants,  had  left, 
leaving  only  the  women  and  children,  consisting  of  four  families.  On 
landing  we  found  11  bales  of  cotton  near  the  landing,  which  was  sent 
on  board  the  Ariel ,  together  with  four  contrabands  captured  in  the  town. 
We  also  found  a  large  quantity  of  loose  cotton  in  an  old  building, 
and  about  32  bales  in  another  building  at  about  a  mile  and  a  quarter 
from  the  landing  place. 

On  the  morning  of  the  11th  instant  the  troops  came  in  and  took  pos¬ 
session  of  the  town.  The  commanding  officer  detailed  a  party  of  men 
to  assist  in  getting'  the  cotton  to  the  landing,  but  before  we  arrived  at 
the  place  where  the  cotton  was  stored  the  buildings  were  set  fire  to  and 
all  the  cotton  destroyed. 

On  the  13th  instant  took  on  board  119  troops  and  5  officers  and  pro¬ 
ceeded  to  Tampa  Bay.  There  we  transferred  them  to  the  steamer 
Ella  Morse.  The  contrabands  were  sent  to  the  U.  S.  S.  Huntsville 
by  order  of  Lieutenant-Commander  R.  Chandler. 

After  watering  ship  I  proceeded  to  my  cruising  ground  and  there 
cruising  until  the  25th  instant,  when  I  proceeded  to  Tampa  Bay  to 
intercept  the  San  Jacinto. 

I  am,  yours,  most  respectfully, 

E.  L.  Robbins, 

Actg.  Ensign,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  Tender  Sea  Bird.

shall  interpose  no  objections  to  her  being  delivered  up  to  her  owner,

Detailed  report  oj  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Dailey ,  T. .  A.  Navy ,  regard¬ 
ed prevalence  of  yellow  fever  and  measures  of  precaution  employed. 

No.  215.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Naval  Warehouse,  Key  West ,  July  07,  186 f 
Sir:  In  my  letter  of  June  19  (Nos.  195,  196)  1  stated  to  the  Depart¬ 
ment  that  indications  had  forced  me  to  the  conviction  that  we  were  to 
have  a  season  of  yellow  fever  at  this  port.  My  worst  fears  have  been 
more  than  realized,  and  for  more  than  two  months  the  disease  has 
held  its  course  without  abatement  and  is  now  as  virulent  as  at  any 
time.  The  season  of  epidemic  lasted  in  1862  nearly  till  the  1st  of 
November,  and  there  seems  no  reason  to  believe  that  it  will  disappear 
sooner  the  present  year,  except  it  shall  have  exhausted  all  the  material 
for  disease  before  that  time. 

I  propose  to  detail  to  the  Department  the  course  the  epidemic  has 
taken  and  the  measures  that  I  have  adopted  to  save  harmless  the  ves¬ 
sels  of  this  squadron  from  its  effects. 

It  was  evident  that  the  first  precaution  to  be  taken  was  to  get  the 
vessels  away  from  Key  West,  the  center  of  the  disease,  as  quickly  as  pos¬ 
sible,  and  the  second  to  provide  some  other  port  than  this  for  coaling 
purposes.  Within  forty-eight  hours  of  the  sailing  of  the  Tioga , 
accordingly,  the  harbor  was  cleared  of  all  vessels  except  such  as  must 
remain,  viz,  the  guard  schooner,  the  ordnance  ship,  and  the  tug.  The 
Huntsville  was  sent  to  Tampa  Bay,  and  I  directed  Lieutenant-Com¬ 
mander  Chandler  to  proceed  at  once  to  erect  a  wharf  at  which  the 
vessels  could  coal  and  a  hospital  that  could  be  used  in  case  of  need, 
capable  of  accommodating  30  patients.  Fortunately  the  lumber  was 
at  hand,  it  having  been  cut  at  West  Pass  and  St.  Andrew’s  Bay  by  the 
blockading  vessels.  Piles  were  sent  up,  and  a  pile  driver,  and  Mr. 
Lane,  a  professional  wharf  builder.  Lieutenant-Commander  Chand¬ 
ler  entered  upon  the  work  with  vigor  and  in  three  weeks  a  wharf  was 
built  of  the  most  substantial  character,  at  which  two  vessels  can  lie  at 
a  time,  and  with  a  depth  of  water  of  4  fathoms.  The  hospital  has  also 
been  completed  and  equipped.  All  this  has  been  done  at  a  very  incon¬ 
siderable  expense. 

I  have  sent  the  coal  vessels  up  to  discharge  and  the  steamers  of  the 
squadron  (except  those  at  St.  Marks  and  St.  George’s  Sound,  which 
coal  at  West  Pass)  are  directed  to  coal  at  Tampa.  Meantime,  while 
this  work  has  been  progressing  at  Tampa,  the  yellow  fever  has  been 
raging  at  this  post  with  a  violence  that  has  exceeded  that  of  1862,  or  I 
believe  of  any  previous  year.  The  vessels  that  have  been  detained 
here  perforce  have  suffered  severely.  The  steamer  Nita  was  under 
repairs  that  rendered  it  impossible  for  her  to  get  away.  Every  per¬ 
son  on  board  but  two  officers  has  been  taken  ill  of  the  fever  and  so

boatswain’s  mate.  The  executive  officer,  Acting  tin  sign  Joseph  A. 
Denman,  the  master’s  mate,  Robert  Wisner,  Acting  Master  Miller  H. 
Johnson  (on  board  under  arrest),  and  Surgeon’s  Steward  Purcell,  the 
only  officers  excepting  the  commanding  officer  living  on  board,  were 
taken  and  all  died.  1  lost  also  four  of  the  barge’s  crew  who  were  on 
board,  and  others  of  the  Dale’s  crew  also  died.  The  T Yandevev  had  but 
three  men;  all  were  taken;  one  died;  the  others  are  in  a  critical  condi¬ 
tion.  The  guard  schooner  Eugenie  has  also  lost  perhaps  one-fourth  of 
her  men.  On  shore  the  sickness  and  mortality  have  been  even  gieatei. 
The  provost-guard  of  45  men  has  lost  more  than  half  its  number,  and  the 
mortality  among  the  citizens  and  refugees  has  been  alarmingly  great. 
Almost  every  unacclimated  person  on  the  island  has  been  attacked.  I 
myself  had  the  disease  in  a  severe  form,  as  did  also  Mr.  Zeller,  the  fleet 
engineer,  Mr.  Bowman,  the  secretary,  Passed  Assistant  Surgeon  [W .  R.] 
Richardson,  the  quartermaster,  all  the  servants,  and  indeed  every  person 
attached  to  these  headquarters  but  one.  Of  these,  only  two  have  died, 
Dr.  Richardson  and  the  printer’s  assistant.  The  doctor  was  attached 
for  general  duty  to  the  Dale  and  lived  at  these  headquarters.  He  was 
taken  the  fourth  day  after  his  arrival  and  died  the  third  day  after  his 
attack. 

The  mortality  on  the  island  I  am  told  has  reached  as  high  as  12  to  15 
in  a  day.  1  concluded  early  in  the  progress  of  the  disease  that  it 
would  be  best  for  me  to  remain  at  this  station.  It  is  the  only  one 
from  which  the  movements  of  the  squadron  can  be  properly  directed 
or  communication  kept  up  with  the  North.  1  have  accordingly 
remained,  causing  those  vessels  that  needed  to  communicate  with  me 
to  anchor  at  Sand  Key  and  sending  out  the  tug  Marigold  to  them.  I 
believe  the  well-being  of  the  squadron  has  not  in  the  least  suffered. 
The  Roebuck  has  been  stationed  as  a  storeship  at  Tampa.  The  coal 
vessels  have  discharged  there  and  the  communication  with  the  squad¬ 
ron,  by  means  of  the  Honduras  making  her  regular  trips,  has  been  unin¬ 
terrupted.  Meantime,  in  spite  of  every  effort,  the  fever  has  manifested 
itself  on  several  of  the  vessels.  The  'Huntsville  has  had  from  20  to  30 
cases.  Her  sick  list  for  to-day  shows  14  cases,  and  those  assuming  a 
more  malignant  type  than  the  previous  ones.  1  can  spare  this  vessel 
as  well  now  as  a  'fortnight  hence.  A  portion  of  her  shaft  is  being- 
forged  at  New  York  and  must  be  nearly  ready,  so  that  a  week  or  two 
sooner  or  later  is  not  of  importance,  as  she  would  necessarily  go  north 
to  receive  the  machinery.  I  am,  however,  very  sorry  to  part  with 
the  Merrimac.  I  am  advised,  however,  by  the  surgeons,  and  my  own 
observation  of  the  nature  of  the  disease  and  its  intensity  this  season 
confirms  their  advice,  that  unless  the  vessel  goes  north  every  person 
on  board  will  in  all  probability  have  the  disease  and  very  many  must 
necessarily  die.  I  have  therefore  concluded  that  in  the  interests  of 
humanity  the  vessel  should  be  sent  north.  She  has  lost  so  far  but  one 
officer — Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineer  Thomas  Cunningham — 
but  several  of  them  are  now  sick,  there  being  at  present  8  cases  in  all, 
as  appears  by  the  surgeon’s  report  enclosed  with  another  communica¬ 
tion  on  this  subject. 

The  other  vessels  in  which  the  disease  has  appeared  are  the  Hondu¬ 
ras ,  the  luka ,  the  Marigold,  the  Honeysuckle ,  and  the  San  Jacinto. 
Deaths  ha\e  occurred  of  officers  and  men  on  these  vessels.  When  I

Report  of^  Captain  Greene, .  If.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  East  Gxdf  Block- 
ad/mg  Squadrcm,  regarding  a  series  of  success/ id  expedit  ions  from  the 
If.  8.  bark  James  L.  Davis. 


/ 

No.  4.]  Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  August  8 ,  186Jh 

.Sir:  Information  has  been  received  at  these  headquarters  of  a  series 
of  successful  boat  expeditions  from  the  U.  S.  bark  J.  L.  Davis ,  Act¬ 
ing'  Master  W.  N.  Griswold,  commanding,  on  the  station  at  Tampa  Bay. 
ihe  first  was  made  on  the  11th  July,  and  resulted  in  the  destruction  of 
some  salt  works  belonging  to  “strong secessionists”  of  Tampa,  Messrs. 
Hay  good  and  Carter.  They  had  been  employed  by  the  rebel  author¬ 
ities  for  sometime,  and  were  fitted  with  pumps,  vats,  and  8  boilers,  and 
produced  about  150  bushels  of  salt  per  day. 

The  second  was  made,  on  the  16th  ultimo,  to  the  factory  of  another 
“strong  rebel,”  named  McCloud,  containing  4  boilers,  with  all  the 
appliances,  tools,  etc.,  necessary  for  the  business,  all  of  which  were 
destroyed. 

Mr.  Griswold  confesses  himself  indebted  to  a  resident  of  Old  Tampa 
(Johnson)  for  the  information  on  which  he  acted  during  these  ex¬ 
peditions. 

The  third  expedition  was  made  on  the  2d,  3d,  and  4th  August  by 
the  tender  schooner  Stonewall ,  attached  to  the  J.  L.  Davis ,  and  com¬ 
manded  by  Acting’  Master  Henry  B.  Carter,  the  commanding  officer 
of  the  Davis ,  with  his  gig’s  crew  of  6  men  accompanying.  Proceed¬ 
ing  up  the  Manatee  River  to  the  town  of  the  same  name  a  large  saw 
and  grist  mill,  with  its  steam  engine  and  fixtures,  was  completely 
destroyed.  Learning  here  that  about  3  miles  up  the  river  was  a  sugar 
mill  belonging  to  Jefferson  Davis,  of  Richmond,  the  party  ascended 
the  river  and  found  an  establishment  which  made  last  year  over  1,500 
hogsheads  of  sugar,  of  which  two-thirds  was  sold  to  the  rebel  commis¬ 
sary  department.  After  breaking  as  much  of  the  machinery  as  was 
possible  with  the  force  at  hand,  loaded  shell  were  placed  in  various 
parts  of  the  engine  and  the  building  fired.  The  shell  exploded  and 
the  factory  was  burned  to  the  ground. 

These  expeditions,  without  loss  of  life  or  limb,  show  a  very  com¬ 
mendable  spirit  on  the  part  of  officers  and  men.  Mr.  Griswold  par¬ 
ticularly  commends  the  conduct  of  Acting  Master  Carter  as  highly 
creditable  and  pleasing. 

Respectfully, 


Tiieo.  P.  Greene, 

Captain ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey ,  U  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
condition  of  the  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto  on  arrival  off  Sandy  Hook. 

U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto, 

At  Sea,  off  Sandy  Hook,  August  12,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  have  availed  myself  of  the 
permission  accorded  in  your  favor  of  the  19th  of  July  to  return  north 
for  the  purpose  of  recruiting  my  health. 


742 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Before  leaving  Key  West  I  turned  over  the  command  of  the  East 
Gulf  Blockading  Squadron  to  Captain  Theodore  P.  Greene,  in  compli¬ 
ance  with  the  directions  of  the  Department. 

The  chief  engineer  of  this  vessel  reports  that  certain  repans  are 
needed  to  the  machinery  which  could  not  have  been  made  at  Key 
West  with  safety  during  the  prevalence  of  the  epidemic.  This  ship 
has  had  27  cases  of  yellow  fever  while  cruising  off  Mobile  and  lying  at 
Tampa  Bay.  Fortunately  the  type  of  the  disease  was  mild,  but  would 
doubtless  have  assumed  a  severe  form  had  I  permitted  the  vessel  to 
enter  the  port  of  Key  West.  I  am  happy  to  be  able  to  report  to  the 
Department  that  but  one  death  has  occurred  on  board,  that  of  Lieu¬ 
tenant  Steece,  and  that  there  have  been  no  new  cases  and  no  deaths 
for  about  three  weeks. 

Before  the  vessel  returns  to  her  station  it  will  be  necessary  to  renew 
a  portion  of  the  crew,  there  being  some  45  on  board  whose  teims  of 
service  expire  by  the  close  of  the  present  month. 

My  address  is  Oyster  Bay,  Long  Island,  N.  Y.,  where  I  shall  await 
the  further  orders  of  the  Department. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodorus  Bailey, 
Acting  Rear-Admiral. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Captain  Greene ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  measures  taken  in 
view  of  a  reported  attack  by  Confederate  ram  upon  the  naval  force  at 
West  Pass ,  Apalachicola. 

No.  8.]  Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  August  13 ,  186 f 

Sir:  Reports  reached  these  headquarters  yesterday  by  the  squadron 
supply  steamer  Honduras  of  a  contemplated  rebel  raid  on  the  naval 
forces  stationed  at  West  Pass,  Apalachicola  [St.  George’s  Sound],  with 
a  purpose  of  raising  the  blockade  at  that  place. 

From  the  accounts  of  a  deserter,  confirmed  by  refugees,  the  ram 
oi  ironclad  gunboat  which  is  known  to  have  been  in  course  of  con- 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


743 


struction  on  the  river  above  Apalachicola  for  more  than  a  year  has  at 
last  been  completed  and  is  about  to  attack  the  vessels  with 'the  help  of 
some  cotton-clad  barges  or  scows. 

The  ram  is  said  to  be  heavily  plated,  with  sloping  sides  and  ends,  and 
to  draw  something  less  than  6  feet  of  water.  Her  armament  is 
unknown,  but  is  reported  to  have  been  taken  from  one  of  the  forts. 

In  view  of  the  possibility  of  truth  in  some  of  these  statements,  it 
seemed  to  me  prudent  to  reinforce  the  vessels  at  that  place,  consisting 
at  present  of  the  Adela ,  an  English  prize  steamer,  Acting  Volunteer 
Lieutenant  Commanding  L.  N.  Stodder,  senior  officer,  and  the  Somer¬ 
set,  ferryboat,  Acting  Master  W.  P.  Rogers,  commanding. 

Th ^  Honduras,  therefore,  was  ordered  to  coal  during  the  night,  and 
has  this  forenoon  sailed  with  orders  for  the  U.  S.  gunboat  Sagamore , 
Lieutenant-Commander  C.  E.  Fleming,  commanding,  senior  officer, 
and  the  ferryboat  Fort  Henry,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  I.  B. 
Baxter,  commanding,  to  proceed  with  all  possible  dispatch  to  West 
Pass,  and  to  remain  there  until  the  necessity  for  so  doing  should  no 
longer  exist.  They  are  in  turn  relieved  by  the  Adela  and  Clyde 
(light  English  prize  steamers),  blockading  East  Pass  and  Cedar  Keys, 
respectively. 

This  arrangement,  concentrating  the  three  best  batteries  in  the 
squadron  at  this  point,  is  the  best  that  I  am  able  to  make,  and  I  trust 
that  my  action  may  receive  the  approval  of  the  Department. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theodore  P.  Greene, 

Captain ,  Commanding  East  Gidf  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Captain  Greene ,  U.  S.  Nary,  transmitting  reports  regarding 
the  prevalence  of  malignant  fever  on  board  the  U.  S.  schooner  James 
S.  Chambers. 


No.  9.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  August  16 ,  186 J 

Sir:  I  enclose  copies  of  two  letters  received  from  the  commanding 
officer  of  the  U.  S.  schooner  Jas.  S.  Chambers  on  blockade  duty  at 
Indian  River,  on  the  east  coast  of  Florida.  Immediately  on  the  receipt 
of  the  second  (dated  August  9)  I  coaled  and  dispatched  the  steam  tug 
Honeysuckle ,  with  Passed  Assistant  Surgeon  J.  H.  Macomber,  who  had 
fortunately  arrived  the  same  afternoon  from  the  North,  the  required 
medical  stores,  and  in  addition  a  supply  of  ice  and  eight  acclimated 
contrabands  to  assist  in  whatever  way  they  could  the  enfeebled  crew  of 
the  Chambers. 

The  Honeysuckle  returned  this  evening  bringing  a  letter  from  the 
officer  then  in  charge,  the  commanding  and  executive  officers  being- 
very  ill,  stating  his  decision  to  take  the  Chambers  to  a  Northern  port. 

I  enclose  a  copy  of  this  letter  also.  As  the  Honeysuckle  is  a  tug  and 
carries  but  a  week’s  supply  of  coal,  Acting  Ensign  Sears  could  do 
nothing  but  return  to  this  place. 

This  of  course  leaves  Indian  River  without  a  blockading  vessel,  but 
I  shall  send  up  the  bark  James  L.  Davis  as  soon  as  possible,  the  only 
vessel  left  at  my  disposal,  and  reducing  the  effective  force  on  the  west 
coast  to  its  lowest  possible  point,  allusion  to  which  will,  however,  be 
made  in  another  communication  of  this  date  to  the  Department. 

Verbal  reports  received  with  the  letter  of  the  9th  convincing  me 
that  no  time  was  to  be  lost,  I  sent  up  the  eight  contrabands  without 
detaining  the  Honeysuckle  for  their  accounts.  I  therefore  respectfully 
request  that  they  be  sent  to  the  naval  storekeeper  at  Key  West,  on 
whose  books  they  are  borne,  by  the  first  opportunity. 

Respectfully, 


Tiieo.  P.  Greene, 

Captain ,  Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Off  Indian  River ,  August  5 ,  186 Ih 
Sir.  Theie  has.  not  anything'  of  importance,  transpired  since  my 
an  i\  al  at  this  station,  other  than  I  regret  to  report  an  unusual  amount 
ot  sickness  on  board.  It  broke  out  about  ten  days  ago;  it  assumed  the 
form  ot  an  epidemic.  My  surgeon  was  among  the  first  taken;  he  has 
not  jet  recovered,  but  is  improving.  Over  one-third  of  my  crew  are 
on  the  list;  the  sickness  is  very  debilitating,  but  no  cases  are  fatal  as 
j  et.  I  have  kept  a  boat  on  guard  duty  in  the  sound  a  portion  of  the 
tune,  but  it  became  necessary  to  withdraw  her  owing  to  our  sick  list 
being  so  large  and  we  being  short  of  our  complement. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  Nickerson,

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


U.  S.  Schooner  J.  S.  Chambers, 

Off  Indian  River  Inlet ,  Florida ,  August  5,  186 f 
Sir:  I  regret  to  be  compelled  to  report  that  since  my  last  communi¬ 
cation  the  sickness  on  board  this  vessel  has  assumed  the  form  of  a  most 
malignant  fever  and  increased  to  an  alarming  extent.  To-day  we  have 
on  sick  and  binnacle  list  38,  over  two-thirds  of  our  number.  Three 
of  my  officers  were  taken  down  last  night  and  are  very  sick.  I  have 
lost  4  men  by  death  since  the  5th  instant,  burying  1  this  morning. 
There  are  a  number  of  others  I  have  but  little  hopes  of.  The  few 
remaining  who  have  thus  far  escaped  are  much  worn  down  by  nursing 
the  sick.  I  can  raise  barely  enough  well  men  to  man  a  boat.  '  I  do  not 
think  it  is  yellow  fever,  but  never  saw  persons  suffer  so  much  and 
become  so  reduced  in  such  short  time.  The  symptoms  are  much  the 
same  as  those  of  that  disease. 

I  am,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  Nickerson, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  T.  Bailey, 

Corndg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  Fla. 


U.  S.  Schooner  J.  S.  Chambers, 

Of  Indian  River  Inlet ,  Florida ,  August  13 ,  186 f

to  a  Northern  port.  Dr.  Macomber  and  Captain  Sears  can  better  state 
the  condition  of  the  ship  than  I  can  write  it.  Not  being  able  to  carry 
out  blockade  orders  by  staying  here,  there  being  not  half  enough  able

Report  of  Captain  Greene ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  condition,  and 
needs  of  the  squadron  under  his  command. 

No.  11.1  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  August  16,  1864-. 

Sir:  I  deem  it  my  duty  to  call  your  attention  to  the  state  and  wants 
of  this  squadron,  and  in  the  statements  and  comparisons  made  will,  for 
the  sake  of  convenience,  refer  to  the  last  squadron  list  prepared  by 
the  captain  of  the  fleet  before  his  departure-on  leave  of  absence  the 
12th  of  May,  and  not  including  the  tenders. 

Seven  vessels  have  since  that  time  sailed  for  the  north,  the  most  effi¬ 
cient  of  the  squadron,  viz,  De  Soto,  with  yellow  fever;  Tioga,  with  yel¬ 
low  fever;  Tahoma ,  with  yellow  fever;  Huntsville,  with  yellow  fever; 
Merrimac,  with  yellow  fever;  Beauregard ,  with  yellow  fever;  James  S. 
Chambers,  with  yellow  fever;  and  to  this  list  may  or  may  not  be  added 
the  San  Jacinto ,  taken  home  by  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Bailey. 

On  the  other  hand,  three  vessels  have  joined  the  squadron — the 
Iuka,  Merrimac,  and  Magnolia — which  leaves  the  disposable  force 
comprised  at  present  in  19  vessels,  the  other  four  being  on  ordnance, 
guard,  hospital,  and  harbor  duty  at  Key  West. 

These  19  vessels  are  of  the  following  classes:  2  iron  prize  steamers, 
English  built;  3  American  river  steamers;  2  ferryboats,  steam;  5 
barks,  sailing;  4  purchased  screw  steamers;  2  tugs;  1  gunboat,  the 
Sagamore’,  total,  19. 

Of  these,  the  prize  steamers  are  unfit  to  cruise,  as  they  can  carry 
but  five  and  eight  days’  coal,  and  unfit  for  blockade  excepting  at  ports 
where  coal  can  be  landed  without  risk  of  capture. 

Of  the  river  steamers  one  is  constantly  engaged  in  supplying  the 
squadron;  another  is  a  small  vessel  purchased  and  fitted  in  Key  West 
for  the  station  at  the  mouth  of  Suwanee  River,  where  she  is  very 
useful,  while  the  third,  the  Magnolia,  is  a  fast  boat  and  capable  of 
doing  good  service  in  fine  weather. 

The  ferryboats  and  gunboat  are  engaged  in  looking  out  for  a  rebel 
ironclad  at  Apalachicola,  as  the  Department  is  informed  by  my  No.  8. 
One  of  them,  however,  as  well  as  the  Sagamore,  is  very  much  out  of 
repair,  having  been  a  long  time  on  the  station,  and  must  come  to  Key 
West,  as  soon  as  the  health  of  this  place  will  allow,  for  repairs,  both 
to  hull  and  machinery. 

Of  the  barks,  four  are  on  blockade.  The  fifth,  Roebuck,  is  unable 
to  take  care  of  herself  from  the  condition  of  her  masts  and  rigging, 
and  is  used  as  storeship  at  Tampa. 

Of  the  purchased  screw  steamers  two  are  required  on  the  blockade 
and  the  other  two  are  cruising  for  blockade  runners,  though  I  fear 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  747 

that  one  must  be  sent  to  St.  Marks  shortly  to  meet  a  rebel  gunboat 
and  barge,  the  Spray,  preparing  to  break  the  blockade.  The  tugs  are 
in  constant  use,  and  like  the  prize  steamers  are,  of  course,  unfit  to 
cruise  under  all  circumstances  of  time  and  weather. 

.  yiew  °f  these  facts  and  of  the  experiences  of  the  summer  to  this 
should  any  other  vessel  become  disabled  through  sickness  or' 
accident,  I  have  but  three  vessels  not  already  on  blockade  to  supply  a 
deficiency,  one  of  which  is  at  present  supplying  the  squadron,  the 
vessel  charged  with  that  duty  having  been  detained  by  fever  on  board, 
and  a  second  likely  to  be  needed  at  St.  Marks  at  any  time.  Of  these 
three,  to  look  at  all  contingencies,  one  is  not  calculated  for  an 
encounter  with  the  enemy,  and  the  other  two  from  their  draft  of  water 
can  not  enter  or  be  of  use  at  many  of  the  blockade  stations. 

Moreover,  these  three  steamers  are  all  I  have  to  look  out  for  the 
Bahama  Banks  and  the  Havana  and  Texas  and  Havana  and  Mobile 
traffic,  or  to  send  out  should  the  Florida  take  her  station  in  view  of 
Sand  Key  light  and  destroy  the  passing  transport  ships.  We  have 
not  a- gunboat  in  Key  West,  and  a  few  howitzers  on  the  Dale  are  all 
the  guaranty  of  safety  for  the  large  amount  of  property  here,  so  far 
as  the  Navy  is  concerned. 

These  statements  are  made  that  the  Department  may  be  fully  aware  of 
the  situation  and  wants  of  the  squadron.  It  may  be  assured,  however, 
that  the  force  at  hand  shall  always  be  employed  for  the  best  interests 
of  the  Government  while  I  remain  in  command. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Theo.  P.  Greene, 

Captain ,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Ensign  Eldredge ,  U  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S. 

schooner  James  S.  Chambers ,  stating  reasons  for  p>roceeding  to  Phila¬ 
delphia  without  orders  from  the  East  Gulf  Squadron. 

U.  S.  Schooner  J.  S.  Chambers, 

At  Quav  cmtine,  near  Philadelphia ,  August  186k. 

Sir:  As  this  vessel  has  been  brought  by  me  from  her  station  in  the 
East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron  without  orders  from  the  officer  in 
command  of  said  squadron,  I  beg  leave  to  lay  before  you  the  follow¬ 
ing  explanatory  statement: 

On  or  about  the  1st  instant,  while  this  vessel,  commanded  by  Acting 
Master  Luther  Nickerson  was  lying  alone  off  Indian  River  Inlet,  Florida, 
having  recently  arrived  thither  from  Key  West,  the  yellow  fever 
made  its  appearance  on  board,  and  in  a  few  days  half  our  crew 
were  prostrated  with  it.  On  the  5th  instant  deaths  occurred,  and  con¬ 
tinued  transpiring  daily.  Two  communications  on  the  subject  by  our 
captain  to  the  admiral  were  forwarded,  the  last  on  the  9th  instant. 
On  that  day  out  of  53  men,  38  were  on  the  sick  list,  only  some  2  or  3 
escaped  attack  altogether,  the  remainder  not  on  the  list  had  suffered,  but 
recovered.  Those  in  health  were  occupied  night  and  da}^  in  nursing, 
and  as  not  even  a  boat’s  crew  could  be  raised  in  the  ship  of  the  strong 
and  able,  burials  were  made  by  dropping  a  cutter  astern  with  the 
current  to  a  distance  of  600  yards,  her  3  or  4  men  drawing  back  by 
the  line.  Up  to  the  morning  of  the  13th  instant  we  lost  12  men  and  1 
officer,  Acting  Ensign  H.  E.  Hoplunson.  Later  on  that  morning  the 
tug  Honeysuckle  arrived  from  Key  W  est  with  a  supply  of  medicines, 
8  contrabands,  and  Past  Assistant  Surgeon  J.  H.  Macomber,  who  had 
been  dispatched  by  the  new  commandant  of  the  squadron,  Captain  T. 
P.  Greene,  to  examine  our  condition  and  remain  as  long  as  he  thought 
necessary,  cooperating  with  our  medical  officer  Acting  Assistant  Sur¬ 
geon  F.  J.  Williams.  A  consultation  was  immediately  held  by  the 
two  surgeons  and  Acting  Ensign  C.  Sears,  in  charge  of  the  tug,  and 
it  was  decided  as  most  proper  that  the  vessel  at  once  proceed  to  a 
Northern  quarantine.  Our  captain  and  executive  officer  being  down 
sick,  the  command  devolved  on  myself.  There  remained  but  one 
other  officer  fit  for  duty,  Acting  Master’s  Mate  J.  F.  Van  Nest.  The 
contrabands  brought  by  the  tug  were  retained  on  board,  their  services 
in  working  the  ship  being  needed.  On  our  passage  at  9  a.  m.  of  the 
14th  instant,  a  seaman  died  of  the  fever,  and  at  1  a.  m.  of  the  15th 
instant  Captain  Nickerson  also  died.  But  two  or  three  new  cases, 
however,  were  reported,  and  at  present  writing  our  men  are  all 
convalescent. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


749 


^ '  sea  at  1  p.  m.,  on  the  15th  instant,  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon 
W  llliams  was  seized  with  nervous  debility  and  insanity,  brought  on  by 
ovei  _  exertion,  anxiety,  and  attention  to  the  sick  for  many  days 
previous.  At  6  p.  m.  on  the  18th  instant,  Acting  Master’s  Mate

Headquarters  East.  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  August  27,  186 f 

Sir:  I  enclose  copy  of  a  letter  this  morning  received  from  Thomas 
Savage,  esq.,  acting  consul-general  of  the  United  States  at  Havana, 
with  a  copy  of  the  “offer”  referred  to. 

I  do  not  place  much  confidence  in  the  man’s  reliability  from  the  tone 
of  his  letter,  but  however  important  it  may  be,  I  am  not  provided  with 
secret-service  money  to  be  appropriated  for  such  purposes. 

1  therefore  refer  the  matter  to  you  for  such  immediate  action  as  you 
deem  best,  and  shall  send  the  same  information  to  the  Department  by 
the  first  opportunity,  which  may  not  be  for  a  week  or  two. 

Respectfully, 


Theo.  P.  Greene, 

Captain,  Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADKON. 


U.  S.  Consulate-General, 

Havana ,  August  25,  186 J^. 

Sir:  The  Anglo-rebel  steamer  Mail  (or  Susanna)  sailed  yesterday 
morning  for  Galveston.  The  Denbigh  is  ready  to  leave  at  any  moment, 
and  carries  a  very  valuable  cargo.  She  cleared  for  Bermuda;  may  go 
to  Wilmington;  but  the  information  I  have  is  that  her  destination  is 
Galveston. 

1  accompany  herewith  a  copy  of  a  letter  that  reached  me  yesterday 
fr.om  Nuevitas,  in  this  island.  I  have  sent  no  answer  to  the  writer, 
because  1  have  no  authority  to  make  the  pecuniary  arrangement  which 
he  proposed.  Are  you  authorized  to  enter  into  it,  and  would  you  do 
so?  The  man  is  unknown  to  me,  and  I  am  unable  to  say  how  reliable 
he  may  be.  If  he  can  give  the  information  which  he  says  that  he  pos¬ 
sesses,  and  is  willing  to  furnish  us,  the  price  demanded  is  not  large,  but 
I  do  not  feel  at  liberty  to  pay  it  on  account  of  the  Government. 

Please  to  advise  me  immediately  what  you  think  about  it  and  whether 
you  would  enter  into  the  arrangement  proposed  by  the  writer  of  the 
letter. 

The  steamer  Frances ,  of  New  York,  has  been  sold  here  to  an  English¬ 
man  named  George  Thomas  Watson  residing  here.  She  is  of  679  tons, 
of  iron,  I  believe,  and  probably  fast,  built  at  Wilmington,  Del.  The 
bill  of  sale  was  for  £20,000.  1  have  no  doubt  she  is  to  be  used  as  a 

blockade  runner.  The  latest  date  we  have  from  New  York  is  to  the 
13th,  in  the  Nassau  papers;  they  give  accounts  of  the  doings  of  the 
privateer  Tallahassee.  She  burned  six  vessels,  some  about  60  miles 
from  New  York;  is  represented  as  a  very  fine,  fast  steamer. 

I  beg  of  you  to  return  me  an  immediate  answer  to  this  letter,  that  I 
may  know  what  to  say  to  the  writer  of  the  letter  from  Nuevitas. 
How  would  it  do  to  send  a  trustworthy  person  there  to  see  the  writer, 
and  if  everything  is  satisfactory,  make  the  arrangement,  provided  that 
you  have  authority  to  pay  such  a  sum  of  money  as  the  man  calls  for? 
Our  latest  date  from  New  Orleans  is  of  the  8th.  We  are  anxious  to 
get  news  from  both  New  York  and  Mobile.  May  I  ask  of  j^ou  the 
favor  to  send  me  late  papers  if  you  have  any. 

With  much  respect,  I  am,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thos.  Savage, 

Acting  Consul-  General. 

Captain  T.  P.  Greene, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

N.  B. — The  Denbigh  can  not  make  over  miles  per  hour,  and  her 
boilers  are  in  a  bad  condition.  Thirteen  schooners,  I  am  advised, 
lately  got  safe  into  the  Suwanee  Biver,  west  coast  of  Florida.

Nuevitas,  Cuba,  August  12,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  very  valuable  and  important  reliable  information  to  give 
to. you  for  the  benefit  of  your  Government.  I  have  just  arrived  from 
Dixie,  and  the  consul  at  Nassau  having  no  authority  to  act  in  the  mat¬ 
ter,  I  apply  to  you.  It  is  of  vital  importance  to  your  shipping  to  know 
at  once,  so  that  your  Government  can  act  on  it.  I  shall  proceed  to 
Principe  on  private  business  and  will  answer  any  telegram  you  may 
send  to  telegraph  office,  Principe.  In  case  of  a  delay  there  for  me  you 
will  look  over  this  list  and  answer  me  by  telegram  yes  or  no.

Report  of  Commander  Shufeldt,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 

Proteus,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner  Ann  Louisa , 

from  Havana. 

U#  ^  Proteus 

At  Sea,  Lat.  <26°  36'  N,  Long.  89°  30'  W,  September  6, 1864,. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  I  have  captured  and 
sent  to  Key  W est  the  British  schooner  Ann  Louisa,  from  Havana  and 
cleared  for  Belize,  Honduras,  but  when  hailed  claimed  to  be  bound  to 
Matamoras. 

You  will  perceive  by  the  above  position  that  the  ship  was  entirely 
out  of  her  course  for  Belize.  This  fact,  together  with  the  character 
of  the  cargo  and  the  owner  and  shippers  in  Havana,  personally  well 
known  to  me  to  be  in  the  blockade-running  business,  induces  me  to 
send  her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication. 

The  prize  list  is  herewith  enclosed. 

Very  respectfully, 

JR..  W.  Shufeldt, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Secretary  of  the  Navy, 

Washington.

Report  of  Commander  Handy ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  requesting  instructions 

regarding  the  disposition  of  a  man  from  St.  Marks ,  Fla.,  desiring 

to  leave  the  Confederacy. 

No  27  1  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  September  13,  186 f 

Sir:  On  the  28th  August  two  men  went  off  from  the  vicinity  of 
St.  Marks  to  the  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieu¬ 
tenant  John  Sherrill,  commanding,  and  desired  a  passage  north,  as 
they  “wished  to  leave  the  Confederacy  for  good.”  One  of  them, 
Edwin  S.  Young,  who  represents  himself  to  have  been  born  in 
Brooklyn,  N.  Y.,  to  have  been  in  the  South  since  a  year  previous  to 
the  war,  and  to  have  been  prevented  by  chronic  illness  from  leaving, 
took  the  oath  of  allegiance  and  has  been  released  on  parole. 

I  now  desire  to  call  the  attention  of  the  Department  to  the  case  of 
the  other,  Roderick  McLennan.  Mr.  McLennan  states  that  he  was 
born  in  Canada,  and  is  a  British  subject;  that  he  is  a  civil  engineer  by 
profession  and  has  been  in  the  South  since  1860.  In  his  possession 
was  found  about  $2,400  in  gold  and  over  $60,000  in  Confederate  bonds 
and  coupons. 

Among  the  papers  found  are  his  exemption  from  military  service 
on  the  ground  of  his  employment  by  the  Southwestern  Railroad 
(dated  Macon,  February  18,  1864),  “his  services  being  essentially 
necessary  to  the  successful  transaction  of  our  (its)  ordinary  business.” 

He  brought  also  letters  which  state  that  the  company  “has  consented 
to  his  going  for  three  months”  and  that  he  has  “  been  here  engineering 
the  railroad  that  is  building  to  Eufaula”  (6th  August,  1864),  and  also  a 
request  to  “bring”  back  certain  articles,  and  also  a  list  of  articles  that 
he  “may  bring  on  a  venture  for  himself  (yourself)  to  make  money.” 

In  view  of  these  circumstances  I  have  taken  possession  of  his  specie, 
Confederate  securities,  and  papers,  and  have  sent  him  to  Fort  J efferson, 
Tortugas,  to  be  detained  until  further  orders. 

Mr.  McLennan  denies  that  he  knew  the  contents  of  these  letters, 
and  claims  that  his  intention  is  to  leave  the  Confederacy  permanently. 

The  case  being  not  one  of  prize,  nor  coming  under  any  instructions 
of  the  Department,  I  respectfully  request  directions  from  the  honor¬ 
able  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  both  as  to  the  disposition  of  his  person 
and  of  his  property. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,  R.  Handy, 

Commander ,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.
