Report  of  Captain  Greene ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  transmitting  report  of  the  cap¬ 
ture  of  steamer  Matagorda,  from  Galveston  for  Havana. 

No.  29.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  September  16,  186 f 

Sir:  By  the  enclosed  report  of  Acting-  Volunteer  Lieutenant  W.  S. 
Cheesman,  commanding  the  U.  S.  S.  Magnolia ,  you  will  be  informed 
of  the  arrival  of  the  Matagorda,  or  Alice,  at  this  port  as  a  prize. 


756 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


I  have  directed  that  she  be  supplied  with  coal,  etc.,  and  she  will  go 
north  so  soon  as  a  suitable  crew  can  be  provided  by  transferring  to 
her  a  number  of  men  whose  times  have  expired.  As  she  was  captured 
without  flag  or  papers,  I  have  placed  the  most  of  her  crew  in  charge 
of  the  army  authorities  for  confinement  in  Fort  Jefferson,  in  obedience 
to  the  directions  of  the  Department  dated  May  9  and  19,  1864.  This 
seemed  to  be  the  proper  course,  more  especially  as  1  am  informed  that 
a  new  blockade  runner  is  waiting  at  Havana  for  this  crew,  it  being  the 
intention  of  her  owners  to  lay  the  Matagorda  up  for  repairs  on  her 
arrival  at  that  port.  1  await  further  directions  as  to  the  term  of  their 
detention,  and  enclose  a  list  (30)  of  them,  with  the  stated  place  of  their 


nativity.  .  . 

It  may  be  proper  to  state  that  the  mate,  John  Lewis,  who  is  sent 
north  under  the  requirements  of  the  new  prize  law,  is  an  old  offender 
and  deserves  imprisonment  on  his  release  by  the  prize  court. 
Respectfully, 

Theo.  P.  Greene, 

Captain ,  Coinmanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

U.  S.  S.  Magnolia  (4th  Rate), 

At  Sea ,  September  10 ,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  at  10  p.  m.  of 
this  date  was  captured  by  this  ship,  in  latitude  22°  50'  N.,  longitude  85° 
47'  W.,  the  nearest  land  being  Cape  San  Antonio,  Cuba,  bearing  from 
ship  S.  E.  \  S.,  distance  75  miles,  the  steamer  Matagorda ,  Captain 
W  illiam  Stumminger,  from  Galveston  for  Havana,  loaded  with  cotton. 
The  deck  load  of  150  to  200  bales  was  thrown  overboard  while  chasing. 
Had  no  papers  or  colors.  We  chased  her  from  3:30  p.  m.  till  10  p.  m. 
Owing  to  the  starboard  boiler  of  the  prize  having  a  bad  leak,  and  our 
own  supply  of  coal  getting  low,  have  concluded  to  convoy  the  prize 
into  Key  West,  Fla. 

Enclosed  is  a  list  of  the  officers  and  men  attached  to  this  ship  at  the 
time  of  capture.

arrival  with  the  prize  steamer  Matagorda  in  safety.  Hoping  that  my 
conduct  in  this  capture  will  meet  with  the  approbation  of  the  Depart¬ 
ment, 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

-Artel,  attached  to  this  vessel,  having  heard  of  the  whereabouts  of  some

Instructions  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Commodore  Stribling,  U.  S. 

Navy ,  upon  assignment  to  command  the  East  Gulf  Blockading 

Sguadron. 

Navy  Department,  September  23,  186 h. 

Sir:  The  Department  has  designated  you  to  command  the  East  Gulf 
Blockading  Squadron,  and  will  detail  the  U.  S.  S.  Neptune  to  carry 
you  to  your  destination.  The  Neptune  is  at  New  York,  but  has  been 
ordered  to  proceed  to  Philadelphia,  from  which  port  you  will  embark. 
When  your  preparations  are  completed,  and  the  Neptune  is  in  all 
respects  ready,  you  will  proceed  in  her  to  sea  and  use  all  practicable 
dispatch  in  reaching  your  station. 

The  squadron  is  under  the  temporary  command  of  Captain  T.  P. 
Greene.  On  relieving  him  of  it,  you  will  hoist  your  flag  on  such  ves¬ 
sel  as  you  may  think  proper.  Captain  Greene  can  be  retained  in  the 
squadron  in  an  appropriate  capacity  should  you  desire  his  services, 
or  return  home  if  it  should  be  his  wish  to  do  so. 

The  headquarters  of  the  squadron  were  removed  to  Tampa  in  conse¬ 
quence  of  yellow  fever,  but  have  been  reestablished  at  Key  West. 

The  limits  of  the  squadron  are  as  follows: 

The  Florida  coast  from  Cape  Canaveral  on  the  east  to  St.  Andrew’s 
on  the  west,  including  the  latter  point  and  the  keys  adjacent  to  the 
coast. 

The  Bahamas  to  as  far  east  as  the  Crooked  Island  Passage. 

The  shores  of  Cuba,  including  the  passage  between  that  island  and 
Yucatan. 

I  transmit  herewith  a  copy  of  the  last  return,  September  1,  of  the 
vessels  of  the  squadron,  showing  their  respective  stations.  During  the 


758 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


summer  several  of  the  vessels  had  to  be  ordered  north  on  account  of 
yellow  fever,  thus  reducing  the  squadron  below  its  usual  standard. 
The  efficiency  of  the  squadron  will  soon  be  restored  by  ordering  them 
to  return  or  by  ordering  others  in  their  places.  rIhe  San  Jacinto , 
repairing  at  Portsmouth,  N.  H.,  will  be  sent  out  to  you  for  your  flag¬ 
ship.  The  schooner  JBea.uregard  and  bark  Midnight  are  under  orders 
to  the  squadron;  also  the  steamer  Isonomia.  The  latter  vessel  was  sent 
out  more  especially  to  cruise  in  the  Bahamas.  The  Neptune which 
carries  you  out,  may  be  retained  by  you  for  service  on  the  station. 

The  Department  will  endeavor  to  provide  you  with  a  squadron  suf¬ 
ficiently  ample  to  maintain  an  effective  blockade,  and  give  pi’otection 
to  the  commercial  interests  of  the  United  States  within  the  limits  of 
your  command.  You  can  exercise  your  discretion  in  sending  home 
vessels  that  are  compelled  to  have  repairs  which  can  not  be  executed 
on  the  station. 

In  carrying  out  the  duties  intrusted  to  you,  you  may  be  brought 
more  or  less  in  contact  with  the  colonial  authorities  of  neutral  powers 
within  the  limits  of  your  station,  and  the  ships  of  these  powers  in 
cruising  in  that  quarter,  and  it  is  very  desirable  that  a  mutual, 
friendly  feeling  should  be  cultivated  and  maintained  between  them  and 
yourself  and  the  officers  of  your  squadron. 

A  strict  regard  for  neutral  rights  and  neutral  waters  is  earnestly 
impressed  upon  you.  The  British  colonial  ports  should  not  be  visited 
by  the  vessels  of  your  squadron  if  it  can  be  avoided,  and  when  neces¬ 
sary  to  enter  them,  or  the  ports  of  any  other  neutral  nation,  the  estab¬ 
lished  regulations,  whatever  they  may  be,  must  be  complied  with.  If 
the  treatment  be  such  as  to  warrant  complaint,  the  facts  and  circum¬ 
stances  can  be  communicated  to  the  Department.  The  practice,  in  a 
liberal  and  generous  spirit,  of  all  customary  courtesies  and  civilities 
goes  a  great  way  toward  allaying  irritations  which  may  exist  and  pre¬ 
serving  friendship.  Your  patience  and  forbearance  may  at  times  be 
taxed  under  the  present  state  of  affairs,  but  the  Department  looks  to 
your  prudence  and  intelligence  to  guide  you  into  the  proper  course. 

The  observance  of  the  neutral  proclamations  of  foreign  powers, 
especially  as  to  the  use  of  their  waters  by  belligerents,  is  a  matter  of 
great  importance  and  one  that  should  never  be  lost  sight  of.  This 
Government  adheres  to,  recognizes,  and  insists  upon  the  principle  that 
the  maritime  jurisdiction  of  every  nation  covers  a  full  marine  league 
from  the  coast,  and  acts  of  hostility  or  authority  within  that  limit  can 
not  be  legally  exercised,  and  if  committed  or  exercised  will  certainly 
bring  upon  the  offending  party  the  displeasure  of  this  Government. 

A  vessel  within  a  marine  league  of  a  neutral  coast  is  regarded  as 
free  from  interruption.  It  is  not  lawful  to  chase,  fire  at,  bring  to,  or 
capture  any  vessel  within  the  waters  or  jurisdiction  of  a  neutral.  Nor 
is  it  proper  to  make  a  convenience  in  any  manner  of  neutral  ports  or 
neutral  territory  for  the  purpose  of  exercising  in  the  vicinity  thereof 
the  belligerent  right  of  search  or  seizure.  The  captain  of  a  vessel 
after  standing  off  and  on  in  neutral  waters  or  lying  in  wait  within  the 
same  for  the  purpose,  although  the  capture  may  have  been  actually 
made  beyond  the  jurisdiction  of  the  neutral,  might  not  be  recognized 
as  valid;  and  the  right  of  search  can  not  be  properly  exercised  when  it 
is  known  previously  that  whatever  the  result  of  the  search,  the  capture 
would  not  be  lawful. 

Your  attention  is  particularly  called  to  the  circular  letter  of  this 


EAST  GITLF  BLOCKADING  SQUADEON. 


759 


Department,  (copies  herewith  enclosed),  issued  August  18,  1862,  reca¬ 
pitulating  the  instructions  that  had  been  given  from  time  to  time,  and 
the  restrictions  and  precautions  to  be  observed  by  our  cruisers  in 
reference  to  the  blockade,  and  the  exercise  of  the  right  of  search  and 
seizure.  These  instructions,  restrictions,  and  precautions  must  be 
faithfully  observed.  Dissatisfaction  has  been  expressed  by  foreign 
governments  that  our  vessels  of  war  on  several  occasions  have,  with¬ 
out  giving  the  customary  notice,  fired  shotted  guns  across  the  bows  of 
vessels  approaching  the  blockaded  coast,  and  sometimes  on  the  high 
seas.  The  recognized  practice  of  ascertaining  the  character  of  a  sus¬ 
picious  vessel  or  of  expressing  a  desire  to  communicate  b}r  firing  a 
blank  cartridge  should  be  adhered  to.  A  vessel  approaching  the 
blockade  at  night  without  making  the  usual  signals  can  not  be  regarded 
as  entitled  to  the  customary  courtesies  of  the  sea. 

Proper  disposition  of  persons  found  on  board  vessels  seized  for 
breach  of  blockade  is  a  matter  requiring  close  attention.  That  you 
may  understand  clearly  the  practice  in  such  cases  and  not  be  embar¬ 
rassed  in  your  action,  I  ti’ansmit  herewith  printed  instructions  sent  in 
May  last  to  the  commanding  officers  of  the  several  blockading  squadrons 
on  the  subject.  It  must  be  particularly  remembered  that  bona  fide 
foreign  subjects,  merely  charged  with  violating  the  blockade,  can  not 
be  treated  as  prisoners  of  war  when  captured  in  neutral  vessels.  They 
may  be  detained  as  witnesses.  The  fact  of  their  having  repeatedly 
violated  the  blockade  gives  no  authority  for  their  detention.  But 
when  such  persons  are  captured  on  board  rebel  vessels,  and  are  serving 
as  officers  or  crew,  they  can  be  treated  as  prisoners  of  war  and  are  to 
be  held  as  such,  subject  to  exchange,  however,  if  coming  within  the 
class  of  passengers  and  have  no  interest  in  vessel  or  cargo,  and  are  not 
connected  with  the  rebel  Government. 

I  transmit  herewith  copies  of  various  printed  general  orders  and 
circulars  issued  by  the  Department  within  the  past  3^  ear  or  two,  copies 
of  laws  of  last  session  of  Congress,  uniform  regulations,  and  plates. 
I  also  transmit  extracts  from  instructions  that  have  been  given  from 
time  to  time  to  the  commanding  officers  of  the  blockading  squadrons 
in  relation  to  matters  and  in  answer  to  questions  which  may  arise  in 
the  course  of  your  command.  They  may  assist  you  much  in  com¬ 
ing  to  a  correct  conclusion  in  parallel  cases,  and  you  may  regard  them 
as  a  basis  for  your  action. 

The  Department  desires  you  to  keep  it  advised  of  your  proceedings 
and  to  communicate  to  it  anything  that  may  suggest  itself  to  you  for 
the  advancement  of  the  Navy  and  the  public  good. 

Forward  to  the  Department  on  the  1st  and  15th  of  each  month  a 
statement  of  the  position  of  each  vessel  of  the  squadron,  similar  to 
that  herewith  enclosed,  with  an  additional  column  showing  the  num¬ 
ber  of  guns  carried  by  each. 

It  is  scarcely  necessary  to  remind  you  that  the  paramount  duty  with 
which  you  are  intrusted  is  the  maintenance  of  a  strict  blockade  of  the 
insurgent  coast  within  the  limits  of  your  command. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Commodore  C.  K.  Stbibling, 

Apptd.  Comd.  East.  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squad.,  Philadelphia.

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  Flagship  Dale, 

Key  West,  August  5,  186J. 

Sir:  In  availing  myself  of  your  permission  to  proceed  north  for  the 
purpose  of  recruiting  my  health,  1  am  desirous  before  my  departure 
of  placing  upon  the  records  of  the  Department  some  recognition  of 
the  very  valuable  services  that  have  been  rendered  to  the  Government 
by  Mr.  Zeller,  the  fleet  engineer. 

The  Department  is  doubtless  aware  of  the  constant  pressure  that  is 
brought  to  bear  upon  the  commanding  officer  of  a  squadron  to  get 
vessels  north  on  the  plea  that  the  boilers  and  machinery  need  exten¬ 
sive  repairs — and  to  meet  this  pressure  on  the  part  of  interested  par¬ 
ties,  he  has  only  the  integrity  and  sound  judgment  of  the  fleet  engineer 
and  his  resisting  power  to  depend  on.  Mr.  Zeller  has  done  his  duty 
so  well  in  this  respect  that  I  am  told  he  has  incurred  much  ill  feeling 
on  the  part  of  those  officers  (I  am  sorry  to  say  not  a  few  in  number) 
to  whose  unpatriotic  efforts  to  take  their  vessels  north  he  has  so  per¬ 
sistently  refused  to  lend  himself,  and  in  the  same  proportion  he  is 
entitled  to  the  just  recognition  of  the  value  of  lus  services  on  my  part. 

This  officer  is  an  enthusiast  in  his  profession,  an  untiring  worker, 
and  a  devoted  servant  of  the  Government.  In  saying  this  in  his  behalf

Report  of  Acting  Master  Martine ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  baric 
Roebuck ,  regarding  the  arrival  of  that  vessel  at  Portsmouth ,  N.  II., 
with  yellow  fever  patients. 

U.  S.  Bark  Roebuck, 
Portsmouth ,  N.  II. ,  September  £8,  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  at  this  port  of  the  U.  S. 
bark  Roebuck ,  under  my  command,  and  in  obedience  to  orders  re¬ 
ceived  from  Captain  Theodore  P.  Greene,  IT.  S.  Nav}r.  I  would 
respectfully  submit  a  detailed  report  of  the  sickness  (yellow  fever) 
which  has  prevailed  on  board  this  vessel. 

July  21,  having  been  relieved  at  Indian  River  Inlet  by  the  U.  S. 
schooner  J.  S.  Chambers ,  in  obedience  to  orders  I  proceeded  with  the 
Roebuck  under  my  command  in  tow  of  U.  S.  transport  Ilussar  toward 
Key  W est,  where  we  arrived  July  24  at  7  a.  m.  Anchored  3  miles 
outside  the  fort.  At  10  a.  m.  the  U.  S.  tug  Marigold  came  down  to 
us,  bringing.orders  for  me  to  come  on  shore,  and  not  to  have  any  other 
communication.  Having  two  small  prizes  in  tow,  the  next  morning,  in 
obedience  to  orders,  took  the  officer  and  two  men,  who  were  among  the 
captors,  up  to  the  prize  commissioners;  the  same  afternoon  received 
on  board  10,000  feet  of  hemlock  lumber;  at  8  p.  m.  received  orders  to 
get  underway  and  proceed  to  Tampa  Bay  in  tow  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Honey¬ 
suckle.  Up  to  this  time  the  bark  was  remarkably  healthy,  not  having 
a  man  on  the  sick  list  for  four  days  previous. 

The  same  night  we  left,  about  12  or  1  o’clock,  two  men  were  attacked, 
and  before  night  again  we  had  6  cases.  On  the  28th  we  arrived  at 
Tampa  Bay,  with  9  more  cases  of  fever  on  board.  1  immediately 
went  on  board  the  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto ,  Captain  Theodore  P.  Greene, 
for  medical  assistance,  there  being  no  medical  officer  on  board  the 
bark.  Captain  Greene  immediately  sent  assistance  and  all  care  taken 
of  the  sick;  the  officers  and  crew  continued  to  be  taken  down,  from  1 
to  5  every  day,  and  at  one  time  we  had  only  5  men  and  1  officer  not 
on  the  sick  list  or  able  to  do  duty.  A  few  days  after  the  San  Jacinto 
left  the  U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson ,  Captain  McDougal,  senior  officer 
of  the  division,  [arrived].  He  immediately  rendered  me  all  assist¬ 
ance;  everything  was  done  that  possibly  could  be  to  check  the  infec¬ 
tion,  but  impossible.  Some  of  the  crew,  after  returning  on  board 
convalescent,  were  taken  the  second  time.  A  medical  survey  was  held 
on  the  bark,  and  September  12th  we  received  orders  to  proceed  to 
Portsmouth,  N.  H. 

On  the  morning  of  the  13th  we  were  towed  to  sea  by  the  U.  S.  S. 
Sunfower ,  and  proceeded  on  our  way.  On  the  13th  one  new  case  of 
fever;  14th,  three  of  the  nurses,  who  had  been  at  the  hospital  tending 


EAST  GULE  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


762 

on  the  sick  all  through  the  worst  stages,  were  taken  down  with  the 
fever,  and  on  the  21st  one  of  them  died.  All  the  clothing  of  the 
officers  and  men  that  have  died  has  been  destroyed.  Everything  in 
the  way  of  disinfectants  has  been  used  that  could  be. 

Copperas  dissolved  in  water  has  been  turned  down  the  pumps,  peak, 
and  run,  and  the  vessel  smoked  throughout  every  morning  with  red 
hot  bolt  dipped  in  tar.  Vessels  containing  chloride  of  lime  and  others 
of  the  copperas  have  been  plentifully  distributed  about  the  ship. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  L.  Martine, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washingotn ,  I).  C.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy,  to  Commodore  Stribling,  U.  S. 
Navy,  transmitting  comnaunication  from  the  Spanish  Government. 


Navy  Department,  October  6,  186 If. 

Sir:  I  enclose  herewith  a  copy  of  a  letter  from  the  Secretary  of 
State  dated  the  26th  ultimo,  and  of  the  papers  therein  referred  to, 
communicating  the  decision  of  the  Government  of  Spain  relative  to 
vessels  of  war  of  foreign  powers,  which  is  adverse  to  their  lying  off 
Havana  and  sending  in  boats,  except  in  case  succor  is  needed. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 


Commodore  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Appointed  to  Command  E. 


Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  Navy.

Legation  of  the  United  States  to  Spain, 

San  Sebastian ,  August  38,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  a  translation  of  the  note  of  Mr. 
Pacheco  dated  the  11th  instant  at  San  Yldefonse  in  which  he  informs 
me  that  the  Government  of  the  Queen  has  decided  to  approve  the 
order  of  the  captain-general  of  Cuba  prohibiting  foreign  men-of-war, 
who  remain  outside  of  the  port  of  Habana  [Havana],  from  sending 
in  their  boats  to  that  port  except  in  the  sole  cause  that  the  vessel  is  in 
need  of  succor. 

With  sentiments  of  the  highest  respect,  sir,  your  obedient  servant, 

Horatio  G.  Perry. 

Hon.  Wr.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State ,  Washington. 

[Translation.] 

Ministerial  Department  of  State, 

San  Yldefonse  August  11,  186 f 

Sir:  In  fulfillment  of  what  was  said  by  this  Department  to  that 
legation  on  the  17th  of  April,  last  year,  I  have  now  the  honor  to  inform 
you  that  the  Government  of  her  Majesty  has  been  pleased  to  approve 
the  measure  adopted  by  the  superior  governor  of  the  island  of  Cuba 
in  respect  to  impeding  the  entrance  into  the  port  of  the  Habana  of  the 
boats  of  foreign  vessels  of  war,  which  themselves  remain  outside.  In 
the  sole  case  that  the  said  vessels  should  be  in  urgent  need  of  succor, 
it  will  be  permitted  to  the  vessel  demanding  it  to  remain,  without  com¬ 
munication,  at  the  entrance  of  the  port,  while  the  consul  of  the  nation 
to  which  the  vessel  belongs  furnish  the  same.  In  the  adoption  of  this 
measure,  observed  by  all  nations  in  their  port  regulations,  the  Govern¬ 
ment  of  her  Majesty  has  had  no  other  object  than  to  put  in  operation 
the  rules  of  maritime  police  and  of  sanitary  police  of  that  island. 

I  avail  myself  of  this  occasion  to  renew  to  you  the  assurance  of  my 
distinguished  consideration. 

G.  F.  Pacheco. 

Charge  d’affaires  of  the  United  States.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Strihling, 

U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  duty  of  the  U  S.  S.  Isonomia. 

Navy  Department,  October  15,  186 I 
c  J-j*  Isonomia  was  sent  to  the  East  Gulf  Blockading 

fequadron  with  the  especial  view  and  instructions  to  cruise  in  the  vicinity 
of  Nassau  and  the  Bahama  Banks.  I  have  just  received  a  dispatch  from 
Captain  Greene,  temporarily  in  command  of  the  squadron,  in  which  he 
says  that,  in  consequence  of  a  report  from  her  commanding  officer  that 
she  was  unfit  for  sea  service,  and  her  incapacitv  to  carry  much  coal  he 
assigned  her  to  blockade  duty  at  West  Pass. 

This  action  is  disapproved.  The  Isonomia  is  very  fast,  and  amongst 
the  Bahamas  can  easily  find  shelter.  Coal  could  be  easily  sent  to  her, 
or  a  vessel  loaded  with  coal  might  accompany  her.  The  vicinity  of 
Nassau  is  a  great  center  for  blockade  runners,  and  the  Isonomia  was 
assigned  to  the  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron  for  the  especial  pur¬ 
pose  of  making  an  effort  to  capture  some  of  them.  Order  her  on  this 
duty,  and  if  a  trial  should  be  unsuccessful  she  can  be  withdrawn  from  it. 

Y ery  respectfully,  etc. , 

Gideon  Welles, 

,  Secretary  of  Navy. 

Acting  Bear- Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Strib- 
hng,  XL  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  reported  agreement  for  the  enlistment 
abroad  of  soldiers  for  the  Confederate  Government. 

Navy  Department,  October  17,  186 J. 
iME.  It  is  reported  that  an  agreement  has  been  effected  between  the 
rebel  Government  and  some  European  power  (Poland,  it  is  intimated) 
by  which  30,000  soldiers  from  abroad  are  to  be  added  to  the  rebel 
Army,  and  that  the  rebel  Government  are  making  arrangements  for 
having  built  in  England  some  50  swift  steamers,  similar  to  the  Colonel 
Lamb ,  for  the  purpose  of  running  these  soldiers  through  the  blockade. 

The  Department  places  little  confidence  in  rumors  regarding  a 
scheme  so  impracticable  in  almost  every  feature,  and  should  such  be 
contemplated  we  will,  without  doubt/ hear  something  reliable  of  it 
hereafter.  In  the  meantime,  however,  I  communicate  the  report  to 
you  for  your  information. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Commandhig  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron,  Key  West. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  XI.  S.  Navy,  transmitting 

report  regarding  the  destruction  of  Confederate  fishery  in  Ocklockonee 

River. 

No.  2'2.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  October  29,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  of  the  destruction  of  a  valuable 
and  extensive  Government  (rebel)  fishery  on  Marsh’s  Island,  north  of 
the  Ocklockonee  River,  by  an  expedition  from  the  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and 
Stripes,  Acting  Volunteer  John  Sherrill,  commanding. 

I  enclose  the  report  of  Lieutenant  Sherrill,  giving  a  detailed  account 
of  the  expedition.  The  happy  issue  of  this  enterprise,  resulting  in 
the  destruction  and  capture  of  a  large  amount  of  rebel  property  and 
the  capture  of  16  Confederate  soldiers,  without  any  loss  on  our  side, 
reflects  credit  on  the  officer  in  charge,  Acting  Master  George  E.  Hill, 
and  I  heartily  concur  with  Lieutenant  Sherrill  in  recommending  his 
promotion. 

I  also  recommend  Acting  Ensign  O.  S.  Roberts  to  the  favorable 
consideration  of  the  Department,  as  he  has  been  represented  as  a  very 
worthy  officer.  The  prisoners  have  been  delivered  to  the  army 
authorities. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Commanding  East  Gidf  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

Off  St.  Marks,  Fla. ,  October  19,  186 J. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  having  learned  of  the 
existence  of  a  valuable  and  extensive  Government  fishery  on  Marsh’s 


768 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Island,  on  the  north  side  of  the  Ocklockonee  River,  1  dispatched  an 
expedition  last  night,  consisting  of  the  launch,  first  and  second  cutters 
of  this  vessel,  with  armed  crews,  the  whole  under  the  command  of 
Acting  Master  George  E.  Hill,  to  destroy  it,  and  do  such  other  injury 
to  the  enemy  as  the  circumstances  and  opportunity  might  permit. 

The  expedition  returned  at  9  o’clock  this  morning,  Mr.  Hill  having 
landed  at  daybreak  with  30  men,  fully  accomplishing  the  object  for 
which  it  was  sent.  All  the  permanent  fixtures  of  the  establishment, 
consisting  of  the  fish  and  dwelling  houses  and  the  kettles  of  the  salt 
works  attached  to  the  fishery,  were  entirely  destroyed,  a  large  and 
valuable  seine  and  2  fishing  boats  captured,  together  with  16  Confed¬ 
erate  soldiers  (2  of  them  sergeants)  detailed  for  the  purpose  of  oper¬ 
ating  and  guarding  the  works.  I  am  happy  to  add  that  the  whole  was 
accomplished  without  any  loss  on  our  part. 

When  I  inform  you  that  this  was  regarded  as  one  of  the  most  impor¬ 
tant  and  reliable  fisheries  on  this  coast,  furnishing  large  supplies  not 
only  to  the  interior  districts  of  this  State,  but  also  to  the  commissariat 
of  the  rebel  Army,  I  think  that  you  will  join  with  me  in  regarding  those 
by  whom  the  expedition  was  so  efficiently  carried  out  as  entitled  to  the 
favorable  consideration  of  the  proper  authorities. 

To  the  enterprise  and  clear  judgment  of  Mr.  Hill  the  success  of  the 
expedition  is  chiefly  due,  and  for  this  and  his  long  and  faithful  services 
in  the  Navy  I  would  most  cordially  recommend  him  for  promotion. 

I  would  further  beg  to  refer  to  Acting  Ensign  O.  S.  Roberts,  who 
displayed  on  this  occasion  that  degree  of  zeal  and  intelligence  that  my 
knowledge  of  his  antecedents  led  me  to  expect  of  him.  His  advance¬ 
ment  to  a  higher  grade  would  be  but  a  just  recognition  of  those 
qualities. 

The  prisoners  belong  mostly  to  the  Second  and  Fifth  Florida  Cav¬ 
alry,  and  I  shall  send  them  to*  Key  West  by  the  first  convenience  for 
your  disposition. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Sherrill, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Navy  Department,  October ■  19,  186 

Sir:  It  is  feared  that  the  steamer  Roanoke,  which  sailed  from 
Havana  on  the  29th  ultimo  for  New  York,  has  been  captured  by  a 
party  of  rebels,  who  are  reported  to  have  taken  passage  in  her.  She 
is  a  side-wheel  steamer  of  about  1,050  tons.

the  fact  of  the  Roanoke  being  missing  ana  direct  them  to  make  a 
search  for  her  within  the  limits  of  their  cruising  grounds.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  U.  S ■.  Navy ,  regarding  the 

destruction  of  salt  works  in  St.  Andrew’s  Ray  by  expedition  from  the 

TJ.  S.  bark  Restless. 

No.  9.]  Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  October  20,  186 f 

Sir:  Reports  received  this  day  from  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant 
W.  P.  Randall,  commanding  U.  S.  bark  Restless ,  on  blockade  duty  at 
St.  Andrew’s  Bay,  Fla.,  contain  details  of  a  successfu’  expedition  on 
the  5th  and  6th  instant,  by  boats  from  that  vessel  under  the  command 
of  Acting  Ensign  Henry  Eason. 

It  resulted  in  the  destruction  of  50  boilers  for  salt  making,  500  to 
1,000  gallons  each;  90  kettles  for  salt  making,  65  to  200  gallons  each; 
300  bushels  of  salt;  31  wagons  and  several  large  casks;  500  cords  of 
wTood;  150  buildings,  dwelling  houses  for  the  employes,  and  sheds, 
storehouses,  etc.,  besides  other  damage. 

All  this  was  the  property  of  the  Confederates,  and  although  it  is 
probable  that  they  may  again  be  rebuilt,  it  is  certain  that  a  severe 
blow  has  been  struck  at  the  rebel  forces  in  Georgia. 

In  consideration  of  the  intelligence,  energy,  and  judgment  displayed 
in  this  expedition,  I  respectfully  recommend  that  Acting  Ensign 
Henry  Eason  be  promoted  to  be  an  acting  master. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Lieutenant-  Ccrmmander  Ale  Doug  al ,  U.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  IT.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson,  regarding  the  capture ,  October  21, 
186 f  of  the  British  schooner  Lucy,  from  Bahia  Honda. 

U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson, 

Tampa  Bay,  October  23,  186 f 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  English  schooner 
Lucy,  with  an  assorted  cargo,  by  the  U.  S.  schooner  Sea  Bird,  a  tender 
to  this  vessel,  the  circumstances  of  which  are  as  follows: 

On  the  morning  of  the  21st  of  October,  while  the  Sea  Bird  was 
cruising  off  Bayport,  a  sail  was  discovered  and  chase  given.  The 
stranger  evincing  no  disposition  to  heave  to,  fire  was  opened  on  him 
and  he  finally,  seeing  the  hopelessness  of  his  case,  ran  ashore,  and  all 
hands,  with  the  exception  of  one  man,  took  the  only  boat  belonging  to 
her,  deserted  her,  and  pulled  for  the  shore,  closed  pursued  by  an 
armed  boat  from  the  Sea  Bird,  which,  however,  was  unsuccessful  in 
their  attempt  to  capture.

On  boarding-  the  vessel  she  was  found  to  be  the  English  schooner

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Smith,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  S.  Nita,  regarding  the  capture  of  schooner  Unknown,  of 
Clearwater  Harbor. 

U.  S.  S.  Nita, 

Tampa  Bay,  Fla. ,  October  186 f. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Unknown , 
under  the  following  circumstances,  viz: 

At  8:30  a.  m.  of  this  day,  being  off  Clearwater  Harbor  in  fathoms 
water,  discovered  a  schooner  at  anchor  close  in  to  the  land. 

Headed  the  ship  for  her,  and  soon  discovered  a  boat  containing  two 
or  three  persons  pulling  toward  the  mainland.  At  the  same  time  dis¬ 
covered  a  smoke  arising  from  her,  forward  and  aft. 

At  9: 30  a.  m.  anchored  near  her,  and  sent  two  armed  boats  (furnished 
with  water  buckets)  in  charge  of  Acting  Ensign  P.  Pease  to  board  her. 
He  soon  subdued  the  fire.  No  person  was  found  on  board  and  no 
papers  of  any  kind.  An  English  ensign  was  the  only  thing  found  by 
which  her  nationalty  could  be  judged.  The  crew  escaped. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Smith, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Lieutenant- Commander  Simpson,  U.  S.Navy,  giving  infor¬ 
mation  received  from  refugees  regarding  affairs  in  Colwnbus ,  Ga. 

U.  S.  S.  Isonomia, 

West  Pass,  St.  George! s  Sound ,  Fla.,  November  11,  186 f 
Sir:  I  forward  to  Key  West  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Isonomia  two  refugees, 
foreigners,  who  have  lately  left  Columbus,  Ga. 


EAST  GUILE  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


773 


Mrs.  Kelley  is  a  Scotch  woman,  whose  husband  left  Columbus  in 
August  and  was  forwarded  from  here  some  time  in  September  by  the 
Union.  Mrs.  Kelley  is  following  her  husband. 

The  other  refugee  is  Mr.  Peter  Farrell  (a  tailor),  who  has  his  cer¬ 
tificate  of  foreign  birth.  From  the  statement  of  this  man  I  find  that 
foreigners  are  being  forced  into  the  conscription  for  the  Southern 
Army.  The  manner  in  which  this  is  effected  is  as  follows:  The  for¬ 
eigner  is  directed  that  in  the  course  of  the  following  ten  da}rs  he  must 
enlist  in  one  of  the  companies  organized  (ostensibly)  for  the  defense 
of  the  city,  or  leave  the  State;  if  he  joins  a  company,  as  soon  as  it  is 
thoroughly  organized  it  is  sent  to  the  front,  and  he  finds  himself  a 
soldier  of  the  Confederacy  without  any  hope  of  relief.  If  he  chooses 
the  other  alternative  and  leaves  the  State  he  receives  a  similar  warning 
as  soon  as  he  is  domesticated  in  his  new  abode.  In  this  dilemma  those 
who  are  desirous  to  leave  the  country  turn  their  attention  to  the 
Union  fleet,  but  their  movements  in  this  direction,  I  fear,  will  be 
retarded  by  the  circular  relating  to  refugees,  of  May  13,  1861,  the 
purport  of  which,  I  perceive,  is  known  on  shore.  They  will  fear 
being  refused  by  the  fleet,  even  if  they  should  succeed  in  reaching  the 
coast. 

1  respectfully  suggest,  in  this  connection,  that  the  only  effect  that 
can  be  produced  by  the  circular  referred  to  is  to  add  men  to  the 
ranks  of  the  enemy.  If  we  receive  all  that  offer,  coming  with  or  with¬ 
out  their  families,  no  matter  whether  they  enter  the  service  or  not, 
we  must  reduce  the  ranks  of  the  enemy  one  able-bodied  man  for  every 
family  we  receive.  I  respectfully  ask  the  attention  of  the  commander 
in  chief  to  this  circular. 

The  two  foreign  refugees  that  I  now  forward  have  been  residents 
of  Columbus,  Ga.,  for  some  time,  and  their  statements  embrace  the 
following  interesting  facts:  Columbus  had  a  population  of  about 
11,000  or  12,000  inhabitants,  which  is  now  much  increased  by  the 
influx  of  refugees  from  Atlanta  and  that  region  of  country.  These 
refugees  are  mostly  women  and  children,  the  men  having  been  con-  - 
scripted.  Huts  are  built  about  the  city  for  their  accommodation  and 
are  extended  for  a  distance  of  100  miles  along  the  railroads  from  Fort 
Valley  to  Columbus  and  from  Fort  Valley  to  Eufaula.  Some  of  the 
old  rolling  stock  of  the  roads  is  used  for  the  purpose  of  sheltering  the 
refugees.  Their  condition  is  described  as  perfectly  destitute;  they  are 
supplied  by  the  State  with  enough  corn  meal  to  prevent  them  from 
starving.  Columbus  has  several  factories  in  operation — - 

1st.  Naval  Iron  Works,  employing  400  white  men. 

2d.  Hayman’s  factories,  one  of  which  is  devoted  to  the  manufacture 
of  pistols  and  the  other  to  that  of  swords,  bayonets,  etc.,  employing 
175  wrhite  men. 

3d.  Ordnance  Department,  under  Major  Humphreys,  C.  S.  Army, 
divided  into  two  establishments,  one  for  the  manufacture  of  saddles, 
bridles,  harness,  and  equipments  for  artillery,  while  the  other  estab¬ 
lishment  is  devoted  to  casting  shot  and  shells,  and  to  the  work  of  a 
laboratory.  The  department  of  Major  Humphreys  employs  about  150 
white  men  and  150  women. 

4th.  Major  Dillard,  Quartermaster,  C.  S.  Army,  has  a  large  tannery 
and  shoemaking  establishment,  in  which  are  employed  about  225  white 
men  detailed  from  the  Army.  Major  Dillard  has  also  about  25  men 
employed  at  tailoring  for  the  army. 


774 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADEON. 


In  addition  to  the  establishments  already  enumerated,  there  are  three 
cotton  factories  in  operation,  one  belonging  to  Grant,  working  about 
75  white  men;  one  belonging  to  Brown,  working  about  200  white  men; 
one  belonging  to  Fountain,  working  about  60  white  men.  _ 

There  is  also  a  paper  mill  worked  by  a  man  named  Winters,  who 
employs  about  25  white  men.  It  is  to  be  understood  that  in  all  these 
factories,  workshops,  etc.,  the  working  force  is  increased  by  a  large 
number  of  negroes. 

The  Naval  Iron  Works,  mentioned  first,  are  occupied  exclusively  in 
the  manufacture  of  machinery  and  boilers,  and  it  is  from  here  that 
these  valuable  equipments  have  been  provided  for  the  rebel  ironclads 
in  the  South. 

As  far  as  I  can  discover,  there  are  no  guns  being  cast  in  Columbus 
at  the  present  time. 

There  are  engineer  officers  employed  on  the  defenses,  working  a  large 
force  of  negroes;  the  works  are  intended  to  surround  the  entire  city, 
those  designed  for  the  pi’otection  of  the  city  in  front  being  constructed 
in  Alabama  on  the  west  side  of  the  Chattahoochee  River. 

There  are  no  regular  troops  stationed  at  Columbus,  but  for  the 
defense  of  the  town  all  the  workmen  in  the  different  factories  and 
workshops  are  organized  into  companies  and  battalions,  supposed  to 
make  up  a  force  of  about  2,000  men. 

The  Muscogee  (ironclad)  and  Chattahoochee  (wooden  gunboat)  are  at 
Columbus.  The  Muscogee  was  originally  constructed  shorter  than  the 
other  rebel  vessels  of  this  class,  and  her  casemate  was  carried  down  to 
the  rail  forward  and  aft,  but  the  armature  has  never  been  placed  on  it. 
An  effort  was  made  to  launch  her  last  December,  but  a  powerful 
steamer,  tugging  at  her,  could  not  drag  her  off  the  ways  in  16  feet  of 
water.  Her  casemate  was  reduced  in  size,  uncovering  a  portion  of  the 
original  deck;  her  hull  has  also  been  lengthened  in  hopes  to  give  her 
more  buoyancy;  the  new  casemate  has  as  yet  no  armor  on  it,  nor  is 
there  any  armor  on  the  new  portion  of  the  hull;  there  is  difficulty  in 
procuring  the  iron.  All  seem  so  well  satisfied  that  she  is  a  failure  that 
there  seems  little  probability  that  the  work  of  completing  her  arma¬ 
ture  will  be  continued,  or  that  any  further  attempt  will  be  made  to 
launch  her.  Work,  however,  is  still  continued  on  her,  the  woodwork 
not  being  all  completed.  The  Chattahoochee  has  been  of  no  use  since 
her  first  boiler  burst  on  her  way  down  the  river.  At  present  she  has 
no  boiler  in  her,  or  she  has  boilers  not  at  all  adapted  to  the  engine  that 
is  in  the  boat  (accounts  differ  on  this  point),  but  whichever  account  is 
correct  it  is  certain  that  she  requires  a  new  boiler  before  she  can  be  of 
service.  She  now  lies  at  Columbus  waiting  for  a  new  boiler,  but  all 
the  work  of  this  kind  which  is  completed  at  the  Naval  Iron  Works  is 
at  once  transported  to  Charleston  or  Savannah,  and  the  Chattahoochee 
still  waits  unprovided.  Her  engine  is  in  order,  but  she  has  no  guns  on 
board. 

There  are  no  troops  on  the  river  between  Columbus  and  Chatta¬ 
hoochee,  but  at  the  latter  place  there  is  stationed  one  large  company, 
under  Captain  J.  L.  Dunham,  C.  S.  Army,  numbering  (itis  said)  140  men, 
and  having  with  them  a  battery  of  4  guns.  Captain  Dunham  has  his 
headquarters  on  board  the  side-wheel  river  boat  IF  II.  Young ,  in 
which  he  cruises  down  the  river  about  40  or  50  miles  in  a  straight  line 
to  a  plantation  called  Iola,  Florida,  below  Rickoe’s  Bluff.  This  town 
is  considerably  more  than  halfway  from  Chattahoochee  to  the  obstruc¬ 
tions.  The  camp  for  the  portion  of  this  company  that  is  quartered  on 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON, 


775 


shore  is  about  a  half  mile  out  from  Chattahoochee,  above  the  city  and 
near  the  arsenal,  which  is  now  devoted  to  the  accommodation  of  the 
families  of  the  troops  forming-  this  command.  There  are  no  tents  in 
the  encampment,  the  men  sleeping  out  as  a  regular  practice. 

The  river  steamboats  that  are  now  running  from  Columbus  to  Chat¬ 
tahoochee  are  Jackson ,  stern  wheel,  drawing  2  feet  2  inches;  Munnerlyn , 
stern  wheel,  drawing  2  feet  2  inches;  Mist ,  stern  wheel,  drawing  2  feet 
2  inches. 

The  following  are  repairing  at  Columbus:  Euchee ,  side-wheel,  draw¬ 
ing  3  feet  3  inches;  Marianna ,'  side-wheel,  drawing  3  feet  3  inches. 

On  Friday,  the  28th  ultimo,  Mrs.  Kelley  stopped  at  Fort  Gadsden, 
where  she  met  but  five  men  and  a  corporal  as  a  picket  guard,  and  she 
is  confident  that  there  are  no  guns  in  the  work. 

There  is  no  reason  why  this  information  should  not  be  considered 
authentic,  and  I  submit  it  as  the  most  satisfactory  statement  of  affairs 
that  I  have  yet  received.  Should  3mu  desire  any  more  elaborate  state¬ 
ments  on  any  particular  point  the  witnesses  will  be  at  hand  to  supply 
the  information. 

I  have  nothing  to  add  in  the  way  of  report  except  that  the  blockade 
has  been  strictly  observed  since  my  last  communication  of  28th  ultimo. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  Simpson, 

Lieutenant-  Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present . 

Acting  Rear- Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling,

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  transmitting 
report  regarding  a  reconnoissance  in  Tampa  Bay ,  with  a  view  to  the 
destruction  of  salt  works. 

Hdqrs.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  November  If  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  received  a  report  dated  November  12  from  Acting  Vol¬ 
unteer  Lieutenant  R.  B.  Smith,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Nita,  of  an 
expedition  sent  to  destroy  rebel  salt  works  in  Tampa  Bay,  in  which 
one  man  was  wounded  and  captured  and  five  men  supposed  to  have 
deserted.  I  presume  these  men  straggled  from  the  party  sent  on  shore 
and  were  captured  by  the  rebels.  Such  expeditions  must  of  necessity 
be  left  to  the  discretion  of  commanding  officers  at  the  blockaded  ports, 
and  are  too  frequently,  I  fear,  undertaken  without  due  caution  and 
without  regard  to  consequences,  in  hope  of  doing  something  to  bring 
themselves  prominently  into  notice. 

I  take  occasion  to  bring  to  the  notice  of  the  Department  the  fact  that 
at  this  time  all  the  vessels  on  the  .^ockade  are  commanded  by  volunteer 
officers,  and  1  have  no  vessels  commanded  In-  regular  officers  of  the 
Navy,  except  those  employed  to  cruise  after  blockade  runners. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

U.  S.  S.  Nita, 

Tampa  Bay ,  Fla. ,  November  12, 1861+. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report:  On  the  10th 
instant  I  proceeded  up  this  bay  on  a  reconnoissance  in  order  to  ascer¬ 
tain  the  cause  of  many  fires  in  the  vicinity  of  Gadsden’s  Point  and  Old 
Tampa  Bay.  Having  received  from  the  Hendrick  Hudson  Acting 
Master  Alex.  Wallace  and  10  men,  and  the  weather  being  thick  and 
rainy,  on  the  lltli  instant  I  advanced  nearly  to  the  head  of  Old  Tampa 
Bay  and  landed  there.  Finding  no  indications  of  any  movements  on 
the  part  of  the  enemy  in  that  direction,  I  scouted  for  some  distance 
inland  and  gave  the  order  to  return  on  board.  The  weather  at  this  time 
was  very  thick  and  rainy.  On  mustering  the  shore  party  five  of  the 
Hudson's  men  were  missing,  and  as  I  kept  my  position  all  night  and 
made  signal  from  time  to  time,  as  well  as  sending  several  boats  in  quest 
of  them,  it  is  to  be  presumed  that  they  have  deserted.  Early  on  the 
morning  of  the  12th  instant  I  proceeded  slowly  down  the  bay,  and  when 
near  Rocky  Point  discovered  evidences  of  quite  extensive  salt  works  a 
short  distance  inland.  I  anchored  as  near  the  shore  as  possible,  and  dis¬ 
patched  a  force  in  charge  of  Acting  Masters  Partridge  and  Wallace  to 
reconnoiter.  They  found  the  water  so  shoal  as  to  oblige  them  to  leave 
the  boats  and  wade  for  some  distance  in  order  to  reach  the  shore.  The 
necessary  pickets  having  been  thrown  out,  they  advanced  through  a 
dense  undergrowth  ai)d  swamp  in  the  direction  of  the  salt  works,  but 
after  they  had  proceeded  some  distance  a  body  of  horsemen  were  seen 
from  the  masthead  of  this  ship,  endeavoring  to  cut  them  off.  A  gun 
was  immediately  fired  and  a  recall  set,  and  Mr.  Partridge  ordered  a 
retreat.  The  picket  on  the  right,  Francis  Lupke,  seaman,  by  a  direct 
disobedience  of  the  orders  given  him,  came  out  in  the  open  ground  and 
was  wounded  and  captured.  With  this  exception,  the  whole,  party 
reached  the  boats  in  safety  and  returned  on  board.  During  the  return 
of  my  force  I  caused  the  bushes  to  be  shelled  vigorously,  and  believing 
that  my  force  was  too  small  to  effect  the  destruction  of  the  salt  works, 
I  returned  to  this  station.  The  works  are  quite  extensive  and  belong 
to  the  rebel  Government.  It  is  my  intention  to  attempt  to  destroy 
them  this  week. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  B.  Smith, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding .

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Stodder ,  L.  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  U.  S.  S.  Adda ,  regarding  the  capture  of  Confederate  schooner 
Badger. 

U.  S.  S.  Adela, 

Key  West ,  Fla..  November  16,  186 L 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  the  Confederate  schooner 
Badger ,  from  St.  Marks  bound  to  Havana,  was  taken  ^  possession  of 
by  the  boats  from  this  vessel  off  the  middle  entrance  of  St.  George’s 
Sound,  Fla.,  on  the  6th  of  November,  1864.  The  following  are  the 
circumstances  attending  the  affair: 

On  the  6th  of  November,  1864,  whilst  lying  at  anchor  at  Middle 
Pass,  St.  George’s  Sound,  Fla.,  a  strange  sail  was  reported  from  the 
masthead.  I  gave  orders  to  get  up  steam,  but  before  it  could  be  done 
the  sail  was  close  to  the  breakers  on  the  beach.  I  dispatched  all  the 
boats  and  had  one  of  them  hauled  across  to  the  outside  and  launched 
through  the  breakers,  which  was  gallantly  done  by  Acting  Ensign  F. 
A.  Strandberg,  who  reached  her  and  brought  her  in  safety  alongside. 
She  proved  to  be  the  Confederate  schooner  Badger,  S.  B.  Caldwell, 
master,  bound  from  St.  Mark’s  to  Havana,  with  a  cargo  of  cotton,  25 
packages  of  which  were  captured  with  the  vessel.  The  captain  threw 
overboard  his  papers,  also  the  deck  load,  consisting  of  9  bales.  1 
subsequently  dispatched  boats  up  and  down  the  coast  and  succeeded  in 
picking  up  5  bales  and  a  quantity  of  loose  cotton.  Accompanying  I 
forward  prize  list. 

I  am,  sir,  with  much  respect,  your  obedient  servant, 

Louis  N.  Stodder, 

Acting  Volunteer'  Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  transmitting 
report  of  the  toted  destruction  of  salt  works  in  Tampa  Bay. 

No.  52.1  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  December  3,  186 Jh 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  destruction  of  a  set  of  saltworks 
on  Rocky  Point,  Old  Tampa  Bay,  by  detachments  from  the  Nita, 
Stars  and  Stripes,  Hendrick  Hudson ,  and  the  tenders  Ariel  and  Two 
Sisters. 

The  expedition  was  made  at  the  instance  and  under  the  orders  of 
Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  R.  B.  Smith,  of  the  Nita, . and  was  in 
every  respect  a  complete  success,  resulting  in  the  demolition  of  seven 
large  boilers  and  everything  of  value  connected  with  the  works,  with¬ 
out  a  single  casualty  on  our  part. 

1  enclose  a  copy  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Smith’s  report, 
and  take  this  opportunity  to  recommend  that  officer  to  the.  Department 
for  his  zeal  and  energy  and  good  judgment  manifested  in  this  enter¬ 
prise,  which  was  conceived  with  clearness  and  executed  with  order  and 
dispatch. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Commanding  East  Gulf  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  T).  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Wells,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  bark 
Midmight,  regarding  the  destruction  of  salt  works  in  St.  Andrew's 
Bay. 

U.  S.  Bark  Midnight, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay,  Fla.,  December  f  186 f 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  following  since  relieving  the 
U.  S.  bark  Restless  on  this  station:  I  have  had  reason  to  believe,  by 
what  1  could  glean  from  refugees,  that  there  was  considerable  salt 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


781 


making  on  the  baj^s  above  here.  Consequently,  on  the  30th  of  Novem¬ 
ber  last  I  dispatched  an  expedition  with  24  men,  in  command  of  Acting 
Master  Charles  H.  Cadieu,  accompanied  by  Acting  Ensign  E.  O.  Drew 
and  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  Edward  W.  Avery,  up  the  bay  to  destroy 
salt  works  and  salt,  which  they  did  effectually.  They  captured  anci 
brought  away  with  them  the  16  salt  makers,  whom  I  have  since  paroled. 
Three  contrabands,  who  are  here;  1  has  enlisted,  and  the  others  object 
to  enlist  on  the  ground  that  they  have  left  their  families  in  Secessia. 
The  expedition  also  captured  2  Confederate  cavalry  pickets,  with  their 
horses.  The  prisoners  of  war  I  shall  send  to  Key  West,  for  your  dis¬ 
posal,  by  the  earliest  opportunity.  The  expedition  captured  the  fol¬ 
lowing  firearms:  Two  flintlock  muskets,  1  flintlock  rifle,  1  breech¬ 
loading  carbine;  also,  1  double-barreled  fowling  piece. 

I  respectfully  enclose  with  this  a  copy  of  the  details  of  the  expedi¬ 
tion  as  handed  to  me  by  Acting  Master  C.  H.  Cadieu,  and  would  sug¬ 
gest  that  a  tender  be  attached  to  this  blockade  for  cruising  up  the  bav 
and  keeping  these  salt  works  down.  The  upper  bays  are  so  large  and 
numerous  that  it  takec  seme  time  to  make  the  circuit  of  them  in  open 
boats,  and  it  leaves  men  exposed  to  the  weather  for  a  considerable 
length  of  time.  If  the  admiral  should  deem  it  proper  to  attach  a  ten¬ 
der  to  this  blockade,  I  would  respectfully  recommend  Acting  Master 
C.  H.  Cadieu  to  the  command  of  her. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  C.  Wells, 

Actg.  Master ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  Comdg.  U  S.  Bark  Midnight. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blkg.  Squadron ,  Key  West ,  J7la.

Rep>ort  of  Acting  Master  loring,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 
Sunflower,  regarding  the  capture  of  sloop  Pickwick. 

U.  S.  S.  Sunflower, 

West  Pass ,  St.  George's  Sound,  December  If  186 f 

Sir:  On  the  night  of  December  6,  1864,  at  9:10  p.  m.,  1  seized 
the  sloop  Pickwick  for  attempting  to  violate  the  blockade.  By  the 
prize  master  I  sent  all  the  papers  found  on  board,  together  with  the 


782 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


captain  and  crew,  to  Key  West.  I  captured  her  near  the  coast  of 
Florida,  in  latitude  28°,  longitude  83°  10',  the  nearest  land  bearing 
east,  12  miles  distant.  My  reasons  for  regarding  her  as  a  prize  are: 

1st.  The  position  in  which  she  was  found  when  captured,  taken  with 
the  captain’s  statement  that  he  was  bound  from  Havana  to  Matamoras, 
and  had  steered  west  ever  since  leaving  port. 

2d.  The  fact  that  when  first  seen  the  vessel  had  all  sail  set,  but 
about  the  time  she  must  have  seen  us  the  sails  were  lowered  and  she 
came  to  anchor. 

3d.  Although  we  saw  the  sloop  lower  here  sails,  yet  when  we  hailed 
her,  ten  minutes  after,  all  hands  pretended  to  be  asleep. 

4th.  The  character  of  the  cargo  and  the  class  of  vessel,  one  consist¬ 
ing  of  the  articles  most  required  in  the  rebel  States  and  the  other  being 
peculiarly  adapted  to  running  the  blockade  at  the  place  where  she  was 
captured. 

No  other  vessel  was  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture.  Enclosed 
I  send  the  prize  list. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  G.  Loring  3d, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  forwarding 
information  regarding  an  expected  raid  on  the  blockade  in  St. 
George's  Sound. 

No.  68.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  Fla.,  December  17,  186 f. 
Sir:  I  enclose  a  copy  of  a  letter  just  received  from  Acting  Volun¬ 
teer  Lieutenant  I.  B.  Baxter,  the  senior  officer  of  the  blockade  in  St. 
George’s  Sound,  [Apalachicola  Bay].  I  have  directed  him  to  be  pre¬ 
pared  to  repel  the  rebel  vessels  if  they  should  attempt  to  raise  the 
blockade. 

This  information  is  similar  to  former  reports,  and  although  I  doubt 
the  account  given  of  the  draft  of  water  and  force  of  the  ironclad  and 
other  vessels  referred  to,  I  regret  that  it  is  not  in  my  power  to 
increase  the  force  now  in  St.  George’s  Sound.  The  Somerset ,  now 
there,  can  be  used  only  as  a  floating  battery,  her  boilers  being  worn 
out  and  her  steam  power  useless. 


784 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  Fort  Henry  schooner  Beauregard,  and  steam  tugboat  Sunflower 
are  the  only  other  vessels  at  that  place.  Simply  to  keep  up  the 
blockade,  they  are  sufficient,  but  not  enough  if  attacked  by  such  a 
force  as  referred  to  in  the  enclosed  letter. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Fad  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  0.

U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry, 

West  Pass,  St.  George’s  Sound,  [. Apalachicola  Bay],  Fla., 

December  12,  186 p 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  the  following  information  was 
received  from  the  prisoners  John  Elision,  Lawrence  Brannan,  Michael 
Riley,  and  Charles  Parsons:  That  the  ironclad  gunboat  building  at 
Columbus,  Ga.,  is  about  completed  and  ready  for  launching. _  She  has 
all  her  machinery  on  board  and  will  carry  a  battery  of  6  7-inch  rifled 
guns,  and  is  not  intended  to  draw  above  6  feet  of  water  with  her 
armament  and  a  full  supply  of  fuel  and  stores  on  board.  . 

She  is  clad  with  2-inch  iron  below  the  knuckle  and  4  inch  above  it 
and  is  considered  a  more  formidable  vessel  than  the  Tennessee.  Theie 
is  a  torpedo  boat  building  at  the  same  place  which  is  nearly  completed, 
and  also  the  gunboat  Chattahoochee  is  there  undergoing  thorough 
repairs  on  hull,  machinery,  and  boilers;  and  [they]  are  making  every 
preparation  to  make  a  raid  on  the  blockade  at  this  place. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

I.  B.  Baxter, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling,

Report  of  Acting  Master  Thacker ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S. 
schooner  O.  II.  Lee ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Sort,  of 
Nassau ,  New  Providence. 

U.  S.  Schooner  O.  H.  Lee, 

Cedar  Keys,  December  17,  186 f. 

Sir:  1  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  the  capture  of  the  English 
schooner  Sort,  of  Nassau,  New  Providence.  I  captured  the  vessel 
under  the  following  circumstances:  December  the  10th,  1864,  latitude 
28°  38'  N.,  longitude  83°  4'  W.,  Anclote  Keys  bearing  S.  E.  i  E.,  dis¬ 
tance  from  land  24  miles.  Saw  a  schooner  bearing  N.  E.,  steering  to 
the  westward;  hauled  to  wind,  beat  to  quarters.  At  6:30  a.  m.  tired 
bow  gun  as  a  signal  for  her  to  heave  to.  She  immediately  backed  ship 
and  stood  in  for  the  land,  making  all  possible  speed.  On  nearing  her 
fired  a  shot  across  her  bow.  She  not  changing  her  course,  and  evidently 
determined  to  escape,  fired  several  shells  at  her,  the  last  one  bursting 
between  her  masts.  Wind  dying  away,  lowered  first  and  second  cut¬ 
ters,  armed  and  manned  them,  and  sent  them  in  chase.  She,  seeing 
escape  impossible,  hauled  down  her  jib.  On  coming  up  with  her 


EAST  GULP  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


785 


found  her  to  be  the  English  schooner  Sort ,  of  Nassau,  New  Provi¬ 
dence,  having  run  the  blockade  loaded  with  78  bales  of  cotton  from 
the  W  ithlacoochee  River;  overhauled  her  and  found  her  crew  con¬ 
sisted  of  captain  and  4  men  and  6  passengers.  All  documents  found 
on  board  were  sealed  up  and  handed  to  prize  master.  Having  put  a 
prize  crew  on  board,  I  sent  her  to  Key  West  for  adjudication.  No 
vessel  in  sight  at  time  of  capture. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Oliver  Thacher, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  U  S.  Schooner  0.  II.  Lee.

Secretary  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Report  of  Captain  Meade,  IT.  S.  Navy,  late  commanding  IT.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto. 

No  Name  Cay,  Abaco  Island,  Bahamas, 

January  1865. 

Sir:  It  has  become  my  painful  duty  to  report  to  you  the  loss  of  the 
U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto ,  lately  under  my  command.  She  struck  the  reef 
off  this  place  at  0h  40'  on  the  morning  of  the  1st  instant,  about  14 
miles  to  the  northward  and  westward  of  Elbow  Cay. 

After  making  every  exertion  to  relieve  the  ship  without  success, 
and  finding  her  to  be  bilged,  I  was  reluctantly  compelled  to  abandon 
the  hope  of  saving  her,  and  to  turn  my  attention  to  the  saving  of  the 
lives  of  my  men  and  officers,  my  guns,  ordnance  stores,  and  such  other 
Government  property  as  might  be  possible. 

The  wind  blew  a  strong  gale  during  the  remainder  of  the  night  and 
the  following  day,  but  I  am  happy  to  say  that  the  crew  were  all  landed 
safely,  notwithstanding  the  sea  broke  heavily  alongside  and  ahead  of 
the  ship. 

On  the  2d,  wind  and  sea  having  moderated,  I  succeeded  in  landing 
the  men’s  bags  and  hammocks,  with  three  weeks’  provisions,  sails  and 
light  spars  to  make  shelter,  with  view  to  the  health  and  comfort  of  the 
men  and  officers, 


788 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


I  have  chartered  a  schooner  of  76  tons  to  receive  the  guns  and  ord¬ 
nance  stores  (hoping  to  save  them  all),  at  $25  per  day  detention,  and 
at  $1,000  to  deliver  them  at  Key  West,  all  to  be  paid  in  gold. 

This  will  be  handed  you  by  Acting  Master  Pilot  William  Richardson, 
who  will  proceed  in  a  sloop,  chartered  at  $400  United  States  currency 
to  carry  this  communication.  He  is  a  reliable  officer,  and  will  furnish 
you  all  the  information  which  you  may  require  with  regard  to  the 
circumstances  as  they  exist  at  present  and  those  preceding  our  mis¬ 
fortune,  and  pilot  a  steamer,  if  you  advise  the  same,  to  receive  my 
crew. 

May  I  beg  to  request  that  the  Department  may  be  informed  of  the 
loss  of  the  ship  and  of  my  earnest  desire  that  a  court  of  enquiry  be 
convened,  at  as  early  a  period  as  the  exigencies  of  the  service  will  per¬ 
mit,  to  investigate  the  circumstances. 

I  desire  this  with  the  abiding  confidence  that  my  conduct  and  course 
of  action  throughout  will  be  sustained  by  every  officer  and  man 
belonging  to  my  command,  without  myself  entering  into  detail. 

I  throw  my  case  entirely  upon  that  decision  of  the  Government 
which  may  result  from  any  trial.  1  therefore  respectfully  request 
that  a  copy  of  this  communication  may  be  forwarded  to  the  Depart¬ 
ment. 

The  sloop  which  I  have  chartered  is  named  the  Garibaldi,  of  Key 
West,  J.  Albury,  master,  who  is  a  brother  of  the  postmaster  at  that 
place. 

I  am,  admiral,  most  respectfullv,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  W.  Meade, 

Captain. 

Forwarded. 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  assistance  rendered  to 

Captain  Meade,  IT.  S.  Navy. 

No.  8.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  January  10,  1865. 

Sir:  On  the  8th  instant  I  received  information  of  the  loss  of  the  San 
Jacinto  on  No  Name  Cay,  near  Great  Abaco.  1  immediately  sent  the 
Honduras  (the  only  vessel  in  port  not  under  repairs)  to  the  assistance 
of  Captain  Meade,  and  shall  send  the  Magnolia  as  soon  as  she  arrives 
(expected  every  hour  with  the  Glaucus  from  San  Domingo). 

These  vessels  can  take  on  board  the  crew  of  the  San  Jacinto.  Cap¬ 
tain  Meade  has  already  made  arrangements  for  bringing  here  the  guns, 
etc.,  saved  from  the  ship.  I  am  happy  to  report  that  all  the  crew  of 
the  San  Jacinto  were  safely  landed  and  are  not  suffering  for  provi¬ 
sions,  having  saved  from  the  ship  abundant  supplies.  The  crew  are 
sheltered  by  tents  made  of  sails,  etc. 

I  have  to-day  received  Captain  Meade’s  report  of  the  loss  of  the  San 
Jacinto,  with  a  letter  to  the  Department.  Both  are  herewith  enclosed. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Com  ay.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  referring  to  arrangements  for  a 

court  of  enquiry. 

No.  23.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  January  27 ,  1865. 

Sir:  By  the  arrival  of  the  Magnolia  from  the  wreck  of  the  San 
Jacinto  I  learn  that  the  wreckers  have  burned  the  ship  to  the  water’s 
edge,  to^  facilitate  their  taking  the  copper,  etc.,  from  the  ship.  I 
expect  Captain  Meade  in  the  Honduras  in  a  day  or  two,  as  his  remain¬ 
ing  there  any  longer  will  be  of  little  service.  I  expect  him  to  appoint 
a  person  on  the  part  of  the  United  States  to  receive  anything  saved 
from  the  wreck  by  the  wreckers  and  to  have  the  property  sent  here. 
As  soon  as  Captain  Meade  arrives  I  shall  make  arrangements  for  send¬ 
ing  the  officers  and  crew  north,  or  such  of  them  as  may  be  necessary 
in  any  investigation  the  Department  may  order  as  to  the  loss  of  the 
San  Jacinto.  I  could  not  have  a  court  of  enquiry  here,  for  the  want 
of  proper  officers  to  compose  a  court  without  detaining  vessels  in  port 
about  to  leave  on  cruises  or  blockades. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  etc., 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdy.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  departure  of  officers 
ordered  to  appear  before  the  court  of  enquiry. 

No.  55.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  February  26,  1865. 

Sir:  I  informed  you  on  the  27th  ultimo  that  I  should  send  Captain 
Meade  and  the  officers  of  the  San  Jacinto,  and  such  of  the  crew  as 
might  be  supposed  to  know  anything  about  the  loss  of  the  ship,  to  the 
North,  as  I  had  not  the  means  of  organizing  a  proper  court  here  for  an 
investigation.  At  the  request  of  Captain  Meade,  I  have  permitted  him 
to  return  north  via  Havana.  A  portion  of  the  officers  left  here  in  the 
Fo-rt  Morgan  on  the  14th  instant,  and  the  remainder  of  them  will  take 
passage  in  the  Bermuda,  with  such  of  the  crew  as  above  referred  to, 
and  all  the  marine  guard  not  required  to  fill  up  the  complement  of 
marines  allowed  to  vessels  on  the  station. 

I  will  take  this  occasion,  without  referring  to  the  cause  of  the  loss 
of  the  San  Jacinto,  to  state  that  Captain  Meade  appears  to  have  been 
untiring  in  his  efforts  to  save  the  public  property  after  the  loss  of  the 
ship. 

All  the  guns,  much  of  the  ordnance  stores,  anchors  and  cables,  boats, 
sails,  and  rigging,  and  much  other  valuable  property,  were  saved  and 
brought  here.  The  expense  of  doing  this  has  been  considerable  for 
freight  and  salvage.  Some  more  property  will  be  saved  from  the 
wreck,  which  I  shall  send  for,  upon  which  a  salvage  of  50  per  cent  has 
been  promised. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Adm  iral,  Conidg.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  letter  from  police 

magistrate  at  Abaco.

No  Name  Cay,  Bahamas,  Abaco, 

,  January  7,  1865. 

Sir:  I  would  respectfully  inform  you  that  two  blockade  runners 
have  lately  visited  this  port,  one  of  which,  losing  her  men,  has  been 
endeavoring  to  get  my  men  to  desert.  The  numerous  wreckers  on 
the  different  cays  have  in  large  bodies  been  here,  and  have  aided  and 
abetted  in  the  desertion  of  46  of  my  men.  Since  the  6th  instant  I 
have  had  no  desertions,  having  asked  the  assistance  of  Police  Justice 
J.  [Nibbs]  Brown,  who  has  been  very  vigilant  with  the  very  small  force 
at  his  command  to  render  me  much  service  in  warning  them  from  my 
camp. 

My  crew  consists  of  “bounty  men,”  having  received  large  sums 
from  State  and  Government,  in  some  cases  amounting  to  $1,400,  other¬ 
wise  largely  in  debt  to  the  Government  in  the  usual  advance  granted. 
I  respectfully  enclose  a  descriptive  list  of  these  deserters,  many  of 
whom,  I  am  informed,  have  reached  Nassau.  Eight  of  them  shipped

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  the  Secretary  of  State,  complaining  of  lack  of 
international  comity  on  the  part  of  the  British  authorities  in  the  Bahamas. 

Navy  Department,  April  12,  1865. 

Sir:  The  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto,  under  the  command  of  Captain  R.  YV. 
Meade,  having  been  recently  wrecked  on  a  reef  near  the  Island  of 
Abaco,  Bahamas,  Captain  ]\leade  deemed  it  expedient  to  avail  himself 
of  the  services  of  a  police  magistrate  of  Abaco,  named  J.  Nibbs  Brown, 
as  an  agent  for  supervising  the  affairs  of  the  wrecked  vessel  and  taki no- 
charge  of  the  property  saved  from  it. 

A  dispatch  received  by  the  Department  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral 
Stribling,  commanding  the  East  Gulf  Squadron,  to  which  the  San 
Jacinto  was  attached,  enclosed  a  copy  of  a  letter  from  Mr.  Brown,  in 
which  he  states  that  “  his.  excellency  the  governor  of  the  Bahamas”  has 
directed  him  to  relinquish  the  agency  for  the  wrecked  vessel.  Mr. 
Brown  further  writes  to  Rear-Admiral  Stribling  in  these  words: 

The  emergency  or  necessity  connected  with  the  wreck  having  ceased,  it  will  not 
be  practicable  for  me  to  permit  one  of  your  armed  vessels  to  enter  this  port  for  the 
transmission  of  the  articles  in  warehouse.  You  will  therefore  be  pleased  to  arrange 
for  their  transport  by  a  vessel  of  other  description.  Should  you  advise  it.  I  may  be 
able  to  procure  a  vessel  here  at  a  reasonable  rate. 

I  beg  leave  to  call  your  attention  to  this  proceeding  on  the  part  of 
the  British  authority  in  the  Bahamas,  which  wears  the  appearance  of 
an  unnecessary  departure  from  international  comity. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Hon.  Wm.  H.  Seward, 

Secretary  of  State. 

Report  of  Captain  Meade,  B.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  expenses  of  sending  a  vessel  to  the 

scene  of  the  wreck. 

Brooklyn,  N.  Y.,  A pril  If  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  forward  for  your  examination  a  copy  of 
the  correspondence  between  Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 
commandingEast  Gulf  BlockadingSquadron;  James  Nibbs  Brown,  esq., 
police  magistrate,  Abaco,  Bahamas,  and  myself,  in  reference  to  the 
expenses  incurred  in  dispatching  a  vessel  from  Green  Turtle  Cay,  the 
scene  of  the  wreck  of  the  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto ,  conveying  the  intelli¬ 
gence  of  the  disaster  to  the  U.  S.  consul  and  to  the  governor  of  the 
Bahamas  at  Nassau,  New  Providence,  and  in  relation  thereto  I  respect¬ 
fully  submit  the  following  statement: 

The  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto  grounded  upon  the  reef  off  Green  Turtle 
Cay,  Bahamas,  at  nearly  1  o’clock  a.  m.,  January  1,  1865.  The  usual 
signs  of  distress  were  exhibited,  and  were  answered  some  time  after 
daylight  by  the  appearance  on  board  of  James  Nibbs  Brown,  esq., 
police  magistrate  of  Abaco,  at  great  risk  to  himself,  resulting  in  serious 
injury  to  his  leg  and  foot,  from  which  he  is  suffering. 

Finding  that  there  was  no  hope  of  saving  the  ship,  he  returned  to 
the  shore. 

During  the  night  and  following  morning  the  weather  forbade  any 
approach  to  the  San  Jacinto ,  and  Mr.  Brown,  having  no  opportunity 
to  consult  with  me,  took  the  responsibility  of  dispatching  a  vessel  to 
Nassau  with  letters  to  the  U.  S.  consul  and  governor  relating  to  the 
wreck.  The  governor  immediately  sent  a  British  vessel. of  war  to  our 


794 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


assistance,  the  Medea ,  Captain  D’Arcy  Preston,  R.  N.  I  did  not  desire 
at  any  time  to  communicate  with  Nassau,  and  hence  did  not  avail 
myself  of  the  advantages  offered  by  the  officials  there.  The  aid  ten¬ 
dered  me  might  have  been  of  the  utmost  value  earlier,  but  circum¬ 
stances  were  such  (the  ship  having  bilged)  as  to  render  it  too  late  and 
make  me  independent  of  any  such  tender.  The  expense  incurred  was 
$300  in  gold,  which,  in  view  of  all  the  circumstances,  1  trust  will  be 
paid  by  our  Government. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

R.  W.  Meade,

Charges  and  specifications  of  charges  preferred  by  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  against 
Richard  W.  Meade,  a  captain  in  the  naval  service  of  the  United  States. 

Navy  Department,  January  J,  1866. 

Charge  1:  Violation  of  the  seventh  section  of  the  seventh  article  of 
the  rules  for  the*  better  government  of  the  Navy. 

_  Specification:  In  this,  that  on  or  about  the  first  day  of  January, 
eighteen  hundred  and  sixty-five,  the  said  Captain  Richard  W.  Meade, 
at  that  time  commanding  the  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto ,  then  cruising  in 
the  neighborhood  of  Elbow  Key,  so  called,  did  negligently  and  inat¬ 
tentively  give  the  orders  and  direct  and  command  the  navigation  of 
said  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto,  and  did  unlawfully  suffer  the  said  San  Jacinto, 
a  vessel  of  the  Navy,  to  be  run  upon  a  rock. 

Charge  2:  Culpable  inefficiency  in  the  discharge  of  his  duty. 

Specification:  In  this,  that  at  the  time  and  place  mentioned  in  the  fore¬ 
going  specification  the  said  Captain  Richard  W.  Meade,  being  then  in 
command  of  the  U.  S.  S.  San  Jacinto ,  did,  through  culpable  inefficiency , 
fail  to  make  his  orders  for  the  navigation  of  the  vessel  intelligible  to 
those  to  whom  they  were  given,  and  did  fail  to  give  to  the  execution  of 
his  said  orders  that  personal  attention  which  it  was  his  duty  to  have  done. 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Finding  of  the  court. 

Navy  Yard,  Philadelphia, 
Saturday ,  February  10,  1866. 

The  court  met  at  11  o'clock  a.  m.,  pursuant  to  adjournment.  Present, 
Captain  William  K.  Latimer,  president;  captains  Charles  Boarman, 
John  P.  Gillis,  Oliver  S.  Glisson;  commanders  T.  Darrah  Shaw,  John 
C.  Carter,  Edward  R.  Thomson,  members,  and  A.  Thomas  Smith  esq 
judge-advocate. 

Ihe  record  of  the  proceedings  of  yesterday  was  read  and  approved. 

Ihe  court  was  then  cleared,  and  after  full  and  mature  deliberation 
upon  the  charges  and  specifications,  the  evidence  adduced,  and  the 
defense  of  the  accused,  it  doth  find  that: 

Ihe  specification  of  the  first  charge  is  proven,  except  the  words 

give  the  orders  and.” 

And  the  said  Captain  Richard  W.  Meade  is  guilty  of  the  first  charge. 

The  specification  of  the  second  charge  is  proven,  except  the  words 

fail  to  make  his  orders  for  the  navigation  of  the  vessel  intelligible 
to  those  to  whom  they  were  given,  and  did.” 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADKON.  795 


And  the  said  Captain  Richard  W.  Meade  is  guilty  of  the  second 
charge. 

And  the  court  doth  sentence  the  said  Captain  Richard  W.  Meade  to 
be  suspended  from  rank  and  command  for  the  term  of  three  years. 

In  coming  to  this  conclusion,  the  court  would  remark  that,  from  a 
careful  review  of  all  the  evidence  in  this  case,  it  appears  that  the 
accused  did  not  exercise  proper  care  and  vigilance  in  the  navigation  of 
the  ship  in  the  vicinity  of  a  dangerous  coast  at  night,  in  not  keeping 
the  lead  going  when  running  for  the  land.  Acting  Master  [William  G.] 
W right,  the  navigating  officer,  proves  that  the  kedge  was  let  go  in  4 
fathoms  water,  80  or  100  fathoms  from  the  ship  after  she  struck;  and 
that  soundings  could  have  been  obtained  at  about  8  ship’s  lengths  from 
where  she  was  aground. 

Notwithstanding  the  state  of  the  weather  was  such  that  a  light  could 
have  been  seen  at  a  greater  distance  from  aloft  than  from  the  deck  of 
the  ship,  a  lookout  was  not  stationed  aloft;  nor  does  it  appear  that 
orders  were  given  to  the  officer  of  the  deck  or  to  any  of  the  look¬ 
outs  to  keep  a  bright  lookout  for  a  light-house,  nor  was  the  direction 
of  the  light-house  given.  The  position  of  the  ship  was  not  ascertained 
by  sights  for  the  chronometer  on  the  afternoon  of  the  31st  of  Decem¬ 
ber,  1864,  although  it  appears  that  they  might  have  [been]  taken  up  to 
3  o’clock  p.  m.  The  speed  which  the  vessel  is  shown  to  have  made  by 
the  revolutions  of  the  engine,  as  testified  to  by  the  engineers  on  watch 
on  that  night  and  by  the  log,  would  not  have  brought  her  to  the.  reef 
if  the  position  indicated  on  the  chart  at  8  o’clock  p.  m.  of  that  day 
had  been  cori’ect,  as  from  the  testimony  of  Acting  Master  Wright  the 
ship  could  have  been  run  from  there  for  25  miles  on  a  S.  by  W.  course 
with  safety,  and  if  she  had  been  run  20  miles  she  would  then  have  been 
11  miles  from  the  point  of  danger.  It  further  appears  that  when  the 
accused  came  on  deck,  after  10  o’clock  on  that  night,  he  did  not  observe 
the  course  the  ship  was  heading  by  compass.  Either  the  commanding- 
officer  himself  or  one  of  the  masters  on  board  should  have  been  on  deck 
on  the  lookout  while  running  for  the  light  on  “Elbow  Key,”  especially 
when  from  the  dangerous  character  of  the  navigation  in  that  vicinity, 
as  testified  to  by  Acting  Master  Wright  before  the  court-martial  at 
Brooklyn,  where  he  swore  that  he  would  not  venture  himself  within 
20  miles  of  the  coast  in  the  night,  it  was  not  proper  that  the  vessel 
should  then  have  been  left  entirely  in  charge  of  an  acting  ensign  as 
officer  of  the  deck. 

W.  K.  Latimer, 

President  of  the  Court.
