Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  March  6,  1865. 

Sir:  I  enclose  herewith  the  report  of  Acting-  Master  Wells  of  an 
expedition  from  the  Midnight  for  the  purpose  of  capturing  a  steamer 
on  the  Chattahoochee  Iiiver,  and  though  it  did  not  succeed  in  captur¬ 
ing  the  vessel,  it  was  otherwise  successful  in  capturing  16  soldiers 
and  bringing  off  13  contrabands  without  any  loss  of  men. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  I).  C. 

[Enclosure.] 


U.  S.  Bark  Midnight, 

St.  Andrew’s  Bay,  Fla.,  January  29,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  you  the  following  report  of  an 
expedition  sent  from  this  ship  in  command  of  Acting  Master  Charles 
H.  Cadieu,  accompanied  by  Acting  Assistant  Surgeon  E.  W.  Avery, 
Acting  Ensign  W.  H.  Grubb,  Acting  Master’s  Mate  J.  R.  Mitchell, 
with  the  launch,  howitzer,  and  second  cutter,  containing  30  armed 
men.  The  object  of  the  expedition  was  to  capture  the  steamer  that 
runs  from  Columbus,  Ga.,  to  Ricoes  [Rickoe’sJ  Bluff,  with  supplies 
for  the  Confederate  Army.  The  details  of  the  expedition  I  state  here¬ 
under  as  given  to  me  by  Acting  Master  Charles  H.  Cadieu.  They  are 
as  follows: 

On  the  16th  instant,  in  obedience  to  your  orders,  at  2  p.  m.  I  left 
the  ship  with  the  expedition,  taking  young  man  Parker  (refugee)  as 
pilot.  I  proceeded  up  St.  Andrew’s  Bay,  and  at  10:30  p.  m.  landed  at 
Barge  Bluff,  situated  on  Wretappo  Creek,  1  mile  from  the  head  of 
East  Bay.  Here  we  encamped  for  the  night,  and  at  daylight  on  the 
following  morning  proceeded  up  the  Wetappo.  At  8  a,  m.  we  arrived 


798 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


at  the  lagoon,  where  I  concealed  the  launch.  Transferring  the  howitzer 
and  ammunition  to  the  second  cutter,  I  sent  it  up  the  creek  to  what  is 
known  as  the  old  salt  house.  I  proceeded  by  land  with  the  balance  of 
the  party,  and  reached  the  salt  house  at  noon  on  the  17th  instant.  Here 
I  was  joined  by  three  deserters,  who  met  me  by  a  previous  appoint¬ 
ment.  Having  sent  a  party  to  guard  the  old  telegraph  road,  which 
the  rebel  cavalry  were  said  to  patrol,  1  started  in  company  with  one 
of  the  deserters,  by  the  name  of  Tate,  for  the  house  of  his  father,  who  is  a 
strong  Union  man.  I  procured  from  him  a  wagon  and  two  yoke  of  oxen, 
so  as  to  transport  the  second  cutter  across  the  country  to  the  Chipola 
River.  I  then  returned  to  the  salt  house,  where  I  arrived  at  11  p.  in. 
At  5  a.  m.  I  got  the  boat  ready  for  transportation,  and  at  8  o’clock  we 
started.  The  road  running  from  the  salt  house  to  White’s  Bluff  was 
in  a  very  bad  condition,  so  that  our  progress  was  slow.  We  arrived 
at  the  Bluff  at  10  p.  m.,  a  distance  of  11  miles.  The  Chipola  enters 
the  Apalachicola  20  miles  below  White’s  Bluff;  but  8  miles  above  the 
bluff  there  is  a  cut-off  which  connects  with  the  Apalachicola. 

At  daylight  we  took  in  the  pickets  from  the  old  Telegraph  road, 
and,  having  embarked  part  of  the  men  in  the  second  cutter  and  the 
remainder  in  canoes,  we  proceeded  up  the  river.  We  landed  at  the 
house  of  Mr.  Whitehard,  whose  son  was  with  us,  and  remained  there 
for  the  day  and  night.  I  here  found  a  runaway  negro  who  was  well 
acquainted  with  the  country  and  who  promised  to  be  our  guide.  At 
3  p.  m.  1  started  for  the  house  of  Mr.  Caraway  to  get  information  in 
regard  to  a  steamer  said  to  ply  in  the  Apalachicola  between  Chatta 
hoochee  and  Ricoes  [Rickoe’s]  Bluff  and  which  I  was  hoping  to  cap¬ 
ture.  I  remained  there  the  night  and  returned  on  the  morning  of  the 
20th.  At  2  p.  m.  we  embarked  and  proceeded  through  the  cut-off  into 
the  Apalachicola.  The  river  being  very  high  and  weather  rainy,  we 
made  slow  progress.  At  8  p.  m.  we  arrived  at  Atkin’s  Landing  and 
encamped  for  the  night.  At  10  a.  m.  on  the  21st  we  reembarked  and 
kept  up  the  river  to  a  place  which  I  learned  from  our  guide  was  suit¬ 
able  for  concealment.  Here  the  fields  were  overflown  to  a  depth  of  3 
and  4  feet.  Accordingly  we  took  the  boat  and  canoes  across  the  field 
behind  a  clump  of  trees,  where  they  were  concealed  from  the  river. 
Leaving  a  guard  in  the  boats,  I  proceeded  with  the  remainder  of  the 
party  along  a  high  ridge  about  a  mile  and  selected  a  very  dense  place 
for  our  camp.  At  1  p.  m.  I  left  the  camp  with  two  men  and  the 
guide  to  reconnoiter  the  vicinity  of  Ricoes  [Rickoe’s]  Bluff,  7  miles 
distant.  We  went  up  the  Apalachicola  2  miles  and,  turning  into  the 
Florida  River,  proceeded  to  the  junction  of  the  Wepaluxet  Creek;  pro¬ 
ceeding  up  the  creek  5  miles,  we  landed  at  a  place  1  mile  in  the  rear 
of  Rickoe’s  Bluff.  On  the  bluff  is  the  residence  of  a  planter  named 
Nixon.  My  guide,  being  acquainted  with  all  the  negroes  on  the  plan¬ 
tation,  called  out  one  that  was  deemed  trustworthy,  and  from  him  I 
received  the  following  information,  viz:  That  the  steamer  was  expected 
daily  and  that  there  was  a  picket  of  13  men  at  the  bluff,  commanded 
by  a  lieutenant.  I  approached  so  close  to  the  picket  station  as  to  be 
able  to  see  the  sentinel  on  duty  and  ascertain  where  the  guard  slept. 
I  then  returned  to  the  camp,  arriving  at  lip.  m.  We  remained  in 
camp  during  the  following  <kvy  and  night.  On  the  23d  at  2  p.  m.  we 
embarked,  and  at  5  p.  m.  we  arrived  at  an  old  gin  house  on  the  banks 
of  the  Wepaluxet  Creek,  1^  miles  from  Rickoe’s  Bluff.  Here  we 
remained  through  the  night,  intending  to  return  to  our  encampment 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


799 


the  following  day  if  the  steamer  did  not  arrive  that  night.  At  7  p.  m. 
on  the  24th  a  little  negro  girl  came  in  sight  of  our  picket,  and,  being 
frightened,  ran  away,  contrary  to  our  orders  to  stop.  Seeing  that  we 
were  discovered,  I  immediately  held  a  consultation  with  the  officers. 
V\  e  concluded  that  the  best  course  to  pursue  under  the  circumstances 
was  to  capture  the  pickets  and  return.  Accordingly  at  dusk  we  started 
for  the  camp,  which  is  about  a  mile  from  the  bluff.  Arriving  in  sight 
of  the  camp  fires,  we  halted  and  concealed  ourselves  until  about  8  p.  m., 
when  everything  seemed  favorable  for  the  attack.  After  stationing  5 
men  as  pickets  to  prevent  any  escape,  I  divided  the  remainder  of  the 
party  into  four  squads,  each  under  command  of  an  officer,  with  instruc¬ 
tions  to  quietly  surround  the  houses  that  had  lights  and  fires  in  them. 
In  this  way  we  charged  together  upon  the  houses,  burst  open  the 
doors,  and  took  everyone  prisoner  without  firing  a  gun.  We  captured 
here  1  lieutenant,  1  sergeant,  and  3  privates;  also  10  horses,  8  car¬ 
bines,  2  shotguns,  1  musket,  and  1  rifle.  Leaving  our  prisoners  under 
guard,  we  started  for  the  bluff,  where  a  picket  of  4  men  was  stationed. 
At  the  same  time  Mr.  Grubb  with  4  men  surrounded  the  house  of  Mr. 
Nixon  and  succeeded  in  capturing  his  son,  who  is  a  sergeant  in  Smith’s 
cavalry  company,  he  being  home  at  the  time  on  a  furlough.  With 
the  remainder  of  the  party  I  captured  the  picket  at  the  bluff.  We 
then  returned  to  the  camp  with  our  prisoners.  Leaving  the  camp, 
Dr.  Avery,  myself,  and  a  boy  as  guide  started  for  a  house  a  mile  and  a 
half  distant,  where  we  captured  the  only  remaining  picket  at  the  station. 
Returning  to  the  camp,  we  remained  there  until  daylight,  when  we  left 
for  the  bluff.  Here  upwards  of  30  negroes,  men,  women,  and  child¬ 
ren,  were  collected,  desiring  to  go  with  us.  On  the  bluff  was  a  Gov¬ 
ernment  storehouse  containing  a  large  quantity  of  corn,  which  I 
destroyed  by  fire.  Embarking  all  the  prisoners  and  negroes,  I  pro¬ 
ceeded  down  the  creek,  taking  the  precaution  to  remove  all  boats  at 
Rickoe’s  Bluff  and  on  the  creek,  to  prevent  pursuit.  I  was  obliged  to 
leave  the  horses,  having  no  means  of  transporting  them  across  the 
river.  Arriving  at  the  mouth  of  the  creek,  I  sent  Mr.  Grubb  with 
the  negroes  and  prisoners  down  the  river  to  White’s  Bluff.  Taking 
4  men,  I  started  for  Freeman’s,  a  planter,  who  owned  about  a  dozen 
negroes.  I  arrived  there  at  4  p.  m.  and  took  every  negro  on  his  plan¬ 
tation,  also  one  rifle  and  one  double-barreled  fowling  piece.  I  imme¬ 
diately  proceeded  down  the  river  to  White’s  Bluff,  arriving  on  the 
following  morning  at  9:30  a.  m.  I  found  that  Mr.  Grubb  had  sent 
the  prisoners  and  negroes  across  the  country  toward  the  salt  house, 
keeping  a  boat’s  crew  with  him  at  the  bluff.  Procuring  a  team  from 
Mr.  Tate  to  transport  the  baggage,  I  sent  the  remainder  of  the  negroes 
across  the  country.  I  then  ordered  Mr.  Grubb  to  proceed  down  the 
river  with  the  second  cutter  and  a  crew  of  11  men  to  capture  a 
picket  of  0  men  which  was  stationed  at  old  Fort  Gadsden,  and  proceed 
down  the  river  and  report  to  blockading  vessel  at  Apalachicola  Bay 
and  return  to  the  Midnight  along  the  coast.  I  then  returned  to  the 
salt  house  and  down  the  creek  to  the  place  where  the  launch  was  con¬ 
cealed.  Here  1  encamped  for  the  night.  On  the  morning  of  the  27th 
1  sent  the  contrabands  down  the  creek  in  charge  of  Mr.  Mitchell  with 
orders  to  land  them  at  Barge  Bluff.  The  prisoners  were  sent  down  to 
the  ship  in  charge  of  Dr.  Avery  with  orders  to  report  to  you  to  send 
back  the  launch  in  tow  of  the  first  cutter.  I  remained  at  the  salt  house 
with  two  men  to  forward  the  baggage  to  the  bluff,  where  I  arrived  on 


800 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


the  morning  of  the  28th.  At  5  p.  m.  the  launch  and  first  cutter  arrived 
from  the  ship.  At  6  p.  m.  we  embarked  and  proceeded  to  the  ship, 
where  we  arrived  at  4  a.  m.  on  the  29th. 

The  following  are  the  details  of  the  expedition  of  Acting  Ensign 
W.  H.  Grubb  in  obedience  to  orders  received  from  Acting  Master 
Charles  H.  Cadieu,  in  Apalachicola  River: 

U.  S.  S.  Midnight, 

St.  Andrew's  Bay,  Fla.,  January  81,  1865. 

Sir:  Id  obedience  to  Mr.  Cadieu’s  orders,  I  left  White’s  Bluff  at  1:30  p.  m.  of  the 
26th  instant  in  the  second  cutter  with  a  crew  of  11  men.  Passing  down  the  Chipola 
River  through  Gum  Swamp,  I  arrived  at  Fort  Gadsden  shortly  after  dark,  a  distance 
of  35  miles.  Having  been  informed  that  the  jacket  was  in  the  habit  of  staying  in  a 
scow  in  the  middle  of  the  river,  I  took  in  my  oars  about  2  miles  above  the  fort  and 
drifted  silently  down  the  stream,  having  hands  ready  with  boat  hooks  to  grapple  as 
we  came  alongside.  But  no  scow  was  there,  it  having  sunk  about  two  weeks  before. 
Having  drifted  past  the  fort,  I  landed  my  party  one-half  mile  below  and  attempted 
to  march  up,  but  was  stopped  by  a  wide,  deep  creek,  which  we  could  not  cross. 
Embarking  my  party  again  and  muffling  the  oars,  pulled  up  the  river  about  1  mile 
and  landed  at  Brick  Yard  Bluff.  Moving  quickly  across  the  fields,  we  captured  the 
sentry,  and,  entering  the  guardhouse,  found  a  sergeant  and  one  man,  which  was 
all  that  were  on  the  station  at  that  time,  three  men  having  permission  to  pass  the 
night  at  their  homes.  Taking  the  three  prisoners  and  their  arms,  we  went  to  the 
house  of  a  Mrs.  Buckles  and  encamped  for  the  remainder  of  the  night.  At  8  a.  m. 
of  the  27th  I  started  for  the  house  of  a  man  named  Wellington,  5  miles  down  the 
river.  As  we  approached  the  house  he  started  for  the  woods  and  escaped.  I  secured 
his  carbine,  shot  his  horse,  and  started  for  a  place  called  Bloody  Bluff,  where  two 
men  lived,  belonging  to  the  same  company.  We  found  them  at  home  and  took  them 
and  their  arms.  At  1:30  p.  m.  we  started  for  the  blockade  at  Apalachicola.  Arriv¬ 
ing  at  10  p.  in.,  I  reported  immediately  to  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Baxter,  com¬ 
manding  the  U.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry,  who  ordered  the  U.  S.  S.  Sunflmuer  to  take  us  to 
St.  Andrew’s  Bay.  We  left  West  Pass  at  4:30  p.  m.  of  the  29th  instant  and  arrived 
at  8  a.  m.  next  morning,  bringing  5  prisoners  and  6  stand  of  arms. 

The  result  of  the  above  expeditions  are  briefly  this,  viz:  The 
capture  of  1  lieutenant,  3  sergeants,  12  privates,  and  19  stand  of 
arms,  besides  bringing  away  43  contrabands  and  destroying  a  govern¬ 
ment  storehouse  which  contained  150  bushels  of  corn  belonging  to  the 
Confederate  Government.  1  would  further  state  that  1  can  not  speak 
too  highly  of  the  officers  and  men  (without  exception)  belonging  to 
this  ship  for  their  bravery  and  the  amount  of  good  judgment  shown 
on  their  numerous  expeditions. 

Very  respectfully,  J.  C.  Wells, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  Officer. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron ,  Bey  West ,  Fla. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  transmitting 
report  regarding  the  probable  loss  of  the  U.  S.  tender  Annie. 

Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  January  26,  1865. 
Sir:  The  schooner  Annie,  tender,  left  here  on  the  30th  day  of 
December  for  Charlotte  Harbor  for  blockade  service  at  that  place. 
Since  then  she  has  not  been  heard  of  and  I  fear  she  has  been  lost. 
The  wreck  of  a  schooner  was  seen  near  Cape  Roman  several  days  since. 
Every  effort  will  be  made  along  the  coast  to  discover  the  crew,  as  they 
may  have  leached  shore  after  the  vessel  was  lost.  1  enclose  herewith

a  copy  of  Acting  Master  Carter’s  report  giving  information  of  the 
probable  loss  of  the  Annie.

C.  K.  Stribling,

U.  S.  Bark  Restless, 
Charlotte  Harbor ,  Fla. ,  January  20,  1865. 

feiiu  I  ha\  e  the  honor  to  report  my  arrival  at  this  place  Monday, 
the  16th  instant.  I  found  the  schooner  Ariel  here  from  Tampa  Bay, 
with  refugees  for  Fort  Myers.  Having  no  means  of  transportation 
at  my  disposal  but  the  ship’s  boats,  I  accordingly  armed  and  manned 
the  first  cutter  next  morning  and  sent  them  down  under  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  Alex.  Hinckley. 

The  first  cutter  returned  to-day  (20th)  and  Mr.  Hinckley  reported 
to  me  that  the  captain  of  the  schooner  Matchless ,  lying  at  Point  Rosa 
[Punta  Rasa  ?],  informed  him  “that  about  12  miles  to  the  northward 
of  Cape  Roman  he  passed  the  wreck  of  a  schooner  with  her  mainmast 
gone  and  foremast  broken,  and  that  night  he  saw  a  large  fire  ashore.” 

The  wreck  I  concluded  to  be  that  of  the  schooner  Annie ,  which  left 
Key  West  for  this  port  about  two  weeks  ago.  I  again  and  immedi¬ 
ately  armed,  manned,  and  provisioned  the  first  cutter,  under  charge  of 
Acting  Ensign  Alex.  Hinckley,  to  ascertain  if  my  surmises  were 
correct,  and,  if  so,  to  render  assistance  or  succor  to  those  of  her  sur¬ 
vivors  that  might  need  it. 

Captain  [Jonathan  W.]  Childs,  commanding-  post  at  Fort  Myers, 
informs  me  of  his  intention  of  sending  a  party  across  to  Cape  Roman. 

Hoping  my  action  in  this  matter  may  meet  with  your  approval, 

I  remain,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

II.  B.  Carter, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding . 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
cruises  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Isonomia  in  the  vicinity  of  Nassau  and  the 
Bahama  Banks. 

No.  23.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  January  27 ,  1865. 
Sir:  Referring  to  your  letter  of  the  15th  of  October  last.  The 
Isonomia  was  immediately  withdrawn  from  the  blockade  at  West  Pass, 
and  has  since  made  two  unsuccessful  cruises  in  the  vicinity  of  Nassau 
and  the  Bahama  Banks.  In  both  cruises  blockade  runners  were  chased 
and  escaped  by  superior  speed  or  running  within  neutral  territory.  In 
both  cruises  much  of  the  time  was  spent  under  shelter  of  the  cays  in 
the  Bahama  Banks,  and  it  was  only  when  the  weather  was  moderate 
she  could  keep  the  open  sea.  On  her  last  cruise  the  Isonomia  received 

N  W  R — VOL  IT - 51 


802 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


considerable  damage  to  her  sponsons  and  wheelhouses.  Having 
received  information  from  the  consul-general  at  Havana  that  a  steamer 
was  about  to  attempt  to  enter  the  port  of  St.  Marks,  I  dispatched  the 
Isonomia  to  cruise  near  that  place  in  the  hope,  with  her  speed  in 
smooth  water  the  vessel  might  be  captured.  Upon  her  return  from 
this  service  she  will  have  to  be  repaired.  The  inability  of  the  Isonomia 
to  keep  the  sea  in  rough  weather,  and  taking  shelter  under  the  cays  on 
the  Bahama  Banks,  and  want  of  speed  except  in  very  smooth  sea,  ren¬ 
der  her,  in  my  judgment,  unfit  for  the  service  for  which  she  was 
intended  by  the  Department.  The  authorities  of  the  Bahamas  find 
fault  with  our  vessels  (the  Isonomia  is  the  only  one)  seeking  shelter 
under  the  cays  in  bad  weather  and  ready  to  take  the  first  opportunity 
of  wind  and  weather  to  chase  vessels  bound  to  or  from  Nassau.  Her 
light  draft  of  water  and  the  vicinity  of  harbors  will  make  her  a  useful 
vessel  near  St.  Marks  and  Cedar  Keys. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  /A  G.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Russell,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle,  regarding 

the  capture  of  schooner  Augusta. 

U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  January  21,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  receiving  information  on  the 
morning  of  the  17th  instant  from  a  Union  refugee  that  a  suspicious 
looking  boat  containing  5  men  had  boarded  him  about  20  miles  up  the 
coast,  representing  themselves  as  belonging  to  the  U.  S.  S.  Honduras , 
and  wishing  him  to  come  with  them  and  pilot  her  into  the  Suwanee 
River,  as  they  were  after  two  blockade  runners,  supposed  to  be  there, 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  803 


and  also  that  the  steamer  was  lying  about  5  miles  to  the  northward 
theni  a  ln*orann£  °f  his  ignorance  of  the  channel,  he  left 

Communicating  this  intelligence  to  me,  I  at  once  dispatched  Acting 
Cnsign  Charles  N.  Hall,  and  Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineer  Charles 
Li.  label’ 'with  two  armed  boats  to  ascertain  if  there  was  any  vessel 
After  a  toilsome  pull  of  over  seven  hours,  on  the  afternoon 
01  tue  17th  instant,  they  succeeded  in  overhauling  a  schooner  at  the 
entrance  to  Suwanee  River,  endeavoring  to  enter  the  river  by  the 
west  channel.  She  proved  to  be  the  English  schooner  Augusta ,  55 
tons,  Jerome  Lakin,  master,  from  Havana,  January  3,  with  a  clearance 
tor  IVlatamoras.  The  crew  consisted  of  six  men,  captain  included,  who 
all  acknowledged  that  they  were  endeavoring  to  violate  the  blockade. 

lhe  cargo  consists  of  pig  lead,  flour,  gunny  cloth,  and  coffee. 

lhe  lead  was  consigned  to  Edward  Hobard,  special  agent  of  War 
Department,  Niter  and  Mining  Bureau,  Tallahassee,  Fla. 

The  customary  papers  were  all  captured  on  the  schooner,  with  the 
exception  of  the  register. 

A  small  portion  of  the  cargo  was  thrown  overboard  to  lighten  the 
vessel,  previous  to  the  capture. 

There  were  no  vessels  in  sight  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 

Owing^  to  the  intricacy  of  the  channel,  and  unfavorable  weather, 
Acting  Ensign  Hall  was  unable  to  reach  this  place  with  the  schooner 
until  the  21st  instant. 


I  send  the  prize  schooner  to  Key  West  for  adjudication,  in  charge 
of  Acting  Ensign  Charles  N.  Hall,  with  6  men  as  a  prize  crew,  also  the 
master  and  mate  as  the  required  witnesses.  The  remaining  4  of  the 
schooner’s  crew  I  retain  for  passage  to  Key  West  by  the  first  naval 
conveyance. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  J.  Russell, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C.

U.  S.  Schooner  (Tender)  Fox, 

Off  St.  Marks,  Fla.,  January  35,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  23d  instant,  at  meridian, 
while  cruising  between  St.  Marks  and  Deadman’s  Ba\r,  I  discovered 
a  schooner  at  anchor,  near  the  mouth  of  Warrior  River,  bearing 
E.  N.  E.  I  immediately  steered  in  that  direction,  and  at  2  p.  m. 
anchored  near  her.  On  boarding  her  she  proved  to  be  the  British 
schooner  Fannie  McRae,  from  Havana,  cleared  from  Matamoras,  with 
an  assorted  cargo.  As  the  captain  acknowledged  that  he  was  endeavor¬ 
ing  to  run  the  blockade  into  the  Aucilla  River,  I  have  taken  possession 
of  her  and  brought  her  to  this  station  as  a  prize.  Herewith  are  all 
the  papers  found  on  board  of  her.  At  the  time  of  capture  she  was 
within  3  miles  of  the  shore. 

Respectfully, 

F.  Burgess, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding. 


Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  French,  U.  S.  Navy,  com¬ 
manding  TJ.  S.  ship  Ino,  regarding  expedition  to  Manatee  River  for 
the  capture  of  cotton  and  sugar. 

U.  S.  Ship  Ino, 

Tampa  Bay,  Fla.,  January  31, 1865. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  a  boat  loaded  with 
cotton  and  12  barrels  of  sugar  on  the  27th  instant,  under  the  following 
circumstances:  Having  received  information  from  reliable  persons 
that  a  certain  rebel  agent  residing  on  the  Manatee  River  had  Gov¬ 
ernment  stores  on  his  premises,  I  accordingly  proceeded  on  board 
tender  Ariel  and  one  armed  boat’s  crew  up  the  Manatee  River,  with 
the  design  also  to  destroy  a  small  salt  work. 

At  the  mouth  of  said  river  captured  a  boat  loaded  with  cotton,  which 
was  the  property  of  a  rebel  army  officer  named  Maloney,  of  which 
circumstance  I  had  previous  information.  After  the  capture  of  the 
boat,  proceeded  to  the  residence  of  one  called  McNeal,  who  being  then 
absent,  I  proceeded  to  examine  his  premises  and  found  12  barrels  of 
sugar,  which  his  wife  affirmed  belonged  to  the  rebel  Government,  and 
which,  with  the  captured  boat,  I  brought  to  this  vessel.  For  more 
minute  particulars  1  would  refer  you  to  my  reports*  of  the  expedition. 

The  captured  sugar  and  boat  I  will  forward  the  first  opportunity  to 
Key  West,  Fla. 

Enclosed  please  find  a  prize  list,  signed  by  the  paymaster  of  tills 
vessel  and  myself. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Charles  A.  French, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


*Not  found.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Hill,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  schooner 
Matthew  Vassar,  regarding  the  capture  of  schooner  John  Hale,  of  St. 
Marks,  Fla. 

U.  S.  Schooner  Matthew  Vassar, 

Off  St.  Marks,  Fla.,  February  f  1865. 
Sir:  I  have  honor  to  inform  the  Department  of  the  capture  of  the 
schooner  John  Hale  on  the  3d  instant  after  a  sharp  chase  of  four  hours, 
iu  which  I  expended  33  shell.  I  first  saw  him  about  10  miles  offshore, 
and  9  miles  to  the  eastward  of  the  Econfenee  River.  As  soon  as  he 
made  us  out  he  immediately  altered  his  course  to  the  southward, 
crowding  on  all  canvas.  I  boarded  him  in  29°  46'  north  latitude  and 


806 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADKON. 


84°  10'  west  longitude,  St.  Marks  light-house  bearing  N.,  distant  18 
miles.  The  boarding  officer  could  find  no  ship’s  paper.  The  vessel 
was  in  charge  of  the  mate,  a  citizen  of  Galveston,  Tex.,  who  said  that 
the  captain  and  supercargo  had  taken  the  papers  ashore  with  them 
early  in  the  morning  to  go  to  Tallahassee.  As  near  as  I  could  make 
out  these  men  were  landed  at  or  about  Point  Edwards.  The  cargo 
consists  mostly  of  lead,  blankets,  shelter  coverings,  and  rope.  For 
about  half  an  hour  before  she  was  boarded  the  crew  were  throwing 
overboard  what  I  think  must  have  been  arms.  I  could  find  nothing- 
floating.  I  herewith  enclose  a  list  of  the  officers  and  crew  entitled  to 
share  in  the  said  prize. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

G.  E.  Hill, 

Acting  Master ,  Commanding . 

Hon,  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  tit  e  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  ■  Commander  Gibson ,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding 

U.  S.  S.  Mahaska ,  of  arrival  at  Key  West  for  duty  in  East  Gulf 

Blockading  Squadron. 

U.  S.  S.  Mahaska, 

Key  West ,  February  f  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  I  arrived  here  this  morning, 
ten  days  from  Boston,  and  in  obedience  to  your  order  reported  to 
Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling  for  duty  in  the  East  Gulf  Squadron. 

We  had  rough  weather  in  crossing  the  Gulf  Stream,  and  a  strong 
N.  W.  gale,  with  a  large,  heavy,  combing  sea  between  Hatteras  and 
Bermuda.  I  ran  the  Mahaska  pretty  well  before  it,  and  she  shipped 
but  little  water  and  behaved  well  generally.  Being  a  double-ender, 
with  a  steering  apparatus  specially  adapted  to  river  service  and  deeply 
laden  with  her  armament  and  stores,  1  was  agreeably  surprised  to  fin'd 
her  a  fair  sea  boat,  and  think  the  fact  worth  mentioning  to  the  Depart¬ 
ment. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  Gibson, 

Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Report  of  Acting  Rear- Admiral  Stribling ,  17.  S.  Navy ,  transmitting 
account  of  the  finding  and  ra  ising  of  the  wreck  of  the  U.  S.  schooner 
Annie. 

N°-  31.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  February  8 ,  1865. 
Sir:  I  informed  the  Department  on  the  27th  ultimo  of  the  probable 
loss  of  the  schooner  Annie ,  commanded  by  Acting  Ensign  H.  W. 
A  ells.  Orders  were  given  to  search  for  the  vessel,  and  1  now  enclose 
a  copy  of  the  report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  C.  II.  Rockwell, 
commanding  the  Hendrick  Hudson ,  giving  a  full  account  of  the  finding 
of  the  wreck  of  the  schooner  and  its  condition.  From  the  account  of 
Lieutenant  Rockwell,  I  think  there  is  reason  to  believe  that  the  Annie 
was  accidentally  blown  up.  I  have  ordered  the  accounts  of  the  crew 
of  the  Annie  to  be  forwarded  to  the  Fourth  Auditor,  and  will  forward 
to  the  Department  a  list  of  the  crew  as  soon  as  received  from  the  Rest¬ 
less,  where  the  accounts  were  kept. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blkdg.  Squadron. 
Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C 

[Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Hendrick  Hudson, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  February  7,  1865. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  of  this  ship  under  my 
command  in  this  port,  in  obedience  to  your  orders  of  the  21st  ultimo. 
Upon  being  relieved  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes ,  and  after  turn¬ 
ing  over  to  her  paymaster  the  accounts  of  the  O.  H.  Lee  and  Fox,  I 
took  the  mails  brought  up  by  the  Stars  and  Stripes  to  West  Pass,  and 
having  received  the  mails  for  Key  West  from  the  vessels  on  that  sta¬ 
tion  left  there,  after  laying  six  hours  on  the  2d  instant.  On  the 
morning  of  the  4th,  being  oft'  Charlotte  Harbor,  I  ran  in  to  ascertain  if 
anything  had  been  heard  from  the  ill-fated  schooner  Annie  and  to  get 
the  mails  from  the  Restless.  I  was  there  informed  that  the  mast  of  a 
vessel  had  been  seen  oft  Cape  Roman.  Leaving  Charlotte  Harbor  the 
same  day,  I  ran  as  far  as  Malco  Inlet  [Marco  Pass?]  and  anchored  at 
midnight.  On  the  5th  I  again  weighed  anchor,  and,  with  a  smooth  sea 
and  very  favorable  circumstances,  succeeded  at  1  p.  m.  in  discovering 
the  mast  referred  to  in  6  fathoms  of  water,  Cape  Roman  bearing  N.  E. 
by  N.,  distant  about  10  miles.  I  immediately  hauled  the  bow  of  this' 
ship  alongside  of  the  mast,  and  with  such  means  as  I  possessed  suc¬ 
ceeded  at  11  p.  m.  in  raising  the  wreck  sufficiently  to  bring  her  bow 
out  of  water  and  identify  her  as  the  Annie,  and  discovered  her  condi¬ 
tion.  The  catastrophe  by  which  she  was  wrecked  is  still  a  mystery, 
and  unless  her  crew  have  been  saved  1  fear  must  remain  so.  From 
her  foremast  aft  her  deck  is  entirely  gone,  with  the  exception  of  the 
port  side  of  the  trunk  cabin  aft.  From  just  abaft  the  fore  rigging,  on 
the  starboard  side,  she  is  entirely  gone — deck,  bottom,  timbers,  and 
everything  from  the  keel  out  being  completely  cut  off,  with  the  excep¬ 
tion  of  two  or  three  of  her  floor  timbers.  No  vestige  of  her  mainmast 
or  the  sail  could  be  discovered,  not  even  the  stump.  The  pole  of  the 


808 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


main  topmast  was  found  fast  to  the  jib  stay,  the  pennant  halyards  being 
wound  around  it  with  the  toggle  and  head  of  the  pennant.  On  the 
port  side,  from  the  fore  rigging  aft,  her  rail  was  entirely  gone,  but  I 
think  her  plank-sheer  was  whole  on  that  side  as  far  as  the  cabin.  A 
more  complete  wreck  could  scarcely  be  imagined.  Everything  that 
could  be  found  was  saved.  Her  gun  could  not  be  discovered,  and  I 
am  satisfied  was  not  on  board.  The  foresail  and  everything  connected 
with  it  was  gone.  I  procured  her  anchors  and  chains  with  the  jib  and 
a  few  other  articles — a  list  of  which  I  enclose  and  which  I  hold  subject 
to  your  order.  An  octant  in  its  case  was  found  with  the  chains  for¬ 
ward.  On  the  6th,  at  9  a.  m.,  finding  that  nothing  more  could  be 
saved,  -I  caused  the  wreck  to  be  hung  by  the  mast,  and  cutting  the 
rigging  as  far  down  as  it  could  be  got  at  the  mast  drew  out  and  was 
saved,  and  the  ill-fated  schooner  sank  in  6  fathoms  of  water.  With 
the  grapnels  and  other  appliances  the  whole  hull  w^as  felt  over  to 
ascertain  if  any  of  the  bodies  of  the  crew  could  be  discovered,  but 
nothing  was  found  except  some  clothing  and  bedding.  Nothing  could 
be  found  to  throw  any  light  on  the  manner  of  her  loss.  As  1  dis¬ 
covered  her  no  vessel  could  have  run  her  down  and  injure  her  to  the 
extent  seen  by  a  single  blow,  although  much  may  have  washed  off 
from  her  since  her  loss.  From  all  I  could  see  I  think  she  must  have 
been  blown  up,  and  can  account  for  it  in  no  other  way. 

Very  respectfully, 

C.  H.  Rockwell, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

Key  West,  Fla. ,  February  23,  1865. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  schooner  Delia 
under  English  colors,  near  Bayport,  on  the  17th  instant,  by  the  Mahaska,

Lieutenant-Commander  Gibson  commanding,  with  a  cargo  of  pig  lead

•  [Enclosure.] 

U.  S.  S.  Mahaska, 

Off  Bay  port,  Fla.,  February  17,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  this  day,  with  the  boats  of  this 
vessel,  I  captured  a  schooner  purporting  to  be  the  Delia. 

We  discovered  her  about  8  o’clock  this  morning  steering  out  from 
the  vicinity  of  Bay  port  on  a  wind  to  the  southward.  Upon  seeing  us 
she  made  all  sail  for  the  nearest  land.  We  chased  her  until  stopped 
by  shoal  water,  firing  at  her  with  the  Parrott  100-pounder  about  a 
dozen  times.  I  then  sent  a  boat  in  pursuit,  followed  soon  after  by 
another. 

The  leading  boat  went  alongside  of  her,  finding  her  with  all  sail  set, 
the  English  flag  at  the  main  and  the  rebel  flag  at  the  fore,  and  aban¬ 
doned,  the  boats  of  the  deserters  and  people  on  the  beach  in  view.  No 
papers  except  one  or  two  trifling  memoranda,  from  which  the  name  of 
the  vessel  is  inferred  (as  also  from  a  burgee),  were  found  on  board. 
The  boat  which  first  boarded  the  schooner  was  in  charge  of  Acting 
Master’s  Mates  J.  C.  Boteler  and  J.  W.  Sanderson.  When  boarded 
her  cabin  was  partially  in  flames,  and  in  addition  a  slow  match  was 
discovered  in  a  bucket  of  turpentine.  I  wish  to  commend  the  judg¬ 
ment  and  promptitude  displayed  by  these  gentlemen  in  extinguishing 
the  fire  and  throughout  the  whole  affair. 

The  Delia  is  a  center-board  schooner  of  apparently  about  80  tons 
burden.  Her  cargo  consists  of  pig  lead  and  some  cases  of  sabers. 
Part  of  her  cargo  was  thrown  overboard."  I  have  taken  some  15  gal¬ 
lons  of  rum  belonging  to  her  on  board  this  ship  for  safe-keeping. 

I  forward  herewith  a  muster  roll  of  the  officers  and  crew. 

No  other  naval  vessel  was  in  sight. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  Gibson, 

Dieuten  ant-  Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  transportation  afforded 
to  troops  under  the  command  of  General  Newton,  1J.  S.  Army. 

Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  March  3 ,  1865. 

Sir:  An  expedition  left  here  on  the  23d  ultimo,  under  General 
Newton,  for  the  west  coast  of  Florida,  intended  for  St.  Marks  or  some 
place  near  it. 

I  was  happy  to  cooperate  with  the  army  by  affording  the  general 
transportation  for  the  troops  in  the  Magnolia  and  Honduras,  there 
being  no  army  transports  here  at  the  time,  and  by  ordering  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Gibson,  the  senior  officer  on  the  blockade  at  St.  George’s 
Sound,  to  unite  with  General  Newton  with  all  the  vessels  on  the 
blockade  and  cruising  from  St.  George’s  Sound  to  Tampa,  leaving  a 
sufficient  force  to  keep  up  the  blockade  at  the  different  ports.  Several 
of  the  vessels  can  enter  the  river  at  St.  Marks  and  will  be  of  great 
service  if  the  general  should  attack  that  place.  We  have  not  heard  of 
the  expedition  since  it  left  here. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  East  Gidf  Blkdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C. 


Detailed  Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  tbe  expedition. 

No.  74.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  March  Uh  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  of  the  result  of  the  expedition 
to  St.  Marks  which  1  reported  on  the  3d  instant  left  here  on  the  23d 
ultimo.  The  vessels  from  St.  George’s  Sound  under  Lieutenant- 
Commander  Gibson,  and  the  vessels  with  the  troops  under  the  com¬ 
mand  of  General  Newton,  arrived  simultaneously  off  St.  Marks. 

The  naval  force  then  consisted  of  the  Mahaska,  Fort  Henry ,  Spirea, 
Stars  and  Stripes,  Hibiscus ,  Honduras,  Magnolia ,  Britannia  (steamers), 
and  the  schooners  Matthew  Vassar,  0.  H  Lee,  and  Two  Sisters. 
Subsequently  the  force  was  increased  by  the  Proteus ,  Iuka ,  Isonomia, 
and  Hendrick  Hudson.  Commander  Shufeldt,  being  the  senior  officer, 
assumed  the  command  of  the  naval  forces  cooperating  with  the  army! 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.

814 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADKON. 


Arrangements  were  immediately  made  for  landing  the  troops  and  for 
such  of  the  vessels  to  enter  the  river  as  drew  the  least  water.  The 
Honduras ,  Fort  Henry ,  Hibiscus ,  and  Britannia  succeeded  in  getting 
up  the  river  some  distance  after  great  efforts.  The  Mahaska ,  Spirea , 
and  Stars  and  Strives  got  aground,  the  Stars  and  Strives .  just  below 
the  Hibiscus ,  the  Mahaska  near  the  light-house,  and  the  Spirea  farther 
out.  While  the  vessels  were  attempting  to  ascend  the  river,  the  troops 
were  landed  near  the  light-house  and  commenced  their  march  into  the 
interior  toward  Tallahassee.  Every  effort  was  made  by  Commander 
Shufeldt  to  get  the  vessels  up  the  river  to  attack  the  forts.  On  the 
6th  instant  information  was  received  that  the  army  was  falling  back. 
By  this  time  the  vessels  named  above  had  succeeded  in  getting  within 
a  mile  and  a  half  of  Port  Leon.  Commander  Shufeldt,  deeming  it, 
under  the  circumstances,  useless  to  attempt  to  ascend  higher,  Lieuten¬ 
ant-Commander  Gibson  was  ordered  to  send  a  party  on  shore  to  hold 
the  bridge,  which  was  accomplished,  and  after  the  army  had  crossed 
the  bridge  was  burned  by  Acting  Ensign  Whitman,  who  had  charge 
of  the  party.  On  the  morning  of  the  7th,  after  an  interview  with 
General  Newton,  the  squadron  was  ordered  to  drop  back  to  an  anchor¬ 
age  off  the  light-house.  General  Newton  stated  to  Commander  Shu¬ 
feldt  that  he  had  accomplished  all  that  he  contemplated  at  present. 
There  is  no  doubt  that  preparations  had  been  made  by  staking  out  the 
channel,  removing  obstructions,  and  garrisoning  the  fort,  to  make  St. 
Marks  in  some  sort  a  compensation  for  the  loss  of  Wilmington.  Com¬ 
mander  Shufeldt  states  “as  the  navy  now  has  possession  of  the  mouth 
of  the  river,  the  only  point  which  is  of  any  naval  importance  whatever, 
I  consider  the  object  so  far  as  we  are  concerned  fully  gained.” 

This  effectually  closes  the  river  so  long  as  we  keep  an  adequate  force 
there.  I  enclose  a  sketch  of  the  mouth  of  the  river  and  the  distance 
it  was  ascended  by  several  vessels  of  the  squadron.  It  affords  me 
great  pleasure  to  report  the  zealous  cooperation  of  the  Navy  with  the 
Army  on  this  occasion.  All  worked  with  a  will,  and  the  only  regret 
felt  by  the  officers  and  men  was  their  not  being  able  to  get  under  fire. 
The  arrangements  made  by  Lieutenant-Commander  Gibson  before  the 
arrival  of  Commander  Shufeldt  were  judicious,  and  the  zeal,  intelli¬ 
gence,  and  industry  of  Commander  Shufeldt,  ably  supported  as  he 
was  by  the  officers  and  crews  of  the  vessels,  in  ascending  the  rivers, 
is  worthy  of  commendation.  I  beg  to  commend  to  your  favorable 
notice  Acting  Ensign  Whitman  and  the  four  men  named  in  the  letter 
of  Commander  Shufeldt,  herewith  enclosed. 

Although  the  expedition  has  not  been  attended  with  the  success 
expected,  it  has  been  the  means  of  showing  the  temper  of  the  officers 
and  men  of  this  squadron  who,  from  the  nature  of  the  blockade  serv¬ 
ice,  have  not  been  so  situated  as  to  render  any  brilliant  service  but 
are  ready  and  anxious  for  an  opportunity  to  show  that  they  are  made 
of  the  same  stuff  that  gained  such  glorious  victories  at  New  Orleans, 
Fort  Morgan,  and  Fort  Fisher. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Bear- Admiral,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  1).  C.

Detailed  report  of  Brigadier-General  Newton,  D  S.  Army,  regarding  expedition. 

Hdqrs.  District  of  Key  West  and  Tortugas, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  March  19,  1865. 

Colonel:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  the  following  report  of  oper¬ 
ations  in  this  district. 


816 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


February  23. — Headquarters  were  embarked  on  the  steamer  Hon¬ 
duras,  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Harris,  commanding,  and  likewise 
three  companies,  A,  B,  and  K,  of  the  Second  U.  S.  Colored  Infantry, 
destined  for  Punta  Rasa. 

February  21 — Reached  Punta  Rasa,  where  the  Magnolia  was  found. 
Both  steamers  sailed  for  Cedar  Keys  at  3  p.  m. 

February  25. — Arrived  at  Cedar  Keys  at  6  p.  m.  Major  Weeks, 
commanding  post,  being  absent  on  a  raid,  he  was  directed  to  return. 
No  chance  to  cut  off  or  intercept  the  enemy’s  force  in  the  South  Penin¬ 
sula  appeared  to  offer  itself. 

February  27. — Major  Weeks  returned.  Companies  C,  D,  and  E, 
Second  Florida  Cavalry  (dismounted),  and  Companies  E,  G,  and  H, 
Second  U.  S.  Colored  Infantry,  were  embarked  on  the  Magnolia ,  leav¬ 
ing  at  Cedar  Keys  a  sufficient  detail  from  the  companies  above  men¬ 
tioned  to  protect  the  place  in  our  absence.  Transferred  headquarters 
to  the  Alliance,  which  had  arrived  from  Key  West. 

February  28. — Arrived  off  Ocklockonee  buoy,  near  St.  Marks  Bar, 
13  miles  from  land,  where  the  naval  force  was  directed  to  assemble. 
The  fog  was  dense. 

March  1  and  2. — Steamers  Mahaska ,  Honduras ,  Magnolia ,  Stars 
and  Stripes,  Spirea,  Fort  Henry;  schooners  0.  II.  Lee,  Matthew 
Yassar ,  and  Two  Sisters  assembled  together.  Heavy  fog.  Lieutenant- 
Commander  William  Gibson  commanded  the  naval  force.  After  full 
and  free  consultation  the  following  plan  of  operations  was  adopted: 
First,  to  land  a  party  of  seamen  and  of  the  Second  Florida  Cavalry  on 
Light-House  Island  on  the  night  of  the  3d  to  take  possession  of  the 
bridge  over  East  River,  and  to  surprise  and  capture  the  pickets  there 
if  possible;  second,  to  land  the  troops  on  the  same  night  in  readiness 
to  start  at  daylight  on  the  4th;  third,  the  land  expedition  was  to  march 
to  Newport,  destroy  the  public  establishments  there,  cross  the  river 
St.  Marks,  take  St.  Marks  in  rear  or  strike  the  railroad  between  St. 
Marks  and  Tallahassee,  attacking  isolated  bodies  of  the  enemy  to  pre¬ 
vent  a  concentration  and  destroying  and  capturing  such  property  as 
might  be  useful  to  the  enemy;  fourth,  in  order  to  effect  these  objects, 
parties  were  landed  to  destroy  the  railroad  and  other  bridges  over  the 
Ocklockonee  River,  the  trestle  or  bridge  over  the  Aucilla  River,  and 
to  break  up  the  railroad  between  St.  Marks  and  Tallahassee;  fifth, 
the  naval  force  was  to  endeavor  to  silence  the  batteries  at  St.  Marks 
and  capture  it,  to  land  a  force  of  500  to  600  seamen  at  Port  Leon 
to  cover  the  land  expedition,  to  prevent  the  enemy  crossing  in  its 
rear  between  St.  Marks  and  Newport,  and  to  threaten  St.  Marks. 
There  was  no  doubt  entertained  that  this  landing  at  Port  Leon  would 
be  effected. 

March  3. — The  fog  having  risen,  the  whole  fleet  put  to  sea,  sailing 
until  after  dark  in  order  to  deceive  the  enemy,  should  he  have  discov¬ 
ered  the  presence  of  the  vessels.  After  dark,  returned  to  the  bar, 
which  the  pilot  in  vain  endeavored  to  cross,  though  he  had  indicated 
no  difficulty  previously.  A  heavy  gale  sprang  up  and  the  vessels 
were  of  necessity  anchored  until  morning,  by  which  the  landing  of  the 
troops  was  unfortunately  delayed.  In  the  meantime  Major  Weeks, 
with  60  men  of  the  Florida  cavalry  and  30  seamen  under  Acting  En¬ 
sign  Whitman,  surprised,  but  did  not  succeed  in  capturing  the  enemy’s 
pickets  at  the  bridge  over  East  River. 

March  L — Early  in  the  morning  the  fleet  got  underway  (the  Spirea 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


817 


leading)  for  the  light-house.  The  pilot  ran  the  Spirea  hard  and  fast 
aground;  the  Honduras ,  containing  troops,  likewise  grounded.  In 
the  meantime  Major  Weeks’  expedition  returned  to  the  light-house, 
because  his  position  at  the  bridge  was  too  advanced  in  the  absence  of 
the  main  force.  The  enemy’s  cavalry  followed  him,  skirmishing. 
The  steamers  Hibiscus ,  Proteus ,  and  Iuka  arrived.  The  last  two  an¬ 
chored  and  remained  outside.  After  the  delays  arising  as  above  stated 
from  the  fog  and  from  the  grounding  of  the  vessels,  the  troops  were 
finally  debarked  by  -i  p.  m.,  and  the  whole  command  was  moved  for¬ 
ward  about  2T  miles  upon  a  spot  of  elevated  ground  suitable  for  an 
encampment,  where  we  were  to  await  the  landing  of  the  artillery,  am¬ 
munition,  and  ambulances.  This  being  effected  about  8  a.  m.  on  the 
5th,  the  whole  command  advanced  upon  the  road  leading  to  the  bridge 
over  East  Itiver,  where  we  found  the  planking  of  the  bridge  taken  up 
and  the  enemy’s  cavalry,  with  one  piece  of  artillery,  upon  the  opposite 
bank  prepared  to  dispute  the  passage.  *  *  * 

The  expedition  returned  because  the  navy  was  unable  to  cooperate 
in  any  manner;  the  ammunition  was  nearly  expended,  and  our  com¬ 
munications,  owing  to  the  failure  to  land  a  force  of  seamen  at  Port 
Leon,  as  agreed  upon,  would  have  been  assuredly  cut  in  less  than  eight 
hours.  The  whole  force  of  the  expedition  was  893  enlisted  men,  2 
navy  boat  howitzers,  and  1  light  12-pounder  captured  from  the  enemy. 
The  artillery  was  drawn  by  hand  the  whole  distance.  Our  wounded 
were  all  brought  off  with  the  exception  of  8  fatally  wounded,  left  at  a 
house  2  miles  from  the  field  of  battle.  Our  loss  was  ITS  killed, 
wounded,  and  missing,  of  which  35  are  missing.  This  number  will  be 
further  reduced,  it  is  reasonable  to  anticipate.  The  force  of  the 
enemy  is  stated  by  a  prisoner  (an  officer  of  militia)  to  have  been  from 
1,500  to  2,000,  and  further  reinforcements  were  continually  arriving. 
The  enemy  was  liberally  supplied  with  field  artillery.  The  bridges 
over  the  Ocklockonee  and  the  Aucilla  were  not  damaged,  nor  the  rail¬ 
road  obstructed,  so  far  as  known.  Indeed,  the  party  for  the  Ock¬ 
lockonee  returned  without  making  a  serious  attempt  to  reach  the 
bridge.  The  men  sent  were  picked,  and  had  a  good  knowledge  of  the 
country,  and  they  would,  with  little  risk  to  themselves,  have  obstructed 
for  several  days  these  railroads.  A  refugee  is  known  to  have  left  one 
of  the  blockading  vessels  and  to  have  given  the  enemy  two  weeks’ 
notice  of  the  expedition;  hence  their  large  concentration  of  force,  a 
party  of  which  is  said  to  have  come  from  Georgia  and  from  the  vicin¬ 
ity  of  Pensacola.  The  expedition,  though  it  did  not  effect  all  that  was 
anticipated,  was  far  from  being  unfruitful  in  its  results.  Two  impor¬ 
tant  bridges,  one  foundry,  and  two  large  mills  were  burned;  extensive 
saltworks  partially  destroyed,  and  laid  open  for  the  future  to  raiding- 
parties.  It  is  proper  fo  state  that  this  expedition  has  likewise  estab¬ 
lished  the  blockade  vessels  off  the  light-house  instead  of  outside  the 
bar  as  before.  St.  Marks  is  now  thoroughly  blockaded.  The  enemy  has 
little  to  boast  of  in  the  military  operations  of  this  expedition.  Though 
having  two  weeks’  notice,  he  was  obliged  to  burn  the  important  bridge 
at  Newport,  so  useful  to  him,  and  was  finally  driven  off  the  field  near 
the  Natural  Bridge,  having  allowed  an  inferior  force  to  march  25  miles 
into  his  territory  and  return  without  losing  an  article  of  public  prop¬ 
erty,  but,  on  the  contrary,  carrying  off  one  captured  piece  of  artillery. 
It  is  unnecessary  to  state  that  we  were  in  ignorance  of  the  fact  that  in¬ 
formation  had  been  furnished  the  enemy  until  the  expedition  was  over.

We  would  otherwise  not  have  landed.  St.  Marks  and  neighborhood  pre¬ 
sented  the  greatest  if  not  the  sole  inducements  for  a  raid  or  expedition 
within  the  limits  of  this  district.  The  absence  of  large  numbers  of  rebel 
troops  in  the  South  Peninsula,  as  before  stated,  fixed  the  proper  moment 
for  the  attempt,  and  it  was  not  suitable  to  pass  unnoticed  the  attempt 
of  the  rebels  to  capture  Fort  Myers  and  annoy  the  garrison  at  Cedar 
Keys.  The  rebel  troops  at  Chattahoochee,  Tallahassee,  St.  Marks,  and 
as  far  east  as  Madisonville  were  by  unanimous  testimony  put  at  less 
than  600  men.  It  was  likewise  thought  that  the  expedition  from  Pen¬ 
sacola,  of  which  I  had  heard,  would  naturally  draw  the  rebels  from  the 
neighborhood  of  Tallahassee  and  St.  Marks,  though  it  is  now  known 
that  the  information  of  our  intended  operations  in  that  vicinity  drew 
their  troops  in  the  opposite  direction;  a  great  advantage,  at  all  events, 
to  our  column  starting  from  Pensacola  into  the  interior.  After  the 
expedition  was  over,  all  the  troops  were  returned  to  the  posts  at  Cedar 
Keys,  Punta  Rasa,  and  Key  West.  Fort  Myers  has  been  broken  up. 
The  officers  and  men  of  the  expedition  behaved  nobly  under  the  most 
trying  circumstances,  marching  50  miles  in  forty-four  hours,  of  which 
they  rested  only  five  hours,  and  fought  or  skirmished  most  of  the  time. 
When  we  recrossed  the  bridge  at  East  River  we  found  there  a  guard 
of  40  seamen  under  command  of  Acting  Ensign  Whitman.  For  this 
precaution  we  were  indebted  to  the  foresight  of  Commander  Shufeldt, 
who  in  my  absence  had  relieved  Lieutenant-Commander  Gibson  of  the 
command  of  the  naval  force. 

I  can  not  close  this  communication  without  expressing  the  obliga¬ 
tions  I  am  under  to  Rear-Admiral  Stribling  for  the  hearty  cooperation 
which  he  ordered  his  officers  to  afford,  and  his  own  endeavors  to  make 
the  expedition  a  complete  success.  And  this  desire  of  the  admiral  was, 
so  far  as  I  could  perceive,  cheerfully  responded  to  by  his  officers.  I 
will  forward  a  list  of  recommendations  for  gallant  services  in  the  field. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

John  Newton, 

Brigadier-  General ,  Commanding. 

Lieutenant-Colonel  C.  T.  Christensen, 

A.  A.  G.  Ildqrs.  Alii.  Div.  of  West  Miss. ,  New  Orleans ,  La.

lT.  S.  S.  Mahaska, 

St.  Marks  River ,  Florida ,  Afarch  21,  1865. 

Sir.  I  have  the  honor  to  forward  a  communication  received  on  the 
18th  instant  by  a  flag  of  truce  from  Major-General  Sam  Jones,  com¬ 
manding  at  Tallahassee,  with  a  copy  of  my  reply.  On  the  20th  the 
enemy  sent .another  flag,  only  to  say  that  if  we  wished  to  communicate 
we  should  hre  a  gun  at  8  a.  m.  and  they  would  meet  us  at  Four-mile 
1  oint.  Quite  a  number  of  refugees,  white  men  and  contrabands,  have 
recently  come  on  board.  From  two — a  one-legged  white  man  named 
dames  Wetzel,  who  claims  to  have  been  taken  prisoner  from  the  U.  S. 
Army,  and  a  colored  man  named  Charles  Amos— I  have  information 
which,  as  it  was  received  at  different  times  and  closelv  tallies,  may  be 
considered  reasonably  reliable.  I  send  you  the  men  that  you  may  per¬ 
sonally  question  them.  On  the  18th  instant  Captain  Strickland  and 
one  private  of  his  party  were  executed  by  the  rebels  (shot).  The  salt 
works  here  are  of  vital  importance  to  the  rebels.  After  our  attack  salt

went  from  $30  to  $50  per  bushel,  Confederate  money.  About  2,000  of 
the  enemy  encountered  General  Newton  at  the  Natural  Bridge,  near 
Newport.  A.  moiety  was  collected  from  the  vicinity,  old  men  and 
young  boys  included,  and  1,000  well-drilled  volunteer  troops  from

magazine  for  the  largest  rifle  gun  is  at  the  other  extremity.  In  antici¬ 
pation  of  the  attack,  all  the  guns  had  been  removed  from  the  Spray  and 
mounted  on  the  fort.  Two  smooth-bore,  old-pattern,  ringed,  cascabel 
32-pounders  were  left  on  the  lighter  alongside  the  Spray.  The  arma¬ 
ment  of  the  fort,  thus  increased,  was  two  32-pounders,  rifled;  one  rifle 
gun,  described  as  a  Parrott  (probably  30-pounder),  and  one  12-pounder 
rifle  gun,  captured  from  us,  and  two  smoothbore  32-pounders,  similar 
to  those  on  the  lighter.  But  at  the  time  of  the  attack  (they  state)  there 
were  only  three  men  left  in  the  fort,  and  trains  were  laid  and  orders 
left  to  blow  up  both  the  fort  and  vessel  on  the  near  approach  of  the 
gunboats.  Wetzel  says  there  are  no  good  artillerists  in  the  fort.  As 
regards  obstructions,  a  flatboat  was  sunk  in  the  river  a  short  distance 
below  Port  Leon  a  long  time  since.  Recently  (as  our  own  people  had 
seen)  many  of  the  stones  were  taken  out  of  her  and  she  was  floating  to 
one  side,  leaving  a  channel,  the  soldier  says,  to  the  left  of  her  going- 
up.  At  the  time  of  the  fleet  moving  up  there  were  no  obstructions 
between  Port  Leon  and  the  fort.  Pens  (to  be  sunken  with  stones) 
were  being  made,  and  pine  logs  chained  together,  with  spearheads 
pointing  downstream  (such  as  they  had  at  Charleston),  were  to  be  sub¬ 
merged  in  what  was  intended  to  be  an  inviting  channel  between  the 
pens.  These  were  not  in  readiness,  and  withal  would  have  been  only 
100  yards  from  the  fort.  We  have  reason  to  believe,  from  watching 
the  movements  of  the  Spray's  boat  and  from  the  talk  of  some  of  the 
contrabands,  that  they  are  dropping  torpedoes  in  the  river.  They 
have  thrown  up  rifle  pits  in  rear  of  the  fort. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  Gibson, 

Lieutenant-  Commander , 

Commanding  First  Dim. ,  East  Gulf  Blkdg.  Squadron. 

In  the  fight  near  Newport  the  enemy’s  loss  is  reported  to  be  more 
severe  than  ours.  Individual  information  states  3  officers  killed  and 
30  men  killed  and  wounded. 

Wm.  Gibson, 

Lieutenant  -  Commander. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron.

EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


Report  of  Brigadier-General  Newton,  IT.  S.  Army,  commanding  expedition. 

Headquarters  District  of  Key  West  and  Tortugas, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  April  19 ,  1865. 

General:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  herewith  a  report  of  the 
operations  in  this  district  during-  the  months  of  February  and  March. 
This  report,  although  previously  sent  to  headquarters  Military  Divi¬ 
sion  of  West  Mississippi,  is  likewise,  by  advice  from  thence,  trans¬ 
mitted  direct  to  Washington.  *  *  * 

The  expedition  started  with  893  men,  but  the  detachments  at  New¬ 
port  and  outposts  up  and  down  the  river,  together  with  losses  in 
action,  had  reduced  this  number  to  500  men  at  the  moment  when  the 
enemy  became  reinforced.  With  500  men,  therefore,  a  force  of  four 
to  five  times  its  number  was  decisively  repulsed.  All  the  troops 
engaged  at  the  Natural  Bridge  were  black  troops  of  Second  and 
Ninety-ninth  Colored  Infantry.  The  boldness  of  our  attack  gave  the 
enemy  the  idea  of  a  much  superior  force  on  our  part,  which  they  actu¬ 
ally  believed  to  have  been  nearly  2,000.  The  disposition  made  of  our 
troops  was  such  that  the  enemy  could  use  but  a  portion  of  their  avail¬ 
able  men,  and  their  papers  declared  that  one-half  at  least  did  not  fire 
a  shot.  The  result  was  that  the  rebels  could  make  but  little  use  of 
vastly  superior  forces.  The  enemy  evacuated  St.  Marks,  leaving  but 
three  men  to  blow  up  the  fort  there,  destroy  their  gunboat,  the  Spray , 
plying  between  St.  Marks  and  Newport,  and  burn  500  bales  of  cotton 
at  the  depot  at  St.  Marks;  and,  had  the  navy  advanced,  all  the  objects 
contemplated  in  the  expedition  could,  I  think,  have  certainly  been 
accomplished.  The  navy  did  not  get  to  Port  Leon  nor  land  the  600  sea¬ 
men  there,  as  promised,  and  in  consequence  I  could  not  cross  between 
Newport  and  St.  Marks  after  the  destruction  of  the  bridge  at  New¬ 
port,  which  was  effected  by  the  retiring  enemy;  neither  could  I  draw 
upon  my  ammunition  and  provisions  on  shipboard.  The  expedition 
was  a  raid  of  a  small  body  of  infantry,  there  being  no  mounted  men  in 
this  district,  and  was  intended,  besides  the  destruction  of  the  enemy’s 
public  property,  to  give  them  employment  near  home  and  prevent  them 
organizing  expeditions  against  our  small  forts  on  the  southern  penin¬ 
sula  of  Florida,  an  object  which  has  been  fully  accomplished.  I  learn 
also  that  it  effected  a  powerful  diversion  in  favor  of  Steele’s  column 
marching  from  Pensacola,  which  was  a  contemplated  benefit  of  the 
expedition.  The  naval  force,  which  exaggerated  the  importance  of  the 
expedition  in  the  public  eye,  being  unable  to  perform  the  part  assigned, 
was,  to  say  the  least,  of  no  benefit  to  our  operations.-  The  expedition 
was  not  undertaken  to  go  to  Thomasville,  capture  Tallahassee,  or 
occupy  any  part  of  the  country,  unless  it  should  afterwards  appear  that 
St.  Marks  possessed  great  advantages  for  the  latter  purpose.  A  great 
deal  of  the  information  imparted  in  this  communication  has  been  gained 
since  my  report  to  General  Canby’s  headquarters.  I  send  herewith  a 
sketch*  of  the  country.  The  enemy’s  available  force,  when  the  expe¬ 
dition  started,  did  not  exceed  700  men. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Newton, 

Br  igadier  -  General ,  Commanding . 


*See  Army  War  Records,  Volume  XLIX,  pt.  1,  p.  68.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling, 
U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  reduction  of  naval  expenses. 

Navy  Department,  February  2f  1865. 

Sir:  The  Department  is  of  opinion  that  the  fall  of  Fort  Fisher  and 
Charleston  will  enable  it  to  reduce  the  expenses  of  the  maintenance  of 
the  Navy. 

You  will  therefore  send  north  such  purchased  vessels  as  appear  by 
surveys  to  require  very  extensive  repairs  and  such  as  are,  in  your 
opinion,  the  most  inefficient  and  all  those  no  longer  required. 

These  will  probably  be  sold  or  laid  up.  You  will  also  send  home 
any  stores  that  are  not  required.  Further  requisitions  must  be  care¬ 
fully  examined  before  approval,  and  the  commanders  of  squadrons 
are  expected  to  use  every  possible  exertion  and  care  to  reduce  the 
expenses  of  their  squadrons. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  requesting  an 

additional  sailing  vessel. 

No.  56.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  P  la. ,  February  26,  1865. 
Sir:  We  are  much  in  want  of  a  sailing  vessel  to  carry  coals,  provi¬ 
sions,  etc.,  to  places  where  they  are  required,  and  to  bring  back  wood 
for  the  use  of  the  vessels  here.  It  frequently  happens  that  for  the  want 
of  such  a  vessel  one  has  to  be  chartered  at  heavy  expense. 

One  of  the  mortar  boats  would  be  about  the  description  of  vessel  for 
this  service.  One  howitzer  is  all  the  armament  she  would  require. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  J).  C. 


Report  of  Commander  Shufeldt,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ.  S.  S. 
Proteus,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  steamer  Ruby,  from  'Havana. 


U.  S.  S.  Proteus, 

At  Sea,  February  27,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that  I  have  this  day  captured 
and  sent  to  Key  West  the  steamer  Ruby,  from  Havana,  and  cleared  for 
Belize,  [Honduras],  but  according  to  the  statements  of  some  of  the 
officers  and  passengers  on  board  bound  to  St.  Marks,  Fla.  Some  of  the 
cargo  appears  to  have  been  thrown  overboard  during  the  chase;  the 
remainder  consists  of  lead  and  sundries. 

This  ship’s  position  at  the  time  of  the  capture  was  latitude  26°  10'  N., 
longitude  83°  30[  W.,  Tortugas  bearing  S.  S.  E.,  95  miles  distant. 

The  prize  list  is  herewith  enclosed. 

Very  respectfully, 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


R.  W.  Shufeldt, 

Commander.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Russell,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Honeysuckle ,  regarding  the  capture  of  British  schooner  Sort ,  from, 

Havana. 

U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle, 

Cedar  Keys,  Fla.,  March  H,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  February  28,  at  7 :30  a.  m., 
while  lying  at  anchor  abreast  of  Sea  Horse  Key,  a  schooner  was  reported 
bearing  E.  by  S.,  standing  inshore.  The  water  being  too  shoal  in  that 
direction  for  me  to  chase  her  with  the  steamer,  I  dispatched  two  armed 
boats  to  endeavor  to  intercept  her,  which  they  were  unable  to  do  owing 
to  a  strong  souther^  wind  which  was  blowing  at  the  time.  They  suc¬ 
ceeded  in  working  to  windward  of  the  schooner  and  forcing  her'in  on 
St.  Martin’s  Reef,  when  she  stood  directly  for  Crystal  River.  Three 
days  previous  to  that  time  I  had  dispatched  Acting  Ensign  Charles  N. 
Hall  with  a  boat  manned  and  armed  for  the  purpose  of  watching  in 
that  vicinity.  Fortunately  Mr.  Hall  was  near  the  entrance  to  the  river, 
and,  seeing  the  schooner,  immediately  made  sail  to  head  her  off.  The 
schooner  then  stood  in  for  the  nearest  land,  striking  on  a  reef  about 
5  miles  from  Crystal  River.  The  crew  lowered  the  sails,  abandoned 
her,  and  succeeded  in  escaping  to  the  mainland.  Mr.  Hall  boarded  and 
took  possession  of  her  at  about  11:30  a.  m.  She  proved  to  be  the 
English  schooner  Sort,  33  tons,  from  Havana,  with  an  assorted  cargo, 
i  he  papers  were  all  found  on  board.  Some  20  demijohns  were  found 
broken;  they  had  contained  liquor  and  were  evidently  destroyed  at  the 
time  of  abandoning  the.  vessel.  There  were  no  vessels  in  sight  at  the 
time  of  capture.  This  is  the  same  schooner  captured  in  December  last 
b}r  the  U.  S.  schooner  0.  II.  Lee. 

I  send  the  schooner  to  Key  West  for  adjudication,  in  charge  of  Act¬ 
ing  Master’s  Mate  M.  C.  Easterbrook  and  a  prize  crew  of  four  men. 

1  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  J.  Russell, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle.  - 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Snerrill ,  IT.  S.  Navy ,  com¬ 
manding  U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes,  regarding  the  running  ashore  and 
firing  of  the  schooner  Bob  Boy  by  her  own  crew. 

U.  S.  S.  Stars  and  Stripes, 

St.  Marks  River ,  March  12,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  the  schooner  Fox  (a  tender  to 
this  vessel),  while  Ring  at  anchor  at  Deadman’s  Bay  on  the  2d  instant, 
discovered  a  strange  schooner  at  anchor  on  the  south  side  of  the  bay 
near  the  shore.  An  armed  boat  was  sent  to  attempt  her  capture,  from 
which  she  endeavored  to  escape;  but  unable  to  effect  this,  was  run  ashore 
and  tired  by  her  crew.  The  flames  spread  with  such  rapidity  and 
had  obtained  such  a  control  by  the  time  the  boat’s  crew  got  alongside 
that  it  was  found  impossible  to  extinguish  them.  She  proved  to  be 
the  Bob  Boy ,  of  Belize,  Honduras.  A  small  portion  of  the  cargo  was 
saved  in  a  damaged  condition.  The  saved  portion  consisted  of  a  lot 
of  cavalry  sabers  and  farming  and  mechanical  implements.  The  Bob 
Boy  was  of  about  60  tons  burden. 

The  articles  saved  will  be  sent  to  the  prize  court  at  Key  West  for 
adjudication.  I  enclose  herewith  a  complete  list  of  the  officers  and 
crew  entitled  to  share  in  the  above  capture. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  Sherrill, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Comma/nding . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Bear- Admiral  Stribling ,  IT.  S.  Navy ,  requesting 
additional  light-draft  vessels  with  heavy  batteries  for  the  protection 
of  the  blockade  of  St.  George's  Sound. 

No.  73.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  March  1.1,  1865. 

Sir:  The  rebels  have  for  a  long  time  been  rebuilding  a  vessel  at 
Columbus  and  plating  her  with  iron.  W e  have  recently  been  informed 
that  this  vessel  has  been  launched,  and  it  is  not  improbable  she  may, 
with  other  vessels  said  to  be  in  the  Chattahoochee,  attempt  to  raise  the 
blockade  of  St.  George’s  Sound.  We  are  sadly  deficient  in  vessels  of 
any  force  with  sufficient  light  draft  of  water  to  enter  St.  George’s  Sound 
or  to  occupy  the  position  now  held  by  us  near  the  light-house  at  St. 
Marks.  As  long  as  we  can  hold  this  position  it  is  almost  impossible  for 


826 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


a  vessel  to  pass  up  to  St.  Marks.  The  Somerset's  boilers  can  not  be  used, 
and  she  is  reported  to  be  otherwise  in  a  very  bad  condition.  I  have 
ordered  her  to  this  place  and  will  report  result  of  the  examination  of 
her  as  soon  as  made.  The  Fort  Henry  is  the  only  other  vessel  of  light 
draft  and  heavy  battery  fit  for  either  of  these  places.  The  Hendrick 
Hudson  and  Stars  and  Stripes  are  the  next  best.  The  Tallapoosa  and 
Mahaska  have  powerful  batteries,  but  are  too  long  to  be  managed  in 
the  narrow  and  tortuous  channels  of  St.  George’s  Sound  and  the 
entrance  to  St.  Marks.  Under  these  circumstances,  as  none  of  the 
vessels  recently  joined  the  squadron  have  heavy  batteries  and  light 
draft  of  water,  I  respectfully  request  that  three  or  four  vessels  of 
light  draft  and  heavy  batteries  may  lie  ordered  here  as  soon  as  prac¬ 
ticable.  The  Galena  would  be  the  most  efficient  I  know  of  for  the 
service.  Some  of  the  large  navy-built  gunboats  with  heavy  batteries 
would  be  the  next  best. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

.  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg .  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg .  East  Gulf  Rlockdg .  Squadron . 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  G.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Browne ,  II  S.  Navy,  command¬ 
ing  TJ.  S.  bark  Pursuit,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
Mary,  of  Alb aco,  Bahama  Islands. 


U.  S.  Bark  Pursuit, 

Off  Indian  River,  Florida,  March  18,  1865. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  British  schooner 
Mary,  of  Abaco,  Bahamas,  on  the  morning  of  the  16th  instant,  in  Indian 


828 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


River,  72  miles  to  the  northward  of  this  inlet.  The  captain  and  owner 
(David  Stone),  who  is  an  American,  with  a  crew  of  two  men  (both  British 
subjects),  states  that  he  cleared  from  Green  Turtle  Cay,  Bahamas,  on 
the  6th  instant,  for  Key  West,  Fla.,  and  was  forced  through  stress  of 
weather  to  run  into  Jupiter  Inlet,  45  miles  to  the  southward  of  this 
place  for  a  harbor,  consequently  the  distance  of  the  place  where  cap¬ 
tured  being  greater  from  the  port  cleared  for  than  where  he  put  in  for 
a  harbor,  leaves  no  doubt  of  his  character  and  intentions.  I  have  sent 
her,  with  captain  and  crew,  together  with  all  papers  and  cargo  (which 
last  consists  of  only  1  box  of  shoes,  1  barrel  of  rum,  and  1  box  of  sun¬ 
dries  containing  a  large  quantity  of  percussion  caps),  to  Key  West, 
Fla.,  for  adjudication. 

I  am  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

W.  R.  Browne, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Master  Russell ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  commanding  U.  S.  S. 

Honeysuckle,  regarding  the  capt  ure  of  sloop  Phantom. 

U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle, 

Cedar  Keys ,  Fla. ,  March  2%,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  2d  instant  at  8  p.  m., 
while  steaming  in  from  the  beacon  toward  the  bar  buoy,  a  light  was 
observed  in  the  direction  of  the  Suwanee  River.  I  at  once  dispatched 
Acting  Ensign  Charles  N.  Hall  and  Acting  Third  Assistant  Engineer 
Charles  E.  Taber  with  an  armed  boat  and  crew  to  that  vicinity. 

At  daybreak  on  the  morning  of  the  3d  instant,  at  about  3  miles  out¬ 
side  of  the  entrance  to  the  Suwanee  River,  Mr.  Hall  overhauled  and 
captured  the  sloop  Phantom,  Piento  Peso,  master,  from  Port  Mariel, 
Cuba,  bound  up  the  Suwanee  River.  The  sloop  is  about  20  tons 
capacity,  has  no  papers  or  flag,  and  is  loaded  with  about  3,000  pounds 
of  bar  iron  and  a  quantity  of  liquors.  There  were  three  men  (master 
included)  captured  on  board.  They  freely  admit  that  they  were  en¬ 
deavoring  to  violate  the  blockade.  There  were  no  vessels  in  sight  at 
the  time  of  capture.  The  prisoners  I  sent  to  Key  West  on  the  U.  S.  S. 
Honduras. 

During  a  severe  gale  on  the  night  of  March  9  the  sloop  was  driven 
ashore  on  Sea  Horse  Key.  After  removing  the  cargo  I  have  succeeded 
in  getting  her  afloat. 

The  liquors  I  have  sent  to  Key  West  in  the  prize  schooner  Sort  and 
have  replaced  the  rest  of  the  cargo.  I  send  the  sloop  to  Key  West  for 
adjudication  in  charge  of  Acting  Master  and  Pilot  Nathaniel  Thrift. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

James  J.  Russell, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Honeysuckle. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
division  of  his  command  for  better  service. 

-N°*  95.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  March  27,  1865. 

.  SlR:  Referring  to  that  part  of  my  letter  No.  41,  relating  to  the  divi¬ 
sion  of  the  vessels  of  the  blockade,  the  closing  of  the  ports  of  Charles¬ 
ton  and  Wilmington  renders  it  certain  that  the  rebels  will  make  greater 
exertions  than  heretofore  to  run  vessels  into  the  many  small  rivers  and 
shallow  bays  on  this  coast,  and  make  it  more  important  to  keep  a  vigi¬ 
lant  lookout  for  blockade  runners  and  to  guard  well  the  I  dockaded  ports. 
As  a  means  of  doing  this  I  have  divided  the  vessels  on  the  blockade  and 
cruising  on  the  coast  into  two  divisions.  The  first  division  is  composed 
of  the  vessels  from  St.  Andrew’s  to  St.  Marks,  both  inclusive,  and  com¬ 
manded  by  Lieutenant-Commander  Gibson,  of  the  Mahaska.  The  sec¬ 
ond,  all  the  vessels  from  St.  Marks  to  Charlotte  Harbor,  the  latter 
included,  and  commanded  by  Lieutenant-Commander  De  Haven,  of  the 
Tcdlapoosa.  .  These  officers  have  the  general  supervision  of  the  vessels 
within  the  limits  prescribed,  and  can  upon  an  emergency  act  without 
waiting  for  order's.  When  each  officer  on  the  blockade  acted  independ¬ 
ently,  it  was  frequently  weeks  before  I  could  receive  their  reports  and 
give  the  necessary  orders  in  matters  requiring  prompt  action. 

1  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Bl-ockdg.  /Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Report  of  Acting.  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  IT.  S.  Navy ,  regarding 
injuries  to  the  JJ.  S.  S.  Fort  Henry. 

No.  100.]  Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  April  1,  1865. 

Sir:  I  expect  to  leave  this  place  to-day  to  visit  and  inspect  the  ves¬ 
sels  at  all  the  blockaded  places  except  Indian  River,  and  shall  be 
absent  from  Key  West  eight  or  ten  days. 

I  have  a  report  that  the  Fort  Henry  grounded  on  her  anchor  and 
filled  with  water.  Everything  was  taken  out  of  her,  and  she  is  again 
afloat,  but  I  have  not  been  informed  whether  she  can  be  kept  on  the 
blockade  without  being  docked. 

If  the  Fort  Henry  has  to  be  withdrawn  from  the  blockade  at  St. 
Marks  or  St.  George’s  Sound  it  will  make  us  still  more  deficient  in 
suitable  vessels  for  the  blockade  of  those  places  referred  to  in  my 
No.  73  of  the  11th  ultimo. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C.
