Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant- Commander  Randall ,  U.  S. 

Nary,  announcing  his  arrival  at  New  York  with  the  prize  steamer 

Ruby. 

Prize  Steamer  Ruby, 

New  York ,  Ap>ril  Ilf,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  of  the  prize  steamer 
Ruby ,  which  left  Key  West  on  the  26th  ultimo.  On  the  2d  instant 
we  encountered,  when  off  Frying  Pan  Shoals,  a  hard  gale  from  the 
northeast,  during  which  the  vessel  sustained  such  injuries  as  to  make 
it  necessary  to  go  into  Beaufort  for  repairs.  She  commenced  break¬ 
ing  in  two  amidships,  one  of  the  iron  plates  on  the  port  side  breaking 
open  for  about  2  feet  6  inches.  I  have  forwarded  to  the  Bureau  of 
Equipment  and  Recruiting-  a  correct  list  of  the  officers  and  crew 
attached  to  this  vessel.  I  also  forward  to  you  a  copy  of  my  orders 
received  from  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling. 

I  have  the  honor  to  remain,  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  P.  Randall, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant-  Commander ,  TJ.  A.  Navy , 

New  Bedford ,  Mass. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  an 
inspection  of  the  vessels  on  the  blockade. 

No.  104.]  Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  April, If  1865. 

Sir:  I  returned  yesterday  in  the  Magnolia  from  an  inspection  of  the 
vessels  on  the  blockade.  On  Saturday  last  I  spent  a  few  hours  at  the 
Pensacola  navy  yard.  On  my  return  here  I  found  that  the  Proteus 
and  Luka  had  returned  from  a  cruise,  and  the  Sagamore ,  from  Phila¬ 
delphia,  and  the  Aries,  from  Norfolk,  had  arrived.  1  did  not  find  the 
vessels  generally  in  as  good  condition  as  I  expected.  The  report  of 
the  inspection  will  be  forwarded  to  the  Bureau  of  Ordnance,  as  required 
by  general  order  of  the  Nav}r  Department  dated  April  5,  1861. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral  Corndg.  Bast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Martine ,  U  S.  Navy ,  com¬ 
manding  U.  S.  S.  Hibiscus ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  Confederate 
sloops  Florida  and  Annie ,  off  Crystal  River. 

U.  S.  S.  Hibiscus, 

Cedar  Keys ,  April  16 ,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  rebel  sloop  boat 
Florida ,  with  5  persons  on  board  and  a  cargo  of  cotton,  also  the 
rebel  sloop  boat  Annie ,  with  2  persons  on  board  and  a  quantity  of 
loose  cotton.  These  captures  were  made  on  the  morning  of  the  11th 
of  April,  oft  Crystal  River,  b}r  the  U.  S.  schooner  Sea  Bird ,  tender  to 
this  vessel,  Acting  Master  E.  L.  Robbins  in  command.  Both  vessels, 
in  my  opinion,  being  unfit  to  send  to  Key  West,  I  have  taken  every¬ 
thing  of  value  on  board  this  vessel  and  destroyed  the  vessels  and  will 
send  their  cargoes  and  the  prisoners  to  Key  West  by  first  opportunity. 
Enclosed  please  find  list  of  the  names  of  all  the  persons  attached  to  this 
vessel  at  the  time  of  the  capture. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Wm.  L.  Martine, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding. 
Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 

U.  S.  schooner  J.  L.  Davis. 

No.  114.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gule^  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  April  <21,  1865. 

Sir:  In  consequence  of  the  extensive  repairs  required,  I  have  ordered 
the  James  L.  Davis  to  Philadelphia.  I  have  sent  to  the  Bureau  of 
Construction  and  Repairs  report  of  survey  upon  this  vessel. 

The  J.  L.  Davis  is  a  sailing  vessel  and  not  calculated  for  the  Navy 
except  upon  such  service  as  we  had  in  keeping  up  the  blockade  of  the 
coast. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Utter  from  the U. \  S. .  consul  at  Nassau,  New  Providence,  to  Acting 
Heat -Admiral  Stnblmg,  XL  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  seizure  of  the 
American  schooner  St.  Mary's  by  party  commanded  by  John  O.  Braine. 


U.  S.  Consulate, 

Nassau,  [New  Providence ],  April  %°2,  1865. 

Dear  Sir:  Since  I  wrote  you  a  few  days  since  there  has  arrived  at 
this  port  the  American  schooner  St.  Mary’s,  of  Baltimore,  with  full 
cargo,  captured  from  her  master  by  10  persons  coming  alongside  of 
her  m  Chesapeake  Bay  about  1  o'clock  on  the  morning  of  April  1 
lb65,  saying  they  were  American  soldiers  crossing  from  Barren  Island 
to  1  oint  Lookout;  they  were  taken  on  board  and  immediately  seized 
the  vessel.  A  few  days  afterwards  they  boarded  a  schooner  loaded 
v  ith  w  ood,  put  the  master  and  part  of  the  crew  and  3  passengers  on 
board  the  schooner  bound  to  New  York,  bringing  two  of  the  crew  of 
the  captured  vessel  here  with  them.  I  immediately  applied  to  the 
government  here  to  have  the  vessel  seized,  with  her  piratical  crew. 
1  hey  declined,  saying  she  was  a  legitimate  prize,  and  she  put  to  sea 
again,  having  put  in  here  under  the  plea  of  distress.  She  is  com¬ 
manded  and  was  seized  by  a  gang  headed  by  the  notorious  John  C. 
Biaine,  of  steamers  C  liGSG^jfscLke  and  Roo.'ixokc  notoriety.  It  is  supposed 
here  that  he  has  gone  to  Spanish  Wells  or  Harbour  Islands  to  get 
H.  A.  Paw,  who  is  there  and  who  is  one  of  them;  both  this  man 
Braine  and  Paw  I  made  a  requisition  upon  the  government  here  for,  on 
the  charge  of  piracy  and  murder  on  board  the  Chesapeake.  I  trust  you 
may  be  able  to  procure  this  man’s  capture,  that  an  end  may  be  put  to 
his  career  of  guilt.  I  he  name  of  the  schooner  has  been  erased.  It  is 
rumored  that  guns  were  put  on  board  of  her  here,  but  I  have  not  been 
able  to  ascertain  clearly  whether  it  is  true.  He  will  undoubtedly 
endeavor  to  get  rid  of  his  cargo. 

Yours,  in  haste, 

Thomas  Kirkpatrick. 

Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling. 


Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  commanding  off  cers  of  blockading 
squadrons,  enjoining  vigilance  m  preventing  the  escape  of  President 
Davis  and  his  Cabinet. 

Navy  Department,  April  28,  1865. 
Sir:  Lieutenant-General  Grant  telegraphs  to  the  War  Department, 
under  date  of  the  26th  instant,  from  Raleigh,  N.  C.,  that  Jeff  Davis 
with  his  Cabinet  passed  into  South  Carolina,  with  the’  intention,  no 
doubt,  of  getting  out  of  the  country,  either  via  Cuba  or  across  the 
Mississippi.  All  the  vigilance  and  available  means  at  your  command 
should  be  brought  to  bear  to  prevent  the  escape  of  the  leaders  of  the 
rebellion. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

G.  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  II.  K.  Thatcher, 

Commanding  West  Gulf  Squadron,  New  Orleans,  La.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling , 

U.  S.  Navy ,  enjoining  vigilance  regarding  the  C.  S.  ram  Stonewall. 

Navy  Department,  April  38,  1865. 

Sir:  Information  has  been  received  from  the  U.  S.  consul  at  Tene- 
riffe  to  the  effect  that  the  rebel  ram  Stonewall  left  that  place,  where 
she  obtained  a  supply  of  coal,  April  1  at  6  p.  m.  and  steamed  away 
rapidly  to  the  south.  Her  destination  is  believed  to  be  some  point  on 
our  coast,  and  every  precaution  should  be  taken  by  you  to  guard  against 
surprise  and  to  prevent  her  inflicting  serious  injury  should  she  make 
her  appearance  an37where  within  the  limits  of  your  command,  and  the 
best  means  in  }’our  power  used  to  capture  or  destroy  her. 

Very  respectfully, 

G.  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Comdg.  Eastern  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron,  Key  West,  Fla. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding 
condition  of  the  TJ.  S.  bark  Pursuit. 

No.  120.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  April  39,  1865. 

Sir:  The  Pursuit  requiring  repairs*  that  would  take  three  months 
to  complete  here,  I  have  ordered  her  to  New  York.  I  have  forwarded 
to  the  Chief  of  the  Bureau  of  Construction,  etc.,  report  of  survey 
upon  this  vessel.  The  Pursuit  is  a  good  vessel,  and,  the  repairs  being 
made,  she  would  be  serviceable  for  some  time;  but  I  do  not  consider 
her  fit  for  naval  purposes,  except  for  such  temporary  duty  as  she  has 
been  employed  upon. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron.

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding 
measures  for  the  capture  of  President  Davis  and  Cabinet. 

No.  130.]  IIdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  May  3,  1865. 

Sir:  On  the  evening  of  the  1st  instant  an  aid  of  General  Sherman 
arrived  here  with  information  that  Jefferson  Davis  and  Cabinet,  with 
considerable  treasure,  passed  Charlotte,  N.  C.,  on  the  23d  ultimo, 
escorted  by  a  large  cavalry  force,  and  that  it  was  supposed  they  would 
attempt  to  make  their  escape  from  the  coast  of  east  or  west  Florida. 
To-day  I  received  a  dispatch  from  Admiral  Dahlgren  giving  me  the 
same  information.  1  dispatched  a  vessel  to  the  west  coast  }'esterday 
morning  to  give  the  information  and  ordered  all  fishing  and  other 
boats  from  this  place  to  return  immediately  to  Key  West.  The  ves¬ 
sels  at  the  blockaded  ports  will  remain  at  their  stations  and  all  cruis¬ 
ing  vessels  have  been  ordered  to  guard  with  vigilance  the  coast,  and,  if 
possible,  prevent  the  escape  of  the  rebels.  I  also  sent  off  yesterday 
two  boat  expeditions  to  cruise  inside  the  reef  and  amongst  the  ke}Ts  to 
Cape  Florida. 

I  have  to-da}^  ordered  an  expedition  under  Commander  Cooper  to 
take  possession  of  Key  Biscayne  and  to  guard  the  passage  to  the  Gulf 
from  it  and  Bear’s  Cut  to  the  eastward  of  the  key.  It  is  not  improba¬ 
ble  the  rebels  may  attempt  to  leave  the  United  States  by  one  of  these 
inlets,  as  there  is  a  land  route  to  Fort  Dallas,  at  the  mouth  of  the 
Miami  River.  All  that  region  of  Florida  is  well  known  by  Mr.  Mal¬ 
lory.  1  think  we  shall  be  able  to  prevent  their  escape  from  any  place 
they  can  reach  in  this  vicinity.  The  west  coast  will  be  more  difficult 
to  guard,  from  its  great  extent.  Admiral  Dahlgren  has  sent  a  num¬ 
ber  of  vessels  along  the  east  coast,  and  I  have  requested  him  (he 
offered  to  do  so)  to  guard  the  coast  from  Key  Biscayne,  as  we  had 
not  vessels  enough  to  do  it  and  guard  other  parts  of  the  coast. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  G%df  Blockdg,  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

[Enclosures.] 

U.  S.  Consulate, 

Nassau ,  [ New  Providence\,  April  17,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  enclose  to  you  a  letter  from  the  colonial 
secietaiy  ot  the  Bahamas,  with  copies  of  letters  and  correspondence 
in  leg  aid  to  visits  of  United  States  ships  of  war  at  Inagua,  which  the 
governor  desires  should  be  laid  before  you  with  a  view  to  a  stop  being 
put  upon  these  irregularities  on  the  part  of  our  commanders.  The  con¬ 
struction  which  the  governor  puts  upon  that  proclamation,  “that  he 
can  only  give  permission  to  anchor  in  case  of  deep  distress,”  is,  in  my 
judgment,  neither  its  true  intent  nor  meaning.  It  says  “  they  shall  not 
anchor,  etc.,  in  the  harbor  of  Nassau  or  in  any  roadstead  of  the 
Bahamas,  etc-.,  without  the  permission  of  the  governor,  etc.,”  or  “in 
case  of  distress,  etc.,”  but  his  construction  would  render  it  impossible 
even  to  find  out  that  they  are  in  distress,  by  refusing  to  let  them  send 
a  boat  on  shore  to  report  the  fact  His  predecessor  did  not  so  construe 
it;  he  in  almost  every  case  when  permission  was  asked  to  anchor  for 
a  short  period  granted  the  request,  and  the  local  authorities  at  the  out 
islands  were  delegated  with  authority  to  grant  permission  there.  Now 
it  seems  they  are  to  be  shutoff  from  communicating  with  the  shore  or 
the  consuls  of  their  governments  in  any  case,  except  such  cases  of 
distress  as  may  appear  such  from  conjecture,  not  from  enquiry  on  the 
part  of  the  governor. 

I  submit  the  papers  enclosed  to  you,  knowing  that  you  will  do  what 
you  believe  to  be  right  in  the  premises  and  give  your  orders 
accordingly. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  Kirkpatrick. 

Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Commanding  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron,  Key  West.

No.  2.] 


Mathew  Town, 
Inagua ,  March  25,  1865. 


Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  for  the  information  of  his 
excellency  the  governor  that  the  U.  S.  S.  Nereus ,  Commander  How¬ 
ell,  anchored  in  this  roadstead  on  the  19th  March,  instant. 

In  less  than  twenty  minutes  after  I  received  a  letter,  a  copy  of  which 
is  annexed,  addressed  to  me  from  the  commander,  which  I  had  scarcely 
read  when  two  of  the  officers  called  on  me  and  stated  that  they  [were] 
desired  by  him  to  express  regret  at  his  inability  to  pay  his  respects 
personally,  as  he  had  been  for  some  time  unwell,  and  to  ask  if  there  was 
any  harm  to  remain  at  anchor  for  a  few  hours.  I  replied  “Harm! 
The  Queen’s  proclamation  should  be  respected,  gentlemen.  I  have  no 
authority  to  sanction  her  anchoring  here  any  time.” 

Whether  it  was  the  result  of  this  answer  or  no  I  am  unable  to  say, 
but  in  less  than  half  hour  after  the  officers  were  on  board  and  the  ves¬ 
sel  steaming  off,  having  been  less  than  one  hour  in  port. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  etc. , 


W.  H.  PlNDER, 

Acting  Resident  Justice. 


Hon.  Charles  R.  Nesbit, 

Colonial  Secretary.

No.  154.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron,

lachicola,  1  have  to  request  that  you  will  inform  me  if  it  will  make  anj^

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Voorhees ,  II.  S.  Navy ,  com¬ 
manding  U.  S.  S.  Isonomia ,  regarding  the  capture  of  the  British 
bark  George  Douthwaite. 

U.  S.  S.  Isonomia, 

Egmont  Key ,  Tampa  Bay ,  Fla.,  May  10,  1865. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  capture  of  the  English  bark 
George  Douthwaite,  of  South  Shields,  England,  Captain  George  Davis, 
on  the  8th  instant,  off  the  Warrior  River,  west  coast  of  Florida,  loaded 
with  sugar,  rum,  wool,  ginger,  and  mahogany,  from  Jamaica,  West 
Indies,  twenty -two  da}^s  out,  under  the  following  circumstances:  On 
the  morning*  of  the  8th  instant,  while  cruising  under  slow  speed  be- 
tween  the  rivers  Steinhatchee  and  Aucilla,  at  about  6  a.  m.,  sighted  a 
strange  sail  bearing  N.  N.  W.  by  compass,  heading  N.  by  W.  £  W., 
undei  foie  and  aft  sails,  with  the  square  sails  clewed  up.  MTe  were 
steeling  N.  \\  .  by  compass  in  3^  fathoms  of  water,  land  in  full  view; 
gave  chase,  and  at  7  a.  m.  beat  to  general  quarters  and  fired  a  blank 
cartridge  from  30-pounder  Parrott,  being  then  about  2  miles  distant 
from  the  chased  vessel,  which  was  heading  for  the  land,  but  hauled 
head  offshore  soon  after  and  set  the  foresail  and  foretopsail.  At  7:30 
a.  m.  passed  under  his  stern  and  found  her  in  15  feet  of  water;  sent 
the  executive  officer  and  armed  boat’s  crew  on  board  to  take  charge, 
and  to  send  the  captain  with  his  papers  on  board  this  vessel.  She  had 
one  boat  in  the  water  alongside  and  the  launch  hoisted  out  and  hanging 
by  the  yard  tackles  ready  for  lowering,  with  no  colors  hoisted, &but 
having  the  English  ensign  on  a  ratlin  on  th.e  starboard  mizzen  rigging 
after  I  had  asked  where  his  flag  was. 

o 


EAST  GTTLE  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


843 


I  hailed  him  twice  to  heave  to  and  shorten  sail,  but  he  did  not  until 
our  men  had  got  on  deck  and  ordered  them  to  shorten  sail  and  began 
to  do  so  themselves.  When  I  asked  him  what  he  was  doing  inside  the 
blockade,  the  captain  said  he  was  bound  for  London  and  had  grounded 
at  4  a.  m.  that  morning,  and  that  he  did  not  know  where  he  was  or 
how  he  got  there.  At  8  a.  m.  it  came  on  stormy,  and  an  S.  S.  W.  gale 
setting  in  I  sent  the  captain  on  board,  and  ordered  the  prize  master  to 
make  sail  and  follow  me,  1  then  ran  for  St.  Marks  for  a  harbor  of 
safety  for  this  vessel  and  the  prize,  where  we  anchored  at  meridian  in 
19  feet  of  water,  and  the  prize  anchored  soon  after  near  this  vessel. 
On  the  morning  of  the  9th  instant,  being  short  of  coal  and  being  fine 
weather,  at  5  a.  m.  I  took  the  prize  in  tow  and  started  for  Tampa  Bay 
with  prize  master  and  two  men  on  board  in  charge  of  prize,  and  safely 
anchored  her  in  this  bay.  At  8  a.  m.  the  wind  was  S.  S.  E.  and  S.  W. 
swell  setting  in,  the  men  were  employed  in  unbending  and  repairing 
sails  and  otherwise  putting  the  vessel  in  order  to  proceed  to  Key  West 
with  the  first  slant  of  wind.  I  send  all  the  officers  and  men  to  Key 
West  in  the  vessel,  12  in  number.  I  am  informed  that  the  second  officer 
of  the  prize  is  acquainted  on  this  coast  and  has  sailed  from  St.  George’s 
Sound  before  the  war.  The  captain  asked  one  of  our  men  when  they 
boarded  the  vessel  where  the  river  Steinhatchee  was.  One  of  the  crew 
has  sailed  out  of  Apalachicola  since  the  war,  as  he  told  two  of  our  men 
that  he  knew  me  when  I  was  on  board  the  Port  Royal ,  blockading  Apa¬ 
lachicola.  I  send  Acting  Master  James  F.  Alcorn  and  5  men  in  charge 
of  the  prize,  and  Acting  Master  [and]  Pilot  N.  Thrift  from  the  U.  S.  S. 
Honeysuckle  to  pilot  the  vessel  to  Key  W7  est. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

L.  D.  D.  Voorhees, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant ,  Commanding  U.  S.  S.  Isonomia. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  I).  C. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  requesting 
vessels  in  place  of  the  IT.  S.  steamers  Fort  Henry  and  Somerset  in  view 
of  the  destruction  of  Confederate  vessels  at  Columbus ,  Ga. 

No.  158.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  May  11,  1865. 

Sir:  The  destruction  of  the  rebel  ram  and  ironclads  so  long  pre¬ 
paring  at  Columbus,  Ga.,  to  oppose  which  we  have  had  the  Fort  Henry 
and  Somerset  stationed  off  Apalachicola,  renders  these  vessels  useless 
for  that  purpose.  These  vessels  were  originally  New  York  ferryboats, 
and  are  only  fit  for  such  service  as  that  upon  which  they  have  been 
employed.  I  would  respectfully  request  two  small  steamers  to  be 
sent  here  to  replace  them,  as  they  both  require  extensive  repairs.  I 
would  send  them  north  at  once,  but  at  present  their  services  can  not 
be  dispensed  with  without  weakening  the  blockade  where  it  is  most 
important  to  have  it  effective. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  veiy  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Str idling,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
movements  of  the  G.  S.  ram  Stonewall. 

No.  159.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  May  1%,  1865. 

Sir:  I  have  a  dispatch  this  morning  from  the  consul-general  at 
Havana  informing  me  that  the  Stonewall  arrived  there  yesterday 
morning  and  that  it  was  reported  that  she  would  leave  to-day  for  Gal¬ 
veston.  It  is  difficult  to  say  what  would  he  the  result  if  she  comes 
here  unless  the  fort  could  stop  her.  I  fear  we  could  not  successfully 
resist  her. 

The  Powhatan  and  Aries  are  the  only  vessels  in  port  and  unless  we 
could  board  her  and  overpower  her  crew,  we  could  hardly  succeed  in 
capturing  this  vessel,  if  she  is  so  powerful  as  represented.  You  may 
depend  upon  our  doing  our  best  to  destroy  her  if  she  comes  here. 

The  consul-general  also  informs  me  that  telegraphic  dispatches 
report  the  arrival  of  Jeff.  Davis  and  others  at  Matanzas  on  the  10th 
instant  in  the  steamer  Imogene ,  from  Galveston.  They  could  not  have 
come  in  the  vessel  from  Galveston,  as  there  has  not  been  sufficient  time 
for  Davis  to  have  gone  from  Charlotte,  [N.  C.],  on  the  24th  ultimo  to 
that  place  and  have  gone  to  Matanzas,  as  only  sixteen  days  elapsed. 
If  they  are  at  Matanzas  they  must  have  been  taken  on "  board  the 
Imogene  from  some  place  on  the  Florida  Reef. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.

Surrender  *  of  the  G.  S.  ram  Stonewall ,  at  Havana ,  Cuba ,  May  19, 1865. 

Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  copy  of  letter  to  the 

U.  S.  consul-general  at  Havana. 

No.  164.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  May  16,  1865. 

Sir:  Having  some  reason  to  suppose  that  there  was  a  disposition  on 
the  part  of  the  commander  of  the  rebel  vessel  Stonewall  to  surrender 
her  to  the  United  States,  I  yesterday  addressed  a  letter  to  the  consul- 
general  at  Havana,  of  which  the  enclosed  is  a  copy.  As  my  letter  to 
the  consul-general  explains  my  object,  it  is  useless  for  me  to  remark 


*See  also  Series  I,  volume  3. 


846 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


upon  it.  At  the  same  time  I  gave  Commander  Werden  instructions 
in  relation  to  the  surrender,  etc.,  if  it  should  be  offered. 

Some  days  since  I  observed  in  the  newspapers  that  a  proclamation 
would  soon  be  issued  by  the  President  by  which  the  rights  of  bellig¬ 
erents,  heretofore  conceded  to  rebel  cruisers,  would  be  withdrawn,  and 
to-day  I  observed  the  correspondent  of  the  New  York  Herald,  dated 
Washington,  May  the  9th,  gives  a  synopsis  of  the  proclamation. 

If  I  had  received  this  information  (though  not  official)  before  making 
the  offer  I  did  yesterday,  I  should  not  have  done  so;  but  having  made 
it  in  good  faith,  I  believe  the  Department  will  approve  the  course  I 
have  taken,  if  the  surrender  is  made  by  the  rebel  officers.  Under  this 
belief  I  shall  await  the  result  of  my  offer  and  trust  to  the  Department’s 
approval. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Hear- Admiral,  Comdg.  Hast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington ,  D.  C. 

[Enclosure.] 

Headquarters  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  May  15,  1865. 

Sir:  If  the  officers  of  the  Stonewall  are  sensible  men  they  must  be 
aware  of  the  desperate  state  of  the  rebel  cause  and  may  be  disposed 
to  surrender  the  vessel  if  the  officers  and  crew  can  be  paroled  on  the 
same  terms  that  Lee  and  others  surrendered  their  armies.  You  will, 
therefore,  in  such  manner  as  you  may  think  best,  let  it  be  known  that 
upon  the  surrender  of  the  Stonewall  to  Commander  Werden,  com¬ 
manding  the  Powhatan,  and  fleet  captain  (who  is  authorized  to  receive 
the  surrender),  with  her  armament  and  all  public  property,  the  officers 
and  crew  will  be  paroled  on  the  same  terms  as  were  granted  to  Gen¬ 
eral  Lee  and  his  army — the  officers  to  retain  their  side  arms  and 
officers  and  men  to  retain  their  private  effects.  And  to  put  them  on 
an  equality  with  Lee’s  army,  I  will  send  them  to  such  port  as  may  be 
agreed  upon. 

There  may  be  some  rebel  navy  officers  at  Havana  not  belonging  to 
the  Stonewall,  and  as  they  may  have  influence,  or  even  control,  over 
her  commander,  they  will,  if  they  desire  it,  be  included  in  the  agree¬ 
ment  and  have  the  same  privilege  of  retaining  personal  effects  and 
being  landed  at  the  same  place  as  the  officers  and  crew  of  the  Stonewall. 

It  is  needless  for  me  to  say  anything  further,  as  it  must  be  evident 
to  the  commander  of  the  Stonewall  that  he  can  not  hope  to  make  cap¬ 
tures  and  carry  them  into  any  port  for  their  benefit.  If  they  can  not 
do  this  there  is  no  other  means  of  support,  and  whatever  means  they 
may  now  have  will  soon  be  exhausted.  If  they  surrender  now,  what¬ 
ever  private  means  they  have  will  be  saved. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  K.  Stribling, 

Acting  Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blkdg.  Squadron. 

Wm.  T.  Miner,  Esq., 

TJ.  S.  Consul-General,  Havana,

Rep°rt  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  transmitting  correspondence  with 
the  Captain-General  of  Cuba  regarding  the  status  of  the  C.  S.  ram  Stonewall. 


No.  161.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West ,  Fla. ,  May  15 ,  1865. 

UP<»  bearing  of  the  arrival  of  the  Stonewall  at  Havana,  Gen¬ 
eral  Newton  and  myself  addressed  a  note  to  the  captain-general  of 
Luba,  hoping  m-tt  such  a  communication  might  induce  him  to  recon- 
sider  the  decision  in  considering  rebel  vessels  entitled  to  the  privileges 
or  belligerents.  1  he  surrender  of  the  great  armies  and  the  flight  of 
Hat  is,  we  argued,  pi’oved  the  rebellion  to  have  no  further  existence, 
as  there  was  no  longer  any  organized  military  force  to  support  it.  I 
enclose  copies  of  the  note  to  the  captain-general  and  his  answer. 

Commander  Werden  proceeded  to  Havana  in  the  Powhatan ,  on  the 
13th  instant,  and  had  a  personal  interview  with  the  captain -general. 

t  he  Powhatan  and  Aries  are  the  only  vessels  of  any  force  I  have 
here.  They  will  be  stationed  off  Havana,  at  sea,  out  of  Spanish  juris¬ 
diction,  to  watch  the  Stonewall  and  try  to  keep  her  in  port,  and  as 
soon  as  the  Tallapoosa  and  Mahaska  join  them  Commander  Werden 
will  be  directed  to  attack  the  Stonewall  if  she  goes  to  sea.  The  Tal¬ 
lapoosa  and  Mahaska  are  now  cruising  on  the  coast,  and  it  may  be  two 
or  three  days  before  they  can  get  my  orders  and  return  to  this  place. 
It  is  my  intention,  at  present,  to  watch  the  movements  of  the  Stone¬ 
wall  as  long  as  she  remains  at  Havana. 

I  do  not  consider  that  this  will  be  any  violation  of  neutrality,  as  the 
vessels  will  be  cruising  on  the  high  seas.  If  I  err  in  this,  I  beg  to  be 
informed  without  delay. 

The  Department  will  have  been  informed  of  the  arrival  of  the 
Stonewall  and  have,  I  hope,  sent  the  necessary  reinforcements  here  to 
enable  me  to  capture  or  destroy  this  vessel.  Two  or  three  heavy 
vessels,  with  good  speed,  will  be  sufficient.  I  would  suggest  a  heavy 
sloop  of  war  and  two  of  the  largest  double-enders,  if  no  ironclads  or 
monitors  are  available.  The  vessels  I  have  at  present  here  will  not 
be  sufficient  to  watch  and  attack  the  Stonewall  if  she  comes  out,  as 
some  of  them  will  have  to  be  withdrawn  from  time  to  time  for  sup¬ 
plies.  The  Powhatan ,  Tallapoosa ,  and  Mahaska  are  the  only  vessels 
on  the  station  sufficiently  strong  to  run  her  down,  and  in  the  absence 
of  either  of  them  I  do  not  think  it  would  be  proper  to  attack  her. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  etc. , 


C.  K.  Stribling, 

Actg.  Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  Fast  Gulf  Blockdg.  Squadron. 


Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Headquarters  U.  S.  Forces,  Naval  and  Military, 

Key  West ,  Fla.,  May  12,  1865. 

Sir:  We  have  understood  that  the  ram  Stonewall  has  arrived  in  the 
port  of  Havana. 

The  rebel  armies  under  Lee,  Johnston,  and  Taylor — in  fine,  all  their 
troops  east  of  the  Mississippi — have  surrendered. 

The  Stonewall  can  not  cruise  except  under  a  piratical  flag,  because 
the  Confederate  Government  has  no  representation,  civil  or  military, 
in  this  country.

If,  therefore,  this  vessel  is  allowed  to  proceed  to  sea,  the  Spanish 
Government  must  account  for  tolerating  piracy. 

This  dispatch  will  be  delivered  to  you  by  Commander  Reed  Wer- 
den,  fleet  captain  of  the  East  Gulf  Squadron. 

We  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  excellency’s  most  obedient  servants, 

C.  K.  Stribling,

[Translation.] 

Office  of  the  Superior  Civil  Government 

of  the  Ever  Faithful,  Island  of  Cuba, 

Havana ,  May  13 , 1865. 

Excellent  Sir:  I  have  received  a  communication  signed  by  your 
excellency  and  Mr.  John  Newton,  brigadier-general  of  the  United 
States  Army,  commanding  the  district  of  Key  West  and  Tortugas,  in 
which  you  state  that  in  consequence  of  the  arrival  in  this  port  of  the 
ram  Stonewall ,  that  if  this  vessel  is  permitted  to  proceed  to  sea  that 
the  Spanish  Government  will  beheld  responsible  for  tolerating  piracy, 
as  the  Confederate  Government  has  no  representative,  either  civil  or 
military. 

Through  the  newspapers  of  the  United  States  I  have  learned  that 
the  Confederate  troops  commanded  by  General  Lee  and  others  have 
surrendered.  But  having  no  new  instructions  from  my  Government, 
I  have  to  confine  myself  to  those  in  existence,  which  date  from  June 
and  December,  1861,  in  which  I  am  directed  to  observe  the  strictest 
neutrality  in  the  contest  between  the  Federal  States  of  the  Union  and 
the  Confederate  States  of  the  South. 

This  neutrality  has  never  been  infringed  since  that  period,  and  I 
will  continue  to  observe  it  until  new  orders  to  the  contrary  are 
received;  and  your  excellencies  will  permit  me  to  say  that  such  com¬ 
munications,  of  the  class  to  which  I  reply,  are  only  proper  and 
permitted  from  one  nation  to  another  through  its  legitimate  represent¬ 
atives  ad  hoc,  which  neither  of  your  excellencies  nor  myself  is. 

The  ram  Stonewall  entered  this  port  on  the  11th  instant  with  damage 
to  her  steam  machinery,  which  is  now  being  repaired.  As  soon  as  she 
is  ready  I  will  cause  her  to  leave  this  port,  under  the  conditions  pre¬ 
scribed  in  the  royal  decree  of  my  Government,  dated  17th  June,  1861, 
unless  some  unforeseen  occurrence  should  give  occasion  for  longer 
detention,  of  which  I  will  inform  your  excellencies. 

I  am  desirous  that  the  good  relations  existing  between  my  Govern¬ 
ment  and  that  of  the  United  States  should  continue,  and  I  am  satisfied 
that  I  will  not  be  the  cause  of  any  interruption  of  the  same,  as  the 
Government  of  the  Union  will  understand  by  the  just  explanation 
contained  in  this  communication. 

God  preserve  your  excellencies  many  years. 

Domingo  Dulce. 

His  excellency  Mr.  Stribling, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  East  Gulf  U.  S.  Squadron.

Havana,  May  19,  1865. 

Excellent  Sir:  On  the  13th  of  the  present  month  I  had  the  honor 
to  reply  to  a  communication  signed  by  your  Excellency  and  by  Briga¬ 
dier-General  Newton,  of  the  Army  of  the  United  States,  commanding 
the  Department  of  Key  West  and  Tortugas,  with  reference  to  the 
arrival  of  the  ram  Stonewall. 

Since  that  period  I  have  been  endeavoring  to  prevent,  in  a  manner 
consistent  with  dignity,  decorum,  and  humanity,  and  with  due  respect 
to  the  good  understanding  which  my  Government  wishes  to  preserve 
toward  the  United  States,  the  unnecessary  shedding  of  any  more  pre¬ 
cious  blood  between  two  kindred  people  as  are  the  North  and  the  South, 
which  constitute  the  United  States. 

To-day  I  have  the  satisfaction  of  having  obtained  that  the  Stonewall 
cease  to  be  one  of  the  vessels  of  war  of  the  enemies  of  the  United 
States. 

This  morning  the  commander,  Mr.  Thomas  J .  Page,  has  surrendered 
for  safe-keeping,  and  subject  to  the  disposal  of  the  Queen  of  Spain,  the 
said  steamer  lately  under  his  command. 

I  will  communicate  this  success  to  my  Government  b}r  the  first  mail 
and  ask  for  instructions  in  reference  thereto. 

All  the  crew  has  been  discharged  and  the  Stonewall  remains  in  the 
custody  of  the  navy  of  her  Catholic  Majesty. 

The  commander  of  the  ram  would  not  adopt  any  other  course,  but, 
notwithstanding,  this  vessel,  once  an  enemy  of  the  United  States,  has 
ceased  to  be  so. 

God  preserve  your  Excellency  many  years. 

Domo  Dulce. 

His  Excellency  Mr.  Stribling, 

Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  U.  S.  East  Gulf  Blkdg.  Squadron.

Key  West ,  Fla.,  May  36,  1865. 

Sir:  The  capture  of  Jeff.  Davis  and  the  surrender  of  the  Stonewall 
to  the  Spanish  authorities  enable  me  to  commence  the  reduction  of 
the  squadron. 

As  soon  as  they  arrive  from  their  proper  stations  I  shall  send  north 
the  Fort  Henry ,  Somerset ,  Isonomia ,  and  Britannia ,  as  being,  in  my 
opinion,  inefficient  or  no  longer  required. 

The  Beauregard ,  Ariel ,  Rosalie,  Stonewall,  and  Two  Sisters  are  small 
schooners,  and  can  be  dispensed  with,  and  I  request  the  authority  of  the 
Department  to  have  them  sold  here,  as  they  are  such  vessels  as  would 
sell  for  a  higher  price  here,  I  believe,  than  anywhere  else,  as  they 
are  of  the  size  required  at  this  place.  All  of  them  are  well  worn  and 
will  soon  require  considerable  repairs. 

I  shall,  perhaps  in  a  week  or  two,  add  to  the  above  the  Aries ,  Chero- 
kee,  luka,  and  Sunflower. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

hassee,  Fla. 

No.  177.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla.,  May  37,  1865. 

Sir:  When  the  rebel  land  forces  were  surrendered  at  Tallahassee  on 
the  terms  agreed  upon  between  Generals  Sherman  and  Johnston  a 
small  steamer  called  the  Spray  was  surrendered  by  her  commander, 
H.  H.  Lewis,  to  the  Navy,  and  the  officers  and  crew  paroled  by  the 
provost-marshal  of  General  Cooke. 

The  Spray  is  a  small  high-pressure  steamer,  unseaworthy  but  in  a  condition  to 
move  in  smooth  water.  She  has  a  good  launch  and  one  other  serviceable  boat. 

This  is  the  account  given  of  her  by  Lieutenant-Commander  Gibson. 
I  have  ordered  her  to  be  brought  to  Key  West  if  she  is  in  a  fit  condi¬ 
tion  to  be  moved.  If  upon  examination  the  Spray  is  found  to  be  in  the 
condition  represented,  I  request  your  authority  to  have  her  sold. 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  853 

It  has  been  represented  to  me  that  upon  the  surrender  of  the  Spray 
lieutenant  H.  H.  Lewis,  her  commander,  was  scrupulously  careful  in 
having  the  vessel  and  everything  belonging  to  her,  and  ordnance  and 
ordnance  stores  on  shore,  delivered  in  good  order  to  the  officer  ordered 
to  receive  them.

Report  of  Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant  Conroy,  ZJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding 
the  capture  of  small  boat  containing  persons  supposed,  to  be  prominent 
men  under  fictitious  names. 

U.  S.  S.  Union, 

Navy  Yard,  New  York,  May  27,  1865. 
SIR.  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  of  this  ship  at  this  sta¬ 
tion,  after  having  complied  with  my  orders  from  the  honorable  Sec¬ 
retary  of  the  Navy,  dated  April  17,  1865. 

On  the  morning  of  the  21st  of  May,  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling 
received  official  dispatches  announcing  the  surrender  of  the  rebel 
pirate  ram  Stonewall  to  the  Spanish  authorities  in  Havana. 

The  same  morning  General  Newton,  commanding  the  army  forces 
at  Key  West,  received  information  that  his  pickets  at  Cape  Sable, 
[I  la.],  had  captured  a  boat  containing  7  white  persons  and  1  colored, 
all  armed,  and  to  appearance,  persons  of  importance.  They  had 
embarked  at  Crystal  River,  pulling  and  sailing  along  the  coast  of 
Florida  during  the  night,  and  secreting  themselves  during  the  day. 
Their  object  was  to  get  to  Havana.  They  gave  their  names  as  follows: 
Frank  C.  Anderson,  Frederick  Mohe,  Richard  S.  McCullock,  Thomas  A. 
Harris,  Julius  C.  Pratt,  Isaac  A.  Homer,  Henry  W.  McCormick.  Not 
having  been  received  at  Key  West,  it  is  not  known  ivho  they  are. 
Their  conduct  looks  suspicious  and  leads  to  the  supposition  that  they 
were  men  of  importance  in  the  so-called  Confederacy,  and  that  many 
of  the  names  given  are  fictitious.  It  is  thought  Breckinridge  and 
Mallory  are  among  them. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Edward  Conroy, 

Acting  Volunteer  Lieutenant- Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Sewetary  of  the  Navy. 


Report  of  Acting  Rear-Admiral  Stribling,  ZJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
loss  of  Confederate  torpedo  boat  en  route  to  Key  West  towed  by  the 
U.  S.  S.  Yucca. 

No.  180.]  Hdqrs.  East  Gulf  Blockading  Squadron, 

Key  West,  Fla. ,  May  29,  1865. 

Sir:  Upon  the  capture  of  Columbus  a  small  torpedo  boat  not  entirely 
finished  was  not  destroyed  by  the  rebels,  and  was  sent  down  to 
Apalachicola.  I  ordered  her  to  be  towed  to  this  place,  and  I  regret  to 
report  her  being  lost  on  her  way  here  in  tow  of  the  Yucca.  A  strong 
westerly  wind  prevailed  at  the  time,  and  every  effort  was  made  on  the 


854 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


part  of  Acting  Master  Wade,  commanding  the  Yucca ,  to  save  the  boat. 
I  am  satisfied  that  Acting  Master  Wade  should  not  be  blamed  for  the 
loss  of  the  boat,  as  she  was  not  intended  to  go  to  sea;  but  I  supposed 
at  this  season  of  the  year,  when  light  winds  and  calms  prevail,  she 
might  be  towed  here  in  safety. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant,

Select  the  most  efficient  vessels  for  retention  and  send  to  the  Depart¬ 
ment  a  list  of  them.  Send  all  the  others  to  Philadelphia,  New  York, 
and  Poston  before  the  middle  of  July.  If  any  can  be  sold  at  Key 
West,  so  report  to  the  Bureau  of  Construction. 

hill  up  the  vessels  that  remain  as  the  fixed  force  of  the  squadron 
with  their  complement  of  officers  and  men.  Retain  for  this  purpose 
good  volunteer  officers,  so  far  as  possible,  those  who  wish  to  continue 
a  while  longer  in  the  service,  and  send  north  all  other  volunteer  offi¬ 
cers,  for  the  purpose  of  being  mustered  out  of  the  service.  Of  the 
men,  send  home  those  who  have  the  least  time  to  serve. 

In  forwarding  to  the  Department  a  list  of  the  vessels  retained  send 
with  it  lists  of  the  officers  of  each  and  complete  muster  rolls  of  their 
crews,  the  latter  to  the  Bureau  of  Equipment  and  Recruiting. 

All  property  hitherto  belonging  to  the  rebel  Naval  Department  or 
that  was  under  its  control  will  be  taken  possession  of  by  you,  and  an 
account  taken,  with  an  estimate  of  the  value  thereof,  and  forwarded  to 
this  Department,  If  such  property  is  in  the  possession  of  the  United 
States  military  forces,  make  a  written  request  for  it,  and  report  your 
action  to  this  Department,  that  the  necessary  orders  may  be  given  by 
the  War  Department  for  its  delivery  to  the  Navy. 

Economize  in  the  use  of  coal  and  give  directions  to  all  vessels  to 
keep  steam  down,  except  in  an  emergency,  of  which  the  senior  officer 
shall  judge,  under  the  directions  of  the  commander  of  the  squadron. 

The  title  of  the  squadron  under  }’our  command  will  hereafter  be  the 
“East  Gulf  Squadron.” 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 


G.  V.  Fox, 

Acting  Secretary  of  the  Navy.

lachicola,  i  la. ,  on  the  31st  instant  [ultimo],  at  10  a.  m.,  with  the  U  S

second  U.  fe.  Colored  Infantry  and  30  mounted  men  and  supplies  for 
-Brevet  Major-General  Wilson’s  command  at  Macon,  Ga.,  on  board 
convoyed  by  the  U.  S.  S.  Itasca ,  Lieutenant-Commander  N.  Green 
commanding,  under  instructions  contained  in  enclosed,  in  1  2  and  3. 
1  arrived  at  the  upper  anchorfage]  of  Apalachicola,  after  a  smooth  run 
ot  twenty-three  hours,  at  9  a.  m.  on  the  1st  instant,  and,  landing  with 
the  steamer  Tampico ,  directed  that  the  discharging  of  the  vessels 
should  commence  immediately  and  continue  day  and  night  in  accord¬ 
ance  with  enclosed  orders,  under  4,  5,  and  6.  The  last  steamer  being

disehargcd  °n  the  night  of  the  4th  instant,  I  embarked  at  daylight  on

1  ampico ,  which  remained  at  Apalachicola  as  lighter,  having  been

at  Mobile  Ala.,  and  arrived  here  at  daybreak,  after  a  run  of  twenty

my  instructions  to  Colonel  L.  L.  Zulavsky,  commanding  post,  and 
would  respectfully  request  to  be  informed,  for  my  further  guidance, 
whether  they  meet  the  approval  of  the  major-general  commanding. 
People  are  returning  to  Apalachicola  from  rebeldom  as  well  as  from 
the  North,  anxious  to  resume  their  former  vocations.  I  can  not  speak 
in  too  high  terms  of  Captain  N.  Green,  commanding  U.  S.  convoy 
steamer  Itasca,  who,  by  his  nautical  skill  and  efficiency,  as  well  as  his 
friendly  willingness  to  aid  whenever  required,  materially  contributed 
to  the  successful  trip  and  the  speedy  discharge  of  the  vessels. 

I  am,  colonel,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

A.  Asbotii,

Letter  .from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Acting  Rear- Admired 

Stribling,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  action  of  the  French  and 

British  Governments  in  relation  to  the  Confederacy. 

Navy  Department,  June  22, 1S35. 

^  Sir:  Information  has  been  communicated  to  this  Department  by  the 
Secretary  of  State  that  the  Imperial  Government  of  France  has  removed 
all  restrictions  heretofore  imposed  by  it  upon  naval  intercourse  with 
the  United  States  and  has  withdrawn  from  the  insurgents  the  character 
of  belligerents. 

The  Government  of  Great  Britain  also  withdraws  her  concessions 
heretofore  made  of  a  belligerent  character  from  the  insurgents,  but 
the  withdrawal  of  the  twenty-four  hour  rule  has  not  been  made 
absolute.  Reciprocal  measures  will  be  extended  to  the  vessels  of  that 
country. 

The  blockade  of  the  ports  and  coast  of  the  United  States  will  soon 
cease,  and  with  the  cessation  of  hostilities  the  belligerent  right  of 
search  will  also  cease. 

Very  respectfully, 

G.  Welles, 
Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Acting  Rear-Admiral  C.  K.  Stribling, 

Commanding  East  Gidf  Squadron ,  Key  West,  Fla.

Letter  from  Brigadier-  General  Jones ,  C.  S.  Army ,  to  Captain  Brent , 

C.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  removal  of  naval  stores  from  Pensacola , 

Fla. 

Hdqrs.  Department  Alabama  and  West  Florida, 

Pensacola ,  Fla. ,  March  8 ,  1862. 

Sir:  The  naval  storekeeper  in  Pensacola  was  informed  on  the  4th 
instant,  by  my  direction,  that  the  naval  stores  in  Pensacola  should  be 
removed  to  the  interior. 

*  ****** 

I  suggest,  therefore,  that  you  put  such  naval  stores  now  in  Pensa¬ 
cola  as  you  can  on  the  steamer  Time.  They  can  be  placed  on  her  while 
she  is  at  the  wharf  in  Pensacola,  and  continue  to  perform  the  service 
she  is  now  engaged  in.  *  *  * 

I  hear  that  an  officer  of  the  Navy  has  been  for  some  time  engaged  in 
building  two  gunboats  at  or  near  Milton,  [Fla.],  and  that  they  are  now 
nearly  ready  for  service.  He  should  be  immediately  informed  of  the 
condition  of  things  as  you  know  them  to  be  here,  and  warned  to  be 
constantly  on  the  alert  to  prevent  them  falling  into  the  hands  of  the 
enemy.  If  he  can  not  take  them  up  the  Escambia  or  place  them 
beyond  the  reach  of  the  enemy,  he  should  burn  them  as  soon  as  he 
hears  that  this  place  has  fallen  into  the  hands  of  the  enemy,  and  meas¬ 
ures  should  be  taken  to  give  him  the  earliest  possible  information  on 
the  subject. 

It  is  probable  that  an  attempt  will  be  made  to  run  the  Bradford  and 
Nelms  into  Mobile  Bay,  and  it  may  be  that  they  could  tow  the  two  gun- 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  863 

boats  on  a  dark  night  into  Mobile  Bay.  Yon  are  better  able  to  judge 
oi  that  than  I  can.  Under  no  circumstances  should  they  be  allowed 
to  fall  into  the  hands  of  the  enemy. 

No  time  should  be  lost  in  carrying  out  the  foregoing  suggestions. 
I  he  quartermaster  in  Pensacola  will  give  you  all  the  aid  he  can  in 
moving  naval  stores. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Sam.  J  ones, 

Brigadier-  General ,  Commanding. 

Captain  Thomas  W.  Brent,  C.  S.  Navy, 

Pensacola ,  Fla. 


Report  of  Captain  Blocker ,  C.  S.  Army ,  regarding  expedition  to 

Crooked  River ,  Florida. 

Headquarters  Camp  Gladden, 

Wakulla  County ,  Fla. ,  May  21,  1862. 

General:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  yesterday  morning  at 
3:  30  o’clock  I  left  this  camp  with  a  detachment  of  33  men  for  Crooked 
River,  at  which  point  we  arrived  at  1  p.  m.  In  a  short  time  after  our 
arrival  I  discovered  a  boat  leaving  the  blockading  vessel  and  approach¬ 
ing  the  mouth  of  said  river.  I  immediately  placed  my  men  in  ambush 
on  Carr’s  Hill,  and  when  the  boat  came  opposite  we  opened  fire  on  the 
enemy  and  killed  or  wounded  all  the  party  of  21  except  4.  It  gives 
me  pleasure  to  state  that  my  men  acted  gallantly  throughout  the  whole 
affair.  There  was  no  one  hurt  on  our  side,  although  our  fire  was 
returned  from  the  boat.  Had  my  men  been  properly  armed  not  one 
of  the  enemy  could  have  escaped. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  general,  your  obedient  servant, 

H.  T.  Blocker, 

Captain ,  Commanding  Beauregard  Rangers.  > 

Brigadier-General  Joseph  Finegan, 

Comdg.  Dept,  of  Middle  and  East  Florida ,  Tallahassee ,  Fla. 


Report  of  Brigadier-  General  Finegan ,  C.  S.  Army,  regarding  result  of 

expedition  to  St.  Marks ,  Fla. 

Tallahassee,  Fla.,  June  17,  1862. 

I  have  just  returned  from  St.  Marks.  The  enemy  shelled  the  light¬ 
house  for  several  hours;  sent  fireboats  on  shore  and  burned  the  wood¬ 
work  of  the  light-house  and  the  keeper’s  house  adjoining,  and  burned 
all  the  buildings  on  the  beach.  I  had  a  small  picket  guard  at  the 
light- house.  No  person  hurt. 

The  Seventh  Regiment  will  proceed  at  once  to  Chattanooga. 

Jos.  Finegan, 

Brigadier-  General,  Commanding. 

General  S.  Cooper, 

Richmond ,  Ya.

Letter  from,  Brigadier- General  Cobb ,  C.  S.  Army ,  to  Lieutenant  Jones, 
C.  S.  Navy,  regarding  cooperation  in  Chattahoochee  River. 

Headquarters  District  of  Middle  Florida, 

Quincy,  [Flat],  January  2,  1863. 

Lieutenant:  Yours  of  the  30th  [ultimo]  is  just  received.  I  am 
gratified  to  know  that  I  shall  have  your  cooperation  in  the  defense  of 
the  river,  whilst  I  regret  on  your  account  that  you  can  not  have  a 
larger  and  more  congenial  field  of  operation. 

Every  assistance  that  1  can  render  you  shall  be  cheerfully  given. 
The  Munnerlyn  shall  be  subject  to  your  order  whenever  you  need  her. 
When  not  employed  in  the  urgent  matter  of  the  river  defenses  the 
Munnerlyn  can  also  be  used  for  transporting  the  materials  from  the 
navy  yard  to  Columbus. 

I_ shall  be  happy  to  meet  you  at  Chattahoochee  at  any  time  you  will 
designate.  Indeed,  I  am  anxious  to  do  so. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Howell  Cobb, 

Brigadier-  General ,  Commanding  District. 

Lieutenant  Catesby  ap  R.  Jones, 

Commanding  C.  S.  Chattahoochee.

Letter  from  Lieutenant  Cift,C.  S.  Navy,  to  Lieutenant  Guthrie,  C.  S. 

Navy ,  regarding  plan  for  the  capture  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Port  Royal , 

off  Apalachicola. 

C.  S.  S.  Chattahoochee, 
Chattahoochee ,  Fla.,  May  9,  1863. 

Sir:  Conformably  with  your  request,  I  beg  to  submit  my  views  as 
to  the  feasibility  of  a  descent  upon  the  enemy  at  Apalachicola.  I  pro¬ 
pose  to  take  60  men  and  a  proper  number  of  officers  and  proceed  in 
the  steamer  Swan  to  a  point  6  miles  from  Apalachicola;  there  disem¬ 
bark  at  nightfall  and  march  to  a  point  near  and  in  rear  of  that  city. 
Arrived,  I  would  use  every  precaution  to  prevent  the  fact  of  my  pres¬ 
ence  becoming  known.  I  would  then  send  in  two  or  three  men,  citi¬ 
zens  of  Apalachicola,  apparently  on  leave.  Their  presence  would  be 
reported  to  Morris,  of  the  enemy’s  Port  Royal,  on  the  first  night,  and 
on  the  second  or  third  he  would  make  his  appearance  as  usual,  with 
four  boats’  crews  and  a  guard  of  marines — probably  60  men.  His 
custom  is  to  land  and  put  his  boat  howitzer  in  position  on  shore  and 
leave  with  it  and  his  boats  a  guard  of  10  or  15  men;  with  the  remainder 
of  his  force  he  proceeds  to  search  for  his  prey.  My  plan  would  be, 
first,  to  attack  and  overpower  the  party  at  the  boats  and  gun,  and  then 
attack  the  remaining  force  when  they  return  to  the  assistance  of  that 
party.  Once  in  possession  of  the  boats  and  the  clothes  of  the  prison¬ 
ers,  I  would  consider  the  capture  of  the  Port  Royal  certain. 

The  only  doubt  concerning  the  matter  is  the  getting  of  Morris  on 
shore,  as  I  would  have  no  doubt  of  the  result  of  battle  as  between  the 
splendid  crew  of  the  Chattahoochee  and  a  like  number  of  Yankees  sur¬ 
prised  and  taken  at  disadvantage. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  W.  Gift, 
Lieutenant,  C.  S.  Navy. 

Lieutenant  Commanding  John  Julius  Guthrie,  C.  S.  Navy. 


Report  of  Lieutenant  Cift,  C.  A.  Navy,  submitting  plan  of  operations 
for  injuring  the  enemy’s  commerce  in  the  Great  Lakes. 

C.  S.  S.  Chattahoochee, 
Chattahoochee,  Fla.,  May  11,  1863. 

Sir:  I  respectfully  beg  leave  to  lay  before  the  Department  the  fol¬ 
lowing  plan  of  operations  against  the  enemy’s  commerce  in  the  great 
Northern  lakes.  To  suggest  the  field  is  alone  sufficient  to  startle  one, 
and  although  the  scheme  may  be  as  Quixotic  as  it  is  audacious,  yet  I 
trust  there  is  no  impropriety  in  stating  the  matter. 

My  plan  would  be  to  proceed  to  Canada  by  the  most  practicable 
route  with  a  full  complement  of  officers  for  a  vessel  of  about  this  class. 
I  would  direct  the  officers  to  part  off  into  small  squads  and  proceed  to 
the  northern  shore  of  Lake  Erie.  There  I  would  purchase  a  swift, 
light-draft  propeller  steamer  in  some  port  on  the  lake.  At  another  1 
would  procure  two  heavy  guns  and  carriages;  at  another,  shot  and 
shells  and  ammunition,  equipments,  etc.  A  crew  could  be  easily 
obtained.  I  woidd  go  to  sea  in  the  lake  and  appoint  a  rendezvous 
where  the  necessary  munitions,  etc.,  could  be  received  on  board. 
Then  1  would  commence  operations  against  the  enemy’s  commerce

Executive  Department,

Letter  from  Lieutenant  McLaughlin.  C.  S.  J\avy ,  to  Lieutenant  Jones , 

C.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  accident  on  hoard  the  C.  S.  S.  Chattahoochee. 

Columbus,  Ga.  ,  June  1,  1863. 

My  Dear  Jones:  I  hasten  to  inform  you  of  the  sad  accident  which 
happened  on  board  the  Chattahoochee ,  and  as  the  quickest  method  1 
enclose  the  account  furnished  tire  newspaper  by  Gift,  who,  though  not 
on  hoard  at  the  time,  came  up  on  the  Young.  with  the  wounded.  1  oung 
Mallory  is  badly  hurt  and  his  recovery  considered  doubtful.  The  state¬ 
ments  as  to  how  the  accident  occurred  are  very  conflicting.  Some  say 
that  the  steam  gauge  had  been  out  of  order  the  day  previous.  At  the 
time  of  the  explosion  it  was  showing  only  7  pounds  of  steam.  Others 
say  that  pumping  water  in  the  boiler,  the  water  at  the  time  being  low, 
was  the  cause.  She  was  at  anchor  and  only  waiting  for  steam  to  be 
reported  to  get  underway.  Mr.  Fagan  at  the  time  was  sick,  though 
had  just  gone  into  the  engine  room.  He  was  the  only  one  on  board 
having  any  knowledge  of  the  engines.  The  gunner  is  at  the  vessel  with 
most  of  the  crew.  The  medical  officers  have  moved  their  effects  to 
Chattahoochee.  Captain  Guthrie  is  here.  I  will  write  you  again  soon. 

Yours,  truly, 

A.  McLaughlin. 

Commander  C.  ap  R.  Jones,  C.  S.  Navy.

Gunboat  Chattahoochee  destroyed — Terrible  loss  of  life. 

Just  as  the  steamer  Jackson  was  pushing  out  from  the  wharf  at  Chat¬ 
tahoochee,  Fla. ,  a  courier  arrived  from  below  with  news  that  the  boilers 
of  the  gunboat  Chattahoochee  had  exploded,  killing  the  pilot,  William 
Bilbro,  for  a  long  series  of  years  a  pilot  on  the  Chattahoochee  River, 
and  wounding  nearly  every  officer  on  board.  The  Jackson  could  not 
remain  to  learn  any  further  particulars;  they  have  doubtless  been 
received  before  this/  The  steamer  Munnerlyn  went  down  to  the 
scene  of  disaster.

The  vessel  was  sunk  below  her  decks.  The  wounded  were  brought

Detailed  report  of  Lieutenant  McLaughlin ,  C.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the 
accident  on  loard  the  C.  8.  8.  Chattahoochee. 

Naval  Station,  Columbus,  Ga.,  June  15,  1863. 

My  Dear  Jones:  Your  letter  of  the  8th  has  just  reached  me,  enclos¬ 
ing  a,  letter  to  Gift.  As  he  has  left  here  permanently  with  orders  to 
Mobile,  I  have  done  as  you  directed,  opened  the  document  and  for¬ 
warded  the  letters  of  recommendation,  through  Pembroke  Jones,  at 
Savannah,  with  a  request  that  he  will  hand  them  to  the  men.  I  will 
go  on  to  explain  and  endeavor  to  furnish  you  with  all  the  information 
connected  with  the  lamentable  accident  which  happened  to  the  ill-fated 
steamer.  The  accounts,  such  as  we  get,  are  most  conflicting,  but  Gift, 
having- taken  an  active  part  in  placing  the  information  before  the  pub¬ 
lic,  I  think,  has  prevented  the  matter  from  being-  as  freely  discussed  as 
would  otherwise  have  been  the  case. 

f  he  only  officers  on  board  at  the  time  were  Guthrie,  Midshipmen 
Craig,  Mallory,  and  Gibbs,  Golder,  Dr.  Ford,  and  the  gunner,  and  the 
engineers,  whose  names  have  already  appeared  in  print  with  the  excep¬ 
tion  of  Third  Assistant  H.  (?)  Blanc,  of  New  Orleans,  who,  not  being 
on  duty,  escaped  uninjured.  The  vessel  had  started  for  the  obstruct 
tions,  and  had  gone  but  20  miles  when  it  was  found  there  was  not  suf¬ 
ficient  water  on  the  bar  to  admit  of  her  crossing.  The  vessel  was 
anchored.  The  next  morning  it  was  ascertained  that  the  river  had 
swollen,  when  orders  weie  given  to  raise  steam,  and,  as  near  as  I  can 
learn,  they  commenced  firing  up  at  or  near  10  o’clock  with  wood. 
At  12  m.,  when  the  relief  came  down  (which,  by  the  way,  accounts  for 
the  number  of  deaths),  the  steam  gauge  was  showing  7  pounds  of 


870 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


steam.  It  is  now  understood  that  it  was  out  of  order  the  day  previous. 
A  discussion  now  arose  with  regard  to  the  quantity  of  water  in  the 
boiler.  Mr.  Fagan,  the  senior  engineer,  being  at  the  time  in  his  bunk 
with  a  chill,  hearing  the  dispute,  and  fearing  from  the  length  of  time 
since  the  fires  had  been  started  that  something  was  wrong,  hastened 
to  the  engine  room  and  was  descending  the  ladder  when  the  explosion 
took  place.  Curiosity  had  taken  the  pilot  to  the  engine  room,  and 
some  think  it  was  he  who  started  the  pump.  The  explosion  was 
instantaneous  with  the  starting  of  the  pump.  Guthrie,  at  the  time, 
was  in  his  cabin.  There  is  some  difference  of  opinion  about  the  time 
of  his  arrival  on  deck.  Otherwise  I  do  not  hear  of  his  name  being- 
mentioned,  except  by  Dr.  Ford,  who  speaks  of  his  administering 
baptism  to  those  who  had  been  wounded  and  were  about  to  die. 

It  being  reported  that  an  explosion  of  the  magazine  was  imminent, 
caused  a  panic  among  the  crew.  Three,  I  believe,  were  drowned  in 
trying  to  reach  the  shore.  Among  the  number  was  a  quartermaster 
by  the  name  of  Berry.  No  description,  I  am  told,  could  possibly  be 
given  of  the  scene  on  the  deck  of  the  Chattahoochee ,  men  running 
about  frantic  with  pain,  leaving  the  impression  of  their  bleeding  feet, 
and  sometimes  the  entire  flesh,  the  nails  and  all,  remain  behind  them. 
The  dead  and  wounded  were  taken  on  shore,  where  they  remained 
until  the  next  afternoon,  most  of  the  time  a  terrible  storm  raging. 
Finally  they  were  taken  on  board  the  Young  and  reached  Columbus 
on  Sunday  night,  just  five  days  after  the  accident.  No  attempt  was 
made  to  dress  the  wounds  until  after  their  arrival  here,  which  could 
not  be  avoided.  Poor  Malloiy!  I  shall  never  forget  his  appearance. 
I  would  not  have  known  him  had  he  not  spoken.  His  face,  hands,  and 
feet  were  scalded  in  the  most  terrible  manner;  he  plead  piteously  to 
have  his  wounds  attended  to.  I  urged  the  doctor,  who,  by  the  way, 
was  almost  used  up  himself,  to  pay  Mallory  some  attention.'  He  then 
told  me  that  he  would  have  to  wait  for  some  assistance.  He  then  said 
that  Mallory  could  not  live.  You  would  have  thought  differently  had 
you  seen  him.  I  could  not  make  up  my  mind  that  he  would'  die. 
When  they  first  commenced  to  remove  the' cloths  he  was  talking  cheer¬ 
fully,  but  the  nervous  system  could  not  stand  the  shock.  He  com¬ 
menced  sinking  and  was  a  corpse  before  they  had  gotten  half  through. 
Duffy,  the  fireman,  expired  on  the  next  day.  You  would  have  been 
surprised  to  have  seen  the  effect  produced  on  Mr.  Craig  and  Colder, 
who  were  only  slightly  injured,  Mr.  Craig  in  the  foot,  Mr.  Golder 
side  of  face,  arm,  and  hand.  They  were  so  prostrated  after  their 
wounds  were  dressed  that  they  were  only  roused  by  the  use  of  stimu¬ 
lants.  _  It  seems  almost  useless  to  mention  that  they  received  all  the 
attention  that  could  possibly  have  been  bestowed.'  The  Home  was 
literally  besieged  with  ladies,  and  for  one  week  the  street  in  front  of 
the  Home  was  blocked  up  with  vehicles  of  all  descriptions.  I  really 
looked  on  with  astonishment.  The  four  worst  cases  were  placed  together 
in  the  room  upstairs,  directly  in  front  of  the  steps.  It  was  with  the 
utmost  difficulty  that  I  could  remain  in  the  room  sufficiently  long  to 
ascertain  what  was  required  and  to  see  what  service  I  could  render, 
the  atmosphere  was  so  unpleasant,  yet  the  ladies  did  not  seem  to  notice 
it  and  remained  at  their  post  till  the  last. 

Guthrie  came  up  on  the  boat,  bringing  the  guns,  which,  strange  to 
say,  he  turned  over  to  Major  Humphreys, with  a  request  that  he  would 
hold  them  subject  alone  to  his  order  or  that  of  the  Secretary  of  the 


EAST  GULF  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  871 

Na\^.  I  immediately  made  a  report  of  the  affair.  The  Secretary, 
.rough  the  Office  ot  Ordnance,  replied  promptly  by  telegraph,  direct¬ 
ing  die  guns  and  everything'  pertaining  to  them,  as  well  as  ship’s 
s  oics,  be  turned  over  to  me.  The  matter  caused  considerable  talk 
among-  the  people  in  town.  It  was  not  understood  why  naval  guns 
siould  not  have  been  placed  under  the  contrpl  of  naval  officers.  It 
does  appear  to  me  that  Guthrie’s  conduct  throughout  the  whole  affair 
ias  been  most  singular.  .  He  has  given  leave  of  absence  to  some  of 
ms  crew  to  visit  a  place  in  possession  of  the  enemy,  and  some  13  of 
his  men  left  him  at  Chattahoochee  with  the  intention  of  not  returning1 
Among  the  number  was  a  man  by  the  name  of  Lee,  whom  you  will 
no  doubt  recollect.  After  placing  the  guns  in  charge  of  Major  Hum¬ 
phreys  he  took  his  family  and  started  for  Chattahoochee,  where  [he] 
remained  four  or  five  days,  when  he  again  embarked  for  Columbus, 
bringing  the  crew,  minus  the  13  mentioned  above.  At  that  time  I 
had  in  my  possession  a  telegram  from  Richmond  to  Guthrie,  directing 
him  to  send  the  crew  to  Savannah.  He  remarked  he  would  turn  them 
over  to  rue,  and  I  might  do  what  I  pleased  with  them,  but  he  thought 
I  had  better  wait  for  further  instructions.  As  Guthrie  appeared  to  be 
laboring  under  some  bodily  infirmity,  I  gave  the  men  quarters  in  my 
mold  room,  and  sent  40  of  them  the  next  day  to  Savannah.  They 
arrived  on  the  day  the  Savannah  was  put  in  commission.  The  men 
were  all  nicely  dressed  when  they  left  here,  and  on  their  arrival  at 
Savannah,  being  all  straight  and  in  good  condition,  were  the  cause  of 
many  remarks.  It  was  certainly  reflecting  great  credit  to  those  who 
had  organized  and  disciplined  the  crew.  I  felt  proud  of  them. 
During  their  stay  with  me  there  was  not  one  guilty  of  the  slightest 
impropriety.  Cronin  (?),  May,  and  Rosier  expressed  deep  regret 
that  they  had  not  time  to  put  a  piece  in  the  paper  thanking  the  ladies 
for  their  many  kindnesses,  but  said  they  would  do  so  on  their  arrival 
at  Savannah.  The  crew  of  the  Chattahoochee  will  ever  remember  the 
latter  and  the  paymaster.  They  would  have  been  willing  to  have  gone 
anywhere  to  have  gotten  rid  of  the  vessel.  Webb  was  exceedingly 
anxious  to  get  hold  of  some  of  the  men.  He  will  have  some  of  the 
landsmen;  the  remainder  will  remain  on  the  Savannah.  I  ordered 
Dr.  Jones  and  Midshipman  Gibbs  and  Mr.  Golder  with  the  crew. 
They  are  now  attached  to  the  Savannah. 

The  6.4-inch  rifle  belonging  to  the  Chattahoochee  I  was  directed  to 
send  to  Charleston.  It  is  to  be  double-banded  and  returned,  to  be 
used,  I  suppose,  on  the  Muscogee.  1  am  doing  very  well.  The  calkers 
have  commenced  to-day,  and  I  am  laying  the  spar-deck.  The  engines 
are  about  being’  placed  in  position.  I  will  keep  you  advised  from  time 
to  time  of  the  progress. 

With  kind  regards  to  Simms,  I  remain,  truly,  yours, 

A.  McLaughlin. 

[Commander  Catesby  ap  R.  Jones,  C.  S.  Navy.] 


Additional  report  of  Lieutenant  McLaughlin ,  C.  S.  Navy ,  regarding 
the  accident  on  hoard  the  C.  S.  S.  Chattahoochee. 

Columbus,  Ga.  ,  December  £ 6 ,  1863. 
My  Dear  Jones:  The  Chattahoochee ,  her  officers  and  men,  have  been 
turned  over  to  me.  I  have  succeeded  in  having  her  towed  to  this  place, 


872 


Hart  gulp  blockading  squadron. 


and  will  commence  work  on  her  at  once.  She  is  not  as  badly  damaged 
as  I  had  supposed.  The  deck  immediately  over  the  boiler  on  the  port 
side  was  raised  by  the  explosion  some  6  inches.  Beyond  that  there  has 
been  no  damage  to  the  boiler.  Mr.  Warner  has  not  had  an  opportunity 
to  examine  the  boiler.  From  a  casual  observation  he  thinks  she  can 
soon  be  in  running  order;  the  machinery  has  not  been  injured.  It  has 
been  to  me  still  more  a  matter  of  surprise  why  that  vessel  should  have 
been  allowed  to  sink.  A  pine  plug  driven  into  the  feed  pipe,  which 
had  been  blown  off,  would  have  been  all  that  was  necessary.  She  draws 
in  her  present  condition  6  feet  3  inches  aft,  5  feet  3  inches  forward. 
Nearly  all  her  outfit  has  been  plundered,  and  in  some  instances  sold 
and  given  away  by  those  who  were  left  in  charge.  Things  were  scat¬ 
tered  around,  some  at  the  arsenal,  Johnston’s,  and  Eufaula.  Johnston 
had  the  entire  control  in  raising  the  vessel.  After  she  was  up  she 
remained  in  charge  of  his  negroes.  She  has  been  stripped  of  every¬ 
thing  that  could  be  converted  into  money.  The  paymaster’s  clerk  gave 
furlough  to  the  men,  some  of  which  are  still  away.  There  was  a  regular 
communication  kept  up  with  Apalachicola  by  means  of  the  dingey, 
which  was  at  the  disposal  of  Father  Somebody,  the  Catholic  priest.  No 
doubt  the  enemy  have  been  kept  fully  posted  with  regard  to  movements 
in  the  Confederacy,  more  particularly  with  matters  on  the  river. 

Guthrie  has  made  one  round  trip  on  the  Advance ,  a  vessel  belonging 
to  the  State  of  North  Carolina.  I  was  at  Wilmington  when  he  arrived. 
He  seemed  to  be  perfectly  happy;  says  he  has  now  established  his  rep¬ 
utation.  I  don’t  know  why  he  did  not  continue  on  her.  Crossan  is  out 
with  her  now.  Guthrie  has  been  spending  some  of  his  time  at  Eufaula, 
where  he  has  purchased  a  house,  and  intends  his  family  to  reside  there 
during  the  war. 

Washington  is  here.  He  seems  anxious  to  get  detached.  I  hope  he 
may.  His  conduct  while  down  the  river  was  shameful. 

D.  S.  Johnston  has  taken  a  contract  to  build  Morino  a  barge  90  feet 
long,  22  feet  breadth  of  beam.  The  contract  was  closed  on  Sunday  last. 
He  pledged  to  have  her  ready  by  the  1st  of  January. 

The  Muscogee  is  all  ready  for  launching.  I  am  only  waiting  for  the 
river,  which,  from  present  appearances,  will  not  keep  me  waiting’  long. 
The  internal  arrangements  are  complete,  with  the  exception  of  the 
magazine.  1  wish  I  could  have  the  benefit  of  your  advice  in  fitting 
it  up. 

I  was  pleased  to  hear  that  you  had  met  with  such  success  in  casting 
guns.  I  hope  you  will  be  ready  to  furnish  the  Muscogee  her  battery.  I 
am  told  it  is  the  only  chance.  They  are  not  doing  much  in  Rich¬ 
mond,  Governor  Milton  informs  me  that  so  soon  as  this  vessel  is  ready 
oi  sei  vice,  Apalachicola  will  be  reoccupied.  He  expressed  himself 
thoroughly  disgusted  with  Morino  and  all  his  works.  Morino  wants 
to  make  a  wagon  road  over  the  river,  using  the  obstructions  as  a  founda¬ 
tion.  Old  Milton  says  he  will  blow  them  all  to  the  devil  and  open 
the  river.  He  has  already  communicated  with  the  President  on  the 
sub]ect,  who  thinks  favorably  of  it.  *  *  * 

Hope  soon  to  hear  from  you. 

I  remain,  very  truly,  your  friend, 

[Commander  Catesby  ap  R.  Jones.] 


A.  McLaughlin.
